entry.title: Hodge classes, complex multiplication, and the search for algebraic cycles
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 032 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Polynomial equations describe geometric objects, but topology sees them through different information: loops, surfaces, and their higher-dimensional analogues. Cohomology organizes this information into vector spaces. Which cohomology classes actually come from algebraic subvarieties?

The Hodge conjecture predicts an answer for smooth projective complex varieties. A necessary compatibility with complex coordinates should also be sufficient, once rational linear combinations of subvarieties are allowed. Family 032 claims this for every abelian variety with complex multiplication, a highly symmetric class that includes special elliptic curves and their products.

The family contains five manuscripts, labeled M1–M5 below. M1 supplies the CM theorem and arithmetic consequences. The others address powers of abelian varieties, covers of curves, certain complete intersections, and K3 surfaces. Their boundaries differ considerably. In particular, the current family does not assert an unconditional Hodge theorem for all powers of all projective K3 surfaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

From subvarieties to cohomology

A projective variety is a solution set of homogeneous polynomial equations inside complex projective space. Smoothness excludes singular points. If its complex dimension is ggg, a subvariety of codimension ppp has dimension g−pg-pg−p. An algebraic cycle is a finite formal linear combination of such subvarieties.

The vector space H2p(X,Q)H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)H2p(X,Q) is rational cohomology in degree 2p2p2p. After allowing complex coefficients it decomposes by the numbers of holomorphic and antiholomorphic directions in differential forms. The summand Hp,p(X)H^{p,p}(X)Hp,p(X) has equal numbers of the two. An algebraic cycle of codimension ppp determines a class in

Hdg⁡p(X)=H2p(X,Q)∩Hp,p(X).\operatorname{Hdg}^{p}(X)=H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X).Hdgp(X)=H2p(X,Q)∩Hp,p(X).

Such a class is a rational Hodge class. The conjecture says that every member of this space is obtained from algebraic cycles. Equivalently, the cycle-class map

cl⁡:CH⁡p(X)Q⟶Hdg⁡p(X)\operatorname{cl}:\operatorname{CH}^{p}(X)_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hdg}^{p}(X)cl:CHp(X)Q​⟶Hdgp(X)

is onto. The source identifies cycles under rational equivalence, a relation generated by algebraic families of divisors of rational functions. For understanding the conjecture, the key point is the existence of a cycle with the prescribed cohomology class, rather than the finer equivalence relation.

A divisor is a codimension-one cycle. Intersections of divisors provide many higher-codimension classes, but generally do not provide all of them. Thus solving the divisor case does not settle the conjecture.

Abelian varieties, CM, and powers

An abelian variety is a smooth projective variety with a commutative algebraic group law. Analytically it has the form Cg/Λ\mathbb C^g/\LambdaCg/Λ, with a lattice Λ\LambdaΛ of rank 2g2g2g, satisfying a projectivity condition. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example.

Let End⁡0(A)=End⁡(A)⊗ZQ\operatorname{End}^{0}(A)=\operatorname{End}(A)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb QEnd0(A)=End(A)⊗Z​Q. The variety has complex multiplication, abbreviated CM, if this algebra contains a commutative semisimple rational algebra of dimension 2g2g2g. These extra symmetries split cohomology into particularly manageable pieces. CM does not mean merely that the variety is defined over the complex numbers.

The power AmA^mAm is a product of mmm copies of AAA. Its classes can connect different copies, so a theorem for AAA alone need not settle all powers. The Hodge group records the symmetries preserving the Hodge tensors; additional endomorphisms can make it smaller and create additional classes.

A polarization is an ample line bundle, or the corresponding positive form on cohomology. An imaginary quadratic field is Q(−d)\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})Q(−d​) with d>0d>0d>0. Its action on an abelian variety gives two conjugate eigenspaces. Balanced dimensions can produce determinant-type Hodge classes called Weil classes, which may lie beyond divisor products.

Two stronger or related questions

The generalized Hodge conjecture concerns entire Hodge substructures, not only individual classes of type (p,p)(p,p)(p,p). It predicts that certain cohomology can be supported on algebraic subsets of an appropriate codimension: the classes disappear when those subsets are removed.

Over finite fields, the Tate conjecture replaces Hodge type with invariance under the arithmetic Frobenius symmetry in étale cohomology. The Hodge standard conjecture concerns positivity of an intersection pairing on algebraic classes. These are distinct statements, connected here through previously established implications.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Lefschetz (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) theorem settles the divisor case. Hodge’s broader question asks whether its relationship between complex structure and algebraic geometry continues in higher codimension. Abelian varieties offer a useful testing ground because their cohomology is the exterior algebra of degree-one cohomology, yet this linear-algebra description does not construct the missing subvarieties.

Deligne’s theorem on absolute Hodge classes showed that Hodge classes on abelian varieties retain their Hodge character under the relevant changes of complex realization. This is a strong compatibility property, but algebraicity is a further step. Pohlmann’s balance criterion and work of André and Hazama reduce CM questions to special tensors and Weil-type classes; M1 §1 describes their precise roles and cites the original papers.

There is substantial prior geometry behind the companion results. Markman’s secant-sheaf construction proves algebraicity of the Weil plane on the split sixfolds relevant to M3. M3 explicitly credits that construction and distinguishes it from its further all-powers conclusion. It also discusses earlier all-powers results of Moonen–Zarhin, Floccari, and Floccari–Fu. A new all-powers claim should therefore not be described as the first algebraicity result for those individual varieties.

Kuga and Satake associated abelian varieties with polarized K3 Hodge structures in 1967. The construction supplies a cohomological map; producing a cycle inducing the specified map is a separate conjectural assertion. Special K3 families already admit algebraic constructions. M2 discusses Paranjape’s curve-product method and more recent results before describing its larger quadratic locus.

Finally, Milne’s work on Lefschetz motives supplies the implication from the CM Hodge conjecture to the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields. His work on polarizations supplies the standard-conjecture implication. These consequences do not require each individual Tate class to lift to a Hodge class on a single CM lifting.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: all CM abelian varieties

M1’s Theorem 1.1 asserts that the displayed cycle-class map is onto for every complex CM abelian variety and every codimension. Finite products and powers remain CM, so they are included. The paper then states the generalized Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties, the Tate conjecture for all abelian varieties over finite fields, and the Hodge standard conjecture for abelian varieties in arbitrary characteristic, using the indicated earlier implications.

The arithmetic conclusion is broader than “CM reductions only.” Conversely, it is not a Hodge theorem for every complex abelian variety. The distinction between characteristic-zero geometry and finite-field geometry matters.

M2 and M5: the precise K3 scope

A K3 surface is a smooth simply connected compact complex surface with trivial canonical bundle; here it is projective. Write TST_STS​ for the orthogonal complement of divisor classes in H2(S,Q)H^2(S,\mathbb Q)H2(S,Q), using the cup-product form qqq. This is its transcendental quadratic space.

M2 assumes a rational isometric embedding

(TS,q)↪UQ⊕2⊥⟨−1⟩4.(T_S,q)\hookrightarrow U_{\mathbb Q}^{\oplus2}\perp\langle-1\rangle^{4}.(TS​,q)↪UQ⊕2​⊥⟨−1⟩4.

Here UUU is the two-dimensional hyperbolic plane with matrix (0110)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)(01​10​); the target has dimension eight and signature (2,6)(2,6)(2,6). An embedding must preserve the actual rational quadratic form, not just its dimension or real signature.

On this locus, M2 claims algebraic cycles realizing every prescribed standard even-Clifford Kuga–Satake tensor, and ordinary and generalized Hodge conjectures for all self-powers of SSS. It includes all ample PPP-polarized surfaces for P=U⊕D8(−1)⊕D4(−1)P=U\oplus D_8(-1)\oplus D_4(-1)P=U⊕D8​(−1)⊕D4​(−1), including points where extra divisor classes appear. Here the Dj(−1)D_j(-1)Dj​(−1) are negative root lattices, and a PPP-polarization embeds this lattice into the divisor lattice with an ample class in its image.

For an arbitrary projective K3, M2 also gives an implication from algebraicity of one exact standard Kuga–Satake tensor. M5 provides a different conditional reduction: at a full-orthogonal-Hodge-group point, one algebraic nonzero map from primitive degree-two cohomology into an abelian variety’s degree-two cohomology recovers the prescribed full correspondence. If that input exists very generally throughout a polarized component, the conclusion extends across that component. The existence of this initial map remains a hypothesis.

M3 and M4: extensions beyond CM

M3 claims the rational Hodge conjecture on every self-power of a six-dimensional abelian variety with an imaginary-quadratic action and a compatible polarization whose rational Hermitian form is hyperbolic of signature (3,3)(3,3)(3,3). Hyperbolic means that it has a three-dimensional totally isotropic subspace over the quadratic field. The actual rational form is required; the signature alone is insufficient.

M3 also treats every abelian variety of dimension at most five admitting an imaginary-quadratic action, again on all powers. Both statements include nonsimple varieties and special points with extra endomorphisms. They use M1’s CM theorem.

M4 treats Jacobians, the abelian varieties associated with curves, arising from connected abelian covers of curves. At every tensor Hodge-generic point of the full marked variation, it claims the Hodge conjecture on all powers, also after taking a product with any CM abelian variety. This means that rational tensors which are Hodge at the chosen point are already Hodge throughout that variation. The base genus and compatible branching pattern are unrestricted.

M4 also claims all-power results for a very general smooth diagonal complete intersection cut out by at most two equations of one common degree at least two. “Very general” excludes a countable union of proper algebraic subsets of the full labeled parameter space. It is not a statement about every member of an arbitrarily constrained subfamily.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The CM Hodge conjecture is a central algebraic-cycle problem with consequences reaching into arithmetic geometry. Its claimed resolution, together with the Tate and positivity implications, would affect a substantial part of the theory of abelian varieties.

The companion results emphasize a second point: understanding cohomology on all powers controls correspondences between factors, not merely subvarieties of one object. Exact correspondences can transfer questions between K3 surfaces, curves, and abelian varieties. This is why an apparently technical distinction between an arbitrary injection and the prescribed Kuga–Satake map has mathematical consequences.

The score measures the significance of these claims if correct. It does not treat the different manuscripts as five independent solutions of the unrestricted Hodge conjecture.

6. The main idea

Balanced tensors become a geometric construction

M1 uses the CM symmetries to divide degree-one cohomology into lines indexed by field embeddings. The Hodge condition becomes a balance condition: holomorphic and antiholomorphic contributions must match at every conjugate embedding. The paper reduces general balances to elementary four-factor relations, schematically

v1+v2=v3+v4,v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4,v1​+v2​=v3​+v4​,

where the viv_ivi​ encode the signs describing CM types. Auxiliary factors and polarization pairings allow these elementary pieces to be assembled and contracted back to the desired tensor.

To realize one piece algebraically, M1 constructs a projective surface carrying four degree-one classes whose product has nonzero integral. A map from that surface to a product of abelian varieties then gives an actual cycle. Algebraic divisor correspondences isolate the required component. Theta one-forms on arithmetic complex-ball quotients produce the nonzero period, while arithmetic operators identify the prescribed rational CM sources of those forms. Both the nonzero period and the rational-source identification are needed.

Supply the missing determinant classes

M3 and M4 use invariant theory: tensors fixed by the relevant symmetry groups are built from pairings and determinant lines. Pairings correspond to divisors. The harder pieces are supplied by algebraic correspondences from CM varieties, where M1 makes rational Hodge lifts algebraic.

M3 combines this with the split-sixfold Weil-plane construction and analyzes the actual Hodge group, including its changes at special points. M4 constructs determinant sources through finite quotients of curve powers and Fermat-type geometry. A Gale correspondence, relating complementary linear configurations, transfers the curve construction to the stated diagonal complete intersections.

Recover and transport an exact K3 tensor

M2 constructs a curve source for a K3-type cohomology space through auxiliary surfaces and pencils. Representation theory then recovers the full even-Clifford tensor from that source. Parameter spaces of algebraic cycles transport the specified action to other periods, with special care when the divisor lattice grows.

M5 isolates this recovery-and-specialization mechanism as a conditional theorem. It explains what a sufficient geometric input would look like without asserting that such an input exists for every K3 surface.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Rational coefficients are essential throughout. These statements do not supply integral representatives with prescribed denominators, nor do they identify all relations among algebraic cycles modulo rational equivalence.

The CM hypothesis, M2’s rational quadratic embedding, M3’s action and polarization requirements, and M4’s genericity conditions must remain attached to their conclusions. All-powers assertions in one of these settings cannot be transferred automatically to arbitrary abelian varieties or arbitrary K3 surfaces.

The repository’s withdrawal notice withdraws three other manuscripts concerning split eightfold Weil classes, general K3 Kuga–Satake algebraicity, and products of K3 surfaces, citing a sign error and dependent constructions. Those withdrawn manuscripts are not among the five current sources listed here. Their unrestricted conclusions are not adopted in this digest.

The current sources are reported as stated. In particular, the remaining existence hypothesis in M5 is a mathematical boundary of that reduction. Finding the initial correspondence beyond the established loci, and understanding integral refinements of the cycle statements, remain natural further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §§1–3 and 7–8 give the CM statement, the elementary-tensor reduction, and the consequences. M2 §§1–2 specify the K3 locus and exact-tensor criterion. M3 §§1–3 explain the all-powers extension and its debt to earlier Weil-class constructions. M4 §1 separates marked genericity from algebraic very-generality. M5 §1 states the conditional input explicitly.

For background, Deligne’s account and Milne’s papers linked above explain why compatibility, algebraicity, and arithmetic consequences are separate questions. Optional introductions to Hodge theory and complex multiplication can help with terminology; the definitions needed for the claims are given here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The rational Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Algebraic Kuga–Satake correspondences and Hodge conjectures on a K3 quadratic locus (September 30, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Weil classes and Hodge classes on abelian powers (October 6, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Abelian covers, Gale correspondences, and the Hodge conjecture for powers (October 6, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, A Conditional Reduction for Algebraic Kuga–Satake Correspondences (September 10, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Adding the complexity of a base and its fibers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 033 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Suppose a geometric space is organized as a family of smaller spaces. A surface might be made of curves, one above each point of another curve. Can the complexity of the whole be estimated from the complexity of the base and a typical fiber?

Dimension itself adds: a family of one-dimensional curves over a one-dimensional base is two-dimensional. Kodaira dimension measures a subtler kind of complexity, using global differential forms. Iitaka’s conjecture asks whether this complexity is at least the sum of the contributions from base and fiber.

Family 033 contains five manuscripts. They claim ordinary, logarithmic, and orbifold lower bounds; a stronger bound that measures how much the fibers change; an equality under smoothness conditions; and a semiampleness theorem for the moduli part of a Kähler fibration. These are related questions, but the equality needs assumptions that the lower bounds do not.

2. Background and essential definitions

Counting differential forms

For a smooth complex variety XXX of dimension nnn, the canonical line bundle KXK_XKX​ has local sections of the form f dz1∧⋯∧dznf\,dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_nfdz1​∧⋯∧dzn​. A section of mKXmK_XmKX​ is an mmm-fold tensor power of such a top-degree form. Here additive notation for line bundles means tensor product.

The space H0(X,mKX)H^0(X,mK_X)H0(X,mKX​) consists of global holomorphic sections. Ratios of sections define a rational map to projective space. The largest image dimension among these maps is the Kodaira dimension κ(X)\kappa(X)κ(X). If every positive-degree space is zero, its value is −∞-\infty−∞. Otherwise it lies between zero and dim⁡X\dim XdimX. A variety is of general type when these two dimensions agree.

For smooth projective curves, genus zero gives −∞-\infty−∞, genus one gives zero, and genus at least two gives one. These examples show that Kodaira dimension measures more than ordinary dimension: all three kinds are curves, but their canonical forms behave differently.

More generally, κ(X,L)\kappa(X,L)κ(X,L) denotes the same construction for a line bundle or rational divisor LLL. A rational divisor has rational coefficients; sufficiently divisible multiples have integer coefficients. We use κ(point)=0\kappa(\mathrm{point})=0κ(point)=0 and −∞+a=−∞-\infty+a=-\infty−∞+a=−∞.

Fibrations and boundaries

A fibration here is a proper surjective map f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y with connected fibers. A general fiber FFF avoids the exceptional parameters where behavior changes. The geometric generic fiber is the corresponding object over an algebraic closure of the function field of YYY.

A boundary Δ=∑iδiDi\Delta=\sum_i\delta_iD_iΔ=∑i​δi​Di​ records specified hypersurfaces with weights 0≤δi≤10\leq\delta_i\leq10≤δi​≤1. Simple normal crossings, abbreviated SNC, means they look locally like distinct coordinate hyperplanes. A reduced boundary has all nonzero coefficients equal to one.

If U=X∖DU=X\setminus DU=X∖D, with XXX smooth projective and DDD reduced SNC, define

κ‾(U)=κ(X,KX+D).\overline\kappa(U)=\kappa(X,K_X+D).κ(U)=κ(X,KX​+D).

This is logarithmic Kodaira dimension. It permits controlled poles along the missing boundary and is independent of the chosen smooth compactification. For example, C∗\mathbb C^*C∗ has logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero, although its compactification P1\mathbb P^1P1 has ordinary Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty−∞.

A compact Kähler manifold has a positive closed real differential form of type (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), giving a metric compatible with its complex structure. Projective manifolds are Kähler, but the converse fails. Fujiki class C\mathcal CC consists of spaces bimeromorphic to compact Kähler spaces. Bimeromorphic maps are analytic analogues of birational maps: they become isomorphisms on dense open subsets.

Variation and positivity

The variation Var⁡(f)\operatorname{Var}(f)Var(f) measures how many parameters are needed to define the whole generic fiber up to birational equivalence. Zero variation means that, after an appropriate field extension, its birational type is constant. This invariant must retain the entire function field of the fiber, not merely a canonical model or one associated period map.

A line bundle is semiample if one positive tensor power is generated by global sections everywhere. Such sections define a morphism. Nefness is a weaker positivity condition: in the projective setting it says that every curve has nonnegative degree. Nefness by itself does not guarantee global sections.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Iitaka’s theory of dimensions of divisors put the addition question into a birational framework. The target inequality for a smooth projective fibration is

κ(X)≥κ(F)+κ(Y).\kappa(X)\geq\kappa(F)+\kappa(Y).κ(X)≥κ(F)+κ(Y).

The key difficulty is global: forms available separately on fibers do not automatically fit together into enough forms on the total space.

Kawamata established major cases involving curve bases and fibers with good minimal models. Viehweg developed weak positivity of direct images of pluricanonical bundles, and Kollár treated general-type fibers. These results draw positivity from different places. A good minimal model is a birational model whose canonical divisor is semiample, while a general-type base provides enough canonical positivity to absorb auxiliary twists. M1 §1 and M4 §1 give the original references and distinguish these hypotheses.

Birkar proved the ordinary conjecture through total dimension six. Other work treats special bases, including abelian varieties and varieties of maximal Albanese dimension, which map generically finitely to their Albanese tori. Logarithmic results of Kovács–Patakfalvi and Hashizume allow boundaries under specified positivity or abundance conditions on the fibers.

Popa’s conjectural framework separates variation lower bounds from stronger additivity questions for smooth families. Earlier results on the reverse inequality required hypotheses such as good models for fibers of the base’s own Iitaka fibration. Those are not the same as assumptions on the original fibers of fff.

The moduli-part question has its own history. Ambro developed its birational formulation; Fujino–Gongyo proved important positivity properties. M5 credits the algebraic b-semiampleness theorem of Bakker–Filipazzi–Mauri–Tsimerman and addresses a compact Kähler extension allowing nonprojective morphisms. It should not be presented as the first projective b-semiampleness theorem.

The introductions also acknowledge earlier broad preprint claims of Tsuji and Maehara. They are not used as inputs in these manuscripts. The exposition here follows the current statements rather than making an independent priority assessment.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 and M4: lower bounds

M4 asserts ordinary subadditivity for every surjective projective morphism with connected fibers between smooth connected projective varieties over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. There is no dimension bound or good-minimal-model assumption on the generic fiber.

M1 gives the broader rational-SNC orbifold statement in Fujiki class C\mathcal CC:

κ(X,KX+Δ)≥κ(F,KF+Δ∣F)+κ(f∣Δ).\kappa(X,K_X+\Delta)\geq\kappa(F,K_F+\Delta|_F)+\kappa(f\mid\Delta).κ(X,KX​+Δ)≥κ(F,KF​+Δ∣F​)+κ(f∣Δ).

The last term is Campana’s birationally defined orbifold-base Kodaira dimension. Multiple fibers and source boundary coefficients contribute to it. For a base divisor DDD, its multiplicity is computed from

m(f,Δ;D)=min⁡E→Dord⁡E(f∗D)1−ΔE,m(f,\Delta;D)=\min_{E\to D}\frac{\operatorname{ord}_E(f^*D)}{1-\Delta_E},m(f,Δ;D)=E→Dmin​1−ΔE​ordE​(f∗D)​,

where EEE runs over divisors dominating DDD, and division by zero means infinity. The base coefficient is 1−1/m(f,Δ;D)1-1/m(f,\Delta;D)1−1/m(f,Δ;D). Taking the specified birational invariant is part of the theorem; one arbitrary base model is not the whole definition.

Coefficient-one boundaries are allowed. Ordinary and logarithmic subadditivity follow as stated consequences, including the characteristic-zero projective formulations.

M2: changing fibers contribute

For a projective surjection f:U→Vf:U\to Vf:U→V with connected fibers between smooth complex quasi-projective varieties, M2 assumes κ‾(V)≥0\overline\kappa(V)\geq0κ(V)≥0 and claims

κ‾(U)≥κ(F)+max⁡{κ‾(V),Var⁡(f)}.\overline\kappa(U)\geq\kappa(F)+\max\{\overline\kappa(V),\operatorname{Var}(f)\}.κ(U)≥κ(F)+max{κ(V),Var(f)}.

Singular fibers are permitted. There is no abundance or semiampleness assumption on FFF. The variation is that of the whole geometric generic fiber. When variation exceeds the logarithmic complexity of the base, this improves the ordinary lower bound.

M3: equality under stratum smoothness

Let f:(X,E)→(Y,D)f:(X,E)\to(Y,D)f:(X,E)→(Y,D) be a connected-fiber surjection of smooth projective complex reduced-SNC pairs, with Supp⁡(f∗D)⊆Supp⁡(E)\operatorname{Supp}(f^*D)\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(E)Supp(f∗D)⊆Supp(E). Assume the total space and every boundary stratum are smooth over Y∖DY\setminus DY∖D. A stratum is an irreducible component of an intersection of boundary components.

M3 claims the reverse inequality. Combining it with M1 gives

κ(X,KX+E)=κ(Y,KY+D)+κ(F,KF+E∣F).\kappa(X,K_X+E)=\kappa(Y,K_Y+D)+\kappa(F,K_F+E|_F).κ(X,KX​+E)=κ(Y,KY​+D)+κ(F,KF​+E∣F​).

Horizontal boundary components are allowed. Both −∞-\infty−∞ cases are included: if either contribution on the right is −∞-\infty−∞, all positive log-pluricanonical section spaces upstairs vanish. This is a substantive assertion, whereas a lower bound by −∞-\infty−∞ would be automatic.

M5: a moduli line defines a map

Suppose f:Y→Xf:Y\to Xf:Y→X is a connected-fiber surjection between smooth compact connected Kähler manifolds, with effective rational SNC boundary Δ\DeltaΔ of coefficients in [0,1][0,1][0,1], and

KY+Δ∼Qf∗L.K_Y+\Delta\sim_{\mathbb Q}f^*L.KY​+Δ∼Q​f∗L.

Rational linear equivalence here means equality of the corresponding actual holomorphic line bundles after a common positive multiple. The canonical bundle formula separates LLL into a canonical part, a discriminant measuring singularities, and a moduli line.

M5 claims that on some smooth compact Kähler modification S→XS\to XS→X, the moduli line MSM_SMS​ is semiample, and on every higher smooth modification ν:S1→S\nu:S_1\to Sν:S1​→S one has MS1=ν∗MSM_{S_1}=\nu^*M_SMS1​​=ν∗MS​ as rational holomorphic lines. This is b-semiampleness. It allows coefficient-one horizontal boundary and does not assume projectivity or orbifold Iitaka subadditivity.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Iitaka subadditivity is a central structural question about the birational classification of varieties. The claimed inequalities cover arbitrary dimension and connect canonical forms, family variation, and analytic positivity.

The equality statement adds information that lower bounds cannot provide, especially when the base has no logarithmic pluricanonical forms. The Kähler moduli theorem would make a numerical-looking contribution into an actual map, allowing geometric constructions that require sections rather than just positivity.

These results also serve as inputs elsewhere in the collection. Keeping their assumptions visible is essential when applying them to abundance or minimal-model claims.

6. The main idea

Replace the fiber by the part seen by its forms

A relative Iitaka map separates a fibration into a part carrying the fiber’s pluricanonical image and a remaining part of Kodaira dimension zero. The latter has essentially one pluricanonical generator in suitable degrees. Taking a cyclic root of that generator produces a differential form on a cover.

As the base varies, this form spans a Hodge line, a line inside a family of cohomology spaces. Its positivity measures some of the variation. The canonical bundle formula packages singular-fiber effects and this moduli contribution while comparing actual section spaces.

M1 and M4 develop the needed positivity on a projective period image and control boundary and ramification terms. Their addition arguments combine sections with auxiliary positive and negative twists so that the twists cancel. This exact comparison is what returns the lower bound to the original canonical divisor.

Keep all parameters of the fiber

M2 needs more than a period map which detects only part of the geometry. It first identifies a parameter field from logarithmic forms. A flat highest Hodge line is used to obtain birational constancy of the Kodaira-zero part. A separate descent argument retains the coordinates of the relative Iitaka base and finite normalization data.

Together these steps claim that the entire fiber is defined over the controlled parameter field. Bounding its transcendence degree then bounds Var⁡(f)\operatorname{Var}(f)Var(f). Forgetting the second step would control a simpler associated object instead of the variation appearing in the theorem.

Use a section’s zero to control the upper bound

For M3, the crucial case is a base of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero. The paper constructs a base pluriform from a total-space pluriform, retaining a zero on a specified smooth fiber. A suitably chosen general base point avoids the zero sets of all nonzero base pluriforms. Restriction to that fiber must therefore be injective on total-space sections, giving the upper growth bound.

For M5, residue constructions handle coefficient-one boundaries. An exact order calculation identifies the extended Hodge line with the threshold-defined moduli line. Product decompositions, period compactifications, and descent supply global generation. Tracking the actual line prevents an undetected flat twist from changing its section spaces.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower inequalities and the equality are not interchangeable. M2 requires nonnegative logarithmic Kodaira dimension of the base. M3 requires smoothness of every boundary stratum over the open base. Removing these assumptions is not part of their statements.

The discriminant used for M5’s moduli line is defined by log canonical thresholds, which measure how much a fiber divisor can be added before singularities cross the allowed limit. It is distinct from M1’s inf-multiplicity orbifold divisor.

The ordinary algebraic theorem is in characteristic zero. The analytic results concern compact Kähler or class-C\mathcal CC spaces under the stated conditions, not arbitrary compact complex manifolds. M5 supplies some globally generating multiple, without a uniform numerical bound for that multiple across all fibrations.

Natural further questions concern effective bounds, positive-characteristic analogues, and extensions beyond the specified singularity and compactness settings. The manuscripts’ claims and dependencies are reported here without an independent mathematical verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 specifies the orbifold invariant and the lower inequality. M2 §1 defines whole-fiber variation and identifies its two constancy steps. M3 §1 states the stratum-smooth upper bound and explains the negative-infinity cases. M4 §§1 and 6–7 give the projective Hodge-line route. M5 §§1 and 4 distinguish the threshold moduli line from numerical positivity.

The linked work of Birkar and Popa supplies accessible entry points into the earlier partial results and conjectural landscape. For terminology, see the optional overview of Kodaira dimension.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Orbifold and logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Logarithmic Kodaira dimension and whole-fiber variation (September 26, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The reverse logarithmic Kodaira inequality and additivity (September 26, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Projective Hodge lines and ordinary Iitaka subadditivity (September 27, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, B-semiampleness for compact log-smooth Kähler fibrations (September 10, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When one numerical direction becomes a fibration in positive characteristic
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 035 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Imagine that the canonical geometry of a three-dimensional algebraic variety has only one direction of numerical growth. Should that direction come from a genuine map to a curve?

The abundance conjecture predicts that a nef canonical divisor, including a specified boundary when appropriate, is generated by sections after taking a positive multiple. Family 035 addresses the numerical-dimension-one case over fields of positive characteristic. Its first manuscript, M1, claims the result for log canonical threefold pairs. The second, M2, treats terminal threefolds without boundary and develops the structural obstruction used by M1.

The distinction between “one numerical direction” and “a map to a curve” is the problem itself. A small intersection dimension does not automatically produce a family of curves on which the divisor has degree zero, let alone global sections defining a morphism.

2. Background and essential definitions

The ambient geometry

A threefold is an algebraic variety of dimension three. Projective means that it embeds in projective space; normality rules out certain defects in its local rings while allowing controlled singularities. The field kkk is algebraically closed and has characteristic p>3p>3p>3, so ppp is a prime, beginning with five, and adding the number one to itself ppp times gives zero.

The canonical divisor KXK_XKX​ represents top-degree differential forms on the smooth part of XXX. A boundary BBB is an effective rational combination of hypersurfaces, and L=KX+BL=K_X+BL=KX​+B is the log canonical divisor. A divisor is Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier when some positive integer multiple defines a line bundle. All section statements use such multiples.

The pair (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) is log canonical if, on resolutions, the coefficients of the boundary obtained from

KY+BY=π∗(KX+B)K_Y+B_Y=\pi^*(K_X+B)KY​+BY​=π∗(KX​+B)

are at most one. This condition measures the allowed singularities of both the space and its boundary. Terminal singularities are a more restrictive condition on a boundary-free variety. A variety is Q\mathbb QQ-factorial if every Weil divisor has a Cartier positive multiple. M1 does not require either terminality or Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality of the original threefold.

Three dimensions associated with a divisor

A divisor LLL is nef when L⋅C≥0L\cdot C\geq0L⋅C≥0 for every curve CCC. For a nef divisor on a threefold and an ample divisor HHH, numerical dimension one means

L⋅H2>0,L2⋅H=0.L\cdot H^2>0,\qquad L^2\cdot H=0.L⋅H2>0,L2⋅H=0.

The first intersection detects a nontrivial positive direction; the second says that two copies of LLL do not produce positive growth. This condition is independent of the ample divisor used to test it. Write it as ν(L)=1\nu(L)=1ν(L)=1.

The Iitaka dimension κ(L)\kappa(L)κ(L) instead measures the largest dimension of a rational image obtained from ratios of global sections of mLmLmL. It is −∞-\infty−∞ if all positive section spaces vanish. A single section only gives nonvanishing; obtaining two sections with a nonconstant ratio can produce a positive-dimensional image.

The nef dimension n(L)n(L)n(L) comes from the nef reduction, which groups together directions traced by curves of LLL-degree zero through very general points. “Very general” means outside a countable union of proper closed subsets, after working over an uncountable algebraically closed field when needed. On a threefold, n(L)=3n(L)=3n(L)=3 means there are no such zero-degree curves through a very general point.

These invariants ask different questions. The difficult configuration in these papers is

ν(L)=1,κ(L)=0,n(L)=3.\nu(L)=1,\qquad\kappa(L)=0,\qquad n(L)=3.ν(L)=1,κ(L)=0,n(L)=3.

Numerical growth is small, there are too few section ratios to define a curve map, but zero-degree curves do not sweep out the space.

Semiampleness and its geometric meaning

A line bundle is semiample if a positive power is generated by global sections at every point. For nef LLL with ν(L)=1\nu(L)=1ν(L)=1, this yields a morphism with connected fibers

f:X⟶C,mL∼f∗A,f:X\longrightarrow C,\qquad mL\sim f^*A,f:X⟶C,mL∼f∗A,

where CCC is a normal projective curve and AAA is ample. Here ∼\sim∼ denotes linear equivalence, hence an identity of the associated line bundles. The fibers are surfaces, and LLL has degree zero on their curves. This is the actual geometric structure sought in the opening question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Over the complex numbers, Miyaoka’s numerical-dimension-one theorem studied effective pluricanonical divisors and their neighborhoods. Kawamata’s abundance theorem completed the minimal-threefold picture and gave a related approach using finite covers and infinitesimal deformations. Keel–Matsuki–McKernan established log abundance for threefolds, with the correction cited in M1.

Positive characteristic requires different tools. Frobenius can help with line bundles and differential forms, but characteristic-zero vanishing arguments cannot simply be imported. Keel’s base-point-freeness criterion and later work of Cascini–Tanaka–Xu established important foundations. Hacon–Xu, Birkar, and subsequent authors developed the threefold minimal model program for characteristic greater than five; Hacon–Witaszek treated characteristic five.

Nonvanishing also has a substantial prior history. Xu–Zhang proved it for terminal minimal threefolds in characteristic greater than five. Witaszek’s canonical-bundle-formula work proved further nonvanishing and low-nef-dimension abundance results. These are advances toward obtaining and using sections, rather than consequences of the new manuscripts.

Zheng Xu’s characteristic-greater-than-three theorem supplies nonvanishing for pseudoeffective lc adjoints and abundance in the low-nef-dimension cases used here. His subsequent numerical-dimension-two result treats a different slice of the problem. M2 explicitly identifies the remaining task in its setting: exclude numerical dimension one with Kodaira dimension zero and maximal nef dimension.

Thus the new step is not obtaining the first section from scratch. It is forcing additional section growth, then applying the established passage from positive Kodaira dimension to semiampleness. M1 extends the companion’s obstruction to arbitrary rational lc boundaries.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the log canonical statement

Let kkk be algebraically closed of characteristic p>3p>3p>3, and let (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) be a normal projective log canonical threefold pair. Assume that B≥0B\geq0B≥0 is rational and that L=KX+BL=K_X+BL=KX​+B is Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier, nef, and of numerical dimension one. M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that LLL is semiample.

There is no terminality or Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality assumption on XXX, and boundary coefficients are arbitrary rational coefficients compatible with log canonicity. Auxiliary birational models may satisfy stronger conditions, but these should not be added to the original theorem’s hypotheses.

The conclusion gives κ(L)=1\kappa(L)=1κ(L)=1 and the curve fibration described above. It does not assert that a particular specified low multiple already generates the line.

M2: the boundary-free case and its obstruction

M2 assumes that XXX is normal, projective, Q\mathbb QQ-factorial, and terminal, with KXK_XKX​ nef and ν(KX)=1\nu(K_X)=1ν(KX​)=1. Its Theorem 1.1 claims a positive Cartier multiple with at least two linearly independent sections, and hence κ(KX)=1\kappa(K_X)=1κ(KX​)=1 and semiampleness.

No restriction is imposed on irregularity, the Albanese map, or the first Betti number. The manuscript works directly in characteristic ppp; it does not assume that XXX can be lifted to characteristic zero.

For M1, the crucial companion output is a nonexistence theorem for a specially prepared effective divisor on a smooth threefold. It combines numerical dimension one, maximal nef dimension, a torsion normal line on the whole possibly nonreduced divisor, and a local canonical relation. M1 constructs precisely this configuration from a hypothetical counterexample with boundary.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The result would close a significant numerical-dimension case of threefold log abundance in positive characteristic, including characteristic five and the broader lc singularities. It connects intersection theory with an actual fibration in a setting where familiar characteristic-zero methods are unavailable.

The scope is substantial but specific: dimension three, p>3p>3p>3, and numerical dimension one. The score reflects that central contribution within birational geometry without treating it as an all-dimensional or all-characteristic abundance theorem.

The companion’s mechanism also has independent explanatory interest. It turns a geometric failure to find enough sections into a conflict between divisibility of line bundles and integer-valued intersection degree.

6. The main idea

Isolate the problematic divisor

Prior nonvanishing gives an effective Cartier divisor N∼m(KX+B)N\sim m(K_X+B)N∼m(KX​+B). Assume that the desired abundance fails. The earlier low-nef-dimension results reduce attention to n(N)=3n(N)=3n(N)=3.

M1 first separates the boundary from NNN: each boundary component is either part of its support or disjoint from it. The argument uses bend-and-break, a technique that extracts rational curves from families of curves with negative canonical degree. In this situation a failure of separation would produce zero-NNN-degree curves through very general points, contradicting maximal nef dimension.

A sequence of controlled birational operations then isolates a component, and surface abundance gives torsion along it. “Torsion” means that some positive tensor power of the restricted line is trivial. The papers retain this property on the full Cartier thickening, including multiplicities, rather than only on the reduced support.

Study all finite neighborhoods

On a smooth model the construction yields a connected divisor DDD, with primitive multiplicities, which is nef and numerically trivial on each of its components. Its normal line OD(D)\mathcal O_D(D)OD​(D) is torsion, and a power of the canonical bundle has a local divisor supported on DDD.

M2 studies successively thicker infinitesimal neighborhoods of DDD. These retain derivatives transverse to the divisor even though their underlying point set stays the same. Estimates for differential forms and finite jets control cohomology when poles of finite order along DDD are allowed.

The resulting object is a punctured formal neighborhood: it remembers all finite thickenings while allowing the local equation of the divisor to be inverted. It is an algebraic formal construction, not simply an ordinary open subset of the original threefold.

Divisibility conflicts with integer degree

Cartier descent is a characteristic-ppp method relating suitable differential data to Frobenius pullback. M2 uses it to claim that every line bundle on this formal neighborhood has a ppp-th root. Its Picard group, the group of line bundles under tensor product, would therefore be ppp-divisible.

At the same time, intersections with an ample divisor give a nonzero homomorphism from this group to Z\mathbb ZZ. The incompatibility is elementary once these constructions are available. If every group element can be divided by ppp repeatedly, every integer in the homomorphism’s image must be divisible by pep^epe for every e≥1e\geq1e≥1. Only zero has that property.

The geometric constructions instead give a positive degree, proportional to D⋅H2>0D\cdot H^2>0D⋅H2>0. The contradiction rules out the prepared configuration, forcing positive Iitaka dimension and then semiampleness through the cited earlier theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The characteristic restriction is p>3p>3p>3; neither characteristic two nor three is covered. The ground field is algebraically closed. Extensions to more general fields require separate descent and singularity arguments.

Numerical dimension one must not be replaced by nef dimension one. The hard part explicitly allows nef dimension three before excluding it. Nor does the result assert abundance for every nef divisor: the canonical-plus-boundary form is essential.

The proof’s stronger singularity conditions occur on intermediate models. M1’s final conclusion concerns the original lc pair, while M2 retains its terminal and Q\mathbb QQ-factorial hypotheses. The argument uses established positive-characteristic minimal-model, nonvanishing, and surface-abundance inputs in addition to the companion obstruction.

The statements give no uniform bound on the generating multiple or a classification of the resulting surface fibers. Such effective bounds, smaller characteristics, and higher-dimensional analogues are further questions. The claims here are reported from the manuscripts without proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §§1–2 state the log canonical theorem and the exact companion obstruction; §§3–6 explain boundary separation and the construction of the prohibited divisor. M2 §§1–2 describe the terminal case and prepared cycle; §§3–6 develop the formal-neighborhood and divisibility mechanism.

The linked papers of Miyaoka, Kawamata, Witaszek, and Zheng Xu locate the new claims among prior partial solutions. For optional terminology, see nef line bundles and Frobenius endomorphisms.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Log abundance in numerical dimension one for threefolds in positive characteristic (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Abundance in numerical dimension one for terminal threefolds in positive characteristic (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: From nef canonical bundles to maps: abundance and uniform degrees
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 034 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A line bundle can look nonnegative when measured on every curve yet have too few global sections to describe a map. The abundance conjecture predicts that canonical line bundles, which encode top-degree differential forms, are special: their numerical nonnegativity should produce an actual geometric fibration.

Family 034 combines fourteen manuscripts addressing this prediction and its quantitative refinements. There are three successive questions. Does a positive power have even one nonzero section? Does some power have sections generating the line at every point? Can one choose a degree depending only on dimension and specified boundary coefficients?

The answers claimed here range from projective varieties to compact Kähler spaces, which need not be projective. The leading Kähler theorem explicitly assumes logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity. A fourfold minimal-model paper is also expressly conditional. These dependencies are part of the mathematical statements, even though related manuscripts in the collection claim the needed inputs.

2. Background and essential definitions

Divisors, singularities, and adjoints

The canonical bundle KXK_XKX​ of a smooth complex nnn-fold consists of holomorphic top-degree forms. A divisor is a formal sum of hypersurfaces; a rational divisor permits rational coefficients. A pair (X,Δ)(X,\Delta)(X,Δ) adds an effective boundary Δ\DeltaΔ, and its adjoint is D=KX+ΔD=K_X+\DeltaD=KX​+Δ.

On a singular space, a divisor need not itself define a line bundle. It is Cartier when it does so locally by one equation, and Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier when some positive integer multiple is Cartier. The manuscripts concern actual multiples and their section spaces, not only their intersection classes.

The singularity conditions can be expressed on a resolution π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X: write

KY+BY=π∗(KX+Δ).K_Y+B_Y=\pi^*(K_X+\Delta).KY​+BY​=π∗(KX​+Δ).

The pair is log canonical, or lc, when all coefficients encountered in these crepant boundaries are at most one; it is Kawamata log terminal, or klt, when they are strictly less than one. The latter is more restrictive. Divisorial log terminal, or dlt, is an intermediate controlled setting in which the coefficient-one boundary supports inductive arguments. Semi-log-canonical, or slc, also permits components joined along double loci, with lc behavior after normalization and inclusion of the joining divisor.

Three levels of positivity

For a projective variety, DDD is nef if D⋅C≥0D\cdot C\geq0D⋅C≥0 for every curve CCC. It is pseudoeffective if its numerical class is a limit of effective divisor classes. On a compact Kähler space these notions use curvature classes and positive currents, generalized differential forms which can concentrate along subvarieties.

Nonvanishing means H0(X,mD)≠0H^0(X,mD)\ne0H0(X,mD)=0 for some positive Cartier multiple. Semiampleness means that some such multiple is generated by global sections everywhere. One section can vanish along a large divisor; global generation requires, at each point, a section which does not vanish there.

Kodaira or Iitaka dimension κ(X,D)\kappa(X,D)κ(X,D) is the largest dimension of a rational image defined by ratios of sections of multiples of DDD, with value −∞-\infty−∞ when there are no sections. For a nef divisor, numerical dimension ν(D)\nu(D)ν(D) instead measures nonzero intersection powers. These two dimensions need not agree merely by definition. Abundance is precisely a bridge from numerical positivity to section geometry.

A minimal model is a birational model with nef adjoint and the required singularity comparison. A good minimal model has semiample adjoint. Birational means that dense open subsets are isomorphic. The minimal model program simplifies a variety through contractions and flips; finding a nef endpoint and proving it good are separate tasks.

Uniformity and the full Iitaka field

If D∼Q0D\sim_{\mathbb Q}0D∼Q​0, some multiple defines the trivial line bundle. Its least positive trivializing degree is the index. Uniform index bounds must work across all pairs in a stated class.

For a rational divisor, define

Vm(D)=H0(X,OX(⌊mD⌋)),K(D)=k(s/t: s,t∈Vm(D)∖{0}, m>0).V_m(D)=H^0\bigl(X,\mathcal O_X(\lfloor mD\rfloor)\bigr),\qquadK(D)=k\bigl(s/t:\ s,t\in V_m(D)\setminus\{0\},\ m>0\bigr).Vm​(D)=H0(X,OX​(⌊mD⌋)),K(D)=k(s/t: s,t∈Vm​(D)∖{0}, m>0).

The floor rounds each coefficient down; on a normal variety the indicated divisorial sheaf is interpreted reflexively when it is not a line bundle. The field K(D)K(D)K(D) is the Iitaka field inside the function field k(X)k(X)k(X). Recovering it in one degree is stronger than obtaining an image of the correct dimension: a proper finite subfield has the same transcendence degree.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The threefold story already separated the main difficulties. Miyaoka treated numerical dimension one, Kawamata completed canonical abundance for minimal threefolds, and Keel–Matsuki–McKernan established the logarithmic result. Fujino’s slc work addressed the additional problem of gluing sections across components. M4 §1 gives these original references and explains how their boundary methods enter its induction.

Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan established fundamental minimal-model and finite-generation results. These do not make every nef lc adjoint semiample automatically. In particular, finite generation alone does not supply a nonzero section when all positive section spaces vanish.

The Kähler theory required analytic replacements for projective tools. Höring–Peternell constructed threefold minimal models, Campana–Höring–Peternell treated canonical abundance, and Das–Ou proved log abundance for compact Kähler lc threefolds. M1 and M14 carefully distinguish these lower-dimensional inputs from the new higher-dimensional claims.

Uniform effectivity developed along another route. Fujino–Mori’s canonical bundle formula, Viehweg–Zhang’s results for surface bases, and Birkar–Zhang’s effective Iitaka theorem controlled degrees using additional fiber invariants. The new uniform claims seek to remove those extra dependencies under their specified coefficient assumptions.

For indices, Jiang–Liu established slc bounds through dimension three and important non-klt fourfold cases. M2 extends the dimension range, with substantial companion inputs. M8 also explicitly credits Zou’s theorem for the same zero-Kodaira-fiber conclusion that it proves by a different route. Its contribution should not be described as first establishing that particular statement.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Abundance and its stated inputs: M1, M3, M4, M14

M1 assumes logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity for smooth projective complex fibrations with compatible reduced simple-normal-crossing boundaries. Under that assumption, every analytically nef Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier adjoint of a normal irreducible compact Kähler lc pair with effective rational boundary is semiample, in every dimension. The conclusion concerns the given holomorphic line, with no unrecorded flat twist.

M4 claims projective rational-boundary log abundance over every algebraically closed characteristic-zero field. Over C\mathbb CC, it also claims canonical nonvanishing for smooth projective varieties and a stronger good-model induction. It states its logarithmic-subadditivity input explicitly; its sole use in the nonvanishing argument is an ordinary Albanese-fibration case, which the paper notes is also covered by earlier external theorems. The collection’s corresponding subadditivity claims are explained in family 033.

M3 concerns compact Kähler klt fourfolds with pseudoeffective actual adjoint and global strong Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality: every rank-one reflexive sheaf on the whole space has an invertible positive reflexive power. This is not simply a local condition on each open chart. Its good-model conclusion assumes the stated orbifold Iitaka inequality, the specified ordinary fourfold program, and abundance after nonvanishing. The manuscript identifies the program as an independent companion input; its remaining conditional premises are stated rather than suppressed.

M14 supplies abundance after nonvanishing for normal compact Kähler klt fourfolds with effective rational boundary. It assumes analytic nefness and κ(X,D)≥0\kappa(X,D)\geq0κ(X,D)≥0, and requires neither projectivity nor Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality. When κ(X,D)=0\kappa(X,D)=0κ(X,D)=0, it claims an actual trivial positive Cartier multiple. It does not itself manufacture the initial section required by its hypothesis.

Obtaining and extending sections: M5, M6, M7, M8

M5 claims that a minimal-singularity semipositive metric on the pullback of a nef projective klt adjoint has zero Lelong numbers everywhere on every projective log resolution. Lelong numbers measure logarithmic concentration of the metric’s singularities; zero does not mean the metric is smooth. A separate injectivity theorem in degree-one cohomology, for strictly interior rational SNC boundaries and zero-Lelong metrics at both endpoints, yields extension of sections from an entire divisor scheme.

M6 claims canonical nonvanishing for every smooth projective complex fourfold with pseudoeffective canonical divisor, without assumptions on numerical dimension, irregularity, or Euler characteristic. It derives nonvanishing for nef rational lc adjoints through dimension four. The result is qualitative: it does not bound the first degree.

M7 starts with a nonzero effective Cartier divisor G∼q(KV+C)G\sim q(K_V+C)G∼q(KV​+C) on a projective Q\mathbb QQ-factorial dlt pair, supported on the coefficient-one boundary. If its line bundle is semiample on the whole reduced support of GGG, it claims positive ambient Iitaka dimension. It derives projective lc abundance after nonvanishing through dimension four, and an all-dimensional reduction assuming smooth canonical nonvanishing. Agreement across intersections is part of the support hypothesis.

M8, using the good-model input from M4, claims the Campana–Peternell inequality

m0KX−D pseudoeffective,D≥0⟹κ(X)≥κ(X,D)m_0K_X-D\text{ pseudoeffective},\quad D\geq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \kappa(X)\geq\kappa(X,D)m0​KX​−D pseudoeffective,D≥0⟹κ(X)≥κ(X,D)

for a smooth projective complex variety and effective Cartier divisor DDD. For a connected-fiber fibration f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y, an ample Cartier HHH on YYY, and pseudoeffective m0KX−f∗Hm_0K_X-f^*Hm0​KX​−f∗H, it obtains κ(X)=κ(F)+dim⁡Y\kappa(X)=\kappa(F)+\dim Yκ(X)=κ(F)+dimY, plus sections of mKX−f∗HmK_X-f^*HmKX​−f∗H in all sufficiently large divisible degrees. The ample comparison is an essential hypothesis.

Uniform indices and uniform maps: M2, M9–M13

M10 claims a degree m(d)m(d)m(d), depending only on dimension, whose complete pluricanonical system recovers the full Iitaka field of every smooth projective characteristic-zero ddd-fold with nonnegative Kodaira dimension. It also claims a uniform normal lc log-Calabi–Yau index for coefficients in a fixed rational DCC set. DCC means there is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence. Its good-model input is M4, not merely the established big-adjoint theory.

M2 extends uniform indices to connected projective equidimensional slc log-Calabi–Yau pairs in every fixed dimension at least four, with a fixed finite rational coefficient set. One integer makes the adjoint Cartier and trivial, independently of the number of components. Together with earlier dimensions at most three, this is the finite-coefficient slc claim. M2 uses the normal index theorem from M10 and good models from M4.

M13 gives uniform complete rounded log-Iitaka systems for projective complex lc fourfolds with fixed finite rational boundary coefficients and pseudoeffective adjoint. It also claims a uniform boundary-free klt fourfold canonical index. Its passage from pseudoeffectivity to a first section uses M4.

M9 gives the analogous full-field conclusion in dimensions at least five over algebraically closed characteristic-zero fields, assuming nonnegative Iitaka dimension and fixed finite rational coefficients. Its supporting result controls moduli denominators, including horizontal boundary, using M4, M10, and M12.

M11 treats log-Calabi–Yau fibrations with lc total space of dimension at most four and positive-dimensional base. For fixed finite rational coefficients, it selects an exact canonical-bundle-formula presentation with uniformly bounded trivializing degree and moduli Cartier denominator. If the base adjoint is big, uniform rounded systems recover its full function field. The denominator bound concerns this normalized presentation, not every rationally equivalent representative.

M12 supplies an arithmetic bound. For an ordinary projective lc log-Calabi–Yau pair (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) of dimension ddd over any characteristic-zero field kkk, with H0(X,OX)=kH^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=kH0(X,OX​)=k, a prime boundary component SSS of coefficient at least t>0t>0t>0 satisfies

[kS:k]≤N(d,t),[k_S:k]\leq N(d,t),[kS​:k]≤N(d,t),

where kSk_SkS​ is the relative algebraic closure of kkk in k(S)k(S)k(S). This controls the finite arithmetic constant field encountered when restricting to boundary components. It is the contraction-to-a-point form stated in that paper, not an unqualified theorem about all fibrations.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Abundance is a central missing bridge in birational classification: a minimal model should reveal a canonical map, rather than merely have nonnegative curve intersections. The all-dimensional projective and conditional Kähler statements are therefore exceptionally consequential if correct.

Uniform degrees would strengthen an asymptotic description into one degree shared across an entire class. Uniform indices also matter when varieties degenerate into several components, because local trivializations must agree globally. The rating reflects the family as a whole; it does not imply equal novelty for each supporting manuscript.

6. The main idea

Move information off the boundary

The abundance arguments repeatedly restrict an adjoint to lower-dimensional boundary components, where induction supplies sections. Those sections must first be glued on the whole boundary. Finite covers and Hodge-theoretic residue calculations then control obstructions to extending them through thicker and thicker neighborhoods.

The intended geometric outcome is a moving family of subvarieties on which the adjoint is trivial. Such families constrain the directions where a nef divisor can remain positive. The papers use that constraint to obtain a fibration and ultimately generation of the actual adjoint line.

Force the first section

Nonvanishing cannot be assumed while proving it. M4 and M6 instead analyze a hypothetical variety with no canonical sections. Reductions constrain its possible fibrations and moving curves. Estimates for jets, which record successive derivatives of sections at a point, then produce incompatible bounds on vanishing orders.

One comparison uses reduction of fixed algebraic data to positive characteristic and Frobenius, the map raising coordinates to the characteristic power. The resulting rank deficit along a diagonal forces more determinant vanishing than the geometric upper bound permits. This is a proof strategy reported from the manuscripts, not a claim that the final theorem is in positive characteristic.

Bound the obstruction to a uniform degree

For uniformity, the obstacle is often a finite character: continuation around a singular fiber multiplies a volume form by a root of unity. The order of that scalar affects denominators and trivializing degrees. The papers aim to bound the relevant character even when a larger covering degree is uncontrolled.

On a reducible slc space, one can picture normalization components as vertices of a graph and their intersections as edges. Trivializations differ by scalars along edges. Products around closed walks obstruct gluing. M2 interprets these products through birational actions on smaller strata and bounds their orders uniformly. Taking one common power then makes the forms agree.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The analytic and algebraic statements have different hypotheses. M1 remains an implication from logarithmic subadditivity; M3 retains its explicit program and abundance premises; M14 assumes nonvanishing. None should be shortened to an assumption-free theorem for arbitrary compact complex spaces.

Numerical equivalence, rational linear equivalence, and global generation are different. A flat twist can preserve a curvature class while changing sections. The conclusions here repeatedly require the actual line bundle. Likewise, a uniform Cartier denominator for a moduli divisor is not a uniform base-point-free multiple.

Finite rational coefficient sets in M2, M9, M11, and M13 must not be silently enlarged to arbitrary real boundaries. M10’s normal index statement has its separately stated rational DCC scope. The uniform bounds are existential; practical formulas or small numerical degrees are not supplied by the headline claims.

Effective values, broader coefficient classes, and positive-characteristic analogues remain further directions. All mathematical claims and dependencies are taken as stated; these expositions do not audit their proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

For the central logical distinctions, read M1 §1, M3 §§1–2, M4 §1, and M14 §1. M5–M7 explain metrics, first sections, and supported-boundary extension. M8 states its numerical comparison and credits the earlier zero-fiber theorem. M9–M13 specify the uniformity parameters and the equality of embedded section fields; M2 explains the extra gluing problem for slc pairs.

The linked BCHM and Jiang–Liu papers supply primary context for model existence and index bounds. The optional minimal model program overview introduces the birational operations used throughout.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Log abundance for compact Kähler spaces under logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Uniform indices for semi-log-canonical log Calabi–Yau pairs (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Conditional good minimal models for compact Kähler fourfolds (October 6, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Log abundance in characteristic zero (September 24, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Minimal metrics and interior injectivity for nef adjoints (September 27, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Fourfold nonvanishing by minimal metrics and moving jets (September 27, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Lifting sections from the reduced support of an adjoint (September 27, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, Schnell fiber spaces and good canonical models (September 24, 2026).
  • M9. OpenAI, Uniform log Iitaka fibrations and bounded moduli denominators (October 4, 2026).
  • M10. OpenAI, Uniform Pluricanonical Iitaka Fibrations (October 3, 2026).
  • M11. OpenAI, Relative denominators and effective systems for log Calabi-Yau fibrations (September 27, 2026).
  • M12. OpenAI, Arithmetic Stein-degree bounds for log Calabi–Yau pairs (September 25, 2026).
  • M13. OpenAI, Uniform effective log Iitaka fibrations for fourfolds (September 26, 2026).
  • M14. OpenAI, Abundance after nonvanishing for compact Kähler fourfolds (September 27, 2026).

entry.title: Numerical semiampleness and the existence of minimal models
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 036 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Can the numerical positivity of a line bundle determine a map, even when the line itself has no sections? This question sounds contradictory until one distinguishes a bundle from its numerical class. Different bundles can have identical degrees on every curve but very different spaces of sections.

Family 036 studies canonical divisors with an additional nef contribution. Two manuscripts claim that the resulting class has a semiample representative: a different bundle with the same numerical information and enough sections to define a map. Another claims existence of minimal models or Mori fiber spaces for generalized log canonical pairs. A fourth gives a separate minimal-model construction in numerical dimension one.

These conclusions concern different stages of birational classification. Existence of a nef model is not itself semiampleness, and numerical semiampleness does not generally make the originally specified bundle semiample.

2. Background and essential definitions

Divisors and their numerical classes

A line bundle assigns a one-dimensional vector space to each point, varying algebraically or holomorphically. Global sections can define a map to projective space if they do not all vanish at any point. A bundle is semiample when some positive tensor power has this property.

For a projective variety, a rational Cartier divisor represents a rational line bundle: an integral multiple is an actual line bundle. It is nef if its degree on every curve is nonnegative. It is pseudoeffective if its numerical class is a limit of classes of effective divisors. Two divisors are numerically equivalent, written D≡LD\equiv LD≡L, if they have the same degree on every curve.

The canonical divisor KXK_XKX​ records top-degree differential forms. A rational boundary B≥0B\geq0B≥0 records weighted hypersurfaces, and KX+BK_X+BKX​+B is an ordinary adjoint. A pair is klt, short for Kawamata log terminal, when its log discrepancies are positive. Concretely, on a resolution with

KY+BY=π∗(KX+B),K_Y+B_Y=\pi^*(K_X+B),KY​+BY​=π∗(KX​+B),

all coefficients of BYB_YBY​ are less than one. Log canonical, or lc, allows equality to one. These conditions control singularities so that birational comparison and extension methods can be used.

The simplest reason for a numerical conclusion

Take a complex elliptic curve EEE, whose canonical bundle is trivial. Let MMM be a non-torsion line bundle of degree zero, meaning that no positive power is trivial. Every M⊗mM^{\otimes m}M⊗m has degree zero and has no nonzero section: a section would have an effective zero divisor of degree zero, so would vanish nowhere and trivialize the bundle.

Nevertheless, MMM is nef and numerically equivalent to OE\mathcal O_EOE​, the trivial bundle, which is generated by a constant section. Therefore numerical semiampleness is possible even though semiampleness of MMM is false. This is why adding an arbitrary nef line to a canonical divisor changes the appropriate target.

Kähler classes and generalized pairs

A compact Kähler manifold has a positive closed real differential form compatible with its complex structure. It need not embed in projective space. The first Chern class of a holomorphic line bundle lies in real Bott–Chern cohomology HBC1,1(X,R)H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)HBC1,1​(X,R), which records closed real (1,1)(1,1)(1,1)-forms modulo the appropriate second derivatives of functions. Equality there captures curvature information but can forget a flat line-bundle factor.

A generalized pair (X,B+M)(X,B+M)(X,B+M) permits the nef contribution to live on a higher birational model. One fixes a nef rational Cartier divisor on that model and uses its compatible pullbacks and pushforwards elsewhere. This compatible collection is a nef b-divisor. Its trace on XXX appears in KX+B+MK_X+B+MKX​+B+M, but the higher-model data must remain fixed when discrepancies are compared.

A minimal model is a birational model with nef adjoint and improved discrepancies, extracting no new divisors. A Mori fiber space has a map to a lower-dimensional base, with negative adjoint along the fibers and relative Picard number one. The last condition says that only one independent numerical divisor direction remains relative to that base.

Numerical dimension before nefness

The fourth manuscript uses Nakayama’s section-growth invariant κσ(X,D)\kappa_\sigma(X,D)κσ​(X,D). For a smooth projective nnn-fold, it is the largest integer jjj for which some fixed ample Cartier divisor AAA satisfies

lim sup⁡m→∞h0(X,OX(mD+A))mj>0.\limsup_{m\to\infty}\frac{h^0(X,\mathcal O_X(mD+A))}{m^j}>0.m→∞limsup​mjh0(X,OX​(mD+A))​>0.

The ample twist is chosen once before taking the limit. Numerical dimension one in this convention rules out positive quadratic growth for every fixed twist. It does not assert a uniform linear upper bound, and it does not manufacture a section of the untwisted mDmDmD.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mori’s contraction and flip methods made birational simplification into a systematic program. The subsequent theory of singular pairs is developed in Kollár–Mori’s monograph. The work of Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan supplied minimal models and finite-generation results in crucial projective settings, particularly the big-boundary and general-type ranges.

Approaching a merely pseudoeffective divisor is harder than treating each positive perturbation. A finite program for every positive perturbation parameter does not imply that the combined sequence stops when the parameter tends to zero. Weak Zariski decompositions, which separate positive and effective parts on birational models, became an important route to this limit problem.

Lazić–Peternell formulated generalized abundance as numerical semiampleness. Their On Generalised Abundance, I, cited in M1 and M2, proves the surface case and a threefold case where the ordinary adjoint has positive numerical dimension. Their broader reductions identify an additional obstacle on varieties with numerically trivial canonical class. Subsequent work studies numerical nonvanishing and restricted nef-reduction dimensions.

For generalized minimal models, Birkar, Han–Li, Lazić–Tsakanikas, and Tsakanikas–Xie developed the decomposition and transfer machinery described in M3 §1. M3 credits these earlier transfer theorems and aims to supply their missing smooth input. It does not claim to originate the generalized-pair framework.

At numerical dimension zero, Nakayama’s methods and results of Druel and Gongyo established important existence and termination statements. M4 addresses the next numerical dimension using a separate surface argument. In the analytic setting, the compact Kähler threefold work of Höring–Peternell and the subsequent abundance results provide precedents, while the present all-dimensional numerical statement uses substantial companion inputs from family 034.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: a semiample representative of a Kähler class

Let XXX be a smooth connected compact Kähler manifold. Let B≥0B\geq0B≥0 be a rational simple-normal-crossing boundary with coefficients strictly less than one, and let MMM be a nef rational holomorphic line bundle on XXX. Assume

KX+B is pseudoeffective,D=KX+B+M is nef.K_X+B\text{ is pseudoeffective},\qquad D=K_X+B+M\text{ is nef}.KX​+B is pseudoeffective,D=KX​+B+M is nef.

M1 claims a semiample rational line bundle LLL on the same manifold with

c1(L)=c1(D)in HBC1,1(X,R).c_1(L)=c_1(D)\quad\text{in }H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R).c1​(L)=c1​(D)in HBC1,1​(X,R).

The conclusion allows changing the flat part. It does not state that DDD itself is semiample. Nor does it allow replacing the nef line on XXX by arbitrary higher-model nef data in the starting hypothesis.

M1 uses the projective positive-part theorem of M2 and the ordinary Kähler decomposition and model constructions of family 034, together with the stated logarithmic Iitaka input from family 033. These are explicit inputs to its argument.

M2: projective generalized abundance

For a projective klt rational pair over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, M2 assumes pseudoeffective KX+BK_X+BKX​+B, a nef Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier divisor MMM on XXX, and nef D=KX+B+MD=K_X+B+MD=KX​+B+M. It claims a semiample Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier divisor LLL with D≡LD\equiv LD≡L.

In particular, if KX+B≡0K_X+B\equiv0KX​+B≡0, every nef rational Cartier divisor is numerically semiample. This still permits the elliptic-curve phenomenon above. The proof uses the companion ordinary log-abundance theorem and specified terminating programs. Ordinary abundance is an input, not a new consequence established independently by setting M=0M=0M=0.

M3: existence with fixed generalized nef data

M3 treats projective generalized lc rational pairs in characteristic zero. If D=KX+B+MD=K_X+B+MD=KX​+B+M is pseudoeffective, it claims a minimal model. If it is not pseudoeffective, it claims a Mori fiber space. The fixed nef b-divisor is retained, and discrepancies improve in the specified sense.

Neither the original variety nor the endpoint is assumed Q\mathbb QQ-factorial in the statement. The conclusion supplies a terminating choice of program. It does not assert termination of every arbitrary program, semiampleness of the endpoint generalized adjoint, or a nonzero pluricanonical section.

M4: a separate numerical-dimension-one construction

For a smooth connected complex projective variety of dimension at least three, M4 assumes pseudoeffective KXK_XKX​ and κσ(X,KX)=1\kappa_\sigma(X,K_X)=1κσ​(X,KX​)=1 in the fixed-twist convention above. It claims a finite canonical-negative sequence ending at a projective Q\mathbb QQ-factorial terminal variety YYY with nef KYK_YKY​.

On a common resolution, the canonical pullback from XXX equals the pullback from YYY plus an effective exceptional divisor, with the required strict comparison for contracted divisors. This records that the endpoint is a minimal model, not just some birational variety with a nef class.

M4’s construction does not use a general minimal-model existence theorem. Its further good-model corollary invokes the separate log-abundance theorem from family 034.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims broad progress on two central problems: existence of generalized minimal models and numerical abundance of nef adjoint classes. Together they would provide both birational endpoints and geometric representatives of classes which otherwise offer only intersection data.

The Kähler extension matters because projective constructions cannot be assumed on the original space. The numerical-dimension-one argument is also useful as a distinct route with a carefully specified growth hypothesis.

The score reflects the breadth of the family if its claims are correct. It does not erase the dependence of its abundance statements on the companion theorems.

6. The main idea

Reduce numerical abundance to a core positivity problem

M2 follows generalized-abundance reductions to the case of a nef divisor on a klt Calabi–Yau pair, where the ordinary adjoint is numerically trivial. The central additional claim is that full nef dimension forces bigness. Full nef dimension says every curve through a very general point has positive degree; bigness says the divisor has positive volume. These are different conditions.

Moving-point jet estimates and a Frobenius comparison are used to rule out full nef dimension with zero volume. Once the needed positive-part statement is available on a birational model, the proof descends a semiample numerical representative to the original variety.

M1 extends this strategy to compact Kähler manifolds. Algebraic reduction maps a modification to a projective base carrying its meromorphic functions. The challenge is to descend the nef contribution and control flat twists, which may vary from fiber to fiber. The paper uses families of cycles and countably many global choices to organize that descent, then applies the projective theorem. A separate argument handles algebraic dimension zero.

Control indices in an attempted infinite program

M3’s local input concerns singularities with cyclic symmetry. It selects divisorial valuations, measurements of orders of vanishing, whose discrepancies stay bounded while their values detect the symmetry characters. The manuscript connects this to the canonical indices appearing along a hypothetical infinite smooth program.

Its global contradiction first bounds those indices, then uses generation and vanishing results to force an adjoint divisor to be both globally generated and negative on a contracted curve.
