A generated line has nonnegative degree there, so the two properties conflict. The established relative and generalized transfer results then produce the stated endpoints.

Use two different surfaces

M4 starts with shrinking positive boundary perturbations. After a finite prefix, their adjoints are generated outside subsets of codimension at least three. A very general surface avoids those subsets; if the limiting canonical square there were positive, extension of sections would force quadratic growth with a fixed ample twist, contradicting κσ=1\kappa_\sigma=1κσ​=1.

That surface might miss a hypothetical negative curve. A second surface is chosen through a point of such a curve. Vanishing-order estimates would force a fixed exceptional contribution with uniformly negative square, making the perturbations have positive square bounded away from zero. This contradicts the zero-square limit. The two surfaces have different jobs, and together they establish nefness of the finite endpoint.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The numerical conclusions do not recover the flat part of the original bundle. The elliptic-curve example shows that this limitation is unavoidable without additional hypotheses. M1’s equality is in real Bott–Chern cohomology; M2’s is projective numerical equivalence.

Both numerical-abundance statements require pseudoeffectivity of the ordinary adjoint KX+BK_X+BKX​+B, not merely of the total sum. Their nef contribution lives on the original space. M3 permits higher-model nef data, but its weaker conclusion is existence of an endpoint, without generalized semiampleness.

M4 uses a precise fixed-ample-twist numerical invariant before a nef model exists. Replacing it by an intersection formula for a non-nef canonical divisor would change the hypothesis. The theorems are characteristic-zero statements, despite positive-characteristic techniques inside some arguments.

Uniform effective degrees, recovery of the original flat factor, and stronger termination assertions are additional questions. The current claims and their dependencies are reported without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 explains the flat ambiguity and its Kähler inputs. M2 §§1–2 state projective numerical abundance and the reduction to full-nef-dimension positivity. M3 §§1 and 3 distinguish existence from arbitrary termination. M4 §1 defines its numerical invariant and outlines the two-surface argument.

For the foundational birational framework, see the linked Kollár–Mori and BCHM sources. Lazić–Peternell’s On Generalised Abundance, I is listed in M1 and M2 with precise theorem references. An optional introduction to numerical equivalence can help separate class-level and line-bundle statements.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Numerical semiampleness of nef adjoint classes on compact Kähler manifolds (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Numerical Semiampleness of Nef Adjoint Divisors (October 3, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Minimal models and Mori fibre spaces for generalized log canonical Q-pairs (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Minimal models in numerical dimension one (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fujita freeness: how much positivity removes every base point?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 038 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A collection of polynomial-like functions can describe a geometric space only where they do not all vanish. If every available section vanishes at the same point, the associated map has a hole there. How much positive twisting guarantees that these base points disappear?

Fujita’s freeness conjecture predicts a remarkably simple answer. On a smooth complex projective variety of dimension nnn, adding n+1n+1n+1 copies of any ample line bundle to the canonical bundle should make it globally generated. The threshold depends only on dimension, not on the variety’s equations, degree, or topology.

Family 038 consists of one manuscript, M1, claiming this sharp bound in every dimension. Its subject is freeness: sections should define a morphism everywhere. The stronger requirement that the morphism embed the variety belongs to the separate very-ampleness part of Fujita’s conjecture.

2. Background and essential definitions

Line bundles and maps defined by sections

A line bundle LLL has a one-dimensional vector space LxL_xLx​ over each point xxx, with compatible local coordinates. A global section is a choice of vector in each fiber which varies algebraically. The finite-dimensional vector space of all global sections is written H0(X,L)H^0(X,L)H0(X,L).

Suppose s0,…,sNs_0,\ldots,s_Ns0​,…,sN​ form a basis. At a point where they do not all vanish, their values define projective coordinates

x⟼[s0(x):⋯:sN(x)].x\longmapsto[s_0(x):\cdots:s_N(x)].x⟼[s0​(x):⋯:sN​(x)].

Changing the local trivialization multiplies all these coordinates by the same nonzero scalar, so the projective point is well-defined. A base point is a point where every section vanishes. The line bundle is globally generated, or base-point-free, when there are no base points.

Equivalently, the evaluation map

H0(X,L)⟶LxH^0(X,L)\longrightarrow L_xH0(X,L)⟶Lx​

is onto for every xxx. Since the target is one-dimensional, this just asks for at least one section nonzero at each prescribed point. The section can depend on the point. It does not ask for one section which is nonzero everywhere.

Ample and very ample

A line bundle is very ample if its sections define an embedding into projective space. It is ample if some positive tensor power is very ample. An ample line bundle itself need not be globally generated, and it may have no nonzero sections at all.

Global generation is weaker than very ampleness. Sections may define a constant map or identify distinct points. Very ampleness requires enough sections to distinguish points and infinitesimal tangent directions. Confusing these properties would turn the claimed theorem into a stronger assertion.

The canonical bundle KXK_XKX​ consists of top-degree holomorphic differential forms. In local coordinates on an nnn-fold, a form looks like f dz1∧⋯∧dznf\,dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_nfdz1​∧⋯∧dzn​. An adjoint bundle combines canonical geometry with a positive twist.

M1 uses additive notation:

KX+mL:=KX⊗L⊗m.K_X+mL:=K_X\otimes L^{\otimes m}.KX​+mL:=KX​⊗L⊗m.

The plus sign is tensor product, not an addition of spaces of sections. In particular, global generation of one adjoint does not automatically imply global generation after tensoring with an ample bundle which is not itself generated.

Orders of vanishing and singularity centers

A section’s order at a smooth point records the first nonzero term of its local Taylor expansion. More general weighted orders, called valuations, measure vanishing along selected directions or exceptional divisors after blowing up the variety.

A blowup replaces a subvariety by its normal directions. If EEE is an exceptional divisor on a smooth birational model π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X, its log discrepancy is

AX(E)=1+ord⁡E(KY−π∗KX).A_X(E)=1+\operatorname{ord}_E(K_Y-\pi^*K_X).AX​(E)=1+ordE​(KY​−π∗KX​).

It measures the canonical cost of using that divisor to detect vanishing. The center of this order is the subvariety downstairs where it is concentrated.

A log canonical center arises when a weighted effective divisor reaches the limiting singularity strength allowed by discrepancy. In freeness arguments, one tries to create a controlled center at a prescribed point and use a vanishing theorem to extend a nonzero value there to a global section.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Fujita formulated the dimension-dependent adjoint prediction in the development of polarized varieties. A polarized variety is a variety together with a chosen ample line bundle. The conjecture asks for a universal rule applying to every such polarization, rather than a bound tailored to a particular embedding.

For curves, the sharp freeness statement follows from Riemann–Roch. For surfaces, it follows from Reider’s theorem. Ein–Lazarsfeld treated threefolds, Kawamata handled dimension four, and Ye–Zhu treated dimension five. M1’s introduction lists the precise earlier statements and references.

In arbitrary dimension, Angehrn–Siu established a quadratic sufficient bound,

m≥n2+n+22.m\geq\frac{n^2+n+2}{2}.m≥2n2+n+2​.

Subsequent improvements reduced its growth: Helmke developed multiplicity estimates for singular centers, Heier obtained a bound of order n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3, and Ghidelli–Lacini reached order nlog⁡log⁡nn\log\log nnloglogn.

The recent preprint of Jingjun Han gives the linear bound m≥⌈C0n⌉m\geq\lceil C_0n\rceilm≥⌈C0​n⌉, with C0C_0C0​ approximately 1.77631.77631.7763. This is a substantial improvement in the same direction, but it is still larger than n+1n+1n+1 in high dimension. The distinction between a linear bound and the sharp linear coefficient is the remaining issue addressed by M1.

M1 also acknowledges Chan’s withdrawn 2024 preprint. The withdrawal notice identifies a local extension step that did not preserve the required vanishing order. That earlier announced solution is therefore not treated here as an established theorem.

Across these approaches, the recurring difficulty is controlling a positive-dimensional singular center while retaining enough positivity to cut it down. A center can be highly singular or have large degree; a universal bound cannot quietly depend on either quantity.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that for every smooth connected projective complex variety XXX of dimension n≥1n\geq1n≥1 and every ample line bundle LLL, the bundle

KX+(n+1)LK_X+(n+1)LKX​+(n+1)L

is generated by global sections. Corollary 6.3 extends this to every integer m≥n+1m\geq n+1m≥n+1.

There is no assumption that LLL itself is generated or effective. Connectedness serves only to simplify notation; the same assertion can be applied separately to connected components. In dimension zero, every line bundle is globally generated.

Why the threshold cannot be lowered

On projective space, let X=PnX=\mathbb P^nX=Pn and L=OPn(1)L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(1)L=OPn​(1). Its canonical bundle is OPn(−n−1)\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(-n-1)OPn​(−n−1), so

KX+(n+1)L≃OX,KX+nL≃OPn(−1).K_X+(n+1)L\simeq\mathcal O_X,\qquad K_X+nL\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(-1).KX​+(n+1)L≃OX​,KX​+nL≃OPn​(−1).

The first has a constant nonzero section and is generated. The second has no nonzero global sections. Thus no theorem with nnn replacing n+1n+1n+1 can hold uniformly for all smooth polarized varieties.

This example also emphasizes the difference from very ampleness. The generated trivial bundle defines a constant map, not an embedding of positive-dimensional projective space.

Why all larger exponents follow

Because LLL need not be generated, simply tensoring by extra copies does not justify the corollary. M1 instead applies the sharp statement to a product with projective space. For r=m−n−1≥0r=m-n-1\geq0r=m−n−1≥0, use

X×Pr,L⊠OPr(1),X\times\mathbb P^r,\qquad L\boxtimes\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(1),X×Pr,L⊠OPr​(1),

where ⊠\boxtimes⊠ means the tensor product of the two pulled-back bundles. The resulting adjoint is

(KX+mL)⊠OPr(n).(K_X+mL)\boxtimes\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(n).(KX​+mL)⊠OPr​(n).

Restricting a generated bundle to X×{z}X\times\{z\}X×{z} gives generation of KX+mLK_X+mLKX​+mL. The product argument retains the arbitrary-ample hypothesis.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Fujita freeness is a central effective-positivity conjecture with a sharp and easily stated threshold. Its claimed resolution would replace bounds depending on more geometry, or larger functions of dimension, by the optimal universal number of ample twists.

The practical mathematical gain is control of an actual map. Ampleness already promises that sufficiently large powers eventually behave well. The conjecture says exactly how the canonical correction makes that behavior uniform across all smooth projective complex varieties.

The sharpness example shows that the constant is structural, rather than an artifact of a particular proof. The score concerns the significance of the stated theorem if correct and does not include the still stronger very-ampleness conclusion.

6. The main idea

Convert a base point into excessive vanishing

Fix a point xxx and suppose that every section of KX+(n+1)LK_X+(n+1)LKX​+(n+1)L vanishes there. The manuscript first translates this failure into a strict asymptotic statement about sections of high powers qLqLqL: bases adapted to ordinary vanishing at xxx have normalized mean order exceeding n/(n+1)n/(n+1)n/(n+1).

This moves the problem to a large finite-dimensional space where sections can be counted. The goal is to show that the resulting excess cannot coexist with the geometric constraints on their vanishing orders.

Minimize a quantity that tracks discrepancy and section orders

The paper considers bases (si)(s_i)(si​) of H0(X,qL)H^0(X,qL)H0(X,qL) and weighted monomial orders vvv whose closed centers contain xxx. For a parameter t<n+1t<n+1t<n+1, the quantity is

1h0(X,qL)∑iexp⁡(AX(v)t−v(si)q).\frac{1}{h^0(X,qL)}\sum_i\exp\left(\frac{A_X(v)}{t}-\frac{v(s_i)}{q}\right).h0(X,qL)1​i∑​exp(tAX​(v)​−qv(si​)​).

The discrepancy term charges for the singularity detector; the section-order term rewards simultaneous vanishing. Varying the scale and tangential directions gives different inequalities from the same objective.

An infimum alone would be insufficient: the argument needs an attained minimizer. M1 encodes simultaneous order conditions on a parameter space of section flags and uses threshold semicontinuity and a fixed resolution to obtain one. It does not assume that all possible bases or all possible birational models form a compact space.

Rule out a positive-dimensional center

Suppose a minimizing order were centered on a positive-dimensional subvariety through xxx. Tangential variation gives an upper bound on a weighted moment of leading Taylor exponents. A restriction-space estimate and the Brunn–Minkowski inequality give a conflicting lower bound.

Brunn–Minkowski is a convex-geometric principle controlling how volume grows under addition of sets. Here the sets organize possible leading exponents of sections. The manuscript’s required uniformity is over all centers of a fixed dimension, including centers with unbounded degree or singularity complexity.

Eliminating those centers leaves an order concentrated at the prescribed point. This is the geometric reduction needed for the final extension step.

Extend one nonzero value

A rational perturbation isolates a reduced divisor above xxx where the discrepancy equality occurs. Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing then yields surjectivity of a restriction map on the resolved space. A nonzero value in the one-dimensional fiber over xxx can be lifted and descended to a global section nonzero at xxx.

This contradicts the assumed base point. The manuscript controls the needed singularities near the equality locus; it does not assume a globally log canonical boundary at that stage. Since the starting point was arbitrary, removing every possible base point proves the claimed generation statement.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns smooth projective varieties over C\mathbb CC and ample line bundles. It is not stated for arbitrary singular varieties, positive characteristic, or arbitrary nef bundles. Ampleness supplies quantitative section growth used throughout the argument.

Global generation does not imply an embedding. Fujita’s very-ampleness prediction concerns separation of points and tangent directions at the next threshold, and is not claimed here. Stronger formulations using prescribed intersection numbers rather than one ample line also require their own statements.

The bound is uniform and sharp, but the manuscript is not an algorithm for computing a basis of sections from arbitrary defining equations. The claimed existence of a nonzero section at each point is a geometric result, not a stated computational complexity bound.

The historical withdrawal and earlier quantitative theorems are reported with attribution. The present exposition takes M1’s claim as stated and does not independently verify its proof.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 states the theorem and reviews the preceding bounds. Section 3 turns a base point into an order inequality, §4 establishes attainment, §5 excludes positive-dimensional centers, and §6 constructs the final section. Corollary 6.3 contains the product argument for all larger exponents.

The linked Reider, Ein–Lazarsfeld, Angehrn–Siu, Ghidelli–Lacini, and Han papers describe important stages of the development. For optional background, see ample line bundles and linear systems of divisors.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Fujita’s freeness conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The ordinary double point as the largest singular volume
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 037 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A smooth point and a singular point can belong to the same algebraic variety, yet their small neighborhoods have very different geometry. Can one number distinguish the smooth case and then identify the least severe singularity?

Normalized volume is designed to measure a singularity through all possible ways of assigning orders of vanishing to local functions. In dimension nnn, its largest value is nnn^nnn, attained exactly at smooth points. The ordinary-double-point gap conjecture predicts the next maximum among singular points.

Family 037 contains two manuscripts. M2 claims the sharp four-dimensional case, and M1 uses it as a base case for the theorem in every dimension at least two. The proposed maximizer is an ordinary double point: a nondegenerate quadratic cone. The statement ranges over all boundary-free complex algebraic klt germs, not just singularities already known to be hypersurfaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

Local geometry and the simplest cone

A germ (X,x)(X,x)(X,x) means the geometry of XXX near a chosen point xxx, ignoring what happens far away. Smoothness means the germ has local coordinates like an open subset of Cn\mathbb C^nCn. A singular point fails this condition.

An ordinary double point in complex dimension nnn has analytic local equation

z02+z12+⋯+zn2=0inside Cn+1.z_0^2+z_1^2+\cdots+z_n^2=0\quad\text{inside }\mathbb C^{n+1}.z02​+z12​+⋯+zn2​=0inside Cn+1.

The quadratic form is nondegenerate: its matrix has full rank. There are n+1n+1n+1 ambient coordinates and one equation, so the hypersurface has dimension nnn. Analytic equivalence allows a local holomorphic change of coordinates, which is stronger information than merely sharing a numerical invariant.

The embedding dimension is the number of independent first-order local coordinates required. Algebraically, if mx\mathfrak m_xmx​ is the ideal of functions vanishing at xxx, it is

edim⁡(X,x)=dim⁡Cmx/mx2.\operatorname{edim}(X,x)=\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2.edim(X,x)=dimC​mx​/mx2​.

At a smooth nnn-dimensional point it is nnn; at an ordinary double point it is n+1n+1n+1.

Valuations and volumes

A real valuation vvv assigns an order of vanishing to local functions, with

v(fg)=v(f)+v(g),v(f+g)≥min⁡{v(f),v(g)}.v(fg)=v(f)+v(g),\qquad v(f+g)\geq\min\{v(f),v(g)\}.v(fg)=v(f)+v(g),v(f+g)≥min{v(f),v(g)}.

It is centered at xxx when it is nonnegative on the local ring and positive on its maximal ideal. Ordinary vanishing order at a smooth point is a basic example; other valuations inspect weighted directions or exceptional divisors on birational models.

For t>0t>0t>0, the valuation ideal

at(v)={f∈OX,x:v(f)≥t}\mathfrak a_t(v)=\{f\in\mathcal O_{X,x}:v(f)\geq t\}at​(v)={f∈OX,x​:v(f)≥t}

contains functions vanishing to at least that order. The quotient by this ideal records the finite amount of local function data below the threshold. Its length is its dimension as a complex vector space. The asymptotic growth defines

vol⁡(v)=lim⁡t→∞n! length⁡(OX,x/at(v))tn.\operatorname{vol}(v)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{n!\,\operatorname{length}(\mathcal O_{X,x}/\mathfrak a_t(v))}{t^n}.vol(v)=t→∞lim​tnn!length(OX,x​/at​(v))​.

This is not the Euclidean volume of a ball. It is a normalized count of local algebraic data.

Discrepancy supplies the normalization

The log discrepancy AX(v)A_X(v)AX​(v) measures how a canonical form changes under the birational viewpoint encoded by vvv. For a prime divisor EEE on a resolution π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X,

AX(ord⁡E)=1+ord⁡E(KY−π∗KX).A_X(\operatorname{ord}_E)=1+\operatorname{ord}_E(K_Y-\pi^*K_X).AX​(ordE​)=1+ordE​(KY​−π∗KX​).

The canonical divisor must be Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier so this pullback makes sense. The klt condition means these discrepancies are positive for the relevant divisors. It restricts the severity of the singularity. The papers use zero boundary, so no extra weighted hypersurfaces are included in this calculation.

Normalized volume is

vol⁡^(x,X)=inf⁡v centered at xAX(v)nvol⁡(v).\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(x,X)=\inf_{v\text{ centered at }x}A_X(v)^n\operatorname{vol}(v).vol(x,X)=v centered at xinf​AX​(v)nvol(v).

Multiplying vvv by a positive constant multiplies discrepancy by that constant and divides volume by its nnn-th power. Their product is unchanged. Taking the infimum therefore compares genuinely different ways of viewing the germ, rather than arbitrary choices of units for an order of vanishing.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Chi Li introduced normalized volume to connect singularity theory with K-stability and canonical metrics. The motivating metric picture concerns limits of Kähler–Einstein spaces, where tangent cones encode small-scale geometry. Spotti–Sun formulated the ordinary-double-point gap in that setting and its algebraic version for arbitrary klt germs.

Low dimensions supplied evidence and complete cases. Surface quotient calculations give normalized volume 4/∣G∣4/|G|4/∣G∣ for the relevant quotient by a finite group GGG. Liu–Xu’s threefold work established the unrestricted three-dimensional gap and equality characterization. Liu later treated local complete intersections in all dimensions. These results already settle the conjecture when a sufficiently restrictive local equation is known.

Toric singularities, built from combinatorial cone data, admit a different sharp bound involving (16/27)nn(16/27)n^n(16/27)nn. Smooth polarized Fano cones also have earlier results. Neither setting covers every isolated klt singularity, so one cannot begin the general argument by assuming a convenient cone presentation or smooth quotient base.

A second line of work made the infimum itself accessible. Blum proved existence of minimizing valuations; Xu proved their quasi-monomial structure; Xu–Zhuang established uniqueness up to scaling and finite generation. The resulting stable-degeneration theory replaces a germ by an algebraic cone while retaining its normalized volume. M1 and M2 cite these primary results in their introductions and explain which versions they use.

The remaining issue is structural: a volume-preserving degeneration is not automatically a hypersurface. M2 aims to force small embedding dimension from a sufficiently large normalized volume. M1 then develops the higher-dimensional estimate and returns the equality information to the original germ.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The sharp local gap

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that every singular closed point of a normal complex algebraic nnn-fold, for n≥2n\geq2n≥2, with Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier canonical divisor and klt singularities near the point, satisfies

vol⁡^(x,X)≤2(n−1)n.\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(x,X)\leq2(n-1)^n.vol(x,X)≤2(n−1)n.

Equality holds precisely when the analytic germ is the nondegenerate quadratic hypersurface displayed above. The point need not be isolated in the original singular locus, and no complete-intersection, quotient, or smoothability assumption is imposed.

The comparison with smooth points is easy to display:

Complex dimensionSmooth maximumClaimed singular maximum
242
32716
4256162

These are normalized-volume values under the log-discrepancy convention used in the manuscripts.

M2’s four-dimensional structural statement

M2 proves the stated fourfold bound 162=2⋅34162=2\cdot3^4162=2⋅34, with the same equality case and unrestricted boundary-free scope. Its central reduction claims

vol⁡^(x,X)≥162⟹edim⁡(X,x)≤5.\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(x,X)\geq162\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{edim}(X,x)\leq5.vol(x,X)≥162⟹edim(X,x)≤5.

For a singular normal fourfold, that forces a hypersurface presentation. The established complete-intersection theorem then supplies the bound and rigidity. Thus the new structural claim is what permits an earlier theorem to finish the argument.

M1 uses M2 as its sole companion input, alongside the cited established results. Its higher-dimensional proof is not independent of the fourfold paper.

A global consequence

A Q\mathbb QQ-Fano variety is normal, projective, and klt, with ample anticanonical divisor −KV-K_V−KV​. K-semistability is a condition controlling how its geometry behaves under algebraic degenerations; it is central to the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics. The relevant global size is the top intersection number (−KV)n(-K_V)^n(−KV​)n.

Combining the local gap with the established local-to-global inequality, M1 obtains, for singular K-semistable Q\mathbb QQ-Fano varieties,

(−KV)n≤2(n2−1n)n<2nn.(-K_V)^n\leq2\left(\frac{n^2-1}{n}\right)^n<2n^n.(−KV​)n≤2(nn2−1​)n<2nn.

The paper does not claim that this smaller singular bound is sharp. Together with Li–Miao’s smooth theorem, it states that a K-semistable Q\mathbb QQ-Fano variety other than projective space has anticanonical volume at most 2nn2n^n2nn, with equality exactly for a smooth quadric or P1×Pn−1\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^{n-1}P1×Pn−1. The smooth equality classification is credited to that prior theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. A sharp local invariant would single out the ordinary double point among every singularity in a broad class, without assuming a local equation. This connects asymptotic algebra, birational geometry, and metric degeneration theory.

The equality statement is as important as the inequality. A bound says how large the invariant can be; rigidity identifies the entire analytic germ when that bound is reached. The global consequence shows that a sufficiently mild-looking singularity still imposes a strict cost on the size of a K-semistable Fano variety.

The score reflects a major structural advance with several connections, while recognizing that the theorem concerns one singularity invariant under specific klt and boundary assumptions.

6. The main idea

Preserve the minimum while simplifying the germ

Both manuscripts use stable degeneration to pass to a cone with a positive grading. A grading assigns weights to functions, analogous to assigning different degrees to variables. Its minimizing real direction is a Reeb vector. The cone reduction preserves the infimum over all centered valuations, not merely the best value among a restricted family of gradings.

A large-volume hypothesis and earlier bounds constrain the cone: the difficult high-volume case becomes isolated and Gorenstein, meaning its canonical sheaf is locally a line bundle. These are conclusions of the reduction, not assumptions added to the original theorem.

Four dimensions: turn volume into few coordinates

M2 examines finite stabilizers of the grading action and counts transverse jets, finite Taylor data on slices. A stabilizer that is too large would furnish a valuation with smaller normalized volume than the minimizing one. Excluding it gives both discrepancy bounds and restrictions on the Hilbert series, the generating function that counts homogeneous functions by weight.

A Fourier-based estimate then supplies low-weight functions. Applying related estimates to suitable lower-dimensional centers controls a singularity threshold. A general hyperplane section becomes a terminal Gorenstein threefold, whose known hypersurface structure bounds the embedding dimension of the original fourfold.

This explains the logical route: high normalized volume constrains weights and thresholds; those constraints force a short local equation; the established hypersurface gap finishes the argument.

Higher dimensions: close an estimate involving a supremum

M1 separates gradings with small stabilizers from those with large stabilizers. In the first case, rational curves and tensor-weight bounds force a projective-space or quadric quotient. In the second, leading Taylor exponents form a semigroup, a set closed under addition. Positivity and adjoint lifting give enough exact control of this set to construct a comparison singularity.

The comparison has the same dimension, so ordinary induction alone would not suffice. Instead, put

pn=2(n−1n)n,Mn=sup⁡vol⁡^(x,X)nn,p_n=2\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^n,\qquad M_n=\sup\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(x,X)}{n^n},pn​=2(nn−1​)n,Mn​=supnnvol(x,X)​,

where the supremum ranges over singular boundary-free klt nnn-fold germs. The manuscript derives a comparison bounded by (pn+Mn)/2(p_n+M_n)/2(pn​+Mn​)/2. Applying it to values approaching the supremum forces Mn≤pnM_n\leq p_nMn​≤pn​; attainment of the supremum is not assumed.

For equality, stricter counting returns the cone to the small-stabilizer case. Further local information forces a nondegenerate quadratic part in the original germ, completing the claimed analytic characterization.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is for complex algebraic klt germs with zero boundary. It does not give the same formula for arbitrary singularities, positive characteristic, or pairs with nonzero boundary. Dimension one is excluded because a normal complex algebraic curve is smooth.

Normalized volume is an infimum over all centered valuations. Computing one convenient valuation only gives an upper bound and cannot by itself establish equality. The manuscripts explicitly use the minimizing and degeneration theory to address this distinction.

The singular global bound is not presented with a sharpness claim or an equality classification. More refined gaps below the ordinary-double-point value, boundary versions, and effective ways to compute the invariant remain further directions.

The conclusions above report the two manuscripts and their stated dependencies. No proof or novelty verification is part of this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 states the all-dimensional local and global claims and maps the prior cases; §7 explains the supremum argument and §8 treats equality. M2 §§1–2 state the fourfold theorem and structural reduction; §§3–6 develop the stabilizer, Hilbert-series, and hyperplane-section steps.

For the global connection, see Liu’s local-to-global volume work. The linked Spotti–Sun and Liu–Xu papers give primary context for the conjecture and its three-dimensional predecessor. An optional introduction to valuations supplies further examples of orders of vanishing.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The ordinary-double-point gap in every dimension (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The normalized-volume gap in dimension four (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 040 — Bloch’s conjecture: when points on a surface have no hidden differences
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 040 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Take two points on a smooth complex algebraic surface. Topologically, they represent the same class: a point is a point. Algebraic geometry asks a finer question. Can one transform one into the other using the zeros and poles of rational functions on curves lying in the surface?

On the projective plane the answer is yes. Join the points by a line, identify that line with the projective line, and choose a rational function with a zero at one point and a pole at the other. On more complicated surfaces, such transformations can leave a large collection of differences that topology cannot see.

Bloch’s conjecture predicts when these hidden differences disappear, or are completely measured by an associated complex torus. Family 040 contains one manuscript claiming the conjecture for every smooth projective complex surface with no holomorphic two-forms. Its central new case has no holomorphic one-forms either. In that case, it claims that the only invariant of a finite integral combination of points is its total coefficient.

The strength lies in the word algebraic: an equality of topological classes would be automatic and would not answer the question.

2. Background and essential definitions

Points, functions, and the Chow group

A zero-cycle on a surface SSS is a finite formal sum

z=∑ini[pi],ni∈Z.z=\sum_i n_i[p_i],\qquad n_i\in\mathbb Z.z=i∑​ni​[pi​],ni​∈Z.

Its degree is deg⁡z=∑ini\deg z=\sum_i n_idegz=∑i​ni​. If a rational function on a curve has zeros at some points and poles at others, with their multiplicities, its divisor defines a degree-zero cycle. Rational equivalence allows us to add or subtract such divisors, including their images from curves mapping into the surface.

The resulting group is the Chow group CH⁡0(S)\operatorname{CH}_0(S)CH0​(S). Its subgroup of degree-zero classes is CH⁡0(S)0\operatorname{CH}_0(S)^0CH0​(S)0. Thus [p]−[q]=0[p]-[q]=0[p]−[q]=0 in this group means an actual finite chain of algebraic relations exists, although the relation need not come from a single curve through the two points.

Saying CH⁡0(S)=Z\operatorname{CH}_0(S)=\mathbb ZCH0​(S)=Z via the degree map means precisely that every degree-zero class vanishes. It does not mean the surface is the projective plane, or even that the surface can be parametrized by rational functions.

Two numerical measurements of differential forms

The geometric genus and irregularity are

pg(S)=dim⁡CH0(S,ωS),q(S)=dim⁡CH1(S,OS).p_g(S)=\dim_{\mathbb C}H^0(S,\omega_S),\qquadq(S)=\dim_{\mathbb C}H^1(S,\mathcal O_S).pg​(S)=dimC​H0(S,ωS​),q(S)=dimC​H1(S,OS​).

Here ωS\omega_SωS​ is the line bundle of holomorphic two-forms; OS\mathcal O_SOS​ is the sheaf of holomorphic functions. For a smooth projective complex surface, qqq also counts independent holomorphic one-forms. These are different invariants: assuming pg=0p_g=0pg​=0 does not automatically mean q=0q=0q=0.

The Albanese variety Alb⁡(S)\operatorname{Alb}(S)Alb(S) is a complex torus, in fact an abelian variety, of dimension qqq. Integrating one-forms along paths produces the Albanese map on degree-zero cycles,

alb⁡S:CH⁡0(S)0⟶Alb⁡(S)(C).\operatorname{alb}_S:\operatorname{CH}_0(S)^0\longrightarrow \operatorname{Alb}(S)(\mathbb C).albS​:CH0​(S)0⟶Alb(S)(C).

Bloch’s prediction is that when pg=0p_g=0pg​=0, this map has no kernel. It is already surjective. When also q=0q=0q=0, its target is zero, so the prediction reduces to CH⁡0(S)0=0\operatorname{CH}_0(S)^0=0CH0​(S)0=0.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mumford’s work on rational equivalence of zero-cycles showed that a nonzero holomorphic two-form forces the group of zero-cycles to be too large to be described by a finite-dimensional parameter space in the relevant sense. Differential forms therefore impose a real obstruction to simple algebraic relations between points. Bloch’s conjecture asks for a converse after accounting for the Albanese variety.

An early broad theorem of Bloch, Kas, and Lieberman established the prediction for surfaces with pg=0p_g=0pg​=0 that are not of general type. A surface is of general type when its pluricanonical sections grow as fast as the dimension permits. These surfaces form the part of the classification where the canonical bundle carries the richest geometry. They remained the main difficulty.

Many general-type examples were then settled using their special constructions or symmetries. Work of Inose–Mizukami, Barlow, and later authors exploited group actions, coverings, and correspondences between surfaces. Numerical Godeaux, Campedelli, Burniat, and Inoue surfaces supplied important testing grounds, but a collection of named constructions does not exhaust all surfaces with the same numerical invariants.

Voisin’s work on Catanese and Barlow surfaces developed another route through families and correspondences. It showed that one could obtain zero-cycle relations without requiring each individual surface to display an especially simple symmetry. This was a major enlargement of the methods available, while still relying on geometric properties of the families involved.

The present manuscript also discusses overlapping recent proposed solutions, including Guletskii’s 2025 preprint and a 2026 proposal of Banerjee for the general-type case with canonical self-intersection nine. It presents its own argument through moduli spaces of quotient sheaves. The account here follows those attributions; it does not settle priority or the correctness of competing proofs.

The remaining conceptual gap was a uniform mechanism that works without a special presentation of the surface. The manuscript proposes such a mechanism by constructing an algebraic relation for its diagonal.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An integral theorem for every regular surface in scope

Theorem 1.1 of M1 states: if SSS is a smooth connected projective surface over C\mathbb CC, and

pg(S)=q(S)=0,p_g(S)=q(S)=0,pg​(S)=q(S)=0,

then the degree homomorphism is an isomorphism

deg⁡:CH⁡0(S)→ ∼ Z.\deg:\operatorname{CH}_0(S)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Z.deg:CH0​(S) ∼ ​Z.

The coefficients here are integers. There is no assumption that SSS is minimal, simply connected, or obtained from a particular covering construction. Every pair of complex points would have equal classes, and every degree-zero integral cycle would vanish.

Corollary 1.2 combines this with the earlier non-general-type theory to give the full stated surface formulation: whenever pg(S)=0p_g(S)=0pg​(S)=0, the Albanese map is an isomorphism. The possibility q>0q>0q>0 is retained in this formulation; one must not replace its conclusion by CH⁡0(S)=Z\operatorname{CH}_0(S)=\mathbb ZCH0​(S)=Z.

Consequences for cycles on larger spaces

For pg=q=0p_g=q=0pg​=q=0, M1 also states that all rational algebraic cycles on products of SSS, and on its Hilbert schemes of points, are determined by their cohomology classes. A Hilbert scheme S[n]S^{[n]}S[n] parametrizes length-nnn finite subschemes, including configurations where points merge with infinitesimal structure.

More precisely, for Y=SmY=S^mY=Sm or S[n]S^{[n]}S[n], the cycle-class maps are isomorphisms

CH⁡i(Y)⊗Q→ ∼ H2i(Y,Q),H2i+1(Y,Q)=0.\operatorname{CH}^i(Y)\otimes\mathbb Q\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{2i}(Y,\mathbb Q),\qquad H^{2i+1}(Y,\mathbb Q)=0.CHi(Y)⊗Q ∼ ​H2i(Y,Q),H2i+1(Y,Q)=0.

The manuscript derives these statements from established results on Chow motives, which package algebraic correspondences into a common structure. It identifies the rational motive of SSS as a sum of elementary pieces. These further consequences have rational coefficients; the integral claim above concerns zero-cycles on SSS itself.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this would settle a central conjecture about the gap between algebraic cycles and their cohomological shadows, across an entire class of surfaces.

Even on a surface with pg=q=0p_g=q=0pg​=q=0, having only algebraic cohomology classes does not immediately determine rational equivalence. Homologically invisible cycles are precisely what makes the subject difficult. The claimed theorem would show that in this setting there is no residual degree-zero information at all.

The generality also matters. Numerical invariants can be shared by surfaces with very different fundamental groups and constructions. A theorem applying uniformly would replace many separate calculations with one principle. Its consequences for all powers and Hilbert schemes would propagate that principle into arbitrarily high dimensions, though only for these particular spaces.

The proposed method is significant independently of the list of examples: it uses enumerative geometry to create a relation in the Chow group itself, retaining information that an ordinary numerical integral would discard.

6. The main idea

Make the identity correspondence vanish on degree-zero cycles

The diagonal ΔS⊂S×S\Delta_S\subset S\times SΔS​⊂S×S consists of pairs (x,x)(x,x)(x,x). Viewed as a correspondence, it acts as the identity on cycles. M1 seeks a relation of the form

0=c[ΔS]+Γin CH⁡2(S×S)⊗Q,c≠0,0=c[\Delta_S]+\Gamma\quad\text{in }\operatorname{CH}^2(S\times S)\otimes\mathbb Q,\qquad c\ne0,0=c[ΔS​]+Γin CH2(S×S)⊗Q,c=0,

where Γ\GammaΓ is a sum of products of cycles from the two separate copies of SSS. Those product terms act trivially on degree-zero zero-cycles. Applying the relation would therefore give cz=0c z=0cz=0 for every such rational cycle zzz, hence its vanishing.

This must be a Chow relation, not merely a cohomology relation. The latter would erase the information one is trying to control.

Keep two marked outputs in a moduli-space calculation

The construction uses a Quot scheme, a parameter space for quotient sheaves of a fixed bundle. Here the starting bundle is a sum of two line bundles, equipped with opposite weights for a one-dimensional torus action. Fixed points of that action split the quotient into simpler pieces involving divisors and finite subschemes.

Such parameter spaces can have singularities and unexpected dimension. A virtual class supplies the intersection-theoretic replacement for a fundamental class, using the specified deformation and obstruction data. Localization expresses its contribution through the torus-fixed pieces.

The crucial design choice is to retain two marked outputs on the surface. Instead of integrating everything to a number, the calculation produces a cycle on S×SS\times SS×S. Recursive formulas for Hilbert schemes then separate contributions where the outputs coincide, giving the diagonal, from contributions that factor through the two independent surfaces.

Show the diagonal really occurs

Obtaining a relation with coefficient c=0c=0c=0 would prove nothing. The manuscript reduces to minimal general-type surfaces and treats two numerical cases for KS2K_S^2KS2​, the self-intersection of the canonical divisor.

For KS2≤8K_S^2\le8KS2​≤8, it uses the intersection lattice and a limited number of point blowups to choose a class of negative square. Pairing the constructed relation with that class expresses the diagonal coefficient through nonnegative squares, with a nonempty positive contribution.

For KS2=9K_S^2=9KS2​=9, that lattice direction is unavailable. M1 instead compares universal coefficients with an auxiliary Cartwright–Steger surface having the same relevant Chern numbers but nonzero holomorphic forms. Its geometry detects the needed coefficient. The two branches are parts of the same strategy, but neither is presented as a substitute for the other.

Finally, the Chow relation initially gives vanishing with rational coefficients. An integral class could still be torsion, meaning some nonzero integer multiple vanishes. Roitman’s torsion theorem, together with q=0q=0q=0, removes that remaining possibility. Birational invariance returns the conclusion from the modified surface to the original one.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns smooth projective surfaces over the complex numbers. It does not assert the analogous statement for arbitrary singular surfaces, nonprojective compact complex surfaces, or varieties over fields of positive characteristic.

The assumption pg=0p_g=0pg​=0 is structural: Mumford’s result explains why positive geometric genus leads to a different picture. When q>0q>0q>0, the Albanese variety remains as genuine information. The conclusion is then that it captures all degree-zero classes, not that those classes vanish.

The integral surface theorem and the rational motivic consequences should also remain separate. The latter do not claim integral cohomology determines every cycle on every product. Nor does the theorem supply an efficient algorithm that, given two points, prints a short collection of curves and rational functions relating them.

These are the manuscript’s stated results and approach. Questions beyond its scope include corresponding principles for higher-dimensional varieties, arithmetic fields, and more explicit descriptions of the relations between individual points.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the integral statement in Theorem 1.1, the Albanese formulation in Corollary 1.2, and the rational motivic consequences in Corollary 1.3. Its introduction explains the earlier surface cases and the distinction between the two coefficient calculations.

The historical papers linked above provide the underlying questions and partial results. For a first encounter, the definitions of a Chow group and an Albanese variety are useful companions. The essential point to retain is that rational equivalence carries much more information than equality in cohomology.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bloch’s conjecture for surfaces with p_g=0 (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 041 — Hyperkähler fibrations: turning a boundary class into a map
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 041 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A polynomial equation can define a geometric space; a collection of functions on that space can define a map to a simpler one. In complex geometry, line bundles organize the functions that may be used together. A basic difficulty is that a line bundle can have the right numerical properties for such a map while apparently supplying no functions at all.

For hyperkähler manifolds, a particularly important numerical condition predicts a map whose fibers have exactly half the dimension of the original space. The fibers should be Lagrangian: the ambient symplectic form becomes zero when restricted to them. This is the holomorphic version of a fibration picture closely related to mirror symmetry.

Family 041 contains two complementary claims. M2 says that every nonzero nef isotropic line bundle on a compact irreducible hyperkähler manifold actually produces the expected fibration. M1 says that, for a projective Lagrangian fibration in its stated setting, the base is ordinary complex projective space, even if it was initially allowed to be singular.

The first question is whether the map exists on the given manifold. The second is what its target can be.

2. Background and essential definitions

The geometry carried by a hyperkähler manifold

In these manuscripts, the relevant object is a compact irreducible holomorphic symplectic Kähler manifold XXX. It is simply connected and has a holomorphic two-form σ\sigmaσ that is nondegenerate everywhere; all its holomorphic two-forms are scalar multiples of σ\sigmaσ. Its complex dimension is even, written 2n2n2n.

“Kähler” means the complex structure has a compatible closed positive differential two-form. A hyperkähler metric provides a family of related complex structures on the same underlying real manifold. Changing the complex structure within this family is called hyperkähler rotation. A submanifold that is real and specially positioned in one complex structure can become a complex submanifold in another.

A complex nnn-dimensional submanifold is Lagrangian if the restriction of σ\sigmaσ is zero. A Lagrangian fibration is a surjective holomorphic map with connected fibers whose components have this half-dimensional property. Smooth fibers in the setting here are abelian varieties, hence complex tori with an algebraic polarization.

Positivity on the boundary

A line bundle LLL has a first Chern class c1(L)c_1(L)c1​(L), recording its topological curvature class. It is nef when this class belongs to the closure of the Kähler cone. Thus it is a limit of positive classes, but need not itself be positive in every direction.

Hyperkähler manifolds carry a quadratic form qXq_XqX​ on second cohomology, the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form. It controls top intersections through

∫Xa2n=cXqX(a)n,cX>0.\int_X a^{2n}=c_X q_X(a)^n,\qquad c_X>0.∫X​a2n=cX​qX​(a)n,cX​>0.

A class is isotropic when qX(a)=0q_X(a)=0qX​(a)=0. A nonzero nef isotropic class therefore has vanishing top self-intersection, but still has positive mixed intersections through dimension nnn. This is the numerical pattern expected of a class pulled back from an nnn-dimensional base.

A line bundle is semiample if some positive power is generated by global sections everywhere. Such sections give a holomorphic map with no unresolved points of definition. Nefness and isotropy are numerical conditions; semiampleness is a statement about actual holomorphic sections. Bridging that gap is the main existence problem.

For a K3 surface, where n=1n=1n=1, the model picture is an elliptic fibration over the projective line. The higher-dimensional question asks for an analogous structure with higher-dimensional torus fibers.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The special Lagrangian fibration picture arose in the mirror-symmetry proposal of Strominger, Yau, and Zaslow. Hyperkähler rotation relates that real-geometric picture to holomorphic Lagrangian fibrations. Hassett–Tschinkel and Sawon formulated early versions involving nef isotropic divisors.

Matsushita established the remarkable rigidity of nontrivial fibrations from projective irreducible symplectic manifolds: the base has half the dimension, and the fibers are Lagrangian. This identifies the geometry once a suitable map exists, but does not manufacture sections of an arbitrary nef isotropic bundle.

Two approaches produced substantial partial progress. Analytic positivity results gave sections or semiampleness under extra metric assumptions. Constructions using moduli spaces of sheaves, stability conditions, and monodromy handled the known deformation types, including manifolds related to K3 surfaces, generalized Kummer varieties, and the two O’Grady examples.

A particularly decisive reduction is the Soldatenkov–Verbitsky deformation theorem: for the fixed isotropic class in the appropriate deformation component, finding one semiample deformation suffices to obtain semiampleness at every nef point. This already establishes the strong conjecture for the known deformation classes. The remaining task is to construct the needed deformation without restricting to those classes.

The base question developed alongside the existence question. Hwang proved that a smooth base of a projective irreducible symplectic fibration is projective space. Greb–Lehn extended the smooth-base statement to compact Kähler total spaces. Other work treated known deformation types, four-dimensional total spaces, and particular classes of base singularities. The unresolved issue in the general projective setting was therefore the possible singularity of the base, rather than a shortage of candidates for a smooth base.

These earlier results are essential inputs, not conclusions first supplied by this family. M2 addresses the missing class-preserving construction; M1 addresses singular bases in arbitrary dimension and deformation type.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: the strong hyperkähler SYZ statement

For every compact irreducible holomorphic symplectic Kähler 2n2n2n-fold XXX, M2 claims

c1(L)≠0,L nef,qX(c1(L))=0⟹L semiample.c_1(L)\ne0,\quad L\text{ nef},\quad q_X(c_1(L))=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L\text{ semiample}.c1​(L)=0,L nef,qX​(c1​(L))=0⟹L semiample.

It asserts this for the original line bundle on the original manifold. No birational replacement is required, and no restriction on deformation type or the second Betti number is added.

More explicitly, there are a positive integer mmm, a normal projective variety BBB, an ample line bundle AAA on BBB, and a map

f:X⟶B,L⊗m≃f∗A,dim⁡CB=n.f:X\longrightarrow B,\qquad L^{\otimes m}\simeq f^*A,\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}B=n.f:X⟶B,L⊗m≃f∗A,dimC​B=n.

The map is surjective with connected fibers. Every component of every fiber has dimension nnn, and σ\sigmaσ vanishes on its smooth part. This includes singular fibers; it does not say all fibers are smooth tori.

M1: the base in the projective setting

M1 starts with a projective surjective holomorphic map from such an XXX to a normal projective nnn-fold BBB, with connected Lagrangian fibers as specified above. It claims

B≃PCn.B\simeq\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}.B≃PCn​.

Here projective map means a relatively ample line bundle exists. Together with a projective base, this makes the original total space projective. The theorem should therefore not be silently extended to every nonprojective total space covered by M2.

After identifying the base, existing theorems exclude codimension-one multiple fibers: for a prime divisor D⊂BD\subset BD⊂B, the multiplicities of the components of f∗Df^*Df∗D have greatest common divisor one. Individual components may still occur with multiplicity greater than one.

A finiteness consequence with an extra hypothesis

M2 combines its semiampleness claim with Engel–Filipazzi–Greer–Mauri–Svaldi’s boundedness theorem to claim finitely many smooth deformation types in each complex dimension among manifolds with

b2(X)≥5.b_2(X)\ge5.b2​(X)≥5.

Here b2b_2b2​ is the dimension of second real cohomology. This restriction belongs to the finiteness deduction, not to the semiampleness theorem. The deduction uses a theorem on indefinite rational quadratic forms to produce an isotropic vector when at least five variables are available.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims solutions to two central structural problems in hyperkähler geometry, with no limitation to currently familiar examples.

The existence theorem would turn a computable boundary condition in cohomology into a global geometric decomposition. Instead of merely suggesting a hidden family of tori, the line bundle would define that family everywhere. The base theorem would then say that the projective versions all organize their fibers over the simplest possible compact base of the right dimension.

The finiteness consequence is also substantial: constructing examples is very different from knowing that only finitely many deformation types can occur in a fixed dimension. It remains a finiteness statement with its stated Betti-number condition, not an explicit classification or a list of all types.

6. The main idea

Produce one torus while remembering the desired class

M2 follows the deformation reduction, but must preserve the particular isotropic class supplied at the start. It constructs a degeneration whose monodromy remembers that class as a labelled integral vector. Monodromy is the change in cohomological coordinates obtained by moving once around the degeneration parameter.

Near the degeneration, the manuscript rescales Ricci-flat metrics and uses estimates to obtain a smooth flat cylinder in logarithmic coordinates. The cylinder contains an angular torus. A perturbation produces a special Lagrangian torus, on which the Kähler form vanishes and the holomorphic volume form has constant phase.

The torus’s position in the coordinate system matters: it connects the analytic construction back to the prescribed monodromy class. Producing an unrelated torus somewhere on a deformation would not suffice.

Hyperkähler rotation then makes this torus holomorphic and Lagrangian on a nonprojective deformation. An existing Greb–Lehn–Rollenske theorem supplies a fibration there. The manuscript arranges that the relevant rational isotropic direction is the original one, and the Soldatenkov–Verbitsky theorem carries semiampleness back to (X,L)(X,L)(X,L).

Remove the base singularities in two stages

M1 first excludes singularities that are not finite quotients of smooth local spaces. Its local tensor analysis associates a hypothetical bad locus with an Euler-characteristic obstruction. Deformations that keep the same base supply incompatible global restrictions. The argument treats small second Betti number separately, including a case requiring a second Lagrangian fibration.

It then eliminates the remaining finite-quotient singularities. The second fibration supplies an abelian variety mapping finitely onto the base. Combining this cover with the original fibration produces translation and ramification constraints incompatible with nontrivial local stabilizers. Once the base is smooth, Hwang’s theorem identifies it with projective space.

M1 uses M2’s semiampleness theorem in constructing the second system. M2’s additional projective-base corollary uses M1 only after its own semiampleness argument. Their primary claims and their subsequent consequences therefore have distinct roles in the exposition.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The line bundle in M2 must have a nonzero integral first Chern class, be nef, and be isotropic. An arbitrary real boundary class need not come from a line bundle, so the theorem does not assign a holomorphic map to every such real class.

The conclusion is semiampleness on a compact irreducible holomorphic symplectic Kähler manifold. It is not a general semiampleness theorem for every variety with trivial canonical bundle. Nor is it the full metric SYZ conjecture for all Calabi–Yau manifolds.

The projective-space conclusion here uses M1’s projectivity hypotheses. The finiteness corollary retains b2≥5b_2\ge5b2​≥5, even though the main existence theorem does not. Neither paper supplies an effective universal power mmm, an explicit list of deformation types, or a classification of singular fibers.

These distinctions leave substantial geometric questions after the stated claims: how to describe the resulting fibrations concretely, determine their degenerations, and turn abstract finiteness into an explicit classification.

8. Sources and further reading

M2’s Theorem 1.1 is the semiampleness claim; Corollaries 1.2 and 1.3 separate the finiteness and projective-base consequences. M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the base theorem and spells out projectivity. Their introductions describe the earlier deformation, fibration, and analytic results used in the arguments.

For background, hyperkähler manifolds connect differential geometry to the holomorphic symplectic language used here. The basic distinction throughout is between a numerical cohomology class and the global sections needed to turn it into a map.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Projective-space bases of Lagrangian fibrations (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The strong hyperkähler SYZ conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 042 — Oka K3 surfaces: extending holomorphic maps with freedom
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 042 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Suppose a holomorphic map is defined only near a small closed region in complex Euclidean space. Can it be approximated there, as accurately as desired, by a holomorphic map defined on the whole Euclidean space?

For complex-valued functions on a convex set, polynomial approximation offers a familiar model. If the values must lie on a curved complex surface, however, one cannot simply approximate each coordinate independently: the resulting coordinates might fail to describe a point of the surface. Global restrictions on the target can obstruct the approximation altogether.

An Oka manifold is a target with a particularly strong form of holomorphic flexibility. Family 042 claims that every complex K3 surface has this property, including nonprojective K3 surfaces that contain no algebraic curves. It then derives consequences for entire curves and several classes of compact complex surfaces.

The claim concerns approximation of every local map in every source dimension. Merely producing a single interesting holomorphic curve on the surface is much weaker.

2. Background and essential definitions

K3 surfaces

A complex K3 surface is a compact connected complex surface that is simply connected and has trivial canonical bundle. The latter condition means it possesses a holomorphic two-form that never vanishes. Every complex K3 surface is Kähler, but not every one can be embedded in projective space.

A smooth quartic surface in P3\mathbb P^3P3 is a standard projective example. Nonprojective examples can have no curves at all, so a proposed argument based solely on moving algebraic curves cannot immediately handle the whole class.

“Surface” here means complex dimension two, hence real dimension four. A holomorphic map from C\mathbb CC traces a complex curve in it; a map from C2\mathbb C^2C2 can have full-rank derivative and explore a whole local neighborhood.

Convex approximation

A compact set K⊂CmK\subset\mathbb C^mK⊂Cm is convex if it contains every real line segment joining two of its points. Let fff be holomorphic on a neighborhood of KKK, with values in a complex manifold XXX.

The convex approximation property says that for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, there is an entire holomorphic map F:Cm→XF:\mathbb C^m\to XF:Cm→X with

sup⁡z∈KdX(F(z),f(z))<ϵ.\sup_{z\in K}d_X(F(z),f(z))<\epsilon.z∈Ksup​dX​(F(z),f(z))<ϵ.

Here dXd_XdX​ is a distance from a smooth Hermitian metric. For compact targets, the qualitative property does not depend on the chosen metric. “Entire” means defined on all of Cm\mathbb C^mCm; it does not mean polynomial, injective, or surjective.

Requiring this in every positive integer dimension mmm characterizes the Oka property. Its equivalent formulations include deforming continuous maps from suitable complex source spaces into holomorphic ones, with approximation and prescribed holomorphic data. The standard sources are Stein spaces, the complex-analytic counterparts of affine geometric spaces, with enough global holomorphic functions to distinguish points and control compact sets.

Several different kinds of flexibility

A surface is dominable by C2\mathbb C^2C2 if one entire map has full-rank derivative somewhere. It is strongly dominable if this can be arranged through each target point. These are existence statements about particular maps.

An entire curve is a map C→X\mathbb C\to XC→X. It is an immersion when its derivative is never zero. Prescribing a jet means prescribing its value and finitely many derivatives in local coordinates. The Oka property controls such interpolation and approximation in a much wider setting than dominability alone.

Likewise, the Oka-1 property concerns maps from open Riemann surfaces, which have complex dimension one. It does not automatically imply approximation from all Cm\mathbb C^mCm.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Oka principle developed from the observation that some holomorphic existence problems are governed principally by topology. Gromov’s work on holomorphic sprays gave a powerful geometric mechanism for this flexibility. A spray is a holomorphic family of maps that can move a point in all tangent directions.

Forstnerič’s convex approximation theorem turned a local-looking approximation test into a characterization of the global Oka principle. It is this characterization that makes the main theorem of M1 a full Oka statement.

K3 surfaces posed a difficult test because their geometry combines strong cohomological structure with potentially few algebraic subvarieties. Buzzard–Lu proved dominability for elliptic and Kummer K3 surfaces. Forstnerič–Lárusson strengthened the Kummer conclusion to strong dominability and studied flexibility throughout the compact-surface classification.

Other work removed obstructions without proving the full property. Kamenova–Lu–Verbitsky showed that the Kobayashi pseudodistance vanishes on every complex K3 surface, using period dynamics with a later correction. This pseudodistance measures resistance to holomorphic discs. Its vanishing is compatible with great flexibility, but does not construct the approximating maps demanded by Oka theory. Alarcón–Forstnerič obtained Oka-1 results for elliptic and Kummer K3 surfaces.

A close predecessor is Xie–Zhao’s 2026 work. It proves Oka properties for explicit K3 examples, including smooth hypersurfaces of multidegree (2,2,2)(2,2,2)(2,2,2) in (P1)3(\mathbb P^1)^3(P1)3, and establishes dense sets of Oka K3 parameters. These are substantial full-Oka results, beyond the earlier dominability and one-dimensional statements.

Density still leaves a logical gap: a dense set can omit particular points, or even many points. M1 seeks to cover every K3 period, including exceptional configurations not reached by a generic argument. It also uses Chen–Gounelas’s families of genus-one curves for the projective case, rather than treating algebraic curves as a new ingredient invented here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Every complex K3 surface is Oka

Theorem 1.1 of M1 states the convex approximation property for every complex K3 surface, every m≥1m\ge1m≥1, every nonempty compact convex K⊂CmK\subset\mathbb C^mK⊂Cm, every local holomorphic map near KKK, and every positive error tolerance.

There is no restriction on projectivity, the number of divisor classes, or the existence of an elliptic fibration. The target is the given K3 surface, not merely a nearby deformation of it.

Dense entire immersions with a prescribed tangent vector

For any x∈Xx\in Xx∈X and any nonzero v∈TxXv\in T_xXv∈Tx​X, Corollary 1.2 claims an entire immersion satisfying

f:C⟶X,f(0)=x,f′(0)=v,f(C)‾=X.f:\mathbb C\longrightarrow X,\qquad f(0)=x,\qquad f'(0)=v,\qquad \overline{f(\mathbb C)}=X.f:C⟶X,f(0)=x,f′(0)=v,f(C)​=X.

The closure is in the ordinary complex topology. In the projective case this implies Zariski density as well. Density is not surjectivity, and immersion is not injectivity. The prescribed derivative is the actual vector vvv, not only its direction.

The manuscript also states approximation and discrete jet interpolation from open Riemann surfaces in a prescribed continuous homotopy class, and strong dominability by C2\mathbb C^2C2.

Consequences for compact surfaces

M1 derives the Oka property for every Enriques surface, whose unramified double cover is a K3 surface. Together with established cases for tori, bielliptic surfaces, and Kodaira surfaces, this gives the assertion that every connected minimal compact complex surface of Kodaira dimension zero is Oka.

Here minimal means there is no exceptional curve that can be contracted to a smooth point. Kodaira dimension measures the growth of sections of powers of the canonical bundle. These qualifications delimit a part of the surface classification, not all compact complex surfaces.

For minimal class VII surfaces, characterized here by first Betti number one and Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty−∞, M1 claims that precisely the Hopf and Enoki surfaces are Oka. This classification additionally uses the global spherical shell theorem claimed in family 060. That companion is not an input to the K3 theorem itself.

Finally, projective K3 surfaces and Enriques surfaces have global dominating holomorphic sprays, by combining the claimed Oka result with an existing theorem for projective Oka manifolds. The manuscript does not extend this spray conclusion to nonprojective K3 surfaces.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the main theorem would settle a prominent flexibility question for a fundamental class of complex surfaces and complete important portions of the Oka surface picture.

Its force comes from the quantifiers. Every local map can be approximated, not just a carefully chosen map; every complex Euclidean source dimension is allowed; every K3 surface is covered. These features would supply a reusable tool for constructing holomorphic maps with specified behavior.

The nonprojective case is especially striking. A surface may contain no compact curves while admitting entire curves dense in its ordinary topology. There is no contradiction: the image of a noncompact source need not be a closed algebraic curve.

The result also connects areas that often use different languages: approximation in several complex variables, algebraic families of curves, symplectic gluing, and arithmetic dynamics on period spaces.

6. The main idea

Extend in one direction while retaining all parameters

M1 first isolates a local operation that enlarges the domain of a holomorphic map in one complex variable. The remaining variables are retained as holomorphic parameters. Two transverse strip maps supply complete directions of motion, one along each coordinate.

The extensions initially disagree on an overlap. Splitting and contraction estimates correct that disagreement. The argument then enlarges polydiscs and removes the real faces of a containing polytope one at a time, passing from the planar operation to approximation on arbitrary convex sets.

Keeping the passive parameters is essential. Without it, the construction would establish only a one-dimensional approximation property.

Find the required directions geometrically

For projective K3 surfaces, two families of genus-one curves provide complete complex directions. Their different degrees force independence at general points, and a propagation argument handles the exceptional set.

For nonprojective surfaces, M1 builds long chains of annuli and joins them by symplectic coordinate changes. Naively correcting the joins could consume all the available transverse width. The proposed sewing theorem keeps the estimates uniform in the length of the chain. Exactness removes a period obstruction, and a quadratic iteration retains a positive width through infinitely many joins.

This constructs suitable open regions in the space of K3 periods. A period plane is the real two-plane spanned by the real and imaginary parts of the holomorphic two-form, after identifying second cohomology with a fixed lattice.

Reach every period, not merely a dense collection

The final transfer separates period planes according to whether they contain zero, one, or two independent rational directions. Arithmetic orbit results and Torelli theory carry the local approximation property through the appropriate orbit in each case. Rational planes fall into the projective case; the other cases require the different open regions built earlier.

Thus the argument does not simply say that approximation survives passage to an arbitrary limit of Oka surfaces. It supplies a route for each type of period plane.

Once Oka interpolation is available, the dense entire immersion is obtained by prescribing nonzero first derivatives and values at a discrete sequence of source points, choosing the target values to form a dense sequence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The principal claim concerns complex K3 surfaces. It does not prove every higher-dimensional Calabi–Yau or hyperkähler manifold is Oka. Numerical similarities between these classes do not transfer the approximation theorem automatically.

The surface-classification consequences are restricted to the minimal cases stated above. The manuscript makes no classification claim for arbitrary blowups or all properly elliptic surfaces. Its class VII conclusion has the separate family 060 dependency.

Entire maps here are holomorphic, not necessarily algebraic or given by an explicit finite formula. The approximation statement gives no effective complexity bound for finding one. Dense immersions need not be embeddings, and strong dominability is not a global covering map.

The projective restriction on global sprays is also retained. Understanding stronger global structures on nonprojective K3 surfaces, and how these methods extend to higher dimensions, remains beyond the stated conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives convex approximation, Corollary 1.2 gives dense entire immersions, and Section 10 separates the interpolation, surface-classification, and spray consequences. Its introduction distinguishes the earlier dominability, Oka-1, and full-Oka results.

The papers of Forstnerič, Forstnerič–Lárusson, and Xie–Zhao linked above provide direct accounts of the relevant earlier advances. Background on K3 surfaces helps locate the examples, while the approximation inequality in Section 2 is the central definition needed to read this digest.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Every complex K3 surface is Oka (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 043 — P = W: two ways to organize the same cohomology
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 043 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

The same topological space can carry two very different algebraic descriptions. Each description may organize its holes and higher-dimensional cycles in a different way. Nonabelian Hodge theory provides a striking example: one description uses vector bundles equipped with a field, while the other uses matrices describing transport around loops on a surface.

The P=WP=WP=W conjecture predicts that two filtrations on their common cohomology agree. One comes from the singular fibers of the Hitchin map; the other comes from mixed Hodge theory on a character variety. Their agreement is unexpected because the correspondence between the spaces is analytic and topological, rather than algebraic.

Family 043 claims the remaining composite-rank comparison for the smooth, fixed-determinant, trace-free setting in coprime degree. Combined with earlier prime-rank theorems, the manuscript says this gives the comparison in every coprime rank. It concerns the entire rational cohomology, including a part not recovered by simply imposing fixed determinant on the known general-linear-group result.

2. Background and essential definitions

From bundles to a map of moduli spaces

Let CCC be a smooth projective complex curve of genus g≥2g\ge2g≥2. Topologically, it is a closed oriented surface with ggg handles. A rank-nnn vector bundle EEE attaches an nnn-dimensional vector space to every point, varying holomorphically.

A Higgs field is a holomorphic map

θ:E⟶E⊗KC,\theta:E\longrightarrow E\otimes K_C,θ:E⟶E⊗KC​,

where KCK_CKC​ is the line bundle of holomorphic one-forms. Locally, it is a matrix of one-forms. We fix a line bundle LLL of degree ddd, require det⁡E≃L\det E\simeq LdetE≃L, and impose tr⁡θ=0\operatorname{tr}\theta=0trθ=0.

A Higgs bundle is stable if each proper nonzero subbundle preserved by θ\thetaθ has smaller slope, where slope means degree divided by rank. The moduli space XXX parametrizes stable objects up to isomorphism. Assuming gcd⁡(n,d)=1\gcd(n,d)=1gcd(n,d)=1 places us in the smooth setting used by the theorem.

The Hitchin map remembers the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of θ\thetaθ:

h:X⟶A,A=⨁i=2nH0(C,KC⊗i).h:X\longrightarrow\mathcal A,\qquad\mathcal A=\bigoplus_{i=2}^{n}H^0(C,K_C^{\otimes i}).h:X⟶A,A=i=2⨁n​H0(C,KC⊗i​).

The linear term is absent because the trace is zero. Writing R=(n2−1)(g−1)R=(n^2-1)(g-1)R=(n2−1)(g−1), the source has complex dimension 2R2R2R and the base dimension RRR. The fibers form an algebraic integrable system, with important singular fibers as the characteristic polynomial degenerates.

The matrix description

On the other side, assign matrices Aj,Bj∈SLn(C)A_j,B_j\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb C)Aj​,Bj​∈SLn​(C) to the two standard loops around each handle. The determinant-one condition explains the notation SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​. The matrices satisfy

∏j=1g[Aj,Bj]=ζIn,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1,ζ=e2πid/n.\prod_{j=1}^{g}[A_j,B_j]=\zeta I_n,\qquad[A,B]=ABA^{-1}B^{-1},\qquad\zeta=e^{2\pi i d/n}.j=1∏g​[Aj​,Bj​]=ζIn​,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1,ζ=e2πid/n.

Tuples are identified under simultaneous conjugation, which changes the basis used to record transport. The resulting twisted character variety is denoted XBX_BXB​. The scalar twist retains the degree information. Nonabelian Hodge theory gives a diffeomorphism between XXX and XBX_BXB​, hence identifies their rational cohomology.

What is being filtered?

A filtration is a nested sequence of subspaces

⋯⊂Fk−1H⊂FkH⊂Fk+1H⊂⋯ .\cdots\subset F_{k-1}H\subset F_kH\subset F_{k+1}H\subset\cdots.⋯⊂Fk−1​H⊂Fk​H⊂Fk+1​H⊂⋯.

It records more than the dimension of HHH: it assigns levels to its elements. On the Higgs side, the perverse Leray filtration PPP organizes cohomology according to the direct image of the Hitchin map, taking the dimensions of supports and singular-fiber contributions into account. “Perverse” is a technical term for the sheaf-theoretic indexing, not a negative judgment.

On the character-variety side, Deligne’s weight filtration WWW measures the different Hodge-theoretic weights that can occur on a noncompact algebraic variety. Smooth projective varieties have pure cohomology of a given degree; these character varieties need not.

These descriptions explain the origin of the two filtrations without requiring their sheaf-theoretic construction. The theorem compares the actual subspaces under the specified nonabelian-Hodge identification.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hitchin’s work introduced the Higgs-bundle moduli spaces and their integrable systems. The correspondence with flat connections and representations rests on foundational work of Hitchin, Donaldson, Corlette, and Simpson.

Arithmetic calculations by Hausel–Rodriguez-Villegas revealed unexpected symmetries in the weights of character-variety cohomology. De Cataldo–Hausel–Migliorini formulated P=WP=WP=W and established the rank-two case. Their comparison explained weight symmetries on one side through the geometry of the Hitchin map on the other.

Higher-rank progress used tautological classes, cohomology classes naturally extracted from universal bundles. Results of Markman and others provided generators in the general-linear setting, while Shende determined their weights. De Cataldo–Maulik–Shen proved the general-linear comparison in genus two and obtained further bounds in arbitrary genus.

Maulik–Shen then proved the coprime GLn\mathrm{GL}_nGLn​ conjecture in arbitrary rank and genus. Other proofs use the operator methods of Hausel–Mellit–Minets–Schiffmann and the Fourier-transform methods of Maulik–Shen–Yin.

Fixed determinant introduces an extra issue. The finite group of degree-zero nnn-torsion line bundles acts by tensoring EEE. The known general-linear result controls the invariant part of the fixed-determinant cohomology, but does not automatically recover its complementary part. De Cataldo–Maulik–Shen’s prime-rank work, combined with the later general-linear theorem, handles prime rank.
