For composite rank, earlier endoscopic correspondences related the missing pieces to geometry on covers of the curve and were compatible with perverse filtrations. M1 identifies the remaining task as a comparison on full cohomology, rather than another proof restricted to the invariant subspace.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Equality on every cohomological degree

For every composite n≥4n\ge4n≥4, every g≥2g\ge2g≥2, every degree ddd coprime to nnn, and every fixed determinant LLL of that degree, Theorem 1.1 of M1 claims

PkHm(XB,Q)=W2kHm(XB,Q)=W2k+1Hm(XB,Q)P_kH^m(X_B,\mathbb Q)=W_{2k}H^m(X_B,\mathbb Q)=W_{2k+1}H^m(X_B,\mathbb Q)Pk​Hm(XB​,Q)=W2k​Hm(XB​,Q)=W2k+1​Hm(XB​,Q)

for all m,k≥0m,k\ge0m,k≥0. The perverse filtration has been transported from XXX through nonabelian Hodge theory.

The factor two is part of the theorem, not an optional convention that can be dropped. M1 uses the standard Hitchin normalization in which the perverse index runs from zero through 2R2R2R. Equality with both weight steps says no additional piece appears at the intervening odd step.

Combining this claim with established prime-rank cases gives the smooth coprime fixed-determinant statement for every n≥2n\ge2n≥2.

The complementary cohomology is included

Let

Γ=Pic⁡0(C)[n]\Gamma=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)[n]Γ=Pic0(C)[n]

be the group of line bundles whose nnn-th power is trivial. Tensoring by an element of Γ\GammaΓ preserves the fixed determinant. Averaging its action projects onto invariant cohomology; the kernel is called variant cohomology.

M1 asserts the filtration equality before taking invariants. After allowing complex coefficients, this includes every nontrivial character of Γ\GammaΓ, meaning every simultaneous eigenspace for this finite abelian group action. A proof of equality only on the average would not establish the advertised theorem.

Corollary 9.2 also derives an exact weight-image compatibility for the specified endoscopic operator associated with a cyclic unramified cover of CCC. This uses the new full equality together with the known general-linear comparison on the cover side. It is a consequence for that particular transported correspondence, not a blanket assertion about every operator on cohomology.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the result would finish an important fixed-determinant portion of a central comparison in nonabelian Hodge theory, including cohomology invisible to the simplest reduction from GLn\mathrm{GL}_nGLn​.

It is stronger than matching Betti numbers or even the dimensions of individual graded pieces. Two filtrations can have equally sized steps while placing different vectors in those steps. The statement says the subspaces themselves coincide under a geometrically meaningful correspondence.

This allows information to travel between descriptions: the geometry of Hitchin fibers constrains Hodge weights, while weight calculations can organize the topology of the integrable system. The claimed method also illustrates how a common operator can identify structures that initially arise from unrelated constructions.

The rating reflects this substantial completion while retaining credit for the earlier general-linear and prime-rank theorems. It is not a claim to establish every version of P=WP=WP=W for arbitrary groups or singular moduli spaces.

6. The main idea

Use one raising operator and construct one lowering operator

Cup product with a distinguished degree-two cohomology class gives an operator eee. On each side, a version of hard Lefschetz supplies symmetry around the middle level: repeated applications of eee connect corresponding levels below and above the center.

M1’s strategy is to construct a single operator fff, lowering cohomological degree by two, that simultaneously satisfies

f(Pk)⊂Pk−2,f(Wj)⊂Wj−4,[[f,e],e]=−2e.f(P_k)\subset P_{k-2},\qquad f(W_j)\subset W_{j-4},\qquad [[f,e],e]=-2e.f(Pk​)⊂Pk−2​,f(Wj​)⊂Wj−4​,[[f,e],e]=−2e.

Here [a,b]=ab−ba[a,b]=ab-ba[a,b]=ab−ba is the commutator of linear operators. Together with the two Lefschetz symmetries, these relations allow a linear-algebra argument to recover both filtrations from eigenspaces of the same operator [e,f][e,f][e,f]. The task is therefore geometric construction of a genuinely common fff, not merely dimension counting.

Move a pole and compare two limits

The construction enlarges the moduli problem by allowing a logarithmic pole at a moving point of the curve and choosing a full flag there. A full flag is a nested sequence of subspaces of dimensions one through nnn. The logarithmic connection parameter interpolates between Higgs bundles and connections.

The manuscript modifies two eigenline lattices in opposite directions, preserving the determinant condition. On the connection side, the resulting translation is interpreted through monodromy as eigenvalues move. A suitable logarithm of that monodromy, followed by operations along the flag correspondence, produces the proposed lowering operator.

Different arguments control its two filtrations. A finite diagram of algebraic fibers supplies the weight bookkeeping; specialization over a Higgs parameter supplies the perverse bound. M1 stresses that the diagram assigns weight zero to the cochains of the moving-point base. Those are not the ordinary Hodge weights of that curve viewed as an algebraic variety.

Finally, a characteristic-class calculation establishes the commutator relation. Throughout, the construction must retain full cohomology. Averaging over Γ\GammaΓ too early would discard the very classes the new theorem needs to reach.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The hypotheses include a smooth projective complex curve of genus at least two, fixed determinant, trace-free Higgs field, and coprime rank and degree. Coprimality is important for smoothness. The claim does not settle versions involving noncoprime degree, where singular moduli spaces and intersection cohomology may enter.

The coefficients are rational. An integral comparison would need to address torsion and is not asserted here. The theorem also does not turn the nonabelian-Hodge diffeomorphism into an algebraic isomorphism: it matches these specific cohomological structures despite the distinct algebraic descriptions.

Other structure groups, parabolic conditions, and singular variants require their own statements. The endoscopic consequence retains its designated operator and normalization. These boundaries leave a broader comparison program beyond the smooth coprime SLn\mathrm{SL}_nSLn​ case addressed by this family.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the composite-rank equality; its introduction explains the variant-cohomology obstruction and the common-operator strategy. Section 9 combines prime and composite ranks and gives the endoscopic consequence.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 trace the development from rank two to the general-linear and prime-rank cases. Optional background on Higgs bundles helps with the moduli-space language. The central comparison is the equality of nested subspaces displayed in Section 4, with its factor-two indexing.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, P=W in composite rank for fixed determinant (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 044 — Hikita’s conjecture: cohomology hidden inside a fixed scheme
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 044 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A space’s cohomology records its topology, while its ring of functions records algebraic geometry. Hikita’s conjecture predicts a surprising bridge: for certain paired spaces arising from quivers, the cohomology ring of one is the ring of functions on a fixed locus in the other.

The fixed locus must be understood with its full scheme structure. Counting its ordinary points would lose the information the conjecture is designed to capture. A fixed locus consisting of one visible point can still carry nonzero functions whose powers vanish, and those functions can represent positive-degree cohomology classes.

Family 044 contains one manuscript claiming the equivariant cohomological comparison for arbitrary finite quivers, including loops and repeated arrows. Its hypotheses require a stability choice yielding a smooth quotient with free gauge-group action. The assertion preserves the natural coefficient classes and all algebraic relations, not just the dimensions of vector spaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

A quiver turns linear algebra into geometry

A quiver is a finite directed graph. Give each vertex iii a vector space ViV_iVi​ of dimension viv_ivi​, and each arrow a linear map between the corresponding spaces. Additional spaces WiW_iWi​, of dimensions wiw_iwi​, provide a framing: extra linear maps that anchor the representation.

The manuscript uses the representation space

N=⨁a:i→jHom⁡(Vi,Vj)⊕⨁iHom⁡(Vi,Wi),N=\bigoplus_{a:i\to j}\operatorname{Hom}(V_i,V_j)\oplus\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Hom}(V_i,W_i),N=a:i→j⨁​Hom(Vi​,Vj​)⊕i⨁​Hom(Vi​,Wi​),

with change-of-basis group

G=∏iGL⁡(Vi).G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}(V_i).G=i∏​GL(Vi​).

Passing to T∗N=N⊕N∗T^*N=N\oplus N^*T∗N=N⊕N∗ adds dual variables and a natural symplectic form. A moment map μ\muμ packages the equations expressing compatibility with the group action. For (s,p)∈N⊕N∗(s,p)\in N\oplus N^*(s,p)∈N⊕N∗ and an infinitesimal change of basis ξ\xiξ, its convention is

⟨μ(s,p),ξ⟩=⟨p,ξs⟩.\langle\mu(s,p),\xi\rangle=\langle p,\xi s\rangle.⟨μ(s,p),ξ⟩=⟨p,ξs⟩.

One imposes μ=0\mu=0μ=0, selects stable points using a character ν:G→C×\nu:G\to\mathbb C^\timesν:G→C×, and divides by changes of basis. A character is a multiplicative one-dimensional representation. Stability excludes configurations that would give a badly behaved quotient.

The resulting Nakajima variety is

X=μ−1(0)ν-stable/G.X=\mu^{-1}(0)^{\nu\text{-stable}}/G.X=μ−1(0)ν-stable/G.

Here the required regularity means that semistable and stable loci coincide and the action there is free. The free-action clause is part of the hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of choosing an arbitrary character.

Two branches and an extra symmetry

The space XXX is called the Higgs branch. The corresponding Coulomb branch is defined by the Braverman–Finkelberg–Nakajima construction: a convolution algebra built from spaces of formal Laurent-series data gives its coordinate ring. Convolution multiplies classes by composing geometric correspondences, much as matrix multiplication composes linear maps.

A flavor torus FFF, a group isomorphic to a product of copies of C×\mathbb C^\timesC×, acts on the linear data and commutes with GGG. On the Higgs side we retain this symmetry through equivariant cohomology HF∗(X;C)H_F^*(X;\mathbb C)HF∗​(X;C). Unlike ordinary cohomology, this also contains polynomial parameters recording the torus action.

On the Coulomb side, flavor parameters produce a family YfY_{\mathfrak f}Yf​, where f\mathfrak ff is the Lie algebra of FFF. A topological charge grading supplies another torus action, and the stability character determines a one-parameter subgroup of that torus.

Why a fixed scheme is more than fixed points

Consider the algebra C[u]/(u2)\mathbb C[u]/(u^2)C[u]/(u2). It describes one ordinary point, but the class of uuu is nonzero and has square zero. Such an element is nilpotent. Replacing the algebra by the functions on its underlying point would give only C\mathbb CC.

This toy example illustrates how topology could be stored: H∗(P1;C)=C[u]/(u2)H^*(\mathbb P^1;\mathbb C)=\mathbb C[u]/(u^2)H∗(P1;C)=C[u]/(u2), with uuu in degree two. Forgetting the nilpotent would erase its degree-two class. This is an illustration of the algebraic issue, not a substitute for identifying the particular spaces in the theorem.

If the Coulomb algebra AFA_FAF​ decomposes into weight spaces for the stability subgroup, the fixed scheme has coordinate ring

C[Yfν]=AF/⟨(AF)m:m≠0⟩.\mathbb C[Y_{\mathfrak f}^{\nu}]=A_F\big/\langle (A_F)_m:m\ne0\rangle.C[Yfν​]=AF​/⟨(AF​)m​:m=0⟩.

One quotients by all nonzero-weight elements and retains whatever nilpotents remain. This differs from merely taking the weight-zero subalgebra.

3. Development history and previous partial results

A classical precursor describes Springer-fiber cohomology through scheme-theoretic intersections of nilpotent orbit closures with a Cartan subalgebra. Work of de Concini–Procesi and Tanisaki showed how a small algebraic intersection can retain substantial topological information.

Hikita formulated the fixed-scheme correspondence in the setting of symplectic duality and established examples involving the Hilbert scheme of points in the affine plane, alongside related type-A and hypertoric examples. These cases made the role of infinitesimal scheme structure particularly clear.

Nakajima proposed a mathematical construction of Coulomb branches, and Braverman–Finkelberg–Nakajima supplied the convolution-algebra definition. This gave a precise object to compare with quiver varieties beyond the first examples. Later formulations made compatibility with tautological and equivariant parameters part of the conjecture itself.

Krylov–Shlykov proved the Gieseker, or framed Jordan-quiver, case. Dumanski–Krylov compared cohomological, equivariant, and K-theoretic versions. As M1 emphasizes, their finite-type conclusion includes types A, D, and E6E_6E6​, while E7E_7E7​ and E8E_8E8​ carry framing restrictions; an earlier unrestricted ADE formulation needs that qualification.

There are also quantum refinements. Dinkins–Karpov–Krylov treat a refined quantum conjecture for ADE quivers with specified minuscule framings and for the Jordan quiver. Those stronger structures have different hypotheses and should not be conflated with the cohomological result claimed here.

The gap addressed by M1 is a uniform coefficient-compatible comparison for arbitrary finite quiver data under regular stability, including loops, multiple arrows, and arbitrary commuting flavor tori.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 asserts a canonical isomorphism of graded algebras

HF∗(X;C)≃C[Yfν].H_F^*(X;\mathbb C)\simeq\mathbb C[Y_{\mathfrak f}^{\nu}].HF∗​(X;C)≃C[Yfν​].

“Canonical” is specified through the coefficient maps. Let T⊂GT\subset GT⊂G be a diagonal maximal torus and WWW its Weyl group, which permutes coordinates at each vertex. Both sides receive natural maps from

R=HG×F∗(pt;C)=C[Lie⁡T⊕f]W.R=H_{G\times F}^*(\mathrm{pt};\mathbb C)=\mathbb C[\operatorname{Lie}T\oplus\mathfrak f]^W.R=HG×F∗​(pt;C)=C[LieT⊕f]W.

On the Higgs side, gauge parameters become Chern classes of tautological bundles, the bundles whose fibers are the vertex vector spaces. Flavor parameters retain their equivariant meaning. On the Coulomb side, the same parameters map through its coefficient algebra and then to the fixed-scheme quotient.

M1 claims both maps are surjective and have exactly the same kernel. Consequently the isomorphism is an identification of the same quotient of RRR, rather than an unspecified algebra isomorphism. Linear gauge and flavor parameters have degree two.

The quiver may have any finite number of vertices and arrows, with loops and multiple arrows allowed. Dimension and framing vectors are arbitrary. The stability character must satisfy the regularity condition defined above. Empty stable loci are included: the corresponding ring is the zero ring on both sides.

The comparison retains nilpotents and all flavor parameters. It is not restricted to a generic parameter value, and no reduction to the underlying ordinary fixed-point set is taken.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, this would establish a broad form of a central bridge in symplectic duality for quiver gauge theories, beyond the earlier special graph types and framing choices.

The result would convert topological calculations into algebraic relations on a dual geometric object. Conversely, knowledge of the cohomology ring would determine the full fixed scheme, including infinitesimal information invisible in a picture of its points.

Preserving coefficients is especially useful. It tells us where natural geometric classes go and allows deformations and symmetry parameters to remain part of the comparison. An equality of Betti numbers alone would provide much less information.

The rating reflects the breadth of the quiver theorem. Its scope remains a cohomological comparison for this class of gauge groups, rather than a universal statement covering every proposed version of Hikita duality.

6. The main idea

Compare relations before comparing spaces

The manuscript first works with the fixed scheme for the entire topological torus, an intermediate object whose coordinate ring is a quotient of RRR. It compares the kernel of that quotient with the kernel defining equivariant cohomology.

Geometric tests on stable pairs show that each relation on the Coulomb side vanishes in the Higgs cohomology ring. This gives a surjection. Such a map could still discard information, so a second argument must show the source is no larger than the target in each degree.

Add loops to simplify the calculation, then remove them

M1 temporarily adds a loop at every relevant vertex. In that setting, factors contributed by the loops cancel denominators in explicit convolution formulas. A filtration indexed by multipartitions reduces the remaining size estimate to polynomial quotients and a reachability count.

Hausel’s established formula supplies the corresponding cohomological dimensions. The degree-by-degree upper bound, combined with the already constructed surjection, forces equality for the auxiliary quiver.

An auxiliary flavor parameter then separates the added loops from the original data. Localization compares the relations near a specified nonzero parameter value. Homogeneity is used to descend this comparison to the original coefficient ideals. The proposed conclusion is therefore equality before localization, including special parameter values, not merely an isomorphism after generic denominators are inverted.

Distinguish one subgroup from the whole torus

A final issue remains: the conjecture asks for the fixed scheme of the stability one-parameter subgroup. A charge can be nonzero for the full torus yet have weight zero for that subgroup. Consequently the two fixed-scheme quotients cannot simply be identified by terminology.

M1 uses complementary convolution generators, often called monopoles, and Hall-algebra generation to analyze a hypothetical surviving charge. The resulting decomposition would produce a semistable configuration with a positive-dimensional stabilizer. That contradicts the regularity hypothesis.

This establishes the claimed equality of the two defining ideals, retaining scheme structure throughout. The coefficient comparison and the fixed-scheme comparison solve different parts of the problem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is over complex coefficients and uses a gauge group that is a product of general linear groups attached to quiver vertices. It does not extend automatically to arbitrary reductive gauge groups; the manuscript notes failures of proposed identifications outside the stated setting.

Regular stability is essential. Singular quotients or actions with stabilizers require additional formulations. The empty case is allowed, but that does not remove the stability conditions from nonempty cases.

The algebra here is the commutative BFN algebra without the loop-rotation quantization parameter. The theorem does not claim the full quantized, quantum-cohomological, or K-theoretic comparison for arbitrary quivers. Those versions preserve more structure and remain separate questions.

Finally, identifying two rings does not identify the Higgs and Coulomb spaces themselves. The fixed scheme can be much smaller geometrically while retaining the algebra needed to encode the other side’s cohomology.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the coefficient-compatible isomorphism. Its introduction records the earlier finite-type restrictions and separates the full-torus comparison from the stability-subgroup comparison. The four-step strategy there is the basis of Section 6 above.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 explain the original conjecture, Coulomb construction, and earlier quiver cases. Optional introductions to quivers and equivariant cohomology provide more notation. The small algebra C[u]/(u2)\mathbb C[u]/(u^2)C[u]/(u2) is the key example for remembering why nilpotents cannot be discarded.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The equivariant cohomological Hikita conjecture for arbitrary quivers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 046 — Shafarevich’s conjecture: two claimed failures of holomorphic convexity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 046 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

The universal cover of a space unwinds all its loops. For compact complex curves, this leads to the sphere, the complex plane, or the unit disc. These highly structured models invite a higher-dimensional question: how well behaved is the universal cover of a smooth projective variety?

Shafarevich’s holomorphic-convexity conjecture predicts a strong analytic answer. Holomorphic functions should be plentiful enough to prevent the hull of a compact set from spreading indefinitely through the universal cover.

Family 046 contains two manuscripts claiming counterexamples. M2 constructs a projective surface whose universal cover contains an infinite connected chain of compact rational curves. Holomorphic functions must be constant along the whole chain, defeating holomorphic convexity.

M1 gives a different and stronger obstruction under an additional geometric condition: a projective fourfold with large fundamental group, whose universal cover contains no compact positive-dimensional analytic subvariety, but is nevertheless not Stein. The two constructions address different ways the conjecture could fail and should not be merged into one example.

2. Background and essential definitions

Universal covers and fundamental-group images

For a connected manifold XXX, its universal cover X~\widetilde XX is a simply connected manifold mapping locally isomorphically to XXX. If XXX is complex, the cover inherits a complex structure.

The fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X)π1​(X) records loops up to continuous deformation. An inclusion Z⊂XZ\subset XZ⊂X induces a homomorphism from the loops in ZZZ to those in XXX. This map need not be injective: loops essential inside ZZZ may contract in the larger space. Its image determines how a connected lift of ZZZ sits over ZZZ.

When that image is infinite, a connected lift can have infinitely many sheets. Keeping an image infinite after embedding into a projective variety is the main construction problem in both manuscripts.

Holomorphic hulls

For a compact nonempty K⊂VK\subset VK⊂V, its holomorphic hull is

K^V={x∈V:∣f(x)∣≤sup⁡K∣f∣ for every f∈O(V)}.\widehat K_V=\{x\in V: |f(x)|\le\sup_K|f|\text{ for every }f\in\mathcal O(V)\}.KV​={x∈V:∣f(x)∣≤Ksup​∣f∣ for every f∈O(V)}.

The notation O(V)\mathcal O(V)O(V) means all holomorphic complex-valued functions on VVV. A point lies in the hull when no such function separates its size from the values already seen on KKK.

The space VVV is holomorphically convex if every compact set has compact hull. A Stein manifold is a complex manifold with particularly strong global function theory; it is the analytic analogue of an affine variety. In particular, Stein manifolds are holomorphically convex and have no compact positive-dimensional analytic subvarieties.

The converse needs care. Merely having no compact analytic curves does not, by definition, make a manifold Stein. For a holomorphically convex manifold, however, Remmert reduction contracts its compact connected analytic fibers to a Stein space. If there are no positive-dimensional compact analytic subvarieties, this reduction identifies the manifold itself as Stein.

“Large” has a precise meaning

A smooth projective XXX has large fundamental group if every positive-dimensional irreducible subvariety Z⊂XZ\subset XZ⊂X has infinite image

im⁡(π1(Zν)→π1(X)),\operatorname{im}\bigl(\pi_1(Z^\nu)\to\pi_1(X)\bigr),im(π1​(Zν)→π1​(X)),

where ZνZ^\nuZν is its normalization, which separates the branches of singularities. In this setting, largeness is equivalent to the absence of compact positive-dimensional analytic subvarieties in X~\widetilde XX.

This is not a statement that the group has many generators or grows quickly. It is a condition on every subvariety and its induced loops.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Shafarevich’s question extends the uniformization viewpoint for curves to higher-dimensional projective geometry. Campana and Kollár developed reduction maps that organize subvarieties whose normalized fundamental groups have finite image. These are powerful geometric reductions, but a map defined generically on the projective variety does not automatically yield a proper holomorphic reduction of its whole universal cover.

Several major affirmative results impose conditions on the fundamental group. Gurjar–Shastri handled smooth projective elliptic surfaces. Katzarkov treated virtually nilpotent fundamental groups. Work of Katzarkov–Ramachandran and Eyssidieux developed the theory for linear and reductive representations.

The linear Shafarevich theorem of Eyssidieux–Katzarkov–Pantev–Ramachandran proves holomorphic convexity for smooth projective varieties whose fundamental groups admit faithful finite-dimensional complex representations. Campana–Claudon–Eyssidieux extended the linear result to compact Kähler manifolds. More recent reductive-cover and normal-space results further broaden this affirmative theory while retaining specific representation-theoretic hypotheses.

Potential counterexamples also have a history. Bogomolov–Katzarkov proposed constructions using degenerating curves and group quotients. Their proposed failures depended on infinitude assertions for groups after all geometric relations had been imposed. Those conditional constructions did not themselves settle the conjecture.

The infinite-chain obstruction was already understood in work of Lasell–Ramachandran and Katzarkov–Ramachandran. The missing ingredient was an actual projective construction retaining the necessary infinite group image. M2 proposes to supply that ingredient through weighted group presentations. M1 instead uses a cover of an abelian surface and a local method for showing loops survive.

Thus the claimed novelty is not the observation that holomorphic functions are constant on compact curves. It is realizing the required configuration while preserving its global fundamental-group behavior.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: failure already in complex dimension two

M2 claims a smooth connected projective complex surface XXX containing a connected nodal curve Z0Z_0Z0​, all of whose irreducible components are smooth rational curves, such that

im⁡(π1(Z0)→π1(X)) is infinite.\operatorname{im}\bigl(\pi_1(Z_0)\to\pi_1(X)\bigr)\text{ is infinite}.im(π1​(Z0​)→π1​(X)) is infinite.

A rational curve is isomorphic to P1\mathbb P^1P1, hence simply connected. Nevertheless, a union of such curves can have loops formed by its incidence pattern: moving through several components and back can create a loop even though each component separately has none.

In X~\widetilde XX, a connected component above Z0Z_0Z0​ is claimed to be a closed, noncompact, locally finite union of compact rational curves. Every global holomorphic function is constant on it. Consequently even the hull of one point is noncompact, so X~\widetilde XX is not holomorphically convex.

This surface does not have large fundamental group: its rational curves already violate that condition.

M1: failure with large fundamental group

M1 claims a smooth connected projective fourfold XXX containing a simple abelian surface AAA, with

X having large fundamental group,im⁡(π1(A)→π1(X))≃Z.X\text{ having large fundamental group},\qquad\operatorname{im}\bigl(\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(X)\bigr)\simeq\mathbb Z.X having large fundamental group,im(π1​(A)→π1​(X))≃Z.

An abelian surface is a projective complex torus of dimension two. It is simple if it contains no nonzero proper abelian subvariety. Its fundamental group is Z4\mathbb Z^4Z4.

The asserted infinite cyclic image means the kernel has rank three. A connected lift of AAA is therefore diffeomorphic to

R×(S1)3,\mathbb R\times(S^1)^3,R×(S1)3,

and has nonzero third homology. A Stein surface has the homotopy type of a cell complex of real dimension at most two, so this lifted surface cannot be Stein. It is a closed complex submanifold of X~\widetilde XX; closed complex submanifolds of Stein spaces are Stein. Thus X~\widetilde XX cannot be Stein either.

Largeness excludes compact positive-dimensional analytic subvarieties in this cover. Remmert reduction then makes non-Steinness a failure of holomorphic convexity as well. The contradiction uses the complex dimension of the lifted surface, not an incorrect claim that a Stein fourfold cannot have third homology.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these constructions would disprove a central conjecture about universal covers of projective varieties, including its especially direct large-fundamental-group version.

The surface example locates failure in the smallest possible complex dimension beyond curves. The fourfold example would show that removing all compact positive-dimensional analytic subvarieties is still insufficient. These are complementary lessons about the role of topology in complex analysis.

The affirmative linear theory would remain intact. Instead, the examples would identify behavior that faithful finite-dimensional matrix representations cannot capture. In particular, the fundamental groups of the claimed examples cannot be linear over C\mathbb CC, by the established linear theorem.

6. The main idea

M2: leave enough group information after compactification

M2 begins with a family of spheres carrying 48 moving punctures. Near a distinguished parameter, the punctures collide in 24 pairs. After modifications, the special fiber consists of a main sphere with attached rational components. Suitable finite covers preserve the rational nature of those components.

The hard part is making the incidence loops survive in the final compact surface. Filling missing fibers and resolving singularities introduce group relations, and sufficiently many relations can collapse an initially infinite group to a finite one.

The manuscript uses a weighted Golod–Shafarevich method. In a presentation by generators and relations, different relations receive different costs according to their depth in a filtration. A strict inequality leaves room for additional high-depth relations while ensuring the resulting quotient stays infinite. The construction is carried out using inverse limits of finite groups of order a power of two.

After compactification, it chooses a finite quotient that detects each entire local boundary-group image. This is designed to preserve the infinite quotient through normalization and resolution, including the exceptional divisors. The final transfer places that infinite image on the compact rational special fiber.

Once the geometry exists, the analytic obstruction is short: holomorphic functions are constant on each compact rational component by the maximum principle, and intersections force all those constants to agree along the noncompact connected lift.

M1: compress an abelian surface’s loops to one infinite direction

M1 starts from a genus-two curve with simple Jacobian. Arithmetic complex-hyperbolic arrangements impose relations that reduce its group image to a cyclic subgroup. Showing the image is cyclic gives only an upper bound: it might still be finite or trivial.

To establish infinitude, the manuscript uses compatible local covers with path labels modeled on an infinite dihedral group. Its two involutions have a product of infinite order. A local criterion using hyperbolic path graphs is intended to detect every nonzero power after the global geometric identifications.

The labels need not form a representation of the full final fundamental group. That distinction matters because the construction is meant to lie outside the affirmative linear setting.

Two copies of the construction, followed by quotients and projective modifications, produce the required simple abelian surface with cyclic image. A complete intersection in a product with an additional abelian variety then gives a fourfold with large fundamental group, preserving that surface and its group map. The rank-three covering obstruction supplies the final analytic conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are existence claims over C\mathbb CC. They do not classify all projective varieties with nonconvex universal covers or provide a criterion that decides holomorphic convexity from arbitrary equations.

The two examples have different dimensions and properties. M2 contains rational curves and is not large; M1 is a fourfold and excludes compact positive-dimensional analytic subvarieties upstairs. The family does not claim a large-fundamental-group surface counterexample.

M2 also discusses consequences using separate claims about special compact Kähler manifolds and semialgebraic universal covers, covered in family 057 and family 058. Those comparisons are additional dependencies, not needed to formulate the basic infinite-chain obstruction.

Questions about which non-linear fundamental groups still force convexity, and what further geometric hypotheses ensure Steinness in the large case, remain meaningful after the stated counterexamples.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the fourfold and abelian-surface construction; its opening reduction explains the homological obstruction. M2’s Theorem 1.1 states the surface example, and Lemma 1.2 explains why its lifted nodal curve destroys holomorphic convexity.

The primary historical papers linked above distinguish established affirmative theorems from earlier conditional constructions. Background on Stein manifolds and covering spaces is useful, but the hull definition and the two concrete obstructions are enough to understand what the family claims.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A projective fourfold with large fundamental group and non-Stein universal cover (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A surface counterexample to Shafarevich holomorphic convexity (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 048 — Free vector fields on a singular surface
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 048 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

On a smooth surface, a coordinate chart supplies two coordinate vector fields. Every other vector field on the chart can be written uniquely as a function times the first plus a function times the second. Could the converse hold: if vector fields admit such a free local basis, must the surface be smooth?

The Lipman–Zariski conjecture predicts yes in characteristic zero. It is a proposed way to recognize nonsingularity through differentiation, without first finding coordinates or checking a Jacobian matrix.

Family 048 contains one manuscript claiming a counterexample over C\mathbb CC. It constructs a normal affine surface with a singular point, while its entire module of algebraic vector fields is free of rank two. Freeness is asserted on the whole affine surface, including at the singularity, not merely on its smooth part.

The construction first takes place in complex-analytic geometry and then passes to an algebraic surface. It is therefore an existence construction through neighborhoods, contraction, and algebraization, rather than a short hypersurface equation in three variables.

2. Background and essential definitions

Vector fields as derivations

If AAA is the ring of polynomial functions on an affine variety, an algebraic vector field is a derivation

D:A⟶A,D(fg)=fD(g)+gD(f),D:A\longrightarrow A,\qquad D(fg)=fD(g)+gD(f),D:A⟶A,D(fg)=fD(g)+gD(f),

which is linear over C\mathbb CC. The product rule captures the familiar behavior of directional differentiation.

All derivations form an AAA-module, denoted Der⁡C(A)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb C}(A)DerC​(A). Multiplying a vector field by a function gives another vector field. On the affine plane,

Der⁡C(C[x,y])=C[x,y] ∂x⊕C[x,y] ∂y.\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C[x,y])=\mathbb C[x,y]\,\partial_x\oplus\mathbb C[x,y]\,\partial_y.DerC​(C[x,y])=C[x,y]∂x​⊕C[x,y]∂y​.

A module is free of rank two if it has two generators and every element has a unique expression as their linear combination with coefficients in AAA. The associated tangent sheaf records the corresponding vector fields on each open set. Local freeness allows a basis that depends on the open set; global freeness supplies one basis everywhere on the affine variety.

Smoothness and the pointwise tangent space

A local ring at a point is regular if its maximal ideal can be generated by as many elements as the local dimension. For a complex algebraic variety, regularity is equivalent to smoothness at that point.

The Zariski tangent space at a point is dual to m/m2\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2m/m2, where m\mathfrak mm is the maximal ideal. At a singular point its dimension can exceed the dimension of the variety.

This pointwise tangent space must be distinguished from a free module of derivations on a neighborhood. At singularities, taking the dual of the module of differentials and then taking a fiber need not reproduce the dual of the fiber of differentials. Thus one cannot dismiss the conjecture by saying that a free rank-two derivation module automatically makes the pointwise tangent space two-dimensional. That implication is part of the subtlety being investigated.

Normality and resolutions

An integral ring is normal if it is integrally closed in its fraction field. Geometrically, normality rules out some elementary defects, such as branches that should have been separated, but it still permits isolated singularities on surfaces.

A resolution replaces a singular point by a configuration of smooth curves in a smooth surface. These exceptional curves record information hidden at the point. Their genera, intersections, and the behavior of differential forms along them help determine the severity of the singularity.

The manuscript builds the neighborhood of one such curve first and then contracts the curve to produce the singular point.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lipman’s 1965 work established that local freeness of the derivation module forces normality. The conjecture therefore asks whether free vector fields also rule out the normal singularities that remain.

In positive characteristic, the corresponding assertion can fail because differentiation loses information: for example, the derivative of zpz^pzp vanishes in characteristic ppp. Those examples do not settle the complex case, where ordinary differentiation behaves differently.

Strong positive results cover several broad classes in characteristic zero. Hochster treated positively graded algebras with degree-zero part equal to the field. Scheja–Storch handled hypersurfaces, and Källström’s corrected complete-intersection result handles the more general locally complete-intersection setting. Van Straten–Steenbrink proved the isolated-singularity case in dimension at least three using extension of differential forms, leaving surfaces as a distinct difficulty.

The extension viewpoint also connects the problem to birational singularities. Greb–Kebekus–Kovács–Peternell proved the conjecture for Kawamata log terminal spaces. Druel and Graf–Kovács established the log-canonical case, a larger class of mild singularities measured by discrepancies on resolutions.

For surfaces, Graf obtained results in low geometric genus. Bergner–Graf proved smoothness when

pg−g−b≤2,p_g-g-b\le2,pg​−g−b≤2,

where pgp_gpg​ is the geometric genus of the local singularity, ggg the sum of the genera of exceptional curves, and bbb the first Betti number of the resolution’s dual graph. Here the local geometric genus measures a cohomological obstruction on a resolution; it is not the geometric genus of a compact surface from the classification theory.

Another useful distinction is the Lie bracket. Jörder proved smoothness when a tangent basis can be chosen with pairwise commuting vector fields. Arbitrary free vector fields need not commute, whereas coordinate vector fields do.

M1 places its example outside these established classes. The neighborhood is deliberately not a positively graded cone, the singularity is more severe than log canonical, and no commuting tangent frame is claimed.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 asserts a finitely generated normal integral complex algebra AAA of dimension two and a maximal ideal m\mathfrak mm such that

Der⁡C(A)≃A⊕2,Am is not regular.\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb C}(A)\simeq A^{\oplus2},\qquad A_{\mathfrak m}\text{ is not regular}.DerC​(A)≃A⊕2,Am​ is not regular.

The affine surface X=Spec⁡AX=\operatorname{Spec}AX=SpecA can be chosen smooth away from the marked singular point. The claim is therefore a counterexample with an isolated normal surface singularity and a globally free tangent sheaf.

The analytic precursor has one exceptional curve of genus 21 and self-intersection −10-10−10. M1 reports canonical discrepancy −5-5−5 and local geometric genus at least 33. Thus, for this resolution,

g=21,b=0,pg−g−b≥12.g=21,\qquad b=0,\qquad p_g-g-b\ge12.g=21,b=0,pg​−g−b≥12.

These values locate the proposed example beyond the earlier numerical smoothness criterion. The discrepancy is the coefficient measuring the change of the canonical divisor along the exceptional curve; log-canonical singularities require it to be at least −1-1−1.

Two further conclusions follow in the manuscript. First, the smooth locus U=XregU=X_{\mathrm{reg}}U=Xreg​ has logarithmic Kodaira dimension two, by applying an earlier theorem of Biswas–Gurjar–Kolte. Logarithmic Kodaira dimension measures the growth of canonical forms allowed logarithmic poles along a boundary compactifying UUU.

Second, repeatedly blowing up at the module of derivations does not resolve this singularity. The relevant blowup is designed to make the module locally free. Since it already is free, the operation is the identity; normalization also changes nothing because the surface is normal. This addresses the specific derivation-module procedure, not resolution of singularities by arbitrary blowups.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the construction would disprove a longstanding intrinsic criterion for smoothness in characteristic zero, in a dimension central to the remaining difficulty.

Vector fields are among the most basic local geometric objects. A free tangent sheaf looks formally like the tangent bundle of a smooth surface, so a counterexample would show that this module alone can miss singular geometry. The issue is not a shortage of vector fields but the failure of their algebraic organization to force coordinate directions.

The example would also clarify the reach of existing theorems. Their additional hypotheses—mild singularities, low resolution genus, grading, complete intersections, or commuting vector fields—carry essential information. The proposed counterexample does not negate those results; it would show why a general converse requires more than freeness.

6. The main idea

Start with a curve whose neighborhood can be changed

M1 chooses a smooth curve CCC of genus 21 and a degree-ten line bundle LLL satisfying

L⊗4≃KC.L^{\otimes4}\simeq K_C.L⊗4≃KC​.

The dual line bundle L−1L^{-1}L−1 has negative degree. Its zero section gives a starting neighborhood with normal bundle L−1L^{-1}L−1, but the manuscript modifies the holomorphic gluing of that neighborhood. This changes more than the normal bundle records.

In local base and fiber coordinates (z,t)(z,t)(z,t), the construction uses the meromorphic two-form

σ=t−5 dt∧dz.\sigma=t^{-5}\,dt\wedge dz.σ=t−5dt∧dz.

The aim is to build two vector fields whose determinant vanishes to exactly the required order along CCC, while remaining nonzero everywhere off CCC. They then form a tangent frame on the punctured neighborhood.

Match local corrections with global residue constraints

The leading coefficients of the fields have six common zeros on CCC. Correcting the determinant at those points requires local choices, but arbitrary choices need not glue around the whole curve.

An auxiliary elliptic curve and a trace pairing provide meromorphic data whose residues satisfy the needed global cancellation identities. The construction then extends the vector fields and their desired determinant through finitely many Taylor orders. Choosing determinant coefficients separately retains freedom to remove the compatibility obstructions.

The manuscript emphasizes a finite construction. It does not rely on asserting that an uncontrolled infinite sequence of neighborhood changes converges. Cohomological vanishing and formal-functions arguments are used to lift the finite data to actual holomorphic fields after shrinking the neighborhood.

Contract, then pass from analytic to algebraic geometry

Grauert’s contraction criterion collapses the negative curve to a point. The vector fields give a frame away from that point, and M1 uses normality to extend tangent freeness across it. Adjunction records that the resulting point is nonetheless singular.

The volume form dual to the frame has a fifth-order pole along the exceptional curve. The construction therefore does not assume the holomorphic extension of forms that powers many earlier positive results.

Finally, approximation and finite determinacy produce an algebraic local ring with the same completed local ring as the analytic singularity. Completion records all formal infinitesimal orders around the point. The manuscript keeps the equations and their relations together, then uses a Jacobian presentation and faithful flatness to descend freeness of derivations. Shrinking to one affine neighborhood gives the globally free module asserted in Theorem 1.1.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claimed surface is affine and noncompact. It does not contradict the compact classification result identifying compact complex surfaces with globally free rank-two tangent sheaf as complex tori.

Its tangent frame cannot be chosen commuting near the singular point, by the earlier commuting-frame theorem. A reader should therefore not interpret the two generators as the partial derivatives of a hidden coordinate chart.

The example also lies outside the known complete-intersection, graded-cone, and log-canonical affirmative settings. Its construction does not provide a universal classification of singularities with free tangent sheaf or a minimal possible value of the local geometric genus.

The derivation-blowup consequence is restricted to that prescribed operation. General resolution methods remain available in characteristic zero. A natural further question is which additional information about vector-field brackets or differential forms restores an effective smoothness criterion.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the algebraic endpoint. Sections 2–5 construct the analytic germ, Remark 5.5 records its resolution invariants, and Section 6 explains algebraization and the two further consequences.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 describe the earlier affirmative cases. Optional background on derivations and regular local rings helps connect the statement to ordinary differentiation and the algebraic definition of a smooth point.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A singular normal affine surface with free tangent sheaf (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 047 — Affine cancellation: when adding one coordinate hides the difference
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 047 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

If multiplying a geometric space by a line produces ordinary affine space, was the original space already affine space? This is Zariski’s affine-space cancellation problem.

The question resembles cancelling a common factor in arithmetic, but an isomorphism of products can mix the factors. Even if X×A1X\times\mathbb A^1X×A1 is isomorphic to A5\mathbb A^5A5, the new coordinates need not respect the projection onto the added line. Removing that line from the formula is therefore not a legitimate cancellation argument.

Family 047 contains one manuscript claiming an explicit negative answer over the complex numbers in dimension four. It gives a polynomial equation for a fourfold XXX, asserts that one extra variable turns its coordinate ring into a polynomial ring, and asserts that the original ring is not polynomial.

The same equation supplies two related claimed failures: a polynomial that becomes a coordinate only after stabilization, and smooth families all of whose fibers are affine three-space but which are not locally products in the Zariski topology.

2. Background and essential definitions

Affine space and its coordinate ring

Complex affine nnn-space An\mathbb A^nAn has polynomial coordinate ring C[x1,…,xn]\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]C[x1​,…,xn​]. A closed affine variety defined by equations has the quotient ring obtained by imposing those equations.

Algebraic isomorphism means polynomial maps in both directions, with polynomial inverses. This is stronger than being homeomorphic, diffeomorphic, or biholomorphic. A smooth variety can resemble Euclidean space in several ways without having a polynomial coordinate system.

If AAA is the coordinate ring of XXX, the cylinder X×A1X\times\mathbb A^1X×A1 has ring A[w]A[w]A[w], where www is an independent variable. Cancellation asks whether

A[w]≃C[x1,…,xn+1]⟹A≃C[x1,…,xn].A[w]\simeq\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]\quad\Longrightarrow\quadA\simeq\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n].A[w]≃C[x1​,…,xn+1​]⟹A≃C[x1​,…,xn​].

All isomorphisms here preserve the complex scalars.

Coordinates versus equations defining a simple fiber

A polynomial f∈C[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]f∈C[x1​,…,xn​] is a coordinate if it can be completed to a polynomial coordinate system:

C[x1,…,xn]=C[f,g2,…,gn].\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=\mathbb C[f,g_2,\ldots,g_n].C[x1​,…,xn​]=C[f,g2​,…,gn​].

For example, x+y2x+y^2x+y2 is a coordinate of C[x,y]\mathbb C[x,y]C[x,y], since (x,y)↦(x+y2,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x+y^2,y)(x,y)↦(x+y2,y) has inverse (u,v)↦(u−v2,v)(u,v)\mapsto(u-v^2,v)(u,v)↦(u−v2,v).

A coordinate has affine-space fibers. The reverse implication is a separate problem: knowing the quotient by (f)(f)(f) is polynomial does not, on its own, provide an ambient polynomial automorphism containing fff.

A polynomial is one-stably a coordinate if it becomes a coordinate after adjoining one independent variable. A residual coordinate over a parameter ring means it is a coordinate after passing to each residue field of that parameter ring. These properties concern stabilization and specialization respectively, and neither should be confused with already having global coordinates.

Families with affine-space fibers

An A3\mathbb A^3A3-fibration is a morphism whose fibers, including geometric fibers, are affine three-space. Being Zariski-locally trivial is stronger: over each member of an algebraic open cover of the base, the entire family must be isomorphic to the product of that open set with A3\mathbb A^3A3, compatibly with projection.

The Dolgachev–Weisfeiler question asks when affine-space fibers force this local product structure. It concerns polynomial families, not just whether nearby fibers look alike as differentiable manifolds.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cancellation is known for the affine line through work of Abhyankar, Heinzer, and Eakin. The complex affine-plane case was established through work of Fujita, Miyanishi, and Sugie, using the geometry of affine surfaces and cylinder-like open subsets.

Positive characteristic has a different history. Asanuma constructed polynomial-fiber rings with cylinders that are polynomial. Gupta showed that suitable examples are not affine three-space, giving counterexamples in dimension three. Her subsequent work established failure in every dimension at least three over fields of positive characteristic.

The higher-dimensional positive-characteristic result needs its own family of examples. Simply adding variables to a threefold whose first cylinder is already affine space would make the original obstruction disappear. This is also a useful warning when interpreting the dimension-four claim here.

Over characteristic zero, additive group actions have been central to recognizing spaces that are not affine space. Makar-Limanov’s work on the Russell cubic supplied a famous example distinguished through its locally nilpotent derivations. That result did not by itself provide the cylinder isomorphism required for affine-space cancellation.

Residual-coordinate methods address the other side of the problem: how adjoining a variable can simplify a polynomial. El Kahoui–Ouali, followed by Dutta–Lahiri, proved one-stability theorems under the relevant one-dimensional parameter hypotheses. M1 uses this established framework and gives explicit coordinate calculations for its example.

Thus two distinct tasks remain in a cancellation counterexample: construct the polynomial cylinder and show the original variety is not polynomial. The manuscript’s main new obstruction is directed at the second task. Gupta’s survey gives the broader history and links to the related coordinate and fibration problems.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The explicit fourfold

Take five independent variables p,s,u,F,Jp,s,u,F,Jp,s,u,F,J, and abbreviate

x=s2+u3+p2F.x=s^2+u^3+p^2F.x=s2+u3+p2F.

Define the polynomial

H=x2F−(1+2sx)J−p2J2−puH=x^2F-(1+2sx)J-p^2J^2-puH=x2F−(1+2sx)J−p2J2−pu

in those five variables, and let

A=C[p,s,u,F,J]/(H),X=Spec⁡A.A=\mathbb C[p,s,u,F,J]/(H),\qquad X=\operatorname{Spec}A.A=C[p,s,u,F,J]/(H),X=SpecA.

The symbol xxx is an abbreviation, not a sixth independent variable. Theorem 1.1 of M1 claims that AAA is an integral four-dimensional algebra and

A[w]≃C[t1,t2,t3,t4,t5],A≄C[t1,t2,t3,t4].A[w]\simeq\mathbb C[t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5],\qquadA\not\simeq\mathbb C[t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4].A[w]≃C[t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​,t5​],A≃C[t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​].

The subsequent fibration statement makes XXX smooth. Thus the claimed failure is not produced by a singularity that vanishes under an informal change of variables.

Stable coordinates

Corollary 1.2 claims that HHH is not a coordinate in the original five-variable polynomial ring, but becomes one in that ring with www adjoined. This is failure of the Stable Coordinate Conjecture in ambient dimension five after one stabilization.

The direction from the fourfold claim is straightforward to interpret: if HHH were already a coordinate, quotienting by it would leave a polynomial ring in four variables. Its asserted nonpolynomial quotient rules that out.

Two nontrivial affine-space families

M1 also claims that the maps

p:X⟶A1,(p,H):A5⟶A2p:X\longrightarrow\mathbb A^1,\qquad(p,H):\mathbb A^5\longrightarrow\mathbb A^2p:X⟶A1,(p,H):A5⟶A2

are smooth A3\mathbb A^3A3-fibrations and neither is Zariski-locally trivial. The source of the second map is ordinary affine space, making the distinction between simple total space and simple family structure particularly clear.

The manuscript states the affine-space condition over residue fields, not only after algebraic closure. These are claimed counterexamples in relative dimension three over the indicated smooth normal bases.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the example would give a negative answer to a central characteristic-zero recognition problem for affine space, with consequences for two closely connected conjectures.

Cancellation asks whether a polynomial coordinate system can hide essential geometry when one extra direction is available. An explicit counterexample would demonstrate that it can. It would also show that smoothness, affine-space fibers, and a polynomial cylinder do not together recover the missing global polynomial structure.

The equation makes the claim concrete, but its significance is structural rather than computational. The essential issue is whether every possible coordinate system or additive action can be ruled out on the fourfold, while still constructing one after stabilization.

6. The main idea

Make the cylinder polynomial

Away from p=0p=0p=0, the manuscript changes variables so that the equation is linear in one of them. At p=0p=0p=0, a separate linear change in F,JF,JF,J makes the reduced polynomial a coordinate. This establishes the claimed residual-coordinate behavior.

The explicit stabilization uses a locally nilpotent derivation DDD. This is a differentiation-like operator such that, for each polynomial aaa, some power Dk(a)D^k(a)Dk(a) vanishes. The exponential series therefore terminates on each element and defines an algebraic action of the additive group.

M1 constructs such an operator with D(H)=p3D(H)=p^3D(H)=p3. Exponentiating with the extra variable shifts the equation to H+p3wH+p^3wH+p3w. A further polynomial coordinate change, with its inverse supplied in the manuscript, produces the polynomial quotient. Divisibility conditions are retained at p=0p=0p=0; an isomorphism only after inverting ppp would not establish the cylinder theorem.

Assume coordinates exist and extract an impossible action

To distinguish AAA from a polynomial ring, M1 studies orders of vanishing along p=0p=0p=0 in an auxiliary algebra. These define a filtration and an associated graded ring, which keeps the leading terms for that filtration.

If AAA were polynomial, differentiating in a suitable polynomial coordinate would induce a nonzero homogeneous locally nilpotent derivation on this graded ring, with an invariant of positive degree. The manuscript then seeks to rule out precisely such an action.

It lifts the action to the complement of the zero section in a line bundle, where a relevant ideal becomes principal. There are two distinct measurements: the valuation degree coming from ppp, and the weight from scaling the line-bundle fibers. Keeping them separate converts the hypothetical action into a constrained derivation on an explicit determinant ring.

The final obstruction uses the polynomial Mason–Stothers abcabcabc inequality, which bounds degrees in polynomial identities, together with a nonsquare condition in the original fraction field. According to M1, these force the derivation to fix certain generators, while the determinant relation then forces a weight incompatible with the earlier constraint.

Why the fibrations cannot be locally products

If either claimed fibration were Zariski-locally a polynomial family, a theorem of Bass–Connell–Wright would identify its algebra with the symmetric algebra of a projective module over the base. Quillen–Suslin then makes that module free over these polynomial bases. The resulting global coordinates would contradict the nonpolynomiality or noncoordinate conclusion already obtained.

This consequence permits arbitrary polynomial transition maps in the proposed local trivializations; it is not merely a failure to be a vector bundle under preassigned linear transitions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The cancellation example is a complex fourfold. It does not settle characteristic-zero cancellation for affine three-space. Nor does it automatically yield counterexamples in every larger dimension by adjoining variables: the very first added variable is asserted to make this example polynomial.

The stable-coordinate consequence concerns ambient dimension five. The affine-fibration consequences have relative dimension three and the specific bases A1\mathbb A^1A1 and A2\mathbb A^2A2. They do not answer the corresponding relative-dimension-one or relative-dimension-two questions.

All distinctions are algebraic. The manuscript’s assertion that XXX is not affine four-space means no polynomial isomorphism exists; no broader conclusion about every analytic or topological comparison is needed for its theorem.

These limits leave open recognition questions in smaller dimensions and the search for additional hypotheses that force an affine-space fibration to become a locally trivial bundle.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the cancellation statement, Corollary 1.2 gives stable-coordinate failure, and Section 7 states the fibration consequences. Its introductory ring table separates the original algebra, its degeneration, and the line-bundle construction used in the obstruction.

The primary works linked in Section 3 explain the positive-characteristic precedent and the residual-coordinate machinery. For orientation, the Zariski cancellation problem provides useful terminology. The key logical distinction is between having affine-space fibers, being a polynomial family, and becoming polynomial after an extra variable is added.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An explicit failure of complex affine-space cancellation (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 049 — Affine space embedded in a way coordinates cannot straighten
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 049 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A copy of affine three-space can be described by a complicated equation inside affine four-space. Does its complicated appearance always disappear after a polynomial change of ambient coordinates?

The Abhyankar–Sathaye embedding conjecture predicts that a hypersurface isomorphic to affine space can be straightened into a coordinate hyperplane in characteristic zero. It concerns the embedding, not merely the abstract shape of the hypersurface.

Family 049 contains two manuscripts claiming explicit counterexamples in four variables. They demonstrate different phenomena. M1 gives a polynomial that is not a coordinate, becomes one after adding a single variable, and has every fiber isomorphic to affine three-space. M2 gives a different polynomial whose zero fiber is affine three-space but which has a critical point on another fiber.

The critical point makes M2’s obstruction easy to state and preserves it after adjoining any number of unused variables. M1 cannot use that obstruction: its stable-coordinate property requires a subtler argument involving additive group actions.

2. Background and essential definitions

Coordinates are global polynomial data

A polynomial f∈C[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]f∈C[x1​,…,xn​] is a coordinate if other polynomials complete it to a coordinate system:

C[x1,…,xn]=C[f,f2,…,fn].\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=\mathbb C[f,f_2,\ldots,f_n].C[x1​,…,xn​]=C[f,f2​,…,fn​].

Equivalently, a polynomial automorphism carries fff to the first standard coordinate. An automorphism requires a polynomial inverse, not just a locally invertible or analytic change of variables.

For example, x+y2x+y^2x+y2 is a coordinate in two variables because the change (x,y)↦(x+y2,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x+y^2,y)(x,y)↦(x+y2,y) is inverted by (u,v)↦(u−v2,v)(u,v)\mapsto(u-v^2,v)(u,v)↦(u−v2,v). Every fiber is a parabola, and the same ambient automorphism straightens all of them at once.

A polynomial is one-stably a coordinate if it becomes a coordinate after adjoining one new independent variable. The Stable Coordinate Conjecture asks whether this can happen without the polynomial already being a coordinate.

An abstract fiber and its embedding

The fiber f−1(λ)f^{-1}(\lambda)f−1(λ) has coordinate ring

C[x1,…,xn]/(f−λ).\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f-\lambda).C[x1​,…,xn​]/(f−λ).

Saying this ring is polynomial in n−1n-1n−1 variables describes the fiber intrinsically. An isomorphism may use formulas that work only after the equation f=λf=\lambdaf=λ has been imposed.

The embedding is rectifiable if a polynomial automorphism of the entire ambient affine space carries the fiber to a coordinate hyperplane. Extending coordinates off the fiber is the extra requirement. Thus even a full polynomial parametrization of the hypersurface need not solve the embedding problem.

The Abhyankar–Sathaye conjecture asks whether

C[x1,…,xn]/(f)≃C[t1,…,tn−1]⟹f is a coordinate.\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f)\simeq\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ is a coordinate}.C[x1​,…,xn​]/(f)≃C[t1​,…,tn−1​]⟹f is a coordinate.

Critical points give one obstruction

A critical point of fff is a point where all partial derivatives vanish. A coordinate polynomial has no critical points: it is a row of the Jacobian matrix of a polynomial automorphism, and that matrix is invertible everywhere.

This gives a useful asymmetry. A critical point anywhere in the ambient space disproves coordinateness, even when it lies far from the zero fiber. The zero fiber can still be perfectly smooth and abstractly affine space.

This obstruction is unavailable when the polynomial becomes a coordinate after adding unused variables, since its zero derivatives in those new directions would leave any old critical point intact.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The two-variable embedding problem is solved affirmatively by the Abhyankar–Moh theorem and Suzuki’s related work: an affine line embedded as such a plane curve can be straightened.

In three variables, important positive results impose conditions on the equation or its general fiber. Sathaye treated planes defined by polynomials linear in one variable, and Russell extended that result to arbitrary fields. Kaliman proved that a polynomial on C3\mathbb C^3C3 with general fiber C2\mathbb C^2C2 is a coordinate. This does not resolve the full three-variable embedding question from a single affine-plane fiber.

Together with curve and surface cancellation, these results imply the Stable Coordinate Conjecture over C\mathbb CC in at most three original variables, as explained by Shpilrain–Yu. Four variables are therefore the first possible dimension for M1’s stable-coordinate counterexample.

The Vénéreau polynomials have been important candidates and testing grounds in four variables. Lewis proved that the second Vénéreau polynomial is a coordinate. Blanc–Poloni developed affine-bundle and bivariable methods, revisited that result, and established one-stability for a wider family. Exhibiting stable coordinates was thus already possible; ruling out every original coordinate system remained the separate challenge.

For the embedding problem in four variables, Kaliman–Vénéreau–Zaidenberg and Maubach proved affirmative results for equations of the form a(x)y+b(x,z,t)a(x)y+b(x,z,t)a(x)y+b(x,z,t), with the coefficient depending on only one variable. More recent work of Ghosh, Gupta, and Pal treats related linear hypersurfaces under further hypotheses. M2 is designed outside those restricted equation classes.

Shpilrain–Yu used ambient critical loci to distinguish inequivalent embeddings and asked whether an affine-space zero fiber forces the gradient to be nowhere zero. M2 claims a negative answer, while M1 claims an obstruction even with every fiber affine space.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: degree five, all fibers affine, one stabilization sufficient

In four independent variables, put

Q=x22−x42+x1x3,f=x1−2Q(Q(x2+x4)+x1x4).Q=x_2^2-x_4^2+x_1x_3,\qquadf=x_1-2Q\bigl(Q(x_2+x_4)+x_1x_4\bigr).Q=x22​−x42​+x1​x3​,f=x1​−2Q(Q(x2​+x4​)+x1​x4​).

Theorem 1.1 of M1 claims that this degree-five polynomial is not a coordinate of C[x1,x2,x3,x4]\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]C[x1​,x2​,x3​,x4​], but becomes a coordinate after adjoining one variable www.

Corollary 1.2 states that for every λ∈C\lambda\in\mathbb Cλ∈C,

f−1(λ)≃A3,f^{-1}(\lambda)\simeq\mathbb A^3,f−1(λ)≃A3,

and that none of these embeddings in A4\mathbb A^4A4 is rectifiable. If any one fiber could be taken to a coordinate hyperplane, its prime principal ideal would be taken to the ideal of a coordinate. Its defining polynomial would differ from that coordinate by a nonzero constant factor, contradicting the asserted noncoordinateness of fff.

This simultaneously claims failure of stable coordinates in the smallest possible ambient dimension and failure of the embedding conjecture there.

M2: an affine zero fiber with a critical point elsewhere

Use four different independent variables h,u,v,wh,u,v,wh,u,v,w, and define

x=u3+hv,y=−u2+hw,x=u^3+hv,\qquad y=-u^2+hw,x=u3+hv,y=−u2+hw,
s=2u3v+3u4w+h(v2−3u2w2)+h2w3.s=2u^3v+3u^4w+h(v^2-3u^2w^2)+h^2w^3.s=2u3v+3u4w+h(v2−3u2w2)+h2w3.

These abbreviations satisfy x2+y3=hsx^2+y^3=hsx2+y3=hs. Set

p=−2s2x+3sy2−3s3y,F=h−p−1.p=-2s^2x+3sy^2-3s^3y,\qquad F=h-p-1.p=−2s2x+3sy2−3s3y,F=h−p−1.

Theorem 1.1 of M2 claims

C[h,u,v,w]/(F)≃C[t1,t2,t3],∇F(2,0,−1/2,1/2)=0.\mathbb C[h,u,v,w]/(F)\simeq\mathbb C[t_1,t_2,t_3],\qquad\nabla F(2,0,-1/2,1/2)=0.C[h,u,v,w]/(F)≃C[t1​,t2​,t3​],∇F(2,0,−1/2,1/2)=0.

The stated critical point lies on F=−1F=-1F=−1, not on the smooth zero fiber. Hence FFF is not a coordinate despite its affine-three-space zero fiber.

Adding independent variables preserves both the polynomial zero-fiber quotient and the critical point. M2 therefore claims embedding counterexamples in every ambient dimension at least four. In contrast, M1’s particular obstruction disappears after one added variable by design.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, these examples would settle major affine-embedding and stable-coordinate questions negatively, with explicit formulas in the first possible dimension for stable-coordinate failure.

They expose three distinct levels of information: one fiber is affine space; every fiber is affine space; the polynomial is a coordinate. The claimed examples separate all the implications needed for the corresponding conjectures.

M2 would show that the intrinsic simplicity of one fiber says little about critical behavior elsewhere. M1 goes further in a different direction: even uniform affine-space fibers would fail to provide a single ambient coordinate system. Stabilization would erase that obstruction.

Neither manuscript needs an exotic ambient variety. The ambient space is ordinary A4\mathbb A^4A4; the complexity lies in how a distinguished polynomial organizes it.

6. The main idea

M1: coordinates on the ring need not include the chosen element

M1 presents a four-variable polynomial ring as a hypersurface in five variables, with a distinguished element ppp. A determinant-preserving matrix substitution makes the defining equation linear in a new variable. Eliminating that variable identifies the quotient with a polynomial ring and turns ppp into the displayed degree-five fff.

A second explicit substitution, using the exponential of a locally nilpotent derivation, makes ppp part of a coordinate system after one extra variable. A locally nilpotent derivation acts like differentiation along an algebraic additive-group action; its exponential terminates on every polynomial.

To obstruct coordinateness before stabilization, the manuscript places an integer-indexed filtration on the ring, including negative degrees. If ppp were a coordinate, differentiating in another coordinate would induce a prohibited additive action on a simpler graded algebra associated with an affine quadric.

A line-bundle lift makes a key ideal principal. The generator has a highest part factoring as (au−d)(au+d)(au-d)(au+d)(au−d)(au+d). The resulting invariance constraints force a coefficient to be both a polynomial in variables of nonnegative weight and an element of negative weight. M1 presents this incompatibility as the final obstruction. It adapts the method of family 047, but here the original ring itself is already polynomial.

M2: use a cusp relation to build the affine fiber

M2 starts with the cusp parametrization (u3,−u2)(u^3,-u^2)(u3,−u2), for which x2+y3=0x^2+y^3=0x2+y3=0, and perturbs both entries by multiples of hhh. The quotient of x2+y3x^2+y^3x2+y3 by hhh supplies sss.

On the zero fiber, the translation

X=x+s3,Y=y−s2X=x+s^3,\qquad Y=y-s^2X=x+s3,Y=y−s2

turns an auxiliary relation into s=X2+Y3s=X^2+Y^3s=X2+Y3. This identifies an auxiliary algebra with a polynomial ring in two variables. A lifting lemma supplies the third variable by solving compatible linear equations whose coefficients generate the unit ideal.

That unit-ideal condition is important: it allows polynomial formulas valid everywhere, without dividing by a coefficient that could vanish. The appendix records coordinates and their polynomial inverse for the entire zero fiber.

The noncoordinate conclusion then comes from the separately stated critical point in the original ambient four-space. The construction distinguishes a global parametrization of the zero fiber from a global automorphism of the ambient space.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both constructions are over C\mathbb CC. M1 concerns a one-stable coordinate in four original variables, and M2 concerns an affine zero fiber with a persistent critical-point obstruction. M2 is not a stable-coordinate example; adjoining unused variables cannot remove its critical point.

The family does not give an affine-space cancellation counterexample in dimension three. In M1 the ambient fourfold and every fiber are already affine spaces; what allegedly fails is rectification of the chosen polynomial. Cancellation and coordinate questions have relationships, but their negations cannot be exchanged without an argument.

The three-variable Abhyankar–Sathaye problem from a single affine-plane fiber is not addressed. The earlier affirmative special cases remain distinct from the four-variable counterexamples claimed here.

Further questions include identifying additional hypotheses on an affine-space fibration that force a coordinate, and understanding how stabilization changes the possible polynomial embeddings.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the degree-five stable-coordinate claim and Corollary 1.2 its all-fibers consequence. M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the zero-fiber isomorphism and critical point, while its appendix provides explicit inverse coordinate maps.

The primary works linked above trace the low-dimensional embedding theorems, Vénéreau examples, and critical-locus approach. The useful distinction throughout is between coordinates on a hypersurface and coordinates on its entire ambient affine space.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A stable coordinate that is not a coordinate in four variables (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An explicit noncoordinate polynomial with affine three-space zero fibre (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 050 — Ample bundles without Griffiths-positive metrics on the quadric
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 050 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Algebraic geometry and differential geometry have different ways to say that a bundle is positive. Algebraic positivity asks whether enough sections eventually give a projective embedding. Differential positivity asks whether a metric has positive curvature in specified directions.

For line bundles on a smooth projective variety, these viewpoints agree. Griffiths’ conjecture asks whether the same is true for vector bundles: must an ample holomorphic vector bundle admit a smooth Hermitian metric with strictly Griffiths-positive curvature?

Family 050 contains one manuscript claiming counterexamples of rank two on the quadric surface P1×P1\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1P1×P1. Every member of its explicit family is ample, but all sufficiently large members are asserted to admit no metric of the required kind.

The manuscript credits an earlier 2026 counterexample of Du–Xie on an abelian surface. Its contribution is a different construction on a rational surface, an explicit family with quantified algebraic positivity, and a limiting obstruction applying to every smooth strictly positive Hermitian metric on the indicated members.

2. Background and essential definitions

Bundles and metrics

A rank-two holomorphic vector bundle EEE attaches a copy of C2\mathbb C^2C2 to every point of a complex manifold, with holomorphic changes of coordinates between local trivializations. A Hermitian metric is a smoothly varying positive-definite Hermitian inner product on those fibers.

In a local frame, its squared norm has the form

∥v∥h2=∑α,β=12hαβˉ(x)vαvβ‾.\|v\|_h^2=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{2}h_{\alpha\bar\beta}(x)v_\alpha\overline{v_\beta}.∥v∥h2​=α,β=1∑2​hαβˉ​​(x)vα​vβ​​.

The dependence on the fiber variable vvv is quadratic. This restriction will matter: more general homogeneous norms, called complex Finsler metrics, need not arise from an inner product.

The Hermitian metric determines the Chern connection, whose curvature records how the fiber geometry varies around infinitesimal loops in the base. Strict Griffiths positivity requires a positive curvature value for every nonzero base tangent direction ξ\xiξ and every nonzero fiber vector vvv. In local coefficients, the condition is

∑j,k,α,βcjkˉαβˉξjξk‾vαvβ‾>0.\sum_{j,k,\alpha,\beta}c_{j\bar k\alpha\bar\beta}\xi_j\overline{\xi_k}v_\alpha\overline{v_\beta}>0.j,k,α,β∑​cjkˉαβˉ​​ξj​ξk​​vα​vβ​​>0.

Semipositivity replaces >0>0>0 by ≥0\ge0≥0. Excluding strictly positive metrics does not automatically exclude semipositive ones.

Ampleness for a vector bundle

Let P(E)\mathbb P(E)P(E) parametrize one-dimensional quotients of the fibers of EEE. It carries a tautological quotient line bundle OP(E)(1)\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(E)}(1)OP(E)​(1). The vector bundle EEE is ample when this line bundle is ample, meaning some positive tensor power gives a projective embedding.

This definition tests the geometry of the projectivized bundle. It does not initially specify a quadratic norm on EEE itself. A strictly Griffiths-positive Hermitian metric implies ampleness; the conjecture asks for the converse.

A Finsler metric can have the homogeneity of a norm without the quadratic formula above. Positivity results allowing such metrics, or metrics on a determinant twist or symmetric power of EEE, are therefore not automatically statements about the original Hermitian problem.

The base and its power maps

The quadric surface is

S=P1×P1.S=\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1.S=P1×P1.

Its two projections give two families of projective lines, called rulings. The line bundle OS(a,b)\mathcal O_S(a,b)OS​(a,b) has degree aaa along one ruling and bbb along the other. Put P=OS(1,1)P=\mathcal O_S(1,1)P=OS​(1,1), which is ample.
