The map fm:S→Sf_m:S\to Sfm​:S→S raises homogeneous coordinates in each factor to their mmm-th powers. It is finite of degree m2m^2m2, and

fm∗P≃P⊗m.f_m^*P\simeq P^{\otimes m}.fm∗​P≃P⊗m.

Pullback changes the scale of the bundle’s geometry, while the family below adds only one fixed positive twist PPP.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hartshorne’s theory of ample vector bundles organized algebraic positivity through symmetric powers, generation, and the tautological line bundle. Griffiths’ differential-geometric formulation asked for a bridge from such algebraic positivity to a curvature condition on a Hermitian metric.

The bridge is established for line bundles. It is also established for vector bundles on compact complex curves, through work of Umemura and Campana–Flenner, with later analytic approaches including Murakami’s work. Thus rank two and base dimension two are the first possible dimensions for the phenomenon claimed here.

Other positive results modify the bundle. Berndtsson proved Nakano positivity for E⊗det⁡EE\otimes\det EE⊗detE when EEE is ample. Nakano positivity is stronger than Griffiths positivity, but the determinant twist is part of the conclusion. Liu–Sun–Yang obtained further positivity statements for symmetric powers and determinant-twisted bundles. These results do not simply remove the twist and produce the conjectured metric on EEE.

Kobayashi characterized ampleness through negatively curved strongly pseudoconvex Finsler structures on the dual bundle. The freedom to use a nonquadratic norm is crucial. Demailly’s later analytic systems and curvature functionals sought to recover the more restrictive Hermitian structure.

A recent obstruction of Lempert concerns a prescribed equivariant rule for constructing a Hermitian metric from a tautological metric. As M1 notes, those examples still admit positive Hermitian metrics by other means. Failure of one construction rule is weaker than nonexistence of every positive metric.

Most directly, Du–Xie’s preprint of 22 September 2026 states an ample rank-two bundle on an abelian surface without any smooth Griffiths-semipositive Hermitian metric. M1 explicitly credits that earlier claim and gives a different family on the quadric, with the weaker metric exclusion of strict positivity.

A subsequent Liu–Wan preprint of 29 September 2026 states examples on every Hirzebruch surface with additional stability and a stronger Finsler-curvature exclusion. Its curvature condition is on the original bundle, whereas Kobayashi’s ampleness characterization uses negative curvature on the dual. These are related developments with different conclusions and constructions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 of M1 asserts an explicitly constructed rank-two algebraic bundle GGG on SSS for which

Em=fm∗G⊗PE_m=f_m^*G\otimes PEm​=fm∗​G⊗P

is ample for every positive integer mmm. It further claims an integer m0m_0m0​ such that for every m≥m0m\ge m_0m≥m0​, the bundle EmE_mEm​ has no smooth Hermitian metric with strictly Griffiths-positive curvature.

The quantifiers differ on the two sides. Ampleness holds for all m≥1m\ge1m≥1; metric nonexistence is asserted for all sufficiently large mmm. The theorem does not identify which of the finitely many smaller values admit such metrics.

The ampleness statement comes with a numerical bound. Proposition 3.1 states that

OP(Em)(n)is very ample whenever n is even and n−1≥3m.\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(E_m)}(n)\quad\text{is very ample whenever }n\text{ is even and }n-1\ge3m.OP(Em​)​(n)is very ample whenever n is even and n−1≥3m.

“Very ample” means the line bundle itself supplies a projective embedding. This is a concrete statement about enough algebraic sections. In contrast, the threshold m0m_0m0​ is obtained by compactness and is ineffective: the manuscript gives no explicit numerical value.

The excluded metrics are smooth, Hermitian, and strictly Griffiths-positive. Singular metrics, semipositive metrics, nonquadratic Finsler structures, and metrics on modified bundles are different questions unless specifically addressed by another theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the construction would exhibit a broad family separating algebraic ampleness from smooth Hermitian curvature positivity on a particularly simple surface.

The central conjecture already has an earlier counterexample claim credited in the source. This family’s significance is therefore its specific rational base, explicit pullback-and-twist construction, all-parameter ampleness bound, and general limiting argument. It should not be described as having sole priority for the negative answer.

The geometric lesson is substantial: plenty of sections of the tautological bundle need not organize themselves into a smoothly varying quadratic norm with positive curvature on the original vector bundle. Fiberwise quadratic structure is additional information, not a harmless choice of notation.

The result would also distinguish flexibility gained by determinant twists or Finsler norms from the original metric problem. Those positive theories can remain valid while the Hermitian converse fails.

6. The main idea

Encode incompatible symmetries in a bundle

Choose two projective transformations A,BA,BA,B of P1\mathbb P^1P1, each of order three, with no common fixed point, but such that their product acts, after a coordinate change, like

z⟼λz,∣λ∣>1.z\longmapsto\lambda z,\qquad |\lambda|>1.z⟼λz,∣λ∣>1.

The manuscript gives explicit matrix lifts and arranges finite orders for the relative lifts needed at graph intersections. Consider the three graphs of the identity, AAA, and BBB inside SSS.

The bundle GGG is built from pairs of sections of two line bundles, one positive along each ruling, required to agree along those graphs through prescribed identifications. This is an elementary transformation. Compatibility at intersections makes the construction locally free rather than merely a singular sheaf.

Two quotient-line-bundle sequences then control symmetric powers of GGG. Alternating their filtrations and adding the positive twist supplies the stated very-ampleness bound for every EmE_mEm​.

Positive metrics would produce a nonzero quadratic limit

Assume positive metrics exist for infinitely many mmm. Their dual squared norms are plurisubharmonic: restriction to every holomorphic disc has the subharmonic mean-value property.

M1 averages these norms over the finite power maps and normalizes them. The twisting factor becomes asymptotically negligible. Its compactness argument produces a finite nonnegative plurisubharmonic function on G∗G^*G∗ that is a Hermitian quadratic form on every fiber and is not identically zero.

The limit may lose rank, so it is permitted to be only a seminorm. What must survive is nonzero mass and quadratic behavior even over the graph divisor. An almost-everywhere statement alone would not retain the relations imposed there.

The limit would force an impossible invariant measure

On either dual line subbundle, compactness of the opposite projective-line direction forces the limiting seminorm to be independent of that direction. The graph identifications therefore produce one nonzero seminorm on a negative line bundle over P1\mathbb P^1P1, invariant under both AAA and BBB.

Taking curvature in the sense of distributions yields a finite positive measure of nonzero total mass. Invariance under the expanding product ABABAB forces that measure to be supported on its two fixed points: successive disjoint annuli otherwise all have the same positive mass, contradicting finiteness.

Both order-three transformations preserve this support. An order-three permutation of at most two points must fix each point, so they would have a common fixed point, contrary to their construction. This excludes the limiting quadratic object and hence excludes an infinite sequence of positive-metric parameters. Only finitely many small mmm can remain.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the stated rank-two family on P1×P1\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1P1×P1. It does not assert that every ample rank-two bundle on that surface lacks positive metrics; direct sums of suitable positive line bundles provide familiar positive examples.

There is no explicit value of m0m_0m0​, so the claim does not identify a numerically specified first counterexample in the family. The explicit construction of GGG and the effective very-ampleness bound do not make the metric threshold effective.

Strict positivity is essential to the reported exclusion. The theorem should not be upgraded to nonexistence of semipositive Hermitian metrics or every Finsler structure by borrowing conclusions from different examples in the cited literature.

Natural further questions concern the smallest failing parameter, additional hypotheses restoring Hermitian positivity, and the exact relationship among algebraic positivity, singular metrics, and nonquadratic curvature conditions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the family and threshold; Proposition 3.1 gives the very-ampleness bound; Proposition 4.1 gives the limiting quadratic object; Section 5 supplies the invariant-measure obstruction.

The primary historical sources linked above separate the curve theorem, twisted-bundle results, Finsler characterization, and recent counterexample claims. Background on Hermitian vector bundles helps with the metric language. The distinction between a quadratic Hermitian norm and a more general homogeneous norm is the key point throughout.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Ample rank-two bundles on the quadric surface without Griffiths-positive metrics (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 051 — Hyperbolicity forces an ample canonical bundle
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 051 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A compact complex manifold is hyperbolic when holomorphic maps into it are strongly constrained. One concrete formulation says that every holomorphic map from the whole complex plane must be constant. Can this prohibition on curves force the manifold to have enough top-degree differential forms to embed in projective space?

Kobayashi’s canonical-ampleness conjecture predicts that it can, for compact Kähler manifolds. The conclusion is about the canonical line bundle, which packages holomorphic forms of top degree. Its ampleness would connect an analytic restriction on one-dimensional maps with global algebraic positivity in every dimension.

Family 051 contains one manuscript claiming this implication for every smooth compact connected Kähler manifold of positive complex dimension. Projectivity is a conclusion, not an assumption. The claimed advance replaces a negative-curvature metric hypothesis from major earlier theorems by hyperbolicity itself.

2. Background and essential definitions

Entire curves and two notions of hyperbolicity

An entire curve in XXX is a holomorphic map C→X\mathbb C\to XC→X. It need not be an embedding, proper, or algebraic. A manifold is Brody hyperbolic if every such map is constant.

The Kobayashi pseudodistance is an intrinsic distance-like function built by joining holomorphic discs and measuring lengths using the hyperbolic geometry of the unit disc. It may assign distance zero to distinct points. Kobayashi hyperbolicity means it is a genuine distance.

Brody’s theorem makes these two conditions equivalent for compact complex manifolds. Compactness is essential to this equivalence as used here. Throughout this digest, hyperbolicity refers to that compact setting.

A compact hyperbolic manifold contains neither rational nor elliptic curves. A nonconstant map from either kind of curve would yield a nonconstant entire curve after using the usual plane parametrization or universal cover. The converse is false: ruling out only rational curves is a substantially weaker requirement.

The canonical bundle

For a complex nnn-fold, the canonical bundle is

KX=⋀n(T1,0X)∗.K_X=\bigwedge^n(T^{1,0}X)^*.KX​=⋀n​(T1,0X)∗.

Locally its sections are expressions f(z) dz1∧⋯∧dznf(z)\,dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_nf(z)dz1​∧⋯∧dzn​. Sections of KX⊗mK_X^{\otimes m}KX⊗m​ are called pluricanonical forms. If sufficiently many of them separate points and tangent directions, they define a projective embedding.

A line bundle is ample if some positive power defines such an embedding. It is nef if its curvature can be made arbitrarily close to nonnegative, allowing an arbitrarily small negative error relative to a fixed Kähler form. It is big if its spaces of sections grow at the maximal rate proportional to mnm^nmn.

These are different properties. Nefness can occur with zero top self-intersection and very few sections. Bigness supplies many sections, but does not alone guarantee an embedding everywhere. Ampleness is the desired final conclusion.

A curve provides the model

For a compact Riemann surface of genus ggg,

deg⁡KX=2g−2.\deg K_X=2g-2.degKX​=2g−2.

The hyperbolic cases have g≥2g\ge2g≥2, so the canonical bundle has positive degree and is ample. The conjecture asks for a higher-dimensional analogue without assuming a uniformizing disc or a particular negatively curved metric in advance.

A Kähler manifold has a positive closed differential two-form compatible with its complex structure. This is a strong geometric condition, but it does not by itself imply that the manifold is projective.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kobayashi’s intrinsic metric theory and Brody’s compactness theorem established the connection between entire curves and hyperbolicity. The canonical-ampleness question asks how that analytic notion interacts with birational and projective geometry.

A major advance was Wu–Yau’s theorem: a smooth projective manifold with a Kähler metric of negative holomorphic sectional curvature has ample canonical bundle. Holomorphic sectional curvature measures curvature along complex tangent lines.

Tosatti–Yang extended this conclusion to compact Kähler manifolds without assuming projectivity. Diverio–Trapani treated quasi-negative holomorphic sectional curvature, where curvature is nonpositive everywhere and strictly negative in every nonzero tangent direction at one point. Further work allows certain Hermitian metrics while retaining a Kähler ambient manifold.

These results provide crucial analytic precedents, but negative curvature is additional structure. The absence of entire curves does not hand us a smooth metric with the curvature inequalities those arguments use. Removing that extra hypothesis is the gap addressed by M1.

Another affirmative theory uses Kähler hyperbolicity in Gromov’s sense: a Kähler form becomes the exterior derivative of a bounded one-form on the universal cover. Gromov established general-type consequences, and Chen–Yang proved canonical ampleness under that hypothesis. This is a distinct definition and must not be substituted for Brody hyperbolicity merely because both names include “hyperbolic.”

Nefness is also a different, weaker stage of the problem. M1 credits Ou’s uniruledness characterization and Cao–Höring’s rational-curve theorem with giving nefness of the canonical bundle when a compact Kähler manifold contains no rational curves. The further difficulty is to force positive canonical volume and then ampleness.

M1 proposes to obtain that missing quantitative positivity directly from extremal holomorphic discs, using derivative bounds supplied by compact hyperbolicity.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 states that if XXX is compact, connected, Kähler, and of complex dimension n≥1n\ge1n≥1, then

every holomorphic C→X is constant⟹KX is ample.\text{every holomorphic }\mathbb C\to X\text{ is constant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_X\text{ is ample}.every holomorphic C→X is constant⟹KX​ is ample.

In particular, some positive power of KXK_XKX​ defines a holomorphic embedding into complex projective space. The conclusion includes projectivity even when none was assumed initially.

The theorem imposes no prescribed curvature bound on a chosen metric and no restriction to a known class of projective examples. It is stated for smooth manifolds; singular spaces require separate formulations.

Consequences using other manuscript claims

Corollary 10.1 combines canonical ampleness with the Fujita freeness claim in family 038 to state that

KX⊗m is globally generated for every m≥n+2.K_X^{\otimes m}\text{ is globally generated for every }m\ge n+2.KX⊗m​ is globally generated for every m≥n+2.

Global generation means that at every point some section is nonzero. It does not mean that this particular power necessarily gives an embedding; separating points and tangent directions is stronger.

Corollary 10.2 adds an extra assumption: the ordinary universal cover is biholomorphic to a semialgebraic open subset of a projective variety. Semialgebraic means described in affine charts by finitely many real polynomial equalities and inequalities, combined by Boolean operations.

Using the classification claimed in family 058, M1 then obtains a connected finite unramified cover of XXX of the form

(D/Γ0)×F.(D/\Gamma_0)\times F.(D/Γ0​)×F.

Here DDD is a bounded symmetric domain, Γ0\Gamma_0Γ0​ acts freely and cocompactly, and FFF is a simply connected compact hyperbolic projective manifold. Either factor may be a point. Neither companion result is used in the principal canonical-ampleness argument.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem would settle a central conjecture linking complex hyperbolicity to algebraic positivity in the smooth compact Kähler category.

Its hypothesis concerns only holomorphic maps from a one-dimensional noncompact source. Its conclusion produces a positive line bundle governing the entire manifold and an embedding into projective space. This is a strong bridge between analysis and algebraic geometry.

The distinction from earlier negative-curvature theorems is substantial. A theorem from hyperbolicity alone would apply without first solving a separate metric-existence problem. It would also turn projectivity into a consequence of the analytic restriction.

The statement has one direction. It does not say that every manifold with ample canonical bundle is hyperbolic; positive canonical geometry does not automatically exclude every entire curve. Retaining this direction is essential to understanding both its strength and its limits.

6. The main idea

Replace curvature assumptions with an extremal-disc problem

Fix a background Kähler metric kkk on XXX. Compact hyperbolicity supplies a uniform upper bound DDD for the squared norm of the derivative at the center of every holomorphic unit disc.

M1 considers discs with a fixed center and finite area. It maximizes a functional combining the central derivative, a weighted integral of a closed two-form, and a negative area penalty. The penalty controls escape in the optimization problem.

The difficult point is the boundary. Convergence on compact subsets of the open disc does not automatically justify differentiating an integral over the whole disc. The manuscript first obtains boundary regularity from maximality, then constructs a holomorphic frame normalized on the boundary and actual variations that keep the disc’s center fixed.

One Hessian identity supplies two estimates

For a Kähler metric hhh, write its Ricci form as

Rh=−i∂∂ˉlog⁡det⁡h.R_h=-i\partial\bar\partial\log\det h.Rh​=−i∂∂ˉlogdeth.

M1 computes the sum of second derivatives of the area functional along its special variations. The resulting identity relates that Hessian to the integral of RhR_hRh​.

One choice of parameters supplies bounded canonical potentials and hence nefness. A second gives the stated pointwise estimate

hn≥e−D(n2n+D)nknwhenever Rh≥−h.h^n\ge e^{-D}\left(\frac{n}{2n+D}\right)^n k^n\qquad\text{whenever }R_h\ge-h.hn≥e−D(2n+Dn​)nknwhenever Rh​≥−h.

The forms hnh^nhn and knk^nkn are volume forms. The inequality says a whole family of qualifying metrics cannot collapse its volume density to zero, with the bound controlled by the fixed background data. The conclusion is quantitative even though the optimizing discs themselves can vary with the metric.

Convert a volume lower bound into algebraic positivity

Following the Monge–Ampère strategy used in the earlier Wu–Yau theory, M1 solves for metrics hth_tht​ in the classes

2πc1(KX)+t[k],t>0,2\pi c_1(K_X)+t[k],\qquad t>0,2πc1​(KX​)+t[k],t>0,

with Rht=−ht+tkR_{h_t}=-h_t+tkRht​​=−ht​+tk. The volume estimate persists as ttt tends to zero and gives

∫Xc1(KX)n>0.\int_Xc_1(K_X)^n>0.∫X​c1​(KX​)n>0.

Together with nefness, established holomorphic Morse inequalities make KXK_XKX​ big. Its sections then make XXX Moishezon, meaning it has as many algebraically independent meromorphic functions as its dimension. A compact Kähler Moishezon manifold is projective.

Finally, established cone-theorem arguments use the absence of rational curves to upgrade the canonical positivity to ampleness. The manuscript’s new analytic estimate is intended to supply the missing positive-volume step; the later passage through bigness and projectivity uses existing results.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Compactness and the Kähler condition are explicit hypotheses. The theorem does not assert the same conclusion for arbitrary noncompact hyperbolic manifolds or all compact non-Kähler manifolds. Boundary geometry changes the appropriate positivity question in the noncompact case.

Hyperbolicity means no nonconstant entire curves, not merely no rational curves. The weaker condition supports nefness in the cited theory but does not supply the full conclusion here.

The theorem also does not construct a metric of negative holomorphic sectional curvature from hyperbolicity. Its analytic method seeks canonical positivity directly, so it should not be reported as settling that stronger metric-existence question.

The effective global-generation exponent uses family 038, and the finite-cover product uses family 058 plus the additional semialgebraic hypothesis. Neither is an unconditional classification of all compact hyperbolic Kähler manifolds. The general structure of such manifolds and their universal covers remains a broader problem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives canonical ampleness. Sections 3–7 explain the disc optimization, boundary variations, and two estimates; Sections 8–9 make the transition to projective geometry. Section 10 labels the two companion-dependent consequences separately.

The primary papers linked above trace the negative-curvature and rational-curve predecessors. Optional background on the Kobayashi metric and canonical bundle helps connect the analytic hypothesis to the algebraic conclusion.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Canonical ampleness of compact hyperbolic Kähler manifolds (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Nagata’s conjecture and the cost of imposing many multiple points
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 039 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

How complicated must a plane curve be to pass through many prescribed points with high multiplicity? A line can pass through two general points, while a cubic has more freedom. Requiring not only passage but repeated vanishing consumes additional freedom, and the interaction between these conditions can be subtle.

Nagata’s conjecture predicts the exact square-root scale once there are at least ten very general points. Family 039 claims its strict form, allowing different multiplicities at different points. Three companions broaden the question to local positivity on arbitrary polarized varieties and to fields of positive characteristic.

The broader claims are eventual exact equalities: for every point count beyond a threshold depending on the variety and polarization, a Seshadri constant reaches its volume upper bound. That is stronger than approaching the bound as the number of points grows, but it does not give the same sharp threshold ten in all settings.

2. Background and essential definitions

Multiple points as linear conditions

A degree-ddd plane curve is the zero set of a homogeneous polynomial in three variables. Its coefficient space has dimension (d+22)\binom{d+2}{2}(2d+2​). At a point, multiplicity at least mmm means that all local terms of total degree below mmm vanish. On a smooth surface this imposes at most (m+12)\binom{m+1}{2}(2m+1​) linear conditions.

For rrr points with equal multiplicity mmm, the leading terms of these counts balance when

d22≈rm22,ord≈mr.\frac{d^2}{2}\approx\frac{rm^2}{2},\qquad\text{or}\qquad d\approx m\sqrt r.2d2​≈2rm2​,ord≈mr​.

The count explains the predicted scale, but does not prove independence of the conditions. Special configurations, unexpected components, or dependencies can allow a curve even when a naive dimension count predicts none.

An effective curve may be reducible, and components may repeat. Multiplicity includes these repetitions. A nonzero effective curve has positive degree; no irreducibility assumption is made in the plane theorem.

“Very general” is a simultaneous condition

A property holds at very general tuples if its exceptional tuples lie in a countable union of proper algebraic closed subsets of the configuration space. Over C\mathbb CC, such a complement is nonempty. This is stronger than avoiding one obvious special configuration, such as collinearity.

Here the exceptional set must work simultaneously for every degree and every multiplicity vector. A new exceptional set chosen separately for each curve after seeing the tuple would not give the desired statement.

In positive characteristic, the algebraic closure of a finite field is countable. The companion therefore states its result at a geometric generic tuple: the universal tuple over an algebraic closure of the configuration space’s function field. This gives a precise notion of unrestricted algebraic general position without claiming the existence of a suitable tuple over a countable constant field itself.

Seshadri constants measure local positivity

Let XXX be a smooth projective nnn-fold and LLL an ample line bundle. Ampleness means some positive power defines a projective embedding. For distinct points p1,…,prp_1,\ldots,p_rp1​,…,pr​, the ordinary multipoint Seshadri constant is

ε(X,L;p1,…,pr)=inf⁡CL⋅C∑i=1rmult⁡piC,\varepsilon(X,L;p_1,\ldots,p_r)=\inf_C\frac{L\cdot C}{\sum_{i=1}^r\operatorname{mult}_{p_i}C},ε(X,L;p1​,…,pr​)=Cinf​∑i=1r​multpi​​CL⋅C​,

where CCC runs over integral curves meeting at least one marked point. The numerator is the degree of LLL on the curve; the denominator counts how strongly the curve concentrates at the points. Multiplicity is zero at a point outside the curve.

Blowing up the points replaces each point by its tangent directions, giving exceptional divisors EiE_iEi​ and a map π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X. The same constant is the largest t≥0t\geq0t≥0 for which

π∗L−t∑i=1rEi\pi^*L-t\sum_{i=1}^rE_iπ∗L−ti=1∑r​Ei​

is nef, meaning nonnegative on every curve. Thus it measures how much equal local weight can be subtracted while retaining numerical positivity.

If V=LnV=L^nV=Ln is the top self-intersection, the volume bound is

ε(X,L;p1,…,pr)≤(V/r)1/n.\varepsilon(X,L;p_1,\ldots,p_r)\leq(V/r)^{1/n}.ε(X,L;p1​,…,pr​)≤(V/r)1/n.

At that value, the displayed blowup class has top self-intersection zero. In higher dimensions these manuscripts still use the ordinary constant defined by curves, not a different invariant defined by higher-dimensional cycles.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nagata’s 1959 work on Hilbert’s fourteenth problem led to the plane interpolation conjecture and proved its square-point-count cases from sixteen onward. Square counts admit configurations and estimates that do not automatically extend to nonsquares.

Later degeneration methods and rational lower bounds brought the constants close to the predicted value. For ten very general plane points, the bound d/m≥117/37d/m\geq117/37d/m≥117/37 is a notable predecessor discussed in M1. Since 117/37117/37117/37 is close to 10\sqrt{10}10​, the remaining numerical gap is small, but closing it must work for arbitrarily large multiplicities. Checking finitely many multiplicities does not suffice.

The problem extends naturally to arbitrary polarized surfaces through Seshadri constants. Biran’s symplectic packing theorem provides a related stability phenomenon for many equal balls. However, symplectic packing allows geometric flexibility that does not itself prove nefness on blowups of a fixed complex variety. The algebraic and symplectic conclusions must be distinguished.

Harbourne established important square-volume and asymptotic cases. Roé–Ross related constants for different point counts through product inequalities. In higher dimensions, Küchle obtained asymptotically optimal lower bounds. These results explain why the volume bound is the right scale, but do not by themselves imply exact equality for every sufficiently large integer count.

The interpolation techniques used here have direct precedents in Ciliberto–Miranda’s degenerations, Evain’s infinitesimal limits, and Dumnicki’s monomial diagrams. Valuation descriptions of linear series and finite-degree jet comparisons supply a further route from geometry to exponent counting. M1–M4 identify these antecedents while distinguishing their new uniformity claims.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the strict plane inequality

For every integer r≥10r\geq10r≥10, M1 claims that at very general complex plane points, every nonzero effective curve of degree ddd, with multiplicities at least nonnegative integers mim_imi​, satisfies

∑i=1rmi<dr.\sum_{i=1}^r m_i<d\sqrt r.i=1∑r​mi​<dr​.

The inequality is strict, permits unequal multiplicities, and includes reducible and nonreduced curves. At nine points a cubic always exists, so the strict statement cannot start there: its total multiplicity is at least nine, equal to 393\sqrt939​.

For the plane polarization OP2(1)\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)OP2​(1), the consequence is

ε(P2,O(1);p1,…,pr)=1r.\varepsilon(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O(1);p_1,\ldots,p_r)=\frac1{\sqrt r}.ε(P2,O(1);p1​,…,pr​)=r​1​.

When rrr is nonsquare this is irrational. Strictness for each individual curve is consistent with equality of the infimum: curve ratios can approach a value without attaining it. The associated real blowup class has square zero and positive intersection with every curve; that does not make it ample.

M2: arbitrary polarized surfaces

For every smooth integral complex projective surface SSS and ample LLL, M2 claims a threshold r0(S,L)r_0(S,L)r0​(S,L) such that, for each integer r≥r0r\geq r_0r≥r0​,

ε(S,L;p1,…,pr)=L2/r\varepsilon(S,L;p_1,\ldots,p_r)=\sqrt{L^2/r}ε(S,L;p1​,…,pr​)=L2/r​

at very general tuples. The threshold may depend on the polarized surface, and no sharp explicit universal value is asserted. The plane theorem’s strict inequality and threshold ten are a separate refinement.

M3: higher complex dimensions

M3 claims that for every smooth integral complex projective variety of dimension n≥3n\geq3n≥3 and every ample LLL, all sufficiently large point counts satisfy

ε(X,L;p1,…,pr)=(Ln/r)1/n\varepsilon(X,L;p_1,\ldots,p_r)=(L^n/r)^{1/n}ε(X,L;p1​,…,pr​)=(Ln/r)1/n

at very general tuples. Again, the threshold depends on (X,L)(X,L)(X,L). This is exact for each such rrr, rather than a limiting ratio as r→∞r\to\inftyr→∞. The paper adapts the surface method but states that its proof does not use the surface maximality theorem as an input.

M4: positive characteristic

M4 asserts the same eventual maximality at geometric generic tuples for smooth integral projective varieties over any algebraically closed field of characteristic p>0p>0p>0, in dimensions at least two. Characteristic two is included.

The claim is qualitative in the point count and uses the ordinary curve-defined constant. It does not assert the plane threshold ten or strict Nagata inequality for every positive characteristic. The chosen generic-field formulation is part of the statement, not merely a change in terminology.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The plane claim resolves a central interpolation conjecture with exact constants, while the companions assert broad maximal local positivity for arbitrary polarizations and dimensions. The family connects curve geometry, linear systems, blowup cones, and packing-type questions.

Exact irrational Seshadri constants are particularly informative: every individual curve contributes a rational degree-to-multiplicity ratio, yet their infimum can be irrational. Such a boundary is not detected by one exceptional curve computing the minimum.

The result also distinguishes two kinds of uniformity. The plane bound works at every count from ten onward. The general statements allow a variety-dependent threshold but must work above it for every degree and every jet order.

6. The main idea

Turn a geometric counterexample into a rank problem

M1 uses closed incidence conditions to turn a hypothetical failure at very general points into systems existing at all configurations. Multiplying over permutations equalizes the multiplicities. Points are then moved toward a smooth auxiliary curve, producing a polynomial on its normal bundle.

For nonsquare point counts, a cubic supplies an elliptic curve. After further collisions, the required vanishing implies a kernel in a finite jet-evaluation matrix. A theta-function degeneration gives explicit limiting bases whose derivatives become powers of integer exponents. The question becomes whether a concrete matrix has full column rank.

Counting only the total number of exponents is insufficient. M1 groups them into rows and uses interpolation row by row. Polygon widths control the possible row sizes, and the strict gap below r\sqrt rr​ absorbs rounding errors. Full rank contradicts the required kernel.

Surface positivity through injective jet tests

A jet records Taylor coefficients up to a specified order. An injective jet test means that a section vanishing to the required order at every test point must be zero. M2 constructs such tests for sections whose equal vanishing would exceed the critical Seshadri slope.

A nodal curve on the surface constrains leading exponents to polygons. Changes of lattice direction and finite torus subgroups adapt the test to every sufficiently large integer rrr, not only square grids. The subgroup and shape are chosen before the arbitrarily large jet orders.

Open rank conditions transfer successful tests to very general tuples. A further intersection and section argument turns exclusion of equal-order sections into a bound against all curves, including those with unequal point multiplicities.

Higher dimensions through surjective tests

M3 instead constructs surjective jet maps: enough sections to prescribe all required Taylor data independently at the marked points. Jet separation through order aaa by sections of kLkLkL gives a lower bound ε≥a/k\varepsilon\geq a/kε≥a/k.

Leading exponents form finite sets SkS_kSk​ with the multiplication property

Sk+Sℓ⊆Sk+ℓ.S_k+S_\ell\subseteq S_{k+\ell}.Sk​+Sℓ​⊆Sk+ℓ​.

The manuscript reshapes the containing simplex two coordinates at a time, preserving both the relevant section counts and this multiplication rule. Full asymptotic density can then be upgraded to exact filling of compact regions inside the simplex. One-variable Hermite interpolation along its long direction separates jets at rrr points.

M4 replaces analytic limits by formal algebraic substitutions and uses interpolation through the Chinese remainder theorem, valid in every characteristic. Its nodal equation retains two distinct branches even in characteristic two. Each finite test holds on a nonempty open set, and therefore at the geometric generic tuple.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Very general position is essential. Special configurations can lie on low-degree curves and have smaller constants. The results do not furnish the same bounds for an arbitrary tuple supplied by coordinates.

The surface and higher-dimensional statements give eventual exact equality with a threshold depending on the polarized variety. They do not determine that threshold, nor do they give exact values for every small point count. M1’s strict plane conclusion is stronger in this particular respect.

The positive-characteristic result is stated at geometric generic tuples. Over a countable algebraically closed field, it should not be paraphrased as a guarantee about constant-field points outside a countable exceptional union.

Further questions include effective thresholds, special point configurations, and weighted analogues with unequal subtraction parameters. The family permits unequal multiplicities of test curves while defining an equal-weight Seshadri constant; these are different notions of “unequal.” The manuscripts are reported as stated without proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 states strict Nagata and §§2–5 develop the collision and rank argument. M2 §§1 and 4–5 explain the surface threshold, torus tests, and passage to nefness. M3 §§1 and 4–6 give reshaping, interior filling, and higher-dimensional jet separation. M4 §§1–2 specify the geometric generic convention and characteristic-independent transfers.

The linked Nagata, Biran, Roé–Ross, and Evain sources give primary historical context. An optional introduction to Seshadri constants expands on the local-positivity interpretation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Nagata’s conjecture for plane curves (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Maximal Seshadri constants on arbitrary polarized surfaces (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Maximal Multipoint Seshadri Constants in Higher Dimensions (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Maximal multipoint Seshadri constants in positive characteristic (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 054 — K3 structures without rationality for cubic fourfolds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 054 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A polynomial equation can define a space whose points nevertheless admit a rational parametrization. The simplest example is a conic with a chosen point: intersecting it with lines through that point supplies a parameter. In higher dimensions, deciding whether such a parametrization exists becomes much harder than solving the equation locally.

A cubic fourfold is the smooth four-dimensional complex variety cut out by one homogeneous cubic equation in projective five-space. Several of its most informative structures resemble those of a K3 surface. For decades this resemblance has guided proposals for recognizing rational cubic fourfolds.

The manuscript in family 054 claims that this guide has a fundamental limitation. On infinitely many prescribed families of cubics, a very general member is irrational even though its associated category is the ordinary derived category of a K3 surface. It also carries the expected integral K3 cohomological structure. The point is a separation between rational parametrization and powerful structures that had been proposed to characterize it.

2. Background and essential definitions

Rationality and genericity

A complex fourfold XXX is rational if it is birational to P4\mathbb P^4P4: dense open subsets are isomorphic, or equivalently its rational-function field is C(t1,t2,t3,t4)\mathbb C(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4)C(t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​). A birational map may fail on a lower-dimensional subset; it need not extend everywhere.

A very general point of a parameter space lies outside a countable union of proper closed algebraic subsets. A theorem for very general members allows exceptional subfamilies, including rational examples. Moreover, being very general in a chosen divisor is different from being very general in the whole parameter space: the divisor itself might belong to the exceptional set of a theorem about the larger space.

K3 surfaces, lattices, and categories

A K3 surface is a compact simply connected complex surface with trivial canonical bundle. Its second integral cohomology is a lattice: a free abelian group equipped with an integer-valued intersection pairing. The Hodge decomposition further divides complexified cohomology according to holomorphic and antiholomorphic degree. An integral Hodge isometry preserves both structures.

For a cubic XXX, let hhh be the hyperplane class. A special cubic has an additional integral Hodge class in degree four. A Hassett divisor Cd\mathcal C_dCd​ parametrizes cubics with a specified saturated rank-two lattice containing h2h^2h2, whose intersection matrix has determinant ddd. Saturated means the lattice has no missing integral points in its rational span. The positive integer ddd is its discriminant.

The bounded derived category Db(Coh⁡X)D^b(\operatorname{Coh}X)Db(CohX) packages coherent sheaves and complexes, retaining how they map to one another. After removing the three elementary pieces OX,OX(1),OX(2)\mathcal O_X,\mathcal O_X(1),\mathcal O_X(2)OX​,OX​(1),OX​(2), its remaining component is denoted Ku⁡(X)\operatorname{Ku}(X)Ku(X). Calling it geometric K3 means there is an exact equivalence

Ku⁡(X)≃Db(Coh⁡S)\operatorname{Ku}(X)\simeq D^b(\operatorname{Coh}S)Ku(X)≃Db(CohS)

for an actual K3 surface SSS. This is an ordinary, untwisted category. Allowing additional twisting data would give a different condition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical constructions of Fano and Tregub produced rational cubics containing suitable special surfaces. Beauville and Donagi connected the variety of lines on a cubic with holomorphic symplectic geometry; Pfaffian cubics supplied particularly striking rational examples related to K3 surfaces. Hassett subsequently organized special cubics through the divisors Cd\mathcal C_dCd​ and their associated K3 lattices. These constructions explain why K3 geometry became central to the rationality problem. The manuscript’s references include the original papers.

Kuznetsov proposed that rationality should be equivalent to having a geometric K3 component. Addington and Thomas related this categorical condition to Hassett’s Hodge-theoretic condition on a dense open subset of the appropriate divisors. Work on stability conditions by Bayer, Lahoz, Macrì, Stellari and their collaborators extended the categorical correspondence. Thus the K3 side of the new statement builds on substantial earlier theory; the manuscript’s proposed new ingredient is irrationality in that same range. Addington–Thomas.

Several rationality tests must be distinguished. Addington showed that having the variety of lines birational to the Hilbert square of a K3 surface is more restrictive than merely having an associated K3 surface. The Hilbert square parametrizes unordered pairs of points together with their limiting configurations. Addington’s comparison.

The manuscript also places itself after recent irrationality results for very general cubics in the full moduli space and after Fay’s September 2026 obstruction on special divisors. Fay’s obstruction uses a quaternion algebra; it is nonzero on some discriminants but vanishes throughout the admissible range considered here. Consequently that earlier obstruction does not supply the new theorem. Fay’s paper.

There remain rational cubics on special loci. Russo and Staglianò constructed rationality results for particular discriminants, while Yang and Yu found rational subloci inside every Hassett divisor. The manuscript therefore does not assert that a whole large-discriminant divisor consists of irrational cubics. The distinction between its very general points and its exceptional points is essential.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Irrationality inside every sufficiently large admissible divisor

Call ddd admissible if

d>6,d≡0 or 2(mod6), d>6,\qquad d\equiv0\text{ or }2\pmod6,d>6,d≡0 or 2(mod6),

and ddd is divisible by neither 444, nor 999, nor any odd prime congruent to 222 modulo 333.

Theorem 1.1 of M1 claims that there is an integer d0d_0d0​ such that, for every admissible d>d0d>d_0d>d0​, a very general cubic X∈CdX\in\mathcal C_dX∈Cd​ is irrational and has a geometric K3 component. No explicit numerical value of d0d_0d0​ is supplied. The statement is uniform over all sufficiently large admissible discriminants, with a separate very-general exceptional set on each divisor.

The associated polarized K3 surface also realizes the expected integral Hodge structure: the orthogonal complement of the cubic’s rank-two labelled lattice matches the primitive degree-two K3 lattice with the appropriate shift of Hodge degrees and reversal of the pairing. Thus replacing the categorical condition by this integral cohomological condition does not restore sufficiency for rationality.

Stronger K3 resemblance and zero-cycles

For every integer n≥2n\ge2n≥2, set

d=2n2+2n+2.d=2n^2+2n+2.d=2n2+2n+2.

These discriminants are admissible and unbounded. When d>d0d>d_0d>d0​, the manuscript combines its irrationality theorem with Addington’s result to obtain very general irrational cubics whose variety of lines F(X)F(X)F(X) is birational to S[2]S^{[2]}S[2], the Hilbert square of a projective K3 surface. The conclusion is birationality, not an isomorphism; the different K3 surfaces appearing in these descriptions need not be identified with each other.

A further consequence concerns zero-cycles, which are formal integer sums of points modulo relations coming from rational functions on curves. For these irrational cubics, the degree map is an isomorphism after every field extension E/CE/\mathbb CE/C:

deg⁡:CH⁡0(XE)⟶Z.\deg:\operatorname{CH}_0(X_E)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z.deg:CH0​(XE​)⟶Z.

This is universal integral triviality of zero-cycles. The source obtains it from Voisin’s earlier theorem, since admissibility includes 4∤d4\nmid d4∤d. It is not a new zero-cycle calculation. It means these irrational examples pass a major necessary test for stable rationality. It does not decide whether they are stably rational.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the claim would overturn central sufficiency directions in the K3-based picture of cubic-fourfold rationality, across infinitely many specifically identified divisors. It would also demonstrate that several mutually reinforcing indicators can all coexist with irrationality.

The significance lies in the precision of the separation. The cubics have an ordinary geometric K3 category, an integral K3 Hodge description, and universally trivial zero-cycles. An infinite subcollection even has its variety of lines birational to a K3 Hilbert square. These are substantial structures, not merely superficial numerical similarities.

At the same time, the theorem would not make the associated K3 geometry irrelevant. It remains a rich description of the cubic and its moduli. What changes is the inference one may draw from that description: possessing it would no longer guarantee a rational parametrization.

6. The main idea

Count the same exceptional geometry in two ways

The proposed argument assumes a birational map from P4\mathbb P^4P4 to XXX and associates an integer to it. Resolving such a map introduces and removes exceptional divisors. The integer counts these with signs, but only when their underlying geometry contains a K3 surface from a carefully chosen collection.

More precisely, one removes the rationally connected directions from a divisor. The resulting maximal rationally connected quotient records the part that cannot be swept out by rational curves. The test is one if that quotient is birational to one of the selected K3 surfaces, and zero otherwise. Adding the tests of divisors acquired at the target and subtracting those lost at the source defines cu(f)c_u(f)cu​(f).

The selected K3 surfaces have Picard number one, a polarization of degree ddd, and a specified entire integral transcendental lattice. The transcendental lattice is the part of cohomology orthogonal to algebraic classes. Retaining the whole integral lattice is stronger than retaining a rational subspace or only its dimension.

Smooth factorization gives one

Weak factorization expresses a birational map between smooth projective varieties as blowups and blowdowns along smooth centers. In dimension four, surface centers can contribute K3-type cohomology.

The manuscript uses operators constructed from genus-zero curve-counting invariants to distinguish the contributions of whole transcendental lattices. Its proposed calculation says that, under the very-general lattice hypotheses, one selected K3 contribution survives. In its notation,

cu(f)=1.c_u(f)=1.cu​(f)=1.

This step does not assume that every surface’s transcendental lattice is indecomposable. Such a general indecomposability proposal has known counterexamples; the source instead introduces additional operators to control the blocks relevant to this particular calculation.

Mori factorization gives zero

The Sarkisov program decomposes the same birational map into links between Mori fiber spaces, the fibered building blocks of birational geometry. Here the manuscript introduces correction terms attached to each intermediate space. A link’s contribution becomes the difference of the corrections at its two ends.

Summing these differences cancels every intermediate term. For sufficiently large ddd, the source’s boundedness arguments make this calculation uniform, independent of the number of links or the chosen birational map. Both endpoint corrections vanish because the endpoints have point bases. Therefore the second calculation gives

cu(f)=0.c_u(f)=0.cu​(f)=0.

The contradiction supplies the irrationality criterion. Period and lattice results then put very general members of each sufficiently large admissible divisor within its hypotheses. This is the strategy reported by the manuscript, rather than an independent verification of its factorization calculations.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The field is C\mathbb CC, the cubic is smooth, and the theorem requires both admissibility and an unspecified lower bound on discriminant. It does not determine rationality at every small discriminant or for every member of a covered divisor. The known rational subloci are consistent with its very-general formulation.

The categorical and cohomological associations are supplied by earlier results. The principal claimed advance is the birational obstruction that operates despite them. Likewise, universal zero-cycle triviality comes from Voisin’s theorem and should not be read as evidence that the manuscript proves stable rationality.

An effective threshold, explicit individual irrational equations in the stated range, and a satisfactory replacement for the discarded sufficiency criteria are natural further questions. Another is how much rationality information can survive in structures finer than the category or integral Hodge lattice used here.

Finally, the ordinary irrationality conclusion leaves stable rationality open: multiplying by projective space is a separate operation, and the manuscript does not establish that all such products remain irrational.

8. Sources and further reading

M1, Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.4, contains the principal statements. Its Sections 2–6 develop the two factorization calculations; Section 7 applies them to Hassett divisors and derives the consequences from existing K3 and zero-cycle theory.

For the earlier structures, see Addington–Thomas on Hodge theory and derived categories, Addington on the two K3 rationality conditions, and Voisin on universal zero-cycles of cubic hypersurfaces. Fay’s 2026 obstruction explains the adjacent discriminant range already treated by a different method. M1’s bibliography supplies the classical rational constructions and the factorization results used in its argument.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Irrational cubic fourfolds with geometric K3 categories (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 055 — Stability at the Gepner point and at large volume
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 055 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Imagine assigning a complex number to every geometric object, then sorting the objects by the angle of that number. One would like every complicated object to split into a finite sequence of simpler pieces, ordered by angle. The number must also faithfully measure the size of those pieces: arbitrarily large numerical objects should not acquire charges arbitrarily close to zero.

This is the outline of a Bridgeland stability condition. It turns a derived category, a setting containing sheaves and complexes of sheaves, into a space where one can discuss stable constituents, their moduli, and changes of stability.

Family 055 asks for particular stability conditions predicted by geometry and physics. Its first manuscript claims the prescribed symmetry at the Gepner point for every smooth quintic threefold. The second claims exact large-volume charges on every smooth projective threefold with trivial canonical bundle, and separately proves uniform numerical inequalities on arbitrary smooth projective threefolds. Their subject is more specific than the existence of some stability condition.

2. Background and essential definitions

Charges, phases, and support

A coherent sheaf generalizes a vector bundle by allowing fibers of varying dimension and singular behavior. The derived category Db(Coh⁡X)D^b(\operatorname{Coh}X)Db(CohX) also contains finite complexes of sheaves, identifying complexes with the same cohomological information. Its shift operation [1][1][1] moves a complex by one degree.

The numerical Grothendieck group Knum(X)K_{\mathrm{num}}(X)Knum​(X) records additive classes of these objects, identifying classes that have the same Euler pairings with all others. The Euler pairing is the alternating sum of dimensions of the extension groups. A central charge is a homomorphism

Z:Knum(X)⟶C.Z:K_{\mathrm{num}}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb C.Z:Knum​(X)⟶C.

A nonzero semistable object of phase ϕ\phiϕ has Z(E)=meiπϕZ(E)=m e^{i\pi\phi}Z(E)=meiπϕ with m>0m>0m>0. Phases are real numbers, not angles modulo a full turn: shifting by [1][1][1] raises the phase by one. A stability condition specifies the semistable objects and requires every object to have a finite filtration with decreasing phases, called a Harder–Narasimhan filtration.

Its support property is a bound

∥[E]∥≤C∣Z(E)∣\|[E]\|\le C|Z(E)|∥[E]∥≤C∣Z(E)∣

for every semistable object, using a norm on the numerical vector space. It prevents numerical complexity from becoming invisible to the charge. Local finiteness imposes a corresponding finite-length condition in short phase intervals.

Hearts and tilting

A heart is an abelian category inside the derived category where kernels, quotients, and short exact sequences can be used. Coherent sheaves form one heart. A tilt constructs another by shifting a selected class of sheaves and closing under extensions. On threefolds, two successive tilts provide the standard route to geometric stability conditions.

For a sheaf, its Chern character ch⁡(E)\operatorname{ch}(E)ch(E) packages rank, divisor, curve, and point data. A real divisor class BBB gives the twisted character ch⁡B(E)=e−Bch⁡(E)\operatorname{ch}^B(E)=e^{-B}\operatorname{ch}(E)chB(E)=e−Bch(E). An ample class HHH specifies a polarization, and t>0t>0t>0 scales it. In the large-volume problem, ttt becomes large while the geometry of XXX remains fixed.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Douglas’s proposal of stability for D-branes motivated the categorical viewpoint, and Bridgeland supplied its mathematical axioms and deformation theory. Bayer, Macrì and Toda developed the double-tilt approach to threefolds, identifying inequalities involving the third Chern character as a central obstacle. Bridgeland, Bayer–Macrì–Toda.

For a quintic, Toda formulated the desired Gepner symmetry and proposed the relevant pair of tilts. The symmetry functor and its fivefold periodicity were already known. The difficult part was to construct the semistable objects with finite filtrations and support for the prescribed, generally irrational, charge. Li established the existence of numerical stability conditions on every smooth quintic in 2019. Xu subsequently proved a stronger sheaf inequality that M1 uses as an input. Thus M1’s claimed addition is the exact Gepner symmetry, not the first stability condition on a quintic. Toda’s formulation, Li’s theorem, Xu’s inequality.

For large volume, Bayer’s polynomial stability describes asymptotic phase order. A genuine Bridgeland condition at each sufficiently large finite value of ttt requires additional control. The threefold inequalities were established in important cases such as abelian threefolds, but an uncorrected inequality at every parameter is false: Schmidt and Martinez–Schmidt produced counterexamples. Corrections depending on the geometry became part of the problem. Bayer’s polynomial stability, Schmidt’s counterexample.

The historical position changed further in 2026. Li and collaborators developed general constructions; Cheng established full numerical support, while Cheng–Feyzbakhsh identified threefold hearts and proved a weak form of the BMT conjecture. M2 explicitly builds on these results. It claims prescribed ordinary and Todd-corrected charges, a common threshold over a real parameter sector, and stronger uniform inequalities. It does not claim that general nonemptiness was still open. Cheng, Cheng–Feyzbakhsh.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: exact quintic Gepner symmetry

Let X⊂PC4X\subset\mathbb P^4_{\mathbb C}X⊂PC4​ be any smooth degree-five hypersurface. It has trivial canonical bundle. Define

Φ=TOX∘(−⊗OX(1)),\Phi=T_{\mathcal O_X}\circ(-\otimes\mathcal O_X(1)),Φ=TOX​​∘(−⊗OX​(1)),

where tensoring by the hyperplane bundle acts first. The spherical twist TOXT_{\mathcal O_X}TOX​​ is the categorical operation obtained from the evaluation map from copies of OX\mathcal O_XOX​ to an object. The established relation is Φ5≃[2]\Phi^5\simeq[2]Φ5≃[2].

M1 claims a numerical stability condition (Z,P)(Z,\mathcal P)(Z,P) with full support satisfying

Z(ΦE)=e2πi/5Z(E),Φ(P(ϕ))=P(ϕ+2/5),Z(Ox)=−1.\begin{aligned}Z(\Phi E)&=e^{2\pi i/5}Z(E),\\\Phi\bigl(\mathcal P(\phi)\bigr)&=\mathcal P(\phi+2/5),\\Z(\mathcal O_x)&=-1.\end{aligned}Z(ΦE)Φ(P(ϕ))Z(Ox​)​=e2πi/5Z(E),=P(ϕ+2/5),=−1.​

Here P(ϕ)\mathcal P(\phi)P(ϕ) is the category of semistable objects of phase ϕ\phiϕ, and Ox\mathcal O_xOx​ is the sheaf concentrated at a point. The normalization identifies the charge with Toda’s proposed one. The theorem holds for every smooth quintic, without a general-position restriction.

M2: exact large-volume charges

Let XXX be any smooth projective complex threefold with KX≃OXK_X\simeq\mathcal O_XKX​≃OX​. For every chosen real twist B∗B_*B∗​ and ample real direction H∗H_*H∗​, M2 claims neighborhoods V,WV,WV,W and a single threshold TTT working for all B∈VB\in VB∈V, H∈WH\in WH∈W, and t≥Tt\ge Tt≥T.

There are geometric numerical stability conditions with each of the exact charges

ZB,tH(E)=−∫Xe−B−itHch⁡(E),ZB,tHLV(E)=−∫Xe−B−itHch⁡(E)td⁡(X).\begin{aligned}Z_{B,tH}(E)&=-\int_X e^{-B-itH}\operatorname{ch}(E),\\Z^{\mathrm{LV}}_{B,tH}(E)&=-\int_X e^{-B-itH}\operatorname{ch}(E)\sqrt{\operatorname{td}(X)}.\end{aligned}ZB,tH​(E)ZB,tHLV​(E)​=−∫X​e−B−itHch(E),=−∫X​e−B−itHch(E)td(X)​.​

The integral selects the top-degree part of the expression. The Todd class is a characteristic class of the tangent bundle; here its square root is 1+c2(X)/241+c_2(X)/241+c2​(X)/24. “Geometric” means all point sheaves are stable of phase one.

Both constructions have support on the full numerical group. The ordinary charge has the standard double-tilt heart. The Todd-corrected charge has a separately constructed heart; the source does not identify the two hearts. No additional vanishing of H1(X,OX)H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)H1(X,OX​) or H2(X,OX)H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)H2(X,OX​) is required.

An independent inequality on arbitrary threefolds

Fix any smooth projective complex threefold, an integral ample HHH, and a rational divisor class B0B_0B0​. Put B=B0+bHB=B_0+bHB=B0​+bH, with b∈Rb\in\mathbb Rb∈R. For objects semistable at zero slope for

νa,b(E)=Hch⁡2B(E)−a2H3ch⁡0(E)/2H2ch⁡1B(E),\nu_{a,b}(E)=\frac{H\operatorname{ch}_2^B(E)-a^2H^3\operatorname{ch}_0(E)/2}{H^2\operatorname{ch}_1^B(E)},νa,b​(E)=H2ch1B​(E)Hch2B​(E)−a2H3ch0​(E)/2​,

M2 claims constants k≥0k\ge0k≥0 and R∗R_*R∗​, independent of the object and bbb, such that

ch⁡3B(E)≤(a26+k)H2ch⁡1B(E)\operatorname{ch}_3^B(E)\le\left(\frac{a^2}{6}+k\right)H^2\operatorname{ch}_1^B(E)ch3B​(E)≤(6a2​+k)H2ch1B​(E)

for every a>0a>0a>0. For a>R∗a>R_*a>R∗​, the same inequality holds with k=0k=0k=0. This assertion requires finite slope, and has no canonical-bundle assumption. An all-slope quadratic version follows in a corresponding large-volume region. Its parameter is related to the physical volume by t=3 at=\sqrt3\,at=3​a; confusing these normalizations changes the coefficient.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claims would connect two distinguished regions of threefold stability theory with explicit constructions: a highly symmetric point on every quintic and prescribed large-volume charges on all threefolds with trivial canonical bundle. They also address a uniform numerical inequality on arbitrary polarized threefolds.

Exactness matters. A nearby charge, or a charge containing an extra curve-class correction, need not represent the same geometric or physical specification. Likewise, a condition that controls only four intersection numbers may miss numerical directions when the Picard rank is greater than one. Full support and one threshold over an open parameter sector substantially strengthen a collection of isolated existence statements.

The Gepner theorem would resolve a specific longstanding symmetry conjecture. The large-volume theorem would offer a consistent starting region for studying stable complexes and their variation. Neither manuscript claims that all paths between these regions or all resulting moduli spaces have thereby been determined.

6. The main idea

Build support before completing the slicing

M1 begins with Toda’s two tilts, but varies the second cut in two independent numerical directions. Xu’s inequality supplies room for these perturbations. Combining the perturbed hearts with the symmetry Φ\PhiΦ produces a periodic grid of categories whose charges lie in narrow angular sectors.

Testing an object against all perturbations controls its rank and first Chern coordinate. Together with the complex charge, these control the remaining two coordinates of the quintic’s rank-four numerical lattice. This yields support before the final semistable filtration is constructed.

The distinction between a lattice and its image in C\mathbb CC is crucial. The charge image need not be discrete. The full numerical lattice is discrete, however, so a bound on numerical classes gives finite refinement. The source then merges shared boundary phases and establishes the slicing and local finiteness.

Preserve all numerical directions at large volume

M2 embeds the threefold in a product of projective spaces using sufficiently many line bundles. This retains the full numerical class rather than just the degrees along one polarization. It constructs ambient stability conditions with a support estimate after rescaling each Chern-character coordinate by the appropriate power of ttt.

In those scaled coordinates, fixed higher-degree corrections become small at large volume. Deformation and restriction can therefore produce the exact desired charge, with the unwanted Todd factors canceled beforehand. Surface restrictions identify the ordinary charge’s heart as the standard double tilt; the boundary at zero slope receives a separate argument.

The numerical inequality follows by another route. Restriction to surfaces and cohomological estimates give a rank-uniform error bound at one fixed volume. Reduction to positive characteristic and Frobenius pullback remove object-dependent errors in a limit. Moving along stability walls then yields the corrected all-volume inequality and an uncorrected large-volume tail. The manuscript treats this argument as independent of the categorical construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The Gepner statement concerns smooth quintic threefolds, not arbitrary Calabi–Yau varieties or arbitrary hypersurface degrees. Its precise functor order, phase shift, and point-charge normalization belong to the theorem.

The prescribed-charge theorem requires trivial KXK_XKX​, whereas the separate inequality allows arbitrary smooth projective threefolds. Its common threshold is local in the real twist and ample-direction parameters; it is not a single bound for the entire ample cone of every variety.

Known counterexamples to the uncorrected BMT inequality remain relevant. M2 allows a correction at small volume and removes it only past a threshold. Tensoring known counterexamples can move the twist without moving them into arbitrarily large volume, so twist uniformity and volume uniformity are different issues.

Natural further questions concern the global stability manifold, paths connecting distinguished regions, wall-crossing of particular classes, and effective thresholds. Existence with a specified charge does not automatically classify stable objects or prove every predicted enumerative correspondence.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the normalized Gepner claim; Sections 3–4 explain the two-parameter construction and the support-first refinement. M2’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 separate the prescribed-charge and numerical statements; Sections 2–3 and 4–7 develop their independent arguments, and Section 8 compares the known counterexamples.

The primary historical links above give the successive stages: Bridgeland’s axioms, Toda’s conjecture, Li’s quintic existence theorem, Xu’s sheaf bound, and the 2026 constructions of Cheng and Cheng–Feyzbakhsh. For the limitations of uncorrected inequalities, see also Martinez–Schmidt.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Gepner stability condition on every smooth quintic threefold (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Prescribed large-volume charges on threefolds with trivial canonical bundle (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 056 — Why four-dimensional minimal model programs should stop
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 056 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

An algorithm that repeatedly improves an object is useful only if it eventually stops. In algebraic geometry, the minimal model program simplifies a space by contracting curves along which its canonical geometry is negative. Sometimes it removes a divisor. Sometimes it performs a flip, replacing a small exceptional set without reducing the number of divisors.

That second operation makes termination difficult. Local improvement of singularities does not immediately provide a positive integer that decreases at every step. An infinite sequence could, in principle, make ever smaller improvements.

Family 056 contains five manuscripts about four-dimensional spaces. They claim termination in broad projective and compact Kähler settings, with careful distinctions between constructing one finite program, terminating every permitted program, and terminating flip sequences whose individual maps are already supplied. These are different assertions even when their eventual geometric pictures look alike.

2. Background and essential definitions

Pairs and positivity

A pair (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) consists of a normal space and an effective boundary B=∑bjBjB=\sum b_jB_jB=∑bj​Bj​, a weighted sum of hypersurfaces. The adjoint divisor is D=KX+BD=K_X+BD=KX​+B, where KXK_XKX​ records top-degree differential forms. Rational boundary means all bjb_jbj​ are rational numbers.

A divisor is nef if its class is a limit of positive classes; in projective geometry this is equivalent to nonnegative intersection with every curve. It is pseudo-effective if its class is a limit of effective divisor classes. In the Kähler setting the manuscripts use the corresponding definition through positive currents, allowing differential-form classes not represented by divisors.

If a curve direction has DDD-degree negative, the program seeks to contract it. A divisorial contraction removes a hypersurface. A small contraction removes no hypersurface; its exceptional locus has higher codimension. A flip replaces a small contraction X→ZX\to ZX→Z by X+→ZX^+\to ZX+→Z so that −D-D−D is relatively ample on the first side and D+D^+D+ is relatively ample on the second.

A Mori fiber space is the other possible endpoint: a contraction to a lower-dimensional base, with connected fibers, relative Picard number one, and relatively ample negative adjoint. Relative Picard number one means there is only one independent numerical direction for divisors along the fibers.

Measuring singularities

On a resolution p:W→Xp:W\to Xp:W→X, the log discrepancy of a prime divisor EEE is

a(E;X,B)=1+coeff⁡E(KW−p∗(KX+B)).a(E;X,B)=1+\operatorname{coeff}_E\bigl(K_W-p^*(K_X+B)\bigr).a(E;X,B)=1+coeffE​(KW​−p∗(KX​+B)).

Log canonical, abbreviated lc, means every such number is nonnegative. Klt means every one is positive. Canonical and terminal impose, respectively, at least one and greater than one for exceptional divisors, with the additional positivity conditions specified in the manuscripts.

A generalized pair also carries a nef divisor on a higher birational model. Its compatible traces form a nef b-divisor MMM, and the adjoint becomes KX+B+MXK_X+B+M_XKX​+B+MX​. Fixing this higher-model datum throughout a sequence is part of the problem; choosing unrelated nef terms at each step would be a different operation.

Projective versus Kähler

A projective variety embeds in projective space. A compact Kähler space has a compatible positive closed differential form and can be nonprojective. A morphism between nonprojective spaces may nevertheless be projective because it has a relatively ample line bundle.

The Kähler manuscripts require global Weil Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality: every prime divisor defined on the whole space has a positive Cartier multiple, and the canonical sheaf has a positive invertible reflexive power. This is not a claim about every analytic local ring. Their stronger global condition applies to every rank-one reflexive sheaf. These distinctions determine which line bundles and contractions are available.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Three-dimensional minimal model theory established the fundamental pattern of contractions, flips, and endpoints. In higher dimensions, Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan supplied major existence results for klt pairs with positivity assumptions. Existence of flips and existence of selected minimal models did not, by themselves, prove that every possible sequence terminates. BCHM.

Shokurov introduced difficulty, a weighted count of exceptional divisors with small discrepancies. Kawamata–Matsuda–Matsuki combined discrepancy counts with surface-cycle ranks for terminal fourfolds. Fujino extended the approach to canonical fourfold pairs, with an essential correction treating repeated blowups over boundary surfaces. Alexeev–Hacon–Kawamata developed further weighted corrections and obtained termination under a numerical effectivity assumption on the negative adjoint. Fujino’s addendum, Alexeev–Hacon–Kawamata.

For pseudo-effective fourfolds, Chen–Tsakanikas and Moraga proved broad termination results, including generalized lc settings. Han–Liu–Zhuang subsequently treated every klt fourfold program with big boundary. The gap addressed by the projective manuscript is rational-boundary lc termination without either pseudo-effectivity or a big boundary. Non-pseudo-effectivity does not imply that the negative adjoint is numerically effective, so the older assumptions cannot simply be exchanged. Chen–Tsakanikas, Han–Liu–Zhuang.

In compact Kähler geometry, Höring–Peternell developed threefold minimal models. Das–Hacon–Păun obtained fourfold results when the adjoint is rationally equivalent to an effective divisor. Fujino’s analytic relative theory supplies projective operations, while Hacon–Xie’s 2026 work gives generalized cone and base-point-free results and programs in big settings. These are important ingredients and partial solutions, rather than consequences newly created by this family. Fujino’s analytic MMP, Hacon–Xie.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1–M2: termination of supplied Kähler flip diagrams

M1 claims that every sequence of generalized lc flips on globally Weil Q\mathbb QQ-factorial compact Kähler fourfolds terminates, subject to its precise data. The boundary is effective and rational. The fixed nef b-divisor is represented by an analytically nef Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier divisor on a projective modification. The adjoints are actual Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier divisors with compatible canonical representatives.

Each supplied flip diagram has projective small maps with connected fibers to a normal compact Kähler base and the opposite ample signs described above. No scaling rule or pseudo-effectivity is required, and the bases may vary. The theorem concerns these existing diagrams; it does not itself construct every requested contraction or flip.

M2 gives the generalized-canonical case with all discrepancies positive and exceptional ones at least one. Boundary coefficients are less than one, and discrepancy exactly one is permitted. It supplies a more direct discrepancy-and-cycle argument within that narrower singularity class. Its maps also need not have relative Picard number one.

M3: arbitrary projective lc programs

M3 claims that, over every algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every permitted program for a projective lc fourfold with rational boundary terminates. Neither initial Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality nor pseudo-effectivity is assumed.

Its allowed steps include divisorial contractions, flips, and a divisorial contraction followed by a small positive modification. The negative side contracts one extremal ray. Arbitrary blowups, flops, and inserted isomorphisms are not allowed steps. It also claims existence of the required continuation for every selected negative ray.

Every maximal program therefore ends with nef adjoint or a Mori fiber space. A maximal program means one continued until an endpoint is reached, not one stopped by choice halfway through.

M3 separately obtains semiample endpoints using the abundance manuscript in family 034, and local complement and Cartier-section consequences using companion results in families 066 and 068. Those additions use extra theorems; termination alone does not imply them.

M4–M5: ordinary programs starting on the given Kähler space

M4, the October 6 manuscript, claims termination of every maximal ordinary negative-ray program from a globally Weil Q\mathbb QQ-factorial compact Kähler klt fourfold with effective rational boundary. The initial model is exactly the given space. Its contractions are projective, and its endpoint has nef adjoint if the initial adjoint is pseudo-effective; otherwise it is a Mori fiber space over a compact Kähler base.

The conclusion includes the corresponding intrinsic formulation using the canonical rational line bundle, rather than requiring a chosen global canonical divisor. Strong global factoriality, if present initially, persists. No abundance conclusion is included.

M5, the September 24 manuscript with the same title, proves the weaker quantifier: there exists one finite ordinary program with these endpoint alternatives. Its limiting-model construction is a separate route. It should not be described as an additional arbitrary-termination theorem merely because it also produces a finite result.

The family thus contains related constructions with different scopes, rather than five interchangeable formulations of one assertion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Termination is a central structural problem in birational geometry. If correct, these claims would remove major remaining restrictions in dimension four and extend the available picture substantially into nonprojective Kähler geometry.

The projective result strengthens “a suitable path reaches an endpoint” to “every allowed path does.” The analytic results also address the existence and compatibility of operations when no global ample polarization is available. Together, these would make four-dimensional classification less dependent on special choices or positivity assumptions.

The endpoint distinction is equally consequential. A nef canonical adjoint is a minimal-model outcome. Producing sections of its multiples is the further abundance problem. Keeping those stages separate reveals exactly which part of the classification program each theorem would settle.

6. The main idea

A corrected integer that can only decrease

Flips improve discrepancies, but infinitely many valuations can arise from blowing up ordinary boundary surfaces. Counting all of them naively gives an unusable infinite quantity. The difficulty method subtracts the predictable families and retains the exceptional contributions.

M1 and M3 pass to auxiliary terminal models, called junctions, carrying the relevant low-discrepancy divisors. Coefficients can still vary along the sequence. The manuscripts confine persistent variation to divisors mapping to curves or points, where a new branch estimate controls the correction terms.

A boundary component can have several branches over a surface after normalization, which separates local branches into a normal space. If there are rrr branches, rounding their individual weights can exceed rounding the total by as much as r−1r-1r−1. The elementary inequality is

⌈∑j=1rxj⌉≥∑j=1r⌈xj⌉−(r−1).\left\lceil\sum_{j=1}^r x_j\right\rceil\ge \sum_{j=1}^r\lceil x_j\rceil-(r-1).⌈j=1∑r​xj​⌉≥j=1∑r​⌈xj​⌉−(r−1).

The geometric work pays for this deficit using cycle ranks on normalized components and additional divisorial contributions over curves. The resulting corrected difficulty is nonnegative and drops by at least one whenever a relevant flipped surface appears. Topological decomposition and Hodge-theoretic tools enter precisely to control the branch excess.

After those positive-side surfaces disappear, remaining flips remove independent surface-cycle classes on the negative side. A finite-dimensional rank cannot decrease forever. These two decreasing quantities address different stages of a potential infinite sequence.

Canonical witnesses and construction of steps
