Large pseudoindex provided another broad range: Novelli–Occhetta handled ιX≥(n+3)/3\iota_X\ge(n+3)/3ιX​≥(n+3)/3, and Novelli later proved the conjecture whenever ιX>n/3\iota_X>n/3ιX​>n/3. At the boundary n=3ιXn=3\iota_Xn=3ιX​, further results use extra geometric hypotheses. Novelli’s theorem.

Symmetry has also made the problem tractable. Casagrande proved the toric version for suitable Gorenstein varieties in every dimension, and Pasquier treated horospherical varieties. Gagliardi–Hofscheier–Pearson subsequently proved the generalized conjecture for Q\mathbb QQ-factorial spherical Fano varieties. These singular varieties with large group actions form a different scope from the unrestricted smooth theorem claimed here. The spherical result.

The difficulty with the chain approach is not the final dimension estimate. It is constructing enough independent proper families of rational curves with the required incidence properties. M1 first detects numerical curve directions through quantum operators and only needs the stronger proper-family structure when equality occurs. That is its proposed way past the missing geometric construction in the general case.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 claims that every positive-dimensional smooth connected complex projective Fano manifold satisfies

ρX(ιX−1)≤dim⁡X.\rho_X(\iota_X-1)\le\dim X.ρX​(ιX​−1)≤dimX.

There is no upper bound on dimension, no toric or homogeneous assumption, no prescribed extremal contraction, and no large-pseudoindex restriction. Equality holds if and only if

X≃(PιX−1)ρXX\simeq\bigl(\mathbb P^{\iota_X-1}\bigr)^{\rho_X}X≃(PιX​−1)ρX​

as an algebraic variety. Thus all factors in an equality example have the same dimension. The conclusion is an actual product isomorphism, not merely a birational description or a product after finite cover.

If ιX=1\iota_X=1ιX​=1, the left side is zero, so the inequality is strict for positive-dimensional XXX. The substantive argument begins with ιX≥2\iota_X\ge2ιX​≥2. For Picard number one, the inequality becomes ιX≤n+1\iota_X\le n+1ιX​≤n+1, and equality identifies projective space, consistent with the classical extremal model.

A main intermediate claim concerns a curve degree β\betaβ represented by a nonconstant free rational map. Free means the pulled-back tangent bundle is globally generated, allowing the map to move through nearby points. Put d=−KX⋅βd=-K_X\cdot\betad=−KX​⋅β, and choose an integer a>0a>0a>0 for which −aKX-aK_X−aKX​ is very ample. In the pseudoindex-at-least-two setting, the manuscript claims

⟨τd−2(pt)⟩β≥(ad)−(d−1).\left\langle\tau_{d-2}(\mathrm{pt})\right\rangle_\beta\ge(ad)^{-(d-1)}.⟨τd−2​(pt)⟩β​≥(ad)−(d−1).

The left side is the one-point descendant with a point condition and ψd−2\psi^{d-2}ψd−2. Its positivity and quantitative lower bound are used to control the spectrum of quantum multiplication. The manuscript does not assume that the entire virtual class of every map space is effective, or that quantum cohomology is semisimple.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the result would settle a major sharp classification conjecture for smooth Fano manifolds, unifying numerous dimensional, positivity, and symmetry-based cases.

The inequality expresses a useful geometric constraint: many independent numerical directions and large minimum rational-curve degree cannot coexist in a fixed dimension. Its equality statement identifies the unique way to use the entire dimension allowance.

The proposed method also has broader interest. It extracts concrete independent curve degrees from commuting quantum operators without a semisimplicity assumption. That avoids requiring the quantum algebra to split into the simplest possible pieces and may make the strategy relevant to other Fano questions.

The rating reflects a substantial all-dimensional advance within Fano geometry, with a precise extremal classification, rather than an assertion that it classifies all Fano manifolds away from equality.

6. The main idea

Degrees create a limited budget

Choose a numerical divisor basis D1,…,DρD_1,\ldots,D_\rhoD1​,…,Dρ​. Quantum multiplication by these divisors gives commuting matrices Aj(q)A_j(q)Aj​(q) on even cohomology, where the formal variables qqq record curve degrees.

A contribution from curves of anticanonical degree ddd lowers cohomological codimension by d−1d-1d−1. Cohomological codimension ranges only from zero to nnn. Therefore, if the manuscript can find a nonzero product using ρ\rhoρ independent positive curve degrees d1,…,dρd_1,\ldots,d_\rhod1​,…,dρ​, it obtains

ρ(ι−1)≤∑j=1ρ(dj−1)≤n.\rho(\iota-1)\le\sum_{j=1}^{\rho}(d_j-1)\le n.ρ(ι−1)≤j=1∑ρ​(dj​−1)≤n.

The first inequality uses the definition of pseudoindex. The second is the finite grading budget. Producing the nonzero independent product is the central task.

Positivity prevents excessive spectral dependence

The source studies maps through a very general point and contracts components away from the marking. This gives a morphism to a weighted projective parameter space. Boundary images have too small a dimension to contribute to the relevant degree, while the free-map locus provides a nonempty effective contribution. Keeping automorphism denominators gives the explicit descendant lower bound.

Divisor and recursion identities yield finite-shift recurrences for descendant vectors. After factorial normalization, these imply an exponential upper bound. If all joint eigenvalue tuples of the commuting matrices satisfied polynomial relations, the same recurrence would force much faster decay along suitable free curve degrees.

The lower bound excludes that decay. The manuscript concludes that one joint eigenvalue tuple has ρ\rhoρ algebraically independent coordinates. This is more than the existence of a nonzero eigenvalue: it detects all numerical divisor directions simultaneously.

Turn spectra into curves, then classify equality

An alternating trace built from matrix-valued differentials is computed in two bases. In a common triangular basis it detects the independent eigenvalues. In the fixed cohomology basis it detects a nonzero product of curve correspondences in independent degrees. Triangularization, unlike diagonalization, is compatible with nonsemisimple commuting operators.

At equality, every selected degree must be minimal, dj=ιd_j=\iotadj​=ι. The correspondence product then yields an actual chain of rational curves. Minimal degree prevents those curves from splitting into smaller positive-degree pieces, making the relevant full families proper.

The source applies the earlier ordered-chain estimate with the family hypotheses required by its erratum. Cyclically reordering the chain shows that every family covers the manifold. Occhetta’s characterization of products of projective spaces then yields the equality classification. This last rigidity theorem is an established input; the new proposed contribution is the route that supplies its hypotheses.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main theorem concerns smooth projective complex Fano manifolds. It does not assert the same unrestricted theorem for all singular log Fano pairs, nor for varieties with merely nef anticanonical bundle. Earlier singular results in special symmetric classes have their own assumptions.

When ι=1\iota=1ι=1, the inequality gives no useful upper bound on ρ\rhoρ. Even for larger pseudoindex, it is not a classification away from equality. Many different Fano manifolds can satisfy a strict inequality.

The descendant statement is restricted to degrees with a free representative and to the setting in which it is proved. It should not be generalized into positivity of every virtual curve count. Nor does the argument claim semisimplicity of quantum cohomology as a byproduct.

Natural further questions concern near-equality geometry, singular extensions with suitable correction terms, and other numerical inequalities accessible through independent quantum divisor eigenvalues. The source’s descendant and spectral arguments are reported as stated, without an independent verification of their positivity claims.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 contains the inequality and equality classification. Proposition 3.1 gives the point-descendant lower bound, Sections 4–5 obtain independent curve correspondences, and Section 6 invokes the ordered-chain and product-rigidity results at equality.

The original generalized formulation, its author-hosted erratum, Novelli’s large-pseudoindex theorem, and the spherical-variety theorem explain the principal earlier routes and their restrictions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The generalized Mukai conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 064 — Constant Milnor number and an unchanged surface singularity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 064 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Suppose the equation of a singular surface varies holomorphically with a parameter. A nearby smooth level of the equation has a finite amount of middle-dimensional topology, measured by the Milnor number. If that number stays constant, must the singularity remain topologically unchanged?

For isolated hypersurfaces, a classical theorem answers this outside complex surface dimension. The surface case lies exactly where the standard high-dimensional topological argument cannot provide the required product structure. Family 064 claims that missing case.

The conclusion is stronger than saying every individual zero set is homeomorphic to the first one. The manuscript claims a continuously varying family of ambient homeomorphisms, with continuously varying inverses, preserving both the parameter and the numerical value of the defining function. It therefore identifies the zero sets and all nearby levels together.

2. Background and essential definitions

The local family

A holomorphic germ records a function near a point, allowing its domain to be shrunk. Consider a holomorphic function F(x,t)F(x,t)F(x,t), where x=(x1,x2,x3)∈C3x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb C^3x=(x1​,x2​,x3​)∈C3 and ttt lies in a small complex disk Δ\DeltaΔ. Write

ft(x)=F(x,t),Xt={x:ft(x)=0}.f_t(x)=F(x,t),\qquad X_t=\{x:f_t(x)=0\}.ft​(x)=F(x,t),Xt​={x:ft​(x)=0}.

Three ambient complex variables give a hypersurface of complex dimension two, hence the term surface singularity. Assume ft(0)=0f_t(0)=0ft​(0)=0 and the origin is an isolated critical point of every ftf_tft​.

The Milnor number is the finite integer

μ(ft,0)=dim⁡CC{x1,x2,x3}(∂ft/∂x1,∂ft/∂x2,∂ft/∂x3).\mu(f_t,0)=\dim_{\mathbb C}\frac{\mathbb C\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}}{(\partial f_t/\partial x_1,\partial f_t/\partial x_2,\partial f_t/\partial x_3)}.μ(ft​,0)=dimC​(∂ft​/∂x1​,∂ft​/∂x2​,∂ft​/∂x3​)C{x1​,x2​,x3​}​.

The denominator is the ideal generated by the spatial derivatives. Finiteness expresses isolatedness. Topologically, the Milnor fiber, obtained by taking a small nonzero level near the origin, has the homotopy type of a bouquet of μ\muμ two-spheres.

For example, f=x12+x22+x32f=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2f=x12​+x22​+x32​ has derivative ideal (x1,x2,x3)(x_1,x_2,x_3)(x1​,x2​,x3​), so μ=1\mu=1μ=1. The invariant is easy to define but does not obviously remember how the whole singular family sits in its ambient space.

Several meanings of unchanged

Topological right equivalence of two functions means one becomes the other after a homeomorphism of the source, without changing the target value. A family is topologically right-trivial if these homeomorphisms can be selected jointly continuously, together with their inverses.

This is a local topological statement. It does not require holomorphic coordinate changes, differentiability at the singularity, or distance control. Individual homeomorphisms for each parameter would not suffice: they could fail to fit together continuously.

A resolution replaces a singular surface by a smooth one, mapping isomorphically away from the singular point. Its exceptional curves record where the point has been replaced. A simultaneous resolution carries out this process throughout a family, sometimes after a finite change of parameter such as t=uet=u^et=ue.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lê–Ramanujam proved that constant Milnor number gives constant embedded topological type when the hypersurface dimension is not two. Their comparison of Milnor fibers produces a homologically trivial cobordism. In high dimensions the h-cobordism theorem makes it a product; curves can be handled by lower-dimensional topology. Complex surfaces remain outside that argument. Timourian and King established the corresponding local triviality of function families outside the exceptional dimension. M1 cites the original papers for both stages.

A stronger numerical hypothesis was already known to imply geometric regularity. Let μ(j)\mu^{(j)}μ(j) denote the Milnor number of a restriction to a general jjj-dimensional linear subspace. For a three-variable germ, μ(3)=μ\mu^{(3)}=\muμ(3)=μ, while μ(1)\mu^{(1)}μ(1) is multiplicity minus one. Teissier and Briançon–Speder related constancy of the full sequence to Whitney regularity, a condition controlling limiting tangent spaces and secant lines. Their examples also show that topological triviality need not imply Whitney regularity. Briançon–Speder.

Parusiński proved topological triviality for constant-Milnor-number families of the special form f(x)+tg(x)f(x)+tg(x)f(x)+tg(x) in every dimension. Arbitrary holomorphic parameter dependence is broader than this linear form. Parusiński.

Fernández de Bobadilla–Pełka proved that finite constant Milnor number forces constant multiplicity, even for much more general continuous formal families. For surfaces this supplies constancy of μ(1)\mu^{(1)}μ(1), but not automatically of the plane-section invariant μ(2)\mu^{(2)}μ(2). Their theorem is a major ingredient in the history and in M1’s treatment of certain singularities, rather than a complete solution of the topological family problem. Equimultiplicity theorem.

Another route uses resolution invariants. Wahl introduced a logarithmic characteristic number for normal surface singularities. Okuma proved that its constancy gives simultaneous resolutions in the non-log-canonical Gorenstein case after finite base change. M1’s main numerical step is to derive constancy of that invariant from μ\muμ alone. Its introduction also credits recent semistable-degeneration results of Aldasoro Rosales and Peters’s symplectic result under a no-vanishing-folds hypothesis. Peters.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let FFF be any holomorphic one-parameter family as above, with an isolated critical point at the origin for every parameter and

μ(ft,0)=μ(f0,0).\mu(f_t,0)=\mu(f_0,0).μ(ft​,0)=μ(f0​,0).

M1 claims that, after shrinking the disk and representatives, there is a homeomorphism germ

Φ(x,t)=(ϕt(x),t)\Phi(x,t)=(\phi_t(x),t)Φ(x,t)=(ϕt​(x),t)

such that

ϕt(0)=0,ϕ0=id⁡,ft(ϕt(x))=f0(x).\phi_t(0)=0,\qquad \phi_0=\operatorname{id},\qquadf_t(\phi_t(x))=f_0(x).ϕt​(0)=0,ϕ0​=id,ft​(ϕt​(x))=f0​(x).

Both Φ\PhiΦ and Φ−1\Phi^{-1}Φ−1 are jointly continuous on neighborhoods of the origin section over the original parameter disk.

Several details belong to the strength of the claim. The parameter dependence can be arbitrary and holomorphic; it need not be linear. The singularities need not be log canonical. The map is ambient in C3\mathbb C^3C3, so it controls how each surface sits in its neighborhood. It preserves the defining function, so no parameter-dependent change of the target value is inserted.

Although the proof uses finite covers of the parameter disk to obtain resolutions, the final result is asserted over the original disk. Triviality only after replacing ttt by ueu^eue would be a weaker conclusion because monodromy could obstruct descent.

This theorem is local near the distinguished singular section. It does not assert a global trivialization of polynomial fibers throughout C3\mathbb C^3C3 or control behavior at infinity.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the claim would complete the classical isolated-hypersurface μ\muμ-constant picture in the dimension excluded by the Lê–Ramanujam argument, with the stronger function-preserving family conclusion.

It would show that one integer, constant under deformation, controls much more than the homotopy rank of nearby smooth fibers. The family would admit a coherent ambient topological identification, including its singular point and all nearby function levels.

The result would also connect three kinds of information: a local derivative algebra defining μ\muμ, logarithmic intersection theory on resolutions, and continuous ambient transport. That bridge is particularly significant in complex dimension two, where direct high-dimensional cobordism methods are unavailable.

It does not say that equal Milnor numbers classify arbitrary singularities. The existence of the holomorphic constant-μ\muμ family is a substantive hypothesis.

6. The main idea

Convert a constant integer into a constant resolution invariant

For a non-log-canonical surface singularity, the source studies the canonical divisor plus the full reduced exceptional boundary on a resolution. A relative Zariski decomposition separates a nef part from an effective exceptional part. Its local nef cycle PlocP_{\mathrm{loc}}Ploc​ determines Wahl’s invariant

β=−Ploc2.\beta=-P_{\mathrm{loc}}^2.β=−Ploc2​.

“Nef” here means nonnegative intersections with the curves relevant to the relative problem. The square is computed using the exceptional intersection matrix. The manuscript recalls resolution independence in the convention needed for Okuma’s theorem.

To compare this number across the family, it reduces the scalar calculation to algebraic curves of polynomial equations and compactifies them to projective surfaces without adding unwanted singularities. These individual finite-determinacy comparisons concern numerical invariants; they are not already a continuous trivialization of the original family.

Positive contributions must all vanish

Semistable reduction and the threefold log minimal model program produce a central fiber with one component dominating the original surface and additional projective surfaces SaS_aSa​ over the singular point. Each has a carefully retained reduced boundary BaB_aBa​.

After cancellation of the main component, constant Milnor number yields an Euler-characteristic relation

0=∑aχc(Sa∖Ba)+δ,δ≥0.0=\sum_a\chi_c(S_a\setminus B_a)+\delta,\qquad\delta\ge0.0=a∑​χc​(Sa​∖Ba​)+δ,δ≥0.

The compactly supported Euler characteristic χc\chi_cχc​ is the version suited to noncompact boundary complements. The correction δ\deltaδ comes from interior smoothings. A logarithmic surface inequality gives

0≤(KSa+Ba)2≤3χc(Sa∖Ba).0\le(K_{S_a}+B_a)^2\le3\chi_c(S_a\setminus B_a).0≤(KSa​​+Ba​)2≤3χc​(Sa​∖Ba​).

Thus every term contributing to the extra logarithmic squares must vanish. Specialization of intersection numbers then makes β\betaβ constant. Keeping the complete boundary is essential because both the Euler cancellation and the inequality must refer to the same open surfaces.

From resolved surfaces to ambient functions

Okuma’s theorem supplies simultaneous resolutions after finite base change. The manuscript shows that the exceptional curves form the required relative normal-crossing configuration, then constructs transport on resolved neighborhoods. This descends to punctured zero fibers and extends to nearby nonzero levels while preserving the function value.

Properness and reverse transport control both directions at the singular point. An additional correction removes the angular mismatch introduced by t=uet=u^et=ue, returning the trivialization to the original disk.

The log-canonical and double-point cases are handled separately. Equimultiplicity, spectral constancy, and sectional Milnor-number arguments supply the relevant regularity; splitting off a square reduces the double-point case to plane curves. The source does not force every singularity through the non-log-canonical resolution theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The hypotheses require a holomorphic one-complex-parameter family, three spatial variables, an isolated critical point along the fixed origin section, and finite constant Milnor number. The theorem does not address arbitrary nonisolated singularities or multiparameter families with their additional compatibility questions.

A continuous gradient vector field alone would not suffice: continuous fields can lack unique flows. The manuscript explicitly separates smallness near the singular section from the trajectory and reverse-transport control needed for a homeomorphism. The stated conclusion includes both maps and inverses.

Topological right-triviality does not imply Whitney regularity, analytic equivalence, or a bi-Lipschitz trivialization. In particular, the generic plane-section Milnor number is not assumed constant in the general case.

The claim is compatible with family 059, which concerns isolated pairs of equivalent germs with different multiplicities. Such a pair cannot be joined by a continuous constant-μ\muμ family under the established equimultiplicity theorem. A path hypothesis and a pairwise comparison are different problems.

Questions beyond this statement include nonisolated settings, parameter spaces of higher dimension, and stronger regularity of the trivializing maps under additional assumptions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the function-preserving trivialization. Sections 3–7 derive constancy of the logarithmic resolution invariant, Sections 8–9 construct and descend transport, and Section 10 supplies the remaining singularity cases. Appendix B explains why gradient estimates need additional flow control.

The primary links in Section 3 cover Whitney regularity, linear-parameter triviality, equimultiplicity, and the recent symplectic partial result. M1’s bibliography also gives the original Lê–Ramanujam, Timourian, King, Wahl, and Okuma papers that establish the classical problem and the resolution bridge.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Topological triviality of mu-constant families of surface singularities (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Virasoro constraints for projective bundles and complete intersections
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 065 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Counting curves on a complex algebraic variety produces far more than one sequence of numbers. Curves have different genera and degrees; they can be required to meet chosen cycles; and each marked point carries further geometric data. Gromov–Witten theory packages all these counts into one enormous generating function.

The Virasoro conjecture predicts universal differential equations for that function. Their form depends on familiar cohomological data of the target, but their content constrains curve counts in every genus. Why should the same algebra of equations govern such different geometric spaces?

This family approaches the question through two constructions. M1 claims that the equations pass from a smooth projective base to the projectivization of any vector bundle on it. M2 claims them for every smooth complete intersection in projective space. Both include cohomology classes that the simplest reconstruction methods cannot see.

2. Background and essential definitions

Curve counts with insertions

Let YYY be a smooth complex projective variety. A stable map consists of a possibly nodal marked curve CCC, together with an algebraic map C→YC\to YC→Y, with only finitely many automorphisms preserving the data. Its genus is ggg; its curve class β∈H2(Y,Z)\beta\in H_2(Y,\mathbb Z)β∈H2​(Y,Z) records where it lies homologically.

At a marked point, a cohomology class γ\gammaγ imposes an incidence condition. A power of the cotangent-line class ψ\psiψ at that point gives a descendant insertion, written τa(γ)\tau_a(\gamma)τa​(γ). The corresponding invariant is a virtual intersection number on the moduli space of stable maps. “Virtual” matters: these are systematically defined invariants even when curves do not form a finite collection that can be literally counted.

Gather the connected genus-ggg invariants into a formal series FgYF_g^YFgY​, with variables for the insertions and symbols QβQ^\betaQβ for curve classes. The total potential is

ZY=exp⁡ ⁣(∑g≥0ℏg−1FgY).Z_Y=\exp\!\left(\sum_{g\geq0}\hbar^{g-1}F_g^Y\right).ZY​=exp(g≥0∑​ℏg−1FgY​).

Here ℏ\hbarℏ keeps track of genus. No numerical convergence of this entire series is required; equations are read coefficient by coefficient.

What the Virasoro equations say

There are prescribed differential operators LkYL_k^YLkY​, for integers k≥−1k\geq-1k≥−1, acting on the insertion variables. The conjecture asserts

LkYZY=0(k≥−1).L_k^Y Z_Y=0\qquad(k\geq-1).LkY​ZY​=0(k≥−1).

The first equations include familiar rules for adding an unconstrained marked point and respecting degrees. Higher operators combine terms with one derivative and two derivatives, reflecting both modifications of a curve and its splitting into pieces. Their commutators form a version of the Virasoro algebra.

The operators use the cohomological intersection pairing, multiplication by the first Chern class of the tangent bundle, and Hodge degrees. For a class of type (p,q)(p,q)(p,q), the grading here uses p−dim⁡(Y)/2p-\dim(Y)/2p−dim(Y)/2. Replacing this with half the total degree would lose information when p≠qp\neq qp=q. Odd-degree classes also require the usual sign when two odd variables are exchanged.

The two geometric constructions

For a rank-rrr vector bundle E→BE\to BE→B, the projective bundle PB(E)\mathbb P_B(E)PB​(E) has fiber Pr−1\mathbb P^{r-1}Pr−1. M1 uses the convention that its points are lines in the fibers of EEE. The bundle need not decompose globally into line bundles.

A smooth complete intersection is the smooth common zero set of homogeneous equations in projective space, with the expected codimension. Its ambient cohomology comes from projective space. The remaining middle-dimensional classes are called primitive. These extra classes are often precisely where the geometry becomes interesting—and where a result restricted to ambient insertions would be incomplete.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The point target already has a rich theory: its stable-map spaces are moduli spaces of curves. Witten predicted the governing integrable equations, and Kontsevich proved the corresponding intersection-theoretic theorem. Eguchi, Hori and Xiong proposed the extension to general targets; subsequent formulations incorporated the full Hodge grading and odd classes. Getzler’s treatment explains this general framework.

Several major regions were already understood. Liu and Tian established genus-zero constraints. Givental’s quantization formalism, together with Teleman’s classification of semisimple theories, supplies all-genus results when quantum cohomology has a sufficiently simple algebraic decomposition. Semisimplicity means that, generically, the relevant algebra splits into independent field factors; many targets of interest do not satisfy it. Okounkov and Pandharipande proved the constraints for target curves, including their odd cohomology.

For bundles, Coates, Givental and Tseng proved a base–total-space equivalence for toric bundles constructed from sums of line bundles. This already covers split projective bundles. Fan’s reconstruction theorem treats arbitrary projective bundles at the level of Gromov–Witten invariants. Iritani and Koto developed the quantum differential equations of nonsplit projective bundles and their relationship with the base. Reconstruction of invariants, however, does not automatically establish compatibility with every Virasoro operator. M1 addresses that additional issue outside the semisimple setting.

Complete intersections also had substantial prior coverage. Getzler’s theorem already gives all-genus constraints for the Calabi–Yau case with vanishing first cohomology; a smooth quintic threefold should therefore not be advertised as a newly settled example here. More recently, Guo, Zhang and Zhou proved genus-one constraints for ambient insertions on smooth Fano complete intersections. Argüz, Bousseau, Pandharipande and Zvonkine developed reconstruction of complete-intersection invariants through nodal invariants. M2 aims at the full constraints across all genera, with unrestricted primitive insertions, including the nonsemisimple cases left by earlier methods.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: arbitrary projectivization preserves the constraints

Write V(Y)\mathcal V(Y)V(Y) for the full ordinary Virasoro constraints. M1 states that for every smooth connected projective complex variety BBB and every algebraic vector bundle EEE of rank at least two,

V(B) ⟹ V(PB(E)).\mathcal V(B)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal V(\mathbb P_B(E)).V(B) ⟹ V(PB​(E)).

There is no positivity, splitting, or semisimplicity assumption on EEE or the base theory. The conclusion concerns every genus, each actual integral curve class, and arbitrary cohomology insertions. Remembering the complete class is stronger than aggregating all classes with the same degree against one divisor.

Repeated application gives projective-bundle towers over any base already satisfying the conjecture. Curves supply one unconditional starting class through the earlier target-curve theorem. M1 states the forward implication; the stronger equivalence from the earlier split toric setting should not be silently transferred to arbitrary bundles.

M2: every smooth projective complete intersection

M2 states V(X)\mathcal V(X)V(X) for every smooth complete intersection X⊂PNX\subset\mathbb P^NX⊂PN, without restricting its dimension, multidegree, or canonical positivity. The theorem includes Fano, Calabi–Yau and general-type examples, and all primitive and odd insertions.

Both papers concern the ordinary, unreduced Gromov–Witten potential and ordinary descendant classes at marked points. Modified theories and ancestor classes—related classes pulled back from moduli spaces of curves—enter the machinery but are not substitutes for the stated conclusion.

Combining the two claims also gives the constraints for arbitrary projective-bundle towers over smooth complete intersections. M2’s own induction uses the previously established split-bundle theorem; it does not need M1’s arbitrary-bundle extension as an input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. These are broad claims about a central organizing principle in enumerative geometry. Complete intersections supply a basic source of varieties with complicated primitive cohomology, while projectivization is among the most common ways to build new varieties. An all-genus theorem stable under these constructions would enlarge the conjecture’s reach substantially.

The significance is structural. The equations relate different curve counts, and their survival under geometry would make them usable within larger reconstruction arguments. They do not, by themselves, provide a short closed formula for every invariant or imply that every target has semisimple quantum cohomology.

This rating reflects the scope of the claims and their methods, conditional on correctness. It is not an assessment of proof reliability.

6. The main idea

A master space connects the base and bundle

M1 places the two targets inside

W=PB(E⊕OB).W=\mathbb P_B(E\oplus\mathcal O_B).W=PB​(E⊕OB​).

Scaling the trivial summand gives a circle-type algebraic action with fixed pieces BBB and PB(E)\mathbb P_B(E)PB​(E). Localization expresses invariants of the larger space through these pieces, together with contributions from curves moving between them. Those connecting curves occur in families and must retain their full correspondence data.

A shift operator packages the action into a system of differential equations. Its leading spectral branches satisfy an equation of the form

hr(h+λ)=y,h^r(h+\lambda)=y,hr(h+λ)=y,

where λ\lambdaλ records the action and yyy records fiber degree. Near y=0y=0y=0, one branch corresponds to the base and the other cluster to the projective bundle. Analytic continuation around branch points permutes the branches. The proposed mechanism transports the base’s identities through this connected system and collects the bundle branches at the end.

This is applied to fixed coefficients, where suitable ancestor expressions are polynomial in the fiber variable. It is not an assumption that the entire all-genus potential converges. Finally, quantization introduces possible scalar errors; the Virasoro commutators are used to recover the prescribed normalization and remove them.

Degeneration handles complete intersections

M2 splits a defining equation into lower-degree factors. The smooth target degenerates into two simpler pieces meeting along a smooth common divisor; a blowup accounts for the intersection geometry. Induction lowers either dimension or the complexity of the defining degrees.

The difficulty is the primitive cohomology. Such classes need not extend coherently across the degeneration. Merely proving equations for ambient classes would leave a large part of the theorem untouched.

The manuscript instead treats each possible failure of a Virasoro equation as a multilinear tensor. It tests that tensor using compatible classes, inverse intersection pairings, and additional copies of curve-counting data. Chains of ruled spaces allow cutting and gluing operations to be compared. Since a Virasoro operator has at most two derivatives, a sufficiently long chain has an unused position at which a cancellation can be arranged.

These cancellations reduce the tested equations to smaller targets. A final Hodge-theoretic pairing turns the remaining primitive error into a nonnegative squared norm; its vanishing is the proposed means of detecting all primitive components. Extra divisor labels are retained where a single projective degree would fail to distinguish curve classes. The strategy therefore separates transporting equations from recovering information hidden by degeneration.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The targets are smooth and projective over C\mathbb CC. The statements here do not automatically extend to arbitrary singular targets, noncompact varieties, orbifolds, or reduced curve-counting theories.

M1 starts with a base already satisfying the full conjecture. It is a transfer theorem, not a proof for every base. M2 supplies a large additional class of bases, but complete intersections and their bundle towers still do not exhaust smooth projective geometry.

“All genera” and “all insertions” are essential parts of the assertions. They include primitive classes and odd signs, not merely the even ambient sector. Equally, the potential is formal: coefficientwise identities do not assert an analytic sum over all curves and genera.

A natural further direction is to understand which other surgeries preserve the full constraints without semisimplicity, and how broadly the primitive-class detection mechanism can be applied. The manuscripts report specific transport arguments for their stated constructions; a universal surgery principle would require more.

8. Sources and further reading

For the foundational formulation, see Getzler’s Virasoro conjecture paper. For the prior all-genus bundle theorem, see Coates–Givental–Tseng; for the nonsplit quantum-cohomology framework, see Iritani–Koto. The recent Guo–Zhang–Zhou paper helps locate the genus-one ambient frontier. These works provide context for the two source manuscripts below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Virasoro Constraints under Projectivization (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Virasoro Constraints for Projective Complete Intersections (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 052 — From a split tangent bundle to a product of manifolds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 052 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

On a product Y1×Y2Y_1\times Y_2Y1​×Y2​, a tangent vector naturally splits into a direction along the first factor and a direction along the second. Suppose a complex manifold has exactly such a splitting at every point. Must the manifold itself come from a product?

There are two obstacles. First, the chosen directions must fit together into leaves, like coordinate slices. Second, local slices must continue globally without twisting or breaking down. Passing to the universal cover removes loop monodromy, but does not automatically solve the continuation problem.

Family 052 contains two complementary claims. M1 starts with two integrable tangent summands on a compact Kähler manifold and claims a compatible product decomposition of its ordinary universal cover. M2 starts with a rationally connected projective manifold and claims that every two-summand holomorphic splitting is automatically integrable. An earlier theorem then supplies a product of the original manifold itself.

In both statements, compatibility means preserving the particular tangent subbundles supplied at the start. An unrelated abstract product decomposition would not answer the question.

2. Background and essential definitions

Splitting directions and integrating them

The holomorphic tangent bundle TXT_XTX​ consists of the complex tangent spaces of XXX. A specified splitting

TX=E1⊕E2T_X=E_1\oplus E_2TX​=E1​⊕E2​

means each EiE_iEi​ is a holomorphic subbundle and every tangent vector has a unique decomposition into the two summands. Let their positive ranks be r1,r2r_1,r_2r1​,r2​, so dim⁡CX=r1+r2\dim_{\mathbb C}X=r_1+r_2dimC​X=r1​+r2​.

A subbundle EEE is integrable if the Lie bracket of any two local vector fields tangent to EEE is again tangent to EEE. The bracket measures the infinitesimal failure of successive motions to commute. Frobenius’ theorem says integrability is precisely the condition for local submanifolds tangent to the chosen directions to exist.

These local submanifolds fit together into leaves. If both complementary summands are integrable, local coordinates can be separated into two blocks, with one block varying along each leaf. Locally the manifold is a product. The global question remains.

Compatibility is stronger than being a product

An isomorphism X≃Y1×Y2X\simeq Y_1\times Y_2X≃Y1​×Y2​ is compatible with the specified splitting when it identifies EiE_iEi​ with the tangent directions of YiY_iYi​:

Ei≃pr⁡i∗TYiE_i\simeq\operatorname{pr}_i^*T_{Y_i}Ei​≃pri∗​TYi​​

as the actual subbundles of the tangent bundle, not only as abstract vector bundles.

Even a manifold already known to be a product can carry a different, nonintegrable tangent splitting. The manuscript recalls an example on an abelian surface times P1\mathbb P^1P1: adding noncommuting vertical vector fields to two translation directions gives a complementary subbundle whose bracket leaves that subbundle. Product topology alone does not force the specified directions to be product directions.

Covering spaces and rational curves

The ordinary universal cover X~→X\widetilde X\to XX→X is the simply connected topological covering equipped with its lifted complex structure. A product upstairs need not descend to a product downstairs: deck transformations can act on both factors together. Even a finite cover need not remove all such coupling.

A smooth projective variety is rationally connected if two general points lie on a rational curve, the image of P1\mathbb P^1P1. “General” means pairs in a nonempty algebraic open subset of X×XX\times XX×X. This is stronger than uniruledness, which requires a rational curve through a general individual point.

Rational connectedness supplies many moving rational curves and, in the smooth complex projective setting, simple connectedness. M2 uses this abundance of curves to control the Lie brackets of the tangent summands.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Riemannian analogue is de Rham’s decomposition theorem: parallel orthogonal distributions on a complete Riemannian manifold give a product on its universal cover. A holomorphic splitting is weaker. Compactness makes a chosen metric complete, but does not make its given tangent subbundles parallel.

Beauville formulated the compatible splitting problem and proved major cases, including Kähler–Einstein manifolds and compact Kähler surfaces. For multiple summands, the compatible formulation involves integrability of relevant partial sums. In the two-summand setting here, integrability of both summands is the required local hypothesis.

Druel treated projective manifolds whose tangent bundle is a sum of line bundles. Brunella–Pereira–Touzet established splitting when one summand is a line bundle and its complement is integrable. Further work of Pereira–Touzet and Druel–Pereira–Pym–Touzet supplies product decompositions under flatness assumptions or the existence of a compact leaf with finite holonomy.

On the projective side, Höring proved automatic integrability for non-uniruled manifolds with split tangent bundle. He also proved that on a rationally connected projective manifold, integrability of one summand already gives a compatible product. The remaining rationally connected problem was therefore to force integrability without extra hypotheses.

Campana–Peternell obtained important low-rank Fano cases. Höring’s 2026 Fano-type theorem establishes algebraic integrability in a broad singular setting with Fano-type positivity, and gives an actual compatible product for smooth Fano manifolds. M2 claims to remove that positivity restriction in the smooth rationally connected case, with arbitrary positive ranks.

The family thus addresses two different missing steps: M1 globalizes an already integrable local product in general compact Kähler geometry; M2 supplies integrability from rational connectedness.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: a compatible product on the universal cover

Let XXX be a compact connected Kähler manifold of dimension at least two, and assume both positive-rank summands in TX=E1⊕E2T_X=E_1\oplus E_2TX​=E1​⊕E2​ are integrable. M1 claims connected simply connected complex manifolds Y1,Y2Y_1,Y_2Y1​,Y2​ and a biholomorphism

Φ:X~→ ∼ Y1×Y2\Phi:\widetilde X\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Y_1\times Y_2Φ:X ∼ ​Y1​×Y2​

such that

dΦ(π∗Ei)=pr⁡i∗TYi,dim⁡CYi=ri.d\Phi(\pi^*E_i)=\operatorname{pr}_i^*T_{Y_i},\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}Y_i=r_i.dΦ(π∗Ei​)=pri∗​TYi​​,dimC​Yi​=ri​.

Here π\piπ is the covering map. The factors are the universal covers of the intrinsic leaves through a common point. They can be noncompact, and the leaves use their own manifold topology.

Combining this with Höring’s earlier integrability theorem gives the same universal-cover conclusion for every two-summand splitting on a smooth non-uniruled projective manifold.

When KXK_XKX​ is nef and big, M1 also claims that the canonical Kähler–Einstein connection preserves the specified summands on the regular canonical locus. This is the inverse image of the smooth part of the canonical model under the pluricanonical contraction. Nefness means nonnegative degree on every curve; bigness means maximal growth of pluricanonical sections. The additional parallelism is more than the product conclusion already obtained from the non-uniruled case.

M2: rational connectedness forces integrability

For a smooth connected rationally connected projective complex manifold, M2 claims that both summands of every specified holomorphic splitting into two positive-rank subbundles are integrable, with no further rank or positivity condition.

Applying Höring’s established product theorem then yields

X≃X1×X2,Ei=pr⁡i∗TXi,X\simeq X_1\times X_2,\qquad E_i=\operatorname{pr}_i^*T_{X_i},X≃X1​×X2​,Ei​=pri∗​TXi​​,

where both factors are smooth projective manifolds. This is a product of XXX itself, stronger than an upstairs statement for a general compact Kähler manifold.

M2 also applies the result to general fibers of the rationally connected quotient of a uniruled compact Kähler manifold. It supplies integrability of the induced summands there, allowing earlier structure theorems to produce almost-holomorphic fibrations in the corresponding rational directions. When one ambient summand has rank two, those directions have rank two, one, or zero; the resulting conclusions differ accordingly. This is not an assertion that every uniruled manifold with a splitting is a global product.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the family would resolve the two-summand compatible splitting problem under its integrability hypothesis and a central automatic-integrability case beyond known positivity or rank restrictions.

Tangent bundles describe infinitesimal geometry. A theorem recovering a global product from their decomposition turns local linear information into a structural classification tool. Compatibility ensures that the factors explain the original geometry rather than merely provide another way to write the same space.

The complementary hypotheses are useful in different regions of the classification. Rationally connected varieties have many rational curves; non-uniruled varieties do not. M2 uses the former abundance, while M1 combines with earlier work in the latter setting. Neither manuscript erases the separate difficulties for general intermediate uniruled geometry.

6. The main idea

M1: continue rectangles, not just individual paths

With integrable complementary directions, a local map of two complex variables can move in E1E_1E1​ along the first variable and in E2E_2E2​ along the second. M1 calls such a map a holomorphic box. It need not be injective or have full rank.

The manuscript first extends these maps across Hartogs figures, domains in several complex variables where analytic continuation can fill a missing region. A general meromorphic extension could have indeterminacy; the separate tangent conditions are used to exclude the exceptional behavior and make the extension holomorphic.

It then crosses mixed boundaries using area estimates from a Kähler form. Closedness of that form permits Stokes’ theorem, while bounded projections onto the two summands control the relevant directions. No assumption that a metric already makes the summands parallel or orthogonal is introduced.

These extensions combine two disc axes into a whole box and preserve additional holomorphic parameters. Finite grids then combine continuous leafwise paths into rectangles. Continuing both the local product map and its inverse, and passing to simply connected covers, is intended to produce the global compatible biholomorphism.

M2: use rational curves to kill the bracket obstruction

M2 begins without integrability. Given a rational curve g:P1→Xg:\mathbb P^1\to Xg:P1→X, it claims a tangent-adapted map

F:P1×P1⟶X,F(s,s)=g(s),F:\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\longrightarrow X,\qquad F(s,s)=g(s),F:P1×P1⟶X,F(s,s)=g(s),

whose two factor directions map into E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​. The construction starts formally near the diagonal, reconstructs a rational map using section counts, and removes indeterminacy through the tangent identities.

On this box, the pullback of each summand comes from its corresponding factor. Along a factor curve, the complementary summand is therefore trivial. This is the geometric feature needed to test integrability in arbitrary rank.

Failure of integrability is measured by the projected bracket tensor

⋀2Ei⟶Ej,j≠i.\bigwedge^2E_i\longrightarrow E_j,\qquad j\ne i.⋀2​Ei​⟶Ej​,j=i.

Rational connectedness supplies moving curves and sections vanishing at one marked point while spanning the desired tangent directions at another. Applying the bracket tensor gives a section of a trivial bundle on P1\mathbb P^1P1. Such a section is constant; because it vanishes at the first point, it vanishes at the second. The spanning property then forces the tensor to vanish on an open set, and holomorphicity extends the vanishing everywhere.

This separates the construction valid for split bundles from the final step where rational connectedness is essential.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 assumes integrability. It does not claim that every holomorphic splitting on every compact Kähler manifold is integrable; the recalled product example shows why that would be false.

M1 concludes a product of the ordinary universal cover, not necessarily of XXX or a finite cover. M2’s actual product conclusion uses smooth rational connectedness and the earlier product theorem. Singular rationally connected spaces are not covered, and the source cites singular examples where automatic integrability fails.

Both main statements are formulated for two summands. More elaborate splittings require attention to integrability of partial sums; they should not be treated as an automatic restatement with more symbols.

The claims do not classify the individual factors or guarantee compact leaves in M1. Understanding intermediate uniruled cases and the possible deck-group actions remains part of the wider structure problem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 is the integrable universal-cover statement; its corollaries and Section 7 give the projective and canonical-metric applications. M2’s Theorem 1.1 is automatic integrability, Corollary 1.2 invokes Höring for the actual product, and Section 5 states the rational-quotient consequences.

The primary works of Beauville and Höring linked above explain the conjectures and earlier cases. Background on foliations and the Frobenius theorem helps interpret integrability as the passage from directions to local slices.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Universal-cover splitting for compact Kähler manifolds (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Integrability of split tangent bundles on rationally connected manifolds (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Family 053 — A relation beyond Pixton’s original system
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 053 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A ring can be described by generators and relations. Giving many true relations is useful; proving that they are all the relations is a much stronger achievement. The distinction is central to the intersection theory of moduli spaces of curves.

These moduli spaces carry natural geometric classes associated with marked points, differential forms, and degenerations into nodal curves. Pixton proposed a uniform graph-based system of relations among them. The relations are known to be valid. The completeness conjecture says that every relation among these natural classes follows from that system.

Family 053 contains one manuscript claiming a counterexample to completeness. It constructs a formal expression that becomes zero as an algebraic cycle but is not generated by the original Pixton relations, even after their standard gluing, forgetting, and multiplication consequences are included.

The example has extraordinarily large parameters. Its role is to disprove a universal assertion, not to provide a small relation ready for everyday computation.

2. Background and essential definitions

A space whose points are curves

The moduli space Mg,n\mathcal M_{g,n}Mg,n​ parametrizes smooth complex curves of genus ggg with nnn distinct labelled marked points. Its stable compactification M‾g,n\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}Mg,n​ also includes connected curves with ordinary nodes, where two branches cross.

Stability requires only finitely many automorphisms preserving the markings. For example, each rational component needs at least three special points, counting both markings and node branches. The condition 2g−2+n>02g-2+n>02g−2+n>0 gives the stable range.

The natural object is a moduli stack, which remembers finite automorphism groups. For this digest, one can think of an orbifold-like parameter space with rational coefficients accounting for those symmetries. Its complex dimension is

3g−3+n.3g-3+n.3g−3+n.

Boundary strata describe the different ways a curve can break into components. A stable graph records them: vertices represent components and their genera, edges represent nodes, and labelled legs represent markings.

Natural classes and their relations

At the iii-th marked point, the cotangent line has a first Chern class ψi\psi_iψi​. Other classes, called κ\kappaκ-classes, arise by forgetting a marking and pushing forward powers of a cotangent class. Together with boundary gluing operations, they generate the tautological ring.

The ambient Chow ring consists of algebraic cycles modulo rational equivalence, with multiplication given by intersection. We use rational coefficients. A codimension-ddd cycle also has a cohomology class in degree 2d2d2d, but different Chow classes can have the same cohomology class.

To keep formulas separate from their geometric values, introduce a strata algebra Sg,n\mathcal S_{g,n}Sg,n​. Its elements are formal linear combinations of decorated stable graphs, with the standard dimension truncations. Realizing a graph as its geometric boundary class gives a map

qg,n:Sg,n⟶A∗(M‾g,n;Q).q_{g,n}:\mathcal S_{g,n}\longrightarrowA^*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n};\mathbb Q).qg,n​:Sg,n​⟶A∗(Mg,n​;Q).

The image is the tautological ring. The kernel consists of formal expressions that vanish geometrically: exactly the relations one wants to understand.

Validity and completeness

Let Pg,n\mathcal P_{g,n}Pg,n​ be Pixton’s original relation span, including its stated formal consequences. Validity means

Pg,n⊆ker⁡qg,n.\mathcal P_{g,n}\subseteq\ker q_{g,n}.Pg,n​⊆kerqg,n​.

Completeness means equality. A counterexample must do two things for the same formal class YYY: show qg,n(Y)=0q_{g,n}(Y)=0qg,n​(Y)=0, and show Y∉Pg,nY\notin\mathcal P_{g,n}Y∈/Pg,n​. Showing only that a new-looking formula vanishes is insufficient; it might already be a complicated combination of known relations.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mumford initiated the systematic intersection-theoretic study of natural classes on moduli spaces of curves. Faber’s calculations and geometric constructions led to conjectural descriptions of the tautological ring on the smooth unpointed space Mg\mathcal M_gMg​.

Faber–Zagier supplied explicit hypergeometric relations among κ\kappaκ-classes. Pandharipande–Pixton proved those relations in Chow using stable quotients. The compactification requires additional boundary information, developed through the gluing and forgetting calculus of Arbarello–Cornalba and Graber–Pandharipande. In genus zero, Keel gave a presentation of the whole Chow ring by boundary divisors.

Pixton’s 2012 formula extended the relation system to stable pointed curves through decorated graphs and proposed completeness. Pandharipande–Pixton–Zvonkine proved cohomological validity using three-spin cohomological field theory. Janda proved Chow validity through equivariant Gromov–Witten theory of the projective line.

These are validity theorems: they establish that the proposed expressions vanish. They do not automatically identify the entire kernel of the realization map. Likewise, Janda’s comparison of relations produced by certain semisimple field-theory reconstructions compares those methods with Pixton’s system, not every possible source of Chow relations.

A nearby question asks whether the tautological ring is Gorenstein, meaning its multiplication pairings in complementary degrees are nondegenerate in the proposed manner. That is logically different from completeness. Pixton’s September 2026 paper proves that the tautological ring of M25\mathcal M_{25}M25​ is not Gorenstein while also establishing Faber–Zagier completeness there. Other compact-type examples similarly separate the two properties.

M1 therefore targets the original full relation span directly on the stable compactification. It does not infer incompleteness merely from a failure of duality in the ring.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The parameters and the two conclusions

Set

g=1060,D∗=(g3),n=3D∗.g=10^{60},\qquad D_*={g\choose3},\qquad n=3D_*.g=1060,D∗​=(3g​),n=3D∗​.

Theorem 1.1 of M1 claims an explicitly defined class

Y∈Sg,n2D∗Y\in\mathcal S_{g,n}^{2D_*}Y∈Sg,n2D∗​​

for which

qg,n(Y)=0,Y∉Pg,n.q_{g,n}(Y)=0,\qquad Y\notin\mathcal P_{g,n}.qg,n​(Y)=0,Y∈/Pg,n​.

The superscript is codimension. It lies below the dimension 3g−3+n3g-3+n3g−3+n, so the assertion is not simply vanishing because the requested degree exceeds the dimension of the moduli space.

The same class yields a cohomological counterexample in degree 4D∗4D_*4D∗​. The cycle-class map sends its Chow realization to zero, while formal nonmembership in Pg,n\mathcal P_{g,n}Pg,n​ remains unchanged. This implication needs no injectivity of the cycle-class map: Chow vanishing already implies cohomological vanishing.

What “explicit” means at this scale

The construction uses ggg colors. For each increasing triple of colors, it allocates three labelled slots, producing n=3(g3)n=3{g\choose3}n=3(3g​) slots in total.

For a three-slot block J=(a,b,c)J=(a,b,c)J=(a,b,c), the manuscript combines two rational-tail divisor sums and a correction supported on rational bridges:

FJst=D‾ab D‾ac−12βJst.F_J^{\mathrm{st}}=\overline D_{ab}\,\overline D_{ac}-\frac12\beta_J^{\mathrm{st}}.FJst​=Dab​Dac​−21​βJst​.

Here D‾ab\overline D_{ab}Dab​ sums boundary divisors cutting off a genus-zero tail containing a,ba,ba,b. The bridge class βJst\beta_J^{\mathrm{st}}βJst​ inserts a genus-zero component carrying the three labels into an edge, giving two nodes, with specified graph-automorphism coefficients and forgetting pullbacks.

M1 multiplies one factor for every color triple and alternates over all relabelings preserving each slot’s color:

Y=∑τ preserves colorssgn⁡(τ) τ(∏JFJst).Y=\sum_{\tau\text{ preserves colors}}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)\,\tau\left(\prod_JF_J^{\mathrm{st}}\right).Y=τ preserves colors∑​sgn(τ)τ(J∏​FJst​).

Every operation is finite, though the expression is immense. The formula specifies a class without listing all of its terms. “Cubic” in the manuscript refers to its three marked inputs; each factor has Chow codimension two.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, this would disprove a central completeness proposal in the intersection theory of moduli spaces, in both rational Chow and rational cohomology.

The existing Pixton relations would remain true and useful. What changes is the belief that their formal closure accounts for every tautological relation. A missing relation would require a broader presentation of the ring or additional geometric principles generating relations.

The scale of the example affects practical usefulness but not the logic. A universal statement covering all genera and all marking counts fails if even one finite pair fails. The manuscript makes no claim that 106010^{60}1060 is close to the smallest possible genus.

The proposed mechanism is also informative: a formal algebra can satisfy all the tested graph relations while lacking a further identity forced by actual Chow correspondences. This would distinguish formal consistency with a relation system from geometric realizability.

6. The main idea

Use different tools for nonmembership and vanishing

M1 deliberately separates the two required conclusions. To show nonmembership, it constructs a linear detector on formal decorated graphs. To show vanishing, it uses actual algebraic cycles in families of curves and surfaces.

A detector is analogous to a linear functional that vanishes on a subspace but not on a candidate vector. If ℓ\ellℓ vanishes on every element of Pg,n\mathcal P_{g,n}Pg,n​ and ℓ(Y)≠0\ell(Y)\ne0ℓ(Y)=0, then YYY cannot belong to that span. This is an algebraic obstruction to derivability, rather than an attempt to enumerate all possible combinations of relations.

A formal algebra preserves an alternating product

The detector uses a super Frobenius algebra, a multiplication-and-pairing structure with even and odd parts. Odd coefficients anticommute, as in an exterior algebra. There is an independent odd generator θijk\theta_{ijk}θijk​ for each color triple.

The manuscript checks the graph identities needed to annihilate Pixton’s full original span, including the relevant boundary and forgetting operations. The test of YYY retains a nonzero coefficient proportional to the product of the distinct θijk\theta_{ijk}θijk​. This supplies the claimed formal nonmembership.

The detector is not asserted to be the actual Chow theory of a family of curves. That distinction is exactly what allows it to separate the original relation system from the additional geometric identity.

Actual curve correspondences obey a further vanishing law

On the geometric side, the small diagonal of a curve links three point positions. Projecting to the appropriate odd part of the curve’s correspondence structure produces a modified diagonal of the Gross–Schoen type, with corrections needed in families.

M1 studies quotient-sheaf moduli spaces on the square of the curve. Virtual localization and a Hilbert-scheme recursion retain marked outputs rather than integrating everything to a scalar. The resulting relation is intended to force sufficiently long products of the cubic coefficients to vanish in relative Chow theory.

Passing to the stable compactification introduces boundary errors. The rational-bridge correction with coefficient −1/2-1/2−1/2 removes a designated local error. The remaining terms either involve simpler operations or are supported over subsets of smaller dimension in the base.

An induction repeatedly pushes that support into higher codimension. The enormous color budget leaves enough marked inputs for each step until no support remains. This is the claimed Chow vanishing of YYY. The argument retains arbitrary Chow correspondences; replacing them with their cohomology classes would only establish a weaker result.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The target is Pixton’s original relation system with its specified full formal closure, not a deliberately weakened selection of seed relations. The manuscript does not claim that any enlarged relation system is incomplete.

The example lives on M‾g,n\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}Mg,n​ at the displayed enormous parameters. It does not supply a small-genus counterexample, determine the first failure, or automatically disprove every completeness statement on the smooth unpointed or compact-type loci.

It also does not invalidate the known Pixton relations or establish that every non-Gorenstein phenomenon arises from a missing relation. Completeness, validity, and nondegeneracy of multiplication pairings are separate questions.

The remaining program would be to identify smaller examples, understand which additional relations are required, and formulate a replacement completeness conjecture with a geometric explanation for the new identities.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Definition 2.3 specifies the alternating class; Theorem 1.1 gives Chow vanishing and formal nonmembership; Corollary 1.2 gives the rational-cohomological consequence. Its introduction distinguishes the two proof mechanisms and the nearby Gorenstein questions.

The primary sources linked in Section 3 explain the original graph relations and their established validity. Optional background on tautological rings and moduli of algebraic curves can help with the vocabulary. The essential algebraic question is whether a known relation subspace equals the full kernel of geometric realization.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A high-arity counterexample to Pixton completeness in Chow (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Bounded klt complements and uniformly mild hypersurfaces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 066 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Suppose a geometric space has singularities, but none are too severe. Can one choose an equation through any prescribed point without creating much worse singularities? And can one balance the canonical divisor by an effective boundary using a denominator bounded uniformly across a whole class of spaces?

These sound like different questions. One concerns choosing a local hypersurface; the other concerns constructing a global-looking divisor near a fiber. Earlier work shows that, for suitable Fano-type maps, the two are closely connected.

The two manuscripts in this family claim uniform answers in every dimension. The relevant bounds depend on dimension and an initial singularity gap, with a finite coefficient set additionally needed for the complement index. The geometry and the chosen equation may vary freely within the stated hypotheses.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measuring singularities

A pair (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) consists of a normal algebraic variety and an effective boundary divisor BBB, a weighted sum of codimension-one subvarieties. Assume KX+BK_X+BKX​+B is rationally Cartier: an integer multiple is locally given by one equation, or equivalently defines a line bundle. The canonical divisor KXK_XKX​ records top-degree differential forms.

To examine a singularity, pass to a smooth birational model π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X. For a prime divisor EEE on such a model, its log discrepancy is

AX,B(E)=1+ord⁡E(KY−π∗(KX+B)).A_{X,B}(E)=1+\operatorname{ord}_E\bigl(K_Y-\pi^*(K_X+B)\bigr).AX,B​(E)=1+ordE​(KY​−π∗(KX​+B)).

This measures how differential forms and the boundary transform near that divisor. All such divisors, including those visible only after further modifications, must be considered. The pair is log canonical, abbreviated lc, if every discrepancy is nonnegative; Kawamata log terminal, abbreviated klt, if every discrepancy is positive; and ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc if every discrepancy is at least a fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0.

Thus klt is stricter than lc, and ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc specifies a quantitative margin. The margin is imposed on prime-divisor orders in their natural normalization. Multiplying an order function by an arbitrarily small real number also scales its discrepancy, so unrestricted rescaling cannot be used to test this condition.

Fano contractions and complements

A contraction f:X→Zf:X\to Zf:X→Z is a projective surjective map of normal varieties with f∗OX=OZf_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Zf∗​OX​=OZ​. A Fano contraction has −KX-K_X−KX​ ample relative to the base. Relative ampleness concerns positivity in the directions of the fibers.

More generally, XXX is of Fano type over ZZZ if some effective rational boundary CCC makes (X,C)(X,C)(X,C) klt and −(KX+C)-(K_X+C)−(KX​+C) relatively ample. This auxiliary boundary need not be the boundary BBB appearing in the theorem. A divisor is relatively nef when its intersection with every contracted curve is nonnegative.

A monotone klt complement replaces BBB by a larger effective rational boundary B+≥BB^+\geq BB+≥B such that the resulting pair is klt and

N(KX+B+)∼0N(K_X+B^+)\sim0N(KX​+B+)∼0

near the chosen fiber. Here the displayed divisor is integral Cartier and linearly trivial. Linear triviality is stronger than having zero intersection with curves: the corresponding line bundle must actually be trivial. The integer NNN is the complement index.

Thresholds explain the local question

For an effective Cartier divisor DDD on the base, the log canonical threshold of its pullback is the largest allowable coefficient in B+tf∗DB+t f^*DB+tf∗D. It is controlled by ratios

AX,B(E)ord⁡E(f∗D)\frac{A_{X,B}(E)}{\operatorname{ord}_E(f^*D)}ordE​(f∗D)AX,B​(E)​

over divisors with positive denominator. The initial discrepancy bound controls the numerator but says nothing immediately about the denominator. On a smooth curve, a divisor consisting of a point with multiplicity mmm has threshold 1/m1/m1/m. The theorem must therefore choose a good equation; it cannot make every equation good.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Shokurov introduced complements in the study of threefold flips and developed their boundedness systematically in his work on surfaces. Prokhorov and Shokurov developed the higher-dimensional program and methods passing between global and local complements.

Birkar’s bounded-complement theorem established bounded lc complements for Fano-type pairs with suitable coefficient sets in arbitrary dimension. This is a major foundation for the present manuscripts. An lc complement may have a divisor of discrepancy zero, however. Simply reducing its coefficients can destroy the exact linear equivalence that made it a complement, so obtaining a bounded klt complement is a separate problem.

Partial results controlled that stronger requirement. Birkar’s work on Fano fibrations gives bounded klt complements over curves. Toric geometry and weighted blowups provide special settings where orders of equations can be controlled more explicitly; the manuscripts discuss results of Ambro and of Sankaran–Santos in these directions.

The decisive organizing result is Bingyi Chen’s equivalence theorem. It links bounded klt complements to the existence of a uniformly mild Cartier hypersurface through a prescribed point. Chen proves the local surface case and consequently the complement conjecture for bases of dimension at most two. This concerns the dimension of the base, not merely the dimension of the total space.

The new manuscripts use that reduction while proposing different arguments for its remaining all-dimensional input. They also build on normalized-volume theory for singularities, which constructs canonical degenerations by optimizing over orders of vanishing. Existing optimization theorems concern ordinary klt pairs; both manuscripts identify additional work needed to impose their special constraints.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: bounded klt complements

Fix a positive integer ddd and a positive rational ϵ\epsilonϵ. M1 claims an integer N=N(d,ϵ)N=N(d,\epsilon)N=N(d,ϵ) for every ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc Fano contraction f:X→Zf:X\to Zf:X→Z of total dimension ddd, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

For every closed point z∈Zz\in Zz∈Z, there are an effective rational boundary BBB and a Zariski-open neighborhood UUU of zzz such that (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) is klt over UUU and

N(KX+B)∣f−1(U)∼0.N(K_X+B)|_{f^{-1}(U)}\sim0.N(KX​+B)∣f−1(U)​∼0.

Neither relative Picard number one nor positive-dimensional general fibers is required. The boundary and neighborhood depend on the contraction and point; the integer does not.

Over C\mathbb CC, M1 also claims monotone klt complements for ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc pairs (X,Δ)(X,\Delta)(X,Δ) with coefficients in a fixed finite rational set III, provided XXX is of Fano type over the quasi-projective base and −(KX+Δ)-(K_X+\Delta)−(KX​+Δ) is relatively nef. Here the uniform index depends on d,ϵ,Id,\epsilon,Id,ϵ,I. This is the finite-rational-coefficient form of the bounded-klt-complement conjecture.

M2: a uniformly mild Cartier section

M2 claims that for every ddd and ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, there is a positive number τ(d,ϵ)\tau(d,\epsilon)τ(d,ϵ) with the following property. Let (X,B)(X,B)(X,B) be an ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc rational pair of dimension ddd, and let f:X→Zf:X\to Zf:X→Z be a Fano-type contraction of normal quasi-projective varieties in characteristic zero, with positive-dimensional base and −(KX+B)-(K_X+B)−(KX​+B) relatively nef.

For each closed point zzz, one can find an effective nonzero Cartier divisor DDD through zzz, defined on a neighborhood UUU, such that

(f−1(U),B∣f−1(U)+τf∗D)is log canonical.\bigl(f^{-1}(U),B|_{f^{-1}(U)}+\tau f^*D\bigr)\quad\text{is log canonical}.(f−1(U),B∣f−1(U)​+τf∗D)is log canonical.

The constant is independent of boundary denominators, Cartier indices and polarizations. Over C\mathbb CC, the manuscript extends this conclusion to effective real boundaries with real-Cartier log canonical divisor.

M2 separately proves a bounded klt complement statement for birational Fano-type contractions with zero boundary and relatively nef −KX-K_X−KX​. Through Chen’s equivalence, this supplies the Cartier-section claim and the complex finite-coefficient complement consequence. The manuscripts present their principal arguments as independent approaches, rather than one paper merely invoking the other.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claims address a central uniformity problem in the study of Fano varieties and singularities. Complements let geometry with positive anticanonical direction be replaced by a controlled log-Calabi–Yau pair, where the adjusted canonical divisor becomes torsion. Uniform indices make that replacement useful across families.

The local section theorem is equally concrete: a prescribed base point admits an equation whose pullback remains tolerably singular along the whole nearby fiber. It is stronger than controlling thresholds only at generic points of divisors on the base.

The rating reflects the breadth of these claimed all-dimensional results and their relationship with existing boundedness theory. It measures significance if correct, not proof confidence.

6. The main idea

Turn failure of uniformity into concentration

M1 reduces the problem to a lower bound for the threshold of the pulled-back maximal ideal of a base point in the birational, zero-boundary setting. If no such bound existed, one could find a sequence in which orders of that ideal become arbitrarily large relative to discrepancies.

Anticanonical sections are collected into a graded ring, whose spectrum is an affine cone. A bounded lc complement supplies an initial system of fixed degree. The proposed constrained optimization chooses an order function on the cone that both minimizes normalized volume and lies on a prescribed log-canonical boundary condition.

A crucial claimed step realizes that constrained minimizer as the actual minimizer for one small klt perturbation. This enables the established stable-degeneration machinery to produce a finitely generated graded model without losing the concentration information.

Count sections, then recover a genuine divisor

M1 organizes independent directions in the resulting function fields according to the cost of producing sections. Upper estimates limit how many sections can occur at a given cost; independent monomials provide competing lower estimates. Auxiliary reductions to positive characteristic use Cartier trace, an operation on differential forms associated with the Frobenius map, to construct controlled sections.

The endpoint must be more precise than “some real valuation has small discrepancy.” Such smallness can be manufactured by rescaling. The manuscript therefore tracks independent coordinates and denominators until a bounded multiple of the constructed valuation is a positive integral multiple of a prime-divisor order. Its discrepancy then contradicts the original ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc bound in the required normalization.

A second route through characters

M2 starts from cyclic covers and sections transforming under specified characters, meaning scalar multiplication rules for the finite cyclic group. Failure of bounded complements forces every section of a fixed character degree to have a large order.

Dividing such sections by powers of a distinguished function produces invariant rational functions. Requiring both a function and its inverse to have nonnegative order pins their order exactly to zero. The argument repeatedly preserves these equalities while adding algebraically independent functions.

Each successful addition uses one of the finitely many dimensions available in the function field. If the process cannot add another independent function, the remaining character direction is claimed to produce a prime divisor of too-small discrepancy on the quotient. Thus dimension bounds one alternative, while the singularity gap rules out the other. Chen’s equivalence then translates this obstruction into the stated geometric conclusions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are local statements over a neighborhood of each chosen base point. They do not claim one boundary or one hypersurface works simultaneously over an entire arbitrary base without shrinking.

The complement output is klt, but is not asserted to preserve the original ϵ\epsilonϵ-lc bound. The stronger demand for quantitatively bounded discrepancies in the complement remains distinct. Likewise, the finite rational coefficient set enters the complement index even though the Cartier-section coefficient has no such dependence.

The bounds are existence statements, not explicit numerical formulas. The use of positive characteristic in M1 is an auxiliary method inside a characteristic-zero theorem; it does not establish the same result for varieties over arbitrary positive-characteristic fields.

The real-boundary extension is stated over C\mathbb CC. Rational-boundary results have the broader characteristic-zero scope specified above. Preserving these different fields, boundary types and uniformity dependencies is essential to understanding what each manuscript contributes.

8. Sources and further reading

Chen’s paper provides the closest formulation of the conjectures, their equivalence and the surface-base result. Birkar’s bounded lc complements and his work on Fano fibrations explain the main earlier boundedness inputs. For the optimization background, see Xu–Zhuang on stable degenerations.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bounded klt complements for Fano contractions (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Uniform Cartier sections for Fano type contractions (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Nef tangent bundles force homogeneity in dimension six
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 067 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Some algebraic varieties look the same at every point because a large symmetry group moves any point to any other. Projective spaces, quadrics and Grassmannians are familiar examples. Can a numerical positivity condition force a variety to have this much symmetry?

The Campana–Peternell conjecture predicts that a smooth complex Fano variety with nef tangent bundle is rational homogeneous. The hypothesis involves degrees of bundles on curves. The conclusion identifies the entire variety as a quotient of an algebraic group.

The manuscript in this family claims the conjecture in complex dimension six. Its main new case is recognized as the Grassmannian of two-dimensional subspaces of a five-dimensional vector space. The proposed bridge from positivity to symmetry is the geometry of tangent directions to minimal rational curves.

2. Background and essential definitions

Fano varieties and nef tangent bundles
