A smooth projective variety XXX is Fano when its anticanonical line bundle −KX-K_X−KX​ is ample. Here KXK_XKX​ is the bundle of top-degree holomorphic differential forms. Ampleness means that a sufficiently high tensor power supplies an embedding into projective space.

The tangent bundle TXT_XTX​ collects the tangent spaces at all points. A vector bundle EEE is nef, or numerically effective, when the tautological line bundle OP(E)(1)\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(E)}(1)OP(E)​(1) has nonnegative degree on every curve in its projectivization. In this definition, P(E)\mathbb P(E)P(E) parametrizes one-dimensional quotients. Equivalently, after pulling EEE back along a map from a smooth projective curve, every quotient line bundle has nonnegative degree.

Nefness permits zero degrees. It is substantially weaker than ampleness and does not say that one has a Hermitian metric with a particular nonnegative curvature tensor. For tangent bundles, it nevertheless places strong restrictions on how rational curves deform.

A rational homogeneous variety is a space G/PG/PG/P, where GGG is a connected semisimple complex algebraic group and PPP is a parabolic subgroup, so the quotient is projective. The group acts transitively. Its infinitesimal action generates the tangent bundle by global sections, and that implies nefness. The conjecture asks for a converse under the Fano hypothesis.

Two numerical guides

The Picard number ρ(X)\rho(X)ρ(X) is the number of independent divisor classes modulo numerical equivalence. When it equals one, all divisor classes point in the same numerical direction, making independent contractions especially restrictive.

The pseudoindex is

ιX=min⁡{−KX⋅C:C⊂X is an irreducible rational curve}.\iota_X=\min\{-K_X\cdot C:C\subset X\text{ is an irreducible rational curve}\}.ιX​=min{−KX​⋅C:C⊂X is an irreducible rational curve}.

The intersection number is the anticanonical degree of the curve. A rational curve has normalization P1\mathbb P^1P1. The pseudoindex records the smallest degree, rather than the divisibility of −KX-K_X−KX​ in the line-bundle group; the latter is the different invariant called the index.

Choose a covering family of rational curves of this smallest degree. At a general point xxx, collect their tangent directions and take the closure inside the projective space of tangent lines. The result is the variety of minimal rational tangents, often abbreviated VMRT. Think of it as the set of directions in which the simplest algebraic curves can leave the point.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mori’s theorem that a projective manifold with ample tangent bundle is projective space gave a powerful model for positivity-based classification. Campana and Peternell proposed the nef analogue in their 1991 paper, with homogeneous spaces replacing projective space as the expected class.

Campana–Peternell established the conjecture in dimensions at most three and for fourfolds with Picard number greater than one. Mok and Hwang’s methods using minimal rational tangents completed the remaining four-dimensional case. Watanabe treated fivefolds with higher Picard number, and Kanemitsu completed the fivefold classification.

A second theorem of Kanemitsu covers an nnn-dimensional Fano manifold with nef tangent bundle whenever

ρ(X)>n−5.\rho(X)>n-5.ρ(X)>n−5.

For a sixfold this already settles every Picard number at least two. Thus the new theorem does not begin with all sixfolds as unexplored territory: its remaining work lies at Picard number one.

Earlier characterization results then reduce the possibilities to projective space, a quadric, and pseudoindex four or five. Watanabe’s coindex-three paper includes the pseudoindex-four sixfold case. The present manuscript gives another argument for that case, while identifying pseudoindex five as its principal new contribution.

There is also a broader analytic background. Demailly, Peternell and Schneider’s structure theorem for compact Kähler manifolds with nef tangent bundle relates them, after finite unramified cover, to Fano fibers over a complex torus. That reduction explains why one additional Fano dimension can yield consequences for compact Kähler manifolds that are not themselves projective.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The sixfold classification

The main theorem states that every smooth connected complex projective Fano variety XXX satisfying

dim⁡CX=6,TX nef\dim_{\mathbb C}X=6,\qquad T_X\text{ nef}dimC​X=6,TX​ nef

is rational homogeneous. There is no additional assumption on Picard number, Betti numbers, or the existence of a particular group action.

The decisive specialized statement says that when ρ(X)=1\rho(X)=1ρ(X)=1 and ιX=5\iota_X=5ιX​=5,

X≅Gr⁡(2,5).X\cong\operatorname{Gr}(2,5).X≅Gr(2,5).

The Grassmannian on the right parametrizes two-dimensional linear subspaces of C5\mathbb C^5C5. Its dimension is 2(5−2)=62(5-2)=62(5−2)=6, so it has exactly the required size. Combining this case with the previous classification and the manuscript’s treatment of pseudoindex four gives the full theorem.

A universal-cover consequence

For a connected compact Kähler manifold, define its augmented irregularity by

q~(X)=max⁡X′→Xh1(X′,OX′),\widetilde q(X)=\max_{X'\to X}h^1(X',\mathcal O_{X'}),q​(X)=X′→Xmax​h1(X′,OX′​),

where the maximum runs over connected finite étale covers, meaning finite unramified holomorphic covers. The quantity measures the largest torus direction visible after such a cover.

Assume the holomorphic tangent bundle is analytically nef and

0≤dim⁡CX−q~(X)≤6.0\leq\dim_{\mathbb C}X-\widetilde q(X)\leq6.0≤dimC​X−q​(X)≤6.

The manuscript claims that a suitable finite cover has a smooth, holomorphically locally trivial fibration over a complex torus, with rational homogeneous fiber FFF. Moreover, the ordinary universal cover satisfies

X~≅F×Cq~(X).\widetilde X\cong F\times\mathbb C^{\widetilde q(X)}.X≅F×Cq​(X).

The fiber is allowed to be a point. This covers every such compact Kähler manifold of dimension at most six, and also higher-dimensional ones whose remaining fiber dimension is at most six. The finite-cover bundle can stay twisted; the displayed product belongs to the universal cover.

The classification also yields positive Kähler–Einstein metrics on Fano manifolds with nef tangent bundle in dimensions one through six. With the manuscript’s normalization, the Kähler form satisfies Ric⁡(ω)=ω\operatorname{Ric}(\omega)=\omegaRic(ω)=ω and represents 2πc1(−KX)2\pi c_1(-K_X)2πc1​(−KX​).

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. This is a major new-dimensional case of a longstanding classification conjecture. It would show that weak numerical positivity still forces complete homogeneity at the first dimension beyond the established fivefold theorem.

The proposed method also has broader interest: it extracts a rigid geometric model from compatibility between two different fibrations of a space of curves. The Kähler consequence translates the classification into a product description of universal covers.

The score is below the collection’s highest tier because the main classification remains dimension-specific. The all-dimensional Campana–Peternell conjecture is not claimed here. As elsewhere in the series, the score concerns significance if the stated result is correct.

6. The main idea

Look at the same family in two ways

Let VVV parametrize minimal rational curves, and let UUU consist of a curve together with a marked point on it. There are two maps:

V ← π  U → e  X.V\ \xleftarrow{\ \pi\ }\ U\ \xrightarrow{\ e\ }\ X.V  π ​ U  e ​ X.

The map π\piπ forgets the marked point, while eee remembers only its location on XXX. A fiber of π\piπ is a projective line. Nefness of TXT_XTX​ gives the deformation properties needed for these families and evaluation maps to be smooth.

In the pseudoindex-five case, a fiber F=e−1(x)F=e^{-1}(x)F=e−1(x) is a smooth threefold. It parametrizes the minimal curves through xxx. Their tangent directions give a finite map from FFF into P5\mathbb P^5P5. Pulling back the hyperplane bundle gives an ample line bundle LLL on FFF.

At this stage, neither the degree of that map nor the identity of its image is known. The core task is to recover them from the two compatible fibrations of UUU.

A numerical identity narrows the geometry

Chern classes are cohomological invariants of vector bundles; their top-degree products can be integrated to give characteristic numbers. The manuscript combines identities for these numbers from both maps, using Riemann–Roch and Hodge-theoretic fixed-part information.

Integration along a fiber supplies linear relations. The projection formula supplies additional relations in which numbers factor as products. The combination is claimed to force

32−20u+3u2=0,u=c1(TF)⋅L2L3.32-20u+3u^2=0,\qquadu=\frac{c_1(T_F)\cdot L^2}{L^3}.32−20u+3u2=0,u=L3c1​(TF​)⋅L2​.

Thus u=4u=4u=4 or u=8/3u=8/3u=8/3. The manuscript includes an exact arithmetic certificate for this finite elimination. The role of that calculation is to extract the displayed identity from geometric constraints; the classification also needs the geometric steps before and after it.

Take the curve obtained by intersecting two general divisors of LLL. Adjunction computes its genus as

g=1+(1−u2)L3.g=1+\left(1-\frac u2\right)L^3.g=1+(1−2u​)L3.

The tangent image spans P5\mathbb P^5P5, so its degree is at least three, and consequently L3≥3L^3\geq3L3≥3. The choice u=4u=4u=4 would make the genus negative. The other choice forces L3=3L^3=3L3=3, a degree-one tangent map and a degree-three image.

Recognize the tangent directions, then the manifold

The classification of varieties of minimal degree, together with smoothness and normality, identifies this image as

P1×P2↪P5\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^2\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^5P1×P2↪P5

in its Segre embedding. The Segre map sends two vectors to their rank-one tensor; its coordinates are all pairwise products of their coordinates.

This is precisely the tangent-direction geometry of Gr⁡(2,5)\operatorname{Gr}(2,5)Gr(2,5). At a two-plane A⊂C5A\subset\mathbb C^5A⊂C5, the tangent space is Hom⁡(A,C5/A)\operatorname{Hom}(A,\mathbb C^5/A)Hom(A,C5/A). Tangents to lines correspond to rank-one maps, whose projectivization is the displayed product. Mok’s recognition theorem then converts equality of these projective tangent models into an isomorphism of the original manifolds.

The separate pseudoindex-four argument uses a factorization theorem to isolate a possible nonhomogeneous case. Its alternative fibrations impose incompatible cohomological and integral-degree conditions. It rules out that alternative, rather than ruling out homogeneous pseudoindex-four sixfolds themselves.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The principal theorem is for smooth projective Fano varieties over C\mathbb CC, in dimension six. Dropping smoothness, changing characteristic, or replacing the tangent bundle by another bundle requires separate results.

Nef tangent bundle alone does not make a compact Kähler manifold rational homogeneous: complex tori already show why a torus factor must be allowed. The analytic corollary uses the earlier Albanese structure theorem and the condition on the remaining fiber dimension. Its torus base can be nonprojective.

The universal cover is holomorphically convex: enough holomorphic functions remain after contracting its compact homogeneous fibers. It is generally not Stein when FFF has positive dimension, because a Stein space cannot contain such a compact positive-dimensional complex subvariety. Nor does the asserted universal-cover product imply that some finite cover splits as a global product.

The natural next classification question is higher dimension. There the minimal-tangent varieties have more possibilities, and this particular characteristic-number identity does not automatically extend. The manuscript settles its six-dimensional configuration rather than supplying an all-dimensional recognition formula.

8. Sources and further reading

The preceding frontier is described in Kanemitsu’s fivefold theorem, his higher-Picard-number theorem, and Watanabe’s coindex-three work. The source manuscript cites the original Hwang–Mok tangent-recognition results and the Demailly–Peternell–Schneider structure theorem, and gives the precise characteristic-class calculation used in the remaining case.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Campana–Peternell conjecture in dimension six (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: From semipositive anticanonical curvature to algebraic sections
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 068 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A line bundle can be geometrically nonnegative without having any nonzero global section. Curvature and intersection numbers describe positivity; a section is an actual globally compatible algebraic object. Passing from one kind of information to the other is a central difficulty in nonvanishing problems.

For the anticanonical bundle, which comes from the tangent directions of the variety itself, there is reason to expect a stronger connection. This family claims that a smooth semipositive anticanonical metric on a smooth complex projective variety always produces a section of some positive tensor power.

Seven manuscripts develop the headline and several related mechanisms. Their shared obstacles are concrete: sections can acquire poles during birational constructions, and a section on a covering space may fail to descend because it transforms under the covering symmetries.

2. Background and essential definitions

Three levels of positivity and effectivity

For a smooth nnn-dimensional variety XXX, its canonical bundle is KX=⋀nΩX1K_X=\bigwedge^n\Omega_X^1KX​=⋀nΩX1​, the bundle of top differential forms. The anticanonical bundle is its dual,

L=−KX=det⁡TX.L=-K_X=\det T_X.L=−KX​=detTX​.

Additive notation for line bundles is convenient: mLmLmL means L⊗mL^{\otimes m}L⊗m, and L+DL+DL+D means tensoring with the line bundle of the divisor DDD.

A Hermitian metric assigns lengths to vectors in each fiber. In a local frame, write its squared norm as e−φe^{-\varphi}e−φ. Smooth semipositivity means that the curvature form −1 ∂∂ˉφ\sqrt{-1}\,\partial\bar\partial\varphi−1​∂∂ˉφ is nonnegative everywhere. It implies that LLL is nef: L⋅C≥0L\cdot C\geq0L⋅C≥0 for every curve CCC.

A divisor is pseudoeffective if its numerical class is a limit of effective divisor classes. This is weaker still. Numerical information alone cannot distinguish a line bundle from a nontorsion flat twist with the same first Chern class.

A nonzero section of mLmLmL gives an effective zero divisor linearly equivalent to mLmLmL, with the empty divisor allowed. Thus the desired conclusion is actual linear effectivity of a positive multiple, not just an effective representative of its numerical class. It is also weaker than semiampleness, which requires some positive power to have enough sections to be generated at every point.

Symmetry and integrability

An algebraic torus T≅(C∗)rT\cong(\mathbb C^*)^rT≅(C∗)r acting on XXX acts naturally on det⁡TX\det T_XdetTX​ by differentiation. A section is invariant if that induced action fixes it. Changing the action on the line bundle by a character—a homomorphism T→C∗T\to\mathbb C^*T→C∗—changes which sections are invariant, even though the underlying line bundle stays the same.

A singular semipositive metric allows nonsmooth plurisubharmonic weights φ\varphiφ, the complex analogue of subharmonic potentials. Locally bounded weights have both upper and lower bounds, but need not be continuous. Integrability is a different condition: the squared norm of a section may be locally integrable even when that of a nonvanishing frame is not.

For example, on a disk, if e−φ=∣z∣−2ae^{-\varphi}=|z|^{-2a}e−φ=∣z∣−2a, then the section zjz^jzj has integrable squared norm exactly when a<j+1a<j+1a<j+1. The frame itself requires a<1a<1a<1. This difference is why the manuscripts carefully distinguish metrics weighted by a boundary section from unweighted metrics.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The positive-multiple problem under smooth semipositivity is associated with Yau’s anticanonical-section question. Yau’s prescribed-Ricci theorem also supplies a geometric route: the given anticanonical curvature can be realized as the Ricci form of a Kähler metric. Demailly–Peternell–Schneider’s structure theorem and the refinement of Campana–Demailly–Peternell then describe the universal cover using flat, Ricci-flat and rationally connected factors. Rational connectedness means that two general points can be joined by a rational curve.

The broader nef problem has substantial earlier results. Lazić, Matsumura, Peternell, Tsakanikas and Xie prove numerical effectivity for log-canonical threefold pairs with nef anti-log-canonical divisor, under their stated assumptions of rational singularities or Q\mathbb QQ-factoriality.

Müller proves actual nonvanishing for projective klt threefold pairs with nef anti-log-canonical divisor. His higher-dimensional result assumes semiampleness on the general fiber of the maximal rationally connected fibration, which separates the rationally connected directions from the rest. His equivariant theorem constructs naturally invariant sections under commutative linear algebraic groups when the anti-log-canonical divisor is semiample. That is a direct predecessor of the monodromy arguments here.

The recent surface classification of Chen, Filip, Sun, Tosatti and Zhang gives complementary results for semipositive anticanonical metrics. It also illustrates that smooth semipositivity need not imply semiampleness. The new headline therefore uses a stronger assumption than nefness but does not merely restate the semiample case.

Analytically, the papers build on hard Lefschetz theorems with semipositive coefficients, positivity of direct images due to Berndtsson, Berndtsson–Păun and Păun–Takayama, and vanishing theorems controlling singular metrics. Algebraically, determinant methods for twisted differential forms and finite generation of adjoint rings provide ways to turn cohomological data into sections. The claimed contributions concern the precise transfer, boundary and symmetry control needed to combine these ingredients.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The common headline

M1 states that for every smooth connected projective complex variety XXX,

−KX smoothly semipositive⟹H0(X,−mKX)≠0 for some m>0.-K_X\text{ smoothly semipositive}\quad\Longrightarrow\quadH^0(X,-mK_X)\neq0\text{ for some }m>0.−KX​ smoothly semipositive⟹H0(X,−mKX​)=0 for some m>0.

The exponent may depend on XXX. M2–M4, M6 and M7 develop additional routes to this conclusion, while M5 concentrates on transfer statements used within the family. Their roles are distinct, and several use explicitly identified companion results.

M1 and M5: finite volume and controlled poles

Suppose a smooth projective variety ZZZ has no positive-degree holomorphic forms, and D≥0D\geq0D≥0 is an integral divisor. Let sDs_DsD​ be its canonical section. M1 claims that if −KZ+D-K_Z+D−KZ​+D has a semipositive metric making the measure ∣sD∣2|s_D|^2∣sD​∣2 integrable, then every line bundle AAA with a locally bounded semipositive metric satisfies

H0(Z,aA+bD)≠0for some a>0, b≥0.H^0(Z,aA+bD)\neq0\quad\text{for some }a>0,\ b\geq0.H0(Z,aA+bD)=0for some a>0, b≥0.

This allows poles only along DDD when viewed as a rational section of aAaAaA. The volume metric and the bounded metric belong to different line bundles.

M5 develops another treatment of this transfer and gives explicit corrections on a fibration’s base whose pullbacks disappear under birational pushforward. It also claims a dimension-reduction procedure preserving both a generic invariant section and one-dimensional invariant adjoint section spaces, under its stated no-forms, smooth-semipositivity and generic-rank hypotheses. Preserving the rank matters because the next step of integration needs it again.

M2 and M4: remove a fixed error, retain the character

For a compact complex manifold FFF with a holomorphic compact-torus action, define the invariant index

IT(m)=∑q(−1)qdim⁡Hq(F,−mKF)T.I_T(m)=\sum_q(-1)^q\dim H^q(F,-mK_F)^T.IT​(m)=q∑​(−1)qdimHq(F,−mKF​)T.

M2 claims that this is polynomial on positive multiples of some integer, with the polynomial’s value at zero equal to the actual IT(0)I_T(0)IT​(0). This index statement assumes neither projectivity nor positivity, but does require the natural anticanonical action.

Independently, M2 claims that for smoothly semipositive L=−KXL=-K_XL=−KX​, a fixed pseudoeffective Cartier divisor DDD, and unbounded positive integers mjm_jmj​,

H0(X,mjL−D)≠0⟹H0(X,kL)≠0 for some k>0.H^0(X,m_jL-D)\neq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quadH^0(X,kL)\neq0\text{ for some }k>0.H0(X,mj​L−D)=0⟹H0(X,kL)=0 for some k>0.

M4 strengthens this kind of conversion by keeping torus invariance for any specified linearization of LLL, provided the input sections with one fixed negative pseudoeffective error are invariant for that same action. It does not assert unconditional invariant nonvanishing for arbitrary shifted actions. With the natural action and nonzero χ(X,OX)\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)χ(X,OX​), the index supplies the necessary cohomological input. Here χ\chiχ is the alternating sum of structure-sheaf cohomology dimensions.

M3: a singular-pair criterion and torus quotients

M3 treats a projective Q\mathbb QQ-factorial klt pair (W,D)(W,D)(W,D) with effective rational boundary. The first condition means every divisor has a Cartier multiple; the second imposes strictly positive log discrepancies on all birational models.

Set P=−(KW+D)P=-(K_W+D)P=−(KW​+D). If PPP is nef, its pullback to a smooth resolution has a locally bounded semipositive metric, and that resolution has nonzero structure-sheaf Euler characteristic, M3 claims a section of some positive Cartier multiple of PPP.

It applies this criterion to torus quotients, obtaining naturally invariant anticanonical sections on smooth rationally connected projective varieties with smoothly semipositive anticanonical bundle. The singular, metric and Euler hypotheses are part of the criterion, not dispensable technical decoration.

M6 and M7: control corrections and attain zero order

M6 claims that if −KY+C-K_Y+C−KY​+C, for an effective integral divisor CCC, has a singular metric whose curvature dominates a Kähler form and whose distinguished section sCs_CsC​ is locally square integrable, then every pseudoeffective rational divisor MMM becomes rationally effective after adding an effective rational correction supported on CCC. It also gives nearby finite-generation results under a stronger unweighted integrability hypothesis, and another fixed-error conversion argument.

M7 addresses exact vanishing orders. Let α\alphaα be the smooth semipositive curvature of L=−KXL=-K_XL=−KX​, of maximum rank ν\nuν, and choose an ample bundle GGG. For n=dim⁡Xn=\dim Xn=dimX, define

ℓ(D)={D⋅Lν⋅Gn−ν−1,ν<n,0,ν=n.\ell(D)=\begin{cases}D\cdot L^\nu\cdot G^{n-\nu-1},&\nu<n,\\0,&\nu=n.\end{cases}ℓ(D)={D⋅Lν⋅Gn−ν−1,0,​ν<n,ν=n.​

This is nonnegative on effective divisors and satisfies ℓ(L)=0\ell(L)=0ℓ(L)=0. For any fixed line bundle MMM, suppose effective integral divisors satisfy Nj∼mjL+MN_j\sim m_jL+MNj​∼mj​L+M, mj→∞m_j\to\inftymj​→∞, ℓ(Nj)=0\ell(N_j)=0ℓ(Nj​)=0, and v(Nj)/mj→0v(N_j)/m_j\to0v(Nj​)/mj​→0, where vvv is a centered discrete valuation or the zero valuation. M7 claims an effective rational divisor N∼QLN\sim_{\mathbb Q}LN∼Q​L with v(N)=0v(N)=0v(N)=0. A valuation measures order of vanishing; “centered” ensures regular functions at its center have nonnegative order. Exact zero is stronger than a vanishing normalized limit.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The headline would settle an all-dimensional anticanonical nonvanishing problem under a natural differential-geometric positivity assumption. The family also proposes reusable ways to preserve genuine line bundles, exact orders and group actions while passing through fibrations and singular models.

These extra outputs explain why seven manuscripts belong together. Producing a section on a simpler space is useful only if its poles and transformation law allow it to return to the original space. The family addresses those requirements through several related constructions.

The rating concerns the scope of the claims if correct. It does not indicate that seven manuscripts constitute seven independent confirmations of one proof; their stated dependencies and shared geometric inputs remain relevant.

6. The main idea

Produce forms, then transfer positivity

An Euler characteristic is often easier to compute than a space of sections. A nonzero Euler polynomial guarantees some nonzero cohomology at many powers. Hard Lefschetz turns those classes into differential forms twisted by anticanonical powers. Taking determinants of a fixed-rank span produces effective divisors with one fixed error term.

Ratios of sections define a rational fibration. By choosing its base maximally, the papers force relevant relative section spaces to have dimension one. Integrating the norm of that section along fibers then defines a metric on a line bundle on the base. Higher moments, after normalization, approach a fiberwise maximum or essential supremum. This is the proposed source of bounded metrics that permit another conversion step.

Keep the boundary where it can disappear

A section regular on general fibers can still have poles over special fibers. The constructions subtract minimum normalized orders above base divisors, retaining a component where the normalized section does not vanish. This supplies bounds near the boundary.

Some corrections are supported only on exceptional divisors—divisors contracted by the birational map back to the original variety. Once the section is pushed back, those corrections disappear. M6 turns integrability into an effective boundary using multiplier ideals, which record locally integrable holomorphic functions, and then applies existing big-boundary nonvanishing results. M7 uses the resulting finite-generation machinery to attain a limiting order exactly, instead of merely approximating zero.

Descend through monodromy

The universal-cover structure separates Euclidean and Ricci-flat factors from a compact factor carrying the remaining geometry. Even after finite cover, deck transformations can act on that last factor through a compact torus. An arbitrary section there may transform nontrivially and fail to descend.

The papers construct sections or twisted forms fixed by the natural action. These combine with invariant canonical frames on the other factors and descend. A finite étale norm—the product over the sheets, interpreted in line bundles—then returns a nonzero section to XXX, at a possibly larger exponent.

The routes differ. M2 descends invariant forms before ordinary conversion. M3 obtains invariant sections through a stable quotient. M4 preserves characters through conversion. M7 translates orders along generic torus orbits into section weights and combines those weights to obtain an invariant product. M7’s exact-order argument explicitly uses the metric construction of M5 and the finite-generation result of M6.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The headline requires smooth projectivity over C\mathbb CC and a smooth semipositive anticanonical metric. It does not settle anticanonical nonvanishing from nefness alone in arbitrary dimension, nor assert semiampleness.

The positive multiple cannot be replaced by the first power. If EEE is an Enriques surface, its canonical bundle has order two but is nontrivial. The variety E×P1E\times\mathbb P^1E×P1 has smoothly semipositive anticanonical bundle with no first-power section, while the square has sections. Its anticanonical bundle is not itself torsion because it has positive degree on the projective-line fibers.

Natural linearization is essential for the unconditional invariant conclusions. A character shift can remove weight zero from every positive power. The transfer theorem for shifted actions therefore retains its input hypothesis rather than promising invariant sections automatically.

The singular-pair and exact-order results have their own additional assumptions. Bounded weights, finite weighted volume and unweighted integrability are not interchangeable. Likewise, a product description of the universal cover does not remove monodromy from a finite cover. These distinctions delimit the claims and identify where further generalizations would need new arguments.

8. Sources and further reading

For earlier numerical nonvanishing, see Lazić–Matsumura–Peternell–Tsakanikas–Xie; for actual threefold nonvanishing and the equivariant predecessor, see Müller. The semipositive surface classification supplies concrete low-dimensional context. The seven source manuscripts below state their different metric and transfer hypotheses in detail.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Anticanonical nonvanishing from smooth semipositivity (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Invariant anticanonical indices and conversion of twisted differentials (September 26, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Bounded anticanonical metrics on klt pairs and torus quotients (September 26, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Cohomological transfer and equivariant anticanonical sections (September 26, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Metric descent and rank-preserving contractions (September 26, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Integrable metrics and effectivity with controlled boundary (September 26, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Exact orders and invariant anticanonical linear systems (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Quantum geometric Langlands at every irrational level
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 069 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Fourier transformation lets the same problem be described in two different languages. Functions become frequency data, while operations that are complicated on one side can become simple on the other. Quantum geometric Langlands predicts a much more elaborate kind of dual description: whole categories of geometric differential equations for one symmetry group should correspond to those for a dual group.

The parameter controlling the differential equations is called the level. Under the proposed duality it changes to a negative reciprocal, with a correction determined by the root system. The geometry on both sides lives over the same complex algebraic curve, but the bundles being parametrized belong to different groups.

This manuscript claims the global unramified correspondence at every irrational complex level, including non-real levels. The conclusion is an equivalence of full categories, with compatibility under the local operations that identify it as the intended Langlands correspondence.

2. Background and essential definitions

Bundles, their parameter space, and the dual group

Let XXX be a smooth connected projective curve over C\mathbb CC. Analytically, it is a compact Riemann surface. A principal GGG-bundle is a geometric object locally modeled on GGG, with transition functions taking values in GGG. For matrix groups, familiar vector bundles with additional structure provide concrete examples.

The notation Bun⁡G(X)\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)BunG​(X) denotes the moduli stack of such bundles. A moduli space parametrizes objects; a stack also remembers their automorphisms. This distinction matters because different bundles can have different symmetry groups, and those symmetries affect differential equations on the parameter space.

A connected simple complex algebraic group has a root system encoding its infinitesimal symmetries. Its full root datum includes additional integer lattices describing characters and one-parameter subgroups. Exchanging roots with coroots and the corresponding lattices defines the Langlands dual G∨G^\veeG∨.

For example, SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​ and PGL2\mathrm{PGL}_2PGL2​ are dual. They share closely related infinitesimal geometry, but one has a nontrivial finite center and the other has a different global topology. Keeping only the Lie algebra would discard information that the theorem explicitly retains.

Categories of differential equations

On a smooth space, a DDD-module is a sheaf on which functions and differential operators act compatibly. Locally, an equation such as Pf=0Pf=0Pf=0, with PPP a differential operator, can be encoded by a module over the ring of differential operators. This makes systems of equations amenable to algebraic operations.

A category records both objects and maps between them. An equivalence of categories preserves all mapping information and reaches every target object up to isomorphism; it is much stronger than matching a list of dimensions or numerical invariants.

The manuscript uses derived differential graded, or DG, categories. Their objects and mapping spaces are organized by complexes, retaining higher cohomological information. “Full” means all twisted DDD-modules in the specified cocomplete category, rather than only a convenient finite or special subcategory. Cocompleteness allows constructions such as arbitrary direct sums and the limits of increasing diagrams called colimits.

The level and its normalization

A twisted DDD-module uses differential operators glued with an additional line-bundle-dependent correction. A complex exponent specifies that correction; an actual fractional root of the line bundle is not required.

For a principal bundle EEE, let gE\mathfrak g_EgE​ be its associated adjoint vector bundle. The determinant line used here is

LG∣E=det⁡H0(X,gE)⊗det⁡H1(X,gE)−1.\mathcal L_G|_E=\det H^0(X,\mathfrak g_E)\otimes\det H^1(X,\mathfrak g_E)^{-1}.LG​∣E​=detH0(X,gE​)⊗detH1(X,gE​)−1.

The determinant of a vector space is its top exterior power. Thus this construction turns two cohomology groups into one line varying over the bundle stack.

Write h∨h^\veeh∨ for the dual Coxeter number, a positive integer attached to the root system. The manuscript’s shifted-level convention is

Dc(Bun⁡G(X))=D ⁣(LG(c−h∨)/(2h∨)).D_c(\operatorname{Bun}_G(X))=D\!\left(\mathcal L_G^{(c-h^\vee)/(2h^\vee)}\right).Dc​(BunG​(X))=D(LG(c−h∨)/(2h∨)​).

The formula defines the notation on the left. It is needed because an unshifted parameter would give a different-looking reciprocal rule.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ordinary geometric Langlands relates geometric differential equations on a bundle stack to a spectral side built from local systems for the dual group. The quantum version deforms that picture and compares two twisted bundle-side categories.

An early inverse-parameter formulation appears in Stoyanovsky’s account, which attributes the quantum deformation to Drinfeld. Kapustin and Witten developed the gauge-theoretic interpretation through electric–magnetic duality. Gaitsgory’s quantum Langlands notes organized the mathematical correspondence using local categories, localization and Whittaker coefficients.

Important local ingredients were established separately. Feigin–Frenkel duality identifies principal WWW-algebras at inverse shifted levels. These algebras arise by reducing representations of loop Lie algebras, which describe symmetries depending on a formal local coordinate. Arakawa–Frenkel and Raskin developed representation-theoretic and categorical forms of that reduction. Campbell, Dhillon and Raskin proved fundamental local equivalences, supplying the pointwise comparisons used here in the irrational range.

The ordinary geometric Langlands theorem was proved in a five-paper collaboration, with the final multiplicity-one paper by Gaitsgory and Raskin. The present manuscript uses that body of work as an input for global cohomological control. It is not a replacement proof of the ordinary theorem.

Two recent predecessors are especially close. Bogdanova’s quantum Whittaker nonvanishing paper proves a detection result for cuspidal twisted objects for adjoint groups. Her quantum Betti Langlands paper constructs a functor in the topological, or Betti, setting with central compatibility. The current claim is a full global equivalence in the algebraic de Rham setting, not merely the construction of a candidate functor or a restatement of the Betti result.

The remaining bridge is substantial: pointwise local equivalences must fit into families, survive collisions of points and reconstruct all global objects. These are the manuscript’s two principal areas of claimed new work.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let GGG be any connected simple complex algebraic group, with its given global form, and let XXX be any smooth connected projective complex curve. Let rrr be the lacing number: the ratio of squared long-root to short-root lengths, equal to 111, 222, or 333.

For every c∈C∖Qc\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Qc∈C∖Q, the manuscript claims an equivalence

Dc(Bun⁡G(X))≃D−1/(rc)(Bun⁡G∨(X)).D_c(\operatorname{Bun}_G(X))\simeqD_{-1/(rc)}(\operatorname{Bun}_{G^\vee}(X)).Dc​(BunG​(X))≃D−1/(rc)​(BunG∨​(X)).

Each side uses its own group’s determinant line and dual Coxeter number in the convention above. When roots have one length, r=1r=1r=1; for SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​, the dual parameter is simply −1/c-1/c−1/c.

“Irrational” here means outside the rational numbers as a subset of C\mathbb CC. It includes every non-real complex number, and real algebraic irrational numbers as well as transcendental ones. The claim has no additional unspecified exceptional irrational levels.

The equivalence includes all connected components of the bundle stacks and the full twisted categories. It is compatible with localization, Whittaker coefficients, moving marked points, their collisions and insertion of the trivial local object. Fixed pinnings—choices normalizing root directions—and a theta characteristic, a square root of the canonical bundle of the curve, set the construction’s normalizations.

The global form is reflected in a concrete exchange. Source objects have a central character η\etaη, describing how the center acts, and a component label ppp in the algebraic fundamental group. Under the root-datum identifications, the manuscript gives

(η,p)⟼(p,−η).(\eta,p)\longmapsto(p,-\eta).(η,p)⟼(p,−η).

It also claims compatibility between twisting bundles by central torsors and tensoring by the corresponding dual local systems. A torsor is a bundle with the specified group acting freely and transitively on each fiber. These compatibilities retain the finite central data that would disappear on replacing every group by its simply connected or adjoint form.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. A full global quantum geometric Langlands equivalence in this parameter range would resolve a central part of a major duality program linking algebraic geometry, representation theory and mathematical physics.

Its force comes from the combination of breadth and compatibility. It treats every connected simple complex group and every irrational complex level, and it identifies the functor through the operations used to build and analyze geometric objects. An abstract resemblance between categories would provide less usable information.

The rating reflects the significance of the stated result if correct. Rational levels, ramification and other extensions remain outside the headline, so the claim is not the completion of every form of quantum Langlands.

6. The main idea

Whittaker coefficients play the role of a transform

A Whittaker coefficient extracts information by averaging along unipotent symmetries with a chosen nontrivial character. Unipotent matrices have all eigenvalues equal to one; upper triangular matrices with ones on the diagonal provide an elementary model. The character supplies an oscillatory or exponential factor, making the operation resemble Fourier analysis.

A Poincaré construction is meant to reconstruct global objects from those coefficients. The manuscript claims an identity schematically of the form

JsRs≃Id⁡(s∉Q),J_sR_s\simeq\operatorname{Id}\qquad(s\notin\mathbb Q),Js​Rs​≃Id(s∈/Q),

where RsR_sRs​ takes Whittaker coefficients and JsJ_sJs​ is the suitably normalized reconstruction functor. This holds on the entire twisted category. At the ordinary level a residual subcategory complicates the analogous statement, so reconstruction at irrational level requires additional work.

Why irrationality matters

For a determinant exponent sss, the local twisting connection has monodromy

q=exp⁡(2π−1 s).q=\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}\,s).q=exp(2π−1​s).

Monodromy records how a local solution changes after going around a loop. When s∉Qs\notin\mathbb Qs∈/Q, qqq is not a root of unity. This separates the theorem’s range from the special torsion behavior of rational exponents.

The manuscript approximates its global kernel calculations by finite diagrams. For these finite pieces, quasi-unipotent monodromy makes relevant cohomology and map ranks constant away from roots of unity. But finite-piece constancy alone does not control an infinite colimit. The additional claimed mechanism combines logarithmic deformations near q=1q=1q=1 with a uniform cohomological weight bound, using ordinary geometric Langlands. It shows that each potential error is killed at a finite later stage, and transports that vanishing to non-torsion qqq.

A finite Whittaker test detects whether an error object remains. The resulting vanishing supplies the reconstruction identity. Irrational twisting also removes sufficiently unstable bundle directions, allowing the categorical duality arguments to be controlled on bounded geometric regions.

Make local comparisons survive collisions

Local representation theory gives a correspondence near one marked point of XXX. To globalize, one must allow any finite collection of points, move them and let them collide. Data defined only for distinct points can fail to extend coherently when two points meet.

The manuscript sends the local categories for the two dual groups into a common category of WWW-algebra modules. Low-degree cohomological estimates recover maps between objects from this common target. It then uses these recovered maps to identify the boundary data across collision divisors. Separate arguments retain compatibility when objects are inserted in both slots of the pairing.

Finally, localization turns loop-algebra representations into twisted DDD-modules on the bundle stack. The Ran space organizes all finite subsets of the curve at once; integration over it removes the auxiliary marking choices. A global unipotent-period identity makes the local pairings compatible with localization. The two Whittaker reconstruction identities, one for each group, provide inverse functors and hence the claimed equivalence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is unramified: the bundle categories carry no prescribed singular or parabolic data at a fixed set of marked points. Moving auxiliary points in the construction is not the same as proving a ramified Langlands theorem.

The level restriction is exact. Rational levels, including special values with additional representation-theoretic phenomena, are not obtained by continuity from the irrational result. The proof’s non-torsion monodromy mechanism is precisely what distinguishes the two regimes.

The headline concerns connected simple complex algebraic groups and de Rham twisted DDD-modules over complex projective curves. Reductive groups enter intermediate constructions, but the digest does not enlarge the final theorem to arbitrary reductive groups or to positive characteristic.

The categories contain much more information than their simplest objects. A categorical equivalence does not automatically provide an explicit elementary formula for the image of every differential equation, and the compatibility statements are part of what makes the proposed correspondence identifiable. Extending these constructions to rational or ramified settings would require additional arguments addressing their different local behavior.

8. Sources and further reading

For the program’s formulation, see Gaitsgory’s quantum Langlands notes. Kapustin–Witten explains the physical duality motivation. The fundamental local equivalences, ordinary geometric Langlands series, and Bogdanova’s Betti functor locate the main preceding results. The source below specifies the level convention, family comparisons and central data used in the claimed global equivalence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global quantum geometric Langlands at irrational level (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When a random surface becomes a tree and how a particle moves on it
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 211 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A very large network drawn on a sphere can be viewed as a discrete random surface. Its vertices are locations, its edges provide routes, and counting edges along a shortest route gives a distance. If the network is sampled randomly and its size grows, does a definite kind of continuum geometry emerge?

The answer can depend on the statistical mechanics used to weight the network. In the Fortuin–Kasteleyn model, abbreviated FK, a parameter qqq changes the relative likelihood of cluster configurations and therefore changes the geometry of the sampled map itself.

This family claims a complete surface-to-tree transition for specified finite spherical FK maps. For 0<q≤40<q\le40<q≤4, the limit is a random sphere described by Liouville quantum gravity. For q>4q>4q>4, the large-scale distances instead approach those of a continuum random tree.

Three further manuscripts ask how a particle moves on such a random surface. In the FK–Ising and spanning-tree cases, they identify a limiting diffusion and its exact time normalization. The FK–Ising results also describe the convergence of the graph’s relaxation frequencies. These are related questions, but a limit for distances alone does not determine the answer to any of the dynamical ones.

2. Background and essential definitions

Maps and their probability law

A planar map is a connected graph embedded in an oriented sphere, where the way edges surround vertices and faces is part of the data. A distinguished directed edge serves as a root. Loops and multiple edges are allowed here.

For a map MMM, choose an edge subset AAA. It gives a cluster configuration on the original graph. The complementary edges define clusters on the dual graph, whose vertices represent the faces of MMM. Let ℓ(M,A)\ell(M,A)ℓ(M,A) count the interfaces separating the two kinds of clusters.

Among rooted maps with exactly nnn edges, the joint law gives (M,A)(M,A)(M,A) weight proportional to

qℓ(M,A)/2.q^{\ell(M,A)/2}.qℓ(M,A)/2.

A normalizing sum makes these weights into probabilities. The choice is at the FK critical point for every fixed qqq; varying qqq is not the same as varying temperature in one fixed model.

The graph distance dnd_ndn​ uses all original map edges, not only the selected edges of AAA. The natural vertex probability measure is

μn(v)=deg⁡(v)2n,\mu_n(v)=\frac{\deg(v)}{2n},μn​(v)=2ndeg(v)​,

where a loop contributes twice to the degree. This measures mass by incident edge ends and is the stationary distribution of the usual random walk. It is generally different from choosing a vertex uniformly.

Continuum geometry and motion

A Liouville quantum gravity, or LQG, sphere is a random surface with a random area measure and an intrinsic random distance. Its construction starts from a Gaussian random field, a continuum analogue of correlated Gaussian variables. The field is too irregular to be evaluated pointwise in the ordinary way, so defining its area and distance requires limiting constructions.

A parameter γ\gammaγ determines the surface law. In this family, for 0<q<40<q<40<q<4,

q=2+2cos⁡(πγ22),2<γ<2.q=2+2\cos\left(\frac{\pi\gamma^2}{2}\right),\qquad \sqrt2<\gamma<2.q=2+2cos(2πγ2​),2​<γ<2.

The endpoint q=4q=4q=4 corresponds to the critical parameter γ=2\gamma=2γ=2. Each limiting sphere has total quantum area one.

A conformal loop ensemble, written CLEκ\mathrm{CLE}_\kappaCLEκ​, is a distribution of random loops whose law respects angle-preserving changes of coordinates. It describes continuum cluster boundaries. The parameter here is κ=16/γ2\kappa=16/\gamma^2κ=16/γ2, reaching four at the critical endpoint.

A Brownian continuum random tree is a compact random metric tree, encoded by a Brownian excursion. An excursion is a continuous Brownian-type path that starts and ends at zero while staying positive between them. A metric tree has a unique simple route between any two points. It can be highly branched even though it has no cycles.

Finally, Liouville Brownian motion is diffusion on an LQG surface. In a conformal coordinate its spatial motion is Brownian, with the clock changed according to quantum area. Its usual energy convention contains the factor 1/21/21/2; that convention matters when stating an exact discrete time scale.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The discrete and continuum theories developed through several layers. Mullin’s enumeration and later bijections of Bernardi encoded maps decorated by spanning trees using pairs of tree contours. Sheffield’s inventory construction extended the encoding to FK-decorated maps and identified a transition in the limiting contour fluctuations at q=4q=4q=4. His paper is a starting point for the connection between cluster weights and random geometry.

Duplantier, Miller, and Sheffield’s mating of trees theory reconstructs LQG surfaces from correlated Brownian contour data. Miller and Sheffield developed the finite-area sphere version. Gwynne, Mao, and Sun, and Gwynne and Sun, established increasingly detailed convergence results for discrete FK encodings, including the finite-volume setting. The continuum construction explains why Brownian data can encode a random surface.

Convergence of an encoding is weaker than convergence of every graph distance in a prescribed drawing. Separate work constructed and characterized LQG metrics. For uniform random maps, corresponding to q=1q=1q=1 in the present ensemble, Brownian-sphere metric limits were already known through work of Le Gall, Miermont, and others. M1–M7 do not present that special case as a new discovery.

Embedded limits also had important precedents. Gwynne, Miller, and Sheffield treated the Tutte embedding of maps built directly from continuum trees; Holden and Sun treated the Cardy embedding of triangulations. These are different ensembles or embedding prescriptions from the finite spherical FK maps considered here.

For diffusion, Berestycki and Garban–Rhodes–Vargas constructed Liouville Brownian motion. Berestycki and Gwynne later proved time-parametrized walk convergence for mated-CRT maps, with a deterministic exit-time normalization comparable to inverse cell area. The exact asymptotic constant for that normalization was not identified there. Their theorem provides an important predecessor to the present finite-map claims.

Above q=4q=4q=4, an infinite-volume tree limit was established by Feng. The finite compact limit claimed here requires separate control of conditioning on the total size and of distances using every map edge.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M4–M7: the geometric transition

M6 states that, for each fixed 0<q<40<q<40<q<4, there is a deterministic distance scale an→0a_n\to0an​→0 such that

(V(Mn),andn,μn)⟹(S,Dh,μh).\bigl(V(M_n),a_nd_n,\mu_n\bigr)\Longrightarrow\bigl(S,D_h,\mu_h\bigr).(V(Mn​),an​dn​,μn​)⟹(S,Dh​,μh​).

Here V(Mn)V(M_n)V(Mn​) is the vertex set, while SSS, DhD_hDh​, and μh\mu_hμh​ are the limiting sphere, distance, and area. The arrow means convergence in distribution. The comparison simultaneously matches distances and probability measures, in what is called Gromov–Hausdorff–Prokhorov topology.

M6 also treats maps weighted by their numbers of spanning trees, with γ=2\gamma=\sqrt2γ=2​. That is a separate argument, not a substitution of q=0q=0q=0 into the finite FK law.

M4 strengthens the FK conclusion by placing the maps in a specified conformal coordinate. Each edge is divided into incidence triangles, these are made equilateral, and the resulting sphere is conformally mapped to a standard sphere. Three independently sampled area points fix the coordinate ambiguity. Area, the full distance function, and all nested interfaces then converge together. The limiting loops have the law of an independent CLE16/γ2\mathrm{CLE}_{16/\gamma^2}CLE16/γ2​.

M5 constructs the corresponding critical sphere at q=4q=4q=4 and states the joint conformal, area, distance, and nested-loop limit with CLE4\mathrm{CLE}_4CLE4​. It treats this endpoint directly; the result is not obtained merely by letting qqq approach four in a fixed-parameter theorem.

For every fixed q>4q>4q>4, M7 instead states

(V(Mn),c(q)n−1/2dn,μn)⟹(T,dT,μT),\bigl(V(M_n),c(q)n^{-1/2}d_n,\mu_n\bigr)\Longrightarrow\bigl(\mathcal T,d_{\mathcal T},\mu_{\mathcal T}\bigr),(V(Mn​),c(q)n−1/2dn​,μn​)⟹(T,dT​,μT​),

where c(q)>0c(q)>0c(q)>0 is deterministic and the right side is the Brownian continuum random tree. This theorem forgets the root and cluster decoration. All these geometric limits run through every positive integer edge count.

M1–M3: motion and relaxation frequencies

At q=2q=2q=2, the FK–Ising sphere has γ=3\gamma=\sqrt3γ=3​. M1 states that stationary random walks on the finite maps converge to Liouville Brownian motion on that same limiting sphere when time is accelerated by exactly nnn, the number of edges.

The unaccelerated walk makes one attempted move per unit time, choosing uniformly among incident half-edges. Loops can cause an attempt with no displacement. Starting vertices have law μn\mu_nμn​. M1 retains the time parameter and any fixed finite number of conditionally independent walks on the same random map.

M3 gives the corresponding result for spanning-tree-weighted maps, retaining the conditional path law jointly with geometry and area, again with acceleration exactly nnn.

M2 treats FK–Ising spectra. If λn,j\lambda_{n,j}λn,j​ are the ordered eigenvalues of the negative rate-one walk generator, then its claim includes

nλn,j⟹Λjn\lambda_{n,j}\Longrightarrow\Lambda_jnλn,j​⟹Λj​

jointly for all fixed mode indices, with multiplicities and the same limiting surface. It also states convergence of the heat traces

∑je−ntλn,j⟹∑je−tΛj,t>0,\sum_j e^{-nt\lambda_{n,j}}\Longrightarrow\sum_j e^{-t\Lambda_j},\qquad t>0,j∑​e−ntλn,j​⟹j∑​e−tΛj​,t>0,

locally uniformly away from time zero. A heat trace adds the contributions of all relaxation modes, so this goes beyond convergence of a finite list of eigenvalues.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The combined claims would identify a broad geometric phase diagram for a central random-surface ensemble and connect that geometry to precisely normalized diffusion and spectra.

The transition at four changes the type of limiting space: a random sphere on one side and a tree on the other. Finite maps above four still have cycles, but those cycles do not survive as macroscopic loops in the limiting metric space.

The joint nature of the results is equally significant. Knowing an abstract limiting distance does not locate cluster boundaries in a chosen conformal coordinate. Knowing the shape of a walk’s trace does not tell us how fast it moves. The family claims these additional identifications in compatible settings, while preserving which conclusions apply to which ensembles.

6. The main idea

Upgrade a contour encoding to geometry

The starting point is an exact combinatorial encoding by words or pairs of contour paths. Brownian limits describe the large-scale fluctuations of those encodings. The geometric challenge is to recover adjacency, paths, and separating loops without overlooking unusual vertices or small regions that create shortcuts.

The subcritical papers keep detailed local records of the encoded map: which pieces meet, how paths enter and leave, and which parts of the surrounding exploration must be retained. Conditional laws of these records connect discrete passage distances with the local continuum field.

Comparisons across many surrounding annuli then control distances and conformal distortion. A final uniform step extends the comparison from typical sampled points to every vertex. The critical paper performs the analogous work at q=4q=4q=4, where the field and area normalization have additional endpoint features.

Above four, a different description becomes effective. M7 decomposes the map into blocks joined through a branching tree. It states that the relevant offspring law has finite variance and that accumulated distances through the blocks are uniformly comparable to tree distances. A conditioned branching-tree limit then yields the Brownian continuum random tree. Controlling the block contribution is what connects the abstract encoding to the all-edge metric.

Electrical energy determines the clock

Treat every graph edge as a unit conductor. A voltage function fff has energy proportional to

∑uv∈E(Mn)(f(u)−f(v))2,\sum_{uv\in E(M_n)}(f(u)-f(v))^2,uv∈E(Mn​)∑​(f(u)−f(v))2,

counting parallel edges separately. This energy determines the random-walk generator together with the stationary vertex masses.

The diffusion papers identify the continuum electrical energy, using the geometric companions and their stated Brownian and LQG inputs. Planar duality helps fix the effective conductivity to one in their conventions. Controlling functions concentrated on very small-mass regions then prevents hidden spectral contributions or unexplained delays.

M2 uses these estimates to pass to inverse operators, eigenvalues, and heat traces. M1 additionally controls whole trajectories, ruling out rapid macroscopic excursions that finite-time observations might miss. M3 performs the energy and path analysis for the tree-weighted ensemble. These steps explain why an exact walk clock requires more than a metric scaling limit.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The map laws, spherical setting, area normalization, and embeddings are specific. The results do not claim universality for every random planar-map ensemble or every way of drawing a map.

The geometric statements use the degree measure, not the uniform vertex measure. For q≤4q\le4q≤4, the claimed distance normalizers are deterministic, but the main statements do not give explicit power laws or convergence rates. No uniformity as qqq approaches four is asserted.

The walk statements start in stationarity. They do not establish convergence from arbitrary prescribed vertices. The exact factor nnn uses the rate-one half-edge walk and the continuum energy factor 1/21/21/2; changing either convention changes the clock.

The spectral theorem concerns FK–Ising maps, not every qqq, and retains its stated geometric and Brownian/LQG inputs. Further directions include other initial distributions, explicit metric exponents, quantitative convergence rates, and extensions beyond these finite spherical ensembles.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Sheffield, Quantum gravity and inventory accumulation, for the FK encoding and its transition.
  • Duplantier, Miller, and Sheffield, Liouville quantum gravity as a mating of trees, for the continuum construction.
  • Gwynne and Sun, Scaling limits for the critical Fortuin–Kasteleyn model on a random planar map III, for finite-volume contour limits.
  • Berestycki and Gwynne, Random walks on mated-CRT planar maps and Liouville Brownian motion, for earlier time-parametrized diffusion limits in a related ensemble.

M4–M7 provide the geometric claims; M1–M3 provide the diffusion and spectral claims with the conventions described above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Random Walks on Critical FK–Ising Maps and Liouville Brownian Motion (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Spectral convergence for critical FK–Ising planar maps (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A Linear Clock for Random Walk on Tree-Weighted Planar Maps (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Canonical conformal limits of subcritical FK planar maps (September 24, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, The critical Liouville quantum sphere and geometric limits of FK maps at q=4 (September 24, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Metric-measure limits of subcritical FK and spanning-tree planar maps (September 24, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Brownian continuum random tree limits of finite Fortuin–Kasteleyn maps above four (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The shape of random travel times and the absence of infinite shortest lines
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 212 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine a square street grid in which every street segment takes a random amount of time to traverse. The fastest route between two places need not be the route with the fewest blocks. As the scale grows, two natural geometric questions arise.

First, could there be a route stretching infinitely in both directions such that every finite piece of it is a fastest route between its endpoints? Such a path would be a random counterpart of a straight line in Euclidean geometry.

Second, if a traveler starts at the origin and can use every route at once, what is the large-scale shape of the region reachable by a given time? A classical theorem gives a deterministic convex limiting shape, but convexity alone permits both flat sides and sharp corners.

The two manuscripts in this family claim progress on both questions. One excludes all doubly infinite shortest paths for a broad class of continuous edge-weight laws. The other rules out corners and flat sides for exponential weights, and rules out corners for the larger Gamma family. The path theorem does not depend on assuming the shape regularity established in the companion.

2. Background and essential definitions

A random metric on the square lattice

The square lattice Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 has vertices with integer coordinates. Two vertices are joined when they differ by one in exactly one coordinate. Assign each unoriented edge eee a random nonnegative travel time tet_ete​, independently and with the same distribution.

For a finite path PPP, its passage time is the sum of its edge weights. The random distance between vertices is

T(x,y)=inf⁡P:x→y∑e∈Pte,T(x,y)=\inf_{P:x\to y}\sum_{e\in P}t_e,T(x,y)=P:x→yinf​e∈P∑​te​,

with repeated traversals charged repeatedly. Paths are undirected: motion is allowed along an edge in either direction. This is first-passage percolation.

A geodesic is a path achieving the smallest passage time. An infinite geodesic ray has the property that every finite segment is a geodesic. A bigeodesic is a path (vi)i∈Z(v_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}(vi​)i∈Z​, with distinct vertices and adjacent consecutive vertices, satisfying

∑k=ij−1t{vk,vk+1}=T(vi,vj)for every i<j.\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}t_{\{v_k,v_{k+1}\}}=T(v_i,v_j)\quad\text{for every }i<j.k=i∑j−1​t{vk​,vk+1​}​=T(vi​,vj​)for every i<j.

It must minimize between every pair of its own vertices, not merely look straight or have a limiting direction. Two infinite rays coalesce when they eventually join and thereafter follow the same route.

A distribution is nonatomic if no single value has positive probability. It need not have a density. Independent nonatomic edge weights remove ties between distinct finite routes almost surely.

The limit shape and its two kinds of regularity

For suitable edge laws, a shape theorem gives a deterministic norm μ\muμ on R2\mathbb R^2R2, with

T(0,⌊tv⌋)t⟶μ(v)\frac{T(0,\lfloor tv\rfloor)}{t}\longrightarrow\mu(v)tT(0,⌊tv⌋)​⟶μ(v)

for each fixed vector vvv. The rounding symbol chooses nearby lattice coordinates. The unit ball

B={v:μ(v)≤1}\mathcal B=\{v:\mu(v)\le1\}B={v:μ(v)≤1}

describes the scaled region reachable by a large time.

A strictly convex boundary has no nontrivial straight segment. A differentiable boundary has a unique tangent or supporting line at each point, hence no corner. These are different properties: a smooth convex shape can have a flat side, and a strictly convex shape can still have a corner. A C1C^1C1 boundary has a continuously varying tangent.

The exponential law of rate λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 has density λe−λt\lambda e^{-\lambda t}λe−λt for t>0t>0t>0. It is the shape-one member of the Gamma family, whose density is

pκ,λ(t)=λκΓ(κ)tκ−1e−λt,t>0.p_{\kappa,\lambda}(t)=\frac{\lambda^\kappa}{\Gamma(\kappa)}t^{\kappa-1}e^{-\lambda t},\qquad t>0.pκ,λ​(t)=Γ(κ)λκ​tκ−1e−λt,t>0.

Here κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 is the shape parameter, λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 the rate, and Γ(κ)=∫0∞sκ−1e−s ds\Gamma(\kappa)=\int_0^\infty s^{\kappa-1}e^{-s}\,dsΓ(κ)=∫0∞​sκ−1e−sds is the normalizing Gamma function.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hammersley and Welsh introduced first-passage percolation in 1965. Subadditive methods, including Kingman’s ergodic theorem, and work of Richardson and Cox–Durrett established deterministic asymptotic shapes. The difficulty then shifted from the existence of a shape to its fine geometry and the structure of infinite shortest paths.

The no-bigeodesics question is attributed to Furstenberg in Kesten’s account. Licea and Newman obtained coalescence for each direction in a deterministic set of full angular measure, together with exclusions for prescribed end directions. Related conclusions that every ray has a direction required stronger moment and curvature assumptions in Newman’s work.

Damron and Hanson developed stationary Busemann functions and excluded paths in specified supporting sectors under differentiability conditions. Other work treated the half-plane metric, selected geodesic graphs, or simultaneous absence under additional quantitative hypotheses. These results were important but did not exclude every possible bigeodesic in a general environment under M1’s assumptions.

Ahlberg and Hoffman supplied structural results on random coalescing geodesics without assuming regularity of the limiting shape. M1 uses that framework. Its stated remaining obstacle is a quantifier problem: a probability-one statement for each fixed direction or label need not hold simultaneously for a label chosen after seeing the entire random environment. Their work is a principal input to the new argument.

Shape regularity developed along a parallel track. Sufficient conditions for strict convexity were known, and distributions with an atom at their smallest weight can produce flat segments. Marchand determined such flat portions in an oriented-percolation regime, while Auffinger and Damron proved differentiability at their endpoints. Those edge laws differ substantially from the nonatomic exponential law, whose support extends down to zero.

M2 claims regularity for the basic planar exponential model itself. It also extends the differentiability conclusion to every positive Gamma shape and rate. The manuscript distinguishes these claims from existing qualitative midpoint results, which do not require shape regularity.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: no bigeodesic in any direction

Let X1,X2,X3,X4X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4X1​,X2​,X3​,X4​ be independent samples from the common nonnegative edge-weight law. M1 assumes that the law is nonatomic and

E[min⁡{X1,X2,X3,X4}2]<∞.\mathbb E\left[\min\{X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\}^2\right]<\infty.E[min{X1​,X2​,X3​,X4​}2]<∞.

Under these assumptions, it states that almost surely no bigeodesic exists anywhere in the planar lattice.

The four-variable minimum is important. The assumption is not that an individual edge weight has finite second moment, or even finite mean. A minimum can have a much lighter tail than one sample. The statement allows bounded-support and singular continuous laws as well.

The conclusion is simultaneous: the probability-one event excludes every bigeodesic, including any whose end directions depend on the environment. M1 imposes no differentiability, strict convexity, or curvature assumption on the limit shape. It does not claim the version with no moment assumption at all.

M2: regularity of exponential and Gamma shapes

For independent exponential weights of any fixed rate λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, M2 claims that μ\muμ is differentiable at every nonzero vector and that B\mathcal BB is strictly convex. In particular, for distinct boundary points x,yx,yx,y and 0<s<10<s<10<s<1,

μ((1−s)x+sy)<1.\mu((1-s)x+sy)<1.μ((1−s)x+sy)<1.

The boundary is a C1C^1C1 curve with a unique supporting line everywhere. This does not identify the shape with a circle or give an explicit formula for the norm.

For every fixed Gamma shape κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 and rate λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, M2 claims differentiability of μ\muμ away from zero and a C1C^1C1 boundary. Strict convexity is asserted for exponential weights, not for the whole Gamma family. The two parts use separate arguments.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claims would settle major geometric questions in a standard random-growth model. They describe both the impossibility of a globally minimizing infinite line and the regularity of the macroscopic growth boundary.

The no-bigeodesics theorem is particularly strong because it addresses all random directions simultaneously. Excluding one direction selected in advance would leave room for an exceptional route whose direction is chosen by the disorder itself.

The shape theorem addresses a different gap between basic existence and geometric understanding. Convexity follows from general averaging principles, but excluding every corner and flat side in the exponential model requires information about how alternative routes compete.

The two conclusions reinforce a coherent picture of planar random geometry without being interchangeable. M1’s broad distributional scope is not a consequence of M2’s results for special laws.

6. The main idea

Compare travel times toward infinity

For a geodesic ray p=(p0,p1,…)p=(p_0,p_1,\ldots)p=(p0​,p1​,…), a Busemann function compares starting points while sending the destination far away:

Bp(x,y)=lim⁡j→∞(T(x,pj)−T(y,pj)).B_p(x,y)=\lim_{j\to\infty}\bigl(T(x,p_j)-T(y,p_j)\bigr).Bp​(x,y)=j→∞lim​(T(x,pj​)−T(y,pj​)).

It records an asymptotic travel-time advantage. Its large-scale linear behavior gives the ray a directional label. The two ends of a hypothetical bigeodesic carry opposite labels.

M1 combines planar ordering and coalescence information with controlled increases of finitely many edge weights. A selected path is forced to acquire extra passage cost, while the probability law changes only mildly. The changes are spread across a growing region: their cumulative effect along a path can diverge even though their total probabilistic cost stays controlled.

A comparison along a horizontal line then limits how much extra cost many selected paths can absorb. Schematically, the manuscript obtains a finite budget

Mq≤lW,Mq\le lW,Mq≤lW,

where MMM is the forced cost increase, qqq the probability of a marked site, lll a fixed spacing, and WWW the width of a bounded label sector. Here qqq is local notation for a probability, unrelated to the FK parameter in family 211.

The construction keeps the marking probability positive and the spacing fixed while increasing MMM, giving the contradiction. A substantial part of the argument handles environment-dependent labels directly, rather than taking an invalid intersection of uncountably many probability-one events.

Corners and flat sides lead to different contradictions

For differentiability, suppose the norm had a corner. Two different supporting linear functionals would touch it in the same direction. Their separation penalizes sideways travel. M2 turns this into a positive excess cost for every sufficiently long path, conflicting with the asymptotic passage time in that direction.

The Gamma law permits a controlled local change of scale with an explicit likelihood estimate. Local crossing bounds and disjoint witnesses then extend the argument from prescribed strips to all relevant paths. This is why the differentiability part extends beyond exponential weights.

For strict convexity, a hypothetical flat side gives two distinct directions sharing one supporting functional. The exponential argument builds local routes following these directions and measures their excess over the supporting cost. It claims both a positive lower bound on that excess and an improvement procedure that contracts it by a fixed factor on larger scales. Iterating the improvement contradicts the lower bound.

These are geometric explanations of the two mechanisms. Neither identifies the limit shape explicitly, and the strict-convexity argument is not presented as a consequence of differentiability alone.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorems concern independent identically distributed weights on the undirected nearest-neighbor square lattice. They do not automatically apply to directed models, dependent environments, or higher dimensions.

M1 retains its minimum-of-four moment assumption. M2 retains its specific distributional assumptions, with the stronger conclusion restricted to exponentials. Removing those restrictions would require further results.

A C1C^1C1, strictly convex boundary need not have a known positive curvature lower bound, and it need not be twice differentiable. No exact shape, fluctuation exponent, or convergence rate is supplied by the headline statements.

The directional consequences in M2 also retain their fixed-direction probability conventions. M1’s simultaneous exclusion of all bigeodesics is a separate statement. Further questions include finer curvature, the size of passage-time fluctuations, and comparable geometric results for more general edge laws.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Hammersley and Welsh, First-passage percolation, subadditive processes, stochastic networks, and generalized renewal theory, for the model’s origin.
  • Licea and Newman, Geodesics in two-dimensional first-passage percolation, for early directional results.
  • Ahlberg and Hoffman, Random coalescing geodesics in first-passage percolation, for the structural framework used by M1.
  • Damron and Hanson, Bigeodesics in first-passage percolation, for earlier shape-dependent exclusions.

M1 and M2 give their precise assumptions, separate arguments, and further primary references for the shape theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, No bigeodesics in planar first-passage percolation (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Strict convexity and differentiability of the planar exponential first-passage limit shape (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When infinite percolation clusters coexist
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 214 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine independently keeping each road in an infinite network with probability ppp. At small ppp, every connected region is finite. At larger ppp, infinite connected regions appear. Must the first infinite regions immediately join into a single giant component, or can infinitely many of them coexist?

The answer depends on the geometry of the network. A tree keeps producing fresh branches, whereas a Euclidean lattice has many routes that reconnect. The manuscript in this family claims that every sufficiently symmetric nonamenable graph has an interval of coexistence: infinite clusters exist, but none absorbs all the others.

Nonamenability means that every finite region has a boundary comparable to its volume. There is always substantial room through which different clusters can escape. Turning that picture into a theorem for every graph in this class is the longstanding difficulty. The manuscript claims a stronger operator estimate that also gives a common set of critical power laws.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an infinite connected graph. It is locally finite if every vertex has finitely many neighbors, and quasi-transitive if graph symmetries divide its vertices into finitely many types. A transitive graph has just one type. These assumptions imply a uniform bound on degrees.

For a finite nonempty set AAA of vertices, let ∂VA\partial_V A∂V​A be the vertices outside AAA adjacent to it. The graph is nonamenable when

hV(G)=inf⁡0<∣A∣<∞∣∂VA∣∣A∣>0.h_V(G)=\inf_{0<|A|<\infty}\frac{|\partial_V A|}{|A|}>0.hV​(G)=0<∣A∣<∞inf​∣A∣∣∂V​A∣​>0.

Thus no sequence of larger finite regions can make the boundary negligible relative to the interior. Large square boxes in the square lattice do make this ratio tend to zero; regular trees of degree at least three do not.

In Bernoulli bond percolation, every edge is independently open with probability ppp. The open cluster CvC_vCv​ contains all vertices connected to vvv by open edges. Write N∞N_\inftyN∞​ for the number of infinite clusters. Two thresholds matter:

pc=inf⁡{p:Pp(N∞≥1)>0},pu=inf⁡{p:Pp(N∞=1)=1}.\begin{aligned}p_c&=\inf\{p:\mathbb P_p(N_\infty\geq1)>0\},\\p_u&=\inf\{p:\mathbb P_p(N_\infty=1)=1\}.\end{aligned}pc​pu​​=inf{p:Pp​(N∞​≥1)>0},=inf{p:Pp​(N∞​=1)=1}.​

The question is whether pc<pup_c<p_upc​<pu​. This says that existence and uniqueness occur at genuinely different densities.

A useful model is the regular tree with degree d≥3d\geq3d≥3. Away from its starting vertex, a cluster branches on average into (d−1)p(d-1)p(d−1)p descendants. Its existence threshold is pc=1/(d−1)p_c=1/(d-1)pc​=1/(d−1), while pu=1p_u=1pu​=1. A closed edge separates two branches permanently: there is no alternate route around it. General nonamenable graphs may have many cycles, so this tree argument does not settle the question.

The stronger claim uses the two-point function

Tp(x,y)=Pp(x↔y).T_p(x,y)=\mathbb P_p(x\leftrightarrow y).Tp​(x,y)=Pp​(x↔y).

View this array as a matrix acting on functions on the vertices. The space ℓ2(V)\ell^2(V)ℓ2(V) consists of functions with ∑x∣f(x)∣2<∞\sum_x|f(x)|^2<\infty∑x​∣f(x)∣2<∞, using ordinary counting measure. The operator norm ∥Tp∥2→2\|T_p\|_{2\to2}∥Tp​∥2→2​ measures how much this matrix can amplify that square-sum norm. Define p2→2p_{2\to2}p2→2​ as the supremum of parameters at which the operator is bounded.

This is different from the expected cluster size, the row sum χv(p)=∑yTp(v,y)\chi_v(p)=\sum_yT_p(v,y)χv​(p)=∑y​Tp​(v,y). An infinite row sum need not force an infinite square-sum operator norm on a rapidly branching graph.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Benjamini and Schramm’s 1996 paper made percolation on nonamenable graphs a systematic subject and posed the general nonuniqueness conjecture. The contrast with Euclidean lattices suggested that the boundary-to-volume ratio should control more than the mere existence of an infinite cluster. Their formulation helped connect probability with geometric group theory. Benjamini–Schramm

Several important classes were subsequently understood. Planar nonamenable graphs admit powerful duality arguments: open connections in the graph and closed connections in its planar dual constrain one another.
