entry.title: The one-sixth fluctuation scale of the SK spin glass
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 217 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Two pieces of a disordered magnet can have the same size and temperature but different microscopic interactions. Their equilibrium free energies will be close on a per-spin scale, yet not identical. How large are those sample-to-sample differences? After rescaling them, does a stable probability distribution emerge?

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick, or SK, model is a central mathematical model of this situation. Every spin interacts with every other spin, with random positive or negative strengths. Its leading free energy is described by the Parisi formula, but that formula does not determine the much smaller fluctuations around the mean.

This family’s two manuscripts address the zero-field Gaussian Ising model at every fixed inverse temperature β>1\beta>1β>1. They claim that the standard deviation of the log partition function grows like n1/6n^{1/6}n1/6, determine a positive variance prefactor, and establish a limiting law after exact centering and standardization. The scale is much smaller than the n1/2n^{1/2}n1/2 fluctuations familiar from sums of independent terms.

2. Background and essential definitions

There are nnn spins σi∈{−1,1}\sigma_i\in\{-1,1\}σi​∈{−1,1}. For each pair i<ji<ji<j, choose an independent standard Gaussian interaction gijg_{ij}gij​, with mean zero and variance one. In the convention used here,

Hn(σ)=1n∑i<jgijσiσj,Zn(β)=∑σ∈{−1,1}neβHn(σ).H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}g_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,\qquadZ_n(\beta)=\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n}e^{\beta H_n(\sigma)}.Hn​(σ)=n​1​i<j∑​gij​σi​σj​,Zn​(β)=σ∈{−1,1}n∑​eβHn​(σ).

The partition function ZnZ_nZn​ sums the statistical weights of all configurations. A Gibbs sample chooses σ\sigmaσ with probability eβHn(σ)/Zne^{\beta H_n(\sigma)}/Z_neβHn​(σ)/Zn​. The log partition function is Fn=log⁡ZnF_n=\log Z_nFn​=logZn​; physical total free energy is −Fn/β-F_n/\beta−Fn​/β.

There are two kinds of randomness. Thermal randomness chooses a spin configuration for fixed interactions. Disorder randomness chooses the interactions themselves. All variances and expectations of FnF_nFn​ in the main theorem refer to disorder. They do not measure the energy fluctuations of one Gibbs sample.

Write

sn2=Var⁡(Fn),Xn=Fn−EFnsn.s_n^2=\operatorname{Var}(F_n),\qquadX_n=\frac{F_n-\mathbb EF_n}{s_n}.sn2​=Var(Fn​),Xn​=sn​Fn​−EFn​​.

The centered variable removes the exact finite-size mean. Standardization divides by the exact finite-size standard deviation. Convergence in distribution means that the probabilities described by XnX_nXn​ approach a common limiting probability law.

For two configurations, their overlap is

R(σ,τ)=1n∑i=1nσiτi.R(\sigma,\tau)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i.R(σ,τ)=n1​i=1∑n​σi​τi​.

It measures similarity: it is one for identical configurations, minus one for opposite configurations, and near zero for weakly related configurations. Two independent Gibbs samples in the same disorder are often called replicas. Their overlap statistics describe the organization of equilibrium states, and are the main bridge between free energy and the Parisi hierarchy.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Sherrington and Kirkpatrick introduced the model in 1975. Parisi replaced the original single-overlap description with a hierarchy of order parameters. Guerra and Toninelli established the thermodynamic limit, Guerra proved a variational bound, and Talagrand proved the matching Parisi formula. These results identify the leading term of order nnn, leaving fluctuations on smaller scales unresolved. The original SK paper, Talagrand’s Parisi formula

The one-sixth prediction developed separately. Kondor’s replica expansion and the work of Crisanti, Paladin, Sommers, and Vulpiani led to the predicted n−5/6n^{-5/6}n−5/6 fluctuation scale for free energy per spin. Parisi and Rizzo analyzed rare free-energy deviations throughout the low-temperature regime. Inferring the width of typical fluctuations from those rare events requires an additional matching assumption; a large-deviation calculation alone does not supply a variance asymptotic. Parisi–Rizzo

At high temperature, Aizenman, Lebowitz, and Ruelle proved order-one Gaussian fluctuations. Chatterjee’s work on superconcentration showed that fluctuations can be much smaller than a basic concentration bound suggests, and connected this phenomenon to sensitivity under changes of disorder. Critical-temperature results and results with a nonzero external field treat other regimes. Their conclusions cannot simply be continued into fixed low temperature at zero field. Disorder chaos and multiple valleys

The manuscripts identify Aronow and Lopatto’s September 2026 estimates as a direct predecessor. For fixed β>1\beta>1β>1, those bounds place the variance between constant multiples of n4/15n^{4/15}n4/15 and n7/15n^{7/15}n7/15. The predicted n1/3n^{1/3}n1/3 lies between them. The present arguments also use Lopatto’s full-support description of the low-temperature Parisi minimizer, together with earlier uniqueness and variational results. Those inputs are substantive parts of the development, rather than consequences of the new fluctuation law. Aronow–Lopatto, Lopatto

Within this family, M2 first obtains the exponent with arbitrarily small power slack. M1 adds a quantitative comparison between different system sizes, which is what allows an actual prefactor and limiting distribution to be extracted.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The fluctuation exponent and typical magnitude

M2 states, for every fixed finite β>1\beta>1β>1,

sd⁡(Fn)=n1/6+o(1),Var⁡(Fn)=n1/3+o(1).\operatorname{sd}(F_n)=n^{1/6+o(1)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(F_n)=n^{1/3+o(1)}.sd(Fn​)=n1/6+o(1),Var(Fn​)=n1/3+o(1).

It also gives a typical-magnitude statement: for every η>0\eta>0η>0,

P ⁣(n1/6−η≤∣Fn−EFn∣≤n1/6+η)⟶1.\mathbb P\!\left( n^{1/6-\eta}\leq|F_n-\mathbb EF_n| \leq n^{1/6+\eta}\right)\longrightarrow1.P(n1/6−η≤∣Fn​−EFn​∣≤n1/6+η)⟶1.

Thus the variance scale is not explained only by extremely rare samples. The two papers use slightly different deterministic normalizations of the spin sum, but multiplying ZnZ_nZn​ by 2−n2^{-n}2−n only subtracts nlog⁡2n\log2nlog2, so it does not change centered fluctuations.

A positive constant and a full-sequence limiting law

M1 strengthens the claim to

Var⁡(Fn)n1/3⟶a2(β)∈(0,∞),Xn⟹νβ.\frac{\operatorname{Var}(F_n)}{n^{1/3}}\longrightarrow a_2(\beta)\in(0,\infty),\qquadX_n\Longrightarrow\nu_\beta.n1/3Var(Fn​)​⟶a2​(β)∈(0,∞),Xn​⟹νβ​.

The limit holds as nnn tends to infinity through all integers. The probability law νβ\nu_\betaνβ​ has mean zero, variance one, and a finite exponential moment near the origin. It is characterized by convergent finite-system moment formulas. The manuscript does not identify it as a Gaussian, Tracy–Widom, or other named distribution.

A more quantitative theorem introduces an independent Gaussian variable ζn\zeta_nζn​ of variance β2/2\beta^2/2β2/2 and sets

Yn=n−1/6(Fn−EFn+ζn).Y_n=n^{-1/6}\bigl(F_n-\mathbb EF_n+\zeta_n\bigr).Yn​=n−1/6(Fn​−EFn​+ζn​).

For every fixed positive integer kkk, its kkk-th moment converges to a constant aka_kak​ with an error bounded by Ckn−ckC_k n^{-c_k}Ck​n−ck​, where ck>0c_k>0ck​>0. Uniform exponential-moment control makes those moments determine a unique law. The added Gaussian disappears on the n1/6n^{1/6}n1/6 scale, so it does not change the final limit.

For physical free-energy density −Fn/(βn)-F_n/(\beta n)−Fn​/(βn), the standard-deviation scale is n−5/6n^{-5/6}n−5/6, and

Var⁡ ⁣(−Fnβn)∼a2(β)β2 n−5/3.\operatorname{Var}\!\left(-\frac{F_n}{\beta n}\right)\sim\frac{a_2(\beta)}{\beta^2}\,n^{-5/3}.Var(−βnFn​​)∼β2a2​(β)​n−5/3.

Its standardized limiting law is the reflection of νβ\nu_\betaνβ​, because physical free energy has the opposite sign.

Two consequences

Using an earlier comparison theorem, M1 extends the same variance constant and limiting law to an added ferromagnetic term

γ2n(∑iσi)2\frac{\gamma}{2n}\left(\sum_i\sigma_i\right)^22nγ​(i∑​σi​)2

in the Gibbs exponent, for fixed 0≤γ<10\leq\gamma<10≤γ<1. The perturbed model uses its own exact mean and variance. The endpoint γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 is not included.

The variance estimate also yields sufficient scales for disorder chaos. If the original interactions are slightly mixed with independent Gaussian interactions, equilibrium replicas from the two systems have vanishing mean squared overlap once the mixing time times n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3 diverges. A corresponding statement holds when a uniformly chosen fraction of edges is replaced and that fraction times n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3 diverges. These are averaged sufficient conditions, not a claimed sharp transition.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The fluctuation problem is a central refinement of the SK thermodynamic theory. A leading free-energy formula can coexist with many possible fluctuation scales and laws. Resolving the one-sixth scale at every fixed low temperature would explain a longstanding finite-size prediction, and the limiting-law claim goes substantially further.

The positive variance prefactor also has practical mathematical value: it lets comparison results transfer the limiting behavior to a perturbed model and converts general variance inequalities into concrete disorder-sensitivity scales.

The rating concerns these consequences if the claims hold. It does not imply that the limiting distribution has an explicit density or that the same law has been established for every spin glass.

6. The main idea

Compare overlapping hierarchies of Gaussian disorder

Gaussian interpolation gradually changes the covariance of the interactions while differentiating free-energy quantities. The derivatives can be expressed through overlaps. A hierarchy lets several replicas share an initial portion of revealed disorder and then branch into independent continuations.

The Parisi minimizer supplies a scalar reference description along this hierarchy. At the thermodynamic scale, replacing the full system by that scalar description can be sufficiently accurate. At the fluctuation scale it loses too much. The manuscripts instead optimize short comparisons and track the difference between actual overlap statistics and the scalar reference.

A cavity step removes or adds one spin. Several apparently large correction terms cancel only when their signed contributions are combined before taking absolute values. Extra test replicas organize these cancellations. This is the mechanism by which the comparison retains information smaller than the leading free energy.

First find the scale, then compare sizes

M2 controls positive Laplace transforms, quantities of the form

Eexp⁡ ⁣(s(Fn−EFn)).\mathbb E\exp\!\left(s(F_n-\mathbb EF_n)\right).Eexp(s(Fn​−EFn​)).

They measure fluctuations through exponential tests. Transform estimates alone can miss how probability is distributed near the center, so the argument adds an auxiliary exponential variable and uses log-concavity to obtain moment and small-interval bounds. The auxiliary randomness is removed at the end. This yields both standard deviation and typical magnitude with the one-sixth exponent.

M1 then compares a system of size NNN with every size between NNN and 2N2N2N, after scaling by the appropriate one-sixth power. It adjusts covariance and field parameters, changes size, and reverses the adjustments. Carefully combined pressure terms cancel the leading contributions, leaving an error with a positive power saving.

Such an error can be summed over dyadic scales N,2N,4N,…N,2N,4N,\ldotsN,2N,4N,…. The resulting moment sequence is Cauchy, giving a limit rather than only bounded subsequences. Uniform exponential tails identify the probability law from its moments, while the lower fluctuation bounds ensure that the variance limit is positive.

The distinction is useful beyond this example: knowing the exponent of a sequence does not force its normalized values to converge. The cross-size comparison is the extra ingredient that rules out persistent oscillation between different subsequential behaviors.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The temperature is fixed with 1<β<∞1<\beta<\infty1<β<∞. Constants may depend on it, and neither manuscript claims uniform control as β\betaβ approaches one or infinity. The critical window and zero-temperature ground-state fluctuations require separate arguments.

The disorder is Gaussian, the spins are Ising, and the external field is zero. The results do not automatically extend to non-Gaussian interactions, mixed higher-order models, or nonzero field. Those changes can affect the fluctuation problem even when the leading thermodynamic theory has a broader formulation.

Exact finite-size centering matters. Replacing EFn\mathbb EF_nEFn​ by only its leading Parisi term could leave a deterministic correction larger than the fluctuation scale. The theorem does not authorize that substitution without additional control.

The limiting law is specified through moments of finite systems, rather than a closed formula. Identifying a simpler description, determining detailed tails, and understanding universality across disorders remain natural questions beyond the stated result. The disorder-chaos corollary gives sufficient averaged perturbation scales, not matching lower bounds or a statement for each typical disorder separately.

Finally, this is an equilibrium sample-fluctuation result. The relaxation and mixing-time questions discussed in family 227 concern a different aspect of the same model.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 develops the fluctuation-scale estimates; M1 uses and strengthens that framework to obtain a positive variance constant and a limiting law. Their introductions distinguish fixed low temperature from critical-window and external-field results.

For the thermodynamic foundation, see Talagrand’s Parisi formula. For the physical fluctuation prediction, see Parisi–Rizzo. The immediate quantitative predecessor is Aronow–Lopatto, while Chatterjee explains the connection between small free-energy variance and disorder chaos.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The low-temperature Sherrington–Kirkpatrick free-energy limiting law (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The low-temperature Sherrington–Kirkpatrick fluctuation scale (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Gaussian-matrix statistics inside sparse random graphs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 219 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A large random regular graph is extremely sparse: every vertex has exactly the same fixed number of neighbors, even as the graph grows. A Gaussian random matrix is dense, with randomness spread across essentially all entries. Why should their eigenvalues have the same fine-scale spacing patterns?

The distinction between a broad spectral histogram and microscopic spacings is crucial. Two ensembles can have very different overall densities while showing the same local repulsion after distances are measured in units of the average spacing.

This family’s two manuscripts claim that phenomenon for every fixed graph degree at least three. One treats the ordinary adjacency matrix. The other adds a small, fixed random potential at each vertex, obtaining the same microscopic law in the interior of the original spectral band. The limit is the bulk eigenvalue process of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, or GOE.

2. Background and essential definitions

A graph is d-regular if each vertex has exactly ddd neighbors. Choose a graph uniformly among simple labelled ddd-regular graphs on nnn vertices. “Simple” excludes loops and multiple edges; “labelled” distinguishes the vertices. Sizes must be admissible, in particular ndndnd must be even.

The adjacency matrix AnA_nAn​ has entry one when two vertices are joined and zero otherwise. It is real symmetric, so its eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ are real. We use ordinary adjacency, without dividing by d−1\sqrt{d-1}d−1​.

The limiting density for most eigenvalues is the Kesten–McKay density

ρd(E)=d4(d−1)−E22π(d2−E2),∣E∣<2d−1.\rho_d(E)=\frac{d\sqrt{4(d-1)-E^2}}{2\pi(d^2-E^2)},\qquad |E|<2\sqrt{d-1}.ρd​(E)=2π(d2−E2)d4(d−1)−E2​​,∣E∣<2d−1​.

The open interval in this formula is the spectral bulk. The familiar eigenvalue ddd, coming from the constant vector, lies outside it and does not affect an interior microscopic window.

Near a bulk energy EEE, a short interval of length Δ\DeltaΔ contains roughly nρd(E)Δn\rho_d(E)\Deltanρd​(E)Δ eigenvalues. The average spacing is therefore about 1/(nρd(E))1/(n\rho_d(E))1/(nρd​(E)). Unfolding rescales the eigenvalues by that local density:

Ξn,E=∑i=1nδ nρd(E)(λi−E).\Xi_{n,E}=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\,n\rho_d(E)(\lambda_i-E)}.Ξn,E​=i=1∑n​δnρd​(E)(λi​−E)​.

Here δx\delta_xδx​ denotes a unit point at xxx. The random measure Ξn,E\Xi_{n,E}Ξn,E​ records all nearby eigenvalues together, with average density one in the limit.

The normalized GOE is a real symmetric matrix whose independent upper-triangular entries are Gaussian, with variance 1/n1/n1/n off the diagonal and 2/n2/n2/n on it. Its limiting density at zero is 1/π1/\pi1/π, so its unit-density reference process uses the scaling (n/π)μi(n/\pi)\mu_i(n/π)μi​, where μi\mu_iμi​ are its eigenvalues.

For the disordered model, put

Hn=An+wdiag⁡(ω1,…,ωn),H_n=A_n+w\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n),Hn​=An​+wdiag(ω1​,…,ωn​),

where the ωv\omega_vωv​ are independent uniform variables on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], independent of the graph. The diagonal term is a random on-site potential. This is a finite-graph Anderson model.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kesten’s work on regular trees and McKay’s random-graph calculation identified the macroscopic density. Jakobson, Miller, Rivin, and Rudnick later formulated the GOE spacing prediction for fixed-degree regular graphs and supplied numerical evidence. Knowing the density does not settle the prediction: equally spaced points, independent random points, and repelling points can all have the same average density. McKay’s density theorem, Eigenvalue spacings for regular graphs

Local laws brought finer control. They estimate resolvents and eigenvalue counts in shrinking windows. Bauerschmidt, Knowles, Huang, and Yau developed these estimates and proved bulk universality in ranges where the degree grows with graph size. Huang and Yau established fixed-degree spectral control for every d≥3d\geq3d≥3. Huang, McKenzie, and Yau obtained optimal rigidity and GOE edge universality. Edge statistics describe extreme nontrivial eigenvalues, a different regime from a fixed interior energy. Bulk statistics at growing degree, Fixed-degree edge universality

The clean manuscript also credits Bourgade and Huang’s 2026 fixed-energy result for a degree range starting above a power of log⁡n\log nlogn. Its remaining fixed-degree conjecture is the target here. The important advance is therefore both fixed degree and fixed energy, rather than an average over a moving spectral window. Bourgade–Huang

Eigenvectors provide another ingredient. Backhausz and Szegedy used entropy inequalities to relate almost-eigenvectors of random regular graphs to Gaussian waves on the infinite tree. Their qualitative weak limits could lose some variance. The new argument needs quantitative moment control that preserves the full variance at microscopic energies. Almost eigenvectors

For Anderson disorder, Klein proved extended spectral behavior on the infinite regular tree at weak disorder in compact subsets of the clean band. Later work refined stability and established quantum ergodicity on suitable finite graphs. These statements concern spectral type or spatial equidistribution, rather than the joint spacing process of finite-graph eigenvalues. M1 addresses that additional microscopic question. Klein’s extended-state theorem

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Clean fixed-degree graphs

M2 states that for every fixed integer d≥3d\geq3d≥3 and every fixed energy

−2d−1<E<2d−1,-2\sqrt{d-1}<E<2\sqrt{d-1},−2d−1​<E<2d−1​,

the unfolded point process Ξn,E\Xi_{n,E}Ξn,E​ converges to the GOE bulk process along all admissible graph sizes. No conditioning on connectedness, nonbipartiteness, or another graph property is imposed.

The theorem is expressed through Laplace functionals. For every nonnegative continuous compactly supported test function fff, it compares

Eexp⁡ ⁣(−∫f dΞn,E)\mathbb E\exp\!\left(-\int f\,d\Xi_{n,E}\right)Eexp(−∫fdΞn,E​)

with the corresponding GOE quantity. Since the integral is a sum of fff over the local eigenvalues, these tests encode the entire point-process law. The conclusion is stronger than a mean density or one spacing statistic.

Fixed weak diagonal disorder

M1 fixes a distance κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 from the clean spectral edges and considers

Id,κ=[−2d−1+κ, 2d−1−κ].I_{d,\kappa}=[-2\sqrt{d-1}+\kappa,\,2\sqrt{d-1}-\kappa].Id,κ​=[−2d−1​+κ,2d−1​−κ].

For sufficiently small fixed w>0w>0w>0, depending on ddd and κ\kappaκ, the infinite-tree Anderson operator has a continuous, strictly positive density of states ρd,w\rho_{d,w}ρd,w​ on this interval. Its measure is defined by averaging the root spectral measure over the independent tree potentials.

For each fixed E∈Id,κE\in I_{d,\kappa}E∈Id,κ​, M1 claims GOE convergence after unfolding with

nρd,w(E)(λi−E).n\rho_{d,w}(E)(\lambda_i-E).nρd,w​(E)(λi​−E).

The density is that of the disordered infinite-tree operator, not the clean Kesten–McKay formula. The strength www remains positive and fixed as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞. The degree, energy, and test function are likewise fixed first.

The stated eigenvalue convergence averages over both graph and potential randomness. An environment-conditioned Gaussian statement for eigenvector marks is an intermediate ingredient; it should not be confused with a separate quenched eigenvalue-universality theorem for every fixed potential realization.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The clean claim resolves the fixed-degree bulk-universality problem, including degree three, where the graph remains sparse at every size. The extension with a fixed weak random potential connects that universality to a basic model of disordered quantum transport.

The result would show that local tree geometry and GOE eigenvalue repulsion are compatible. Tree structure determines the local density and eigenvector covariance, while the global finite graph supports the same microscopic spectral statistics as a dense Gaussian matrix.

Its reach is substantial, but the theorem remains in the bulk and, for the Anderson model, in a specified weak-disorder regime. It does not describe the entire localization phase diagram.

6. The main idea

Use the tree as a local reference

Most fixed-radius neighborhoods of a random regular graph look like trees when nnn is large. For a matrix HHH, the resolvent (H−z)−1(H-z)^{-1}(H−z)−1, with Im⁡z>0\operatorname{Im}z>0Imz>0, records smoothed spectral information.

On a tree, deleting the edge to a parent leaves independent child branches. The diagonal branch resolvent satisfies

g(z)=(V−z−∑j=1d−1gj(z))−1,g(z)=\left(V-z-\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}g_j(z)\right)^{-1},g(z)=(V−z−j=1∑d−1​gj​(z))−1,

where VVV is the root potential and the gjg_jgj​ are branch values. In the clean case this reduces to a deterministic equation. With disorder, the limiting resolvent remains random, even though the averaged density of states is deterministic.

M1 controls this random recursion near the clean bulk and compares finite-graph cavity resolvents with it. Replacing the random tree response by only its mean would lose information needed later.

Recover Gaussian eigenvector marks

Normalize an eigenvector so its squared coordinate sum is nnn. Its value at a uniformly sampled vertex then has average square one. In the clean model, the manuscript obtains joint Gaussian moment approximations for finitely many eigenvectors sampled at graph-edge endpoints. The two endpoints have covariance E/dE/dE/d, reflecting their adjacency.

The argument combines counts of local colored configurations with entropy and Fisher-information inequalities. Gaussian smoothing turns the counting constraint into an analytic comparison. Quantitative control of the equality case forces Gaussian moments and prevents variance from escaping into rare large coordinates.

With disorder, the marks are Gaussian conditional on the tree environment, with variance proportional to the imaginary part of the local tree resolvent. That variance varies from place to place. Keeping it conditional is part of the extension’s substance.

Insert Gaussian noise without changing the ensemble

A degree-preserving edge switch changes only a small part of a regular graph and can be chosen reversibly, preserving its distribution. In the disordered model, suitable exchanges of intervals in the potential law play a related role.

The effect on microscopic eigenvalues can be written using the Gaussian marks. Many weak changes then approximate an additive GOE perturbation. The number of changes is increased inside an already constructed limiting marked process, after the graph-size limit; the method does not assume a growing-dimensional eigenvector theorem for finite graphs.

Finally, fixed-energy Dyson Brownian motion results identify the local statistics of the Gaussian-perturbed matrices. The manuscripts match the density normalization and control eigenvalue counts so that the conclusion concerns the full point process. Fixed-energy Dyson Brownian motion

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The degree is a fixed integer at least three. Degree two gives unions of cycles and is outside both claims. The energy stays in the open clean bulk; the disordered theorem keeps a prescribed positive distance from its edges. No conclusion is asserted here for edge fluctuations, spectral outliers, or energies drifting toward a band boundary with nnn.

The random potential is independent and uniform on a bounded interval. The theorem does not automatically extend to arbitrary potential distributions, correlated disorder, or disorder strong enough to produce localization. Its smallness threshold depends on the degree and the chosen interior energy range.

Universality of eigenvalue statistics does not mean that eigenvectors have constant local variance in a disordered environment. Nor does it by itself prove a transport theorem on every finite or infinite graph. The density, local tree response, and point-process limit describe different aspects of the model.

Natural further questions include the boundary of the GOE regime as disorder grows, other potential laws, and the transition to localized spectral statistics. These require information beyond the compact weak-disorder bulk treated here.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 develops the clean fixed-degree theorem and the entropy-to-switching mechanism. M1 adapts it to random tree resolvents and positive fixed diagonal disorder.

For earlier milestones, see McKay on the limiting density, Backhausz–Szegedy on Gaussian-wave eigenvectors, and Huang–McKenzie–Yau on fixed-degree edges. The final analytic comparison uses Landon–Sosoe–Yau’s fixed-energy universality theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Fixed-energy universality for weak Anderson disorder on random regular graphs (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, GOE bulk universality for fixed-degree random regular graphs (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why weakly perturbed Ising models would keep the same large-scale geometry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 218 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

The critical square-lattice Ising model has an exceptionally rich mathematical description. Its spin correlations transform predictably under conformal maps, and the boundary between plus and minus regions approaches a particular random curve. But how much of that structure survives if the microscopic model is changed?

There are two natural changes. One can add small, fixed interactions among several nearby spins. Or one can randomly vary the strength of each bond, then hold that environment fixed while sampling the spins. Both changes destroy the special homogeneous nearest-neighbor formulas.

This family contains six manuscripts claiming that much of the critical behavior survives. They cover mixed spin-and-energy correlations, full spin-interface laws, and the slow residual effect of random bonds on correlation fluctuations. A technical companion supplies comparisons that remain valid after an interface exploration reveals an irregular boundary.

The common theme is universality: different microscopic interactions can produce the same macroscopic fields and curves after the correct temperature and field normalizations are chosen.

2. Background and essential definitions

An Ising spin is σx∈{−1,1}\sigma_x\in\{-1,1\}σx​∈{−1,1}. The basic ferromagnetic model gives configurations weight

exp⁡ ⁣(β∑e={x,y}Jeσxσy),Je>0.\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{e=\{x,y\}}J_e\sigma_x\sigma_y\right),\qquad J_e>0.exp​βe={x,y}∑​Je​σx​σy​​,Je​>0.

Positive bonds favor agreement, while β\betaβ is inverse temperature. In the homogeneous model with Je=1J_e=1Je​=1, the critical coupling is

K0=12log⁡(1+2).K_0=\frac12\log(1+\sqrt2).K0​=21​log(1+2​).

A spin correlation averages products of spins. A local energy observable is a neighboring product σxσy\sigma_x\sigma_yσx​σy​, centered by subtracting its expectation. At criticality, their scaling dimensions are respectively 1/81/81/8 and one: mesh-normalized fields use factors δ−1/8\delta^{-1/8}δ−1/8 and δ−1\delta^{-1}δ−1.

A conformal map preserves angles locally. Conformal covariance of a correlation means that mapping its domain changes it by explicit powers of the map’s local scale factor ∣ϕ′∣|\phi'|∣ϕ′∣. It is more information than knowing a power-law decay in the plane.

Fix plus spins along one boundary arc and minus spins along the other. These Dobrushin boundary conditions force an interface joining the two arc endpoints. Its proposed limit is chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution with parameter three, abbreviated SLE3. In the upper half-plane it is generated by

∂tgt(z)=2gt(z)−3Bt,\partial_t g_t(z)=\frac{2}{g_t(z)-\sqrt3 B_t},∂t​gt​(z)=gt​(z)−3​Bt​2​,

where BtB_tBt​ is ordinary one-dimensional Brownian motion. The maps gtg_tgt​ remove a growing curve; conformal mapping gives the law in other simply connected domains. The parameter three specifies the randomness of the driving motion.

For random bonds, quenched means that the Gibbs law is normalized separately for each fixed environment ω\omegaω. Only afterward may one average those laws over environments. The environment is not weighted by its partition function. Thus a quenched correlation is itself a random variable depending on the sampled bonds.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Onsager’s exact free energy and Yang’s spontaneous magnetization made the nearest-neighbor model a foundation of critical statistical mechanics. Conformal field theory organized its spin and energy fields, and discrete complex analysis later established rigorous continuum limits. Chelkak, Hongler, and Izyurov proved conformal convergence of bulk spin correlations and developed the theory of mixed primary fields. Spin-correlation convergence

For interfaces, Smirnov’s fermionic observables and the work of Chelkak and Smirnov supplied the analytic ingredients. Chelkak, Duminil-Copin, Hongler, Kemppainen, and Smirnov obtained convergence of critical spin interfaces to SLE3. The associated random-cluster interface has a different limit, SLE with parameter 16/316/316/3. The distinction matters when comparing later random-bond results. Interface convergence

Universality beyond the exactly solvable model also has substantial predecessors. Giuliani, Greenblatt, and Mastropietro proved energy-correlation limits for weak finite-range pair perturbations. Antinucci, Giuliani, and Greenblatt extended energy universality to cylinders with even multispin interactions of either sign. Cava, Giuliani, and Greenblatt treated boundary spins in the free half-plane. Thus signed interactions and actual-state energy centering were already features of earlier work; the broader mixed bulk correlation problem remained. Plane energy universality, Cylinder energy universality

Greenblatt and Peltola constructed an interface martingale for non-integrable models and formulated estimates that would lead to SLE3. Their work supplies a route to the problem, rather than already proving the full interface limit claimed here. Non-integrable spin interfaces

Random bonds introduce a different difficulty. Harris’s criterion leaves two-dimensional Ising disorder at a borderline case. The analyses of Dotsenko and Dotsenko, Shalaev, Shankar, and Ludwig developed the prediction of unchanged leading exponents with logarithmic corrections. Earlier rigorous random-bond interface results cited by the manuscripts concern disorder that vanishes with the mesh and random-cluster interfaces. Here the disorder strength stays fixed and the claimed limit concerns spin interfaces.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Mixed bulk correlations under deterministic interactions

M4 starts with nearest-neighbor Ising and adds a fixed, sufficiently small finite-range potential on even sets of spins. “Even” means invariance under flipping every spin. The potential is translation invariant and invariant under square-lattice rotations and reflections; its coefficients may have either sign.

The manuscript constructs one temperature branch βc(λ)\beta_c(\lambda)βc​(λ) and two nonzero factors Zσ(λ)Z_\sigma(\lambda)Zσ​(λ), Zϵ(λ)Z_\epsilon(\lambda)Zϵ​(λ). For any fixed number of distinct interior insertions, the mixed correlation limit is

Zσ(λ)nZϵ(λ)mCDb(x1,…,xn;y1,…,ym),Z_\sigma(\lambda)^n Z_\epsilon(\lambda)^m\mathcal C_D^b(x_1,\ldots,x_n;y_1,\ldots,y_m),Zσ​(λ)nZϵ​(λ)mCDb​(x1​,…,xn​;y1​,…,ym​),

where CDb\mathcal C_D^bCDb​ is the corresponding critical nearest-neighbor correlation with nnn spin and mmm energy insertions. The same branch and factors work in all bounded simply connected domains with twice continuously differentiable Jordan boundary, with free, plus, or minus boundary conditions, and in the periodic thermodynamic plane state.

Each energy is centered in its actual interacting state and domain. Under a conformal map ϕ\phiϕ, the limit acquires factors

∏i=1n∣ϕ′(xi)∣1/8∏j=1m∣ϕ′(yj)∣.\prod_{i=1}^n|\phi'(x_i)|^{1/8}\prod_{j=1}^m|\phi'(y_j)|.i=1∏n​∣ϕ′(xi​)∣1/8j=1∏m​∣ϕ′(yj​)∣.

The theorem concerns separated bulk points, not coincident or boundary insertions.

Deterministically perturbed interfaces

M5 considers sufficiently weak, finite-range, square-symmetric perturbations of the contour energy, allowing many-edge interactions of either sign. It claims a domain-independent temperature at which the full oriented spin interface converges to SLE3.

Here domains need only have Jordan boundaries: simple closed boundary curves, without a smoothness assumption. Their lattice boundaries must approximate the limiting boundary uniformly through homeomorphisms. The specified interactions across the boundary are retained, and admissible exterior contours may vary with the mesh.

The convergence keeps the order of traversal, modulo increasing changes of speed. It is stronger than convergence of the curve’s image as an unparameterized compact set. For the signed deterministic models, the critical branch is established through the stated massless or interface behavior; one should not replace it by a magnetization-threshold definition without an additional argument.

Fixed weak random bonds

M2 treats independent fair bonds Je=1±εJ_e=1\pm\varepsilonJe​=1±ε. M1 extends the interface claim to

Je=1+εξe,J_e=1+\varepsilon\xi_e,Je​=1+εξe​,

where the ξe\xi_eξe​ have any fixed bounded, nondegenerate, mean-zero independent identical law. After rescaling the bound, one may take their support in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1]. The positive strength ε\varepsilonε must be sufficiently small for that law and remains fixed as the mesh shrinks.

The temperature is the physical threshold where the disorder-averaged plus-state magnetization becomes positive. For deterministic Jordan-domain approximations, the quenched oriented interface law converges in probability over environments to the deterministic SLE3 law. This is not an almost-sure assertion for every environment or permission to choose the domains after observing the disorder.

For fair binary bonds, the critical point is identified by

sinh⁡ ⁣(2βc(1−ε))sinh⁡ ⁣(2βc(1+ε))=1.\sinh\!\bigl(2\beta_c(1-\varepsilon)\bigr)\sinh\!\bigl(2\beta_c(1+\varepsilon)\bigr)=1.sinh(2βc​(1−ε))sinh(2βc​(1+ε))=1.

For general mean-zero bounded laws, M1 gives βc=K0+O(ε2)\beta_c=K_0+O(\varepsilon^2)βc​=K0​+O(ε2), without an analogous closed self-dual formula.

Logarithmic fluctuations remain visible

M3 assumes the specified deterministic reference estimates and treats the fair binary disorder. Let Cω(r)C_\omega(r)Cω​(r) be the critical spin correlation in a fixed environment, after the free-box thermodynamic limit. Its relative second moment is

Rε(r)=Eω[Cω(r)2]Eω[Cω(r)]2.R_\varepsilon(r)=\frac{\mathbb E_\omega[C_\omega(r)^2]}{\mathbb E_\omega[C_\omega(r)]^2}.Rε​(r)=Eω​[Cω​(r)]2Eω​[Cω​(r)2]​.

The manuscript states

Rε(r)=(log⁡r)1/4+o(1).R_\varepsilon(r)=(\log r)^{1/4+o(1)}.Rε​(r)=(logr)1/4+o(1).

Since Rε−1R_\varepsilon-1Rε​−1 is the variance divided by the squared mean, this detects sample-to-sample variability even while the macroscopic interface law becomes universal. It is an exponent statement, not a positive-amplitude equivalent. At zero disorder the ratio is identically one; the theorem fixes a positive disorder strength before sending rrr to infinity.

A comparison theorem supporting the family

M6 gives likelihood-ratio bounds for finite ferromagnetic Ising systems with arbitrary common pinned spins. It also claims that, after exploring across a band of fixed positive width, finitely many regular signed barriers approximate the good conditional laws on a separated target in total variation. Total variation controls the probability of every target event simultaneously, so the test observable may change with the mesh.

This is a statement about the pure reference model and its conditioned laws. It supplies tools used by the other manuscripts, rather than being another random-bond scaling theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family addresses universality for central observables that lie beyond the reach of the original exact solution: mixed bulk fields, whole interfaces, and fixed weak disorder.

The deterministic results would connect a broad class of microscopic perturbations to the same conformal theory using only one temperature adjustment and two field factors. The random results would show that a typical fixed environment loses its macroscopic directional irregularities in the interface law, while retaining measurable logarithmic effects in another observable.

The strength of that combination is precisely that universality is not presented as complete disappearance of all microscopic information. Amplitudes, the critical temperature, and disorder moments can change even when the limiting geometric law remains SLE3.

6. The main idea

Keep the important fields and shrink the rest

A change of scale replaces a local interaction by its conditional average in the pure critical model. Most resulting directions contract. The spin and energy fields are the important low-dimensional components, and changing temperature controls the expanding thermal direction.

The difficulty is uniformity. Repeated averaging creates functions of many microscopic spins; convergence of a fixed list of spin correlations does not control all such functions. M6’s buffered comparisons and finite descriptions of explored boundaries make it possible to approximate their effect on distant regions uniformly over bounded tests.

M4 and M5 then construct exact transformations of the local interactions. The temperature is chosen so the thermal component does not grow. Marked spin and energy insertions retain their leading components with model-dependent factors, while the remaining interactions become negligible at a fixed physical separation.

Convert local errors into geometric control

A local change deep inside a region can alter a macroscopic crossing only if several long interface strands reach it. For the pure spin model, the four-arm exponent is 21/8>221/8>221/8>2: the rarity of such configurations beats the two-dimensional count of possible change locations. Separate boundary and corner estimates complete the comparison.

The signed perturbations need not preserve the usual ferromagnetic ordering for the physical spins. The manuscript therefore uses restricted boundary comparisons with auxiliary variables, retaining the actual cross-boundary interaction. Further passage estimates prevent a curve from tracing the right set in the wrong order.

Track slowly decaying random variance

For random bonds, a supremum over all environments would be too strong. The construction tracks environmental moments and treats rare concentrations of large local effects through positive conditional weights. It also records which original random bonds each effective interaction depends on.

After tuning the mean thermal component, the leading disorder variance gjg_jgj​ follows a marginal recursion of the form

gj+1=gj−cgj2+smaller terms,c>0.g_{j+1}=g_j-cg_j^2+\text{smaller terms},\qquad c>0.gj+1​=gj​−cgj2​+smaller terms,c>0.

Thus gjg_jgj​ decays like 1/j1/j1/j, rather than exponentially. Its accumulated effect can produce powers of a logarithm. In M3, each distant spin insertion contributes half of the relative-second-moment exponent; the local dependence records allow their leading factors to separate.

Finally, the tuned temperature must be identified with the physical transition. Binary disorder permits a self-dual comparison. For a general law, M1 tunes primal and dual descriptions separately and uses finite-torus duality and monotonicity to show that the temperatures agree. Crossing and magnetization arguments then identify the threshold used in the theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All perturbations are sufficiently weak and fixed before the continuum limit. The deterministic potentials have finite range and square symmetries. The random bonds are independent, bounded, and ferromagnetic. Strong disorder, correlated environments, and general anisotropic interactions are outside these claims.

The random interface conclusion is convergence in probability of quenched laws, not uniform convergence over environments. The logarithmic correlation-moment result is stated for fair binary disorder and with its deterministic companion assumptions; M1’s broader interface theorem does not automatically broaden that moment theorem.

Domain regularity and boundary prescriptions differ between the correlation and interface results. M6 also requires positive geometric separation for its buffered comparisons; its constants need not remain controlled as that separation vanishes.

The family does not assert every boundary-field limit, every multiply connected geometry, or an entire loop-ensemble theorem for each perturbation. Extending the methods to those observables, and resolving further disorder-dependent logarithmic factors, remain separate questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M4 covers deterministic bulk fields, M5 deterministic interfaces, and M6 the pure conditional-comparison tools. M2 establishes the binary random-bond interface result; M1 extends its environment law; M3 studies a distinct random-correlation observable with explicit reference assumptions.

Useful predecessors include the pure interface theorem, energy universality under weak interactions, and Greenblatt–Peltola’s interface framework. The source introductions give the primary references for the historical logarithmic-disorder predictions and the earlier vanishing-disorder results.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Quenched SLE₃ limits for general weak random-bond Ising models (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Quenched SLE₃ Universality for the Weak Random-Bond Ising Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Logarithmic Relative Fluctuations in the Weakly Disordered Planar Ising Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Conformal universality of bulk Ising correlations under weak interactions (September 23, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, $\mathrm{SLE}_3$ universality for weak finite-range Ising interactions (September 23, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Buffered comparison and stopping-band resolution in critical Ising (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The XY transition: a quarter-power law, logarithms, and an exponential length scale
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 216 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A two-dimensional magnet can change phase without acquiring a preferred direction. In the planar XY model, each spin is an arrow constrained to a circle. At high temperature, distant arrows rapidly forget one another. At low temperature, their correlations persist as a power of distance, even though there is no ordinary spontaneous magnetization.

The Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless, or BKT, picture predicts unusually precise behavior at the boundary between these phases. The critical correlation should decay with exponent 1/41/41/4, multiplied by a small logarithmic correction. Approaching the transition from the high-temperature side, the correlation length should grow faster than any power of the distance to criticality.

The six manuscripts in this family claim these critical asymptotics for the ordinary cosine XY model and identify its critical continuum spin field. A broader companion also treats rough height surfaces and low-temperature spin fields. Together they describe both individual correlations and a random field built from many spins at once.

2. Background and essential definitions

Write the spin at x∈Z2x\in\mathbb Z^2x∈Z2 as eiθxe^{i\theta_x}eiθx​, where angles are taken modulo 2π2\pi2π. In a square box, the probability density is proportional to

exp⁡ ⁣(b∑{x,y}cos⁡(θx−θy)),\exp\!\left(b\sum_{\{x,y\}}\cos(\theta_x-\theta_y)\right),exp​b{x,y}∑​cos(θx​−θy​)​,

relative to independent uniform angles. Every nearest-neighbor edge occurs once. The parameter bbb is inverse temperature: heating decreases it.

For free boundary conditions, first send the box size to infinity while keeping two sites fixed. Let Cb(r)C_b(r)Cb​(r) be their expected cosine difference when they are rrr steps apart along a coordinate axis. Then define

m(b)=lim⁡r→∞−1rlog⁡Cb(r),bc=inf⁡{b>0:m(b)=0}.m(b)=\lim_{r\to\infty}-\frac1r\log C_b(r),\qquadb_c=\inf\{b>0:m(b)=0\}.m(b)=r→∞lim​−r1​logCb​(r),bc​=inf{b>0:m(b)=0}.

A positive mass m(b)m(b)m(b) means exponential decay. Its reciprocal ξ(b)=1/m(b)\xi(b)=1/m(b)ξ(b)=1/m(b) is the axis correlation length. The infinite-volume limit comes before the separation limit. The threshold is defined through this observable, rather than by presupposing the desired critical exponent.

A vortex is a configuration in which the angle winds by a nonzero multiple of 2π2\pi2π around a closed circuit. Smooth angle fluctuations are called spin waves. In the BKT picture, vortex pairs remain bound at low temperature; unbinding destroys the slowly decaying phase.

A second description uses integer-valued heights on faces of the lattice. Fourier expansion of the spin interaction turns angle integration into conservation of integer currents. Rotating these currents gives height differences. For the cosine model the edge weights involve modified Bessel functions, so this dual height model is not simply a discrete Gaussian model.

The continuum Gaussian free field, or GFF, is a random distribution whose covariance is the inverse Laplacian. In a domain DDD with zero boundary values, its covariance kernel has local behavior

GD(z,w)=12πlog⁡1∣z−w∣+a smooth remainder.G_D(z,w)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\log\frac1{|z-w|}+\text{a smooth remainder}.GD​(z,w)=2π1​log∣z−w∣1​+a smooth remainder.

Pointwise variance diverges, but averages against smooth functions are well defined. A spin field is related to an imaginary exponential of this Gaussian field, rather than to the Gaussian field itself.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Berezinskii’s early analysis predicted a low-temperature phase with algebraic correlations. Kosterlitz and Thouless explained the transition through vortex binding and unbinding, and Kosterlitz’s renormalization calculation predicted both the critical exponent and the essential singularity of the correlation length. The important variable is the effective stiffness seen after averaging over small-scale fluctuations, which need not equal the original coupling. Kosterlitz–Thouless, Kosterlitz

McBryan and Spencer obtained algebraic upper bounds. Fröhlich and Spencer’s 1981 multiscale analysis proved a low-temperature algebraic regime for planar rotators and related models. This established a central part of the phase picture without fixing the exact critical correlation asymptotic. Fröhlich–Spencer

Van Engelenburg and Lis later gave a current-and-loop approach yielding an exponential-versus-polynomial dichotomy for the ordinary XY model. Their polynomial lower bound also holds at the threshold. This is an essential endpoint input in the present manuscripts, although its exponent is not the predicted 1/41/41/4. Van Engelenburg–Lis

Height methods supplied another route. Aizenman, Harel, Peled, and Shapiro connected height depinning with BKT behavior, using discrete Gaussian comparison inequalities. Lammers related the XY and dual-height correlation lengths exactly and developed a localization dichotomy. These results identify the relation between the two transitions; determining the effective coefficient precisely at the endpoint remains additional work. Depinning and BKT phases, Bijecting the BKT transition

Rigorous renormalization also established detailed Gaussian limits and logarithmic corrections in related settings. Bauerschmidt, Park, and Rodriguez treated high-temperature discrete Gaussian heights, while Falco analyzed a dilute Coulomb gas at criticality. Such results are important methodological predecessors. Their hypotheses and observables differ from those of the fixed nearest-neighbor cosine model at its physical transition, so their conclusions cannot simply be transferred unchanged.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Critical bulk and boundary correlations

M5 first states

Cbc(r)=r−1/4+o(1).C_{b_c}(r)=r^{-1/4+o(1)}.Cbc​​(r)=r−1/4+o(1).

This fixes the exponent but allows slowly varying multipliers. M1 sharpens it to

Cbc(r)=B r−1/4(log⁡r)1/8(1+o(1)),0<B<∞.C_{b_c}(r)=B\,r^{-1/4}(\log r)^{1/8}(1+o(1)),\qquad 0<B<\infty.Cbc​​(r)=Br−1/4(logr)1/8(1+o(1)),0<B<∞.

The amplitude BBB is model-specific. The logarithm grows more slowly than every positive power of rrr, but it means that r1/4Cbc(r)r^{1/4}C_{b_c}(r)r1/4Cbc​​(r) does not approach a finite nonzero constant.

For a different observable, fix every boundary angle of [−n,n]2[-n,n]^2[−n,n]2 to zero and let

an=En,bc0cos⁡θ0.a_n=\mathbb E^0_{n,b_c}\cos\theta_0.an​=En,bc​0​cosθ0​.

M2 states, using its specified companion inputs,

an=A n−1/8(log⁡n)1/16(1+o(1)),0<A<∞.a_n=A\,n^{-1/8}(\log n)^{1/16}(1+o(1)),\qquad 0<A<\infty.an​=An−1/8(logn)1/16(1+o(1)),0<A<∞.

This is magnetization at the center caused by an aligned boundary. It is not the root-mean-square spatially averaged magnetization in a periodic box. The two amplitudes AAA and BBB also need not be equal.

The near-critical correlation length

M4 claims that, approaching from the massive side b<bcb<b_cb<bc​,

bc−b log⁡ξ(b)⟶Aξ,0<Aξ<∞.\sqrt{b_c-b}\,\log\xi(b)\longrightarrow A_\xi,\qquad 0<A_\xi<\infty.bc​−b​logξ(b)⟶Aξ​,0<Aξ​<∞.

Equivalently,

ξ(b)=exp⁡ ⁣(Aξ+o(1)bc−b).\xi(b)=\exp\!\left(\frac{A_\xi+o(1)}{\sqrt{b_c-b}}\right).ξ(b)=exp(bc​−b​Aξ​+o(1)​).

The constant is not evaluated in closed form and depends on the temperature convention. This logarithmic asymptotic does not assert a multiplicative equivalent with a fixed prefactor outside the exponential.

The critical continuum spin field

M3 works in D=(−1,1)2D=(-1,1)^2D=(−1,1)2 with mesh 1/n1/n1/n and boundary angles zero. Set K∗=2/πK_*=2/\piK∗​=2/π. Let GnG_nGn​ be the inverse of the unscaled nearest-neighbor Dirichlet graph Laplacian. The normalized spin distribution is

Sn=1n2∑x∈Dn∘exp⁡ ⁣((Gn(x,x)−Gn(0,0))/(2K∗))aneiθx δx.S_n=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{x\in D_n^\circ}\frac{\exp\!\left((G_n(x,x)-G_n(0,0))/(2K_*)\right)}{a_n}e^{i\theta_x}\,\delta_x.Sn​=n21​x∈Dn∘​∑​an​exp((Gn​(x,x)−Gn​(0,0))/(2K∗​))​eiθx​δx​.

Here Dn∘D_n^\circDn∘​ is the set of interior mesh sites and δx\delta_xδx​ evaluates a test function at xxx. The exact center magnetization removes the microscopic amplitude; the Green-function correction adjusts its spatial dependence.

The claimed limit is

V∗=lim⁡ε↓0exp⁡ ⁣(iΦD,εK∗+EΦD,ε22K∗),V_* =\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\exp\!\left(\frac{i\Phi_{D,\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{K_*}}+\frac{\mathbb E\Phi_{D,\varepsilon}^2}{2K_*}\right),V∗​=ε↓0lim​exp(K∗​​iΦD,ε​​+2K∗​EΦD,ε2​​),

interpreted after integration against smooth test functions. The regularized GFF ΦD,ε\Phi_{D,\varepsilon}ΦD,ε​ averages over small circles. The positive variance term compensates for the vanishing mean of the unnormalized imaginary exponential. It uses the entire variance, including its finite position-dependent part.

M3 claims convergence along all integer meshes in a local negative Sobolev topology, a topology for distributions, together with all mixed smeared moments. Both spins and their complex conjugates are included, without requiring equal numbers. The theorem uses the exact ana_nan​, so its formulation does not depend on first knowing M2’s asymptotic.

Rough heights and low-temperature universality

M6 treats discrete Gaussian heights with values in 2πZ2\pi\mathbb Z2πZ, for any finite interaction set JJJ invariant under square symmetries and containing nearest neighbors. If

vJ2=12∣J∣∑y∈Jy12,v_J^2=\frac{1}{2|J|}\sum_{y\in J}y_1^2,vJ2​=2∣J∣1​y∈J∑​y12​,

its effective height temperature at the physical roughening threshold satisfies

βeff(J,βc(J))=8πvJ2.\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(J,\beta_c(J))=8\pi v_J^2.βeff​(J,βc​(J))=8πvJ2​.

Mean-subtracted macroscopic torus heights converge to a GFF with covariance coefficient βeff/vJ2\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}/v_J^2βeff​/vJ2​, including at the threshold. The paper also gives differentiability above the threshold, an infinite right slope there, and asymptotics for interactions extending over increasingly large neighborhoods. The height temperature β\betaβ is a separate parameter from the spin inverse temperature bbb.

For the ordinary XY and Villain spin models, M6 proves imaginary-GFF field limits at sufficiently low fixed temperatures, with model-dependent stiffness and amplitude. The Villain interaction is a periodic sum of Gaussian angle weights. The low-temperature theorem does not itself reach either spin model’s transition; M3 supplies the additional critical XY result.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family addresses several signature predictions of one of statistical mechanics’ central unconventional phase transitions. It connects the critical exponent, its logarithmic refinement, the divergence of the correlation length, and a full continuum spin field for the original cosine interaction.

These are complementary achievements. An exponent is a coarse summary of decay. A positive finite amplitude with a logarithmic correction requires finer control. A field limit organizes arbitrary collections of spin averages. A near-critical theorem explains how the finite correlation length becomes infinite as the transition is approached.

The height results add a broader universality statement across finite-range interactions. Their normalization also shows why numerical constants such as 8π8\pi8π and 2/π2/\pi2/π must always be tied to the precise field and Laplacian convention.

6. The main idea

Identify the critical Gaussian coefficient

The first stage uses finite comparison inequalities and changes to the height graph to construct an effective covariance coefficient a(b)a(b)a(b). For the dual XY heights, the manuscripts establish the alternative a=0a=0a=0 or a≥8πa\geq8\pia≥8π.

The known critical polynomial lower bound rules out zero at bcb_cbc​. A separate openness argument says that a coefficient strictly above 8π8\pi8π would keep the model massless in a neighborhood extending below bcb_cbc​, contradicting the threshold definition. Thus the endpoint is a(bc)=8πa(b_c)=8\pia(bc​)=8π.

Spin insertions create prescribed windings in the height description. Their energy then gives exponent 2π/a=1/42\pi/a=1/42π/a=1/4. Controlling ordinary height averages is insufficient: one must also compare the partition functions with these winding defects.

Accumulate a small correction across scales

At criticality, the renormalized interaction approaches its limiting Gaussian form slowly. If jjj counts geometric length scales, the relevant deviation has size proportional to 1/j1/j1/j. Summing that deviation gives ∑j≤N1/j∼log⁡N\sum_{j\leq N}1/j\sim\log N∑j≤N​1/j∼logN. Since physical size grows exponentially with NNN, exponentiating the accumulated correction produces a power of log⁡n\log nlogn.

The center observable acquires power 1/161/161/16; the bulk two-point function acquires power 1/81/81/8. To obtain a positive finite amplitude, the remaining errors must be summable, not merely smaller than the leading term. Comparing nested geometries with identical microscopic insertions lets otherwise troublesome normalization factors cancel exactly.

Turn a departure scale into a physical length

Near criticality, two coupled coordinates track stiffness and the first periodic height interaction. Their leading recursion has the form

xj+1−xj≈−yj2,yj+1−yj≈−xjyj.x_{j+1}-x_j\approx-y_j^2,\qquady_{j+1}-y_j\approx-x_jy_j.xj+1​−xj​≈−yj2​,yj+1​−yj​≈−xj​yj​.

M4 controls how changing the original temperature moves the system away from the critical trajectory. The exit occurs after order (bc−b)−1/2(b_c-b)^{-1/2}(bc​−b)−1/2 scale steps. Exponentially growing block sizes then suggest the essential singularity.

The manuscript must additionally show that this analytic exit scale is the actual correlation length. It does so through height fluctuations, annular winding estimates, and a finite-size criterion for spin decay. Without that connection, a recursion time would not yet be an observable of the original magnet.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The critical XY statements concern the square lattice with its ordinary nearest-neighbor cosine interaction. They do not give a closed-form value of bcb_cbc​, the amplitudes, or AξA_\xiAξ​. Universality of exponents does not mean equality of microscopic constants.

The boundary conventions differ across conclusions. Bulk correlations use a free thermodynamic limit; center magnetization and the continuum spin field use aligned boundary spins on a square. The transfer between these geometries requires additional estimates and is not automatic from a field limit.

Similarly, the discrete Gaussian height theorem reaches its physical roughening threshold, while M6’s spin theorem covers only a sufficiently low-temperature range. The critical XY result relies on the companion’s specific critical-height inputs. This family does not silently extend that conclusion to the Villain endpoint or to arbitrary planar-spin interactions.

The claims concern distributions and integrated moments, not pointwise convergence of the angle field. They also leave more detailed questions about interfaces, finite-size corrections, and other domains beyond the particular assertions stated here.

8. Sources and further reading

M5 introduces the critical exponent and height coefficient; M1 and M2 refine the bulk and center asymptotics. M3 constructs the critical spin field, M4 treats the massive approach to criticality, and M6 supplies the broader height and low-temperature framework.

For the development of the physical picture, see Kosterlitz’s 1974 analysis. For established rigorous phase information, see Fröhlich–Spencer, van Engelenburg–Lis, and Lammers’ spin–height relation. The six source manuscripts identify precisely which companion inputs each argument uses.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The critical logarithmic correction for the planar XY model (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Critical Center Magnetization in the Planar XY Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The Critical Spin Field of the Planar XY Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Essential Singularity of the Correlation Length in the Planar XY Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, The critical correlation exponent of the planar XY model (September 24, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, BKT universality for height and planar spin fields (September 24, 2026).

entry.title: When escape through a random environment forces a definite direction and speed
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 220 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine a walker moving through a landscape of local instructions. At each site, a randomly chosen probability vector tells it how likely it is to move to each neighboring site. The instructions remain in place: returning to a site means encountering the same biases again.

Two basic questions arise. Can the walker have a probability strictly between zero and one of eventually escaping in a prescribed direction? And if it does escape in that direction almost surely, must it make linear progress, or can increasingly long delays reduce its speed to zero?

This family contains three manuscripts claiming answers under carefully distinguished hypotheses. Two establish directional zero–one laws, including an extension to environments with dependence over a finite range. The third claims that almost-sure directional escape implies positive speed in independent uniformly elliptic environments in dimension at least two.

The distinction between escape and speed is central. A sequence can tend to infinity as slowly as log⁡n\log nlogn; reaching arbitrarily distant levels says little by itself about how much time the journey takes.

2. Background and essential definitions

The walker lives on Zd\mathbb Z^dZd and takes nearest-neighbor steps from

U={±e1,…,±ed},U=\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_d\},U={±e1​,…,±ed​},

where eie_iei​ is the iii-th coordinate vector. An environment assigns a row of transition probabilities ω(x,⋅)\omega(x,\cdot)ω(x,⋅) to each site:

ω(x,e)≥0,∑e∈Uω(x,e)=1.\omega(x,e)\geq0,\qquad\sum_{e\in U}\omega(x,e)=1.ω(x,e)≥0,e∈U∑​ω(x,e)=1.

For a fixed environment, the walk is a Markov chain with transition probability ω(x,e)\omega(x,e)ω(x,e) from xxx to x+ex+ex+e. Its law is called quenched. Averaging that law over the environment gives the annealed law P0P_0P0​, when the walk starts at zero.

An iid environment has independent identically distributed rows at different sites. The entries within a row are not required to be independent; indeed they must sum to one.

There are two positivity assumptions:

  • Strict ellipticity: every allowed transition probability is positive almost surely.
  • Uniform ellipticity: one deterministic constant κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 bounds every transition probability below, at every site.

Strict ellipticity permits exceptionally small transition probabilities. Uniform ellipticity prohibits them, though larger regions can still delay a walker.

For a fixed nonzero real vector ℓ\ellℓ, define the directional escape event

Aℓ={Xn⋅ℓ⟶+∞}.A_\ell=\{X_n\cdot\ell\longrightarrow+\infty\}.Aℓ​={Xn​⋅ℓ⟶+∞}.

A directional zero–one law says P0(Aℓ)∈{0,1}P_0(A_\ell)\in\{0,1\}P0​(Aℓ​)∈{0,1}. Ballisticity is stronger: the displacement divided by elapsed time approaches a vector vvv with v⋅ℓ>0v\cdot\ell>0v⋅ℓ>0.

The dependent-environment manuscript uses finite-range dependence. There is a fixed range RRR such that all rows in two deterministic sets are independent whenever the sets are more than RRR apart in maximum-coordinate distance. This concerns the full collections of rows, including infinite sets. Merely having pairwise correlations that decay with distance is weaker.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Solomon’s one-dimensional theory showed that transience and positive speed can separate even in uniformly elliptic iid environments. A walker may escape to the right while spending enough time in unfavorable stretches to have zero limiting speed. Higher dimensions offer routes around obstacles, but making that geometric intuition quantitative has been difficult. Solomon’s paper

Kalikow’s work initiated much of the directional-transience theory. The classical zero–one statement concerns the union Aℓ∪A−ℓA_\ell\cup A_{-\ell}Aℓ​∪A−ℓ​: escape in one of two opposite directions is either almost sure or has probability zero. That leaves open the possibility that the two signs each have positive probability.

Zerner and Merkl settled the one-sign question for planar iid elliptic environments. Their argument exploits the fact that suitably opposed paths must intersect in the plane. Zerner later simplified the proof. Higher-dimensional paths can pass around one another, so the same geometric mechanism does not extend directly. Zerner–Merkl, Zerner’s revised proof

Sznitman and Zerner developed regeneration times, which cut a transient walk into independent pieces after conditioning against backtracking. Finite mean duration of those pieces gives a law of large numbers with positive speed. The difficulty is that finite duration almost surely does not imply finite expected duration. The regeneration law of large numbers

Many sufficient conditions for ballisticity were subsequently proved. Kalikow-type drift conditions, Sznitman’s slab-exit conditions and effective criterion, and polynomial exit criteria all supply quantitative control strong enough to rule out excessive trapping. The conjecture addressed here starts from only qualitative escape in one direction. Fribergh and Kious explicitly formulate that gap and study the role of local trapping. Local trapping

Dependence changes the picture again. Bramson, Zeitouni, and Zerner constructed stationary, uniformly elliptic, polynomially mixing environments in higher dimensions with positive probabilities of escape in opposite directions. Thus a theorem for finite-range dependence cannot be replaced by a vague assertion that sufficiently weak correlations should suffice. The source manuscripts carefully preserve exact independence beyond the stated range.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A zero–one law with only strict ellipticity

M2 states that for every dimension d≥3d\geq3d≥3, every iid nearest-neighbor environment with strictly positive transition probabilities, and every fixed nonzero real direction ℓ\ellℓ,

P0(Aℓ)∈{0,1}.P_0(A_\ell)\in\{0,1\}.P0​(Aℓ​)∈{0,1}.

There is no uniform lower bound, inverse-probability moment condition, drift assumption, reversibility assumption, or positive-speed premise. The direction need not have rational coordinates. The theorem is asserted for each fixed direction; it does not require a single exceptional null set that works simultaneously for every real direction.

An extension to finite-range dependence

M1 gives the same directional conclusion for d≥3d\geq3d≥3 when the row environment is stationary, ergodic, uniformly elliptic, and finite-range dependent. Stationarity means that translating the whole environment preserves its law; ergodicity rules out nontrivial translation-invariant random alternatives.

The assumptions differ from M2 in two ways: independence of all sites is weakened, but uniform ellipticity is imposed. Combining the headlines into a theorem with both arbitrary finite-range dependence and mere strict ellipticity would go beyond what is stated.

Directional escape implies positive velocity

M3 states that for an iid uniformly elliptic nearest-neighbor environment in every dimension d≥2d\geq2d≥2,

P0(Aℓ)=1⟹Xnn⟶vP0-almost surely,v⋅ℓ>0,P_0(A_\ell)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{X_n}{n}\longrightarrow v\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},\qquad v\cdot\ell>0,P0​(Aℓ​)=1⟹nXn​​⟶vP0​-almost surely,v⋅ℓ>0,

where vvv is deterministic and depends on the environment law. No regeneration-time moment is assumed; obtaining the required duration control is part of the claim.

For d≥3d\geq3d≥3, combining this with M2 upgrades positive-probability directional escape to the same positive-velocity conclusion. If one such direction exists, the manuscript identifies all deterministic escape directions:

{u∈Sd−1:P0(Au)>0}={u∈Sd−1:P0(Au)=1}={u∈Sd−1:v⋅u>0}.\{u\in S^{d-1}:P_0(A_u)>0\}=\{u\in S^{d-1}:P_0(A_u)=1\}=\{u\in S^{d-1}:v\cdot u>0\}.{u∈Sd−1:P0​(Au​)>0}={u∈Sd−1:P0​(Au​)=1}={u∈Sd−1:v⋅u>0}.

They form the open hemisphere pointing along the velocity. Each fixed equatorial direction, with v⋅u=0v\cdot u=0v⋅u=0, has zero escape probability. This last conclusion uses the combined theorems; convergence of Xn/nX_n/nXn​/n alone would not rule out slower unbounded motion in an equatorial direction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Directional zero–one behavior and ballisticity are foundational questions about motion in a persistent random medium. The claims would settle both the higher-dimensional iid directional conjecture and the uniformly elliptic ballisticity conjecture, while adding an exact finite-range-dependent extension of the first.

The results separate two kinds of uncertainty. The zero–one theorem rules out a probabilistic choice between opposite eventual escape signs under its hypotheses. The speed theorem rules out indefinite slowdown once almost-sure escape is known under stronger ellipticity and independence assumptions.

The common methods also aim to extract quantitative information from very weak qualitative premises. That is a significant change from requiring a strong drift or a pre-established exit estimate at the outset.

6. The main idea

Cut the path where the past stops mattering

A regeneration point is a new height record below which the future path never returns. After such a point, the walk can use fresh environmental rows. Successive pieces then have a factorization that resembles independent increments.

These times depend on the future, so they are not ordinary stopping times. Independence must be established from the weights of finite path pieces. A particularly useful detail is that a path uses the row at a site when it departs, not merely when it arrives. Stopping on first arrival leaves that row available to a fresh continuation.

Under strict ellipticity, a short prescribed path through previously unused rows has positive annealed probability given by a product of positive row averages. There is no need for one uniform lower bound across all environments.

Rule out coexistence by counting contacts two ways

The zero–one arguments suppose that escape in both signs has positive probability. They first derive finite mean spatial radius for regeneration pieces. Very large sideways excursions could otherwise be spliced to an opposite continuation, forcing incompatible probabilities for arbitrarily large finite height maxima.

Next, two independent sequences of regeneration pieces are placed in opposed arrangements. The manuscripts estimate how many geometric scales contain contacts between them. An entropy comparison with independent bridges makes contacts relatively scarce. A second argument starts one path near the other’s random endpoint and forces more contacts.

Selecting that endpoint naively would be too costly. The proof tracks posterior probabilities of possible endpoints as a vector of martingales, controlling their accumulated maxima. The two resulting contact counts are incompatible, excluding coexistence.

For finite-range dependence, disjoint paths are not necessarily independent. M1 inserts short sequences of environment-independent forced steps to cross a gap wider than the dependence range. Contacts are then defined by proximity within that range, and all transfers retain the actual row information already used.

Control time only after controlling space

Ballisticity requires more than spatially finite regeneration pieces. A piece can stay in a modest region for a very long time. M3 studies the quenched probability of reaching a high level before a backward level and seeks to show that extremely small success probabilities are exceptionally rare.

The argument compares two walks in the same environment with two walks in independent environments, using spatial moments and truncated variances rather than assuming a central limit theorem based on positive speed. It then follows the distribution of successful endpoints across scales.

If survival repeatedly lost too much probability, normalized endpoint profiles would have to sustain that loss in a stationary construction. Entropy bounds restrict how their mass can diffuse or split among separated groups. An order comparison in the distant tails contradicts persistent loss. The resulting crossing estimate supplies finite mean regeneration duration, after which the renewal law of large numbers gives the positive velocity.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The nearest-neighbor assumption is present throughout. The stated results do not cover arbitrary long jumps or environments that evolve in time.

The three hypotheses should remain separate. M2’s zero–one theorem needs only strict ellipticity but iid rows. M1 allows finite-range dependence but requires uniform ellipticity. M3’s speed theorem requires both iid rows and uniform ellipticity. It does not claim ballisticity for every strictly elliptic environment or for the dependent class of M1.

Dimension also matters: the speed theorem begins at two, and the one-dimensional counterexamples remain valid. The zero–one manuscripts address dimensions at least three, building on the earlier planar result.

A positive limiting velocity does not by itself specify Gaussian fluctuations, quantitative slowdown probabilities, or an explicit formula for the speed. Nor does the theorem decide which environment laws are directionally transient in the first place. It determines the consequences once that escape premise is met.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 is the iid strict-ellipticity directional theorem, M1 its uniformly elliptic finite-range-dependent extension, and M3 the ballisticity theorem. Their introductions explain the differences between spatial radius, projected width, and elapsed time in regeneration arguments.

For context, read Solomon on one-dimensional environments, Zerner’s planar zero–one proof, and Fribergh–Kious on trapping and the ballisticity conjecture. These predecessors make clear why positivity of transition probabilities, independence, and dimension play distinct roles.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A directional zero-one law for finite-range-dependent random environments (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A directional zero–one law under strict ellipticity (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Directional transience implies ballisticity (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A hierarchical formula for the free energy of diluted spin glasses
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 221 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

In a dense spin glass, each spin interacts with a number of others that grows with the system. In a diluted spin glass, each spin participates in only a finite average number of interactions. The system remains locally irregular no matter how large it becomes.

The cavity method tries to understand such a system by adding one spin and asking how its neighbors influence it. A single effective field may suffice in a simple phase. When many competing states contribute, the proposed description becomes a hierarchy of probability distributions over fields.

The manuscript in this family claims that this hierarchical prescription gives the exact limiting pressure for a specified class of diluted Ising models. Earlier work had established that every finite hierarchy gives an upper bound. The new assertion is that optimizing over all finite depths and all trial laws reaches the actual value.

This is a statement about a variational formula, not a claim that one small hierarchy always suffices or that an optimizer can be computed efficiently.

2. Background and essential definitions

There are NNN spins σi∈{−1,1}\sigma_i\in\{-1,1\}σi​∈{−1,1}. Fix an even interaction size p≥2p\geq2p≥2 and a density α>0\alpha>0α>0. The number of interactions is a Poisson random variable MNM_NMN​ with mean αN\alpha NαN. Each interaction chooses ppp site indices independently and uniformly with replacement.

Let θk\theta_kθk​ be independent copies of a random function on ppp spins, and let hih_ihi​ be independent external fields. The statistical weight is

exp⁡ ⁣(∑k=1MNθk(σi1,k,…,σip,k)+∑i=1Nhiσi).\exp\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{M_N}\theta_k(\sigma_{i_{1,k}},\ldots,\sigma_{i_{p,k}})+\sum_{i=1}^N h_i\sigma_i\right).exp(k=1∑MN​​θk​(σi1,k​​,…,σip,k​​)+i=1∑N​hi​σi​).

The partition function ZNZ_NZN​ sums these weights over all 2N2^N2N configurations. The pressure is the expected log partition function per spin,

FN=1NElog⁡ZN.F_N=\frac1N\mathbb E\log Z_N.FN​=N1​ElogZN​.

The expectation averages the disorder. If inverse temperature β\betaβ has been included in θ\thetaθ and hhh, physical free energy per spin is −FN/β-F_N/\beta−FN​/β. This sign explains why an upper pressure bound is often called a lower free-energy bound in the literature.

A message x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R represents a one-spin probability distribution

qx(s)=exs2cosh⁡x,s∈{−1,1}.q_x(s)=\frac{e^{xs}}{2\cosh x},\qquad s\in\{-1,1\}.qx​(s)=2coshxexs​,s∈{−1,1}.

Its mean spin is tanh⁡x\tanh xtanhx. The cavity approximation replaces the influences from different neighboring branches by messages. A random message law captures variation among local environments. A hierarchy adds distributions of message laws, then distributions of those distributions, allowing nested variation among competing states.

The simplest, depth-zero prescription is called replica symmetric. Positive depth incorporates replica symmetry breaking. Here replicas simply mean independent spin samples from the same Gibbs system; the hierarchy is a trial construction rather than an assumed literal decomposition of the original finite system.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Viana–Bray model supplied a basic diluted two-spin glass. Mézard and Parisi developed a hierarchical cavity description for the Bethe-lattice spin glass, including a one-step symmetry-breaking functional.
