Their work explained why a distribution of local fields must itself fluctuate across states. The Bethe lattice spin glass revisited

Franz and Leone adapted Guerra’s interpolation method to diluted systems, obtaining replica-symmetric and one-step bounds for even-arity models. Panchenko and Talagrand then established arbitrary finite-level hierarchical bounds for the interaction class used here. Their conjecture asked whether the infimum of those bounds equals the limiting pressure. Panchenko–Talagrand

Other exact variational descriptions already existed. De Sanctis used random multioverlap structures for Viana–Bray models. Panchenko’s spin-distribution approach gave exact formulas over invariant exchangeable spin distributions. These are broader ways of recording the state of the system; an exact formula over such a class does not automatically reduce to the specific finite hierarchy of independent message laws. Spin distributions

Later results clarified pieces of the hierarchy. Panchenko obtained single-site hierarchical representations for finite-symmetry-breaking asymptotic measures of suitably modified models. Other work proved exact replica-symmetric formulas in high-temperature or low-connectivity regimes, and developed variational bounds for random regular graphs.

The remaining issue addressed by this manuscript is the equality for the Poisson model at arbitrary fixed interaction density and temperature, within the stated factorization and positivity class. The distinction between Poisson and fixed-degree graph ensembles is important: the historical Bethe-lattice motivation does not make the theorem an assertion about every regular factor graph.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The precise interaction class

Write

B(θ)=max⁡s∈{−1,1}p∣θ(s)∣.B(\theta)=\max_{s\in\{-1,1\}^p}|\theta(s)|.B(θ)=s∈{−1,1}pmax​∣θ(s)∣.

The integrability assumption is only

EB(θ)+E∣h∣<∞.\mathbb E B(\theta)+\mathbb E|h|<\infty.EB(θ)+E∣h∣<∞.

The interaction must admit the factorization

eθ(s1,…,sp)=a(1+b∏ℓ=1pfℓ(sℓ)),e^{\theta(s_1,\ldots,s_p)}=a\left(1+b\prod_{\ell=1}^p f_\ell(s_\ell)\right),eθ(s1​,…,sp​)=a(1+bℓ=1∏p​fℓ​(sℓ​)),

where a>0a>0a>0, the fℓf_\ellfℓ​ are independent copies of one random function, and bbb is independent of them. For every spin tuple, the product term has absolute value strictly below one. The further positivity requirement is

E[(−b)k]≥0(k=1,2,…).\mathbb E[(-b)^k]\geq0\qquad(k=1,2,\ldots).E[(−b)k]≥0(k=1,2,…).

These are substantive restrictions. The theorem is not stated for an arbitrary random interaction on a sparse graph. The multiplier aaa may depend on the other variables, and no separate moment assumption on log⁡a\log aloga is imposed.

The variational equality

For clarity, first describe the cavity terms. If ppp independent message spins enter one interaction, its average weight is

Cθ(x1,…,xp)=∑s1,…,speθ(s1,…,sp)∏ℓ=1pqxℓ(sℓ).C_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_p)=\sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_p}e^{\theta(s_1,\ldots,s_p)}\prod_{\ell=1}^p q_{x_\ell}(s_\ell).Cθ​(x1​,…,xp​)=s1​,…,sp​∑​eθ(s1​,…,sp​)ℓ=1∏p​qxℓ​​(sℓ​).

For a new spin fixed to sss, let Uθ(x1,…,xp−1;s)U_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1};s)Uθ​(x1​,…,xp−1​;s) be the logarithm of the same average over the other p−1p-1p−1 spins. A new site sees a Poisson number KKK of interactions with mean αp\alpha pαp, giving

Vsite=12∑s=±1exp⁡ ⁣(hs+∑j=1KUθj(xj1,…,xj,p−1;s)).V_{\mathrm{site}}=\frac12\sum_{s=\pm1}\exp\!\left(hs+\sum_{j=1}^K U_{\theta_j}(x_{j1},\ldots,x_{j,p-1};s)\right).Vsite​=21​s=±1∑​exp(hs+j=1∑K​Uθj​​(xj1​,…,xj,p−1​;s)).

The interaction correction uses Vedge=Cθ(x1,…,xp)V_{\mathrm{edge}}=C_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_p)Vedge​=Cθ​(x1​,…,xp​). Its role is to remove the excess counting caused by assigning interactions to their incident sites.

At depth rrr, choose hierarchy parameters 0<m1<⋯<mr<10<m_1<\cdots<m_r<10<m1​<⋯<mr​<1 and a law ζ\zetaζ for the nested message distributions. Starting from the deepest message level, average a positive quantity through successive conditional power means

W⟼(E[Wmj∣earlier message levels])1/mj.W\longmapsto\bigl(\mathbb E[W^{m_j}\mid\text{earlier message levels}]\bigr)^{1/m_j}.W⟼(E[Wmj​∣earlier message levels])1/mj​.

Call the complete operation T0\mathcal T_0T0​. Physical interaction and field disorder is held fixed during these message averages. Different message labels have independently drawn hierarchical roots.

The trial functional is

Br(ζ,m)=log⁡2+Elog⁡T0Vsite−α(p−1)Elog⁡T0Vedge.\mathcal B_r(\zeta,m)=\log2+\mathbb E\log\mathcal T_0V_{\mathrm{site}}-\alpha(p-1)\mathbb E\log\mathcal T_0V_{\mathrm{edge}}.Br​(ζ,m)=log2+ElogT0​Vsite​−α(p−1)ElogT0​Vedge​.

At depth zero, omit the power-mean operations and use independent ordinary messages. The manuscript’s main theorem is

lim⁡N→∞FN=inf⁡r≥0 inf⁡ζ,mBr(ζ,m).\lim_{N\to\infty}F_N=\inf_{r\geq0}\ \inf_{\zeta,m}\mathcal B_r(\zeta,m).N→∞lim​FN​=r≥0inf​ ζ,minf​Br​(ζ,m).

The limit exists. The infimum ranges over finite depths, but does not require that any finite depth or trial law attain the optimal value. No moment condition is needed on the trial messages themselves.

Examples and zero temperature

The class includes diluted even-spin interactions θ=βJ∏ℓsℓ\theta=\beta J\prod_\ell s_\ellθ=βJ∏ℓ​sℓ​ with symmetric coupling JJJ, and independent external field βH\beta HβH, assuming E∣J∣+E∣H∣<∞\mathbb E|J|+\mathbb E|H|<\inftyE∣J∣+E∣H∣<∞. The case p=2p=2p=2 is Viana–Bray.

It also includes soft random even-K SAT: each violated clause incurs a finite nonnegative energy penalty. Independent nonnegative clause weights with finite mean are allowed. “Soft” means that violations are penalized rather than forbidden outright.

For these named models, the manuscript obtains the limiting expected optimal energy by sending β→∞\beta\to\inftyβ→∞ after the pressure limit. The error between pressure divided by β\betaβ and the expected optimal score per spin is at most log⁡2/β\log2/\betalog2/β. For unit-weight SAT, this yields the limiting expected minimum violation density.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claim turns an established family of hierarchical bounds into an exact thermodynamic formula for a broad class of sparse disordered models. It would justify a central cavity prescription beyond the regimes where a single message distribution is already known to suffice.

The first-moment scope is useful: the result permits unbounded interaction and external-field laws as long as their mean absolute sizes are finite. The zero-temperature consequence connects equilibrium pressure with optimization on random sparse instances.

The rating also reflects the theorem’s boundaries. It identifies a variational value for a specific even-arity Poisson class, without solving the optimization explicitly or covering all sparse constraint models.

6. The main idea

The previously known interpolation inequality supplies one side: every admissible trial functional lies above the pressure. The new task is to extract trial messages from a large physical system whose value comes arbitrarily close to that pressure.

Retain more than pairwise overlaps

For replicas indexed by a finite set SSS, define the multioverlap

RS=1N∑i=1N∏a∈Sσia.R_S=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\prod_{a\in S}\sigma_i^a.RS​=N1​i=1∑N​a∈S∏​σia​.

Pair overlaps use sets of size two. A diluted interaction can depend on a whole pattern of replica spins at a site, and the probabilities of those patterns involve multioverlaps of every fixed finite order. Pairwise information alone is therefore insufficient.

The manuscript adds a sublinear number of bounded auxiliary perturbations, so their contribution per spin vanishes. These perturbations yield identities for replicas with prescribed branching patterns in a finite auxiliary hierarchy. The hierarchy is introduced as a tool; no ultrametric organization of the physical Gibbs states is assumed.

Turn a reservoir into independent messages

A large Gibbs system serves as a reservoir for comparing the partition functions before and after one spin is inserted. Concentration identities control multioverlaps averaged over branching depths. Moving branching points one level later gives an induction that controls the necessary conditional fluctuations.

The control need not be uniform over every possible tree. The cavity expansion averages over finite trees, and the exceptional branching patterns receive vanishing total weight. This matches the estimate to the quantity actually being computed.

At a uniformly sampled reservoir site, successive conditional laws encode a hierarchical message. Multioverlap concentration then permits the message roots attached to different sites to be redrawn independently without losing the cavity increment. The resulting object belongs to the prescribed Panchenko–Talagrand trial class and nearly achieves the pressure.

Remove boundedness without changing the target

The construction first handles bounded interactions. A scalar shift removes the potentially troublesome multiplier aaa from the factorization while preserving the relevant pressure difference. Truncation and estimates uniform over all trial laws then pass to first-moment interactions and fields.

The order of limits matters: system size tends to infinity at each fixed hierarchy depth, and only afterward is the depth increased. This establishes equality of variational values without constructing one infinite-depth Gibbs hierarchy or asserting attainment.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Even arity is part of the theorem. In particular, the soft-SAT application does not cover random 3-SAT. The manuscript explicitly distinguishes the separate companion formula for that model, whose trial messages have a different form.

Interactions are counted by a Poisson variable, and their site positions are sampled with replacement. The result should not be silently transferred to every fixed-degree graph ensemble or every conditioned hypergraph model.

The formula is exact but not automatically an effective numerical algorithm. It does not bound the depth needed for a prescribed accuracy, prove existence of an optimal finite trial law, or identify which parameters exhibit a particular number of symmetry-breaking levels.

The zero-temperature conclusion concerns an expected optimal energy density. A vanishing minimum violation density does not itself determine whether a random SAT instance is completely satisfiable with high probability. Exact thresholds require additional information about rare violations and finite-instance probabilities.

8. Sources and further reading

The source manuscript states the interaction assumptions, full power-mean functional, equality theorem, and named-model applications. Its main conceptual distinction is between an exact formula over general spin distributions and reduction to the specific finite hierarchical message class.

Read Mézard–Parisi for the cavity proposal, Panchenko–Talagrand for the hierarchical bounds and equality question, and Panchenko’s spin-distribution formulation for the broader variational viewpoint that precedes the new reduction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Mézard–Parisi formula for diluted spin glasses (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random-cluster interfaces: conformal shapes, natural length, and perturbations
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 223 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Draw a large random network on a fine square grid, and trace the boundary between an open cluster and the surrounding closed connections. The microscopic path makes innumerable right-angle turns. Does its large-scale law remember the grid, or does it become invariant under smooth angle-preserving changes of coordinates?

The Fortuin–Kasteleyn random-cluster model, usually abbreviated FK, asks this question in one family containing independent percolation, Ising connectivity, and Potts connectivity. The predicted continuum objects are Schramm–Loewner evolution, or SLE, for one distinguished interface, and conformal loop ensembles, or CLE, for collections of loops.

Family 223 claims those limits across broad ranges of the cluster parameter. It also asks two more demanding questions. Does counting lattice steps converge to the continuum curve’s natural measure? And what survives when Ising couplings acquire weak fixed randomness or the temperature moves away from criticality on the scale of the mesh?

The six manuscripts address these questions with different hypotheses. A curve’s shape, its nesting among other loops, and its occupation measure are separate conclusions.

2. Background and essential definitions

A probability law for connected clusters

On a finite graph with edge set EEE, a configuration is a subset A⊆EA\subseteq EA⊆E of open edges. Its FK probability is proportional to

p∣A∣(1−p)∣E∣−∣A∣qkξ(A).p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E|-|A|}q^{k_\xi(A)}.p∣A∣(1−p)∣E∣−∣A∣qkξ​(A).

Here q>0q>0q>0 rewards or penalizes the number of connected components, and ξ\xiξ specifies which boundary vertices are identified when counting them. Isolated vertices count as components. At q=1q=1q=1, the cluster factor disappears and edges are independent. At q=2q=2q=2, the model represents Ising spin connectivity.

A wired boundary arc is counted as a single connected block; a free arc has no such identifications. These bookkeeping connections must be distinguished from an actual open path using graph edges. Dobrushin boundary conditions put one wired and one free arc between two marked boundary points. A medial-lattice interface separates the primal open cluster from the dual cluster made by crossing closed primal edges.

The self-dual square-lattice parameter and predicted SLE parameter are

pq=q1+q,κ(q)=4πarccos⁡(−q/2).p_q=\frac{\sqrt q}{1+\sqrt q},\qquad\kappa(q)=\frac{4\pi}{\arccos(-\sqrt q/2)}.pq​=1+q​q​​,κ(q)=arccos(−q​/2)4π​.

For q≥1q\geq1q≥1 up to four, the first quantity is the known critical edge probability. Below one, the corresponding manuscript states its theorem directly at the self-dual parameter without assuming an infinite-volume critical-point identification.

Curves and their continuum laws

Chordal SLE describes a random curve between two boundary points of a simply connected domain. In the upper half-plane, the conformal maps removing the growing curve satisfy

∂tgt(z)=2gt(z)−Wt,Wt=κBt,\partial_t g_t(z)=\frac{2}{g_t(z)-W_t},\qquad W_t=\sqrt\kappa B_t,∂t​gt​(z)=gt​(z)−Wt​2​,Wt​=κ​Bt​,

where BtB_tBt​ is standard Brownian motion. Conformal maps transport this law to other domains. The parameter κ\kappaκ controls the curve’s roughness; for κ≤8\kappa\leq8κ≤8, its dimension is d=1+κ/8d=1+\kappa/8d=1+κ/8.

CLE describes a compatible random collection of loops, including loops nested inside others. Retaining traversal order matters: two curves can trace the same set while visiting its pieces in different orders. Likewise, a collection can contain two distinct loops with the same limiting image. The source statements retain this information.

For a fractal curve, ordinary arc length is generally infinite. Its ddd-dimensional Minkowski content instead rescales the area within distance rrr of the trace by rd−2r^{d-2}rd−2, then sends rrr to zero. This produces the natural occupation measure relevant to counting lattice steps.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Fortuin and Kasteleyn’s representation united several statistical-mechanical models through random connectivity. Exact solutions and Coulomb-gas calculations then predicted exponents and relations between cluster weights and continuum parameters. Schramm’s introduction of SLE turned a conformal-invariance prediction into a precise candidate law for interfaces.

Smirnov proved conformal invariance and Cardy’s crossing formula for critical triangular-lattice site percolation. FK–Ising on the square lattice became another major example through fermionic observables and the interface theorem of Chelkak, Duminil-Copin, Hongler, Kemppainen, and Smirnov. These achievements did not settle general square-lattice FK weights.

A substantial intermediate advance was rotational invariance for critical planar FK models by Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Krachun, Manolescu, and Oulamara. Rotation invariance is weaker than identifying the complete SLE or CLE law. M1 also acknowledges overlapping square-bond percolation claims by Tsai–Yam–Zhou and Zhou, with the latter’s stated boundary regularity and separation conditions. The present family should be read in that context.

For occupation measures, the dimension prediction was only a first step. Lawler and collaborators developed SLE natural parametrization and its identification with Minkowski content. Garban–Pete–Schramm and Holden–Li–Sun connected triangular-site percolation interface measures to that content; Lawler–Viklund did so for loop-erased random walk. These were important precedents, with different lattice models and normalizations.

Away from criticality, Makarov and Smirnov formulated the massive-SLE program. Park’s massive FK–Ising observable theorem supplied near-critical observables and crossing estimates. M4 claims the further steps needed to identify a unique interface law. Weak random bonds raise another difficulty: the Ising disorder is marginal, so microscopic randomness can decay only slowly under changes of scale.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Critical curves and all nested loops

M1 claims that, for every fixed 1≤q<41\leq q<41≤q<4, square-lattice Dobrushin interfaces converge to chordal SLEκ(q)\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa(q)}SLEκ(q)​. M6 includes the endpoint q=4q=4q=4. The domain may be any bounded Jordan domain, meaning its boundary is a simple closed curve, with lattice boundaries and marked points converging through uniform boundary parametrizations.

The convergence is of the entire oriented curve, modulo increasing changes of traversal speed. For the free infinite-volume lattice law, the complete nested loop collection converges to whole-plane CLEκ(q)\mathrm{CLE}_{\kappa(q)}CLEκ(q)​, retaining multiplicities and traversals. A spherical metric controls the plane together with its point at infinity. These statements hold along every mesh sequence for each fixed parameter.

Thus q=1q=1q=1 gives SLE6\mathrm{SLE}_6SLE6​, q=2q=2q=2 gives SLE16/3\mathrm{SLE}_{16/3}SLE16/3​, and q=4q=4q=4 gives SLE4\mathrm{SLE}_4SLE4​. The endpoint uses a separate field argument; it is not obtained by silently sending q↑4q\uparrow4q↑4 in estimates valid strictly below four.

M2 claims the Dobrushin curve limit for every fixed 0<q<10<q<10<q<1, where 6<κ(q)<86<\kappa(q)<86<κ(q)<8, in bounded smooth Jordan domains with its specified polygon approximations. It does not state the same general-Jordan or complete-loop theorem as M6.

Square-bond crossings and exponents

At q=1q=1q=1, M1 and M6 claim Cardy’s formula for actual open crossings with all boundary edges free and independently sampled. Map four successive boundary marks a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d to 0,x,1,∞0,x,1,\infty0,x,1,∞ in the upper half-plane. The limiting probability of connecting arc [a,b][a,b][a,b] to arc [c,d][c,d][c,d] is

∫0x[t(1−t)]−2/3 dt∫01[t(1−t)]−2/3 dt.\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^x[t(1-t)]^{-2/3}\,dt}{\displaystyle\int_0^1[t(1-t)]^{-2/3}\,dt}.∫01​[t(1−t)]−2/3dt∫0x​[t(1−t)]−2/3dt​.

M1 additionally states square-bond exponent consequences. At criticality, the probability of an open connection from the origin to distance RRR is R−5/48+o(1)R^{-5/48+o(1)}R−5/48+o(1). For 2k2k2k disjoint, cyclically alternating primal-open and dual-open arms across an annulus with fixed sufficiently large inner radius, the exponent is (4k2−1)/12(4k^2-1)/12(4k2−1)/12.

Its near-critical consequences include an infinite-cluster density exponent 5/365/365/36, a finite-cluster susceptibility exponent 43/1843/1843/18, and a second-moment correlation-length exponent 4/34/34/3. Susceptibility here counts only finite clusters. These stated exponent corollaries concern q=1q=1q=1, not every FK parameter or every choice of arm colors.

Natural occupation measure

M5 works in the unit square, with opposite marked corners and its precise wired/free drawing convention, for fixed 1≤q<41\leq q<41≤q<4. Let NnN_nNn​ be the number of full medial-edge traversals at mesh 1/n1/n1/n, and zn,jz_{n,j}zn,j​ their midpoints, projected into the closed square when necessary. It claims a constant c(q)>0c(q)>0c(q)>0 such that

(ηn,  c(q)n−d∑j=1Nnδzn,j)⟹(η,μη),d=1+κ(q)8.\left(\eta_n,\;c(q)n^{-d}\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}\delta_{z_{n,j}}\right)\Longrightarrow (\eta,\mu_\eta),\qquad d=1+\frac{\kappa(q)}8.(ηn​,c(q)n−dj=1∑Nn​​δzn,j​​)⟹(η,μη​),d=1+8κ(q)​.

Here δz\delta_zδz​ is unit point mass, η\etaη is SLE, and μη\mu_\etaμη​ is the Minkowski-content measure of that same sample. In particular, c(q)n−dNnc(q)n^{-d}N_nc(q)n−dNn​ converges to its total mass. Boundary traversals count; the two terminal half-edges do not. The constant depends on these units. A single constant times a power is stronger than knowing only the exponent, because it excludes an undetermined slowly varying correction.

Disorder and thermal perturbations at q=2q=2q=2

M3 takes independent fair signs ξe\xi_eξe​ and ferromagnetic couplings Je=1+εξeJ_e=1+\varepsilon\xi_eJe​=1+εξe​. For sufficiently small fixed positive ε\varepsilonε, it claims the critical FK interface still converges to SLE16/3\mathrm{SLE}_{16/3}SLE16/3​. Criticality is the physical plus-state magnetization threshold; the FK edge probabilities are 1−e−2βcJe1-e^{-2\beta_cJ_e}1−e−2βc​Je​.

The environment is fixed before sampling the interface. Its conditional curve law converges in probability over environments to the deterministic SLE law, in every deterministically approximated bounded Jordan domain of the stated class. This is stronger than averaging the curve over disorder, but does not claim almost-sure convergence along the full sequence. The companion weak-disorder critical-point and scale-transformation results discussed in family 218 are substantive inputs.

M4 instead changes the thermal parameter on the mesh scale, retaining a fixed nonzero continuum mass mmm. It treats angle-bounded isoradial lattices: faces lie on circles of the common mesh radius, and the associated rhombi stay uniformly nondegenerate. Its elliptic weights use a nome rδr_\deltarδ​ satisfying rδ/δ→∣m∣/2r_\delta/\delta\to|m|/2rδ​/δ→∣m∣/2, with the negative branch defined by duality.

For every bounded simply connected marked limit domain, M4 claims a lattice-independent massive SLE16/3\mathrm{SLE}_{16/3}SLE16/3​ limit. Domain convergence is measured conformally from an interior point; approximating domains may have unbounded diameters. Curves are compared after mapping them to the unit disk.

For positive mass, the driving Brownian motion keeps variance rate 16/316/316/3 and acquires a drift determined by a boundary problem in the evolving physical domain:

Δh=−4m∣∇h∣,\Delta h=-4m|\nabla h|,Δh=−4m∣∇h∣,

with value one on the primal-wired bank and zero on the dual-wired bank. The manuscript claims uniqueness in a class where the drift has locally finite squared time integral. Negative mass follows by duality and reversal. The mass records a physical length scale, so this law is a deformation of critical SLE rather than ordinary conformal invariance at fixed mass.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Identifying square-lattice FK interfaces throughout the claimed ranges would settle central conformal-limit predictions beyond the previously established special models. The complete nested ensemble would determine how interfaces fit together, not merely what one boundary looks like.

Natural occupation adds a quantitative geometric observable: the limiting amount of interface inside each region. The disorder and thermal results ask how robust the critical picture is and what replaces it when a macroscopic correlation scale remains.

Together these claims connect microscopic probabilities, continuum random curves, and measurable geometric quantities. Their breadth supports the highest relative rating, while the separate parameter ranges remain essential to interpreting that breadth.

6. The main idea

A central device is a boundary observable with four changes of boundary condition. Its limiting value depends on the conformal positions of four marked points. After part of an interface is revealed, conditional crossing probabilities become martingales. Two suitable tests identify the variance and drift of the limiting Loewner driver.

The difficult passage is from a formula on a fixed shape to one valid in a random slit domain. The sources develop physical crossing estimates, local comparisons, and control of narrow passages, preserving the difference between actual open paths and artificial boundary identifications. Analytic winding observables then supply the conformal information.

Below q=1q=1q=1, the usual positive-association inequality is unavailable. M2 builds restricted connection and gluing comparisons instead. At q=4q=4q=4, M6 uses a whole-plane height-field input, including the six-vertex field result discussed in family 225, and develops the additional finite-domain and conditional field arguments needed to identify interfaces.

For occupation, M5 must calibrate individual-edge visits against continuum neighborhood area. Quantitative comparisons between successive scales produce an actual amplitude, while boundary estimates prevent mass from disappearing near the square’s edges. For disorder, fixed-domain comparisons are transferred to adaptive explorations without assuming a uniform rate over every possible slit. For the massive law, energy estimates identify the drift and then support uniqueness.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The family does not supply one theorem covering all combinations of lattice, cluster weight, disorder, and temperature. The broad critical curve theorem is square-lattice; the occupation theorem is restricted to a square and q<4q<4q<4; the below-one theorem assumes a smooth limiting boundary. Neither endpoint-uniform estimates nor a q=4q=4q=4 occupation theorem follow from these statements.

The random-bond result concerns weak symmetric two-valued disorder at q=2q=2q=2, with deterministic domain approximations. The thermal result concerns its prescribed isoradial near-critical weights and nonzero mass. It does not address arbitrary off-critical perturbations of every FK model.

Natural questions include extending occupation convergence to broader domains and parameters, treating other disorder laws, and obtaining useful rates of convergence. The manuscripts’ claims are reported as stated; the distinctions between curve, loop, and measure convergence are part of their mathematical scope.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary historical links above describe the Ising interface theorem, rotational invariance, earlier square-bond claims, and the massive observable input. For the continuum occupation concept, see Lawler and Rezaei, Minkowski content and natural parametrization for SLE.

M1 and M6 cover critical interfaces and nested loops, with M6 including four. M2 treats parameters below one. M3 treats fixed weak disorder, M4 thermal mass, and M5 natural occupation. These labels correspond to the six source manuscripts below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Square-lattice FK interfaces and nested loops for 1 ≤ q < 4 (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Self-dual random-cluster interfaces below one (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quenched SLE Universality for Weakly Disordered FK–Ising Interfaces (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Thermal FK–Ising interfaces and massive SLE (October 5, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Natural Occupation Measures for Critical Square-Lattice FK Interfaces (October 5, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Conformal Limits of Critical Square-Lattice Random-Cluster Interfaces (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Voronoi percolation: Cardy crossings and the near-critical window
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 224 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Scatter points randomly across the plane. Give each point the region closer to it than to any other point, and color these regions independently black or white. Can a connected black path cross a prescribed rectangle or a more complicated shape?

This is Poisson–Voronoi percolation. Unlike a square or triangular lattice, its geometry is itself random, with cells of many shapes and sizes. Yet its large-scale critical behavior is expected to agree with that of familiar planar lattice models.

Family 224 asks three increasingly detailed questions. At the critical coloring probability, is a crossing probability given by Cardy’s conformal formula? If black becomes slightly more likely, do the thresholds at which many crossings appear have the same joint limit as on the triangular lattice? Finally, can the precise width of that transition window be written as a constant times a power of the microscopic scale?

The three manuscripts form a dependency chain. M3 claims the critical crossing formula. M1 takes that formula as an explicit input and claims a joint near-critical universality theorem. M2 uses the same input, together with results from M1, to determine the pivotal normalization more sharply.

2. Background and essential definitions

A random tessellation with two kinds of randomness

Let ηε\eta_\varepsilonηε​ be a homogeneous Poisson point process of intensity ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}ε−2. This means that a region of area AAA contains on average Aε−2A\varepsilon^{-2}Aε−2 points, and counts in disjoint regions are independent. Typical neighboring points are a distance of order ε\varepsilonε apart.

The closed Voronoi cell of a point vvv is

Vv={z∈R2:∣z−v∣≤∣z−w∣ for every w∈ηε}.V_v=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z-v|\leq|z-w|\text{ for every }w\in\eta_\varepsilon\}.Vv​={z∈R2:∣z−v∣≤∣z−w∣ for every w∈ηε​}.

Color each cell black with probability ppp, independently of the geometry and other colors. The critical value is p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2.

An annealed probability averages over both points and colors. A quenched probability first fixes the point configuration and averages only the colors. Consequently, a quenched crossing probability is a random number depending on the tessellation. Showing that this number becomes nearly deterministic is an additional statement beyond computing its average.

A quadrilateral, or quad, is a bounded Jordan domain with four distinct boundary marks a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d in cyclic order. Its sides can be curved. A crossing between arcs [a,b][a,b][a,b] and [c,d][c,d][c,d] means a connected subset of the black cells, clipped to the closed domain, meeting both arcs. The cells come from the full-plane tessellation. Cells centered outside the domain can participate, and boundary points are not artificially wired together.

Coupling all coloring probabilities

Attach to every point an independent uniform mark Uv∈[0,1]U_v\in[0,1]Uv​∈[0,1], and declare its cell black when Uv≤pU_v\leq pUv​≤p. Increasing ppp then only adds black cells. This monotone coupling lets us ask when each crossing first appears, while preserving dependencies between different crossing events.

A cell is color pivotal for a crossing if flipping its color alone changes the answer. Let NεN_\varepsilonNε​ count these cells for a left-to-right crossing of the unit square at p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2, including cells whose centers lie outside the square. Define the deterministic scale

rε=1ENε.r_\varepsilon=\frac1{\mathbb E N_\varepsilon}.rε​=ENε​1​.

The expectation includes geometry and colors. It is not a normalization chosen separately for each tessellation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cardy’s conformal-field-theory calculation predicted a crossing probability determined only by the conformal shape of a marked domain. Smirnov established this formula for critical site percolation on the triangular lattice. Subsequent SLE and loop-limit theory supplied a detailed continuum description there. Smirnov’s original crossing paper is the foundational rigorous example.

Voronoi percolation has exact rotational symmetry in distribution, but that alone does not determine its crossing probabilities. Bollobás and Riordan established its critical probability of one half. Tassion proved scale-uniform box-crossing estimates. These estimates keep crossing probabilities away from zero and one for fixed rectangle shapes; they do not identify their exact limits.

Ahlberg, Griffiths, Morris, and Tassion showed concentration of quenched crossing probabilities and developed quenched noise sensitivity. Vanneuville’s annealed scaling relations and quantitative quenched arm estimates supplied further control of rare connections and shared random geometry. The new crossing claim builds on this probabilistic foundation.

The near-critical mechanism was clarified by Kesten’s scaling relations: a macroscopic crossing changes when one of its rare pivotal sites changes color. Garban, Pete, and Schramm constructed triangular-lattice near-critical and dynamical scaling limits using continuum pivotal measures. M1 uses that model as its reference, with an explicit normalization through the mean pivotal count.

There is also a distinction between exponents and amplitudes. An exponent predicts a power only up to smaller logarithmic-scale errors. A limiting amplitude gives a fixed positive multiplicative constant. Sharp triangular-lattice arm asymptotics were already known in work of Du, Gao, Li, and Zhuang; M2 concerns a specific Voronoi pivotal observable under its stated crossing input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Cardy’s formula for the random-cell model

M3 claims that every fixed bounded Jordan quad has the annealed critical crossing limit

lim⁡ε↓0P(Cε)=F(x)=∫0x[u(1−u)]−2/3 du∫01[u(1−u)]−2/3 du.\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(C_\varepsilon)=F(x)=\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^x[u(1-u)]^{-2/3}\,du}{\displaystyle\int_0^1[u(1-u)]^{-2/3}\,du}.ε↓0lim​P(Cε​)=F(x)=∫01​[u(1−u)]−2/3du∫0x​[u(1−u)]−2/3du​.

Here a conformal map to the upper half-plane sends a,c,da,c,da,c,d to 0,1,∞0,1,\infty0,1,∞, and sends bbb to x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1)x∈(0,1). Thus changing the domain while preserving this conformal parameter preserves the limiting probability. For the symmetric square crossing, the value is one half.

The domain need not have a smooth boundary; the Jordan property is the stated assumption. The theorem concerns the exact closed-cell crossing event, averaged over both sources of randomness. M3 explicitly does not claim the full interface law or a quenched crossing theorem for every Jordan domain as its main result.

For a fixed rectangle, however, combining the claimed limit with established quenched concentration gives

Egeom ⁣[∣P(Cε∣ηε)−F(x)∣2]⟶0.\mathbb E_{\rm geom}\!\left[\left|\mathbb P(C_\varepsilon\mid\eta_\varepsilon)-F(x)\right|^2\right]\longrightarrow0.Egeom​[∣P(Cε​∣ηε​)−F(x)∣2]⟶0.

This is a mean-square statement over tessellations, and implies convergence in probability. No coupling of tessellations at different meshes is required.

A common joint law of near-critical thresholds

For a real parameter λ\lambdaλ, set

pε(λ)=max⁡{0,min⁡{1,12+λrε}}.p_\varepsilon(\lambda)=\max\{0,\min\{1,\tfrac12+\lambda r_\varepsilon\}\}.pε​(λ)=max{0,min{1,21​+λrε​}}.

For a quad QQQ, let τε(Q)\tau_\varepsilon(Q)τε​(Q) be the first λ\lambdaλ at which its crossing occurs in the monotone coupling. This is random because the cell marks are random, even after fixing the geometry.

M1 fixes a countable list of all simple rational polygonal quads with rational boundary marks. It records the entire vector of their thresholds. It defines the same object for triangular-lattice site percolation, normalizing that model by its own expected unit-square pivotal count.

Assuming the scalar Cardy statement of M3, M1 claims that the triangular threshold vectors have a limiting law ν△\nu_\triangleν△​, and that

Law⁡ ⁣((τε(Q))Q∣ηε)⟶ν△\operatorname{Law}\!\left((\tau_\varepsilon(Q))_Q\mid\eta_\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow\nu_\triangleLaw((τε​(Q))Q​∣ηε​)⟶ν△​

in probability over tessellations, in a metric for weak convergence of laws. The threshold coordinates are compactified by allowing ±∞\pm\infty±∞, and the topology records every finite set of coordinates.

In concrete terms, choose finitely many polygonal regions and finitely many near-critical parameters. The joint distribution of all their crossing answers converges to the triangular reference under the same monotone coupling. This includes their dependencies. Equality of one crossing probability at λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 would not supply that information.

A sharp amplitude for pivotal cells

Under the same scalar Cardy assumption, M2 claims a constant cV∈(0,∞)c_V\in(0,\infty)cV​∈(0,∞) such that

ENε∼cVε−3/4,rε∼cV−1ε3/4.\mathbb E N_\varepsilon\sim c_V\varepsilon^{-3/4},\qquadr_\varepsilon\sim c_V^{-1}\varepsilon^{3/4}.ENε​∼cV​ε−3/4,rε​∼cV−1​ε3/4.

The symbol ∼\sim∼ means that the ratio tends to one. The constant refers to the specified unit square, intensity convention, closed-cell event, and count of color-pivotal cells. Its positivity and existence are claimed; a numerical value is not supplied by this statement.

Why does 3/43/43/4 appear? A bulk pivotal cell needs four alternating black and white connections from its neighborhood to macroscopic distance. The predicted four-arm probability has exponent 5/45/45/4, while there are order ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}ε−2 candidate cells. Multiplying suggests ε−2ε5/4=ε−3/4\varepsilon^{-2}\varepsilon^{5/4}=\varepsilon^{-3/4}ε−2ε5/4=ε−3/4. This explains the exponent but not the limiting constant. M2’s additional content is that no unresolved slowly varying or oscillatory multiplier remains.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family targets a central universality question for a planar model with genuinely random geometry. The claimed crossing theorem would identify its conformal law, while the companion results would transfer substantially richer near-critical information from the triangular lattice.

The quenched conclusion is especially informative: a typical fine tessellation would have the same limiting threshold law after averaging only colors. The randomness of the cells would cease to create a separate macroscopic law.

The amplitude makes the scale explicit. Doubling spatial resolution would shrink the density window by the corresponding 3/43/43/4 power, with a fixed model-dependent conversion factor. That factor need not match the triangular model’s factor; universality appears after each model is normalized in its own units.

The importance rating applies to this combination of claims as stated. The conditional structure of the companion theorems remains part of the result, rather than being hidden by the shared family label.

6. The main idea

M3 must recover an analytic observable from irregular geometry. On the dual triangulation, local triangles can be compared with equilateral ones by affine maps. Their displacement fields split into a conformal part and a geometric defect. Exact identities around closed cluster boundaries control these quantities, but an interface calculation requires control along open pieces.

The manuscript describes a transport construction that closes those pieces using prescribed local configurations and connecting corridors. Comparing different closures isolates endpoint contributions and a common bulk term. The resulting cancellation identifies a holomorphic limit, whose boundary values determine a conformal map to an equilateral triangle and hence Cardy’s function. This addresses the irregular embedding rather than treating rotational symmetry as a substitute for conformal invariance.

M1 then extracts joint critical information by exploring colors on a fixed geometry and applying crossing tests in the unexplored regions. To change density, it expands the effect of changing finitely many color histories. Alternating-arm estimates control the contributions of multiple nearby pivotal locations.

A local comparison replaces a microscopic color insertion by a small-square modification. It retains the signs of the resulting differences, which ordinary absolute-probability estimates could lose. Two independent color replicas on the same tessellation finally control variation over geometry and yield the quenched conclusion.

M2 sharpens the scale by studying transmission of connection information across long annuli. When four interfaces survive, the relevant difference has one dominant component. For a symmetric signed insertion, that component cancels, giving faster decay for distant geometric changes. Integrating these effects controls the derivative with respect to Poisson intensity and produces a summable error around the predicted exponent. A qualitative Cardy limit is enough to start the multiscale contraction; no rate in that input is assumed.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The critical theorem averages geometry and colors in arbitrary fixed Jordan quads. The near-critical theorem is a stronger conditional-law statement, but is formulated for the specified countable rational polygonal family and monotone coloring coupling. It is not automatically a theorem in every possible topology on time-dependent interfaces.

The tessellation stays fixed as ppp varies. This differs from moving the Poisson points or refreshing colors dynamically. Earlier dynamical-percolation work motivates the methods, but these main conclusions concern monotone thresholds.

The pivotal amplitude is annealed and model-specific. It does not assert that every sampled tessellation has exactly that pivotal count, nor that an arbitrary random planar tessellation shares the same constant. All statements concern the planar homogeneous Poisson model with independent coloring.

Questions beyond the displayed claims include quantitative rates, other random geometries, and stronger path-space descriptions of near-critical interfaces. Extending such conclusions requires additional arguments; scalar crossing convergence alone is not interchangeable with a full coupled continuum model.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary papers linked in the history section explain criticality, box crossings, quenched concentration, and the triangular near-critical reference. The Voronoi diagram offers optional geometric background; all definitions needed for the main claims are given above.

Read M3 first for the claimed scalar Cardy theorem, M1 for its transfer to joint near-critical thresholds, and M2 for the sharper pivotal amplitude. Their source numbering below follows the repository rather than this dependency order.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, From critical crossings to quenched near-critical universality in Voronoi percolation (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Pivotal Amplitude for Voronoi Percolation from Cardy’s Formula (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Cardy’s formula for critical Poisson–Voronoi percolation (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Six-vertex heights and the Gaussian free field across the balanced critical range
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 225 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Place an arrow on every edge of the square lattice, requiring exactly two arrows to enter and two to leave each vertex. There are six allowed local arrangements, which gives the six-vertex model its name. Although the rule is local, it couples arrows over long distances.

These arrows can also be read as the slopes of an integer-valued random surface. What does that surface look like when the lattice spacing becomes very small? The expected answer in the critical regime is the Gaussian free field, the two-dimensional analogue of a Gaussian random process whose correlations are governed by a Green function.

Family 225 contains one manuscript claiming this limit for the balanced plane model with weights a=b=1a=b=1a=b=1 and every fixed 0<c≤20<c\leq20<c≤2. It also gives the exact fluctuation coefficient. The choice of infinite-volume state, the units of height, and the meaning of field convergence are essential parts of the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

From arrows to heights

Assign weight ccc to the two vertex types whose horizontal arrows both point inward or both point outward, and weight one to the other four types. The probability of a finite configuration is proportional to the product of its vertex weights. Changing ccc changes the interaction while preserving the two-in, two-out rule.

Give the face to the left of an arrow height one more than the face to its right. The ice rule ensures that following different routes between two faces gives the same height difference. Absolute height remains arbitrary: adding a constant changes no arrows.

The manuscript selects its plane state through rectangular tori of horizontal size MMM and even vertical size LLL. In every vertical column of horizontal edges, it conditions on exactly L/2L/2L/2 left-pointing and L/2L/2L/2 right-pointing arrows. It first sends M→∞M\to\inftyM→∞, then even L→∞L\to\inftyL→∞, in the sense of probabilities of every fixed finite arrow pattern. This defines the balanced plane law Pc\mathbb P_cPc​.

This is a prescribed thermodynamic construction. It should not be replaced by an arbitrary boundary condition or a simultaneous torus limit without an additional result.

At physical mesh δ\deltaδ, the rescaled surface is

hδ(x)=h(x/δ),h_\delta(x)=h(x/\delta),hδ​(x)=h(x/δ),

with the discrete height extended constantly over each face. There is no extra power of δ\deltaδ multiplying the height. What converges is the surface as a generalized function, tested over regions, rather than its value at each point.

What a Gaussian free field means

The plane Gaussian free field Γ\GammaΓ, modulo additive constants, is specified by the kernel

G(x,y)=−12πlog⁡∣x−y∣.G(x,y)=-\frac1{2\pi}\log|x-y|.G(x,y)=−2π1​log∣x−y∣.

For smooth compactly supported functions f,gf,gf,g with integral zero, its averaged values are centered jointly Gaussian and satisfy

Cov⁡(⟨Γ,f⟩,⟨Γ,g⟩)=∬G(x,y)f(x)g(y) dx dy.\operatorname{Cov}(\langle\Gamma,f\rangle,\langle\Gamma,g\rangle)=\iint G(x,y)f(x)g(y)\,dx\,dy.Cov(⟨Γ,f⟩,⟨Γ,g⟩)=∬G(x,y)f(x)g(y)dxdy.

The zero-integral condition removes the arbitrary additive constant. One example is the difference between two smooth regional averages. The logarithmic singularity means that a point value is not an ordinary finite-variance Gaussian random variable.

The theorem also allows compactly supported signed measures μ\muμ of total mass zero when

∬log⁡+ ⁣1∣x−y∣ ∣μ∣(dx)∣μ∣(dy)<∞,\iint \log^+\!\frac1{|x-y|}\,|\mu|(dx)|\mu|(dy)<\infty,∬log+∣x−y∣1​∣μ∣(dx)∣μ∣(dy)<∞,

where log⁡+t=max⁡{log⁡t,0}\log^+t=\max\{\log t,0\}log+t=max{logt,0} and ∣μ∣|\mu|∣μ∣ is total variation. This finite-energy requirement controls the singularity without canceling infinite positive and negative contributions. Smooth zero-mass densities qualify; a difference of two point masses does not.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lieb’s solution of square ice determined the exact entropy at c=1c=1c=1, and the wider exact-solution program made the six-vertex model a central example of an interacting system with accessible algebraic structure. The Coulomb-gas approach predicted Gaussian height fluctuations and their parameter-dependent coupling. The manuscript credits the work of Di Francesco, Saleur, and Zuber for the corresponding normalization after converting height units.

At the free-fermion value c=2c=\sqrt2c=2​, a relation to dimers supplies determinant formulas. Kenyon’s Gaussian-free-field theorem for domino tilings established a foundational example of this kind of scaling limit. Near that special point, interacting-fermion and dimer methods gave correlation asymptotics, logarithmic variance, and, for appropriate models, Gaussian field limits.

A broader probabilistic advance was logarithmic delocalization of six-vertex heights by Duminil-Copin, Karrila, Manolescu, and Oulamara. Logarithmic variance identifies the size of fluctuations, but a non-Gaussian field can have the same covariance growth. A full GFF theorem must identify all joint fluctuations as well.

The particularly relevant predecessor is the March 2026 GFF convergence theorem of Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers, and Manolescu, treating 3≤c≤2\sqrt3\leq c\leq23​≤c≤2 in the isotropic model. It includes the same exact multiplier in the stated height convention. The new manuscript explicitly builds on this work: it uses its conditional amplitude theorem for 1≤c<21\leq c<21≤c<2, and its endpoint argument after supplying the required rotation input at two.

There is also related finite-domain progress. The October 2026 paper of Avérous, Duminil-Copin, He, Lammers, and Manolescu states Dirichlet GFF convergence with piecewise constant boundary data in parameter ranges including those near Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0 and −1≤Δ≤−1/2-1\leq\Delta\leq-1/2−1≤Δ≤−1/2. That addresses boundary-value problems distinct from this family’s full-range balanced plane statement. It prevents interpreting the plane theorem as the whole current story of six-vertex conformal limits.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A full-range plane field with a fixed coefficient

For every fixed c∈(0,2]c\in(0,2]c∈(0,2], the manuscript claims that the iterated balanced-torus plane state exists and that

hδ⟹σ(c)Γ,σ(c)2=1arcsin⁡(c/2).h_\delta\Longrightarrow\sigma(c)\Gamma,\qquad\sigma(c)^2=\frac1{\arcsin(c/2)}.hδ​⟹σ(c)Γ,σ(c)2=arcsin(c/2)1​.

Equivalently, with the usual parameter Δ=1−c2/2\Delta=1-c^2/2Δ=1−c2/2,

σ(c)2=2arccos⁡Δ.\sigma(c)^2=\frac2{\arccos\Delta}.σ(c)2=arccosΔ2​.

The displayed number is the variance multiplier, not the multiplier of the field itself. The latter is its positive square root. With the source’s unit height jumps and Green kernel, some examples are

ParameterModel pointVariance multiplier
c=1c=1c=1Square ice6/π6/\pi6/π
c=2c=\sqrt2c=2​Free-fermion point4/π4/\pi4/π
c=2c=2c=2Endpoint2/π2/\pi2/π

For any finite collection of zero-mass finite-energy measures, their integrals against hδh_\deltahδ​ converge jointly to a centered Gaussian vector. Its covariance is σ(c)2\sigma(c)^2σ(c)2 times the corresponding Green-kernel energy. This is a statement about the whole joint law, not only its second moments.

Convergence as a rough field

The manuscript also claims tightness and convergence in negative-regularity distribution spaces on every bounded open set. For example, it gives convergence in restriction Hölder–Besov spaces of regularity α\alphaα for −1<α<0-1<\alpha<0−1<α<0, together with the stated Besov and Sobolev variants.

Negative regularity is a way to measure generalized functions too rough to evaluate pointwise. Convergence in such a space controls a large family of smoothed observations simultaneously. No regularity of the open set’s boundary is required, because the restriction spaces inherit norms from the whole plane.

Constants can be removed by choosing a smooth compactly supported density ρ\rhoρ of integral one and replacing a field XXX by X−⟨X,ρ⟩X-\langle X,\rho\rangleX−⟨X,ρ⟩. The same convention must be used for the discrete field and the limit. This pins an average; it does not assert a finite pointwise value of the GFF.

Separated height increments

A further claim concerns products of increments

∏i=1k(hδ(ui′)−hδ(ui)),\prod_{i=1}^k\bigl(h_\delta(u_i')-h_\delta(u_i)\bigr),i=1∏k​(hδ​(ui′​)−hδ​(ui​)),

when the endpoint sets of different increments are disjoint. Their expectations converge to the Gaussian pairing rule. For two increments the limiting covariance is σ(c)2C12\sigma(c)^2 C_{12}σ(c)2C12​, where

Cij=G(ui′,uj′)−G(ui′,uj)−G(ui,uj′)+G(ui,uj).C_{ij}=G(u_i',u_j')-G(u_i',u_j)-G(u_i,u_j')+G(u_i,u_j).Cij​=G(ui′​,uj′​)−G(ui′​,uj​)−G(ui​,uj′​)+G(ui​,uj​).

For an even number of increments, sum the products of these covariances over all pairings; for an odd number, the limit is zero. Convergence is uniform on compact families of separated endpoint configurations.

This does not say that the variance of one fixed-endpoint increment stays finite as the mesh vanishes. Repeating the same increment would violate the separation condition. The source’s logarithmic variogram describes the growing variance, while the displayed mixed moments isolate finite correlations between distinct increments.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The six-vertex model is a central interacting height model, and the claim covers the entire stated balanced critical interval rather than only an exactly determinantal point, a perturbative neighborhood, or a previously treated subinterval.

The exact multiplier matters as much as the Gaussian shape. Different microscopic interactions can lead to the same type of continuum field while retaining different fluctuation strengths. The formula specifies precisely how the parameter survives in the limit.

The field theorem also provides information used by related loop and interface problems, including the endpoint discussion in family 223. A height limit does not automatically identify all level curves, but it supplies a major ingredient for those further arguments.

The rating reflects the breadth and centrality of the claimed full-range plane result, while crediting the substantial pre-existing GFF and amplitude theory on which parts of it rely.

6. The main idea

The model has exact finite-dimensional row transfer matrices: operators that add one row of vertices and encode its weights. Bethe-ansatz identities express selected scalar products and marked-row quantities through determinants. A mark records a local height increment.

Exact finite formulas alone do not give a continuum theorem. The manuscript develops estimates allowing row length to grow, including control of root tails and simultaneous large parameters in determinant expressions. These estimates produce a plane representation in which angular transfer operators have a tractable spectrum.

The long-distance height fluctuations are then organized into two current components, corresponding to holomorphic and antiholomorphic behavior. Contributions outside the leading modes are damped. The surviving current correlations obey a Wick recursion: higher moments reduce to sums of pairwise contractions, which is the characteristic structure of a Gaussian field.

Identifying Gaussianity still leaves an unknown multiplicative coefficient. For c≥1c\geq1c≥1, the manuscript uses the earlier conditional normalization theorem after establishing its required convergence. For c<1c<1c<1, it compares two independently derived bounds: a stiffness calculation controlling the response to a small slope, and a bound from a staggered vacuum overlap. Their stated agreement fixes the coefficient in physical height units.

Moment bounds and removal of smoothing extend the current calculation to ordinary field averages, signed finite-energy measures, and rough distribution spaces. At c=2c=2c=2, the argument is separate: fair orientations of associated FK loops supply rotation information, after which the earlier endpoint GFF framework is used.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns one balanced, zero-slope plane state and one specified order of thermodynamic limits. It does not assert uniqueness among all Gibbs states, cover every slope, or evaluate arbitrary boundary-conditioned finite domains.

The parameter is fixed before the mesh limit. The coefficient diverges as c↓0c\downarrow0c↓0, and the manuscript states no uniform estimate in that limit. The endpoint c=0c=0c=0 and the regime c>2c>2c>2 are outside its assertion. Anisotropic weights also require their own statement and embedding conventions.

Field convergence does not imply pointwise convergence or immediate convergence of contour ensembles. Those observables need additional control. Conversely, the separated-increment theorem is meaningful even though point evaluations of the limiting GFF are not ordinary random variables.

Natural directions include quantitative convergence rates and the relation among different slope and boundary regimes. Existing finite-domain results should be read alongside those questions, rather than treating every boundary problem as still untouched. Throughout, the manuscript’s mathematical claims are reported as stated.

8. Sources and further reading

The source’s introduction gives a detailed account of the exact-solution, dimer, delocalization, and GFF predecessors. The March and October 2026 primary papers linked above are especially relevant for understanding which parts of the landscape are already covered by related work.

For an introduction to the continuum object, see Sheffield, Gaussian free fields for mathematicians. The main normalization in this digest is fixed by the unit height jumps and Green kernel displayed in section 2.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Gaussian free field limit of the balanced six-vertex model with variance multiplier 1/arcsin(c/2) (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Double-dimer loops: from topological records to nested CLE₄ curves
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 226 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A perfect matching of a graph pairs every vertex with exactly one neighbor. Draw two independent perfect matchings on the same square grid. An edge selected twice becomes a doubled edge; the other selected edges arrange themselves into alternating loops.

These double-dimer loops are predicted to approach a conformally invariant continuum ensemble called nested CLE₄. Earlier work already identified extensive topological information about that limit. Family 226 asks for the stronger geometric statement: do the actual loop curves converge, including every nested generation and the order in which each loop traverses its trace?

The distinction is visible in a simple example. A loop can make a long, extremely thin excursion and return without enclosing any of a chosen finite set of test points. A record of which points lie inside the loop will miss the excursion. Even identifying the limiting trace does not exclude running backward along part of it before continuing forward.

The manuscript claims to rule out these possibilities for the standard half-plane Temperleyan double-dimer model, thereby upgrading existing topological convergence to convergence of complete loop collections as curves.

2. Background and essential definitions

Matchings and the half-plane law

A dimer is an edge occupying its two endpoints. A dimer covering, or perfect matching, uses exactly one incident edge at every vertex. On a finite graph that admits coverings, the uniform dimer law gives every perfect matching equal probability.

The infinite domain here is the upper half-plane

H={z∈C:Im⁡z>0},Hδ=H∩δZ2.\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\},\qquad\mathbb H_\delta=\mathbb H\cap\delta\mathbb Z^2.H={z∈C:Imz>0},Hδ​=H∩δZ2.

An infinite-volume law needs a boundary convention. The manuscript takes simple lattice polygons in the coarse grid (0,δ)+2δZ2(0,\delta)+2\delta\mathbb Z^2(0,δ)+2δZ2, keeps the fine-grid graph in their closure, and deletes one coarse boundary vertex, called the root. These are the specified Temperleyan graphs. Their polygons exhaust the half-plane while their roots escape to infinity. The local limit of uniform matchings defines the law used in the theorem.

Sample two matchings independently with this same law. In their superposition, each vertex has degree two if a doubled edge is counted twice. Under this particular half-plane law, the components are almost surely doubled edges and finite simple even cycles. Remove the doubled edges and call the collection of cycles Lδ\mathcal L_\deltaLδ​.

The loops alternate between edges of the first and second matchings. They are treated as unrooted and unoriented: neither a starting point nor a preferred direction is part of the final observable.

What nested CLE₄ describes

A conformal loop ensemble is a random collection of loops whose law transforms naturally under conformal maps. For parameter four, the individual loops are simple and disjoint. The nonnested ensemble gives the outermost layer. Nested CLE₄ repeats the same construction independently inside each loop, conditional on its boundary, and continues recursively.

The source uses the standard normalization whose outermost ensemble can be constructed from a Brownian loop soup of central charge one. This identifies the conventional CLE₄ law, rather than a new loop process with an adjustable intensity. A Brownian loop soup is a Poisson collection of Brownian loops; its cluster boundaries provide this continuum construction.

Every fixed positive size cutoff leaves only finitely many loops in the disk, even though there are loops at arbitrarily small scales. This local finiteness is what makes comparison of whole collections possible.

A topology that remembers curves

To compare the unbounded half-plane globally, use

F(z)=z−iz+i,F(z)=\frac{z-i}{z+i},F(z)=z+iz−i​,

which maps it to the unit disk. All distances and diameters in the theorem are measured after this map. Thus infinity is handled through a compact conformal coordinate.

Two loops are close when one can choose starting points and either orientation, then continuously change traversal speed so that corresponding points remain uniformly close. Pauses do not matter; a backward detour cannot generally be removed by a monotone change of speed.

Two loop collections are close if their macroscopic members can be matched one-to-one, with close matched curves, leaving only small loops unmatched. Distinct loops remain distinct entries even if their limiting images coincide. This retains multiplicity as well as geometry.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kasteleyn and Temperley–Fisher developed exact dimer enumeration through determinant and Pfaffian methods. Lieb’s transfer-matrix approach offered another way to exploit the model’s algebra. These exact formulas made dimers one of the most tractable interacting planar systems.

At the field level, Kenyon proved Gaussian-free-field limits for dimer heights in suitable Temperleyan domains. This strongly motivates a connection to CLE₄, whose loops are related to Gaussian-field level lines. But a random distribution does not determine the convergence of discrete contours without extra geometric arguments.

Kenyon and Wilson identified limiting boundary pairing probabilities for double dimers and their agreement with Gaussian-field contour predictions. Kenyon’s loop observables then accessed conformally invariant topological data using matrix-valued weights.

Dubédat connected such observables to CLE₄ through isomonodromic tau-functions, analytical quantities encoding how a differential equation changes when punctures move. Basok and Chelkak recovered probabilities of cylindrical events from the corresponding expansion, subject to a continuum tail estimate. Bai and Wan supplied the needed tail control for the nested ensemble.

The source imports the precise half-plane formulation in Basok and Izyurov’s 2025 paper. It states convergence of reduced loop records relative to finitely many punctures, including all nested generations. That work also treats fluctuations of nesting counts and their limiting field.

The proposed advance therefore concerns the remaining geometric information. It does not claim that the CLE₄ candidate or its puncture-record law was previously unknown. The task is to retain entire paths while preventing features invisible to every fixed finite record.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For the half-plane Temperleyan law just defined, the manuscript claims tightness and full convergence

F(Lδ)⟹F(L)(δ↓0),F(\mathcal L_\delta)\Longrightarrow F(\mathcal L)\qquad(\delta\downarrow0),F(Lδ​)⟹F(L)(δ↓0),

where L\mathcal LL is standard nested CLE₄ in H\mathbb HH. The arrow denotes convergence in distribution in the loop-collection topology described above.

Several parts of the claim matter separately. It holds along the full mesh limit, rather than only a selected subsequence. It includes all nested generations, rather than just the outermost boundaries. Every macroscopic loop is matched as a curve, and no extra macroscopic limiting loop is left unidentified.

The target loops lie strictly inside the open disk after applying FFF. The statement includes tightness in that interior collection space, so boundary contact is not simply ignored by first working in a larger closed-disk space.

For comparison, the imported topological theorem works as follows. Choose finitely many distinct interior punctures. Record the homotopy classes of loops relative to them, keeping multiplicities but deleting loops surrounding at most one puncture. Homotopy means deformation without crossing a puncture. This reduced record converges to its CLE₄ counterpart. The new theorem supplements that information with control at successively finer geometric resolutions.

The result concerns unparametrized curves, in the precise sense of allowing changes of speed. It does not attach a limiting travel time, arc-length normalization, or occupation measure to each loop. Those would be additional observables, analogous to the separate natural-measure question discussed in family 223.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Double dimers are a central exactly solvable loop model, and full geometric convergence is a major strengthening of topological identification. The result would complete the stated half-plane Temperleyan version of a prominent CLE₄ scaling-limit prediction.

The stronger topology permits questions about where a loop goes and how it is traversed, not merely which selected points it surrounds. It also ensures that the many nested loops fit into one continuum ensemble with the correct multiplicities.

The rating reflects a substantial advance with potentially reusable methods, while retaining the theorem’s particular domain and boundary law. It is not a claim for every dimer graph or every possible finite-domain approximation.

An instructive general lesson is that exact algebraic observables and geometric compactness solve different parts of a scaling-limit problem. Here the earlier algebraic and topological information identifies the candidate; the new estimates are designed to make that identification valid in a stronger space.

6. The main idea

The manuscript starts in a finite rectangle with a deleted corner, chosen to match the Temperleyan convention. It counts matchings one column at a time. The state along a vertical seam records which dimers cross it; after a change of variables, these states behave like configurations of particles on transverse sites.

The transfer in a sector with a fixed number of particles is an exterior power of a one-particle matrix. This expresses the many-particle calculation through the spectrum of a simpler operator. Moving far from the typical particle number has a quadratic spectral cost.

That cost yields the first geometric estimate: the total number of disjoint crossings of a fixed-width slab is tight. Importantly, repeated crossings by one loop count separately. Controlling only the number of distinct loops would allow a single loop to oscillate arbitrarily often. Bounds of this kind give compactness after suitable reparametrization.

A second estimate controls signed crossing counts through a short transverse interval. The sign records which way an arc crosses. A local two-particle insertion has matrix coefficients that are small quadratically in the interval length. A separate planar positivity identity converts this signed algebra into a probability bound, with weights that decay down nested chains.

This estimate excludes a thin excursion canceling against a nearby return path. Wilson’s spanning-tree algorithm and the Temperley correspondence then transfer the rectangle estimates to bounded windows of the half-plane. These are localization tools; the theorem is not restricted to the auxiliary rectangles.

Finally, the argument couples a subsequential curve limit with its known finite-puncture records. A progressively finer puncture grid identifies each visible trace and rules out invisible macroscopic loops. Another refinement excludes backward traversal along an already identified trace. This separates three tasks that a winding number alone cannot settle: identifying the image, its multiplicity, and its traversal order.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem uses two independent uniform matchings with the specified half-plane Temperleyan law. Changing edge weights, boundary conventions, lattice, or domain requires a separate statement. Conformal invariance of the proposed continuum limit does not by itself transfer the discrete theorem to arbitrary lattice approximations of other domains.

The convergence is measured after the fixed map to the disk. It is consequently a precise compactified geometric statement, rather than uniform Euclidean control over all of the unbounded half-plane.

No convergence rate or natural parametrization is asserted. Nor does convergence of these loops automatically settle every joint observable involving the two original matchings or their heights. The source takes established topological convergence and standard CLE properties as inputs; its claim is the geometric upgrade built on them.

Broader domains and boundary laws, quantitative rates, and simultaneous convergence with naturally normalized loop measures are directions beyond the displayed result. The mathematical claims here are reported as stated in the source.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical papers linked above trace the progression from height fields and boundary pairings to topological loop records. Basok–Izyurov provides the exact half-plane input cited by the manuscript.

For the continuum ensemble and its normalization, see Sheffield and Werner, the Markovian characterization and loop-soup construction of CLE. The source below supplies the claimed geometric estimates and full curve-limit statement.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Curve Scaling Limit of Half-Plane Double Dimers (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random perceptrons: free energy, correlated patterns, and microscopic jamming
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 222 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A perceptron chooses a vector of weights and tests its projections onto a collection of input vectors. Can it satisfy many random requirements at once? If violations are allowed but penalized, how many good choices remain? Near the point where satisfying every requirement becomes impossible, do the nearly binding constraints follow universal power laws?

These questions link a basic learning model to spin glasses and to jamming: the loss of freedom that occurs when too many constraints compete for too few degrees of freedom. The connection concerns the geometry of a high-dimensional optimization problem, rather than the behavior of a particular training algorithm.

Family 222 contains four manuscripts. Two claim general limiting free-energy formulas for independent Gaussian patterns, with either binary or spherical weights. A third treats spherical weights with correlated, rotationally invariant patterns. The fourth claims microscopic gap and force exponents at the jamming transition of a particular negative-margin spherical model. The last result requires additional arguments beyond the bounded-potential free-energy theorems.

2. Background and essential definitions

Patterns, weights, and pressure

Let NNN be the number of weights and M=⌊αN⌋M=\lfloor\alpha N\rfloorM=⌊αN⌋ the number of patterns, where the density α>0\alpha>0α>0 stays fixed as NNN grows. For independent standard Gaussian vectors ga∈RNg^a\in\mathbb R^Nga∈RN, define the field

ba(x)=ga⋅xN.b_a(x)=\frac{g^a\cdot x}{\sqrt N}.ba​(x)=N​ga⋅x​.

The Ising model restricts xxx to {−1,1}N\{-1,1\}^N{−1,1}N; the spherical model imposes ∥x∥2=N\|x\|^2=N∥x∥2=N. In either case, μN\mu_NμN​ denotes the uniform probability measure on the allowed weights. For a real log-potential fff, set

ZN=∫exp⁡ ⁣(∑a=1Mf(ba(x)))dμN(x),pN=1Nlog⁡ZN.Z_N=\int \exp\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^M f(b_a(x))\right)d\mu_N(x),\qquad p_N=\frac1N\log Z_N.ZN​=∫exp(a=1∑M​f(ba​(x)))dμN​(x),pN​=N1​logZN​.

The pressure pNp_NpN​ balances rewards against the scarcity of configurations earning them. Taking f=βφf=\beta\varphif=βφ introduces inverse temperature β\betaβ. The physical free-energy density is then −pN/β-p_N/\beta−pN​/β. Because the prior has total mass one, zero potential gives zero pressure; replacing the Ising prior by counting measure adds log⁡2\log 2log2.

Two independently sampled configurations have overlap R(x,x′)=x⋅x′/NR(x,x')=x\cdot x'/NR(x,x′)=x⋅x′/N. A single typical overlap gives a replica-symmetric description. A hierarchy of overlaps describes clusters, subclusters, and successively closer configurations. The corresponding variational formulas optimize over a whole nondecreasing function, not just one scalar.

Hard constraints and jamming

A hard requirement assigns weight zero to a forbidden configuration. Its log-potential is therefore −∞-\infty−∞, which is outside a theorem for bounded real fff.

For the jamming manuscript, write y=x/Ny=x/\sqrt Ny=x/N​, so ∥y∥=1\|y\|=1∥y∥=1, and let AAA have independent standard Gaussian entries initially. Its constraints are

ha(y)=1+(Ay)a≥0.h_a(y)=1+(Ay)_a\geq0.ha​(y)=1+(Ay)a​≥0.

Thus the required projection is at least −1-1−1: the margin is negative. A positive gap hah_aha​ measures spare room; zero marks contact with a constraint. The energy

HN(y)=12∑a=1M(−ha(y))+2,z+=max⁡{z,0},H_N(y)=\frac12\sum_{a=1}^M(-h_a(y))_+^2,\qquad z_+=\max\{z,0\},HN​(y)=21​a=1∑M​(−ha​(y))+2​,z+​=max{z,0},

penalizes violations. The model is satisfiable, or SAT, if some unit vector has zero energy; otherwise it is UNSAT. Negative margin and the spherical restriction produce a nonconvex feasible-set problem.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gardner introduced the statistical-mechanical storage-volume problem, and Gardner and Derrida studied both spherical and binary weights. Their work made the number and organization of feasible classifiers central objects. Krauth and Mézard subsequently developed the binary storage-capacity prediction. Gardner’s original paper provides the starting point for this history.

Rigorous Ising formulas first covered restricted regimes, including Talagrand’s small-density and high-temperature results. Bolthausen, Nakajima, Sun, and Xu developed a small-density approach using approximate message passing and conditional moment estimates. M1 presents its removal of density and temperature restrictions for bounded log-potentials as the main advance over this line. Separate hard-constraint capacity results do not automatically evaluate every positive-temperature pressure, or vice versa.

For spherical models, Shcherbina and Tirozzi established a Gardner formula in a nonnegative-margin hard-constraint regime. The more general hierarchical finite-temperature expression also predates these manuscripts: Györgyi and Reimann developed continuous replica symmetry breaking, and Montanari and Zhou supplied a related replica derivation alongside rigorous results about algorithmically attainable projections. M4 claims a rigorous evaluation of the general bounded-potential pressure, rather than the invention of the physical functional.

The jamming story grew from the theory of high-dimensional hard spheres. Franz and Parisi proposed the negative spherical perceptron as a minimal model sharing their critical behavior. Franz, Parisi, Sevelev, Urbani, and Zamponi analyzed the SAT–UNSAT transition and its scaling predictions. The predicted exponents and their relation were therefore established targets. M2 claims to derive them with the necessary existence, limiting, and profile-selection arguments.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Independent Gaussian patterns: binary and spherical weights

M1 claims convergence of the Ising pressure, both in expectation and probability, for every bounded Borel real log-potential, every fixed positive density, and every fixed positive temperature. Borel measurability allows discontinuities. There is no symmetry, concavity, or smallness assumption on the potential.

Its formula has the structure

lim⁡N→∞EpN=inf⁡q{αVf(q)+SI(q)}.\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb E p_N=\inf_q\{\alpha\mathcal V_f(q)+\mathcal S_I(q)\}.N→∞lim​EpN​=qinf​{αVf​(q)+SI​(q)}.

Here q:(0,1)→[0,1]q:(0,1)\to[0,1]q:(0,1)→[0,1] is a nondecreasing overlap quantile. The pattern term Vf\mathcal V_fVf​ is obtained by successively averaging Gaussian fields along the hierarchy; SI\mathcal S_ISI​ is the associated binary-spin entropy term, defined through a dual optimization of one-spin log⁡cosh⁡\log\coshlogcosh recursions. The coefficient α\alphaα counts patterns per weight. The two contributions must use the same hierarchy.

M4 gives the spherical analogue for every bounded continuous potential, again at arbitrary fixed density and temperature. Its formula can be described using a nondecreasing function m:[0,1]→[0,1]m:[0,1]\to[0,1]m:[0,1]→[0,1]. Define

Dm(t)=∫t1m(s) ds,S(m)=12∫01(1Dm(t)−11−t)dt.D_m(t)=\int_t^1m(s)\,ds,\qquad\mathcal S(m)=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac1{D_m(t)}-\frac1{1-t}\right)dt.Dm​(t)=∫t1​m(s)ds,S(m)=21​∫01​(Dm​(t)1​−1−t1​)dt.

An infinite value excludes an inadmissibly expensive hierarchy. The pattern term has a stochastic-control description:

Vf(m)=sup⁡vE[f ⁣(B1+∫01m(t)vt dt)−12∫01m(t)vt2 dt].\mathcal V_f(m)=\sup_v\mathbb E\left[f\!\left(B_1+\int_0^1m(t)v_t\,dt\right)-\frac12\int_0^1m(t)v_t^2\,dt\right].Vf​(m)=vsup​E[f(B1​+∫01​m(t)vt​dt)−21​∫01​m(t)vt2​dt].

Here BBB is standard Brownian motion, and vtv_tvt​ may depend on information observed up to time ttt, with finite expected cost. One chooses a drift to improve the terminal reward while paying a quadratic penalty. The claimed limiting pressure is inf⁡m{αVf(m)+S(m)}\inf_m\{\alpha\mathcal V_f(m)+\mathcal S(m)\}infm​{αVf​(m)+S(m)}. The variable ttt indexes the hierarchy; it is not the physical evolution time of a learning process.

Correlated rotationally invariant patterns

M3 replaces the independent-pattern matrix by an M×NM\times NM×N matrix whose distribution is unchanged by orthogonal rotations on either side. Its singular-vector bases are uniformly random, while its singular values can have a prescribed limiting distribution. In this normalization the field is AxAxAx, with the usual independent Gaussian comparison having entries of size N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2.

For bounded continuous fff, a deterministic compact limiting singular-value distribution, and the stated spectral control, M3 claims a deterministic pressure limit in expectation and probability.
