The main theorem excludes singular-value outliers away from the limiting support; an appendix weakens this to control by the interval between its extreme points, with a further allowance for a structural input null space.

The formula optimizes how much squared input norm lies in each singular-value band, together with a hierarchical angular contribution. It permits spectral atoms, gaps, and rank deficiency. Thus the spectrum of correlations enters the answer explicitly; replacing the matrix by an independent Gaussian one would generally change the model.

Microscopic jamming at margin minus one

M2 claims a finite positive critical density αc\alpha_cαc​: SAT probability tends to one for fixed α<αc\alpha<\alpha_cα<αc​, and to zero for fixed α>αc\alpha>\alpha_cα>αc​. It further claims the same threshold and critical conclusions when each matrix entry has distribution

12N(0,1−ε)+12N(0,1+ε),\tfrac12\mathcal N(0,1-\varepsilon)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(0,1+\varepsilon),21​N(0,1−ε)+21​N(0,1+ε),

for sufficiently small fixed ε≥0\varepsilon\geq0ε≥0. This is a particular variance-one non-Gaussian family.

Its microscopic statements use an ordered limit: first N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞, then inverse temperature β→∞\beta\to\inftyβ→∞, then α↓αc\alpha\downarrow\alpha_cα↓αc​ from the UNSAT side. Define GJ(u)G_J(u)GJ​(u) as the limiting fraction of constraints with positive gap at most uuu, excluding the contact atom by first imposing a positive lower cutoff and subsequently sending that cutoff to zero.

For violated constraints, normalize the magnitude −ha-h_a−ha​ by its average over those constraints. The resulting forces have mean one. Their limiting cumulative distribution is FJ(s)F_J(s)FJ​(s). M2 claims

GJ(u)=u1−γ+o(1),FJ(s)=s1+θ+o(1),γ=12+θ,G_J(u)=u^{1-\gamma+o(1)},\qquadF_J(s)=s^{1+\theta+o(1)},\qquad\gamma=\frac1{2+\theta},GJ​(u)=u1−γ+o(1),FJ​(s)=s1+θ+o(1),γ=2+θ1​,

as u,s↓0u,s\downarrow0u,s↓0, with

0.4126930<γ<0.4126934,0.4231063<θ<0.4231088.0.4126930<\gamma<0.4126934,\qquad0.4231063<\theta<0.4231088.0.4126930<γ<0.4126934,0.4231063<θ<0.4231088.

These are cumulative-law statements; differentiating them into density asymptotics would require additional justification. The complete gap law has a contact atom of mass 1/αc1/\alpha_c1/αc​. Since there are approximately αcN\alpha_c Nαc​N constraints, this expresses one contact per degree of freedom, or isostaticity. The positive-gap function itself need not have total mass one.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family addresses both a central thermodynamic quantity across broad classes of perceptrons and the detailed critical geometry of a major jamming model.

The general pressure formulas would replace regime-specific calculations with a common framework for arbitrary bounded rewards. The rotationally invariant extension would show how correlated data change that framework. The jamming claim reaches further than locating a phase boundary: it describes the abundance of almost-binding constraints and unusually weak forces at that boundary.

The connection is mathematically valuable because free energy is a global average, while small-gap and small-force tails resolve a delicate microscopic population. Neither level of information automatically supplies the other. These statements would connect the hierarchical thermodynamics to its most singular geometric predictions.

The rating concerns the mathematical claims as stated. It does not assert that the formulas yield efficient training algorithms or directly predict the behavior of a finite neural network.

6. The main idea

For the independent-pattern pressure, one first enriches the model with auxiliary Gaussian fields that encode candidate overlap hierarchies. Gaussian averaging proceeds level by level, retaining shared randomness for configurations in the same branch. Small perturbations organize overlap identities without changing the limiting pressure.

The upper and lower bounds have different jobs. A variational comparison controls pressure from above despite the nonlinear pattern interaction. A cavity calculation removes and restores a small number of variables or patterns, expressing the pressure increment through the limiting overlap structure. Matching those increments identifies the entropy and pattern terms. Gaussian patterns alone are insufficient to invoke the ordinary spin-glass formula: after applying a nonlinear fff, the Hamiltonian is generally no longer a Gaussian process.

For rotationally invariant matrices, M3 first separates radii from angles. Putting an atypical fraction of the input norm into a spectral band has an entropy cost. Conditional on those radii, random orthogonal subspaces govern the angular problem. Optimizing both parts retains information that a single scalar variance would lose.

The jamming argument needs its own control of the unbounded quadratic penalty. It also must turn small energy into exact feasibility: an energy density tending to zero does not by itself produce a vector satisfying every constraint. M2 describes a repair argument using a small surplus of constraints before removing a fraction of them.

At criticality, its variational description supplies coupled gap and force scales. A selected limiting profile determines both exponents, while conservation and normalization link them. The manuscript reports a finite numerical enclosure for the resulting spectral problem, yielding the displayed intervals. This is an attributed component of the source’s claimed result, not a separate numerical check here.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main free-energy theorems use fixed finite temperature and fixed density. A bounded soft potential cannot simply be replaced by a hard indicator or an infinite penalty without controlling another limit. M2 supplies separate analysis for its specific negative-margin quadratic model; it is not a consequence of substituting that potential into M4’s bounded theorem.

M1 also discusses integrable unbounded potentials and random-sign pattern universality under additional hypotheses. For the latter, bounded potentials must have a discontinuity set of Gaussian measure zero; arbitrary bounded Borel functions do not all qualify. M3 likewise states extensions beyond continuous bounded potentials with their own spectral and integrability conditions.

The jamming theorem fixes margin −1-1−1, approaches from the UNSAT side, and uses the stated order of limits. Its small Gaussian-mixture universality does not cover every independent-entry distribution. It does not state SAT probability at the critical density itself, nor give a universal finite-size scaling window.

Further questions include broader disorder universality, other margins, convergence rates, and the relation between equilibrium predictions and what feasible algorithms actually find. Finite-dimensional particle packings remain a different model; the perceptron’s connection to them is a motivating universality picture, not an identification of their theorems.

8. Sources and further reading

For the origins of the storage problem, begin with Gardner’s paper linked above. Györgyi–Reimann and Montanari–Zhou explain the earlier hierarchical and algorithmic viewpoints. Franz–Parisi and the subsequent SciPost paper develop the physical jamming predictions that M2 targets.

In the source list below, M1 concerns binary weights, M4 independent Gaussian spherical weights, M3 correlated rotationally invariant matrices, and M2 the microscopic jamming transition. Their assumptions should be read separately when applying a particular conclusion.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The free energy of the Ising random perceptron (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Microscopic jamming in the negative spherical perceptron (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The spherical perceptron with bi-orthogonally invariant disorder (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, The free energy of the spherical random perceptron (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Engineering a temperature transition with radial pair interactions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 228 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Can identical particles moving freely in three-dimensional space undergo a mathematically demonstrable temperature transition when their energy is just a sum of radial pair interactions?

This resembles the everyday question of why matter changes phase, but the mathematical task is demanding even as an existence problem. The particles are not attached to lattice sites, their number grows with the volume, and an attractive interaction must avoid catastrophic collapse. One also needs a genuine singularity for one fixed interaction, rather than a corner that appears only in an additional mean-field limit.

Family 228 contains two constructions. Both claim a stable radial pair potential whose canonical free energy has a strict derivative jump at one common positive inverse temperature for every density in an open interval. The potentials differ: one has a divergent repulsive core and an integrable tail; the other has a bounded continuous core and an explicit power-law tail bound.

These are engineered examples. Neither manuscript identifies the phases as ordinary liquid, vapor, or solid, and neither asserts the result for the standard Lennard–Jones potential.

2. Background and essential definitions

Energy, stability, and the thermodynamic limit

For particle positions x1,…,xN∈R3x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3x1​,…,xN​∈R3, a radial pair potential φ\varphiφ gives energy

UN(x1,…,xN)=∑1≤i<j≤Nφ(∣xi−xj∣).U_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(|x_i-x_j|).UN​(x1​,…,xN​)=1≤i<j≤N∑​φ(∣xi​−xj​∣).

Only the distance between each pair matters. There is no fixed spatial grid in this physical interaction and no separate three-body or four-body term.

A potential is stable if some finite constant BBB satisfies

UN≥−BNU_N\geq-BNUN​≥−BN

for every configuration and every particle number. The lower bound grows only linearly with NNN, preventing attraction from producing energy of order −N2-N^2−N2 through collapse. Stability is a statement about total energy; it does not require the pair potential itself to be nonnegative.

Let ΛL\Lambda_LΛL​ be a cube of volume L3L^3L3. At inverse temperature β>0\beta>0β>0, the canonical partition function is

ZL,N(β)=1N!∫ΛLNe−βUN dx1⋯dxN.Z_{L,N}(\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N}\,dx_1\cdots dx_N.ZL,N​(β)=N!1​∫ΛLN​​e−βUN​dx1​⋯dxN​.

The factor N!N!N! accounts for identical particles. The source uses position integration with a fixed, temperature-independent measure. No kinetic or temperature-dependent normalization is included.

At density ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0, take N=⌊ρL3⌋N=\lfloor\rho L^3\rfloorN=⌊ρL3⌋. The free-energy density is

f(β,ρ)=−lim⁡L→∞1βL3log⁡ZL,⌊ρL3⌋(β).f(\beta,\rho)=-\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac1{\beta L^3}\log Z_{L,\lfloor\rho L^3\rfloor}(\beta).f(β,ρ)=−L→∞lim​βL31​logZL,⌊ρL3⌋​(β).

The volume limit is what permits a singularity. For a large finite system, a sharp but smooth crossover can resemble a transition without giving the claimed nondifferentiability.

What derivative jumps mean

The manuscripts claim finite one-sided derivatives satisfying

∂β−f(βc,ρ)>∂β+f(βc,ρ).\partial_\beta^-f(\beta_c,\rho)>\partial_\beta^+f(\beta_c,\rho).∂β−​f(βc​,ρ)>∂β+​f(βc​,ρ).

This is a downward jump as inverse temperature increases. The free energy is continuous at the transition, but its slope changes abruptly.

Where differentiability is available, ∂β(βf)\partial_\beta(\beta f)∂β​(βf) is the configurational energy per volume. Thus a corner in the stated normalization carries an energy discontinuity. The claim is made at fixed density, not merely by varying a chemical potential and observing two densities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Continuum phase transitions form part of the program highlighted in Simon’s problems in mathematical physics. The precise interaction class matters: a theorem for several species, many-body forces, or an altered spatial interaction may address an important model without settling every radial single-species formulation.

Ruelle’s 1971 theorem established a transition in the two-species Widom–Rowlinson system. Israel’s convex constructions also produced coexistence for hard-core continuum particles with radial pair perturbations. A hard core excludes a whole positive interval of pair distances, unlike M1’s potential, which is finite at every positive separation.

Lebowitz, Mazel, and Presutti proved continuum liquid–vapor transitions for a model with attractive pair interactions and repulsive four-body interactions. The many-body repulsion is a substantive feature of that model.

A recent theorem of He, Jauslin, Lebowitz, and Peled treats a finite-range modified Kac pair interaction and distinct-density coexistence. Its interaction uses a fixed partition into boxes. The current manuscripts emphasize that their final physical potentials depend only on particle separation, even though boxes are used to estimate them.

The main long-range tool has a classical origin. Lebowitz and Penrose related weak, spread-out attraction to a mean-field free energy followed by convexification. Extending this idea to one fixed potential requires care: a sequence of smooth free energies can converge to a nonsmooth one even when no member has a transition.

Likewise, two states of different density at a fixed chemical potential do not automatically yield a temperature corner at one prescribed density. Family 228 seeks the stronger supporting-slope geometry needed for that canonical conclusion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A divergent core with an integrable tail

M1 claims a radial Borel potential φ\varphiφ, finite and locally bounded at every positive distance, with φ(0)=+∞\varphi(0)=+\inftyφ(0)=+∞ and

φ(r)⟶+∞(r↓0).\varphi(r)\longrightarrow+\infty\quad(r\downarrow0).φ(r)⟶+∞(r↓0).

It has a genuine attractive interval: for some 0<r1<r20<r_1<r_20<r1​<r2​ and a>0a>0a>0, one has φ(r)≤−a\varphi(r)\leq-aφ(r)≤−a throughout [r1,r2][r_1,r_2][r1​,r2​]. It is stable, and its tail satisfies

∫R∞r2∣φ(r)∣ dr<∞,φ(r)=o(r−3).\int_R^\infty r^2|\varphi(r)|\,dr<\infty,\qquad\varphi(r)=o(r^{-3}).∫R∞​r2∣φ(r)∣dr<∞,φ(r)=o(r−3).

The first condition is absolute tail integrability in three dimensions. The second says that r3φ(r)→0r^3\varphi(r)\to0r3φ(r)→0. Neither statement supplies a fixed positive power margin beyond r−3r^{-3}r−3.

For this potential, the free-cube canonical limit is claimed to exist and be finite for every β>0\beta>0β>0 and every ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0. There is a nonempty open density interval III and one βc∈(1/2,3/2)\beta_c\in(1/2,3/2)βc​∈(1/2,3/2) at which the strict downward derivative jump occurs for all ρ∈I\rho\in Iρ∈I.

A bounded continuous core with a power-law margin

M2 constructs a different stable radial potential, bounded and continuous even at zero, satisfying

∣φ(r)∣≤Cr−3−1/32(r≥1).|\varphi(r)|\leq Cr^{-3-1/32}\qquad(r\geq1).∣φ(r)∣≤Cr−3−1/32(r≥1).

For an open interval of positive densities, its canonical free energy is finite at every positive inverse temperature and has the same kind of derivative jump at a common βc∈[7/8,9/8]\beta_c\in[7/8,9/8]βc​∈[7/8,9/8].

The interval is centered at 5p/35p/35p/3, where ppp is the limiting maximal number of mutually distance-at-least-one points per unit volume. The numerical value of this packing constant is unnecessary for the construction. The temperature bounds use the energy units selected by the construction, rather than naming a temperature for a particular material.

These two results must not be merged into a single potential having every listed property. M1 retains divergence at the origin but proves only its integrable-tail conclusion. M2 proves a fixed algebraic decay margin with a bounded core. Each has its own density interval and transition point.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed constructions would establish a genuine canonical temperature singularity for single-species continuum particles with ordinary radial pair interactions. That is a major existence result in a setting where obtaining mathematically controlled phase transitions has required careful model design.

The common transition temperature across an entire density interval is stronger than separately finding a singularity at unrelated densities and temperatures. It arises from a two-dimensional collection of competing pressure slopes.

The bounded-core result also gives an explicit decay exponent beyond the integrability threshold. That extra margin restricts how the infinitely many attraction scales may be assembled and requires quantitative estimates.

The rating reflects the conceptual advance while preserving its engineered character. The claims do not classify the phases of a standard molecular potential or explain a particular observed fluid transition.

6. The main idea

Small clusters prevent uncontrolled collapse

The short-range reference interaction is strongly repulsive except for a very narrow low-energy shell at a tiny positive distance. Four particles can sit at the vertices of a tetrahedron with every pair distance in that shell. Five points in three-dimensional space cannot all have nearly the same pair distance within the selected tolerance.

This geometric restriction yields a quadratic penalty for large particle populations in small cubes. It is a concrete form of superstability: beyond a linear correction, the energy controls the sum of squared local particle counts. The bound survives the attractive terms added later and supplies thermodynamic limits and occupation estimates.

At a suitable construction scale, three configurations compete: near-vacuum, separated particles, and four-particle clusters. They generate three groups of slopes of a pressure depending on inverse temperature and a field conjugate to density.

Add attraction without losing the corner

A spread-out attraction has the form

−aR−3w(x/R),-aR^{-3}w(x/R),−aR−3w(x/R),

where www is a nonnegative radial kernel of integral one. Its total mass is proportional to aaa, while increasing RRR makes it weaker and longer-ranged. A Kac comparison relates its pressure to an ideal transformation containing a quadratic density reward.

The manuscripts add a summable sequence of such attractions at successively larger ranges. The difficult point is to preserve actual supporting slopes at each finite stage. Uniform approximation alone could round a corner. The construction therefore keeps three separated slope groups and arranges errors to be small compared with the next attraction mass.

M2 gives a quantitative pressure error of order R0/R\sqrt{R_0/R}R0​/R​, where R0R_0R0​ is the range of the previously constructed reference. A sufficiently rapid range schedule and suitably shrinking masses make the losses summable while ensuring the required power-law tail bound.

Recover the fixed-density temperature jump

For a convex pressure Q(β,h)Q(\beta,h)Q(β,h), a supporting vector (e,ρ)(e,\rho)(e,ρ) describes an affine plane lying below the pressure and touching it at the chosen parameter point. The second coordinate is density; the first tracks the energy-related slope.

The construction preserves an entire two-dimensional ball of supporting vectors at one limiting pressure point. A horizontal slice of that ball fixes ρ\rhoρ but leaves two different first coordinates. Partial convex duality then transfers those two supports into distinct one-sided canonical slopes. The ball supplies a whole interval of such densities, all at the same βc\beta_cβc​.

The final interaction is fixed before taking the thermodynamic limit. Its many scales are ingredients of one potential, not an instruction to send the attraction range to infinity together with the volume.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The potentials are infinite-range constructions with tailored short-distance shells and summable attractions. The theorem is not a finite-range radial-potential result and is not a statement for the ordinary 12–6 Lennard–Jones interaction.

M1 explicitly does not establish ∣φ(r)∣≤Cr−3−ϵ|\varphi(r)|\leq Cr^{-3-\epsilon}∣φ(r)∣≤Cr−3−ϵ for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0. M2 supplies such a margin but changes the core. Historical problem formulations requiring both kinds of hypotheses cannot be declared solved by combining conclusions about different potentials.

The claimed singularity does not identify conventional liquid, vapor, or crystalline phases. Nor does it classify all Gibbs states or supply a phase diagram at every density. Those are separate physical and mathematical questions.

Natural extensions would impose simpler interaction shapes, faster or finite-range decay, or stronger geometric descriptions of the coexisting states. The present contribution is the stated existence and slope-jump construction, reported without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

Simon’s problem collection gives the historical motivation. Ruelle, Lebowitz–Penrose, Lebowitz–Mazel–Presutti, and He–Jauslin–Lebowitz–Peled provide the primary continuum precedents linked above.

M1 and M2 below should be read as complementary constructions with different core and tail assumptions. Their introductions state those distinctions explicitly and explain the supporting-slope route from pressure coexistence to a canonical temperature singularity.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A continuum temperature singularity for a radial pair potential (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A radial continuum phase transition with algebraic decay (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Measuring SLE curves beyond their Hausdorff dimension
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 230 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Knowing a fractal’s dimension does not always tell us how to measure it. A curve can have dimension ddd, yet receive zero measure when every small covering set is charged its diameter to the power ddd. A slightly different cost may be needed to obtain a finite, nonzero notion of size.

For Schramm–Loewner evolution, or SLE, the dimension is known, and the critical-power Hausdorff measure is known to vanish. Schramm asked whether a deterministic correction could give a meaningful Hausdorff measure of the trace.

Family 230 contains two proposed answers for every fixed 0<κ<80<\kappa<80<κ<8. The first constructs a gauge from deterministic moment integrals without asserting a simple asymptotic formula. The second claims an explicit power multiplied by an iterated-logarithm correction. It also claims that the larger correction suggested by Schramm gives a measure too large even to be sigma-finite on a nontrivial compact positive-time segment.

The issue concerns arbitrary spatial covers. It is distinct from measuring a curve through its time order or through the area of a thin neighborhood.

2. Background and essential definitions

The random curve

Chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_\kappaSLEκ​ in the upper half-plane runs from zero to infinity. In the source’s time convention, the conformal maps removing its growing hull satisfy

∂tgt(z)=2gt(z)−Wt,Wt=κBt,\partial_tg_t(z)=\frac2{g_t(z)-W_t},\qquad W_t=\sqrt\kappa B_t,∂t​gt​(z)=gt​(z)−Wt​2​,Wt​=κ​Bt​,

where BtB_tBt​ is standard Brownian motion. This is half-plane capacity 2t2t2t parametrization. Capacity time describes how the growing curve changes a conformal map, rather than measuring its ordinary length.

Write the curve as γ\gammaγ, and its whole trace as Γ=γ([0,∞))\Gamma=\gamma([0,\infty))Γ=γ([0,∞)). For 0<κ<80<\kappa<80<κ<8, its almost-sure Hausdorff dimension is

d=1+κ8,1<d<2.d=1+\frac\kappa8,\qquad 1<d<2.d=1+8κ​,1<d<2.

Hausdorff gauges and exact measurement

A Hausdorff gauge is a continuous nondecreasing function hhh with h(0)=0h(0)=0h(0)=0 and h(r)>0h(r)>0h(r)>0 for r>0r>0r>0. For a set EEE, define

Hh(E)=lim⁡δ↓0inf⁡{∑jh(diam⁡Uj):E⊆⋃jUj,diam⁡Uj≤δ}.\mathcal H^h(E)=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\inf\left\{\sum_jh(\operatorname{diam}U_j):E\subseteq\bigcup_jU_j,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_j\leq\delta\right\}.Hh(E)=δ↓0lim​inf{j∑​h(diamUj​):E⊆j⋃​Uj​,diamUj​≤δ}.

The cover can be countable, and its sets can be arbitrary. One chooses the cheapest sufficiently fine cover and then sends the maximum allowed diameter to zero. This digest uses diameters, matching the manuscripts’ convention.

The ordinary ddd-dimensional Hausdorff measure uses h(r)=rdh(r)=r^dh(r)=rd. An exact gauge for the segments in question gives a measure strictly between zero and infinity almost surely. Exactness does not mean that every segment has the same numerical measure.

A measure is sigma-finite on a set if that set can be covered by countably many measurable pieces of finite measure. This is weaker than finite total measure. Failure of sigma-finiteness is therefore stronger than simply saying that one whole segment has infinite measure.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Beffara determined the SLE dimension 1+κ/81+\kappa/81+κ/8. In his overview and collection of problems, Schramm asked for a sigma-finite Hausdorff measure and suggested the gauge rdlog⁡log⁡(1/r)r^d\log\log(1/r)rdloglog(1/r).

Rezaei subsequently proved that the uncorrected rdr^drd Hausdorff measure is zero. This sharpened the problem: the missing ingredient is a refinement at the critical exponent, not a new dimension.

A parallel line developed a natural length for SLE. Lawler–Sheffield constructed natural parametrization in an initial parameter range, Lawler–Zhou extended it throughout 0<κ<80<\kappa<80<κ<8, and Lawler–Rezaei identified it with ddd-dimensional Minkowski content up to normalization. Minkowski content measures the area within distance rrr of the trace, rescaled by rd−2r^{d-2}rd−2.

That natural measure can be nonzero even when Hrd\mathcal H^{r^d}Hrd vanishes. The definitions use different optimization procedures: Minkowski content uses a uniform neighborhood thickness; Hausdorff measure can choose a mixture of spatial scales adapted to the realized set.

Holden and Yuan established a fine-mesh variation characterization of natural parametrization using ordered partitions of the curve. Its logarithmic correction is different again. The family explicitly does not identify its Hausdorff measure with that variation or with Minkowski content.

Multipoint Green-function bounds and higher moments of natural length also have established precedents, notably work of Lawler–Werness and Rezaei–Zhan. M1 uses moment information to construct an exact gauge; M2 seeks quantitative tail and dense-visit estimates strong enough to produce a regular closed formula.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An existence theorem through a moment-defined gauge

M1 claims that for each fixed κ∈(0,8)\kappa\in(0,8)κ∈(0,8), there is a deterministic gauge hκh_\kappahκ​, depending only on κ\kappaκ, such that almost surely

0<Hhκ(γ([s,t]))<∞for every real 0<s<t<∞.0<\mathcal H^{h_\kappa}(\gamma([s,t]))<\infty\qquad\text{for every real }0<s<t<\infty.0<Hhκ​(γ([s,t]))<∞for every real 0<s<t<∞.

The same gauge works for every sample outside one null event and for every such interval simultaneously. It is not selected after seeing a particular curve.

The construction uses moments of a canonical trace mass in a disk, specified by deterministic integrals. These moments determine finite batches of thresholds and spatial radii. The gauge takes a full infimum over the resulting quadratic covering costs. Its scales may be irregular; M1 does not claim a log-log asymptotic for this gauge.

It also claims finite expected gauge measure for the entire trace in every bounded box of the upper half-plane, including the trace’s real-boundary points. That controls all visits to the box together, rather than merely summing separate finite-time bounds.

An explicit exact correction

M2 gives a separate argument for the small-radius formula

h(r)=rd(log⁡log⁡(1/r))(2−d)/2.h(r)=r^d\bigl(\log\log(1/r)\bigr)^{(2-d)/2}.h(r)=rd(loglog(1/r))(2−d)/2.

Choose radii small enough that the expression is positive and increasing, then complete it continuously and nondecreasingly at larger radii. That completion does not affect Hausdorff measure, which uses arbitrarily small covers.

For this explicit gauge, M2 claims the same simultaneous positive-finite conclusion for all 0<s<t<∞0<s<t<\infty0<s<t<∞. For every deterministic radius R<∞R<\inftyR<∞, it further claims

E Hh(Γ∩B(0,R))<∞.\mathbb E\,\mathcal H^h(\Gamma\cap B(0,R))<\infty.EHh(Γ∩B(0,R))<∞.

The expectation covers the whole infinite-time trace inside the disk. It implies almost-sure local finiteness on a countable exhaustion by bounded regions. The positivity statement itself is stated for nontrivial compact positive-time segments.

For example, at κ=4\kappa=4κ=4, one has d=3/2d=3/2d=3/2 and the correction exponent is 1/41/41/4. At κ=6\kappa=6κ=6, the dimension is 7/47/47/4 and the exponent is 1/81/81/8. These are much smaller corrections than multiplying by one full power of log⁡log⁡(1/r)\log\log(1/r)loglog(1/r).

The exponent-one candidate is not sigma-finite

Let

g(r)=rdlog⁡log⁡(1/r)g(r)=r^d\log\log(1/r)g(r)=rdloglog(1/r)

at small radii. M2 claims that Hg\mathcal H^gHg, restricted to any of the positive-time segments above, is not sigma-finite.

The source explains this through gauge comparison. Since (2−d)/2<1(2-d)/2<1(2−d)/2<1, the ratio h(r)/g(r)h(r)/g(r)h(r)/g(r) tends to zero. Every set of finite Hg\mathcal H^gHg-measure consequently has zero Hh\mathcal H^hHh-measure. A countable collection of such sets cannot cover a segment with positive Hh\mathcal H^hHh-measure.

Thus the explicit claimed answer both supplies a working correction and rules out the proposed exponent-one correction. It does not state that M1’s moment gauge is asymptotic to M2’s formula; their asymptotic relationship remains unspecified.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The family addresses a long-standing geometric question for the full non-space-filling SLE parameter range. It would refine dimension into an exact spatial measure and determine an explicit iterated-logarithm exponent.

SLE describes scaling limits of many planar interfaces. A finer understanding of its trace measure therefore enriches the continuum geometry underlying those models, even though transferring such a measure back to a lattice requires additional work.

The result also clarifies why several plausible notions of fractal length differ. Critical-power Hausdorff measure, corrected Hausdorff measure, Minkowski content, and ordered variation respond differently to dense local visits and the freedom to choose covering scales.

The rating reflects a major contribution to random fractal geometry, with scope narrower than a general theorem for all random curves or an automatic identification of every natural parametrization.

6. The main idea

To show positive Hausdorff measure, a useful strategy is to find a positive mass supported on the trace whose mass in every small ball is at most a constant times h(r)h(r)h(r). Any cover must then pay enough total gauge cost to account for that mass.

To show finite Hausdorff measure, one needs the opposite kind of construction: economical covers. Regions where the curve visits unusually densely can be covered cheaply relative to the trace mass they contain. One selects such regions across scales and covers the missed residue separately.

M1 arranges both tasks using all finite moments of a local trace mass. Moderate thresholds give repeated opportunities for useful covering regions; much larger thresholds have summably small costs. The moments choose finite batches of tests, and a quadratic envelope makes their costs compatible with subdividing planar sets. The argument uses conditional restarting and angle mixing, not independence of successive curve pieces.

M2 makes the relevant tail quantitative. Put p=2−dp=2-dp=2−d. In normalized local coordinates, it claims a bound of the form

P{local stopped mass>u}≤Cexp⁡(−cu2/p)\mathbb P\{\text{local stopped mass}>u\}\leq C\exp(-cu^{2/p})P{local stopped mass>u}≤Cexp(−cu2/p)

for large uuu, uniformly under the permitted stopped histories and mesh approximations. At spatial scales r=2−kr=2^{-k}r=2−k, a threshold proportional to (log⁡k)p/2(\log k)^{p/2}(logk)p/2 makes exceptional mass losses summable. Since log⁡k\log klogk has the scale of log⁡log⁡(1/r)\log\log(1/r)loglog(1/r), this explains the correction in the candidate gauge.

For economical upper covers, the paper uses rare dense visits arranged along a serpentine ribbon. A ribbon with order mmm strands supplies mass of order mpm^pmp, at a probability cost exponential in m2m^2m2. Repeated conditional opportunities across scales balance this cost against the number of trials. Selecting disjoint charging regions allows one whole-trace neighborhood measure to pay for the cover.

Separate boundary and cleanup estimates retain visits near the real axis and avoid overlooking points missed by the favorable tests. The lower and upper estimates together yield the claimed exactness; either one alone would leave half the measurement problem unresolved.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The statements concern ordinary chordal SLE in the upper half-plane for each fixed 0<κ<80<\kappa<80<κ<8. The probability-one event can depend on that fixed parameter; no simultaneous assertion over an uncountable range of κ\kappaκ is made. The space-filling endpoint and larger parameters are excluded.

The gauges use spatial diameters and arbitrary countable covers. Their correction should not be substituted into an ordered-variation formula without another theorem. Neither manuscript identifies its Hausdorff measure with natural parametrization, and M2 does not establish the asymptotic equivalence of the two constructed gauges.

The all-time bounded-region estimate gives local finiteness, not finite total measure of the unbounded trace. No convergence theorem for lattice step counts is asserted here. Such questions require a normalization and a separate discrete-to-continuum argument.

The remaining relationships among these measures, their exact proportionality constants where applicable, and extensions to other SLE variants are distinct questions beyond the source claims.

8. Sources and further reading

Schramm’s problem collection, Beffara’s dimension theorem, and Rezaei’s zero-measure theorem frame the question. Lawler–Rezaei and Holden–Yuan explain the related but different notions of natural length.

M1 below supplies the moment-based existence construction; M2 supplies the explicit gauge and its comparison with the exponent-one candidate. Both mathematical claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE: A moment-integral and finite-batch construction (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An explicit exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE: A regular formula from quantitative tails and dense visits (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When noisy descendants remember their ancestor: Potts reconstruction thresholds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 229 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine a message copied down a family tree. Each child receives a noisy version of its parent’s symbol. One distant descendant may remember almost nothing, but there can be exponentially many descendants. Can their combined observations still reveal something about the original message?

This is the reconstruction problem for broadcasting on trees. It connects information theory, statistical mechanics, and community detection in sparse random graphs. A simple second-moment calculation predicts a threshold from the branching rate and the channel’s retained correlation. The prediction is not exact for every alphabet, because nonlinear patterns among descendants can carry information that a linear calculation misses.

Family 229 contains three manuscripts. M1 claims the exact threshold for a ferromagnetic four-state channel on regular and Poisson trees. M2 gives a nonlinear-capacity criterion for that channel on arbitrary bounded-degree deterministic trees. M3 treats the three-state channel with either sign of correlation and derives an exact weak-recovery threshold for a symmetric three-community graph model.

2. Background and essential definitions

Broadcasting and posterior information

Choose the root symbol uniformly from qqq possibilities. Across each edge, independently conditional on the parent, use the channel

Pλ(j∣i)=λ1{i=j}+1−λq.P_\lambda(j\mid i)=\lambda\mathbf1_{\{i=j\}}+\frac{1-\lambda}{q}.Pλ​(j∣i)=λ1{i=j}​+q1−λ​.

For positive λ\lambdaλ, the child favors its parent’s symbol: this is the ferromagnetic regime. For three states, the full allowed range is −1/2≤λ≤1-1/2\leq\lambda\leq1−1/2≤λ≤1. Negative values favor a different symbol. At λ=−1/2\lambda=-1/2λ=−1/2, the child must choose one of the other two colors.

After observing the symbols at distance nnn from the root, form the posterior vector p(n)p^{(n)}p(n), whose coordinates are the conditional probabilities of each root symbol. The uniform vector is u=(1/q,…,1/q)u=(1/q,\ldots,1/q)u=(1/q,…,1/q). Define the average information advantage

an=E[12∑i=1q∣pi(n)−1/q∣].a_n=\mathbb E\left[\frac12\sum_{i=1}^q|p_i^{(n)}-1/q|\right].an​=E[21​i=1∑q​∣pi(n)​−1/q∣].

This is expected total variation distance from having no information. Reconstruction means lim⁡n→∞an>0\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n>0limn→∞​an​>0; nonreconstruction means the limit is zero. It does not require recovering the root perfectly.

A regular ddd-ary tree has exactly ddd children at every vertex. A Poisson Galton–Watson tree has independent offspring counts of mean ddd. Here ddd counts children or their mean, not total undirected degree. The random tree is independent of the root symbol and is observed along with the relevant boundary spins.

Why the square of the channel parameter appears

A correlation transmitted along a path of length nnn is scaled by λn\lambda^nλn. Second-moment information therefore has scale λ2n\lambda^{2n}λ2n, while a regular tree has dnd^ndn descendants. Their competition produces

(dλ2)n.(d\lambda^2)^n.(dλ2)n.

The Kesten–Stigum condition dλ2>1d\lambda^2>1dλ2>1 is a known sufficient criterion for reconstruction. Showing impossibility at or below one requires control of nonlinear posterior updates. Equality is particularly delicate because the linear factor neither grows nor contracts.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kesten and Stigum’s work on multitype branching processes supplied the second-eigenvalue scale. Evans, Kenyon, Peres, and Schulman developed the connection between broadcasting and the Ising model, including the role of tree geometry. For more than two symbols, the spectral criterion can cease to be necessary.

Mézard and Montanari proposed threshold coincidence for small alphabets and its extension across branching parameters. Sly’s Potts reconstruction work established the three-state result for sufficiently large regular degree and demonstrated nonsharpness for at least five states. Four states sit at the boundary between these behaviors, where higher-order terms become decisive.

Mossel, Sly, and Sohn established three- and four-state nonreconstruction at and below the spectral bound for sufficiently large mean degree in tree families covering regular and Poisson offspring. The present regular/Poisson claims remove those large-branching restrictions within their stated channel ranges.

For irregular trees, Pemantle and Peres developed critical Ising criteria through nonlinear capacities and concave recursions. M2 adapts that structural viewpoint to four-state reconstruction. Its capacity combines an L3L^3L3 exponent with squared channel resistances, a different combination from the earlier free- and plus-boundary Ising criteria.

Community detection supplies another motivation. Statistical-physics calculations by Decelle, Krzakala, Moore, and Zdeborová predicted the spectral transition for the assortative three-community model. The established tree-to-graph impossibility transfer and Abbe–Sandon above-threshold algorithms provide the ingredients for M3’s graph consequence once its all-degree Poisson theorem is available.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Four states on regular and Poisson trees

M1 treats q=4q=4q=4 and 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq10≤λ≤1. It claims nonreconstruction whenever

dλ2≤1d\lambda^2\leq1dλ2≤1

for every integer d≥2d\geq2d≥2 in the regular model and every real d>0d>0d>0 in the Poisson model. Combined with the known reconstruction direction above one, this gives the exact threshold, including nonreconstruction at equality.

For Poisson trees, the whole unlabelled rooted tree is given to the observer. The advantage averages over trees and spins without conditioning on survival. An extinct tree contributes no information at sufficiently deep levels. Above threshold, survival has positive probability and the known surviving-tree reconstruction criterion gives positive averaged advantage.

M1 does not treat negative four-state channel parameters. The manuscript explicitly notes that antiferromagnetic four-state behavior can differ from the claimed ferromagnetic threshold.

Three states, including negative correlation

M3 claims the same strict criterion for all −1/2≤λ≤1-1/2\leq\lambda\leq1−1/2≤λ≤1, on every regular tree with at least two children per vertex and every observed Poisson tree with mean d>1d>1d>1.

In its Poisson formulation, the observer receives the unlabelled tree through the observed level and the symbols on that level, without interior symbols or sibling ordering. The average again is not conditioned on survival.

On the negative side, reconstruction occurs precisely when

d>4,−12≤λ<−1d.d>4,\qquad -\frac12\leq\lambda<-\frac1{\sqrt d}.d>4,−21​≤λ<−d​1​.

In particular, at d=4d=4d=4, the proper three-coloring channel λ=−1/2\lambda=-1/2λ=−1/2 is nonreconstructible in both tree models. This is an endpoint conclusion, not something obtained by leaving equality unspecified.

Irregular four-state trees: the capacity criterion

M2 assumes a deterministic infinite rooted tree with at most some finite number BBB of children per vertex, and fixes 0<λ<10<\lambda<10<λ<1. Vertices may have zero or one child, and there is no uniform-growth assumption.

A nonnegative flow θ\thetaθ assigns a number to each edge, conserving incoming and outgoing mass at every nonroot vertex. Its total mass ∣θ∣|\theta|∣θ∣ leaves the root. For an infinite ray ξ\xiξ, let

Vλ(θ,ξ)=∑e∈ξ(λ−2∣e∣θ(e))2,V_\lambda(\theta,\xi)=\sum_{e\in\xi}\bigl(\lambda^{-2|e|}\theta(e)\bigr)^2,Vλ​(θ,ξ)=e∈ξ∑​(λ−2∣e∣θ(e))2,

where ∣e∣|e|∣e∣ is the depth of its child endpoint. Define

Cap⁡3,λ(T)=sup⁡{∣θ∣:sup⁡ξVλ(θ,ξ)≤1}.\operatorname{Cap}_{3,\lambda}(T)=\sup\left\{|\theta|:\sup_{\xi}V_\lambda(\theta,\xi)\leq1\right\}.Cap3,λ​(T)=sup{∣θ∣:ξsup​Vλ​(θ,ξ)≤1}.

The zero flow is allowed. Positive capacity means that some positive amount can be distributed through the tree while keeping the accumulated nonlinear cost bounded on every ray.

M2 claims reconstruction if and only if this capacity is positive. It therefore sees branching bottlenecks and critical geometry that an exponential growth rate alone can miss. On a regular tree, equally splitting flow makes the path costs a geometric series with ratio (dλ2)−2(d\lambda^2)^{-2}(dλ2)−2, illustrating the connection to the regular threshold.

The exclusion of λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 matters: an infinite ray then transmits the root perfectly, while the displayed capacity of a single ray is zero.

Three-community weak recovery

In M3’s graph consequence, assign each of nnn vertices an independent uniform label in {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}{1,2,3}. Join each pair independently with probability a/na/na/n for equal labels and b/nb/nb/n for unequal labels. Assume fixed a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0 and mean degree d=(a+2b)/3>1d=(a+2b)/3>1d=(a+2b)/3>1.

Weak recovery means correctly labeling a fraction greater than 1/31/31/3 by a fixed positive amount, after optimally permuting the three label names. M3 claims the exact condition

(a−b)2>3(a+2b).(a-b)^2>3(a+2b).(a−b)2>3(a+2b).

Above it, an algorithm allowed to depend on a,ba,ba,b achieves weak recovery with probability tending to one in O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) time. At or below it, every graph-based estimator, including randomized ones, has expected optimized overlap tending to 1/31/31/3.

The translation uses λ=(a−b)/(a+2b)\lambda=(a-b)/(a+2b)λ=(a−b)/(a+2b) and established graph results. The conclusion concerns weak recovery, not exact recovery of every vertex label.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The family would complete important all-degree small-alphabet threshold predictions and extend four-state reconstruction to arbitrary bounded-degree tree geometry through an exact criterion.

The equality cases are substantive: they decide whether a barely balanced flow of information can persist indefinitely. The graph consequence then turns the three-state classification into a sharp statistical and algorithmic boundary for a widely studied sparse network model.

The capacity theorem also adds information beyond a single critical number. It describes how uneven branching affects reconstruction, making the geometry of the whole tree relevant rather than just its average size at one depth.

The score reflects a major advance at the intersection of probability and inference. The claims remain specific to the stated alphabets and channels; larger-state Potts models can have different thresholds.

6. The main idea

A posterior vector is updated in two stages. Passing through one edge moves it toward the uniform distribution, multiplying its deviation by λ\lambdaλ. Combining child observations then multiplies likelihoods and renormalizes. This second operation is nonlinear, and the observations are independent only conditional on the parent symbol.

For four states, M1 tracks quadratic information together with an additional polynomial statistic of the law of the posterior. It claims a preserved constraint that makes combining two informative branches lose a strictly positive cubic amount. If mnm_nmn​ is expected quadratic information, the resulting estimate has the form

mn+1≤dλ2mn−cmn3,c>0,m_{n+1}\leq d\lambda^2m_n-cm_n^3,\qquad c>0,mn+1​≤dλ2mn​−cmn3​,c>0,

in the relevant nontrivial parameter regime. At equality, the cubic loss still forces information to vanish. The source reports exact-arithmetic polynomial certificates for the required inequalities; these are components of its claimed proof, not computations performed for this digest.

M2 uses that posterior-law inequality as an essential companion input. In one direction, surviving information is transformed into a positive flow with bounded path cost. In the other, a capacity flow prescribes how much noise to add to observations at each leaf. Tracking a third moment controls losses while preserving a positive amount of root information, even through irregular branches.

M3 uses entropy identities for positive three-state channels. For negative channels, it separates small posterior information from a possible nonuniform fixed point: such a fixed point must exceed a stated positive gap. Analytic inequalities and finite, more-informative comparison experiments rule out the remaining possibilities, with computer-assisted certificates near the coloring boundary. The graph conclusion then invokes the previously established transfer and algorithmic theorems.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The three-state result allows either sign of correlation; the four-state results are ferromagnetic. Their scopes should not be exchanged. M2’s bounded-degree deterministic-tree criterion does not directly include an unbounded-offspring Poisson tree, which is covered separately by M1.

The Poisson advantages average over extinction as well as survival. The results are not statements that a root can be recovered from every sampled tree. Likewise, reconstruction uses an indefinitely distant full level of symbols, rather than an arbitrary incomplete or adaptively chosen sample.

The graph corollary assumes independent uniform labels, three symmetric communities, positive fixed connectivity rates, and mean degree greater than one. It does not settle all asymmetric or many-community block models, nor exact label recovery.

Extensions to other channels and irregular random trees remain separate questions. The source’s certificate claims are reported as stated; no independent certificate execution or proof verification is part of this exposition.

8. Sources and further reading

Sly and Mossel–Sly–Sohn provide the principal threshold predecessors. Abbe–Sandon supplies the above-threshold algorithmic result used for the graph application. For the irregular-tree viewpoint, see Pemantle and Peres, The critical Ising model on trees, concave recursions and nonlinear capacity, Annals of Probability 38 (2010), 184–206.

M1 below is the four-state regular/Poisson theorem, M2 its capacity companion, and M3 the three-state theorem with its community-detection consequence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Reconstruction Threshold for the Ferromagnetic Four-State Potts Model (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Capacity Criterion for Four-State Potts Reconstruction on Trees (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The exact reconstruction threshold for the three-state symmetric channel (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Building the free uniform spanning forest from independent randomness
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 231 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A uniform spanning tree is a global random object: every vertex is included, cycles are forbidden, and distant edge choices can affect one another. On an infinite graph, its free-boundary limit may be a forest with several components.

Can that forest nevertheless be generated from independent random labels placed at the vertices, using a rule that respects every graph symmetry and chooses no special root?

This is the factor-of-IID question. It asks whether the apparent global coordination can be encoded measurably in independent local randomness. The rule may inspect infinitely far, so it is a structural question about random processes rather than automatically an efficient distributed algorithm.

Family 231 contains a manuscript claiming one such rule for every infinite connected locally finite simple unweighted graph. It also gives a broader factor theorem for translation-invariant strongly Rayleigh processes on countable groups, including a class of determinantal processes.

2. Background and essential definitions

Free and wired spanning forests

A spanning tree of a finite connected graph includes every vertex, is connected, and contains no cycle. The uniform spanning-tree measure gives each such tree equal probability.

For an infinite graph GGG, choose an increasing sequence of finite connected subgraphs exhausting all edges. Sample a uniform spanning tree in each and examine probabilities involving any fixed finite set of edges. The free uniform spanning forest, or FUSF, is the limiting law when no boundary vertices are identified. This limit exists and does not depend on the chosen exhaustion.

The wired construction instead identifies the outer boundary before taking the limit. Free and wired forests can differ, so a sampling result for one is not automatically a result for the other.

A graph is locally finite if each vertex has finite degree. Degrees need not have one common upper bound. Simplicity excludes loops and multiple edges; unweighted means all graph edges have the same original weight.

Factors of independent labels

Give every vertex vvv an independent uniform random variable Uv∈[0,1]U_v\in[0,1]Uv​∈[0,1]. A factor rule decides whether an edge eee is present through a measurable function

Φ(G,U,e)∈{0,1}.\Phi(G,U,e)\in\{0,1\}.Φ(G,U,e)∈{0,1}.

Equivariance means that relabeling the graph by an isomorphism and transporting its random labels transports the output in exactly the same way. Root independence means that the construction uses no distinguished vertex. Borel measurability is the standard regularity requirement ensuring that this deterministic map defines a random process.

The output coordinates need not be independent. Their dependencies are created by applying the rule to overlapping portions of the input. For example, an edge rule can depend on random labels shared with nearby edge rules.

A finitary factor has an additional property: each output can be determined from an almost surely finite random neighborhood. An ordinary Borel factor need not have this property. A uniform real label also contains an unlimited sequence of random bits, unlike a fixed finite-alphabet label.

Negative dependence and determinant laws

For a finite binary process X=(Xi)i∈FX=(X_i)_{i\in F}X=(Xi​)i∈F​, its generating polynomial is

g(z)=E∏i∈FziXi.g(z)=\mathbb E\prod_{i\in F}z_i^{X_i}.g(z)=Ei∈F∏​ziXi​​.

The law is strongly Rayleigh if this polynomial is nonzero whenever every ziz_izi​ has positive imaginary part. On a countable set, this is required for every finite-coordinate marginal. The algebraic condition implies robust forms of negative dependence: selecting one coordinate tends to discourage selecting others, and the relevant properties survive certain changes of weights.

A determinantal random subset with kernel KKK is specified by

P(A⊆X)=det⁡(Kg,h)g,h∈A\mathbb P(A\subseteq X)=\det(K_{g,h})_{g,h\in A}P(A⊆X)=det(Kg,h​)g,h∈A​

for every finite set AAA. If KKK is a Hermitian positive contraction, meaning 0≤K≤I0\leq K\leq I0≤K≤I as an operator on square-summable functions, such a law exists and is strongly Rayleigh. The determinant controls joint inclusion probabilities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Pemantle constructed infinite-volume spanning-tree limits on the integer lattice. Benjamini, Lyons, Peres, and Schramm developed the general theory of uniform spanning forests, including the distinction between free and wired limits.

For wired forests on transient graphs, cycle popping and Wilson’s algorithm rooted at infinity already provide an IID construction. Transience means a random walk can escape rather than returning indefinitely. That construction did not settle the free-forest problem on arbitrary graphs.

Determinantal structure supplied another route in group settings. Lyons and Thom proved a stronger Bernoulli-isomorphism conclusion for the relevant invariant determinantal measures on amenable groups. Amenability permits averaging through finite sets whose boundary is small relative to their size. The unrestricted factor problem also includes nonamenable settings where that method of approximation is unavailable.

Timár established free-forest factor results for recurrent unimodular random graphs and, more generally, invariantly amenable unimodular random graphs, with stronger finitary conclusions in the stated amenable setting. The cited December 2025 version still lists the general FUSF factor question as open.

The new construction also has an information-theoretic ancestry. Eldan introduced stochastic localization; El Alaoui and Montanari described its Gaussian observation and innovation formulation. Nam, Sly, and Zhang used Brownian-driven posterior equations for factor constructions of free Ising measures on regular trees. The current manuscript adapts that observation mechanism to a countable collection of negatively dependent binary variables.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

One rule for every graph in the class

The main theorem claims a single Borel, root-independent, equivariant rule Φ\PhiΦ such that, for every infinite connected locally finite simple undirected unweighted graph,

{e∈E(G):Φ(G,U,e)=1}has law FUSF⁡G.\{e\in E(G):\Phi(G,U,e)=1\}\quad\text{has law }\operatorname{FUSF}_G.{e∈E(G):Φ(G,U,e)=1}has law FUSFG​.

The quantifier is graphwise: one rule works across the whole class. It does not first choose a random-graph distribution and tailor the construction to that law.

No amenability, transience, uniform degree bound, or degree-moment assumption is imposed. The output has the joint forest law, rather than merely the correct probability for each individual edge.

As a consequence, the FUSF is a graph factor of IID under every unimodular random-graph law supported on this class. Unimodularity is the mass-transport balance saying that expected total mass sent from a randomly rooted vertex equals expected total mass received, for every invariant nonnegative transport rule. The source does not need this balance for its stronger graphwise construction.

The conclusion is an ordinary Borel factor. It does not state a finite coding radius or a finite input alphabet.

Strongly Rayleigh laws under group translations

Let Γ\GammaΓ be a countable group, and index a binary process by its elements. Left translation acts by

(τgx)h=xg−1h.(\tau_gx)_h=x_{g^{-1}h}.(τg​x)h​=xg−1h​.

For every strongly Rayleigh law ν\nuν invariant under these translations, the manuscript claims a Borel map from independent uniform labels to ν\nuν, commuting with every translation on every label input.

The group need not be amenable or finitely generated, and finite groups are allowed. In this theorem the map may depend on Γ\GammaΓ and ν\nuν, unlike the single graphwise rule in the forest theorem.

The determinantal corollary applies whenever a Hermitian positive-contraction kernel on ℓ2(Γ)\ell^2(\Gamma)ℓ2(Γ) defines a translation-invariant law. A sufficient condition is that KKK commute with left translations. Projection kernels and complex Hermitian kernels are included; no trace-class assumption is imposed on the full operator.

This statement concerns the regular action on the group itself. It is not asserted for every action of a group on every other index set, and a factor map need not be an invertible Bernoulli isomorphism.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The free uniform spanning forest is a canonical infinite random structure. A universal graphwise IID representation would answer a substantial factor question while removing the geometric restrictions present in previous constructions.

The group theorem broadens the significance beyond spanning forests. It would connect a robust algebraic negative-dependence condition with equivariant generation from independent randomness, without relying on amenability.

The result also separates two notions often conflated in informal discussion. A process can be generated measurably from independent labels without admitting a bounded-time or finite-neighborhood sampling algorithm. The structural conclusion is strong even when no such computational guarantee is supplied.

The rating reflects broad consequences within probability on graphs and invariant random processes, while retaining the theorem’s precise distinction between graph isomorphisms and regular group translations.

6. The main idea

Reveal a target sample through Brownian noise

Temporarily suppose a sample Xe∈{0,1}X_e\in\{0,1\}Xe​∈{0,1} from the desired forest law already exists. Observe each coordinate through

Ye(t)=tXe+Be(t),Y_e(t)=tX_e+B_e(t),Ye​(t)=tXe​+Be​(t),

with independent Brownian motions BeB_eBe​. As time grows, the signal dominates the noise: the long-time slope reveals XeX_eXe​.

Given the observations, the conditional mean be(t,Y)b_e(t,Y)be​(t,Y) is a drift. Subtracting its accumulated contribution produces innovations,

W^e(t)=Ye(t)−∫0tbe(s,Y(s)) ds,\widehat W_e(t)=Y_e(t)-\int_0^t b_e(s,Y(s))\,ds,We​(t)=Ye​(t)−∫0t​be​(s,Y(s))ds,

which form independent Brownian inputs under the observation law. If the relation can be inverted deterministically, these independent inputs can generate the original correlated sample.

Negative dependence controls the inverse

For a finite weighted spanning tree, let pep_epe​ be the inclusion probability of edge eee, and let hfh_fhf​ be the logarithm of edge fff‘s weight. Differentiating gives

∂pe∂hf=Cov⁡(Xe,Xf),∑f∣∂pe∂hf∣=2pe(1−pe)≤12.\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial h_f}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_e,X_f),\qquad\sum_f\left|\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial h_f}\right|=2p_e(1-p_e)\leq\frac12.∂hf​∂pe​​=Cov(Xe​,Xf​),f∑​​∂hf​∂pe​​​=2pe​(1−pe​)≤21​.

Different edges have nonpositive covariance, while every spanning tree has the same number of edges. Together these facts bound the entire response of one inclusion probability, uniformly in graph size and weights.

The manuscript passes this response bound to a countable-coordinate drift and solves

Ze(t)=we(t)+∫0tbe(s,Z(s)) dsZ_e(t)=w_e(t)+\int_0^t b_e(s,Z(s))\,dsZe​(t)=we​(t)+∫0t​be​(s,Z(s))ds

by deterministic successive approximation. Only differences between successive approximations need a uniform bound. This matters because infinitely many independent Brownian paths are not uniformly bounded over all coordinates.

Feeding independent Brownian paths into the inverse recovers the observation process, and integer-time slopes recover the forest. Intrinsic edge-centered neighborhoods preserve graph symmetry; independent vertex labels provide independent edge paths by allocating disjoint random coordinates.

For strongly Rayleigh laws, the same covariance-row estimate holds as an inequality after suitable finite extensions. Translates of finite subsets of the group supply compatible coordinate exhaustions. They need not have small boundary, which is why the stated regular-action result requires no amenability.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The graph theorem is stated for simple unweighted locally finite graphs. Weighted finite trees appear inside the proof, but that does not automatically extend the final graphwise claim to arbitrary infinite conductance networks or multiple edges.

The construction has no stated finitary radius, runtime, or finite-bit budget. Measurability and exact equivariance are the conclusions; practical sampling complexity is a separate question. Stronger finitary results already known in special amenable settings remain stronger in that particular respect.

The group theorem allows its factor to depend on the target law and treats only the regular left action. The existence of compatible finite exhaustions is used in that form. General actions and broader negatively dependent processes require additional analysis.

The companion free-Ising factor threshold discussed in family 236 uses a related observation viewpoint with a different recovery mechanism. It is a separate theorem, not an automatic consequence of the forest result. All claims here are reported as stated by the source.

8. Sources and further reading

The uniform-spanning-forest paper and Timár’s work give the main graph-theoretic background. Lyons–Thom explains the earlier amenable-group determinantal result. For the algebraic condition used in the extension, see Borcea, Brändén, and Liggett, Negative dependence and the geometry of polynomials.

The source manuscript below states the graphwise and group-action theorems separately and develops the Brownian observation inverse that connects them.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The joint scaling limit of critical Ashkin–Teller currents
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 233 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A statistical-mechanics model can have several descriptions. One records spins, another draws connected clusters, and a third builds a random height surface. Understanding each separately does not explain how they fit together. Two random objects can have familiar individual distributions while their dependence contains substantial additional information.

The Ashkin–Teller model provides a particularly rich example. Its critical parameters form a line rather than an isolated point. Along that line, a height representation is expected to approach a Gaussian free field, while two coupled collections of current clusters should become geometric structures determined by that same field.

Family 233 contains one manuscript claiming this joint continuum description throughout the stated critical line, including its four-state Potts endpoint. It retains the complete compact supports of the clusters, their nesting at every depth, and the special cluster touching the wired boundary. The proposed limit explains how a random surface encodes two interacting geometries.

2. Background and essential definitions

From spins to currents

The usual Ashkin–Teller model couples two Ising spin systems. Each vertex carries two signs, and the interaction rewards agreements within each system and an additional product of the two agreements. The dimensionless interaction strengths are denoted by JJJ and UUU.

The manuscript fixes

J>0,U≤J,sinh⁡(2J)=e−2U.J>0,\qquad U\leq J,\qquad \sinh(2J)=e^{-2U}.J>0,U≤J,sinh(2J)=e−2U.

These equations specify the critical line under consideration. Two useful parameters are

c=1+e4U,g=8πarcsin⁡ ⁣(c2),1<c≤2,43<g≤4.c=\sqrt{1+e^{4U}},\qquad g=\frac{8}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac c2\right),\qquad 1<c\leq2,\quad \frac43<g\leq4.c=1+e4U​,g=π8​arcsin(2c​),1<c≤2,34​<g≤4.

Here ggg is a continuum coupling parameter, not a lattice spacing. The lattice spacing will be δ\deltaδ.

A current is an edge configuration obtained from an expansion of the spin model. For the theorem, it is enough to describe the equivalent joint construction. Put signs τ\tauτ on square-lattice vertices and signs τ†\tau^\daggerτ† on the centers of bounded faces. The latter form the dual lattice. Fix the primal boundary signs to +1+1+1, and leave the dual boundary free.

Across a pair of crossing primal and dual edges, the two spin systems are forbidden from disagreeing simultaneously. Give an allowed spin configuration weight proportional to ttt raised to its total number of disagreements, where t=1/ct=1/ct=1/c. If the dual signs disagree, open the primal edge and close the dual edge; do the reverse if the primal signs disagree. If neither disagrees, open only the primal edge, only the dual edge, or neither, with probabilities 1−t,1−t,2t−11-t,1-t,2t-11−t,1−t,2t−1, respectively. The primal boundary edges are open.

Thus the two open-edge sets never cross. They are not complements: both edges can be closed. Their connected components are the current clusters. The primal collection has a wired boundary cluster; the dual collection has free boundary conditions.

Heights and Gaussian fields

Define a height HδH_\deltaHδ​, zero on the primal boundary, by the corner increment

Hδ(f)−Hδ(v)=12τ(v)τ†(f),H_\delta(f)-H_\delta(v)=\frac12\tau(v)\tau^\dagger(f),Hδ​(f)−Hδ​(v)=21​τ(v)τ†(f),

where vvv is incident to face fff. The spin constraint makes the increments consistent around closed paths. Heights are integers at vertices and half-integers at face centers.

A two-dimensional Gaussian free field, or GFF, is a random generalized function. Its averages against smooth test functions are jointly Gaussian; individual point values are not ordinary finite random variables. This article uses the manuscript’s field hhh with zero boundary conditions and covariance operator

GD=2π(−ΔD)−1.G_D=2\pi(-\Delta_D)^{-1}.GD​=2π(−ΔD​)−1.

Here −ΔD-\Delta_D−ΔD​ is the positive Laplacian with zero boundary values on the domain DDD. Near coincident points its Green kernel behaves as −log⁡∣z−w∣-\log|z-w|−log∣z−w∣. This factor 2π2\pi2π matters when comparing formulas with other GFF conventions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ashkin and Teller introduced their four-component lattice model in 1943. Its coupled spins later became an important setting for critical behavior that varies continuously with a parameter. The geometric representations used here developed through work relating spin systems, percolation and height functions; Lis gave the precise spin–edge–height framework and current weights on which this manuscript builds. Original model, Lis’s representation.

An essential solved case occurs at U=0U=0U=0, where g=2g=2g=2. The relevant currents are then double random currents. Duminil-Copin and Lis identified their signed nesting field with a dimer height. Duminil-Copin, Lis and Qian subsequently obtained conformally invariant limits of the height and recursive cluster-boundary families. This supplied both a concrete continuum picture and an exploration strategy. Nesting field, double-current limits.

In 2026, Alcalde López, Heeney and Lis described the joint height and complete current-cluster collections at the Ising point, and formulated the extension along the critical line addressed here. Their broader work couples Ising magnetisation fields to a GFF. A separate paper by Alcalde López and Sepúlveda studies a stronger Ising-point excursion decomposition involving additional fields and measures. Those extra conclusions should not be attributed to the present theorem. Critical-line conjecture and Ising coupling, excursion decomposition.

The height is also related to a six-vertex model with weights (1,1,c)(1,1,c)(1,1,c). Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers and Manolescu proved a GFF limit for 3≤c≤2\sqrt3\leq c\leq23​≤c≤2, and developed estimates on a larger interval. The new manuscript uses those estimates while claiming the missing covariance and Gaussianity arguments needed for its full range. The full-plane companion described in family 225 is related, but does not supply the random-domain cluster theorem by itself. Earlier six-vertex work.

The historical gap is therefore specific: extend a known joint picture beyond the Ising point, with the appropriate varying coupling, and identify entire cluster supports even near rough boundaries.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A limit for every admissible approximation

Let DDD be a bounded Jordan domain: its boundary is a simple closed curve, without a smoothness assumption. Approximate it by simple square-lattice polygons whose boundaries converge under parametrization and whose interiors eventually contain every compact subset of DDD.

For every fixed allowed (J,U)(J,U)(J,U), Theorem 2.3 claims the joint limit

(Hδ,Cδw,Cδf,C∂,δ) ⟹ (hπg,Cw,Cf,A−a,a(h)),a=π2g.\bigl(H_\delta,\mathcal C_\delta^{\mathrm w},\mathcal C_\delta^{\mathrm f},C_{\partial,\delta}\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\\left(\frac{h}{\pi\sqrt g},\mathcal C^{\mathrm w},\mathcal C^{\mathrm f},A_{-a,a}(h)\right),\qquad a=\frac\pi2\sqrt g.(Hδ​,Cδw​,Cδf​,C∂,δ​) ⟹ (πg​h​,Cw,Cf,A−a,a​(h)),a=2π​g​.

The superscripts distinguish wired and free collections. The final component singles out the wired boundary cluster. The convergence is along the full mesh limit, with no specially chosen subsequence.

Height convergence is in local Sobolev spaces Hlocs(D)H^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)Hlocs​(D) for every s<−1s<-1s<−1. These spaces permit distributions rather than pointwise functions. Equivalently for the basic interpretation, integrate the lattice height against smooth functions and obtain the corresponding Gaussian averages with the stated normalization.

For clusters, every set above a fixed positive diameter must have a nearby counterpart in Hausdorff distance, in both directions. Hausdorff distance measures whether every point of either compact set lies near the other set. The matching is not required to be one-to-one, and the topology ignores multiplicities and singleton clusters. The distinguished boundary cluster is tracked separately. The continuum collections contain only finitely many clusters larger than any fixed positive size.

How the common field determines the clusters

A two-valued local set A−α,β(h)A_{-\alpha,\beta}(h)A−α,β​(h) is a random closed set determined by the GFF. Once it is exposed, the field in each remaining component is a constant, either −α-\alpha−α or β\betaβ, plus an independent zero-boundary GFF. The parameters satisfy α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0α,β>0 and α+β≥2λ\alpha+\beta\geq2\lambdaα+β≥2λ, where λ=π/2\lambda=\pi/2λ=π/2.

This is a precise conditional description, not a contour drawn through pointwise GFF values. The set with labels ±2λ\pm2\lambda±2λ produces holes whose boundary loops have the law called CLE₄, the conformally invariant loop ensemble with parameter four.

The wired construction starts by retaining A−a,a(h)A_{-a,a}(h)A−a,a​(h). In each remaining component, subtract its constant label and apply the free construction below to the residual GFF.

For the free construction, first expose the CLE₄ holes of a zero-boundary field. A hole has label ξ2λ\xi2\lambdaξ2λ, with ξ=±1\xi=\pm1ξ=±1. Inside it, expose a further two-valued set: use relative labels −2λ,2a−2λ-2\lambda,2a-2\lambda−2λ,2a−2λ if ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1, or −(2a−2λ),2λ-(2a-2\lambda),2\lambda−(2a−2λ),2λ if ξ=−1\xi=-1ξ=−1. Retain this inner set, including its outer boundary, as one cluster. Then repeat in all its remaining components.

Measured relative to the incoming height, the retained split has labels 000 and ξ2a\xi2aξ2a. The initial CLE₄ set is an exploration device, not itself a retained current cluster. Both recursive constructions use the same realization of hhh, which specifies their joint dependence at every nesting depth.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the claim gives a broad geometric description of an interacting critical line, extending a detailed special-case theory to continuously varying parameters and the four-state Potts endpoint.

The gain over a height theorem is substantial. Knowing that a surface becomes Gaussian does not identify which microscopic edges belong to the same macroscopic object. Here, entire cluster supports and the wired boundary component are tied to canonical structures of that Gaussian field.

The result also makes parameter dependence concrete. At the Ising point, g=2g=2g=2; at the four-state Potts endpoint, g=4g=4g=4. The splitting height aaa changes accordingly, so one common family of continuum constructions describes distinct lattice interactions. The score reflects this geometric unification, while recognizing the major foundations already established in the Ising and six-vertex settings.

6. The main idea

The manuscript separates two tasks: identify the random field, then recover the complete geometry coupled to it.

First, it develops exact conditional laws for cutting along suitable explored boundaries. A current and an auxiliary complementary spin percolation are used together. This auxiliary complement must not be confused with the other current in the theorem. An appropriate explored perimeter leaves a region with constant boundary height, making its conditional field accessible.

Second, reflection positivity and estimates from the six-vertex representation constrain the plane covariance. Screening arguments control how local insertions respond to distant boundary information. Moment identities then identify Gaussian limits in the flat regions. The normalization is extracted from the free-energy response only after the necessary Gaussian convergence has been obtained.

Third, stop cluster explorations before their geometry becomes uncontrolled. The conditional limiting field in the remaining regions has the harmonic constants and independent GFF remainders characteristic of two-valued local sets. This connects discrete stopping rules to the recursive continuum constructions.

There remains a geometric problem: some pieces of a current cluster might escape detection by the height jumps around its visible holes. The manuscript uses local passage tests, collar bounds and a no-crossing argument to rule out such missing macroscopic pieces. It then matches the complete collections, including the boundary cluster and all nesting depths.

The guiding principle is that field convergence supplies information about fluctuations, while additional exploration estimates determine which fluctuations belong to the same geometric cluster. Neither step automatically replaces the other.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The parameters are fixed before taking the mesh to zero. There is no stated uniformity as c↓1c\downarrow1c↓1, equivalently g↓4/3g\downarrow4/3g↓4/3. That excluded limiting value cannot simply be added by continuity.

The result uses the specified wired/free coupling on admissible square-lattice approximations of bounded Jordan domains. It does not assert every boundary condition, lattice or off-critical perturbation has the same limit.

Cluster convergence concerns compact supports in the stated noninjective matching topology. It does not assign a limiting area measure, preserve cluster multiplicities, supply natural parametrizations, or identify all spin-domain-wall curves. Nor does it give an exact metric exponent for travelling within a cluster.

The theorem includes the four-state Potts endpoint at a fixed parameter value. This should be distinguished from taking a second limit along the critical line toward that endpoint. Its normalization also belongs to the height convention used here; replacing HHH by the unit-corner-increment height 2H2H2H changes the multiplier.

Natural further problems concern geometric measures, additional spin observables and boundary conditions beyond this coupling. Some richer statements are already known at the Ising point; extending them through the full critical line would require additional conclusions beyond this manuscript.

8. Sources and further reading

The principal source is M1, especially Sections 2.1–2.7 for the model, recursive sets, topology and joint theorem. Its introduction explains the relation to prior double-current and six-vertex results.

For the continuum objects, Aru, Sepúlveda and Werner develop bounded-type thin local sets, while Aru and Sepúlveda study two-valued sets and their geometry. These give the conditional-GFF meaning behind the recursive description. Family 232 offers a related introduction to height limits and the distinction between a field theorem and an interface theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The joint scaling limit of critical Ashkin–Teller currents (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: All-temperature pressure for orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 234 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Knowing a symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues solves a quadratic optimization problem on the Euclidean sphere. It does not solve the same problem when every coordinate must be +1+1+1 or −1-1−1. A rotation preserves the sphere but moves the corners of the cube, so eigenvectors matter to an Ising spin system.

Suppose those eigenvectors are uniformly random. Can the limiting eigenvalue distribution then determine the system’s thermodynamics? Family 234 claims an affirmative answer at every fixed temperature, for compact limiting spectra without asymptotic outliers.
