It also treats deterministic external magnetic fields and derives zero-temperature optimization limits.

The resulting answer is a variational formula: a precisely defined optimization over possible hierarchies of spin overlaps. It need not reduce to an elementary expression, but it turns an exponentially large random sum into a deterministic mathematical problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Random interactions and pressure

There are NNN spins, assembled into a vector σ∈{−1,1}N\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^Nσ∈{−1,1}N. Write the interaction matrix as

JN=UNTΛNUN,ΛN=diag⁡(λ1,N,…,λN,N).J_N=U_N^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_NU_N,\qquad \Lambda_N=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1,N},\ldots,\lambda_{N,N}).JN​=UNT​ΛN​UN​,ΛN​=diag(λ1,N​,…,λN,N​).

The diagonal matrix is initially deterministic. The orthogonal matrix UNU_NUN​ has Haar distribution, the uniform distribution invariant under multiplying by any fixed orthogonal matrix. Thus the spectrum is prescribed while its directions are randomized.

The manuscript uses normalized pressure

PN=1Nlog⁡[2−N∑σ∈{−1,1}Nexp⁡ ⁣(12σTJNσ)].P_N=\frac1N\log\left[2^{-N}\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^N}\exp\!\left(\frac12\sigma^{\mathsf T}J_N\sigma\right)\right].PN​=N1​log​2−Nσ∈{−1,1}N∑​exp(21​σTJN​σ)​.

Larger quadratic values receive greater weight. Inverse temperature and coupling strength are absorbed into ΛN\Lambda_NΛN​. The factor 2−N2^{-N}2−N makes the spin prior a probability measure: pressure is zero when all interactions vanish. Using an unnormalized counting sum adds log⁡2\log2log2.

The empirical spectral measure

μN=1N∑i=1Nδλi,N\mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{\lambda_{i,N}}μN​=N1​i=1∑N​δλi,N​​

records the fraction of eigenvalues in each region; δx\delta_xδx​ denotes a point mass. Its limit is μ\muμ, a probability law supported in a compact interval. The smallest and largest eigenvalues must approach the corresponding endpoints of the support. Weak convergence of μN\mu_NμN​ alone is insufficient, because it can overlook a small number of extreme eigenvalues.

Overlaps and hierarchies

Two independent equilibrium samples at the same interaction matrix are called replicas. Their overlap is

Q(σ,τ)=1N∑i=1Nσiτi.Q(\sigma,\tau)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i\tau_i.Q(σ,τ)=N1​i=1∑N​σi​τi​.

It is 111 for identical configurations, −1-1−1 for opposites, and near zero for largely unrelated signs. In a spin glass, several levels of similarity can survive as NNN grows.

The formula uses a nondecreasing function p:(0,1)→[0,1]p:(0,1)\to[0,1]p:(0,1)→[0,1], interpreted as a quantile description of a trial overlap hierarchy. The nonnegative convention comes from small auxiliary perturbations used in the analysis; it does not mean unperturbed finite systems have no negative overlaps.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model introduced a mean-field spin glass with Gaussian pair interactions. Parisi proposed that its low-temperature behavior requires a hierarchy of overlaps rather than one scalar similarity. Guerra proved the variational upper bound, and Talagrand established the matching pressure formula. Aizenman, Sims and Starr developed a complementary cavity formulation based on adding spins. SK model, Guerra’s bound, Talagrand’s formula, cavity principle.

Orthogonally invariant models ask how much of that picture survives with more general spectra. Statistical-mechanics calculations for the random orthogonal model and related interactions developed spectral and replica-symmetry-breaking predictions. These provided important motivation, but are different from an all-temperature theorem under explicit matrix assumptions. Marinari, Parisi and Ritort, Cherrier, Dean and Lefèvre.

Rigorous results had reached substantial high-temperature regimes. Bhattacharya and Sen treated zero-field pressure. Fan and Wu obtained a replica-symmetric formula with external fields at sufficiently high temperature. The manuscript also credits 2026 work by Fan, Misiakiewicz, Wang and Wen giving an explicit high-temperature criterion for a constant field through dynamical mean-field analysis. Zero-field result, external-field result, 2026 development.

A further ingredient comes from random-matrix theory: Guionnet and Maïda analyzed spherical integrals using the spectral R-transform, including behavior at a spectral edge. A spherical integral averages over continuously varying directions. The quenched Ising pressure averages the logarithm of a sum over cube vertices, so this earlier theorem does not by itself answer the present question. Spherical-integral theorem.

The claimed advance is to remove the high-temperature restriction while retaining the full overlap hierarchy and a general limiting spectrum.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The spectral contribution

Let λ+\lambda_+λ+​ be the top edge of the support of μ\muμ. For x>0x>0x>0, solve

∫μ(dλ)b(x)−λ=x,b(x)>λ+.\int\frac{\mu(d\lambda)}{b(x)-\lambda}=x,\qquad b(x)>\lambda_+.∫b(x)−λμ(dλ)​=x,b(x)>λ+​.

If there is no such solution, set b(x)=λ+b(x)=\lambda_+b(x)=λ+​. Define

R(x)=b(x)−1x,R(0)=∫λ μ(dλ).R(x)=b(x)-\frac1x,\qquad R(0)=\int\lambda\,\mu(d\lambda).R(x)=b(x)−x1​,R(0)=∫λμ(dλ).

This is the manuscript’s edge-extended R-transform. The edge rule is part of the definition, not an assumed analytic continuation.

For a trial overlap function ppp, put

Dp(r)=1−r−∫01(p(s)−r)+ ds,(u)+=max⁡{u,0},D_p(r)=1-r-\int_0^1(p(s)-r)_+\,ds,\qquad (u)_+=\max\{u,0\},Dp​(r)=1−r−∫01​(p(s)−r)+​ds,(u)+​=max{u,0},

and define its spectral cost by

Gμ(p)=12∫01R(Dp(r)) dr.G_\mu(p)=\frac12\int_0^1 R(D_p(r))\,dr.Gμ​(p)=21​∫01​R(Dp​(r))dr.

The function DpD_pDp​ translates the overlap hierarchy into the argument seen by the spectral transform.

The single-spin contribution

A second functional S(p)S(p)S(p) depends on the Ising spin space, but not on μ\muμ. It is built from Gaussian averaging of the single-spin expression log⁡cosh⁡z\log\cosh zlogcoshz.

Here is its finite-step definition. Choose a nonnegative nondecreasing step function hhh, with successive values h0,…,hk−1h_0,\ldots,h_{k-1}h0​,…,hk−1​ and interval lengths w0,…,wk−1w_0,\ldots,w_{k-1}w0​,…,wk−1​ summing to one. Set h−1=0h_{-1}=0h−1​=0 and ζi=∑l<iwl\zeta_i=\sum_{l<i}w_lζi​=∑l<i​wl​. For a standard normal variable ZZZ, define

(Ta,vf)(z)={a−1log⁡Eexp⁡{af(z+vZ)},a>0,Ef(z+vZ),a=0.(T_{a,v}f)(z)=\begin{cases}a^{-1}\log\mathbb E\exp\{a f(z+\sqrt v Z)\},&a>0,\\\mathbb E f(z+\sqrt v Z),&a=0.\end{cases}(Ta,v​f)(z)={a−1logEexp{af(z+v​Z)},Ef(z+v​Z),​a>0,a=0.​

Starting with Fk−1(z)=log⁡cosh⁡zF_{k-1}(z)=\log\cosh zFk−1​(z)=logcoshz, apply these operators backwards:

Fi−1=Tζi,hi−hi−1Fi,ℓ(h)=F−1(0)−hk−12.F_{i-1}=T_{\zeta_i,h_i-h_{i-1}}F_i,\qquad\ell(h)=F_{-1}(0)-\frac{h_{k-1}}2.Fi−1​=Tζi​,hi​−hi−1​​Fi​,ℓ(h)=F−1​(0)−2hk−1​​.

Each step adds a Gaussian field increment and averages it at a specified level of the hierarchy. Finally,

S(p)=sup⁡h{ℓ(h)+12∫01p(s)h(s) ds},S(p)=\sup_h\left\{\ell(h)+\frac12\int_0^1p(s)h(s)\,ds\right\},S(p)=hsup​{ℓ(h)+21​∫01​p(s)h(s)ds},

where the supremum runs over these finite step functions. This definition gives a concrete meaning to the otherwise abstract single-spin term.

The pressure and its extensions

Theorem 1.1 claims

PN⟶F(μ),EPN⟶F(μ),F(μ)=inf⁡p{S(p)+Gμ(p)}.P_N\longrightarrow F(\mu),\qquad\mathbb E P_N\longrightarrow F(\mu),\qquadF(\mu)=\inf_p\{S(p)+G_\mu(p)\}.PN​⟶F(μ),EPN​⟶F(μ),F(μ)=pinf​{S(p)+Gμ​(p)}.

The first convergence is almost sure. The Haar matrices need not be independent across dimensions. Atomic spectral laws, disconnected supports and a point-mass law are allowed; no spectral density or positive variance is required. The infimum over ppp remains outside the supremum defining SSS: the manuscript does not interchange them.

The external-field extension adds ∑ici,Nσi\sum_i c_{i,N}\sigma_i∑i​ci,N​σi​ to the exponent. The empirical law of the deterministic fields must converge in W1W_1W1​, the minimum expected absolute difference over couplings of two probability laws. This controls both distribution and first absolute moments. For finitely many field values, the formula first prescribes a mean spin in each field group, uses the corresponding constrained single-spin functional, and then optimizes those magnetizations. General field laws follow by W1W_1W1​ approximation. It is a separate extension, not merely a substitution into the zero-field expression above.

For zero-field optimization, let μβ\mu_\betaμβ​ be the law of βλ\beta\lambdaβλ when λ\lambdaλ has law μ\muμ. The claimed maximum-energy limit is

12Nmax⁡σσTJNσ⟶lim⁡β→∞F(μβ)β.\frac1{2N}\max_\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}J_N\sigma\longrightarrow \lim_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{F(\mu_\beta)}\beta.2N1​σmax​σTJN​σ⟶β→∞lim​βF(μβ​)​.

This convention maximizes the quadratic reward; physical ground-state energy has the opposite sign when the Hamiltonian is minus that reward.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, an all-temperature formula for this broad matrix class substantially extends the thermodynamic theory beyond high-temperature regimes. It links spin-glass organization to spectral data while preserving the possibility of complicated overlap hierarchies.

The result also reaches Gaussian-pattern Hopfield interactions. If GNG_NGN​ is an ⌊αN⌋\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor⌊αN⌋-by-NNN matrix of independent standard Gaussian entries, then

JN=cNGNTGNJ_N=\frac cN G_N^{\mathsf T}G_NJN​=Nc​GNT​GN​

is covered for every fixed real ccc. Positive and negative signs, followed by zero-temperature limits, determine respectively the largest and smallest lengths of signed sums of the Gaussian columns, with the manuscript’s normalizations. Thus the same thermodynamic formula has consequences for discrete quadratic optimization and Gaussian operator norms.

The score reflects the breadth of this extension, rather than suggesting the variational problem is automatically easy to compute or that an efficient optimization algorithm follows.

6. The main idea

The argument begins with a spectrum taking finitely many distinct values. Rotate equilibrium configurations into spectral coordinates and measure their overlaps separately inside each eigenspace. Their sum is the ordinary spin overlap.

Small perturbations enforce identities relating several replicas. Established ultrametricity and synchronization theory then reduce these many overlap arrays to compatible nondecreasing functions. Rotation identities connect the eigenspace functions to a single total-overlap function. This is the step that makes the eigenvalue law enter through the spectral transform.

For one pressure bound, add hierarchical Gaussian fields to a trial system and vary the interaction strength. The comparison is arranged to keep the supremum over fields inside the infimum over trial overlap functions. Preserving this optimization order is central to the stated formula.

For the other bound, couple systems with slightly different numbers of spins. Random directions within eigenspaces generate approximately Gaussian fields for the added spins. Evaluating this cavity increment produces the same single-spin and spectral terms. A concavity argument identifies the required field supremum.

Finally, approximate general compact spectra by finite alphabets and use concentration on the orthogonal group to turn mean convergence into almost-sure convergence. External fields require an additional constrained-magnetization argument. The common theme is to separate the randomness of directions, the spectral information and the hierarchy of spin similarities without discarding their interactions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The absence of asymptotic spectral outliers is an assumption. A vanishing fraction of eigenvalues can be invisible to the empirical law yet strongly affect the cube’s energy. The manuscript also gives an example showing that weak convergence to an unbounded-support law is not enough for the conclusion.

For random spectra, the conditional eigenvector law must be Haar. Spectral convergence in probability gives pressure convergence in probability; almost-sure spectral hypotheses give almost-sure pressure convergence. Convergence of expectations additionally requires uniform integrability. A random external field dependent on the matrix requires the corresponding Haar condition after conditioning on both spectrum and field data.

The pressure includes diagonal self-interactions. Removing them subtracts half the limiting mean eigenvalue. Physical free energy at inverse temperature β>0\beta>0β>0 is minus the chosen pressure divided by β\betaβ, with the counting-prior correction included if appropriate.

An exact variational characterization need not identify its optimizer explicitly. Determining phase boundaries, fluctuation laws, computational complexity and concrete minimizing hierarchies are further questions. The thermodynamic limit is taken before the zero-temperature limit in the ground-state consequence; the manuscript does not require a uniform all-temperature finite-size estimate to obtain it.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the pressure theorem and definitions in Section 1, random-spectrum and optimization consequences in Section 7, and the magnetic extension in Section 8. These conventions are essential when comparing formulas.

For overlap hierarchies, Panchenko’s ultrametricity theorem provides a central structural result. Family 222 discusses related random-perceptron variational formulas; the present manuscript compares certain Gaussian quadratic cases while treating the formulas as distinct constructions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, All-temperature pressure for orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random SAT thresholds, fluctuations, and computability
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 235 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Begin with an empty Boolean formula and add random clauses one by one. Initially every assignment works. Eventually no assignment satisfies all the clauses. Three questions arise: does the transition approach a definite clause density, how much does its location fluctuate between samples, and can that limiting density be computed to arbitrary accuracy?

These questions sound similar, but they require different answers. A narrow transition may have a center that drifts with system size. A limiting constant may exist without an algorithm to approximate it. An algorithm that computes the constant may still be too slow to produce useful numerical values.

Family 235 contains four manuscripts addressing these distinctions. Their current versions credit Gaia Carenini with priority for resolving the satisfiability conjecture. The family’s contributions are presented as an alternative existence argument, sharper fluctuation bounds, and computability of the threshold for three-literal clauses.

2. Background and essential definitions

The random formula

A Boolean variable takes values zero or one. A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is an “or” of literals. A formula in conjunctive normal form is an “and” of clauses. For example, (x1∨¬x2∨x3)(x_1\lor\neg x_2\lor x_3)(x1​∨¬x2​∨x3​) is a three-literal clause.

Fix a clause size k≥3k\geq3k≥3 and n≥kn\geq kn≥k variables. A proper random clause chooses kkk distinct variables uniformly and gives each an independent fair sign. Whole clauses are sampled independently with replacement: two clauses can be identical, but a variable does not repeat within one clause.

Let

Fn,m=C1∧⋯∧Cm,pn(m)=P(Fn,m is satisfiable).F_{n,m}=C_1\land\cdots\land C_m,\qquad p_n(m)=\mathbb P(F_{n,m}\text{ is satisfiable}).Fn,m​=C1​∧⋯∧Cm​,pn​(m)=P(Fn,m​ is satisfiable).

The density is m/nm/nm/n. Adding clauses cannot restore satisfiability, so pn(m)p_n(m)pn​(m) is nonincreasing.

The first unsatisfiable index is

Hn=min⁡{m≥1:Fn,m is unsatisfiable}.H_n=\min\{m\geq1:F_{n,m}\text{ is unsatisfiable}\}.Hn​=min{m≥1:Fn,m​ is unsatisfiable}.

Consequently, pn(m)=P(Hn>m)p_n(m)=\mathbb P(H_n>m)pn​(m)=P(Hn​>m). The last satisfiable index is Hn−1H_n-1Hn​−1; this one-clause difference matters when stating exact finite-size identities.

Location, width and computation

A limiting threshold αk\alpha_kαk​ means satisfiability tends to probability one at every fixed density below αk\alpha_kαk​, and to zero at every fixed density above it. A central transition window measures how many additional clauses are required to move between two fixed probabilities, such as 0.90.90.9 and 0.10.10.1.

The variance Var⁡(Hn)\operatorname{Var}(H_n)Var(Hn​) measures fluctuations of the entire hitting-time distribution, including its tails. The notation Θk(n)\Theta_k(n)Θk​(n) means upper and lower positive constant multiples of nnn, with constants allowed to depend on fixed kkk.

A real number is computable if one fixed finite algorithm can return a rational approximation with any requested error. This says nothing about whether the algorithm runs quickly.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The two-clause problem was settled through implication-graph methods in work of Chvátal and Reed, Goerdt, and Fernandez de la Vega. For larger fixed clause sizes, Friedgut’s sharp-threshold theorem established a narrow transition around a size-dependent density. It did not prove that these densities converge. Friedgut’s theorem.

Weighted second-moment methods of Achlioptas and Peres located the threshold to leading order as kkk grows. Statistical-physics work by Mézard, Parisi, Zecchina and collaborators developed predictions based on the organization of satisfying assignments into clusters. Ding, Sly and Sun established the predicted limiting threshold for all sufficiently large fixed kkk. This left the small fixed clause sizes outside that theorem. Large-clause threshold theorem.

For transition width, Wilson proved that a fixed central probability drop needs at least order n\sqrt nn​ clauses. Carenini first obtained an upper window bound of order n/log⁡nn/\log nn/logn, then improved it to Ok,η(n1/2+1/k)O_{k,\eta}(n^{1/2+1/k})Ok,η​(n1/2+1/k) between probabilities η\etaη and 1−η1-\eta1−η. Combined with the Abbe–Montanari criterion, her paper made public on 5 October 2026 establishes limiting thresholds for every fixed k≥3k\geq3k≥3. The present manuscripts explicitly acknowledge her priority. Carenini’s resolution, earlier window paper.

The three-clause threshold has a separate numerical history. The computability manuscript recalls established lower and upper bounds of 3.523.523.52 and 4.48984.48984.4898, and the statistical-physics prediction near 4.2674.2674.267. It does not evaluate the threshold or prove equality with that prediction.

Finally, existence and computability are genuinely different mathematical properties: a computable sequence of rational numbers can converge to a noncomputable real. Therefore finite formula enumeration plus an unspecified limiting theorem does not automatically give an algorithm with a certified stopping rule. That is the gap addressed by the fourth manuscript.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: an alternative limiting-threshold argument

For every fixed integer k≥3k\geq3k≥3, M1 claims a finite positive constant αk\alpha_kαk​ such that

lim⁡n→∞pn(⌊cn⌋)={1,0≤c<αk,0,c>αk.\lim_{n\to\infty}p_n(\lfloor cn\rfloor)=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq c<\alpha_k,\\0,&c>\alpha_k.\end{cases}n→∞lim​pn​(⌊cn⌋)={1,0,​0≤c<αk​,c>αk​.​

There is no assertion at c=αkc=\alpha_kc=αk​. The manuscript describes its proof as an alternative to Carenini’s resolution, and does not identify αk\alpha_kαk​ numerically or through the physics prediction for every small kkk.

Its finite-size center is the normalized expectation of the last satisfiable index capped at 2k+1n2^{k+1}n2k+1n. Concentration of this index is combined with comparisons between different system sizes to establish convergence of the center.

M3 and M2: fluctuations of order square root of size

M3 claims

Var⁡(Hn)=Θk(n)(k≥4),\operatorname{Var}(H_n)=\Theta_k(n)\quad(k\geq4),Var(Hn​)=Θk​(n)(k≥4),

and, by its own argument, lower bound cnc ncn and upper bound Cnlog⁡nC n\log nCnlogn for k=3k=3k=3. M2 supplies the additional three-clause estimate that removes the logarithm:

Var⁡(Hn)=Θ(n)(k=3).\operatorname{Var}(H_n)=\Theta(n)\quad(k=3).Var(Hn​)=Θ(n)(k=3).

Together, they give linear variance for every fixed k≥3k\geq3k≥3. The lower bounds come from Wilson’s transition-width theorem; the new claims concern the matching upper bounds.

For a fixed 0<η<1/20<\eta<1/20<η<1/2, define

rn(p)=min⁡{m≥0:pn(m)≤p}.r_n(p)=\min\{m\geq0:p_n(m)\leq p\}.rn​(p)=min{m≥0:pn​(m)≤p}.

The combined results imply

rn(η)−rn(1−η)=Θk,η(n).r_n(\eta)-r_n(1-\eta)=\Theta_{k,\eta}(\sqrt n).rn​(η)−rn​(1−η)=Θk,η​(n​).

Thus the central width is order n\sqrt nn​ clauses, or order n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 in density. These are fluctuations around finite-size locations. They do not establish a Gaussian limiting distribution or show that EHn−αkn\mathbb E H_n-\alpha_k nEHn​−αk​n is of order n\sqrt nn​.

M3 also gives upper variance bounds for hitting times capped at any fixed positive multiple of nnn. Its matching capped lower bound requires a sufficiently late cap; a cap before the transition can remove the randomness being measured.

M4: the three-clause threshold is computable

M4 claims that one deterministic Turing machine, given the unary precision input 1r1^r1r, halts with a rational qrq_rqr​ satisfying

∣qr−α3∣≤2−r.|q_r-\alpha_3|\leq2^{-r}.∣qr​−α3​∣≤2−r.

The machine uses no oracle, advice or noncomputable real constant. It computes the limiting density, not a satisfying assignment for a supplied formula. There is no efficiency bound, no numerical evaluation of α3\alpha_3α3​, and no corresponding computability theorem here for every clause size.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the matching variance bounds settle the fluctuation order of a central random constraint problem, while the computability theorem supplies a distinct conceptual advance beyond existence.

The score accounts for the current priority statements. Threshold existence for all fixed clause sizes is credited to Carenini; this family’s existence paper is an alternative argument. Its sharper width and variance claims remain substantial: they match the earlier square-root lower bound and control the tails that a central-window statement alone need not control.

Computability is also meaningful without practical speed. It asserts that the threshold can be approached with certified error by one finite procedure. This separates a well-defined physical constant from a constant whose value might resist all such effective approximation. It does not turn random SAT into an efficiently solved problem.

6. The main idea

Delete a clause and measure the delay

A clause is pivotal at a prefix if restoring it turns a satisfiable formula into an unsatisfiable one. Delete one clause without renumbering subsequent arrivals, and measure the resulting delay in first failure. A version of the Efron–Stein variance inequality bounds the hitting-time variance by a sum of expected squared delays.

The deleted clause singles out kkk root variables. If it is pivotal, every remaining solution gives these roots the unique assignment that falsifies it. Flipping each root creates a necessary test on the other variables, involving shorter clauses. Away from collisions where another clause meets several roots, these tests can be exposed independently.

A comparison relates how easily shorter clauses destroy a set of assignments to how long it can survive ordinary clauses. Averaging the actual root-incidence counts, instead of imposing a coarse cutoff, yields the linear bound for k≥4k\geq4k≥4. At k=3k=3k=3, the same occupation estimate is borderline and produces a logarithm.

M2 introduces a bounded monotone potential built from probabilities that several two-clauses eliminate an assignment set. Its expected increase controls the time spent in the troublesome regime. This is the claimed extra ingredient removing the three-clause logarithm.

For existence in M1, concentration is followed by an interpolation comparing one large formula to formulas on smaller blocks. Errors that are summable along geometrically increasing sizes prevent the normalized centers from drifting indefinitely.

Search from both sides of the constant

M4 constructs finite certificates for lower and upper bounds on α3\alpha_3α3​. Lower certificates come from explicit deletion estimates and finite enumeration in an auxiliary Poisson clause process. This auxiliary model permits repeated variables within a clause; separate comparisons transfer its threshold conclusions to the proper model.

For upper certificates, soften satisfiability by penalizing each violated clause. If Vn(σ)V_n(\sigma)Vn​(σ) is the number of violations, define

Zn(a,β)=∑σe−βVn(σ),P(a,β)=lim⁡n→∞1nElog⁡Zn(a,β).Z_n(a,\beta)=\sum_\sigma e^{-\beta V_n(\sigma)},\qquad P(a,\beta)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\log Z_n(a,\beta).Zn​(a,β)=σ∑​e−βVn​(σ),P(a,β)=n→∞lim​n1​ElogZn​(a,β).

The parameter aaa is density and β>0\beta>0β>0 is the penalty. Below the threshold this pressure is nonnegative. The manuscript claims that above the threshold a positive density of unavoidable violations makes it negative for some finite penalty.

Finite rational descriptions of hierarchical trials provide computable upper bounds on this pressure and approximate its infimum. A certified negative trial therefore certifies an upper bound on α3\alpha_3α3​, and such a trial exists at every rational density strictly above it.

The algorithm fairly interleaves all lower-certificate calculations and all candidate upper-certificate searches. It stops when the certified interval is short enough. It does not need a computable rate at which finite-size expectations converge, because the interval itself supplies the stopping test.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All fluctuation constants concern a fixed clause size. The statements do not claim uniform estimates when kkk grows with nnn, arbitrary clause distributions, biased signs, or other random constraint languages.

The proper-clause model samples whole clauses with replacement but uses distinct variables inside each clause. Poissonization and repeated-variable clauses occur in intermediate arguments; their equivalence for a particular conclusion requires the transfers stated in the papers.

Linear variance and square-root central windows do not identify a limiting distribution, its variance constant, or the finite-size bias relative to αkn\alpha_k nαk​n. Those finer questions remain outside the claims. Strict-side threshold theorems also leave the probability at the exact critical density unspecified.

The computability result does not confirm the numerical prediction near 4.2674.2674.267, provide a useful runtime, or settle worst-case SAT complexity. Its soft-pressure construction for three clauses is a substantive additional argument; it should not be inferred from an even-clause interpolation theorem such as the one discussed in family 221.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the alternative existence argument. M3 develops the general clause-deletion variance framework, and M2 closes its three-clause logarithmic gap. M4 supplies the two-sided certificate search and the soft-pressure completeness statement needed for computability.

For the historical division between sharpness and convergence, read Friedgut’s theorem alongside Carenini’s October 2026 paper. Ding, Sly and Sun’s large-clause theorem explains the earlier regime where the threshold was already identified with the statistical-physics prediction. Wilson’s On the critical exponents of random k-SAT (2002) supplies the lower window bound credited throughout this family.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Limiting Satisfiability Threshold for Every Fixed Clause Size (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Linear Variance of the Random 3-SAT Hitting Time (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Variance of the Random k-SAT Hitting Time (September 27, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Computing the Random 3-SAT Threshold (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Lipschitz random surfaces: Gaussian fields and a tuned SLE₄ interface
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 232 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Choose a random surface subject only to a local slope restriction: neighboring heights may differ by at most one. Although each slope is bounded, a large surface can wander over many height levels. What is the continuum law of its fluctuations, and what does a contour separating positive from negative heights become?

These questions are basic tests of universality for random surfaces. The expected field is the Gaussian free field, or GFF. In a suitable two-boundary-arc setup, the expected interface is Schramm–Loewner evolution with parameter four.

Family 232 contains three manuscripts about triangular-lattice models. One treats weighted integer heights with zero boundary data. Another treats uniform odd-integer heights with boundary values plus and minus one. The third treats real-valued heights uniformly sampled from a convex polytope, with a specially tuned boundary amplitude for its interface theorem.

The models share a broad physical picture, but their height units, probability measures, boundary conditions, and normalizing constants differ. In particular, the integer field claims do not include an integer-interface theorem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Three versions of a hard slope constraint

The triangular lattice has basis vectors (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) and (1/2,3/2)(1/2,\sqrt3/2)(1/2,3​/2). Its nearest neighbors lie in three unoriented directions. At mesh δ\deltaδ, multiply all spatial coordinates by δ\deltaδ.

For integer heights, the constraint is

h(u)∈Z,∣h(u)−h(v)∣≤1(u∼v).h(u)\in\mathbb Z,\qquad |h(u)-h(v)|\leq1\quad(u\sim v).h(u)∈Z,∣h(u)−h(v)∣≤1(u∼v).

M1 gives an admissible configuration weight xN(h)x^{N(h)}xN(h), where N(h)N(h)N(h) counts unordered adjacent pairs with unequal heights. Thus x=1x=1x=1 is uniform, while smaller xxx penalizes steps. Its boundary layer is fixed at zero.

M2 uses odd integers and neighboring differences zero or two. Two marked boundary points divide the boundary into arcs with heights +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. The transformed height H=(h−1)/2H=(h-1)/2H=(h−1)/2 has integer values, unit allowed steps, and boundary values zero and minus one. This change of units multiplies fluctuation amplitudes by two.

M3 instead permits real heights with ∣h(u)−h(v)∣≤1|h(u)-h(v)|\leq1∣h(u)−h(v)∣≤1. With fixed boundary values, the admissible free coordinates form a bounded convex polytope. Uniform means normalized Lebesgue measure on that polytope, not equal weight on a finite set of configurations.

A hard constraint differs from a smooth energetic penalty. Its interaction is flat where slopes are allowed and infinite outside. Theorems requiring a smooth uniformly convex potential therefore do not apply by direct substitution.

Fields are tested by averages

Let DDD be the limiting planar domain. The zero-Dirichlet GFF ΦD\Phi_DΦD​ is a centered Gaussian random distribution with covariance

E[ΦD(f)ΦD(g)]=∬D×Df(z)GD(z,w)g(w) dz dw,GD=(−ΔD)−1.\mathbb E[\Phi_D(f)\Phi_D(g)]=\iint_{D\times D}f(z)G_D(z,w)g(w)\,dz\,dw,\qquad G_D=(-\Delta_D)^{-1}.E[ΦD​(f)ΦD​(g)]=∬D×D​f(z)GD​(z,w)g(w)dzdw,GD​=(−ΔD​)−1.

Here f,gf,gf,g are smooth compactly supported test functions, and ΔD\Delta_DΔD​ is the Euclidean Laplacian with zero boundary condition. The Green function has singular part (2π)−1log⁡(1/∣z−w∣)(2\pi)^{-1}\log(1/|z-w|)(2π)−1log(1/∣z−w∣).

A lattice field is compared with this object through Euclidean area integrals against tests. Such averages can have finite limiting fluctuations even though the height at a single point has a variance growing logarithmically as the mesh shrinks. No division by log⁡(1/δ)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}log(1/δ)​ is used in these distribution-valued limits.

Nonzero boundary data contribute a deterministic harmonic profile. Harmonic measure ωD(z,A)\omega_D(z,A)ωD​(z,A) is the probability that Brownian motion started at zzz first exits through boundary arc AAA; it gives the harmonic extension of that arc’s indicator.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Schramm’s problem collection separately asks about the odd-integer model with two arcs and the real-valued Lipschitz model. Each has a field question, and the contour question demands further information beyond field convergence.

The loop representation links integer Lipschitz heights on the triangular lattice to the loop O(2) model on its hexagonal dual. Duminil-Copin, Glazman, Peled, and Spinka established macroscopic loops at the predicted critical point. Glazman and Manolescu proved logarithmic variations for the uniform integer model and developed a useful two-spin representation.

Glazman and Lammers extended delocalization and logarithmic fluctuation estimates across a broader parameter range. Subsequent work of Glazman, Harel, and Zelesko supplied another delocalization approach. These results establish roughness, but logarithmic covariance growth alone does not identify a Gaussian joint law.

For real surfaces with smooth uniformly convex interactions, homogenization and coupling methods already yield GFF behavior. Miller’s bounded-domain theorem is a key predecessor, and his contour universality work extends the discrete Gaussian contour picture to smooth gradient models. The hard flat/infinite interaction considered here lies outside those assumptions.

Miłoś and Peled developed delocalization methods for hard-core surfaces, including uniform Lipschitz constraints, on square tori. Further controlled-gradient results provide inputs for the real model. They do not themselves identify the bounded-domain field and contour limits claimed here.

For the integer arguments, reflection positivity, transfer spectra, and harmonic moment analysis also have substantial precedents in the 2026 six-vertex work of Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers, and Manolescu. The triangular models still require their own conditional comparisons, boundary analysis, and normalization; family 225 discusses the distinct square-lattice plane theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Weighted integer heights with zero boundary values

M1 fixes

12≤x≤1.\frac1{\sqrt2}\leq x\leq1.2​1​≤x≤1.

Its domain is bounded with a C2C^2C2 Jordan boundary, approximated from inside by simple hexagonal-lattice cycles. The enclosed faces have triangular-lattice centers. Every compact subset is eventually included, and boundary parametrizations converge uniformly.

For the weighted integer law with zero boundary-layer heights, M1 claims a constant σ(x)>0\sigma(x)>0σ(x)>0, independent of the domain and its admissible approximation, such that

hδσ(x)⟹ΦDin the space of distributions on D.\frac{h_\delta}{\sigma(x)}\Longrightarrow\Phi_D\quad\text{in the space of distributions on }D.σ(x)hδ​​⟹ΦD​in the space of distributions on D.

The height is extended constantly across each hexagonal face, and test weights are the actual face integrals. The statement includes tightness, joint convergence of all finite families of smooth-test integrals, and convergence of their mixed moments.

The constant is implicit. No formula for σ(x)\sigma(x)σ(x), nor independence from xxx, is asserted. The left endpoint is described as the predicted critical value for this loop model; the field theorem does not give a complete phase diagram outside the displayed interval.

The loop correspondence is exact: unequal neighboring heights create mutually vertex-disjoint hexagonal loops, and choosing each loop’s orientation gives its signed height increment. Forgetting orientations produces weight

2#loopsx#occupied edges.2^{\#\text{loops}}x^{\#\text{occupied edges}}.2#loopsx#occupied edges.

M1’s result concerns the field. It does not claim convergence of this entire loop collection.

Uniform odd heights with two boundary arcs

M2 uses bounded smooth simply connected domains and triangular-lattice polygonal approximations with uniformly converging marked boundaries. The discrete marks lie at edge midpoints, so no boundary vertex receives conflicting values.

For uniform odd heights with boundary values +1+1+1 and −1-1−1, M2 claims

hδ⟹gˉ+σoddΦD,hδ−Ehδσodd⟹ΦD.h_\delta\Longrightarrow\bar g+\sigma_{\rm odd}\Phi_D,\qquad\frac{h_\delta-\mathbb Eh_\delta}{\sigma_{\rm odd}}\Longrightarrow\Phi_D.hδ​⟹gˉ​+σodd​ΦD​,σodd​hδ​−Ehδ​​⟹ΦD​.

The height is interpolated affinely over triangles. The function gˉ\bar ggˉ​ is the bounded harmonic extension of the two boundary values, and expectations of smooth-test integrals converge to the corresponding integrals of gˉ\bar ggˉ​. Joint mixed moments converge as well.

The positive constant σodd\sigma_{\rm odd}σodd​ depends only on this lattice model. The manuscript specifies it through an absolutely convergent series of finite-volume counts and Fourier coefficients. This is an implicit normalization, not an elementary numerical formula.

The source uses an annulus estimate from M1 at x=1x=1x=1, but not M1’s weighted field-convergence theorem. The common method does not license identifying the two constants or extending M1 to weighted two-arc data.

Real heights and the tuned zero contour

M3 considers real heights with boundary values +λ∗+\lambda_*+λ∗​ and −λ∗-\lambda_*−λ∗​. It claims the existence of a domain-independent amplitude λ∗∈(0,1/2]\lambda_*\in(0,1/2]λ∗​∈(0,1/2] for which the zero contour between the marked boundary points converges to chordal SLE4\mathrm{SLE}_4SLE4​.

The upper bound on λ∗\lambda_*λ∗​ makes the adjacent boundary prescriptions compatible with unit slope constraints. After affine interpolation, each triangular face has at most one zero segment almost surely; these segments form loops and the distinguished boundary-to-boundary contour.

The claimed convergence retains the entire oriented curve in uniform distance modulo increasing changes of speed. It also gives the centered field limit

hδ−Ehδσreal⟹ΦD,\frac{h_\delta-\mathbb Eh_\delta}{\sigma_{\rm real}}\Longrightarrow\Phi_D,σreal​hδ​−Ehδ​​⟹ΦD​,

with harmonic limiting mean

mD(z)=λ∗(ωD(z,A+)−ωD(z,A−)).m_D(z)=\lambda_*\bigl(\omega_D(z,A_+)-\omega_D(z,A_-)\bigr).mD​(z)=λ∗​(ωD​(z,A+​)−ωD​(z,A−​)).

A positive stationary tangent-flux coefficient AAA determines the constants. With lattice vertex density v=2/3v=2/\sqrt3v=2/3​, the source’s normalization is

σreal2=1vA,λ∗2=π8vA=π8σreal2.\sigma_{\rm real}^2=\frac1{vA},\qquad\lambda_*^2=\frac\pi{8vA}=\frac\pi8\sigma_{\rm real}^2.σreal2​=vA1​,λ∗2​=8vAπ​=8π​σreal2​.

The coefficient measures the effective macroscopic response of the constrained surface to a small tilt. It is defined through the stationary cell construction, without a proposed elementary closed form. The theorem singles out this tuned amplitude; it does not say that every two-arc amplitude produces ordinary SLE₄.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. These are basic hard-constraint random surfaces, with no smooth quadratic energy that directly forces Gaussian behavior. The claimed results would strengthen roughness estimates into full field laws and, for the real model, identify the geometry of a distinguished contour.

The weighted interval connects the uniform integer surface to the predicted critical endpoint. The two-arc theorems retain the actual imposed boundary profile, rather than only a translation-invariant bulk covariance. The real-interface claim supplies information that distributional field convergence alone cannot deliver.

The constants also matter. Gaussian universality permits a model-dependent stiffness, and the contour height must be tuned to that same stiffness. The displayed relation explains how field normalization and interface boundary conditions fit together in the real model.

The rating concerns the combined mathematical claims as stated, while preserving the different models and the earlier delocalization and smooth-potential results on which the developments build.

6. The main idea

For integer heights, the manuscripts encode height residues using two spin variables. Appropriate circuits reveal enough information to cut a region off from its exterior while leaving the correct conditional law inside. In the weighted setting, the recorded exploration history must include the relevant spins as well as auxiliary cell statuses; a less informative conditioning need not preserve the required order inequalities.

Reflection through lattice rows creates a positive transfer operator. Its spectral representation constrains possible large-scale covariances. Combining all three triangular-lattice reflection directions forces the claimed inverse-square frequency structure, the Fourier counterpart of a logarithmic Green kernel. A further identity determines a unique positive coefficient.

That still leaves the true boundary condition and Gaussianity. The papers compare fields with separated pinned regions, control rare conditioning events multiplicatively, and move the pins through reflected configurations. Boundary attachment estimates then recover the harmonic profile. Away from collisions, limiting moment functions are harmonic; their logarithmic collision singularities and boundary values lead to the Gaussian pairing rule for higher moments.

The real model uses the geometry of its convex height polytope. Local slack and volume losses control large averages. Reflected Brownian couplings compare boundary-conditioned surfaces, and a stationary response problem identifies the effective stiffness. Small tilts then determine Gaussian fluctuations.

For the contour, conditioning on an explored segment continually changes the polytope. The source supplies conditional covariance and barrier estimates for those changing domains, then determines the effective height gap across the interface. A stopped harmonic observable identifies the SLE₄ driver, while additional separation and nonreturn estimates retain the whole ordered curve. This extra geometric work is why the field and interface conclusions are separate achievements.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The integer models use discrete counting measures; the real model uses Lebesgue volume. Their normalizations are not interchangeable. Nor should the six-vertex multiplier from family 225 be inserted into these triangular-lattice statements.

M1 assumes zero boundary data and an inside approximation of a C2C^2C2 Jordan domain. M2 and M3 have their own smooth-domain, two-arc approximation conventions. Arbitrary rough boundaries, nonzero macroscopic slopes, or weighted two-arc laws require further results.

The real interface is tuned to one amplitude. The corresponding contour question for uniform odd-integer heights remains separate from M2’s field theorem. The sources do not infer a full loop-ensemble limit merely from the GFF limits.

Pointwise height tightness is not claimed. Finite fluctuations of smooth averages coexist with divergent microscopic variance. Quantitative rates, explicit evaluations of the stiffness constants, and wider boundary or parameter classes remain questions beyond the stated conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

Schramm’s Problems 2.2 and 2.3 distinguish the integer and real questions. Glazman–Manolescu and Glazman–Lammers give the integer roughness background; Miłoś–Peled and Miller explain important hard-constraint and smooth-potential predecessors.

M1 below is the weighted zero-boundary field theorem, M2 the uniform odd-height two-arc theorem, and M3 the real-valued field and tuned-interface theorem. Their current source statements and normalization conventions are used separately throughout this digest.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Gaussian free-field limits of weighted integer Lipschitz heights (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Gaussian free field limit of integer Lipschitz heights with two-arc boundary data (October 6, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Uniform real Lipschitz surfaces on the triangular lattice (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The 3/4 size exponent for honeycomb self-avoiding walks
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 237 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A self-avoiding walk cannot visit the same vertex twice. It is a simple model of a polymer whose different parts cannot occupy the same location. If the walk has nnn steps, how large a region does it occupy?

In two dimensions, the predicted answer is a linear size of order n3/4n^{3/4}n3/4, intermediate between the square-root scale of an ordinary random walk and the linear scale of a straight path. The reciprocal exponent 4/34/34/3 describes how the number of visited sites grows with spatial scale.

Family 237 contains thirteen manuscripts developing this prediction on the regular honeycomb lattice. Its strongest fixed-length statement concerns the diameter, local mass and covering numbers of a uniform walk at every sufficiently large integer length. Other papers treat critically weighted bridges, prescribed boundary chords, polygons, infinite walks and thermally discounted walks.

The sampling law matters throughout. A mean length in a strip is not automatically a theorem about a uniform walk of one exact length, and a diameter lower bound does not force the two endpoints to be far apart.

2. Background and essential definitions

Walks, size and critical weights

Fix a vertex ooo of the honeycomb graph. An nnn-step self-avoiding walk is a sequence γ=(γ0,…,γn)\gamma=(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_n)γ=(γ0​,…,γn​), starting at ooo, with adjacent consecutive vertices and no repeated vertex. Let cnc_ncn​ be their number and choose one uniformly.

Three size statistics are useful:

D(γ)=max⁡i,j∣γi−γj∣,A(γ)=∣γn−o∣,Mγ(z,s)=#{γi:∣γi−z∣≤s}.D(\gamma)=\max_{i,j}|\gamma_i-\gamma_j|,\qquad A(\gamma)=|\gamma_n-o|,\qquad M_\gamma(z,s)=\#\{\gamma_i:|\gamma_i-z|\leq s\}.D(γ)=i,jmax​∣γi​−γj​∣,A(γ)=∣γn​−o∣,Mγ​(z,s)=#{γi​:∣γi​−z∣≤s}.

They are respectively diameter, endpoint distance and local mass in a ball. Let Nγ(s)N_\gamma(s)Nγ​(s) be the fewest radius-sss balls covering the visited vertices. Distances are Euclidean in a fixed regular embedding.

An alternative ensemble allows every length and gives a path of length LLL the critical weight

ρL,ρ=(2+2)−1/2.\rho^L,\qquad \rho=(2+\sqrt2)^{-1/2}.ρL,ρ=(2+2​)−1/2.

The reciprocal 1/ρ1/\rho1/ρ is the honeycomb connective constant, the exponential growth rate of cnc_ncn​. A weight sum is a mass, not a probability until divided by its total.

Boundary paths use ports, midpoints of boundary edges. Their length counts visited vertices, and ports have no weight. This convention lets adjoining path pieces multiply weights exactly. A bridge goes from one strip boundary to the other without another boundary visit; an arch returns to its starting boundary. A polygon is an unoriented simple cycle. Polygon sums modulo translations count each translated shape once.

Reading exponent statements

For a positive deterministic quantity, f(R)=Ra+o(1)f(R)=R^{a+o(1)}f(R)=Ra+o(1) means log⁡f(R)/log⁡R→a\log f(R)/\log R\to alogf(R)/logR→a. It permits subpower corrections and does not assert a limiting amplitude. The stronger notation f(R)≍Raf(R)\asymp R^af(R)≍Ra means upper and lower fixed positive multiples.

For random variables, an exponent statement in probability means that, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, the quantity lies between the two powers with exponents a−εa-\varepsilona−ε and a+εa+\varepsilona+ε with probability tending to one. An almost-sure statement is stronger and is identified separately below.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nienhuis’s analysis of the dilute loop model predicted the honeycomb critical point and the two-dimensional polymer exponents, including 3/43/43/4. Lawler, Schramm and Werner later formulated the conjectural connection between planar self-avoiding walk and SLE₈/₃, a conformally invariant random curve. That picture explains a coherent set of exponent predictions, but a prediction from a conjectured scaling limit is not a lattice theorem. Nienhuis’s work, scaling-limit conjectures.

Duminil-Copin and Smirnov proved the exact connective constant using a parafermionic observable: a weighted sum of paths with complex phases recording their winding. Its local cancellation yields a positive boundary identity after summing over a domain. This determines the critical activity, but not the full size exponent. Connective-constant theorem.

Subsequent work improved control of critical strip crossings. Beaton, Bousquet-Mélou, de Gier, Duminil-Copin and Guttmann proved that crossing mass tends to zero. Glazman and Manolescu obtained further bounds and boundary two-point invariance for a specified class of integrable rhombic deformations. Krachun and Panagiotis proved polynomial decay of strip mass and a quantitative sub-ballistic bound: uniform honeycomb walks remain within order n/log⁡nn/\log nn/logn of their origin with high probability. Strip decay, rhombic boundary results, quantitative sub-ballisticity.

Kesten’s bridge renewal method supplies another foundation. A bridge splits at lines crossed exactly once into irreducible pieces; critically weighted pieces can be concatenated independently. Later work developed infinite half-plane and strip laws through this representation. Kesten’s paper, strip and infinite-walk laws.

This family claims the sharper quantitative inputs and changes of ensemble needed to reach the predicted exponents. Its geometric conclusions rely on the accompanying analytic manuscripts, rather than following from the previously known connective constant alone.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Every fixed length: diameter, mass and covering

M4 claims that for every δ>0\delta>0δ>0 and q>0q>0q>0, with probability at least 1−Cδ,qn−q1-C_{\delta,q}n^{-q}1−Cδ,q​n−q, a uniform nnn-step walk simultaneously satisfies

n3/4−δ≤D(γ)≤n3/4+δ,n^{3/4-\delta}\leq D(\gamma)\leq n^{3/4+\delta},n3/4−δ≤D(γ)≤n3/4+δ,
n−δmin⁡{n,s4/3}≤Mγ(z,s)≤nδmin⁡{n,s4/3},n^{-\delta}\min\{n,s^{4/3}\}\leq M_\gamma(z,s)\leq n^\delta\min\{n,s^{4/3}\},n−δmin{n,s4/3}≤Mγ​(z,s)≤nδmin{n,s4/3},

and

n−δ(1+ns−4/3)≤Nγ(s)≤nδ(1+ns−4/3).n^{-\delta}(1+ns^{-4/3})\leq N_\gamma(s)\leq n^\delta(1+ns^{-4/3}).n−δ(1+ns−4/3)≤Nγ​(s)≤nδ(1+ns−4/3).

The last two bounds hold for every visited vertex zzz and every real 1≤s≤n1\leq s\leq n1≤s≤n. They apply to all sufficiently large integer nnn, with no subsequence or parity restriction for this ordinary vertex-rooted walk.

The paper also claims the same size exponent for the radius of gyration, the root mean square distance of visited vertices from their average position. Every fixed positive moment of diameter or radius of gyration has exponent 3p/43p/43p/4 for moment order ppp. Spans in each of the three lattice-normal directions have matching lower exponents.

These are discrete geometric statements. They do not assert that the rescaled path converges to a continuum curve or identify the Hausdorff dimension of such a limit.

Critical crossings and polygons

M11 claims critical strip-crossing mass Bh≍h−1/4B_h\asymp h^{-1/4}Bh​≍h−1/4, with a fixed source port and terminal port summed over the opposite wall. It also controls a first horizontal-displacement moment of returning paths, of order h3/4h^{3/4}h3/4.

M12 sharpens finite bridge information: the first-length mass is at most Ch13/12Ch^{13/12}Ch13/12, and mass at least ch−1/4ch^{-1/4}ch−1/4 is carried by bridges of length at least ch4/3ch^{4/3}ch4/3. Together with the total mass, this gives a bridge mean comparable to h4/3h^{4/3}h4/3. M8 obtains the exponent for both unrestricted bridges and bridges confined to a sufficiently wide fixed corridor. M9 gives another construction with logarithmically widening confinement.

For unrooted polygon classes, M1 claims

∑D(γ)≥RρL(γ)=R−2+o(1),∑D(γ)≥RL(γ)ρL(γ)=R−2/3+o(1),\sum_{D(\gamma)\geq R}\rho^{L(\gamma)}=R^{-2+o(1)},\qquad\sum_{D(\gamma)\geq R}L(\gamma)\rho^{L(\gamma)}=R^{-2/3+o(1)},D(γ)≥R∑​ρL(γ)=R−2+o(1),D(γ)≥R∑​L(γ)ρL(γ)=R−2/3+o(1),

and a truncated squared-length bound

∑D(γ)≤RL(γ)2ρL(γ)≤R2/3+o(1).\sum_{D(\gamma)\leq R}L(\gamma)^2\rho^{L(\gamma)}\leq R^{2/3+o(1)}.D(γ)≤R∑​L(γ)2ρL(γ)≤R2/3+o(1).

Under either unweighted or length-weighted critical polygon mass, conditioning on L≥nL\geq nL≥n then gives diameter n3/4+o(1)n^{3/4+o(1)}n3/4+o(1) in probability. This is a length-cutoff ensemble, not a polygon of one prescribed length.

Chords and other walk laws

M2 claims length R4/3+o(1)R^{4/3+o(1)}R4/3+o(1) in probability for critical chords between prescribed, macroscopically separated side-interior ports of regular-hexagon approximations. It also treats specified half-plane, parallel-strip and nonparallel-cut geometries with nondegenerate endpoint clearances. Half-plane arches additionally have the matching mean exponent. Its more specialized strip endpoint means retain their density-one-height or critically weighted even-height-mixture conventions.

M10 claims endpoint distance n3/4+o(1)n^{3/4+o(1)}n3/4+o(1) almost surely for the infinite irreducible-bridge walk. Uniform strict bridges have terminal distance and diameter with that exponent for every sufficiently large compatible even vertex length. For unrestricted full-plane and half-plane walks, its endpoint lower law holds on a common density-one set of lengths: the fraction of excluded integers up to NNN tends to zero.

Thermally discounted walks have weight ρLe−L/N\rho^L e^{-L/N}ρLe−L/N. At every large discount scale NNN, M10 claims L=N1+o(1)L=N^{1+o(1)}L=N1+o(1) and endpoint distance and diameter N3/4+o(1)N^{3/4+o(1)}N3/4+o(1), with matching positive-moment exponents. It also treats prescribed thermal endpoints at that spatial scale. Its near-critical inverse correlation scale is t3/4+o(1)t^{3/4+o(1)}t3/4+o(1), and the small-force free energy is s4/3+o(1)s^{4/3+o(1)}s4/3+o(1), with force response s1/3+o(1)s^{1/3+o(1)}s1/3+o(1). These conclusions have their own orders of limits.

How the thirteen manuscripts fit together

Several papers develop overlapping constructions and stronger versions of particular inputs. Their roles can be summarized without treating them as thirteen independent fixed-length theorems.

ManuscriptMain contribution in the family
M1Radial transfer estimates, polygon tails and length-cutoff laws
M2Chords with prescribed boundary ports and qualified endpoint means
M3Separating-loop partition exponents for every fixed positive fugacity; planar nesting
M4Exact-length diameter, local mass, covering and gyration statements
M5Signed cylinder propagation, free-boundary hexagon means and marked-polygon bounds
M6Logarithmic length windows after averaging bridge mass over heights
M7Squared-length polygon estimates and bounds for one marked arc
M8Disk transfer construction and bridge means in a fixed corridor
M9Polynomial transfer states, bridge means and free-boundary hexagon visits
M10Renewal estimates and transfers to infinite, thermal and fixed-length laws
M11Bounded-factor strip-crossing exponent
M12Uniform two-mark bounds, sharp finite bridge moments and positive long-bridge mass
M13Cylinder amplitudes selected by boundary caps and free-boundary triangle means

For instance, at loop fugacity two—an extra factor two per polygon—M3 and M5 obtain cylinder nesting exponent 1/61/61/6 and planar exponent 1/121/121/12. M3 gives a parameter-dependent exponent for every fixed positive fugacity. M12 obtains bounded-factor planar nesting estimates in its stated domains. M13’s triangle chord mean is R4/3+o(1)R^{4/3+o(1)}R4/3+o(1), with both ports summed and a macroscopic diameter cutoff; it is not the prescribed-port law of M2.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the fixed-length size and mass exponents would settle central geometric predictions for a canonical two-dimensional polymer model. The surrounding boundary and polygon results would provide a substantial quantitative theory supporting those exponents.

The local mass statement gives more than a single overall radius: roughly s4/3s^{4/3}s4/3 visited sites lie near each point at scale sss, subject to the stated power slack. The covering statement expresses the corresponding number of spatial pieces needed to describe the trace.

The significance also lies in connecting distinct ensembles carefully. Fixed-length counting, infinite concatenation and critical boundary weights are useful for different purposes. Establishing the normalization and rare-event controls needed to move between them is a major part of the claimed contribution.

6. The main idea

The analytic papers start from exact lattice identities. Finite transfer matrices encode how partial paths and loops connect across a moving cut. Integrable local relations allow changes in those cuts and yield algebraic expressions for selected boundary states and marked observables.

These transformed expressions can have complex or signed terms even though the original walk weights are positive. A formal leading power is therefore insufficient: its coefficient could cancel. The papers develop normalization, nonvanishing and uniform remainder estimates to connect the transformed calculations back to positive path sums. Marking two points on a polygon records a squared-length quantity after summing the marks, providing control over unusually long paths packed into a small region.

The geometric papers then sew paths through corridors while keeping the joining lines recoverable. Recoverability bounds how many input constructions can produce the same output walk. First and second moments give positive mass to long bridges; independent irreducible pieces amplify these estimates through renewal arguments.

For exact-length conclusions, a generating-function estimate is not enough: one needs lower bounds on the coefficient or renewal probability at the chosen length. M10 develops such local renewal estimates for compatible bridge lengths. M4 obtains absolute bounds on the critical mass of bad geometric behavior, controls all subpaths and repeated visits to balls, and divides by a fixed-length normalization bounded below using submultiplicativity.

This last passage is why the family can state a diameter theorem for every length while retaining a weaker density-one qualification for the unrestricted endpoint lower law.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The family concerns the regular honeycomb lattice and the specified critical weights. Integrable deformations used inside arguments are not a universality theorem for every planar lattice.

The ordinary fixed-length diameter theorem does not establish an endpoint-distance lower bound at every length. A long loop-like excursion can have a large diameter while ending near its starting point. The endpoint lower statement summarized from M10 retains its density-one qualification.

No manuscript here claims convergence of the uniform walk to SLE₈/₃. Consequently, continuum conformal invariance, a continuum parametrization and a continuum Hausdorff-dimension theorem should not be read into the discrete exponent conclusions.

Means, typical values and unnormalized masses must also remain distinct. M6’s logarithmic window averages over a range of heights. M13 sums both endpoints. M1 conditions polygon length from below. The prescribed-port, fixed-height and exact-length statements require their own additional estimates and cannot be substituted for these laws without justification.

Exact amplitudes and correction terms are not supplied by an o(1)o(1)o(1) exponent. Removing the endpoint exceptional lengths, establishing the continuum scaling limit and extending the geometric theory beyond the honeycomb setting remain further directions beyond the stated results.

8. Sources and further reading

For the main geometric claims, begin with M4 and M10, then consult their explicitly cited finite inputs. M11 and M12 give comparatively direct statements of the strip and marked-polygon estimates. M2 is the source for prescribed boundary endpoints; the table above locates the other ensembles.

Duminil-Copin and Smirnov’s connective-constant paper explains the critical activity and boundary observable. Lawler, Schramm and Werner’s scaling-limit discussion provides the larger conjectural picture. The exponents reported here are the manuscripts’ lattice claims, rather than consequences assumed from that conjecture.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Radial transfer estimates and polygon length laws for honeycomb walks (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Critical honeycomb chords with prescribed boundary endpoints (September 26, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Cylinder loop weights and planar nesting (September 26, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Mass and covering exponents for fixed-length honeycomb walks (September 26, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Signed cylinder propagation and marked polygons on the honeycomb lattice (September 26, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Cylinder amplitudes and logarithmic bridge-length windows on the honeycomb lattice (September 26, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Marked polygon correlations and one-arc bounds (September 26, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, Disk transfer representations and confined bridge mass (September 26, 2026).
  • M9. OpenAI, Polynomial vacuum representations and bridge mass for honeycomb walks (September 26, 2026).
  • M10. OpenAI, Renewal and changes of law for critical honeycomb walks (September 26, 2026).
  • M11. OpenAI, Critical strip-crossing mass on the honeycomb lattice (September 26, 2026).
  • M12. OpenAI, Uniform marked-polygon estimates and sharp finite bridge moments (September 26, 2026).
  • M13. OpenAI, Cap-selected amplitudes and triangle chords for honeycomb walks (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Optimal-order mixing of the Thorp shuffle
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 238 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Split a deck into equal halves. Pair cards in corresponding positions, independently toss a fair coin to decide the order of each pair, and interleave the pairs. This is one complete Thorp shuffle.

For a deck of n=2dn=2^dn=2d cards, a single card is uniformly distributed after ddd shuffles. Does this mean the whole deck is random? No: different cards share switches, so their positions can retain joint information even when every individual position looks uniform.

Family 238 contains twelve manuscripts claiming that a constant multiple of ddd complete shuffles suffices to randomize the full permutation. Since a simple counting obstruction already requires order ddd, this gives the optimal order Θ(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n)Θ(logn) for decks whose sizes are powers of two.

The family develops several arguments and additional conditional statements. Its constants are bounds, not an identification of the precise number of shuffles needed in the leading asymptotic term.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measuring the full deck

A deck ordering is a permutation in the symmetric group SnS_nSn​, the set of all n!n!n! bijections from card labels to positions. Let UnU_nUn​ be the uniform distribution on this group, and qdq_dqd​ the permutation law of one physical shuffle.

Independent successive shuffles compose permutations. Their ttt-step law is denoted by qd∗tq_d^{*t}qd∗t​, where the asterisk means convolution. For two probability laws,

∥μ−ν∥TV=12∑π∈Sn∣μ(π)−ν(π)∣\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\pi\in S_n}|\mu(\pi)-\nu(\pi)|∥μ−ν∥TV​=21​π∈Sn​∑​∣μ(π)−ν(π)∣

is their total-variation distance. Equivalently, it is the largest difference in probability they assign to the same event. Small full-deck distance therefore controls every statistic of the deck, including joint positions of any selected cards.

The mixing time here is the first integer ttt for which this distance is at most 1/41/41/4. Starting from a different deterministic deck translates the permutation law and leaves its distance from uniform unchanged.

Binary coordinates and sweeps

Label positions by binary strings (x1,…,xd)(x_1,\ldots,x_d)(x1​,…,xd​). A physical Thorp shuffle can be written

(x1,u)⟼(u,x1+ξu),(x_1,u)\longmapsto(u,x_1+\xi_u),(x1​,u)⟼(u,x1​+ξu​),

where addition is modulo two, uuu contains the other bits, and the ξu\xi_uξu​ are independent fair bits.

Removing the deterministic cyclic rotation turns successive shuffles into switch layers along successive coordinate directions of the binary cube. One coordinate sweep visits all ddd directions once. It costs ddd physical shuffles, not one.

A card has each coordinate refreshed once during a sweep, explaining its uniform marginal. The other cards still constrain which collective routes are possible.

Partial observations miss global information

Even observing nearly every card can miss something. A uniformly random even permutation has exactly uniform joint images for any chosen list of at most n−2n-2n−2 labels, yet its full law has total-variation distance 1/21/21/2 from uniform on SnS_nSn​. Its parity is fixed.

This example explains why a proof based on partial decks must separately control the information omitted by those observations. Parity is one obstruction; representation theory organizes all such modes of dependence.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thorp introduced the shuffle in his 1973 study of nonrandom shuffling and Faro. Its simple mechanism became a difficult mixing-time problem because local randomness spreads through a highly structured switching network. Original paper.

Morris obtained the first upper bound polynomial in ddd, of order d44d^{44}d44, using evolving sets and a chameleon process describing conditional card probabilities. Montenegro and Tetali improved the exponent to 292929 through spectral-profile and evolving-set methods. Morris’s first bound, Montenegro–Tetali analysis.

Entropy methods brought further progress. Morris proved an O((log⁡n)4)O((\log n)^4)O((logn)4) bound for arbitrary even deck sizes, then an O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3) bound for n=2dn=2^dn=2d. The optimal logarithmic order remained beyond those estimates. General even decks, dyadic cubic-logarithmic bound.

Partial decks have their own history. Morris, Rogaway and Stegers studied ordered lists of cards in connection with enciphering on small domains. Czumaj and Vöcking showed that order (log⁡n)2(\log n)^2(logn)2 shuffles mix any fixed fraction of the deck strictly below one. Such marginal statements are useful, but they leave a separate passage to the full permutation law. Enciphering application, partial-deck result.

The new family builds on these conditional-flow ideas and on finite-group Fourier analysis, classically used by Diaconis and Shahshahani for shuffling problems. Its claimed improvement is to control the remaining collective information after only a constant number of coordinate sweeps. Fourier method for shuffles.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The headline mixing law

M1 claims the explicit asymptotic bound

∥qd∗(1600d)−Un∥TV⟶0(d→∞).\|q_d^{*(1600d)}-U_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0\qquad(d\to\infty).∥qd∗(1600d)​−Un​∥TV​⟶0(d→∞).

Its proof is given independently of the companion transfer theorems. M2 gives a separate 32800d32800d32800d construction and, combining its stronger fixed-list estimate with M3’s Fourier transfer, states convergence after 512d512d512d physical shuffles. These different constants describe different arguments for the same logarithmic order.

Every physical shuffle uses n/2n/2n/2 independent fair bits. After ttt shuffles there are at most 2tn/22^{tn/2}2tn/2 possible outcomes, so

∥qd∗t−Un∥TV≥1−2tn/2n!.\|q_d^{*t}-U_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\geq1-\frac{2^{tn/2}}{n!}.∥qd∗t​−Un​∥TV​≥1−n!2tn/2​.

Hence

tmix(d)≥⌈2nlog⁡2 ⁣(3n!4)⌉=2d−O(1).t_{\mathrm{mix}}(d)\geq\left\lceil\frac2n\log_2\!\left(\frac{3n!}{4}\right)\right\rceil=2d-O(1).tmix​(d)≥⌈n2​log2​(43n!​)⌉=2d−O(1).

Together, the claimed upper bounds and this support obstruction give tmix(d)=Θ(d)t_{\mathrm{mix}}(d)=\Theta(d)tmix​(d)=Θ(d). They do not show that 2d2d2d is the correct leading mixing time.

Partial and conditional laws

M2 and M4 claim that after 256d256d256d shuffles, the joint images of every specified ordered list of at most 7n/87n/87n/8 cards approach the uniform law on distinct positions, uniformly over the list. M1 instead uses an averaged estimate for a uniformly sampled list after 200d200d200d shuffles. These are different inputs.

M3 proves an abstract transfer: if the images of a uniformly chosen 7n/87n/87n/8 labels approach uniform in average total variation, and the mean permutation sign tends to zero, then the product of two independent permutations with that law approaches uniform on SnS_nSn​. Its general statement assumes nnn tends to infinity through multiples of eight. The parity condition cannot be dropped, as the even-permutation example shows.

M4 retains observed trajectories of base cards while estimating additional cards on the remaining positions, provided a fixed positive fraction of labels is left outside both lists. Its conditional error is averaged over the actual observed paths, not bounded for every possible path history.

M5 goes further: reveal the complete trajectories of half the labels and ask for the entire remaining assignment to be uniform conditional on that environment. After an explicit constant number of sweeps, it claims

EE∥νE−Un/2∥TV⟶0,\mathbb E_{\mathcal E}\|\nu_{\mathcal E}-U_{n/2}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0,EE​∥νE​−Un/2​∥TV​⟶0,

where νE\nu_{\mathcal E}νE​ is the conditional permutation law of the remaining slots. This expresses near-independence from the revealed environment in the joint law. It permits rare exceptional environments. Its separate full-deck consequence uses 16 040 400d16\,040\,400d16040400d physical shuffles; the large constant accompanies a stronger conditional construction, rather than improving the headline numerical bound.

Spectral and stronger-distance statements

M6–M12 develop several representation and moment methods. M8 claims that an absolute number of sweeps gives total-variation distance at most 12n−5\tfrac12n^{-5}21​n−5, uniformly over initial decks. M10 claims convergence of the full density in squared L2L^2L2 distance after a fixed number LLL of sweeps:

EUn∣fd,L−1∣2⟶0,fd,L(π)=n! qd∗(Ld)(π).\mathbb E_{U_n}|f_{d,L}-1|^2\longrightarrow0,\qquad f_{d,L}(\pi)=n!\,q_d^{*(Ld)}(\pi).EUn​​∣fd,L​−1∣2⟶0,fd,L​(π)=n!qd∗(Ld)​(π).

This controls a stronger discrepancy than total variation. The number of sweeps is an absolute constant, independent of deck size.

The roles of the twelve manuscripts are:

ManuscriptMain route or additional information
M1Conditional flow, averaged partial decks and an explicit 1600d1600d1600d full-deck bound
M2Random coordinate frames, uniform fixed-list bounds and the combined 512d512d512d consequence
M3General transfer from complementary partial permutations to Fourier bounds
M4Specified lists and conditional information after observing base trajectories
M5The full remaining permutation in a revealed half-deck environment
M6Routing densities and dimension-dependent representation contraction
M7Row–column symmetry and weighted sweep moments
M8Random-subspace tests and a regular-trace smoothing bound
M9Compatibility entropy controlling a fixed spectral moment
M10Signed tensor representations and full-density L2L^2L2 convergence
M11Conditional coordinate sweeps followed by analytic transfer to binary sweeps
M12A robust four-row permanent inequality driving a recursive moment estimate

These are overlapping approaches and extensions within one result family, with their dependencies stated in the individual papers.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the family resolves the optimal order of mixing for a longstanding, highly structured shuffle on dyadic decks. It improves the earlier cubic power of log⁡n\log nlogn to the smallest possible order.

The full-law conclusion is considerably stronger than randomizing a few cards. It implies that every event defined by the final permutation has almost the same probability as under a uniform deck. The shuffle then generates approximate uniform permutations using O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) fair bits, the same order suggested by the log⁡2(n!)\log_2(n!)log2​(n!) information content of a uniform permutation.

The general partial-information transfer and conditional-environment results may also be useful in other random switching systems. That methodological breadth supports the rating, without implying cryptographic security for a particular finite implementation or a sharp practical round count.

6. The main idea

Expose cards and track the remaining flow

In M1, reveal some card trajectories and track the conditional distribution of the next card over unoccupied positions. At a switch with two free positions, its conditional masses are averaged. At a switch with only one free position, the observed trajectory determines where that free mass must go.

Subtract the uniform distribution on the available positions. Pure averaging across all coordinate directions would annihilate this centered vector in one sweep. The actual update adds a mean-zero noise term arising from switches with one free position.

An exact energy identity records only the noise from the preceding sweep. Looking backward through the other coordinate directions separates the two opposite halves of the cube. Their remaining randomness is independent conditional on the appropriate earlier history, allowing the manuscript to bound the energy of the conditional flow. This yields the averaged large-list estimate.

Recover information hidden from partial decks

Partition the labels into eight blocks. The images outside one block describe a coset of the subgroup that permutes the omitted labels. Suitable complementary marginal bounds let the argument remove a small amount of probability and bound all eight coset densities under one common retained law.

A group representation assigns a matrix to every permutation, respecting composition. Averaging these matrices under the shuffle law gives its Fourier matrices. Repeating independent shuffle blocks multiplies the matrices, so contraction in every nonconstant mode leads to mixing. The sign representation records parity and is handled separately.

M3 controls whole matrix norms through the complementary observations, including multiplicities when a representation is restricted to block subgroups. This stronger transfer explains how two independent blocks can suffice once its marginal assumptions hold.

Other routes control collective modes directly

The later papers analyze the same dependence through routing densities, row–column decompositions, compatibility counts and matrix moments. Their estimates keep the dimension and multiplicity factors needed when all representation modes are summed.

M12 illustrates the role of a small finite inequality. For permutation laws on four elements that are sufficiently close to uniform and have exactly uniform coordinate marginals, it claims a product-function inequality with an exponent strictly below two. The uniform-law permanent inequality was already known; the additional ingredient is robustness under these marginal-preserving perturbations. This saving can be propagated through a four-row decomposition of larger decks. Earlier sharp permanent bound.

Across these approaches, a recurring issue is that a forward sweep is not generally a normal or reversible operator. Bounds for a forward sweep followed by its reverse require a separate matrix-norm argument before they imply bounds for repeated forward shuffles.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The headline result is for n=2dn=2^dn=2d cards. The cube-coordinate argument does not establish optimal-order mixing for every even deck size, despite earlier general-even-size bounds.

The explicit constants such as 160016001600 and 512512512 are sufficient asymptotic choices. The family does not determine a sharp leading constant, a cutoff location, or the width of a cutoff window. Those would describe the transition much more precisely than its order.

Conditional conclusions retain their stated mode of averaging. An expected small error over revealed environments does not assert a uniform bound for every feasible history. M11’s more general conditioned line-law estimates have their own near-uniformity and line-size hypotheses; they are not blanket statements about arbitrary conditioning of the physical shuffle.

One-card uniformity, fixed-list mixing, full-deck total variation and full-density L2L^2L2 convergence are distinct conclusions. The extra transfer and spectral arguments are what connect them here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives a comparatively direct full-deck argument, while M2–M3 explain the stronger partial-information transfer and the 512d512d512d consequence. M4–M5 are the sources for conditional statements, and M6–M12 develop the alternate spectral routes summarized above.

Morris’s entropy-based dyadic bound is a useful predecessor. Diaconis and Shahshahani’s finite-group Fourier approach supplies background for converting matrix contraction into total variation. The binary coordinate description in Section 2 is enough to follow the present problem without prior representation theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Optimal-order mixing of the Thorp shuffle (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Random coordinate frames and partial permutation laws (September 26, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, From partial permutation information to Fourier bounds (September 26, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Conditional information under deterministic coordinate sweeps (September 26, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Conditional permutations in a revealed switching environment (September 26, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Routing densities and representation contraction for Thorp sweeps (September 26, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Row–column symmetry and contraction of coordinate sweeps (September 26, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, Random-subspace tests and trace smoothing for coordinate sweeps (September 26, 2026).
  • M9. OpenAI, Compatibility entropy and the spectrum of a Thorp sweep (September 26, 2026).
  • M10. OpenAI, Signed tensor densities and diagram budgets for the Thorp shuffle (September 26, 2026).
  • M11. OpenAI, Conditional coordinate sweeps and analytic transfer (September 26, 2026).
  • M12. OpenAI, A strict four-row permanent inequality and permutation moments (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The factor-of-IID threshold for the free Ising model on regular trees
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 236 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine giving every vertex of an infinite tree its own independent random number. Can the vertices use one common symmetry-respecting rule to produce correlated spins with exactly the free Ising distribution?
