Székely later gave an influential crossing-number proof by viewing the problem as incidences between points and unit circles. Refinements improved constants and examined near-extremal structure, but a fixed improvement of the exponent required additional information.

The recent lower-bound history matters here. M2 cites the May 2026 OpenAI construction of many unit distances, which gives a fixed exponent above one, and Sawin’s refinement, giving exponent 1.014114 along an unbounded sequence of sizes. These are construction lower bounds. The new upper-bound claim leaves a gap above them and does not restore the older proposed n1+o(1)n^{1+o(1)}n1+o(1) upper bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: large distance fibers occupy a vanishing fraction of pairs

For every fixed s>0s>0s>0, M1’s Theorem 1.1 states

sup⁡∣P∣=n∣{(x,y):x≠y, kP(x,y)≥ns}∣n(n−1)⟶0.\sup_{|P|=n}\frac{\bigl|\{(x,y):x\ne y,\ k_P(x,y)\ge n^s\}\bigr|}{n(n-1)}\longrightarrow0.∣P∣=nsup​n(n−1)​{(x,y):x=y, kP​(x,y)≥ns}​​⟶0.

The supremum ranges over all planar configurations of nnn distinct points. The convergence is uniform over those configurations, with no separation or general-position assumption.

Corollary 1.2 says that for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, all but o(n)o(n)o(n) pins satisfy

∣Dx(P)∣≥n1−ε.|D_x(P)|\ge n^{1-\varepsilon}.∣Dx​(P)∣≥n1−ε.

The source supplies no explicit rate for the exceptional fraction. It cannot exclude every bad pin: points on a circle together with its center give a center that sees only one distance.

M2: a fixed improvement for unit distances

M2’s Theorem 1.1 asserts absolute constants C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ and 1≤β<4/31\le\beta<4/31≤β<4/3 such that

u(n)≤Cnβfor every n≥0.u(n)\le Cn^\beta\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.u(n)≤Cnβfor every n≥0.

Equivalently, the exponent is 4/3−δ4/3-\delta4/3−δ for some absolute δ>0\delta>0δ>0. The count is of unordered pairs. The constants do not depend on the configuration, and no numerical value for the saving is extracted.

These are separate manuscripts with different conclusions. The fiber theorem controls a vanishing proportion of pairs at each fixed power threshold; it does not automatically produce M2’s fixed power saving for one repeated length.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Both claims would break longstanding barriers in planar distance geometry. The pinned theorem approaches linear distance diversity and strengthens existence of one good pin to a statement about almost every location.

The unit-distance result would improve the exponent governing one of the basic incidence problems. Reducing a fixed exponent is a stronger asymptotic change than a constant improvement and calls for structure beyond the standard point–circle incidence estimate.

The rating reflects major advances while retaining the unresolved quantitative gaps. M1 does not reach the sharp pinned scale, and M2 does not determine the optimal unit-distance exponent. Their methods combine arithmetic and probability with Euclidean geometry in a way that may be useful beyond the headline bounds.

6. The main idea

Factor distance in complex coordinates

Both sources use the coordinates

z=x1+ix2,w=x1−ix2.z=x_1+ix_2,\qquad w=x_1-ix_2.z=x1​+ix2​,w=x1​−ix2​.

For two real planar points,

∥x−y∥2=(zx−zy)(wx−wy).\|x-y\|^2=(z_x-z_y)(w_x-w_y).∥x−y∥2=(zx​−zy​)(wx​−wy​).

On a fixed circle around a pin, this product is constant. On a unit edge it equals one, so the two coordinate differences are reciprocals. This converts geometric constraints into multiplicative algebraic relations.

The sources transfer finite systems of distance equalities and inequalities to algebraic coordinates. They then use the product formula for number fields, which balances logarithmic absolute values across all real, complex and prime-adic measurements. A difference that is small in one measurement cannot be treated in isolation from the others.

M1: compare a distance fiber with the whole set

Assuming many pairs lie in large fibers, M1 organizes points into nested partitions according to coordinate closeness at each absolute value. Their overlap counts satisfy an additive identity derived from the product formula.

The source compares sampling uniformly from a fiber with sampling uniformly from the whole configuration. The identity turns the comparison into variance bounds: the two distributions must agree unusually well across many partition cells.

Two scale regimes remain. If the integrated overlap scale grows without bound, the nested partitions behave like weighted trees, and the required concentration of tree distances contradicts their geometry. If the scale stays bounded, normalized coordinate distributions converge to nonatomic limits, meaning no single point has positive mass.

The circle relation becomes a family of fractional linear, or Möbius, maps between those limiting distributions. The independence and variance properties force an incompatible collapse of their spread. This rules out a positive density of large-fiber pairs.

The almost-every-pin deduction is simpler: a pin seeing too few distances must place most of its neighbors into large fibers, so many bad pins would contradict the pair-density theorem.

M2: predict neighbors and extract an algebraic obstruction

M2 begins with a hypothetical sequence approaching the 4/34/34/3 exponent. It restricts the point–circle incidence graph to a part with controlled degrees and sampling laws. Entropy estimates show that two points sampled as neighbors of one center share relatively little information.

A short history of coordinate tests can then predict enough about a point to preserve its compatibility with a fresh neighboring center. Arithmetic height measures the total logarithmic size of algebraic quantities across absolute values.

In a bounded-height regime, predictions force a separated point to approximately satisfy too many unit-circle equations, producing a geometric contradiction. In the unbounded regime, the source extracts ratios that individually have large height while certain rectangular products have negligible height.

Passing to a limiting field converts that separation into algebraic independence. A system of quadratic extensions then permits independent sign changes of square roots that conflict with the required equations. The argument excludes every sequence approaching exponent 4/34/34/3, yielding some fixed gap without estimating its size.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 fixes ε\varepsilonε or sss before taking the large-set limit. It does not provide one explicit exceptional-count formula valid for parameters shrinking with nnn. Exceptional pins are unavoidable in general.

M2 gives existence of an absolute exponent improvement, with no numerical value for δ\deltaδ. It does not establish a near-linear upper bound or match the recent lower constructions. The maximum possible exponent remains undetermined within these claims.

Both results concern finite sets of distinct points in the real Euclidean plane. They do not directly apply to arbitrary norms, finite-field planes or configurations with repeated points.

The global, pinned and repeated-distance statistics should remain separate when applying these results. Each asks a different question about how equal lengths are distributed, even though the same coordinate factorization helps study them.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 give the fiber and pinned statements; Sections 3–7 explain the partition identity and two scale regimes. M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the unit-distance saving; its introduction outlines prediction, height extraction and the final algebraic obstruction.

The primary historical links above distinguish global distance bounds from unit-distance constructions. Wikipedia’s unit distance problem and mutual information pages provide optional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The weak pinned planar distance theorem (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A power saving for planar unit distances (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Can an unlabeled order determine a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 168 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Some mathematical objects are built using detailed labels, yet their essential information may survive after the labels are erased. Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials present a striking instance. Their usual definition uses generators of a group, and their geometric interpretation involves singular spaces. A conjecture asks whether a much simpler object—a finite partially ordered set—already determines each polynomial.

The manuscript in family 168 claims a positive answer in full equal-parameter generality. Whenever two Bruhat intervals have the same abstract order structure, their Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials agree, even if they come from different Coxeter groups.

The point is not that the intervals retain hidden permutation names or geometric coordinates. The proposed theorem uses only which elements lie above which others. Understanding why this is surprising requires separating that order from the richer algebra used to define the polynomial.

2. Background and essential definitions

Coxeter groups and Bruhat intervals

A Coxeter group is generated by reflections SSS, subject to relations s2=1s^2=1s2=1 and specified relations (st)mst=1(st)^{m_{st}}=1(st)mst​=1. An infinite value of mstm_{st}mst​ means no finite-order relation is imposed for that pair. The group together with its chosen generators is a Coxeter system (W,S)(W,S)(W,S).

The symmetric group of permutations is a standard example: adjacent swaps generate every permutation. The length ℓ(w)\ell(w)ℓ(w) is the smallest number of generators needed to express www. Such a shortest expression is called reduced.

Bruhat order can be described by subwords: u≤wu\le wu≤w if a reduced expression for www contains a subword that is a reduced expression for uuu. For u≤bu\le bu≤b, the interval is

[u,b]={x∈W:u≤x≤b}.[u,b]=\{x\in W:u\le x\le b\}.[u,b]={x∈W:u≤x≤b}.

It is finite even when WWW is infinite. Its rank is ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)\ell(b)-\ell(u)ℓ(b)−ℓ(u). An abstract interval remembers the order relation but forgets the words, generators and reflection labels. A poset isomorphism is a bijection preserving the order in both directions.

Where the polynomials come from

The Hecke algebra is a deformation of the group algebra, with basis symbols TwT_wTw​ and a parameter qqq. Products corresponding to length-additive group multiplication satisfy TxTy=TxyT_xT_y=T_{xy}Tx​Ty​=Txy​. For a generator,

Ts2=(q−1)Ts+q.T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q.Ts2​=(q−1)Ts​+q.

At q=1q=1q=1, this returns the relation s2=1s^2=1s2=1. There is a bar operation sending q1/2q^{1/2}q1/2 to q−1/2q^{-1/2}q−1/2 and TsT_sTs​ to Ts−1T_s^{-1}Ts−1​. A distinguished bar-invariant basis has expansions

Cb′=q−ℓ(b)/2∑u≤bPu,b(q)Tu,C'_b=q^{-\ell(b)/2}\sum_{u\le b}P_{u,b}(q)T_u,Cb′​=q−ℓ(b)/2u≤b∑​Pu,b​(q)Tu​,

where Pb,b=1P_{b,b}=1Pb,b​=1 and, for u<bu<bu<b,

deg⁡Pu,b<ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)2.\deg P_{u,b}<\frac{\ell(b)-\ell(u)}2.degPu,b​<2ℓ(b)−ℓ(u)​.

These normalization and invariance conditions characterize the usual equal-parameter Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. The formal symbol qqq records grading; it is not a probability. “Equal parameter” means the same parameter governs all generators.

In Weyl-group settings the coefficients also encode local intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties, a tool for measuring topology near singularities. The theorem can be understood without computing that cohomology: the question is whether the polynomial defined by the algebra is already determined by the smaller order structure.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kazhdan and Lusztig introduced the polynomials in 1979, and their subsequent geometric work connected them with Schubert varieties. The combinatorial invariance conjecture is associated with Lusztig and Dyer.

Dyer showed how the interval order reconstructs the directed Bruhat graph, including reflection edges that are not just immediate order covers. This recovers more than the usual diagram of adjacent levels, but still does not recover the root labels used in geometric constructions.

A major positive case concerns principal lower intervals [1,b][1,b][1,b], starting at the identity. Work by du Cloux, Brenti, Brenti–Caselli–Marietti and Delanoy established broad invariance results using special matchings and order-theoretic recursions. Delanoy’s paper treats arbitrary Coxeter systems in that setting.

The distinction is subtle. Knowing a larger interval [1,b][1,b][1,b] and where uuu sits inside it gives additional information. The full conjecture asks to recover Pu,bP_{u,b}Pu,b​ from [u,b][u,b][u,b] alone, whose bottom may be far from the identity.

Other progress handled short intervals, individual coefficients and special decompositions. Recent work by Barkley, Gaetz and Lam treats the coefficient of qqq in arbitrary Coxeter systems and yields full invariance at low interval rank. Hypercube decomposition methods, including the machine-learning-guided work of Blundell and collaborators, supplied further formulas and conjectures in symmetric groups.

Moment-graph sheaves offer another route. Braden–MacPherson, Soergel, Fiebig, and Elias–Williamson developed algebraic and geometric models recovering the polynomials. Prior comparisons of labeled moment graphs could use compatible maps on root labels. The new manuscript’s task is to compare the relevant information when those label maps are absent.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s Theorem 1.1 takes arbitrary Coxeter systems (W,S)(W,S)(W,S) and (W′,S′)(W',S')(W′,S′). If

[u,b]≅[u′,b′][u,b]\cong[u',b'][u,b]≅[u′,b′]

as abstract posets, it asserts

Pu,bW(q)=Pu′,b′W′(q).P^W_{u,b}(q)=P^{W'}_{u',b'}(q).Pu,bW​(q)=Pu′,b′W′​(q).

The systems may be infinite or noncrystallographic, meaning they need not arise from the integral root systems familiar in Lie theory. No preservation of generator labels or root coordinates is required.

Restricting the poset isomorphism to every subinterval gives equality of all corresponding polynomials inside the interval. The source also recovers the associated RRR-polynomials through standard reciprocity relations. These are related Hecke-algebra polynomials entering the inversion formulas behind the canonical basis.

The claim is specifically for equal parameters. It does not state an unequal-parameter version, where different generators carry different weights. It is a determination theorem: identical order data imply identical polynomials. It does not by itself promise a fast algorithm using only the diagram of the interval.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Full combinatorial invariance would settle a central question connecting algebraic combinatorics, representation theory and geometry. It would identify precisely how much information can be discarded while preserving these important polynomials.

The result’s breadth matters. A statement only for symmetric groups, only for intervals starting at the identity, or only for a few coefficients would leave substantial parts of the conjecture unresolved. The manuscript claims all coefficients for arbitrary intervals across arbitrary Coxeter systems.

The theorem would also clarify a conceptual puzzle: root labels are useful in constructing the invariant, yet the final answer would depend only on order. A successful argument must explain that independence without assuming the labels can somehow be reconstructed unchanged.

6. The main idea

Keep the two label systems separate

A moment-graph sheaf assigns algebraic modules to vertices and edges, with maps recording compatibility across edges. A graded module is organized by degree, and its graded size can be summarized by a polynomial or series. In the relevant sheaf, the module at a vertex records a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial.

The source studies vectors whose restrictions vanish along selected upward edges. With no edge conditions, one has the full vertex module. With all upward edges imposed, a known duality formula describes the opposite extreme. Intermediate choices are harder because their modules must also have the necessary freeness and graded behavior.

Choose a reflection order in the second Coxeter system and transport its edge schedule across the poset isomorphism. It need not become a reflection order for the first system. The argument therefore retains both realizations rather than pretending there is one common set of root labels.

Compare one edge at a time

At an edge from xxx to yyy, impose the conditions coming from later edges and compare the images from its two endpoints. Localizing at a plane spanned by root labels reduces the comparison to dihedral, or two-reflection, models.

The order structure controls the relevant relative dihedral intervals and the counts of later edges. The source obtains an inclusion between graded images with a precisely determined degree shift. This gives an inequality on their Hilbert series, which count dimensions in each degree.

Removing edge conditions in the transported schedule accumulates these inequalities. Dyer’s reflection-path formula identifies the resulting product with an RRR-polynomial matrix in the other system.

Reciprocal comparisons force equality

The argument applies the comparison in both directions and uses the reciprocity relations linking RRR- and Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. Because the intermediate terms are nonnegative in the relevant range, equality of the global quantities forces the individual inequalities to be sharp.

This also establishes the freeness needed for the next step of the induction. Polynomial equality and module structure are proved together, in increasing interval rank. The mechanism therefore avoids assuming at the start the intermediate properties it needs later.

The broad idea is that local order-controlled inequalities, constrained by a two-way algebraic symmetry, leave no room for the richer labels to change the final polynomial.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the usual equal-parameter polynomials. Weighted Hecke algebras, other canonical bases and characteristic-dependent analogues are not included merely because their notation looks similar.

Combinatorial invariance of these polynomials does not mean the entire geometric spaces associated with two intervals are identical. A shared numerical invariant may capture only part of their topology or singularity structure.

The source supplies a structural proof through sheaves, localization and reciprocity. Finding a short direct combinatorial formula, or an efficient label-free computation for arbitrary intervals, remains a different goal. Determination by a poset is weaker than a practical procedure with a controlled running time.

The claim is broad enough to compare intervals from different Coxeter systems, but it still requires an actual order isomorphism. Matching only rank sizes or the total number of interval elements would discard more information than the theorem allows.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states full invariance; Corollary 6.1 records the associated consequences. Sections 2–3 introduce the realizations, sheaves and transported orders. Sections 4–6 give the local comparison and simultaneous induction.

The original and partial-result papers linked in Section 3 trace the problem’s development. Wikipedia’s Coxeter group and Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial pages provide optional examples; the algebra and order conventions needed for the claim are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Positive elementary coefficients for refined graph colorings
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 169 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Counting graph colorings naturally gives positive numbers: every coloring contributes one. But when the same information is rewritten in a different mathematical basis, subtraction can appear. A central question in algebraic combinatorics asks when a more structured expansion still has only nonnegative coefficients.

Family 169 concerns a refinement that remembers an additional statistic of each coloring through a variable qqq. The manuscript claims that the chromatic quasisymmetric function of every natural unit interval graph has nonnegative integer coefficients in the elementary basis, degree by degree in qqq.

It also supplies a combinatorial explanation: a terminating procedure assigns a partition to each admissible permutation, so the elementary coefficients count permutations with specified data. The claim strengthens previously established positivity at q=1q=1q=1, but explicitly does not assert elementary unimodality.

2. Background and essential definitions

The graphs and their colorings

A natural unit interval graph can be specified by a weakly increasing integer sequence h(1),…,h(n)h(1),\ldots,h(n)h(1),…,h(n) satisfying i≤h(i)≤ni\le h(i)\le ni≤h(i)≤n. Its vertices are 1,…,n1,\ldots,n1,…,n, and

{i,j}∈E(G)⟺i<j≤h(i)\{i,j\}\in E(G)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i<j\le h(i){i,j}∈E(G)⟺i<j≤h(i)

for i<ji<ji<j. This ordered graph class includes paths and complete graphs. The labels carry information and are part of the definition of the refined statistic.

A proper coloring fff assigns a positive integer color to each vertex, with adjacent vertices receiving different colors. Let asc⁡G(f)\operatorname{asc}_G(f)ascG​(f) count edges {i,j}\{i,j\}{i,j} with i<ji<ji<j and f(i)<f(j)f(i)<f(j)f(i)<f(j). With variables X=(x1,x2,…)X=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)X=(x1​,x2​,…), define

χG(X;q)=∑f properqasc⁡G(f)∏a=1nxf(a).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{f\text{ proper}}q^{\operatorname{asc}_G(f)}\prod_{a=1}^n x_{f(a)}.χG​(X;q)=f proper∑​qascG​(f)a=1∏n​xf(a)​.

The monomial records how often each color is used; the power of qqq records ascents. Although there are infinitely many color names, this is a well-defined formal homogeneous function of total degree nnn.

The elementary basis

The elementary symmetric function ek(X)e_k(X)ek​(X) is the sum of all products of kkk distinct variables. For example, e1=x1+x2+⋯e_1=x_1+x_2+\cdotse1​=x1​+x2​+⋯, while e2=∑i<jxixje_2=\sum_{i<j}x_ix_je2​=∑i<j​xi​xj​.

A partition λ=(λ1,…,λℓ)\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_\ell)λ=(λ1​,…,λℓ​) of nnn is a nonincreasing list of positive integers summing to nnn. Put eλ=∏jeλje_\lambda=\prod_j e_{\lambda_j}eλ​=∏j​eλj​​. These products form a basis for symmetric functions of degree nnn.

For the graph class above, χG\chi_GχG​ is symmetric in the color variables and has a unique expansion

χG(X;q)=∑λ⊢ncλ(q)eλ(X).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}c_\lambda(q)e_\lambda(X).χG​(X;q)=λ⊢n∑​cλ​(q)eλ​(X).

Elementary positivity means cλ(q)∈N[q]c_\lambda(q)\in\mathbb N[q]cλ​(q)∈N[q]: every coefficient of every power of qqq is a nonnegative integer. This is stronger than cλ(q)≥0c_\lambda(q)\ge0cλ​(q)≥0 at every positive real qqq. For instance, q2−q+1q^2-q+1q2−q+1 is positive for all real qqq but has a negative coefficient.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Stanley introduced the chromatic symmetric function as a refinement of the chromatic polynomial. The latter counts proper colorings with a fixed finite palette; the symmetric function also records color multiplicities.

The Stanley–Stembridge conjecture predicts elementary positivity for incomparability graphs of (3+1)(3+1)(3+1)-free posets. An incomparability graph joins two elements when neither is below the other. The excluded pattern is a chain of three elements together with one element incomparable to all three.

Guay-Paquet’s reduction expresses those chromatic functions as nonnegative combinations of functions associated with unit interval orders. This made the graph class in the present theorem central to the older conjecture.

Shareshian and Wachs introduced the qqq-refinement and formulated elementary positivity together with an additional unimodality prediction. They proved symmetry and positivity in the Schur basis, another important basis of symmetric functions. Positivity in one basis need not survive a change to another, so that achievement did not settle the elementary question.

The refined functions also connect to the cohomology of Hessenberg varieties, spaces of flags satisfying linear-operator constraints. Brosnan–Chow and Guay-Paquet proved the representation-theoretic identity proposed in that connection. This identity is distinct from coefficientwise elementary positivity, even though both are associated with the Shareshian–Wachs program.

Hikita’s proof of the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture established the classical positivity result. M1 explains that Hikita’s formula also supplies numerical nonnegativity at positive real qqq, while its rational weights do not establish membership in N[q]\mathbb N[q]N[q]. The new manuscript targets that remaining graded statement and an individual permutation interpretation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let DG0D_G^0DG0​ be the permutations σ\sigmaσ of 1,…,n1,\ldots,n1,…,n in which every adjacent descent is an edge of GGG. Thus if σi>σi+1\sigma_i>\sigma_{i+1}σi​>σi+1​, their two labels must be adjacent in the graph.

Define the graph-inversion statistic

ginv⁡G(σ)=∣{(i,j):i<j, σi>σj, {σi,σj}∈E(G)}∣.\operatorname{ginv}_G(\sigma)=\bigl|\{(i,j):i<j,\ \sigma_i>\sigma_j,\ \{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\in E(G)\}\bigr|.ginvG​(σ)=​{(i,j):i<j, σi​>σj​, {σi​,σj​}∈E(G)}​.

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic terminating procedure assigning a partition θG(σ)⊢n\theta_G(\sigma)\vdash nθG​(σ)⊢n to each σ∈DG0\sigma\in D_G^0σ∈DG0​, with

χG(X;q)=∑σ∈DG0qginv⁡G(σ)eθG(σ)(X).\chi_G(X;q)=\sum_{\sigma\in D_G^0}q^{\operatorname{ginv}_G(\sigma)}e_{\theta_G(\sigma)}(X).χG​(X;q)=σ∈DG0​∑​qginvG​(σ)eθG​(σ)​(X).

Each elementary coefficient therefore counts admissible permutations of the appropriate partition type and inversion degree. The procedure acts on an individual permutation; it does not first compute the coefficient list and distribute permutations to fit it. Its running time may be large.

For the path 1 ⁣− ⁣2 ⁣− ⁣31\! -\!2\! -\!31−2−3, the stated expansion is

χG(X;q)=q e(2,1)(X)+(1+q+q2)e(3)(X).\chi_G(X;q)=q\,e_{(2,1)}(X) +(1+q+q^2)e_{(3)}(X).χG​(X;q)=qe(2,1)​(X)+(1+q+q2)e(3)​(X).

The admissible permutations are 123,132,213,321123,132,213,321123,132,213,321, with inversion degrees 0,1,1,20,1,1,20,1,1,2. One degree-one permutation contributes to (2,1)(2,1)(2,1), and the remaining three contribute to (3)(3)(3).

Using the established geometric identity, the source also obtains degreewise decompositions of Hessenberg cohomology representations into Young permutation modules. These modules have bases permuted by the symmetric group, with multiplicities given by the same counts. The conclusion is an abstract representation isomorphism, not a preferred geometric basis or compatibility with multiplication of cohomology classes.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Coefficientwise positivity is a substantial strengthening of numerical positivity and the classical q=1q=1q=1 theorem. It says that every separate graded contribution admits a nonnegative count, rather than relying on cancellations between degrees.

The permutation rule adds explanatory value. A polynomial identity can prove that coefficients are nonnegative without revealing what they count. Here the source claims a finite assignment that connects each count to an individual combinatorial object.

The geometric consequence gives the positivity a representation-theoretic meaning as well. The rating reflects a major advance in algebraic combinatorics, while recognizing that the classical Stanley–Stembridge theorem is already established and the additional unimodality claim remains separate.

6. The main idea

Move the coefficient question to another algebra

The first reduction uses an algebra whose monomials encode vertex multiplicities. Multiplication keeps track of the graph’s ordered edges through powers of an auxiliary variable vvv, with q=v2q=v^2q=v2. This is a quantum torus: monomials multiply with a prescribed commutation factor rather than simply commuting.

Sums indexed by independent vertex sets nevertheless commute in the required way. They can therefore play the role of elementary symmetric functions in a formal new alphabet. The source translates the desired elementary coefficient into a monomial coefficient in this graph-based algebra.

This change does not prove positivity by itself. It creates a setting where graded vector spaces and positive factorization can control the coefficients.

Identify the exact positive object

The manuscript constructs systems of algebraic transformations attached to walls between regions. Compatible expressions on those regions are called sections. Earlier Hall-algebra and scattering-diagram ideas motivate this framework, where factorization can reveal nonnegative graded dimensions.

The essential graph-specific step is an identification: the symmetric expression arising from the graph must equal a particular positive section. General positivity elsewhere in the algebra would be insufficient.

An auxiliary triangular graph with distinguished independent vertices, called anchors, provides the coordinates. Repeated interval rotations and support bounds show that the required expression has precisely the anchor form of the positive section. Graded vector-space dimensions then give nonnegative integer coefficients.

Turn algebraic positivity into a permutation assignment

The final stage returns to individual words. It groups vertices into packets, each an independent set in increasing order. Local bijections transport packets to subsets of the anchors while recording weighted changes.

The source uses finite ordering and cancellation procedures to pass from conditions requiring certain ascents to conditions specifying the exact ascent pattern. The surviving terminal data determine a partition for each admissible permutation and preserve its graph-inversion degree.

Thus the two main outputs have separate roles: positive algebraic objects establish coefficientwise positivity, and the packet procedure realizes it as a rule on individual permutations. The latter is stronger than simply knowing the final coefficient totals.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns natural unit interval graphs with their specified labels. It does not assert elementary positivity of the same refined function for every graph or every arbitrary relabeling.

Specializing q=1q=1q=1 recovers classical positivity, but the theorem makes no assertion of elementary unimodality. Unimodality would require each coefficient sequence to increase and then decrease in the prescribed way, a restriction beyond nonnegativity.

The permutation procedure terminates, yet no efficient running-time bound is claimed. Nor does its existence supply a simple closed formula for the partition assigned to every input without performing that procedure.

The cohomological consequence is an abstract decomposition over the complex numbers. It does not automatically identify a canonical basis, a geometric partition of the variety, or a decomposition compatible with the cup product. These stronger interpretations need their own constructions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the positive expansion and permutation rule; Corollary 1.2 gives the representation consequence. Section 2 makes the algebraic reduction, Sections 3–5 establish positivity and the graph-specific identification, and Section 6 constructs the individual witness before Section 7 completes the expansion.

The primary papers linked in Section 3 distinguish the original symmetric function, the refined conjecture, the reduction and Hikita’s theorem. Wikipedia’s symmetric function and elementary symmetric polynomial pages offer optional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Elementary positivity of chromatic quasisymmetric functions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The logarithmic scale of off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 170 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

How large can a network be if it contains neither a small group whose members are all connected nor a large group with no connections at all? Ramsey theory says that such a network cannot grow indefinitely. The difficult part is finding the right scale of the limit.

For fixed integers sss and ttt, the Ramsey number r(s,t)r(s,t)r(s,t) is the smallest number of vertices forcing either a complete subgraph on sss vertices or an independent set of size ttt. In an independent set, no two vertices are joined. Here sss stays fixed while ttt tends to infinity: this is the off-diagonal problem.

The two manuscripts in this family concern every fixed s≥5s\geq5s≥5. They claim to identify the exponent of the logarithm in the asymptotic growth of r(s,t)r(s,t)r(s,t). This is finer information than its main power of ttt, which earlier work had already determined. It still leaves room between upper and lower bounds at smaller scales.

2. Background and essential definitions

A graph here is finite, undirected and simple: there are no loops or repeated edges. Write KsK_sKs​ for the graph with every possible edge on sss vertices. A graph is KsK_sKs​-free if it contains no copy of that graph. Its independence number α(G)\alpha(G)α(G) is the largest size of an independent set.

To prove a lower bound on a Ramsey number, one constructs a graph that avoids both alternatives. If a graph GGG has NNN vertices, contains no KsK_sKs​, and satisfies α(G)<t\alpha(G)<tα(G)<t, then

r(s,t)>N.r(s,t)>N.r(s,t)>N.

An upper bound requires showing that every sufficiently large graph has one of the two structures. Equivalently, color each pair of vertices red when it is an edge and blue when it is not. Then r(s,t)r(s,t)r(s,t) forces a red KsK_sKs​ or a blue KtK_tKt​.

Throughout, log⁡\loglog denotes the natural logarithm. Constants may depend on the fixed integer sss. The notation o(1)o(1)o(1) means a quantity tending to zero as ttt grows with sss held fixed. An exponent a+o(1)a+o(1)a+o(1) is a statement about a limiting exponent; it does not generally identify a constant multiplying the whole expression.

For example, a factor log⁡log⁡t\log\log tloglogt is smaller than every fixed positive power of log⁡t\log tlogt, but it still grows without bound. Such a factor can be hidden inside a logarithmic exponent error tending to zero. This distinction is central to the result.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ramsey’s 1930 theorem established the fundamental finiteness phenomenon. The elementary recursion developed in early Ramsey theory gives the binomial upper bound

r(s,t)≤(s+t−2s−1).r(s,t)\leq\binom{s+t-2}{s-1}.r(s,t)≤(s−1s+t−2​).

For fixed sss, this is of order at most ts−1t^{s-1}ts−1. It says nothing about the logarithmic improvement now expected at that scale.

Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi obtained upper bounds of the form

r(s,t)≤Csts−1(log⁡t)s−2,r(s,t)\leq C_s\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{s-2}},r(s,t)≤Cs​(logt)s−2ts−1​,

with later work sharpening their constants. On the construction side, the triangle case became a benchmark: Kim’s 1995 paper established the matching order r(3,t)=Θ(t2/log⁡t)r(3,t)=\Theta(t^2/\log t)r(3,t)=Θ(t2/logt). Here Θ\ThetaΘ means upper and lower bounds differing by at most constant factors.

Larger fixed cliques were much harder. Probabilistic constructions, including the local lemma and random processes that avoid creating a forbidden clique, supplied important lower bounds without reaching the upper bound’s polynomial exponent in general. Mattheus and Verstraëte’s work on r(4,t)r(4,t)r(4,t) used finite geometry to obtain a lower bound of order t3/(log⁡t)4t^3/(\log t)^4t3/(logt)4, bringing that case within logarithmic factors of the upper bound.

The immediate predecessor for this family is Bradač’s 2026 manuscript. For every fixed s≥3s\geq3s≥3, it gives a lower bound of the form

r(s,t)≥csts−1(log⁡t)2s−4.r(s,t)\geq c_s\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{2s-4}}.r(s,t)≥cs​(logt)2s−4ts−1​.

Thus the power s−1s-1s−1 of ttt was already sharp. The remaining gap relevant here was between logarithmic exponents 2s−42s-42s−4 and s−2s-2s−2. The present manuscripts claim to close that exponent gap for s≥5s\geq5s≥5. They build on an older line of constructions from ordered incidence relations, together with methods that show there are too few descriptions of a hypothetical large independent set.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The common conclusion

Manuscript M1 treats s=5s=5s=5. Manuscript M2 treats every fixed s≥6s\geq6s≥6. Together they claim that for each fixed integer s≥5s\geq5s≥5 and each real ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, all sufficiently large ttt satisfy

ts−1(log⁡t)s−2+ε≤r(s,t)≤Csts−1(log⁡t)s−2.\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{s-2+\varepsilon}}\leq r(s,t)\leq C_s\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{s-2}}.(logt)s−2+εts−1​≤r(s,t)≤Cs​(logt)s−2ts−1​.

The threshold for “sufficiently large” may depend on both sss and ε\varepsilonε. The upper bound is classical; the new claim is the nearly matching lower bound. An equivalent compact formulation is

r(s,t)=ts−1(log⁡t)s−2+o(1).r(s,t)=\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{s-2+o(1)}}.r(s,t)=(logt)s−2+o(1)ts−1​.

More explicitly, the exponent statement reads

lim⁡t→∞(s−1)log⁡t−log⁡r(s,t)log⁡log⁡t=s−2.\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{(s-1)\log t-\log r(s,t)}{\log\log t}=s-2.t→∞lim​loglogt(s−1)logt−logr(s,t)​=s−2.

For s=5s=5s=5, the manuscript therefore replaces the earlier logarithmic denominator exponent six by an exponent arbitrarily close to three. The gain grows without bound with ttt, even though it does not change the main polynomial power.

The construction behind the bound

Set d=s−1d=s-1d=s−1. A central construction in the papers uses a large prime qqq and a fixed small parameter η>0\eta>0η>0. It claims graphs with approximately

N=qdlog⁡qN=q^d\log qN=qdlogq

vertices, no Kd+1K_{d+1}Kd+1​, and independence number smaller than approximately

q(log⁡q)1+η.q(\log q)^{1+\eta}.q(logq)1+η.

The precise statements use integer parts. Choosing η\etaη sufficiently small in terms of the requested ε\varepsilonε, and translating between qqq and the desired independent-set size, yields the Ramsey bound. The result is stated for all sufficiently large integer ttt, rather than only a subsequence indexed by primes.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Off-diagonal Ramsey numbers are central measures of how much disorder a graph can sustain. Determining a logarithmic exponent for every fixed clique size in an infinite range is a major quantitative advance, especially after the polynomial exponents have been identified.

The scale deserves some perspective. Two bounds with the same power of ttt can still differ by an arbitrarily large factor. Replacing a denominator (log⁡t)2s−4(\log t)^{2s-4}(logt)2s−4 by (log⁡t)s−2+ε(\log t)^{s-2+\varepsilon}(logt)s−2+ε permits substantially larger graphs avoiding both forbidden structures. It narrows the uncertainty to effects smaller than any fixed positive logarithmic power.

The methodological interest is also broad. Finite geometry ensures that a clique cannot form; an information argument then limits independent sets. These two tasks pull in opposite directions, and the construction coordinates them without relying on a completely unconstrained random graph. The rating reflects both the central problem and this combination of ideas, while leaving room for stronger constant-factor or leading-constant results.

6. The main idea

Make cliques impossible by linear algebra

Work over the finite field Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, where arithmetic is performed modulo the prime qqq. A projective point represents a one-dimensional subspace of Fqd+1\mathbb F_q^{d+1}Fqd+1​. A projective hyperplane is specified by a nonzero linear equation. A flag is an incident point–hyperplane pair: the point lies in the hyperplane.

Sample a sequence of flags (ai,bi)(a_i,b_i)(ai​,bi​). Each position becomes a graph vertex, even if two positions receive the same flag. For i<ji<ji<j, place an edge when aia_iai​ lies in bjb_jbj​ but aja_jaj​ does not lie in bib_ibi​.

This asymmetric rule uses the order of the positions, although the resulting graph has ordinary undirected edges. The incidence pattern required by a clique forces an incompatible arrangement of independent vectors and hyperplanes. The paper uses this to exclude Kd+1K_{d+1}Kd+1​ deterministically: every sampled sequence has the required clique restriction.

Make independent sets too expensive to describe

It remains to show that some sequence has no large independent set. An independent subsequence must obey many restrictions on its point–hyperplane incidences. Those restrictions ought to make it unusually structured, but counting all possible subsequences directly loses too much.

The manuscripts use entropy, a numerical measure of uncertainty. Suppose a rule selects a long independent subsequence whenever one exists. There are two competing ways to estimate the information needed to specify the selected flags. Random sampling supplies a lower bound on that information. Geometric restrictions supply a compressed description.

Selection changes the distribution: the chosen flags are not simply independent uniform samples. The argument must account for the information lost by selecting them. Ignoring this bias would make the compression comparison unreliable even if each individual geometric estimate were strong.

The compression repeatedly locates parts of the sequence whose allowable point and hyperplane sets have unusually few incidences. Short records then restrict where many flags could lie. A hierarchy of these records reduces the total description length; the construction replaces earlier records where needed instead of paying for every intermediate stage forever.

Higher dimensions introduce additional geometric possibilities. M2 develops projection and polynomial tools to control them, extending the strategy beyond the s=5s=5s=5 case. The intended contradiction is that a selected independent sequence would retain more information than its compressed description can carry. Consequently, some sampled graph has no independent set of the prohibited size.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The statements hold for each fixed s≥5s\geq5s≥5. They do not give uniform estimates when the forbidden clique size grows with ttt. Nor do these two manuscripts settle the corresponding logarithmic question for s=4s=4s=4.

The lower bound contains an arbitrary fixed exponent loss ε\varepsilonε. One cannot set ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0 in the quantifiers: the threshold is allowed to worsen as ε\varepsilonε decreases. The conclusion therefore does not establish

r(s,t)=Θ ⁣(ts−1(log⁡t)s−2).r(s,t)=\Theta\!\left(\frac{t^{s-1}}{(\log t)^{s-2}}\right).r(s,t)=Θ((logt)s−2ts−1​).

A matching constant-factor lower bound, and then a leading asymptotic constant, are stronger targets. The construction is also an existence argument using random flags and information estimates; the headline theorem does not itself provide a practical algorithm for producing optimal Ramsey graphs at a chosen size.

Finally, this family concerns ordinary graphs with a fixed forbidden clique. Related questions for hypergraphs, several colors, or different forbidden subgraphs require their own statements. The logarithmic precision achieved here should be understood within these specific parameters.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the r(5,t)r(5,t)r(5,t) construction and its entropy analysis. M2 develops the higher-dimensional extension and states the result for all fixed s≥6s\geq6s≥6. Their introductions explain the earlier ordered-incidence constructions and the remaining logarithmic gap.

For primary historical context, see Ramsey’s original paper, Kim on triangle-free Ramsey graphs, Mattheus–Verstraëte on r(4,t)r(4,t)r(4,t), and Bradač on general fixed off-diagonal Ramsey numbers. The manuscripts’ bibliographies identify the classical upper-bound papers and the geometric and information-theoretic tools used in the construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The sharp logarithmic exponent of r(5,t) (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Sharp Logarithmic Exponents for Fixed Off-Diagonal Ramsey Numbers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A monochromatic hypercube in a network only a constant times larger
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 171 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Draw every possible connection among a large collection of points, and color each connection red or blue. How many points guarantee a one-color copy of an nnn-dimensional cube?

The cube itself has 2n2^n2n vertices. The question is whether a host network only a fixed constant times larger always suffices, with the same constant for every dimension. Each cube vertex has nnn neighbors, so the required pattern becomes more demanding as the dimension grows. A result for graphs whose degrees stay bounded does not answer this question.

The manuscript claims that an absolute constant does suffice. In the language of Ramsey theory, the Ramsey number of the hypercube has linear order in its number of vertices. This resolves the cube question raised by Burr and Erdős in 1975, according to the manuscript.

2. Background and essential definitions

The binary cube graph QnQ_nQn​ has vertex set

{0,1}n.\{0,1\}^n.{0,1}n.

Two binary strings are adjacent when they differ in exactly one coordinate. Thus Q1Q_1Q1​ is a single edge, Q2Q_2Q2​ is a square, and Q3Q_3Q3​ is the familiar graph of a solid cube. In general it has 2n2^n2n vertices and n2n−1n2^{n-1}n2n−1 edges for n≥1n\geq1n≥1.

For a finite graph HHH, its two-color Ramsey number R(H)R(H)R(H) is the least integer MMM such that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph KMK_MKM​ contains a monochromatic copy of HHH. All edges required by the copy must have one color. Additional edges among its vertices are allowed and may have either color. The copy need not be induced.

The cube is bipartite. Separate its strings according to whether their coordinate sum is even or odd. Every edge crosses between the two classes, each of size 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1. This parity split is a useful structural feature because an embedding can first place one class and then find compatible places for the other.

“Linear order” means that positive constants bound the ratio R(Qn)/2nR(Q_n)/2^nR(Qn​)/2n above and below independently of nnn. It is often written R(Qn)=Θ(2n)R(Q_n)=\Theta(2^n)R(Qn​)=Θ(2n). It does not specify a limiting ratio or a numerical best constant.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Burr and Erdős asked when an entire family of graphs has one common linear Ramsey bound. They considered several sparsity conditions and separately posed the hypercube question. The common constant is essential: an individual finite graph always has some finite Ramsey number.

In 1983, Chvátal, Rödl, Szemerédi and Trotter proved linear bounds for graphs of any fixed maximum degree. The constant could depend on that degree. Much later, Lee obtained linear bounds for each fixed degeneracy. A graph is ddd-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex with at most ddd neighbors. This allows some vertices to have large degree while still imposing global sparsity.

Neither theorem gives a common linear constant for cubes: both their maximum degree and their degeneracy equal nnn, which grows. The cube has about a logarithmic number of edges per vertex relative to its order. It therefore probes a substantially denser regime than fixed-degree examples.

A separate sequence of estimates addressed cubes directly. Shi’s work established a polynomial bound in the cube’s order. Subsequent results approached a quadratic bound: Fox and Sudakov obtained n22n+5n2^{2n+5}n22n+5, Conlon, Fox and Sudakov obtained 22n+62^{2n+6}22n+6, and Lee obtained 22n+n22n2^{2n}+n^2 2^n22n+n22n for sufficiently large nnn.

Tikhomirov then improved the exponent below two when the size is measured as m=2nm=2^nm=2n. His bound has the form 22n−cn+1+22^{2n-cn+1}+222n−cn+1+2 for an absolute c>0c>0c>0. The new manuscript claims the next endpoint: a constant multiple of mmm itself.

There was also strong progress for a cube in one color versus a fixed clique in the other. Those results do not settle the present problem, because here both target graphs grow with nnn. The manuscript draws on their way of dividing a cube into coordinated smaller cubes.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The single manuscript states that there exists an absolute constant C>0C>0C>0 such that

R(Qn)≤C2nfor every integer n≥0.R(Q_n)\leq C2^n\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq0.R(Qn​)≤C2nfor every integer n≥0.

“Absolute” means that CCC is independent of dimension. This is the new upper-bound claim.

A standard coloring gives the complementary lower bound

R(Qn)≥3⋅2n−1−1(n≥1).R(Q_n)\geq3\cdot2^{n-1}-1\qquad(n\geq1).R(Qn​)≥3⋅2n−1−1(n≥1).

For n≥2n\geq2n≥2, take two blocks of sizes 2n−12^n-12n−1 and 2n−1−12^{n-1}-12n−1−1, color edges within each block red, and edges between blocks blue. Neither red component is large enough for a cube. A blue cube would need 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1 vertices in each block, exceeding the smaller block’s size. This construction explains why the upper bound cannot have a constant arbitrarily close to one.

The paper also records consequences for subgraphs of cubes. If HHH is a subgraph of QdQ_dQd​ and

2d≤A∣V(H)∣,2^d\leq A|V(H)|,2d≤A∣V(H)∣,

then R(H)≤CA∣V(H)∣R(H)\leq CA|V(H)|R(H)≤CA∣V(H)∣. The condition says that HHH occupies at least a fixed fraction of the ambient cube’s vertices.

For a spanning subgraph FFF of QdQ_dQd​, the same absolute constant works for every Cartesian power F□kF^{\square k}F□k. Its vertices are kkk-tuples of vertices of FFF; an edge changes one entry along an edge of FFF. Concatenating the binary coordinates embeds the product in QdkQ_{dk}Qdk​, giving

R(F□k)≤C∣V(F)∣k.R(F^{\square k})\leq C|V(F)|^k.R(F□k)≤C∣V(F)∣k.

Examples include powers of paths, and of cycles, whose orders are suitable powers of two.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim settles a longstanding central question about sparse Ramsey theory with a constant uniform across all cube dimensions. The improvement is from a power larger than one in the target’s order to a linear bound, rather than a refinement of a leading constant.

Cubes have a distinctive combination of regularity and increasing local complexity. They are highly organized, yet their degrees grow logarithmically with the number of vertices. Showing that every two-color complete graph of comparable size contains such a structure identifies a strong limit on how effectively coloring can hide it.

The uniformity also produces whole new families of linear bounds through Cartesian products. A theorem whose constant depends exponentially on the number of factors would lose this conclusion. The manuscript’s treatment of simultaneous adjacency requirements and distinct vertex assignments is therefore as significant as the final asymptotic notation.

6. The main idea

Common neighbors are only half the problem

Call a cube vertex a role and a host-graph vertex a label. First assign distinct labels to the odd-parity roles. An even role vvv must then receive a label adjacent, in the selected color, to all already assigned labels of its neighbors. Its candidate set is

Lv=⋂u∼vNG(f(u)),L_v=\bigcap_{u\sim v}N_G(f(u)),Lv​=u∼v⋂​NG​(f(u)),

where f(u)f(u)f(u) is the assigned label, GGG is the chosen color graph, and NG(x)N_G(x)NG​(x) denotes the neighbors of xxx.

Nonempty candidate sets do not suffice: several roles might have only the same label available. Hall’s marriage theorem supplies the exact condition for choosing distinct representatives. Every collection of roles must collectively have at least as many available labels as roles.

One device in the manuscript is to assign each role a probability distribution pvp_vpv​ on its candidate set and show that every label has total load at most one:

∑vpv(x)≤1.\sum_v p_v(x)\leq1.v∑​pv​(x)≤1.

Since each role distributes one unit of mass, any group of roles then needs enough distinct labels to hold its total mass. This gives Hall’s condition.

Use both colors to find usable pieces

If the desired theorem failed, the paper reduces to a sequence of hosts whose sizes are arbitrarily large multiples of the corresponding cube sizes, but which contain no cube in either color. The absence in both colors imposes restrictions on weighted edge densities.

The proof studies patches: pairs of host sets equipped with sampling distributions. A distribution can focus on a smaller region, but its concentration is controlled. If a patch has sufficient bias toward one color, that surplus can help create large common neighborhoods. If no such usable bias is available, the argument derives stronger balance properties across many possible weighted patches.

The host patches receive smaller subcubes formed by fixing initial binary coordinates. The remaining coordinates describe edges inside a piece, while the fixed coordinates identify edges that must run between pieces. A slight density gain can accumulate across many adjacency requirements and compensate for the loss caused by splitting the host.

Finish without collisions

Some branches produce enough surplus to establish the probability-load bound directly. Others preserve candidate lists through a delayed assignment of selected cube roles. These delayed classes are organized using a linear map on binary strings, so each relevant role is affected in a controlled way when a class is reassigned.

The final construction leaves pairs of candidates and bounds the chance that a collection of them violates Hall’s condition. Throughout, the sampling must preserve the correct distributions while avoiding repeated labels. The strategy thus coordinates three demands: the right edge color, enough common neighbors, and injectivity of the whole embedding.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem determines the order of growth, but supplies no numerical value for the absolute constant. It does not determine whether R(Qn)/2nR(Q_n)/2^nR(Qn​)/2n converges, or what its limit would be. Closing that constant-scale uncertainty is a stronger problem.

The copy is a subgraph copy. Requiring all nonedges of the cube to appear in a prescribed way would be an induced Ramsey problem, outside the stated result. Likewise, the theorem concerns two edge colors; additional colors require separate estimates.

The subgraph consequence needs control of the ambient cube’s size. Merely embedding a small graph somewhere in a much larger cube does not give a useful linear constant in that graph’s own order. The Cartesian-power corollary works because the chosen factor spans its cube, preserving the vertex count exactly under products.

Finally, the theorem is an existence statement for every coloring. The headline does not promise an efficient procedure that finds the monochromatic cube or produces an optimized constant for applications.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s introduction gives the historical bounds, the subgraph and Cartesian-product consequences, and a four-phase guide to the embedding argument. Its common-neighborhood formulation is a useful starting point before the technical sampling estimates.

Primary landmarks include Burr–Erdős’s 1975 questions, the bounded-degree theorem, Lee’s degeneracy theorem, and Tikhomirov’s subquadratic cube bound. Hall’s original paper supplies the matching principle used to turn candidate sets into distinct assignments.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The hypercube Ramsey number has linear order (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Which finite shapes must appear in one color
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 172 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Choose a finite shape, perhaps the corners of a triangle or several points on a circle. Color every point of a Euclidean space using finitely many colors. If the dimension is high enough, must there be a copy of the shape whose points all have the same color?

The copy must preserve every distance at the original scale. Rotations and translations are allowed; enlarging the shape is not. The coloring can be completely arbitrary, with no continuity or measurability assumption.

A finite configuration with this property is called Euclidean Ramsey. The manuscript claims a classification of all such configurations by an algebraic condition on their coordinates. Among its consequences, every set of at most five points on a circle is Ramsey, while some larger spherical sets fail the condition. It also separates the Ramsey property from the ability to sit inside a finite set with transitive symmetry.

2. Background and essential definitions

A finite nonempty set AAA is Ramsey if, for every integer r≥2r\geq2r≥2, there is a dimension DDD such that every coloring

c:RD⟶{1,…,r}c:\mathbb R^D\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,r\}c:RD⟶{1,…,r}

is constant on a congruent copy of AAA. The dimension may depend on both AAA and rrr. Congruence means exact preservation of pairwise Euclidean distances.

A set is spherical if all its points lie on one sphere. A circle counts as a sphere in a plane. A finite Euclidean set is transitive if its distance-preserving symmetries can move any point to any other point. A regular polygon is an example. A set is subtransitive if it is congruent to a subset of some finite transitive set, possibly in a larger dimension.

To state the classification, place A={a1,…,as}A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}A={a1​,…,as​} in its affine span, identified with Rd\mathbb R^dRd. The affine span is the smallest translated linear subspace containing it. Let FFF be the smallest field containing the rational numbers and all coordinates of these points.

The tensor product F⊗QFF\otimes_{\mathbb Q}FF⊗Q​F keeps two copies of this field algebraically separate. Its elements are finite sums of symbols x⊗yx\otimes yx⊗y, subject to addition and rational bilinearity. In particular,

(x+x′)⊗y=x⊗y+x′⊗y,(qx)⊗y=x⊗(qy)(x+x')\otimes y=x\otimes y+x'\otimes y,\qquad(qx)\otimes y=x\otimes(qy)(x+x′)⊗y=x⊗y+x′⊗y,(qx)⊗y=x⊗(qy)

for rational qqq. One may multiply symbols by multiplying their two coordinates separately.

There is a map mFm_FmF​ that multiplies the two factors:

mF(x⊗y)=xy.m_F(x\otimes y)=xy.mF​(x⊗y)=xy.

An expression can become zero after applying this map without being zero in the tensor product. Keeping that extra information is the point of the criterion. Ordinary equations describing a sphere see only the multiplied expressions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus introduced Euclidean Ramsey theory in 1973. They proved that every finite Ramsey configuration is spherical. Graham later conjectured that this necessary condition might also be sufficient.

Positive results accumulated for geometrically important classes. Frankl and Rödl proved that nondegenerate triangles, and then all nondegenerate simplices, are Ramsey. A nondegenerate simplex consists of affinely independent vertices, such as a genuine triangle or tetrahedron. Their simplex theorem is a primary landmark. Kříž treated certain transitive symmetry groups and cyclic trapezoids, and Cantwell proved the result for regular polytopes.

A different possible classification emerged from symmetry. Leader, Russell and Walters proposed that Ramsey configurations are exactly the subtransitive ones. This would explain many known positive examples through a common geometric source. In a companion paper, they constructed cyclic quadrilaterals that are not subtransitive, making four-point circle configurations an important test.

The manuscript also places itself after several recent developments. Results on adjoining a point outside the affine span extended the known Ramsey classes, but did not settle arbitrary collections of coplanar circle points. Pálvölgyi’s September 2026 manuscript presents a seven-point circle configuration that is not Ramsey, disproving the spherical characterization. Its author also announced a proof for all finite transitive sets, with exposition still in preparation at the version cited here.

Against this background, the new manuscript claims an exact criterion rather than another isolated positive or negative family. Sphericity and transitive symmetry become consequences or sufficient conditions within a larger algebraic picture.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The exact condition

A singleton is Ramsey. For a configuration of at least two distinct points with affine span Rd\mathbb R^dRd, put

pi=(1,ai)T,B=F⊗QF.p_i=(1,a_i)^T,\qquad B=F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F.pi​=(1,ai​)T,B=F⊗Q​F.

The initial coordinate one allows affine expressions to be written as matrix expressions. The manuscript states that AAA is Ramsey if and only if there is a (d+1)(d+1)(d+1)-by-(d+1)(d+1)(d+1) matrix PPP with entries in BBB satisfying

(pi⊗1)TP(1⊗pi)=0(1≤i≤s),(p_i\otimes1)^T P(1\otimes p_i)=0\qquad(1\leq i\leq s),(pi​⊗1)TP(1⊗pi​)=0(1≤i≤s),

and

mF(Pαβ)=δαβ(1≤α,β≤d).m_F(P_{\alpha\beta})=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\qquad(1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq d).mF​(Pαβ​)=δαβ​(1≤α,β≤d).

Here tensors are formed coordinate by coordinate, and δαβ\delta_{\alpha\beta}δαβ​ is one when the indices agree and zero otherwise. The second condition says that multiplying the entries of the spatial block gives the identity matrix. It imposes no separate condition on the multiplied constant row or column.

The first equations must hold in the tensor ring itself. Applying mFm_FmF​ to them produces an ordinary equation

∥ai∥2+ℓ⋅ai+c=0\|a_i\|^2+\ell\cdot a_i+c=0∥ai​∥2+ℓ⋅ai​+c=0

for suitable ℓ\ellℓ and ccc. Completing the square gives a sphere. Thus the classification retains the classical spherical necessity but adds a stronger algebraic requirement before multiplication.

Geometric consequences

The paper claims that every nonempty subtransitive set satisfies the criterion. It also gives a sufficient condition using quadratic interpolation: quadratic polynomials must be able to prescribe arbitrary values on the chosen points. For spherical configurations satisfying this independence condition, a suitable tensor matrix exists.

This applies to every nonempty set of at most five distinct points on a circle. In particular, the non-subtransitive cyclic quadrilaterals constructed by Leader, Russell and Walters are Ramsey. The necessity direction of their proposed characterization therefore fails, according to the manuscript.

The paper also supplies negative examples illustrating the criterion: nine circle points obtained from algebraically independent parameters, and a twelve-point configuration made from three rotated squares. The nine-point conclusion is not presented as the first spherical obstruction; the earlier seven-point result is explicitly credited.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. A necessary-and-sufficient characterization for an entire classical class is an exceptional advance. It changes the question from which special geometric shapes can be handled to what exact algebraic feature governs all finite configurations.

The result also clarifies two attractive but incomplete intuitions. Lying on a sphere is necessary, yet does not capture every obstruction. Having enough finite symmetry is sufficient, yet is not necessary. The tensor condition identifies information that survives between these two descriptions.

For readers outside Ramsey theory, the striking point is that an assertion about every possible coloring of a continuum is claimed to be equivalent to an exact finite-coordinate certificate. The certificate is algebraic rather than a simple visual rule, so classification does not automatically mean easy computation. Nevertheless, it offers a common language for both constructions and impossibility examples.

6. The main idea

Retain identities that ordinary multiplication erases

The proof first rewrites the matrix condition using tensors of affine functions. An affine function is a linear function plus a constant. Evaluating the tensor at each point gives zero, while its gradient data reproduce the Euclidean metric through an identity matrix.

If no such tensor exists, an algebraic separation argument constructs a finite coloring that avoids the configuration in every dimension. This is the necessity direction: failure of the certificate becomes an obstruction to monochromatic copies.

For sufficiency, the tensor identities are converted into finite lists of affine functions with signed rational multiplicities. At each point of AAA, positive and negative contributions cancel exactly by evaluation value. The paper uses these cancellations to produce two arrays of vectors representing copies at different scales, with matching coordinate multisets.

Those coordinate multisets can be rearranged by permutations. The construction must exploit the rearrangements while retaining exact distances; an approximation argument alone would not work for arbitrary colorings.

Synchronize the scale before asking for a color

The second part uses word and group methods. A word is a finite string over a finite alphabet. The Hales–Jewett theorem guarantees a monochromatic family of words obtained by changing a common set of variable positions together, once the word length is large enough.

When coordinates of Euclidean copies are placed in separate blocks, squared distances add. If a monochromatic word pattern has ttt variable blocks, it can therefore multiply a squared distance by ttt. But the desired copy must have scale one, and ttt is initially unknown.

The manuscript prepares compatible constructions with weights 1,1/2,…,1/n1,1/2,\ldots,1/n1,1/2,…,1/n, where nnn is the chosen word length. Whichever number ttt of variable positions appears, the weight 1/t1/t1/t cancels that multiplier exactly. Additional group constructions align the endpoints associated with the coordinate permutations. Compactness then yields a finite ambient dimension for each prescribed number of colors.

This explains the two demanding parts of the argument: preserving exact algebraic cancellations and coordinating the scale selected by a combinatorial theorem. Neither can be replaced by saying that the resulting shape is merely close to the intended one.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The classification is for finite nonempty configurations, arbitrary finite colorings, and congruent copies at the original scale. Allowing a free dilation would change the problem. Requiring measurable colorings would also change what kinds of obstruction are relevant.

The coordinate-field condition is invariant under replacing the configuration by a congruent representative. It depends on exact relations among coordinates, however. Decimal approximations to arbitrary real coordinates do not supply those relations, so the statement is not a numerical decision algorithm for a drawing or a list of rounded measurements.

The theorem guarantees some finite dimension for each configuration and number of colors. Its headline does not provide a practical optimal dimension bound. Finding usable certificates or obstructions for concrete families, and making the dimension dependence effective and sharp, remain separate tasks.

The five-point circle consequence and the existing seven-point obstruction also leave an evident small-configuration question: how the criterion behaves for six circle points. The classification supplies a framework for that investigation without turning every intermediate case into an immediate corollary.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s first section states the criterion and explains why ordinary sphere equations lose information. Its final section derives the subtransitive, circle-point and negative-example consequences.

For primary background, see Frankl–Rödl on simplices, Leader–Russell–Walters on transitive sets, their cyclic quadrilateral examples, and Pálvölgyi’s non-Ramsey heptagon. The bibliography of M1 gives the original Euclidean Ramsey papers and the word-theoretic sources behind the exact-scale construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Finding a vertex whose second neighborhood is at least as large as its first
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 173 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine a network of one-way links. From a starting point, some vertices are reachable in one step. Others become reachable for the first time in two steps. Must there be a starting point for which the second group is at least as large as the first?

The network may be irregular, disconnected or sparse. The only restriction, beyond finiteness, is that a pair of vertices cannot carry links in both directions. Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture predicts that such a starting point always exists.

The manuscript claims the conjecture in full. Its argument turns a supposed failure at every vertex into an impossible expansion rule for all vertex subsets. A separate pruning principle for pairs of sets supplies the contradiction. The paper also records weighted versions and consequences for short directed cycles.

2. Background and essential definitions

An oriented graph is obtained by assigning directions to the edges of a simple undirected graph. It has no loops, repeated arcs or opposite pair of arcs. Write v→uv\to uv→u for an arc from vvv to uuu.

The first out-neighborhood is

N1+(v)={u:v→u}.N_1^+(v)=\{u:v\to u\}.N1+​(v)={u:v→u}.

The exact second out-neighborhood is

N2+(v)={w∉{v}∪N1+(v): some u satisfies v→u→w}.N_2^+(v)=\{w\notin\{v\}\cup N_1^+(v):\text{ some }u\text{ satisfies }v\to u\to w\}.N2+​(v)={w∈/{v}∪N1+​(v): some u satisfies v→u→w}.

The word “exact” matters. A vertex already reachable in one step does not count in the second group, even if it is also reachable in two steps. Each endpoint counts once, regardless of how many two-step paths reach it.

For example, a directed triangle has one first and one exact second out-neighbor at every vertex. A sink, meaning a vertex with no outgoing arcs, has neither; it satisfies the desired inequality trivially. In a directed chain, the last vertex is a sink, while an interior vertex sufficiently far from the end has one neighbor of each kind.

The outdegree d+(v)d^+(v)d+(v) is ∣N1+(v)∣|N_1^+(v)|∣N1+​(v)∣. The indegree d−(v)d^-(v)d−(v) counts vertices with arcs into vvv. A tournament is an oriented graph with an arc between every pair of distinct vertices. It is a particularly dense special case, not the general setting of the claim.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The conjecture was recorded by Dean and Latka in 1995. The tournament case, also known as Dean’s conjecture, was proved by Fisher in 1996 using a probability distribution obtained from linear programming duality. Havet and Thomassé later gave a combinatorial proof using specially chosen vertex orders.

Those results suggested that the inequality was compatible with very dense directed networks. Further work extended it to tournaments with particular missing-edge patterns, such as a matching or certain stars. These patterns allow some of the tournament structure to remain available even though the underlying graph is no longer complete.

Another approach restricted degrees. Kaneko and Locke established the conjecture when the minimum outdegree is at most six. A 2026 computer-assisted manuscript treats minimum outdegree seven. Such results cover all graphs with a sufficiently low-degree vertex, but leave arbitrary large minimum degrees untouched.

A third line weakened the desired comparison to

∣N2+(v)∣≥λ∣N1+(v)∣|N_2^+(v)|\geq\lambda|N_1^+(v)|∣N2+​(v)∣≥λ∣N1+​(v)∣

for a universal constant λ<1\lambda<1λ<1. Chen, Shen and Yuster obtained approximately 0.6572980.6572980.657298. Huang and Peng raised the theoretical bound to approximately 0.7155380.7155380.715538, and reported a computational bound of 0.745300.745300.74530. The original conjecture asks for the endpoint λ=1\lambda=1λ=1.

Results for orientations of random graphs and for sufficiently dense graphs supplied other substantial partial cases. The manuscript’s principal structural predecessors are the minimal-counterexample and graph-product methods of Brantner, Brockman, Kay and Snively, together with Seacrest’s subset formulation. The new argument claims to combine a strengthened subset inequality with a pruning lemma that is valid for arbitrary finite binary relations.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The unweighted theorem

For every nonempty finite oriented graph, the manuscript states that some vertex vvv satisfies

∣N1+(v)∣≤∣N2+(v)∣.|N_1^+(v)|\leq|N_2^+(v)|.∣N1+​(v)∣≤∣N2+​(v)∣.

There is no connectivity assumption and no lower or upper degree restriction. The statement is existential: it guarantees at least one suitable vertex, rather than the inequality at every vertex.

Two different weighted conclusions

For a nonnegative vertex weighting η\etaη, write

η(S)=∑x∈Sη(x).\eta(S)=\sum_{x\in S}\eta(x).η(S)=x∈S∑​η(x).

The paper invokes Seacrest’s established weighted equivalences to obtain two consequences with different quantifier orders. For every specified weighting, there is a vertex satisfying

η(N1+(v))≤η(N2+(v)).\eta(N_1^+(v))\leq\eta(N_2^+(v)).η(N1+​(v))≤η(N2+​(v)).

Conversely, there exists some nonnegative weighting of total mass one for which this inequality holds at every vertex simultaneously. The weights in that second conclusion may include zeros. It does not say that every weighting works everywhere.

The manuscript also states the corresponding arc-weighted form through the same earlier equivalences. These equivalences are credited as existing results; the new input is the claimed unweighted theorem for all oriented graphs.

A directed-triangle consequence

If an oriented graph on nnn vertices has both minimum indegree and minimum outdegree at least n/3n/3n/3, the manuscript concludes that it contains a directed triangle.

To see the connection, suppose there is no directed triangle. Every exact second out-neighbor of vvv must then be a non-neighbor: an arc back into vvv would close a triangle, while an arc out of vvv is excluded by the exact-distance definition. For the vertex supplied by the main theorem, counting the disjoint groups gives

n−1≥2d+(v)+d−(v).n-1\geq2d^+(v)+d^-(v).n−1≥2d+(v)+d−(v).

Both degree lower bounds would make the right side at least nnn, an impossibility. This consequence uses both directions of degree; it is not the general one-sided minimum-outdegree conjecture about short cycles.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim resolves a central and elementary-to-state problem in directed graph theory. Its simplicity is deceptive: local two-step reachability can overlap heavily with immediate reachability, so an ordinary averaging argument does not directly produce the desired vertex.

The assertion also holds without the global regularity used in many earlier partial cases. Reaching the exact factor one unifies tournament, bounded-degree and approximate-ratio results under a single theorem.

The weighted consequences make the comparison more flexible. Vertices may represent unequal amounts of mass rather than indistinguishable units, while the existence of a favorable viewpoint survives. The new pruning principle is potentially interesting beyond this specific conjecture because its statement concerns general finite relations. The rating reflects the complete conjecture and these structural connections, conditional on the manuscript’s claims.

6. The main idea

Strengthen a local failure into a subset rule

For a vertex subset SSS, let

F(S)={y: some x∈S has x→y}.F(S)=\{y:\text{ some }x\in S\text{ has }x\to y\}.F(S)={y: some x∈S has x→y}.

This is the union of outgoing neighbors; it does not automatically remove vertices of SSS. Applying FFF twice gives all endpoints of two-step walks starting in SSS, again without the exact-distance exclusions used for an individual neighborhood.

Assume every vertex violates the desired theorem and choose a counterexample first with as few vertices, then as few arcs, as possible. The manuscript uses carefully chosen arc deletions to deduce a strict deficit for every nonempty proper subset. It then replaces each vertex by a sufficiently large transitively oriented complete graph, with all arcs between blocks following the original directions.

This enlarged graph is claimed to satisfy

∣U∣+∣F2(U)∣<2∣F(U)∣|U|+|F^2(U)|<2|F(U)|∣U∣+∣F2(U)∣<2∣F(U)∣

for every nonempty proper subset UUU. Thus its first image would always be strictly larger than the average size of the starting set and the second image. The task becomes ruling out such a universal expansion pattern.

Compare two families of ordered pairs

Work in the square of the vertex set. An ordered pair has two coordinates, and each coordinate can advance along a graph arc while the other stays fixed. The argument chooses two families of pairs whose respective coordinate images do not overlap. Both families must contain the diagonal pairs (v,v)(v,v)(v,v).

Let MMM be the combined size of the two families and let ddd count positions left uncovered by their images. Choose compatible families maximizing M+dM+dM+d. Applying the subset inequality to their columns and rows produces larger prospective families, with combined size exceeding M+2dM+2dM+2d.

The prospective families can conflict. Simply deleting every conflict might destroy the gain. The pruning lemma instead restores compatibility while preserving the diagonal and charging its deletion cost partly to positions that remain uncovered afterward.

If d′d'd′ is that new uncovered count, the stated cost is at most d+d′d+d'd+d′. The new objective therefore exceeds

M+2d−(d+d′)+d′=M+d,M+2d-(d+d')+d'=M+d,M+2d−(d+d′)+d′=M+d,

contradicting maximality. The cancellation explains why the uncovered positions belong in the objective: they compensate for part of the later pruning loss.

The lemma itself uses a matching construction and linear algebra, comparing two ways to advance the coordinates. This is the additional mechanism that allows the local neighborhood problem to be closed by a global extremal argument.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The orientation restriction is indispensable to the stated theorem. With two vertices joined in both directions, each vertex has one first out-neighbor and no exact second out-neighbor. Such a directed graph is excluded from the outset.
