Through another published equivalence, it also concludes that every three-edge path in a finite simple cubic, bipartite, 3-connected Pfaffian graph extends to a Hamiltonian cycle. A graph is Pfaffian if it has an orientation in which each even cycle whose deletion leaves a perfect matching has an odd number of edges directed along either traversal of that cycle. This is a matching-theoretic condition that includes planar graphs and also allows some nonplanar ones.

The principal theorem is an existence claim. Although its ingredients include finite matchings and flows, the manuscript does not assert a polynomial-time algorithm for finding the Hamiltonian cycle. The finite weighted sum used to establish existence may involve many states.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. Barnette’s conjecture is a major longstanding problem about when local degree, planarity, connectivity and parity force a global spanning route. The claim removes the face-size restrictions of earlier partial results.

The central difficulty is connectedness of the route. It is comparatively easy to describe a spanning structure that gives every vertex degree two; preventing it from breaking into multiple cycles is much harder. The dual-tree construction builds that global connectedness into the argument.

The prescribed local pattern is also significant. Recursive arguments cut a graph into pieces, but independently chosen solutions may fail to match along their boundaries. Retaining a small boundary condition allows the manuscript to glue the pieces back together while preserving induced trees. The importance rating reflects both the full conjecture and this structural treatment of compatibility.

6. The main idea

Translate one cycle into two trees

Suppose the dual triangulation’s vertices have been split into two induced trees. Every triangular face then has exactly one edge inside a tree class: it cannot have all three vertices in one class, because that would create a cycle.

Discard those tree edges and return to the original graph by duality. Exactly two selected edges meet each original vertex, so the result has degree two everywhere. Complementary planar tree–forest duality supplies connectedness. A finite connected graph of degree two is one cycle, hence a Hamiltonian cycle.

The task is therefore to construct the two-tree partition, including the prescribed pattern on a chosen triangle.

Pair matching states

First assume there is no separating triangle, meaning no triangular cycle with vertices strictly on both sides. Choose one black triangle as the outer face and call its vertices roots.

The remaining black triangles and the nonroot vertices have equal cardinality. A state matches every remaining black triangle to one incident nonroot vertex, using each such vertex once. A pair of states chooses different vertices in every triangle. A planar counting inequality and an integral flow argument establish that such pairs exist.

For the second state sss, select the edge opposite its chosen vertex in each black triangle. Call the selected edge set QsQ_sQs​. The desired intermediate object is a state for which QsQ_sQs​ is a forest.

Cancel the cyclic states, then show something survives

The manuscript introduces a finite weighted sum over pairs of states. The same sum is analyzed in two ways.

When the second state is fixed and QsQ_sQs​ contains a cycle, a reversal changes the first state and pairs two terms with opposite phases but equal real weights. These contributions cancel. Thus only pairs with acyclic QsQ_sQs​ can survive in the total.

To prove that the sum is not zero, the terms are regrouped according to the undirected edges joining the two chosen vertices in each triangle. Their components are cycles, and choosing a pair of states amounts to choosing orientations of those cycles.

Suitable positive circulations determine the real weights. A planar disk identity controls the phases. Near a chosen parameter value, the groups with the fewest cycles have leading contributions with a common phase and positive magnitude, so they cannot cancel each other. Some forest state must therefore exist.

From that forest, complementary plane-tree duality produces the edge structure needed for the two induced trees. This is an existence mechanism based on cancellation and nonvanishing, not a claim that arbitrary local choices already produce the correct forest.

Glue across separating triangles

If a separating triangle is present, split the triangulation into two smaller ones and cap each side along the triangle. Apply the theorem recursively while prescribing matching labels on the shared boundary.

For each tree class, the two smaller induced trees meet in either one vertex or one edge. Gluing trees along such a connected intersection produces a tree. The preserved facial pattern is what makes this final assembly possible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All four graph hypotheses remain part of the main theorem. Tutte’s earlier example already shows that removing bipartiteness from the cubic polyhedral setting does not preserve the conclusion. The manuscript does not claim Hamiltonicity for arbitrary bipartite planar graphs or for graphs with weaker connectivity.

The output is a Hamiltonian cycle, not a uniquely determined one or a lower bound on how many such cycles exist. Avoiding one specified edge is guaranteed, but arbitrary collections of forbidden edges are not covered by that statement.

The Pfaffian extension uses a specific published equivalence and retains cubicity, bipartiteness and 3-connectivity. It is not a blanket nonplanar generalization.

Finally, efficient construction remains separate from the stated existence argument. A matching or flow step can be algorithmic while a later nonvanishing argument is still nonconstructive in its complexity guarantees. Determining useful algorithms, optimized structural criteria or stronger prescribed-route properties requires further results.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s first two pages explain the dual formulation, the paired states and the two distinct regroupings of the weighted sum. Its final section records edge avoidance and the Pfaffian consequence.

Primary background includes Tutte’s non-Hamiltonian cubic polyhedron, Goodey’s quadrilateral–hexagon case, Schnieders’s face-size-eight result, Alt–Payne–Schmidt–Wood’s dual viewpoint, and Gorsky–Steiner–Wiederrecht’s matching equivalences. These distinguish the earlier reductions from the general existence claim explained here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Paired states and Hamiltonian cycles in cubic bipartite planar graphs (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Partitioning every graph into only linearly many cycles and edges
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 181 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A dense graph may have quadratically many edges. Can all of them be organized into only linearly many simple cycles, with individual edges used for the parts that cannot join a cycle?

Single edges are necessary: a tree has no cycle at all. The Erdős–Gallai cycle decomposition conjecture says this allowance is enough. Every graph on nnn vertices should have an edge partition into at most CnCnCn cycles and single edges for one universal constant CCC.

The manuscript claims the conjecture. Earlier general bounds had reduced the extra factor from a logarithm to an iterated logarithm. The new argument claims to eliminate that last growing factor by saving vertices during recursion and using those savings to pay for the work of joining paths into cycles.

2. Background and essential definitions

All graphs in the main theorem are finite, simple and undirected. A simple cycle visits distinct vertices before returning to its start and has length at least three.

An edge partition assigns every graph edge to exactly one part. Here each part must be either the complete edge set of a simple cycle or one individual edge. Different parts may share vertices; they may not share edges.

This differs from an edge cover by cycles and edges, where repeated use of the same edge is permitted. A small cover need not become a small partition when repetitions are removed: cutting edges out of a cycle can break it into many paths.

Write e(G)e(G)e(G) for the number of edges and Δ(G)\Delta(G)Δ(G) for the maximum vertex degree. A graph is Eulerian in this article when all vertex degrees are even; connectivity is not required. Such a graph has a decomposition into cycles, but controlling their number is a further problem.

The notation O(n)O(n)O(n) means at most a constant multiple of nnn, with the constant independent of the graph. The earlier term log⁡∗n\log^*nlog∗n is the number of successive logarithms needed to reduce nnn to at most one. It grows extraordinarily slowly, but it is still unbounded. Removing it changes an almost-linear estimate into a uniform linear theorem.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The conjecture was recorded in the 1966 paper of Erdős, Goodman and Pósa, which distinguished edge-disjoint decompositions from unrestricted covers and gave an O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) upper bound.

Conlon, Fox and Sudakov improved the general bound to O(nlog⁡log⁡n)O(n\log\log n)O(nloglogn) in 2014. Their methods used sparse cuts and reserved edges to organize cycles across different density scales. Bucić and Montgomery subsequently reached

O(nlog⁡∗n),O(n\log^*n),O(nlog∗n),

with the journal version appearing in 2024. Expansion, hypergraph matching and path-closing methods in that work form the principal starting point of the present manuscript.

Linear bounds were already known in important settings. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov proved them for graphs of linear minimum degree and, with high probability, for binomial random graphs. Korándi, Krivelevich and Sudakov obtained asymptotically sharp counts over a broad random-graph range.

For dense graphs, Girão, Granet, Kühn and Osthus obtained a bound of (3/2+δ)n(3/2+\delta)n(3/2+δ)n for every fixed positive δ\deltaδ, provided the minimum degree is a fixed positive fraction of nnn and nnn is sufficiently large. Akbari, Aloni, Beikmohammadi and Clow proved the bound n−1n-1n−1 for graphs of positive order and maximum degree at most four.

The unrestricted covering problem was easier: Pyber proved that n−1n-1n−1 cycles and edges cover every graph of positive order, and later work improved this when a cycle is present. Those results permit overlap and therefore do not settle the edge-partition question.

The new claim handles arbitrary mixtures of sparse regions, dense regions and highly unequal degrees, while preserving a unique assignment of every edge throughout the construction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that there is an absolute constant C>0C>0C>0 such that every graph GGG on nnn vertices has a partition

E(G)=E1∪˙⋯∪˙Em,m≤Cn,E(G)=E_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}E_m,\qquad m\leq Cn,E(G)=E1​∪˙⋯∪˙Em​,m≤Cn,

where each EjE_jEj​ is either a simple cycle’s edge set or a singleton. The dotted union means the parts are disjoint.

The empty partition is allowed when the graph has no edges. Isolated vertices require no separate part. The same constant works for every graph size and every degree pattern.

The paper derives two cycle-only consequences. First, every Eulerian graph on nnn vertices has a partition into at most CnCnCn cycles. To understand the deduction, remove the cycle parts from the main decomposition. The remaining single-edge graph still has even degrees and can itself be decomposed into cycles, using no more parts than the number of leftover edges.

Second, fix δ,p>0\delta,p>0δ,p>0. For sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and sufficiently large nnn, an Eulerian graph satisfying

eG(A,B)≥p∣A∣∣B∣e_G(A,B)\geq p|A||B|eG​(A,B)≥p∣A∣∣B∣

for every vertex partition into two sets of size at least εn\varepsilon nεn has a decomposition into at most

Δ(G)2+δn\frac{\Delta(G)}2+\delta n2Δ(G)​+δn

cycles. Here eG(A,B)e_G(A,B)eG​(A,B) counts crossing edges. This is a large-cut density condition, and the consequence uses a previously established equivalence in the dense-decomposition literature.

The maximum-degree term is unavoidable: each cycle can use at most two edges incident with a fixed vertex. Thus at least Δ(G)/2\Delta(G)/2Δ(G)/2 cycles are necessary, and the corollary approaches this lower bound up to a small linear error under the additional hypothesis.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claim establishes a longstanding universal decomposition principle. A graph with up to quadratically many edges can be described by only linearly many edge-disjoint cyclic pieces and isolated edge pieces, regardless of its irregularity.

The order of the bound is best possible. A tree on nnn vertices requires n−1n-1n−1 single-edge parts. Certain complete bipartite examples require approximately 3n/23n/23n/2 parts, so even the optimal universal leading constant cannot be read off from trees alone.

The advance is subtle because log⁡∗n\log^*nlog∗n is tiny for any ordinary numerical input. Mathematically, however, a uniform linear bound demands a new accounting mechanism: work across arbitrarily many scales cannot repeatedly charge the full vertex set. The manuscript’s vertex-saving recursion is intended to supply that missing mechanism. Its Eulerian consequences also connect the general result with nearly optimal cycle counts in dense settings.

6. The main idea

Separate the graph by scales

A graph has strong cut expansion when every vertex set has many outgoing edges compared with its smaller side. Such regions are useful for routing paths: there are many ways to connect selected endpoints without consuming the same edges repeatedly.

The proof divides the graph into overlapping vertex regions with disjoint assigned edge sets. At each scale it removes a controlled collection of long cycles, extracts expanding pieces, and sends sparser residual graphs to smaller scales. The overlap in vertex counts must be carefully bounded even though the edges remain uniquely assigned.

Processing every expanding piece at every scale would recreate the unwanted logarithmic loss. Instead, the manuscript selects one layer whose total size can pay for a whole earlier portion of the decomposition.

Reserve routes before simplifying

Some edges in the selected expanding pieces are reserved for later connections. The remaining sparse regions are collected into batches. Many vertices have low total degree across the relevant batch, allowing them to be paired and identified.

Identifying two vertices reduces the order of the graph. This gives the induction a smaller problem, but it can create loops or parallel edges. The construction sets aside only a controlled linear number of such troublesome edges and records an original representative for every retained quotient edge.

The quotient graphs are then decomposed recursively. The saved vertex count is the resource that pays for the parts already completed and the edges set aside outside the recursive calls.

Lift quotient cycles back to real cycles

A cycle in the quotient may enter an identified vertex through one original member of the pair and leave through the other. To lift it back, those two original vertices must be joined by a reserved path.

The routing lemma chooses these paths edge-disjointly. It also keeps their interiors away from the representative endpoints and, within each lifted cycle, from one another. These conditions ensure that one quotient cycle becomes one simple original cycle, rather than a closed walk with repeated vertices.

This is why arbitrary contraction would not suffice. The identifications are coordinated with expansion and reserved routes from the beginning. The construction must retain both a smaller recursive graph and enough unused structure to undo its simplification.

Make the savings exceed the overhead

The recursive cost is not bounded merely by writing CnCnCn at every stage. The manuscript proves a slightly stronger estimate Cϕ(n)nC\phi(n)nCϕ(n)n, where ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n) approaches one slowly from below.

Smaller quotient graphs have a smaller value of this factor. That additional decrease absorbs the overlap and rounding costs left after the main vertex savings. The final bound is then at most CnCnCn.

The overall strategy combines classical path decompositions, matching theorems for choosing disjoint routes, and a multiscale induction whose budget is tied to genuine reductions in vertex count.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem gives an unspecified universal constant, not the sharp leading constant. The examples requiring nearly 3n/23n/23n/2 parts remain relevant to the finer optimization problem.

The graph is simple. Temporary quotient multigraphs are cleaned up internally, but that does not amount to a theorem with the same CnCnCn bound for arbitrary parallel-edge inputs. The definition of a cycle remains simple and of length at least three.

Single edges are permitted in the general conclusion. Removing that allowance requires an even-degree condition; otherwise some edges cannot belong to an edge-disjoint cycle decomposition. The Eulerian corollary makes this distinction explicit.

The near-Δ/2\Delta/2Δ/2 count requires the stated density condition across every sufficiently large vertex partition. It is not claimed for every Eulerian graph. Finally, the headline is an existence theorem and does not state an optimized practical algorithm for minimizing the number of parts.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s introduction gives the progression from logarithmic losses to the linear claim and carefully distinguishes covers from partitions. Its roadmap explains how reserved routes allow quotient cycles to be lifted without edge reuse.

The main immediate predecessor is Bucić–Montgomery’s decomposition paper. Akbari–Aloni–Beikmohammadi–Clow gives recent sharp results for restricted degrees and overlapping covers. M1’s bibliography identifies the original Erdős–Goodman–Pósa formulation, Conlon–Fox–Sudakov’s cycle-packing work, and the dense-graph equivalence used for the final corollary.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A linear cycle-and-edge decomposition of every graph (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A power saving for sets avoiding polynomial differences
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 182 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

How many integers can be chosen from 1,…,N1,\ldots,N1,…,N if no two chosen numbers differ by a nonzero square? More generally, what if differences are forbidden whenever they equal a value of a fixed polynomial?

Classical recurrence theorems say that the density of such a set must tend to zero, provided the polynomial has no local congruence obstruction. The quantitative challenge is how quickly it must vanish. A fixed power saving would bound the size by CN1−cCN^{1-c}CN1−c for some constant c>0c>0c>0, crossing a longstanding barrier between subpower decay and polynomial decay.

The three manuscripts claim this improvement for squares, for every intersective polynomial of fixed degree, and for suitable polynomials evaluated only at primes. The prime-argument result uses a separate new zero-free theorem for Dirichlet LLL-functions. Its dependency and its stronger local hypothesis are essential parts of the statement.

2. Background and essential definitions

Write [N]={1,…,N}[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}[N]={1,…,N} and

A−A={a−b:a,b∈A}.A-A=\{a-b:a,b\in A\}.A−A={a−b:a,b∈A}.

A set is square-difference-free when A−AA-AA−A contains no positive square. Since differences occur with both signs, this is equivalent to forbidding a nonzero square as an absolute difference.

An integer polynomial hhh is intersective if it has a root modulo every positive integer qqq: for each qqq, some integer rrr satisfies h(r)≡0(modq)h(r)\equiv0\pmod qh(r)≡0(modq). The roots may vary with the modulus, and hhh need not have a rational root.

This condition is necessary for a general density theorem. If hhh has no root modulo some qqq, all multiples of qqq form a positive-density set whose differences avoid every value of hhh. Squares are intersective because zero is a root modulo every modulus.

When arguments are restricted to primes, the condition becomes prime-intersectivity: for every qqq, there is a root rrr with

gcd⁡(r,q)=1,h(r)≡0(modq).\gcd(r,q)=1,\qquad h(r)\equiv0\pmod q.gcd(r,q)=1,h(r)≡0(modq).

Such a root is called a unit root. It belongs to a residue class compatible with primes not dividing the modulus. The polynomial (x−1)2(x-1)^2(x−1)2 has this property, using r=1r=1r=1. The polynomial x2x^2x2 does not: modulo a prime, its only root is zero.

A power-saving estimate has the form ∣A∣≤CN1−c|A|\leq CN^{1-c}∣A∣≤CN1−c, so the density is at most CN−cCN^{-c}CN−c. This is stronger than

Nexp⁡(−alog⁡N),N\exp\bigl(-a\sqrt{\log N}\bigr),Nexp(−alogN​),

because a fixed power saving corresponds to exp⁡(−clog⁡N)\exp(-c\log N)exp(−clogN). The constants are fixed before NNN grows.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Furstenberg and Sárközy independently proved that every positive-density set of integers contains two elements with nonzero square difference. Furstenberg used ergodic theory; Sárközy used Fourier analysis. Kamae and Mendès France extended the density conclusion to nonconstant intersective polynomials, matching the necessary congruence condition.

Quantitative bounds then improved through increasingly refined density-increment arguments. Pintz, Steiger and Szemerédi introduced a stronger iteration for square differences. Bloom and Maynard improved the logarithmic decay using additive-energy estimates for rational frequencies.

Green and Sawhney obtained

∣A∣≪Nexp⁡(−alog⁡N)|A|\ll N\exp\bigl(-a\sqrt{\log N}\bigr)∣A∣≪Nexp(−alogN​)

for square-difference-free sets. Their arithmetic level inequality connected rational Fourier coefficients with product-space methods. For general intersective polynomials, Lucier developed auxiliary polynomials adapted to arithmetic progressions, and Rice and Arala strengthened the quantitative bounds. Adajar and collaborators extended the newer method to obtain density decay exp⁡(−a(log⁡N)μ)\exp(-a(\log N)^\mu)exp(−a(logN)μ) for every fixed μ<1/2\mu<1/2μ<1/2.

Lower-bound constructions show that square-difference-free sets can still be large. Ruzsa and later authors built examples with power-law size; the manuscript cites Krachun’s lower exponent exceeding 0.75270.75270.7527. Thus even a power-saving upper bound leaves a substantial exponent gap.

The prime-argument problem has its own history. Sárközy treated differences p−1p-1p−1 and p+1p+1p+1, and Green later obtained a power saving for these linear examples. For nonlinear prime-intersective polynomials, Rice proved quantitative logarithmic bounds and recorded the qualitative characterization through unit roots. M2 claims a fixed power saving in this nonlinear setting, using the square and polynomial framework together with its stated analytic companion input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M3: square differences

M3 states that absolute constants c>0c>0c>0 and C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ exist such that every square-difference-free A⊆[N]A\subseteq[N]A⊆[N] satisfies

∣A∣≤CN1−c.|A|\leq CN^{1-c}.∣A∣≤CN1−c.

The exponent is described as extremely small, with no useful numerical value or optimality claim. The result also gives a polynomial bound for square-difference colorings: if

N>(Cr)1/c,N>(Cr)^{1/c},N>(Cr)1/c,

every rrr-coloring of [N][N][N] has same-colored elements a,a+d2a,a+d^2a,a+d2 with d≥1d\geq1d≥1. Only the two endpoints must share a color; ddd has no color requirement.

M1: all intersective polynomials of a fixed degree

For every degree k≥2k\geq2k≥2, M1 claims an exponent ck>0c_k>0ck​>0 common to all intersective integer polynomials of degree kkk with positive leading coefficient. For each fixed such hhh, there are constants Ch,NhC_h,N_hCh​,Nh​ such that

(A−A)∩h({1,2,…})⊆{0}⟹∣A∣≤ChN1−ck(A-A)\cap h(\{1,2,\ldots\})\subseteq\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|A|\leq C_hN^{1-c_k}(A−A)∩h({1,2,…})⊆{0}⟹∣A∣≤Ch​N1−ck​

for N≥NhN\geq N_hN≥Nh​. The leading constant and starting threshold may depend on every coefficient of hhh. Only the saving exponent is uniform across a fixed degree.

Zero values are explicitly permitted in the intersection: a polynomial root contributes no forbidden nonzero difference. Arguments are positive integers, and differences are ordinary integer differences, not merely residues modulo a chosen modulus.

M2: polynomial values at primes

For each fixed prime-intersective integer polynomial hhh of degree at least two with positive leading coefficient, M2 claims constants ch>0c_h>0ch​>0 and Ch≥1C_h\geq1Ch​≥1 such that

(A−A)∩{h(p):p prime}⊆{0}⟹∣A∣≤ChN1−ch(A-A)\cap\{h(p):p\text{ prime}\}\subseteq\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|A|\leq C_hN^{1-c_h}(A−A)∩{h(p):p prime}⊆{0}⟹∣A∣≤Ch​N1−ch​

for every positive integer NNN. Here the exponent may depend on the whole polynomial, not only its degree.

M2 uses the companion claim that every Dirichlet LLL-function is zero-free in Re⁡s>7/8\operatorname{Re}s>7/8Res>7/8, with the principal pole at one allowed. Dirichlet LLL-functions encode arithmetic progressions through multiplicative periodic coefficients; control of their zeros yields estimates for primes in residue classes. This is the specific new input explained in family 003, rather than a classical zero-free estimate silently assumed by the prime argument.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The square-difference problem is a foundational quantitative recurrence problem. Crossing to a fixed power saving changes the scale of the answer, and extending that conclusion to the full local-obstruction class of integer polynomials greatly broadens its reach.

The fixed-degree uniformity in M1 is another substantive feature. Polynomial coefficients can create very different congruence behavior. The claim allows those differences to affect constants and starting scales while keeping one positive exponent for each degree.

The prime result is stronger in a different direction: forbidding only values at prime arguments excludes fewer differences, so avoiding sets could potentially be larger. The manuscript claims power decay even under that weaker avoidance condition, for the appropriate unit-root class and using its stated analytic dependency.

These bounds remain far from an optimal exponent. Their importance lies in establishing a new qualitative rate of decay, not in predicting the largest avoiding set accurately for a practical numerical range.

6. The main idea

Measure more than density

Classical density-increment arguments locate an arithmetic progression where the set becomes denser, then repeat. The manuscripts instead construct a nonnegative multilinear quantity Y(N,A)Y(N,A)Y(N,A) that dominates a fixed power of density:

(∣A∣N)d≤Y(N,A),\left(\frac{|A|}{N}\right)^d\leq Y(N,A),(N∣A∣​)d≤Y(N,A),

where ddd is a fixed even number of slots in an auxiliary construction. They seek a recurrence forcing YYY to decay as a power of NNN.

The construction works first over finite fields. It chooses probability laws on tuples of residue labels so that selected differences are polynomial values, except for a small controlled exceptional part. The laws also satisfy reflection positivity: splitting the tuple along prescribed reflections gives positive semidefinite coupling matrices.

Repeated Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities across these reflections yield a norm-like estimate. This remains valid for signed inputs, which is necessary because the Fourier approximations used later need not be nonnegative.

Connect local residues with actual integer values

A Fourier lift retains selected rational-frequency coefficients of the indicator of AAA. It places the integer set into a product of residue spaces while preserving its mean density.

Residue constraints alone do not ensure an actual square or polynomial difference in the integers. The papers therefore construct a signed kernel supported on genuine polynomial values. Its Fourier transform approximates the pair distribution prescribed by the tuple law.

If AAA avoids those values, the kernel’s contribution on appropriate ordered pairs from AAA vanishes, irrespective of the signs of its weights. This cancellation controls a positive portion of the multilinear expression. Other terms are compared with the same kind of expression on shorter intervals, and exceptional contributions are kept summable.

Preserve the problem when changing scale

For squares, restricting to a progression of square step preserves square-difference avoidance after rescaling. General polynomials change under progression restriction, so M1 organizes them into a compatible family of auxiliary polynomials.

A normalization at chosen local roots makes the structural parameters determining the exponent depend only on the degree. Weighted tuple laws transform compatibly with the auxiliary family, while the signed kernels reproduce their changing polynomial-value distributions.

M2 must additionally restrict arguments to unit residue classes and realize its kernel on values at actual primes. The companion zero-free theorem supplies the needed prime-distribution estimates on the major arcs, the neighborhoods of simple rational frequencies. Other frequencies are controlled by exponential-sum methods. The final contraction follows the same broad architecture, with constants depending on the fixed polynomial.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The power-saving exponents are positive but not optimized or numerically useful. The square problem still has a large gap between known construction exponents and the claimed upper exponent near one.

M1 fixes the polynomial before NNN grows. Uniformity of ckc_kck​ does not make the constants uniform over arbitrarily large coefficients. M2 has a different guarantee: even its exponent may depend on hhh.

Prime-intersectivity is stronger than ordinary intersectivity. In particular, M2 does not apply directly to h(x)=x2h(x)=x^2h(x)=x2 and therefore does not claim the same theorem for forbidding only prime squares. It does apply to (x−1)2(x-1)^2(x−1)2, giving a power saving when the forbidden differences are (p−1)2(p-1)^2(p−1)2.

The prime theorem depends on the specified zero-free companion. M1 and M3 do not require that prime-distribution input. Keeping the dependency separate is necessary to understand what each manuscript establishes within the collection.

Finally, the conclusions force one forbidden difference, not a long polynomial progression or a monochromatic polynomial configuration with every parameter sharing the same color. Such extensions would need additional statements.

8. Sources and further reading

M3 develops the square-difference framework. M1, dated October 5, extends it to general intersective polynomials with a degree-dependent exponent. M2, also dated October 5, adapts the method to prime arguments.

Primary predecessors include Bloom–Maynard, Green–Sawhney, Adajar and collaborators, and Rice on prime-intersective polynomials. The prime-distribution dependency is the September 30 zero-free manuscript, discussed in family 003. M1 and M3 also explain the earlier recurrence theorems and the reflection-positivity background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A power saving for intersective polynomial differences with an exponent depending only on the degree (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Power Saving for Polynomial Differences at Prime Arguments (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A power saving for square-difference-free sets (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A full logarithmic gain from excluding a fixed clique
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 184 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A graph with maximum degree Δ\DeltaΔ can always be colored with Δ+1\Delta+1Δ+1 colors by a greedy procedure. But if the graph contains no large clique, can substantially fewer colors suffice?

Forbidding a triangle is known to save a logarithmic factor. The longstanding question is whether forbidding any fixed clique gives the same order of improvement. A parallel question asks whether every clique-free graph has an independent set larger by a logarithmic factor than the elementary average-degree guarantee.

The two manuscripts claim both conclusions. M1 obtains Or(Δ/log⁡Δ)O_r(\Delta/\log\Delta)Or​(Δ/logΔ) even for correspondence coloring, a generalization of list coloring with edge-specific conflicts. M2 obtains independent sets of size Ωr(nlog⁡d/d)\Omega_r(n\log d/d)Ωr​(nlogd/d), where ddd is average degree. Both remove an iterated-logarithm loss from the earlier general bounds.

2. Background and essential definitions

A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors. The chromatic number χ(G)\chi(G)χ(G) is the smallest palette size allowing this. An independent set contains no adjacent pair, and α(G)\alpha(G)α(G) denotes its maximum size.

A clique KrK_rKr​ is a set of rrr pairwise adjacent vertices. A graph is KrK_rKr​-free when it has no such set. The parameter rrr will be fixed, while graph size and degree may grow.

The maximum degree is Δ\DeltaΔ, the largest number of neighbors of any vertex. The average degree is

d=2∣E(G)∣n,d=\frac{2|E(G)|}{n},d=n2∣E(G)∣​,

where nnn is the number of vertices. These parameters can be very different when a few vertices have many more neighbors than the rest.

In list coloring, each vertex has its own set of allowed colors. A coloring must select an allowed color at every vertex and still avoid equal colors on adjacent vertices. The list chromatic number is the smallest list size that guarantees this for every assignment.

Correspondence coloring goes further. Give each vertex a separate list L(v)L(v)L(v). For every edge uvuvuv, specify a matching between entries of L(u)L(u)L(u) and entries of L(v)L(v)L(v); matched pairs are forbidden together. The identifications may be inconsistent around a cycle. A valid coloring chooses one entry per list while avoiding every forbidden pair.

The correspondence chromatic number, also called the DP-chromatic number, is written χDP(G)\chi_{\mathrm{DP}}(G)χDP​(G). The basic hierarchy is

χ(G)≤χlist(G)≤χDP(G)≤Δ+1.\chi(G)\leq\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\leq\chi_{\mathrm{DP}}(G)\leq\Delta+1.χ(G)≤χlist​(G)≤χDP​(G)≤Δ+1.

Ordinary and list coloring are special cases of correspondence coloring. All logarithms below are natural.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ajtai, Komlós and Szemerédi proved a logarithmic improvement for independent sets in triangle-free graphs. Shearer sharpened this to asymptotic leading coefficient one:

α(G)≥(1−o(1))nlog⁡dd\alpha(G)\geq(1-o(1))\frac{n\log d}{d}α(G)≥(1−o(1))dnlogd​

as the average degree grows. Ajtai, Erdős, Komlós and Szemerédi conjectured in 1981 that the same order holds when any fixed clique is excluded. Their first general bound gained a factor log⁡log⁡d\log\log dloglogd; Shearer later obtained a gain log⁡d/log⁡log⁡d\log d/\log\log dlogd/loglogd.

The coloring story developed in parallel. Kim obtained the sharp asymptotic list-coloring order for graphs with no cycles of length three or four. Johansson proved O(Δ/log⁡Δ)O(\Delta/\log\Delta)O(Δ/logΔ) for triangle-free list coloring and

Or ⁣(Δlog⁡log⁡Δlog⁡Δ)O_r\!\left(\frac{\Delta\log\log\Delta}{\log\Delta}\right)Or​(logΔΔloglogΔ​)

for a general fixed forbidden clique. Molloy sharpened the triangle-free leading constant and gave a new proof of the clique-free estimate.

Dvořák and Postle introduced correspondence coloring, allowing colors to be identified differently across different edges. Bernshteyn extended the triangle-free and clique-free bounds to that stronger setting. The iterated-logarithm factor remained for general fixed cliques.

Other structural restrictions allowed sharper conclusions. Local sparsity in neighborhoods, bounded neighborhood coloring parameters, and particular forbidden subgraphs all supplied logarithmic gains. Davies, Kang, Pirot and Sereni developed a common framework using local occupancy of random independent sets.

More recently, Dhawan, Janzer and Methuku obtained the sharper ordinary-coloring order and leading-coefficient-one independence bounds when a fixed three-colorable graph is forbidden. That does not include every KrK_rKr​-free graph for r≥4r\geq4r≥4. M1 and M2 claim to remove the remaining iterated-logarithm losses for the full fixed-clique setting.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: correspondence coloring

For every fixed integer r≥4r\geq4r≥4, M1 states that constants CrC_rCr​ and Δr\Delta_rΔr​ exist such that every KrK_rKr​-free graph with maximum degree Δ≥Δr\Delta\geq\Delta_rΔ≥Δr​ satisfies

χDP(G)≤⌈CrΔlog⁡Δ⌉.\chi_{\mathrm{DP}}(G)\leq\left\lceil C_r\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\right\rceil.χDP​(G)≤⌈Cr​logΔΔ​⌉.

The constants depend only on rrr, not on the number of vertices, the individual lists or the chosen matchings. Ordinary and list coloring inherit the same bound.

The paper deduces a result for every fixed forbidden graph FFF, where exclusion means ordinary subgraph exclusion, not induced exclusion. Taking r≥max⁡{4,∣V(F)∣}r\geq\max\{4,|V(F)|\}r≥max{4,∣V(F)∣}, a KrK_rKr​ contains FFF, so an FFF-free graph is KrK_rKr​-free. Consequently,

χDP(G)=OF(Δ/log⁡Δ).\chi_{\mathrm{DP}}(G)=O_F(\Delta/\log\Delta).χDP​(G)=OF​(Δ/logΔ).

The manuscript identifies the ordinary-coloring version as the Alon–Krivelevich–Sudakov conjecture. When FFF contains a cycle, the order is optimal up to a constant in general, by high-girth examples with large chromatic number. It is not claimed to be sharp for every acyclic forbidden graph.

M2: independence in terms of average degree

For each fixed r≥4r\geq4r≥4, M2 claims a constant cr>0c_r>0cr​>0 such that every KrK_rKr​-free graph with nnn vertices and average degree d≥2d\geq2d≥2 satisfies

α(G)≥crnlog⁡dd.\alpha(G)\geq c_r\frac{n\log d}{d}.α(G)≥cr​dnlogd​.

This resolves the fixed-clique-size independence conjecture stated above, according to the manuscript. The order is optimal up to constants even in the smaller class of triangle-free graphs.

The average-degree formulation is important: it uses the graph’s actual mean density, not an exceptional high-degree vertex. M2 does not optimize crc_rcr​. Neither manuscript claims the triangle-free leading coefficient one for every fixed clique size.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The family establishes the full logarithmic improvement predicted by two major conjectures, including a coloring framework stronger than ordinary or list coloring.

Clique exclusion is a comparatively weak structural assumption. Neighborhoods may still contain many edges and triangles, and a graph can have high chromatic number despite having no fixed large clique. The bounds quantify exactly how much improvement this local prohibition forces at the level of general asymptotic order.

The two results are related but not interchangeable. A coloring contains a large independent color class, yet a maximum-degree coloring theorem does not immediately give the strongest average-degree statement. Conversely, repeatedly removing large independent sets does not automatically preserve a sharp correspondence-coloring bound. The companion methods address both the structural independence problem and the additional consistency issues of local color lists.

6. The main idea

Choose weights that reveal useful structure

M2 assigns nonnegative weights wvw_vwv​ to vertices and maximizes an entropy-minus-edge expression:

FG(w)=∑vwv(1−log⁡wv)−∑uv∈E(G)wuwv.F_G(w)=\sum_v w_v(1-\log w_v)-\sum_{uv\in E(G)}w_uw_v.FG​(w)=v∑​wv​(1−logwv​)−uv∈E(G)∑​wu​wv​.

The convention 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0 makes the expression continuous. The first term rewards spread-out positive weights; the second penalizes placing much weight on adjacent vertices.

At a maximizing weight, local variations relate a vertex’s weight to the total weight in its neighborhood. Clique exclusion permits additional random weight modifications, producing a bound on weighted edge mass between arbitrary vertex sets.

The key structural theorem then bounds weighted triangle mass by a constant multiple of weighted edge mass. It is designed to survive edge deletion and splitting a vertex into several copies, so the later reductions need not keep the weights at an optimizer.

Split neighborhoods while retaining triangle information

Random walks inside neighborhoods compare probability distributions started at different vertices. An entropy estimate controls how much these distributions change on average over triangles.

Coupling close distributions tends to group the two edges of a triangle together. Splitting a vertex according to these groups reduces the total neighbor weight seen by each copy while losing only a controlled amount of triangle mass. Iterating reaches bounded neighborhood weights, where the triangle-to-edge comparison becomes direct.

To extract an independent set, choose a vertex and delete its closed neighborhood, meaning the vertex together with all its neighbors. The weighted triangle bound controls the drop in the potential. Repeating this selection produces an independent set with the required logarithmic gain. Removing the original graph’s highest-degree vertices first converts a maximum-degree intermediate result into the stated average-degree theorem.

Extend the control to correspondence lists

M1 forms a new graph whose vertices are list entries and whose edges are forbidden pairs. Each list is an independent part. Because each edge correspondence is a matching, an entry has at most one neighbor in any other list. A clique in this conflict graph projects to a clique in the original graph, so clique exclusion survives.

The algorithmic-style argument colors in small random rounds, with nonnegative weights on available entries. Activations select entries while deleting their conflicts. Shared neighbors create correlations: one activation can remove both endpoints of a conflict edge, and the resulting cost is measured by weighted triangles.

A local adjustment lemma, developed from M2’s multiplier and splitting ideas, offsets that triangle cost. It also bounds how many entries from any one list an operation can affect. This extra participation control is necessary for concentration; a small graph-radius operation could otherwise touch many entries from one list.

Concentration estimates and the local lemma make the desired inequalities hold simultaneously across vertices. The rounds reduce remaining degrees faster than the available-list supply, after which a final coloring step completes the assignment.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The forbidden clique size is fixed. The constants and degree thresholds may deteriorate with rrr; these are not uniform estimates for growing clique size.

M1 uses maximum degree and sufficiently large Δ\DeltaΔ. M2 uses average degree d≥2d\geq2d≥2. Exchanging those parameters without an additional argument would change the statements.

For the general forbidden-graph corollary, containment is ordinary, not induced. Induced exclusion can permit large complete graphs and therefore cannot be substituted into the same conclusion.

The optimal leading constants are not determined, and the manuscripts do not supply optimized efficient algorithms for arbitrary input graphs or correspondence assignments. Their headline contribution is the sharp order of the logarithmic gain.

M2 also distinguishes its degree-sensitive statement from the off-diagonal Ramsey exponents in family 170. Those companion Ramsey results are cited for context and are not inputs to its proof. A bound on extremal graph order and a guarantee based on each graph’s average degree answer different quantitative questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 is the October 5 correspondence-coloring manuscript. M2 develops the weighted independence method and its average-degree consequence. Their introductions separately trace coloring and independent-set bounds.

Primary recent background includes Davies–Kang–Pirot–Sereni’s local-occupancy framework, Dhawan–Janzer–Methuku on three-colorable forbidden graphs, and Davies’s weighted local independence methods. The source bibliographies identify the original Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi conjecture, Shearer’s independence bounds, Johansson’s coloring results and the correspondence-coloring extensions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Correspondence coloring graphs with a forbidden clique (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A logarithmic independence bound for clique-free graphs (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fewer balanced lines through a planar point set
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 183 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Place an even number of points in the plane, with no three on one line. Some lines through pairs of points divide all the remaining points equally between their two sides. How many such balanced lines can there be?

This is the halving-line problem. Its formulation is elementary, but it sits at the center of longstanding questions about the complexity of planar separations. The classical general upper bound is of order n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3 for nnn points.

The manuscript claims a fixed power improvement: at most Cn4/3−εCn^{4/3-\varepsilon}Cn4/3−ε halving lines for some absolute ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. It also derives improved bounds for small subsets that can be separated by a line and for levels in arrangements of straight lines. The saving is nonquantitative: the proof supplies no numerical value of the exponent improvement.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let P⊂R2P\subset\mathbb R^2P⊂R2 contain nnn points, where nnn is even and no three points are collinear. An unordered pair {a,b}\{a,b\}{a,b} is a halving pair if its line leaves exactly

n−22\frac{n-2}{2}2n−2​

other points in each open halfplane. The two defining points lie on the line and are not counted on either side. Because no three points are collinear, distinct pairs determine distinct lines. Counting halving pairs and halving lines therefore gives the same number h(P)h(P)h(P).

A kkk-set is a subset of kkk points that can be strictly separated from all remaining points by a line. “Strictly” means no point lies on the separating line. This is a related counting problem for every rank kkk, rather than only a balanced middle split.

A useful way to follow separations is to vary a slope sss and mark the kkk points with smallest values of y−sxy-sxy−sx. These are the points below a suitable line of slope sss. As the slope changes, one marked point can exchange places with one unmarked point. Such an exchange is a switch.

At middle rank k=n/2k=n/2k=n/2, the switches correspond to halving pairs. An interval’s activity counts distinct points that change membership somewhere during that interval. It differs from the number of switches and from the difference between the two endpoint marked sets: a point can leave and later return.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Early work by Lovász and by Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus established an O(n3/2)O(n^{3/2})O(n3/2) upper bound for halving lines. Rotating-line arguments and graphs drawn on the point configuration helped turn the problem into one about crossings.

Pach, Steiger and Szemerédi improved that bound by an iterated-logarithm factor. Dey’s 1998 theorem then gave the bound

O(n(k+1)1/3)O\bigl(n(k+1)^{1/3}\bigr)O(n(k+1)1/3)

for planar kkk-sets in the range 1≤k≤n/21\leq k\leq n/21≤k≤n/2. At middle rank, this yields the familiar O(n4/3)O(n^{4/3})O(n4/3) scale. Dey’s use of convex chains and crossing estimates is the finite combinatorial starting point of the present manuscript.

Lower bounds grew much more slowly. The early constructions gave Ω(nlog⁡n)\Omega(n\log n)Ω(nlogn) halving lines. Tóth obtained examples with

nexp⁡(Ω(log⁡n))n\exp\bigl(\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})\bigr)nexp(Ω(logn​))

halving pairs, and Nivasch simplified the construction and improved its exponential constant. This exceeds every fixed multiple of nnn, but remains below n1+δn^{1+\delta}n1+δ for every fixed δ>0\delta>0δ>0 as nnn grows.

Pinchasi related changes in slope-ordered balanced cuts to measure concentration in the plane. The new manuscript develops a related activity perspective, including points that change status and later return.

More recent work improved a lower-order term in the halving-line upper bound while retaining exponent 4/34/34/3. The claimed advance here is a change in that exponent, using geometric information beyond the crossing estimate alone.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that absolute constants ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ and n0n_0n0​ exist such that

h(P)≤Cn4/3−εh(P)\leq Cn^{4/3-\varepsilon}h(P)≤Cn4/3−ε

for every even n≥n0n\geq n_0n≥n0​ and every nnn-point planar configuration with no three collinear.

An intermediate theorem bounds the number of switches uniformly over all ranks. For a generic NNN-point configuration and any 0≤k≤N0\leq k\leq N0≤k≤N,

Sk(P)≤CN4/3−ε.S_k(P)\leq CN^{4/3-\varepsilon}.Sk​(P)≤CN4/3−ε.

Here genericity adds distinct first coordinates, distinct determined slopes and some noncoincidence conditions on segment intersections. The paper explains how small perturbations preserve the relevant halving relations, so these auxiliary assumptions do not restrict the final theorem. At ranks zero and NNN, the marked set never changes.

The all-ranks conclusion yields a finer kkk-dependent corollary. For absolute constants C0C_0C0​ and ε0>0\varepsilon_0>0ε0​>0, the number of kkk-sets is at most

C0n(k+1)1/3−ε0(1≤k≤n/2).C_0n(k+1)^{1/3-\varepsilon_0}\qquad(1\leq k\leq n/2).C0​n(k+1)1/3−ε0​(1≤k≤n/2).

The same bound controls the complexity of the kkk-th level in an arrangement of nnn nonvertical straight lines, assuming no parallel pair and no three concurrent lines. A level follows points on the lines with exactly kkk other lines strictly below them; its complexity counts vertices and edge pieces in the resulting polygonal chain.

The constants and size threshold are not effective numerical outputs of the proof. The auxiliary geometric exponents appearing in the argument are not the final value of ε\varepsilonε.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. A power improvement over the classical halving-line exponent is a major advance in discrete geometry. The associated kkk-set and line-level bounds affect a broader family of separation-complexity questions.

The improvement is qualitatively stronger than dividing n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3 by a logarithm or adjusting a lower-order term. A fixed positive saving in the exponent eventually beats every such logarithmic improvement.

At the same time, the theorem would not determine the true growth rate. The known lower constructions remain close to linear on the scale of fixed powers, leaving a wide gap. The significance lies in breaking the long-standing upper-bound exponent and in identifying additional geometric restrictions that prevent the classical crossing argument from being sharp for these configurations.

6. The main idea

Turn a sweep into exchange graphs

Take an interval of the slope sweep. Let LLL be points marked at the beginning but not at the end, and GGG those marked at the end but not at the beginning. These sets have the same size, say aaa.

Join every point of LLL to every point of GGG. This produces a complete bipartite exchange graph with a2a^2a2 edges. Convex and concave chain decompositions control how its edges can cross.

The usual crossing argument limits how many disjoint sweep intervals can each have large activity. At activity scale bbb, it gives an upper bound of order (n/b)4/3(n/b)^{4/3}(n/b)4/3. The manuscript seeks a uniform improvement that is little-o of this quantity as n/bn/bn/b grows: the ratio to the classical bound must tend to zero.

Examine a hypothetical near-extremal sequence

Suppose the packing bound remained close to sharp. The paper places configurations into compact rank coordinates, which record smoothed proportions of certain chain graphs lying below a point. It then passes to limiting measures describing vertices, edges and crossings.

Rank coordinates preserve ordering information, but can distort ordinary distances. A tiny region in the coordinate square might correspond to an elongated or collapsed region of the original plane. The manuscript therefore uses sweep information from several separated direction ranges.

Monotonicity and almost-everywhere differentiation produce three transverse limiting families of directions. A rigidity statement says that these families prevent collapse after a suitable linear normalization. This is the step that returns meaningful Euclidean geometry to the compact limiting picture.

Show the activity cannot fit

Crossing estimates and the geometric normalization yield a spatial measure with quantitative bounds on how much mass fits inside a small disk or a thin strip. A narrow angular window can then activate points only in a few thin strips, except for points accounted for by boundary crossings.

To control the latter, imagine a token following a marked point through exchanges. Each token crosses the chosen boundary only a bounded number of times. Summing the strip and boundary contributions contradicts the positive amount of activity retained by the limiting construction.

This rules out asymptotic saturation of the classical packing bound. Choosing one sufficiently large fixed scale turns that little-o gain into a contracting recurrence. Iteration gives the fixed exponent saving, even though the limiting argument does not provide its numerical value.

Pass from middle rank to shallow levels

Uniformity over all ranks is needed because restricting attention to the points active in one block changes the rank. It also lets the paper use a shallow cutting: cover a low line-arrangement level by relatively few cells, each crossed by only O(k+1)O(k+1)O(k+1) lines.

Inside each cell the global level becomes one fixed local rank. Applying the all-ranks bound there and summing over cells produces the sharper dependence n(k+1)1/3−ε0n(k+1)^{1/3-\varepsilon_0}n(k+1)1/3−ε0​. The argument thus turns a global power saving into a rank-sensitive geometric estimate.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The halving-line theorem assumes an even number of points and no three collinear. Its generality is over all configurations satisfying those conditions, not just random or convex-position sets.

The line-arrangement corollary concerns complete straight lines. It does not assert the same improvement for pseudolines, which may be curved but satisfy analogous crossing rules, or for finite line segments. The geometric rigidity used in the proof is specific to the stated setting.

The exponent improvement is existential. The paper does not give a usable numerical ε\varepsilonε, an effective threshold, or a practical finite-size estimate. In particular, the disk and strip exponents used inside the proof should not be substituted into the final theorem.

The sharp order of the maximum number of halving lines remains unresolved by this claim. The gap between the near-linear lower constructions and the improved upper power still leaves substantial room. Related higher-dimensional separation problems are also outside the theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript introduces switches and activity before its limiting-measure argument, then derives the kkk-set and straight-line-level consequences at the end.

Primary landmarks include Dey’s classical exponent, Tóth’s lower construction, Nivasch’s refinement, and Pinchasi’s measure-concentration approach. The Agarwal–Aronov–Chan–Sharir paper supplies the shallow-cutting framework used for the level corollary.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A power saving for planar halving lines (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Where unrestricted infinite matroid packing and covering break down
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 185 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Linear independence and cycle-free edge sets share a common combinatorial structure called a matroid. For finite matroids, powerful theorems explain when independent or spanning sets can be packed, covered or chosen simultaneously in two systems.

How much survives when the ground set is infinite? An unrestricted conjecture proposed a partition into one region admitting disjoint spanning sets and another region admitting an independent covering, with contraction used on the second region.

The manuscript claims a counterexample using only two matroids on a countably infinite ground set. Both are self-dual and are direct sums of uniform matroids, yet they admit neither the proposed packing/covering partition nor an intersection witness. The examples are not finitary, so they do not refute the original finitary intersection conjecture or the established positive results for that setting.

2. Background and essential definitions

A matroid specifies which subsets of a ground set EEE are independent. Familiar examples are linearly independent subsets of a collection of vectors, or edge sets containing no cycle in a finite graph.

Independence is hereditary: every subset of an independent set is independent. There is also an exchange principle allowing a nonmaximal independent set to be enlarged using an element from a maximal one. In the infinite theory, a further axiom requires every independent set to extend to a maximal independent set inside every prescribed containing subset of EEE. This maximal-extension requirement is essential; finite-style exchange rules alone are not enough.

A basis is a maximal independent set. A set is spanning if it contains a basis. The closure cl⁡M(S)\operatorname{cl}_M(S)clM​(S) consists of elements determined by SSS in the matroid sense, analogous to the vectors lying in a linear span. Spanning means cl⁡M(S)=E\operatorname{cl}_M(S)=EclM​(S)=E.

Restriction M↾PM\mathbin{\upharpoonright}PM↾P keeps only the elements of PPP. The dual matroid M∗M^*M∗ has complements of bases as its bases. Contraction onto CCC is defined by

M.C=(M∗↾C)∗.M.C=(M^*\mathbin{\upharpoonright}C)^*.M.C=(M∗↾C)∗.

It models the residual independence structure after the elements outside CCC have been contracted. Restriction and contraction are different operations.

For two matroids, a packing is a pair of disjoint spanning sets, one for each system. A covering is a pair of independent sets whose union is the ground set. A packing/covering partition divides

E=P∪˙CE=P\mathbin{\dot\cup}CE=P∪˙C

so the restrictions to PPP admit a packing and the contractions onto CCC admit a covering.

A matroid is self-dual here when M=M∗M=M^*M=M∗ on the same labeled set, not merely after relabeling. It is finitary when a set is independent whenever all its finite subsets are independent. It is cofinitary when its dual is finitary.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Finite matroid intersection, packing and covering theorems are central results of combinatorial optimization. Extending them to infinity requires replacing numerical rank comparisons with structural witnesses and choosing axioms that support restriction, contraction and duality.

Bruhn, Diestel, Kriesell, Pendavingh and Wollan developed the standard infinite-matroid axioms used here. Bowler and Carmesin formulated the packing/covering conjecture and established its relationships with infinite intersection and separate packing and covering statements.

The intersection question originated in a more restricted form associated with Nash-Williams: finitary matroids. Joó proved intersection for two finitary matroids on a countable ground set. His later packing/covering theorem allows every set-indexed family on a countable ground set whose members are direct sums of finitary and cofinitary matroids.

Uniform matroids form another natural class. In the infinite setting used here, uniformity means that exchanging any basis element with any element outside that basis again produces a basis. Equivalently, every subset is independent or spanning. This should not be interpreted as a fixed finite cardinality cutoff.

Bowler and Geschke constructed countable self-dual uniform examples under additional set-theoretic assumptions, leaving their existence in ZFC open. ZFC is the usual Zermelo–Fraenkel axiom system with the axiom of choice. The new manuscript claims such a uniform matroid in ZFC as a building block.

Joó also proved intersection when one matroid is a direct sum of finitely many uniform matroids and the other is arbitrary. He asked about two partitional matroids on a countable set, where partitional means a direct sum of uniform components. The present construction uses countably infinitely many components and claims a negative answer to that question.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem asserts that in ZFC there are two matroids M0,M1M_0,M_1M0​,M1​ on the same countably infinite set EEE, each self-dual, such that

I0∪I1≠EI_0\cup I_1\ne EI0​∪I1​=E

whenever I0I_0I0​ is independent in M0M_0M0​ and I1I_1I1​ is independent in M1M_1M1​. Thus no independent covering exists.

The paper separately proves that for a self-dual pair, a mixed packing/covering partition would imply an independent covering of the whole ground set. This additional reduction is necessary: failure of a covering alone would not rule out every mixed partition for arbitrary matroids.

Each constructed matroid is partitional. The local component QQQ is a self-dual uniform matroid on a countable set, with every basis and its complement infinite. The manuscript thereby also claims a ZFC solution to the uniform-matroid existence questions described above.

For intersection, the usual witness is a set JJJ independent in both matroids, partitioned as J=J0∪˙J1J=J_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}J_1J=J0​∪˙J1​, with

cl⁡M0(J0)∪cl⁡M1(J1)=E.\operatorname{cl}_{M_0}(J_0)\cup\operatorname{cl}_{M_1}(J_1)=E.clM0​​(J0​)∪clM1​​(J1​)=E.

The manuscript states that its pair has no such witness. This follows through Bowler and Carmesin’s established equivalence between intersection for (M,N)(M,N)(M,N) and packing/covering for (M,N∗)(M,N^*)(M,N∗), together with self-duality.

The paper also deduces that the unrestricted separate universal Packing and Covering conjectures are false. Those deductions use equivalences between universal statements. It does not identify the same pair as the direct witnessing family for every separate formulation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claim sets a sharp boundary on how far finite matroid principles can be generalized without structural assumptions. Countability of the ground set and decomposition into uniform components do not by themselves suffice.

The result also illustrates a characteristic infinite phenomenon. Every finite subset of the constructed ground set is independent, yet the entire set is dependent. Finite tests therefore cannot detect the obstruction. The counterexample exploits precisely the behavior excluded by finitary hypotheses.

The local self-dual uniform construction has independent significance because it is claimed within ordinary ZFC, without the continuum hypothesis or the extra assumptions used in earlier constructions. The rating reflects both the failure of broad conjectures and this new building block, while keeping the established finitary theory clearly outside the negative conclusion.

6. The main idea

Force a quantity to decrease forever

The final obstruction uses ordinals, which generalize nonnegative integers as well-ordered positions. Like nonnegative integers, ordinals cannot form an infinite strictly decreasing sequence: any nonempty collection of them has a least element.

The manuscript equips certain large subsets of a countable set DDD with an ordinal-valued quantity ρ\rhoρ. This is an auxiliary rank, not matroid rank. Largeness is defined by an ultrafilter: a coherent collection closed under supersets and finite intersections that chooses exactly one side of every complementary pair of subsets.

On two labeled copies L,RL,RL,R of DDD, the local matroid QQQ is constructed so that a basis with a large left slice forces a large complement of its right slice and a strict decrease:

ρ(BL)>ρ(D∖BR).\rho(B_L)>\rho(D\setminus B_R).ρ(BL​)>ρ(D∖BR​).

The auxiliary rank also behaves monotonically in the direction needed to pass from independent sets to containing bases.

Arrange the components along a two-sided path

Take vertices indexed by all integers and place a copy of DDD in each bundle between consecutive vertices. At every vertex, place one copy of QQQ on its two incident bundles. Its left coordinate points toward a central bundle, and its right coordinate points outward.

The components at even-indexed vertices form M0M_0M0​; those at odd-indexed vertices form M1M_1M1​. Within either parity, the component supports partition the common ground set, so these are direct sums of uniform matroids.

Suppose independent sets from the two matroids covered everything. They can be made into a partition by removing overlap. Assign each bundle element to the endpoint whose matroid receives it.

The ultrafilter selects one large side of the central bundle. Follow the path outward from that side. At every vertex, extend the received independent set to a basis of its local component. The defining inequality then forces the ordinal rank to decrease strictly at the next bundle. Continuing outward would produce an impossible infinite descending sequence.

Build the local matroid without losing maximal extension

Most of the paper constructs QQQ. It partitions DDD into rapidly growing finite blocks and compares subsets modulo sets whose block densities tend to zero. Within each resulting class, real-valued probes select bases using interval conditions.

Finite exchanges shift these probes by controlled integer amounts, supporting the uniform basis-exchange property. A separate interpolation argument ensures that bases can be found between suitable subset endpoints.

The construction processes all required intervals through a transfinite recursion, choosing complementary classes together to preserve self-duality. Additional reservations keep the ordinal inequalities compatible with earlier choices. The maximal-extension axiom is then established for every prescribed subset, completing the infinite-matroid structure needed for the final path argument.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The counterexample is unrestricted and nonfinitary. It does not refute Nash-Williams’ original finitary intersection conjecture. It also lies outside Joó’s positive countable packing/covering theorem for direct sums of finitary and cofinitary matroids.

Indeed, the manuscript states that its examples have no nonempty finitary or cofinitary direct summand. Their failure is not caused by adding a small pathological component to an otherwise covered class.

The ground set is countable, but its family of subsets is uncountable. The construction uses choice, ultrafilters and transfinite recursion over subset requirements. It is an existence construction in ZFC, not an efficiently encoded finite counterexample or an algorithm for a finite optimization problem.

Self-duality means equality on the same labels and is used in the reduction from a mixed partition to a full covering. Merely knowing that a matroid is isomorphic to its dual would require additional care.

The broader lesson for further questions is structural: which infinite matroid classes still admit intersection or packing/covering witnesses? The theorem excludes the unrestricted formulation while leaving stronger hypotheses meaningful and, in several countable cases, already supported by positive results.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript states its packing/covering and intersection conventions explicitly, constructs the local uniform component, and finishes with the ordinal descent on a two-sided path.

Primary context comes from Bowler–Carmesin’s equivalence framework, Joó’s partitional intersection theorem and question, and Joó’s positive countable packing/covering theorem. The source bibliography identifies the standard infinite-matroid axioms and Bowler–Geschke’s earlier self-dual uniform constructions under additional set-theoretic assumptions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Counterexample to the Infinite Matroid Packing/Covering Conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How narrow must a symmetric random-graph transition be
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 186 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

As the edge probability of a random graph increases, a property such as connectivity changes from unlikely to likely. How wide can that transition be if the property treats every vertex label equally and is preserved when edges are added?

This question concerns the width of the transition, not where it occurs. A theorem locating the threshold near a counting prediction does not automatically determine how rapidly the probability rises through that location.

The two manuscripts claim optimal-order universal width bounds for graphs and the conjectured extension to uniform hypergraphs. M2 gives a squared logarithm in the denominator for graphs. M1 gives exponent r/(r−1)r/(r-1)r/(r−1) for rrr-uniform hypergraphs. Both are driven by stronger sensitivity estimates that hold at every edge probability, even for properties that are not increasing.

2. Background and essential definitions

In G(n,p)G(n,p)G(n,p), each possible edge among nnn vertices is present independently with probability ppp. A graph property is a yes-or-no rule unchanged by every permutation of the vertex labels. Connectivity and containing a triangle are examples.

Write the rule as a Boolean function fff, taking values zero or one. It is increasing if adding edges cannot change a yes to a no. For a nontrivial increasing property, let

q(p)=Epf,pa=inf⁡{p:q(p)≥a}.q(p)=\mathbb E_p f,\qquadp_a=\inf\{p:q(p)\geq a\}.q(p)=Ep​f,pa​=inf{p:q(p)≥a}.

The quantile pap_apa​ is the density at which the probability reaches level aaa. For 0<ε<1/20<\varepsilon<1/20<ε<1/2, the transition width is

p1−ε−pε.p_{1-\varepsilon}-p_\varepsilon.p1−ε​−pε​.

An edge is pivotal for the other edges’ configuration when forcing it present rather than absent changes the property. Its influence is

Ie,p(f)=Pr⁡p(f(xe←1)≠f(xe←0)),I_{e,p}(f)=\Pr_p\bigl(f(x^{e\leftarrow1})\ne f(x^{e\leftarrow0})\bigr),Ie,p​(f)=pPr​(f(xe←1)=f(xe←0)),

and total influence is Ip(f)=∑eIe,p(f)I_p(f)=\sum_e I_{e,p}(f)Ip​(f)=∑e​Ie,p​(f). The probability is over the other coordinates. This convention includes no extra factor p(1−p)p(1-p)p(1−p).

For a Boolean function, the variance is Var⁡p(f)=q(p)(1−q(p))\operatorname{Var}_p(f)=q(p)(1-q(p))Varp​(f)=q(p)(1−q(p)). It is substantial when the outcome is uncertain and small when the property is almost certain or almost impossible.

An rrr-uniform hypergraph replaces ordinary edges by rrr-element vertex subsets. Each possible hyperedge is independently present with probability ppp. A hypergraph property again ignores vertex labels. Throughout, nnn counts vertices, not the (nr)\binom nr(rn​) edge coordinates, and logarithms are natural.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kahn, Kalai and Linial established a fundamental connection between Boolean Fourier analysis and influence. For a function with transitive coordinate symmetry, this forces total influence to grow logarithmically with the number of coordinates when the variance is bounded below. Bourgain, Kahn, Kalai, Katznelson and Linial extended the influence method to product probability spaces.

Friedgut and Kalai’s 1996 theorem used such estimates to prove narrow transitions for increasing properties with transitive symmetry. For graph properties, this gives a universal width of order 1/log⁡n1/\log n1/logn for fixed probability levels.

They conjectured the stronger graph bound 1/(log⁡n)21/(\log n)^21/(logn)2. Vertex relabeling supplies more information than the fact that all individual edges are equivalent: it also constrains how groups of edges overlap. Exploiting that richer action is the source of the additional logarithm.

Bourgain and Kalai approached the conjectured exponent. For every fixed η>0\eta>0η>0, they obtained graph widths of order (log⁡n)−2+η(\log n)^{-2+\eta}(logn)−2+η. For rrr-uniform hypergraphs, their influence estimates at the unbiased density p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2 approach exponent r/(r−1)r/(r-1)r/(r−1) with an arbitrary fixed loss.

Kelman, Kindler, Lifshitz, Minzer and Safra obtained, for graph properties at p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2, total influence at least a constant times

Var⁡1/2(f)(log⁡n)2(log⁡log⁡n)2.\operatorname{Var}_{1/2}(f)\frac{(\log n)^2}{(\log\log n)^2}.Var1/2​(f)(loglogn)2(logn)2​.

The present manuscripts claim to remove the remaining losses and to keep the estimates uniform throughout 0<p<10<p<10<p<1. That uniformity is needed for a general width theorem, since a property’s transition need not occur near one half.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: graph properties

For every vertex-relabeling-invariant Boolean graph property, whether increasing or not, M2 states

Var⁡p(f)≤217(log⁡n)2Ip(f)(0<p<1).\operatorname{Var}_p(f)\leq\frac{2^{17}}{(\log n)^2}I_p(f)\qquad(0<p<1).Varp​(f)≤(logn)2217​Ip​(f)(0<p<1).

For a nontrivial increasing property, it deduces

p1−ε−pε≤219(log⁡n)2log⁡12ε.p_{1-\varepsilon}-p_\varepsilon\leq\frac{2^{19}}{(\log n)^2}\log\frac1{2\varepsilon}.p1−ε​−pε​≤(logn)2219​log2ε1​.

The numerical constants are convenient explicit choices, not optimized ones. The theorem is uniform over all n≥2n\geq2n≥2, all such properties and all 0<ε<1/20<\varepsilon<1/20<ε<1/2.

M1: uniform hypergraphs

For each fixed r≥3r\geq3r≥3, M1 claims a constant CrC_rCr​ such that every relabeling-invariant Boolean property of simple rrr-uniform hypergraphs satisfies

Var⁡p(f)≤Cr(log⁡n)r/(r−1)Ip(f)(n≥r, 0<p<1).\operatorname{Var}_p(f)\leq\frac{C_r}{(\log n)^{r/(r-1)}}I_p(f)\qquad(n\geq r,\ 0<p<1).Varp​(f)≤(logn)r/(r−1)Cr​​Ip​(f)(n≥r, 0<p<1).

Again, monotonicity is unnecessary for this variance–influence inequality. For a nontrivial increasing property, the stated consequence is

p1−ε−pε≤2Cr(log⁡n)r/(r−1)log⁡1−εε.p_{1-\varepsilon}-p_\varepsilon\leq\frac{2C_r}{(\log n)^{r/(r-1)}}\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.p1−ε​−pε​≤(logn)r/(r−1)2Cr​​logε1−ε​.

For fixed ε\varepsilonε, this is the conjectured (log⁡n)−r/(r−1)(\log n)^{-r/(r-1)}(logn)−r/(r−1) width scale. M1 reproduces the graph companion’s analytic restriction argument and adds the combinatorial estimate needed for hyperedge supports.

These are additive widths in the probability parameter ppp. They do not assert that the width divided by the threshold location tends to zero for every property.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claims settle broad quantitative sharp-threshold questions using only vertex symmetry and monotonicity, without a detailed description of the property.

For graphs, the squared-logarithm order is optimal in general at fixed probability levels. Friedgut and Kalai already noted examples involving cliques of order proportional to log⁡n\log nlogn whose widths have this scale. Some familiar properties have much narrower transitions, but a universal theorem must accommodate the worst case.

The stronger influence statement also has independent meaning. A symmetric property whose answer remains uncertain must have many opportunities for a single edge to change that answer. This conclusion survives without monotonicity, although a nonmonotone property need not have one increasing transition to which the width language applies.

The rating reflects the sharp universal graph order, the hypergraph extension and the full-density control. It is distinct from the threshold-location advances in nearby families, which compare where a transition sits with expectation-based predictions.

6. The main idea

Split variation into Fourier degrees

A function of independent edge bits has an orthogonal expansion indexed by edge subsets SSS. Under Bernoulli density ppp, one uses centered, normalized coordinate functions so that the basis remains orthonormal.

If f^(S)\widehat f(S)f​(S) denotes a coefficient, the basic identities are

Var⁡p(f)=∑S≠∅f^(S)2,p(1−p)Ip(f)=∑S∣S∣f^(S)2.\operatorname{Var}_p(f)=\sum_{S\ne\varnothing}\widehat f(S)^2,\qquadp(1-p)I_p(f)=\sum_S|S|\widehat f(S)^2.Varp​(f)=S=∅∑​f​(S)2,p(1−p)Ip​(f)=S∑​∣S∣f​(S)2.

The second sum weights large supports more heavily. Consequently, influence already controls the high-degree part of the variance. The problem is bounding mass on smaller edge subsets.

Restrict through vertices, preserving symmetry

Choose a random block BBB of about n\sqrt nn​ vertices. Keep every edge touching BBB free and fix all edges entirely outside it.

Every permutation within BBB still preserves the restricted function. Each free edge belongs to a large orbit under these surviving permutations, so no individual conditional influence can dominate the total. An elementary Fourier estimate then controls the restricted low-degree mass, with a bound linear in total influence.

Linearity matters because the proof averages over the fixed outside configuration and over the random block. A nonlinear loss at that stage could spoil the desired uniform estimate.

Regard a Fourier support as a small graph

An edge set SSS indexing a coefficient is itself a graph. If it has at most k2/2k^2/2k2/2 edges, it has a nonisolated vertex of degree at most kkk.

With sufficient probability, the random block meets the support only at that vertex. The restriction then retains between one and kkk edges of SSS. Thus a low-degree bound after restriction controls original Fourier supports up to a quadratic degree scale. This is where the graph’s squared logarithm enters.

For an rrr-uniform support with sss edges, the analogous combinatorial observation gives a vertex of positive degree at most rs(r−1)/rrs^{(r-1)/r}rs(r−1)/r. Inverting that relationship produces the exponent r/(r−1)r/(r-1)r/(r−1) in the original support size.

The proof tracks the factor p(1−p)\sqrt{p(1-p)}p(1−p)​ in the Fourier cutoff. In the final combination of low- and high-degree estimates, the bias dependence cancels or remains bounded. This permits densities arbitrarily close to zero or one.

Integrate sensitivity into a width bound

For increasing properties, the Margulis–Russo identity gives

q′(p)=Ip(f).q'(p)=I_p(f).q′(p)=Ip​(f).
