The variance inequality therefore bounds q′(p)q'(p)q′(p) below by a multiple of q(p)(1−q(p))q(p)(1-q(p))q(p)(1−q(p)) times the relevant logarithmic power. Integrating the derivative of log⁡(q/(1−q))\log(q/(1-q))log(q/(1−q)) between the two quantiles yields the stated width estimates. This final step is why monotonicity is needed for the transition conclusion but not for the underlying sensitivity theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The symmetry is invariance under all vertex relabelings. A property singling out a distinguished vertex, edge or labeled pattern need not satisfy the same estimate. Mere transitivity of arbitrary coordinates supplies a weaker general framework.

Hypergraph uniformity rrr is fixed, and its constant may depend on rrr. The claim is not uniform when hyperedge size grows with the number of vertices.

The width bound is additive. If a threshold lies at a much smaller density than (log⁡n)−2(\log n)^{-2}(logn)−2, the universal graph estimate may say little about its relative sharpness or precise transition window. Determining exact locations, leading constants and limiting probability curves remains property-specific.

The manuscripts do not use the integral–fractional comparison or the second Kahn–Kalai theorem in families 175 and 176. Those concern threshold locations; this family’s restriction and influence argument addresses widths directly. Nor does the result settle every broader conjecture about Boolean Fourier coefficients, such as the general Fourier–entropy conjecture.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 gives the graph theorem and the density-uniform variance bound. M1, dated October 5, extends the restriction argument to hypergraphs and derives its quantile inequality.

The central historical source is Friedgut–Kalai’s sharp-threshold paper. Kelman–Kindler–Lifshitz–Minzer–Safra supplies a recent symmetry-sensitive Fourier predecessor. The manuscripts’ bibliographies identify the Kahn–Kalai–Linial influence theorem, Bourgain–Kalai’s group-symmetry refinements, and the Margulis–Russo derivative identity used in the final integration.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A uniform influence bound for hypergraph properties (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Sharp Threshold Bound for Monotone Graph Properties (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Making Snaky in at most twenty-one moves
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 187 · Combinatorics
Importance 1/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Two players alternately claim empty cells of square graph paper. Maker wants to occupy a particular six-cell shape called Snaky. Breaker only wants to prevent this from ever happening. Can Maker force the shape from an empty board without receiving an extra opening move?

The manuscript claims that Maker can win within twenty-one of its own moves, regardless of Breaker’s legal replies. The strategy works on the infinite square board and can be confined to a fixed finite region inside a 171717-by-171717 square.

The result settles the ordinary planar achievement question for this particular shape. Its main device is a finite collection of conditional winning positions that can be combined into larger ones. The endpoint of the construction has no initial Maker holdings, so it applies directly to the empty board.

2. Background and essential definitions

A polyomino is a shape made from unit square cells joined edge to edge. A six-cell polyomino is a hexomino. Snaky is the set of cells indexed by

S={(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(3,1),(4,1)}.S=\{(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(3,1),(4,1)\}.S={(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(3,1),(4,1)}.

Here a cell’s coordinates refer to its lower-left corner. In the small diagram below, # marks a target cell and . an unused location:

Translations, quarter turns and reflections are permitted. Scaling is not. Thus Maker may build the same shape in any location and any of its square-grid orientations.

The board is initially empty. Maker moves first, after which the players alternate, each claiming one previously unclaimed cell. Ownership is permanent. Maker wins as soon as it owns all six cells of an allowed copy; additional Maker cells do not invalidate that copy.

This is a weak achievement game, also called a Maker–Breaker game. Breaker has no independent objective of completing its own shape. In the strong game both players seek a copy, so the rules and possible outcomes differ.

A handicap of one means Maker gets two cells on the opening turn before Breaker’s first response. The theorem here gives no such advantage. Its move bound counts actual cells claimed by Maker, including replacement moves when a planned cell is already Maker-owned.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Polyomino achievement games were introduced in work associated with Frank Harary. Snaky became a difficult small example: its six cells are enough to create several interacting threats, yet its geometry resists simple short strategies.

Earlier work found winning strategies with extra initial resources. Harary, Harborth and Seemann obtained handicap-two strategies. Sieben proved a win in forty-one dimensions, showing that abundant extra directions can overcome the obstruction.

Another line examined pairing defenses. In such a defense, Breaker pairs cells in advance and responds to a Maker claim by taking its partner. If every target copy contains a full pair, this can prevent a win. Snaky was shown to admit no pairing defense, with a later computer-free proof by Csernenszky, Martin and Pluhár. But ruling out one class of defenses does not establish a Maker win against every possible strategy.

Halupczok and Schlage-Puchta proved that Snaky wins in three dimensions, loses on an 888-by-888 board, and has planar handicap number at most one. Ito and Miyagawa also presented a handicap-one construction.

Sieben’s work on proof trees gave a finite proof sequence for that handicap and developed a way to combine local winning situations. The ordinary empty planar-board problem remained distinct: Maker’s extra opening stone could not simply be removed from those arguments.

Computer encodings of finite positional games also studied Snaky and related targets. The new manuscript uses a finite certificate of sufficient conditions for the infinite weak game. It explicitly accommodates Breaker moves outside the displayed local regions, so its conclusion is not limited to an unmentioned finite search board.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that one globally legal Maker strategy completes an allowed copy of Snaky within at most

21 actual Maker claims21\text{ actual Maker claims}21 actual Maker claims

against every legal Breaker continuation from the empty infinite board.

Since Maker moves first, its twenty-first move is the forty-first individual turn. There are at most twenty Breaker replies before that final Maker claim. Thus the theorem is not a claim of winning within twenty-one total alternating turns.

The same bound holds on a finite 171717-by-171717 board. More precisely, the strategy can keep all Maker claims inside a fixed region of 251 cells. The manuscript does not claim that either the move count or the board size is optimal.

The main certificate has 728 numbered conditions, including six elementary base conditions. Its final condition requires no pre-owned Maker cells, uses the 251-cell region, and has height twenty-one. Height is the bound on future actual Maker moves associated with a condition.

The paper also presents independent constructions with bounds of twenty-five and thirty-five Maker moves. They use different representations and openings, so they provide additional descriptions of the local tactics rather than improving the main numerical bound.

These assertions concern the ordinary weak game. They do not assert the same result for the strong game, biased play with several Breaker claims per turn, or an arbitrary smaller finite board.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 1/5. This is a focused contribution to positional games: it resolves a concrete longstanding achievement question for one small shape and gives a finite move bound.

The score measures relative mathematical scope across the collection, not how entertaining or difficult the problem is. Unlike a general theorem for all polyominoes or all Maker–Breaker games, the headline concerns Snaky under one precise rule set.

Its broader methodological interest is the composition of conditional strategies. A finite local condition can be strong enough to survive arbitrary earlier play and replies outside the region under discussion. Combining such conditions offers a way to express an infinite-board strategy through finite data, while retaining a clear accounting of moves and previously occupied cells.

The finite-board consequence is particularly concrete. The claimed infinite-board win does not require Maker to keep searching farther away; a bounded region already contains enough alternative continuations.

6. The main idea

Describe a position by what a tactic needs

A conditional winning position is recorded as a triple (A,T,h)(A,T,h)(A,T,h). The finite set AAA contains cells Maker must already own. The finite envelope TTT must contain no Breaker cell. The number hhh bounds the further Maker moves needed to win.

There may be additional Maker cells anywhere, and Breaker may have cells outside TTT. The condition makes no assumption about how the position arose. It applies whenever it is Maker’s turn and the stated holdings and clear region are available.

The elementary conditions start with five cells of a target already owned and the remaining cell free. One additional claim completes the shape.

Create several continuations that one reply cannot destroy

Suppose Maker has a pivot move after which several child conditions have their required cells. Their envelopes may overlap, but the construction arranges that every cell common to all envelopes is already Maker-owned.

Breaker can claim only one new cell. That cell cannot belong to every child envelope, because their common intersection is unavailable to Breaker. At least one envelope therefore remains clear, and Maker follows that child’s strategy.

The move bound is one for the pivot plus the largest bound among the children:

h=1+max⁡ihi.h=1+\max_i h_i.h=1+imax​hi​.

The bound uses the worst surviving continuation, so Maker does not need to predict Breaker’s choice. Repeating this composition builds a tree of sufficient conditions.

This generalizes the familiar idea of a double threat: if two different cells would each complete a target, Breaker cannot occupy both in one move. Here the alternatives can be multi-move strategies with different local envelopes, not merely immediate completions.

Keep the policy legal under previous ownership

A planned pivot may already belong to Maker because of earlier play. The tactic cannot count claiming it again as a legal move. The manuscript instead uses a fresh replacement claim, still charging one actual move, before proceeding with the same ownership guarantees.

If a target has already been completed, play stops. Otherwise the policy chooses among available cells and surviving child conditions by fixed rules. This turns the existential composition into one strategy selected before Breaker’s play, rather than a different strategy chosen after seeing the whole future.

On the infinite board a fresh cell always exists after finitely many moves. The finite-board argument keeps the policy within the stated envelope and accounts for available replacement cells there as well.

Assemble the finite certificate

Each nonbase condition refers backward to earlier conditions after translations, reflections or quarter turns. The final condition has A=∅A=\varnothingA=∅, so the empty board meets its requirements.

The manuscript prints the exact coordinate data and describes reconstruction and checking programs. Their role is to express the finite identities used by the composition rule. The mathematical claim combines those identities with the rule’s game-theoretic interpretation; a list of coordinates alone would not explain why arbitrary outside replies are covered.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The twenty-one-move figure is an upper bound. The paper does not determine the minimum number of Maker moves against optimal defense. Nor does it determine the smallest winning rectangular board or smallest winning cell region.

Rotations and reflections are allowed, and Maker may own extra cells. Changing either convention produces a different achievement problem. The move order and one-cell-per-turn rule also remain part of the theorem.

A handicap-one result gives Maker an extra initial claim; the present theorem starts from an empty board without that privilege. Conversely, the theorem says nothing about Breaker moving first or claiming several cells each turn.

The strong game is outside scope. A strategy that forces a Maker target while ignoring whether Breaker has already completed its own target need not settle the game where both players can win.

Finally, a win on the stated finite board does not contradict the earlier loss on an 888-by-888 board. The available space and the number of alternative local envelopes are part of what makes the construction work.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript gives the exact target, game rules, composition lemma and three finite constructions. Its main certificate supplies the twenty-one-move conclusion; the later constructions expose different local tactics.

Primary predecessors include Halupczok–Schlage-Puchta’s Achieving Snaky, Sieben’s higher-dimensional result, and Sieben’s proof-tree framework. Shaik and collaborators describe finite-game encodings that provide computational context, with different board and depth conventions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Snaky in 21 Maker moves (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The exact threshold for a red cycle or a blue clique
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 189 · Combinatorics
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine coloring every connection between a group of people red or blue. How many people guarantee either a red cycle through exactly mmm distinct people or a group of nnn people whose mutual connections are all blue?

Ramsey theory studies such unavoidable patterns. Its answers are often difficult even when the patterns sound simple. This family concerns the cycle–clique Ramsey number, where one color must contain a cycle of a prescribed length and the other a complete graph.

There is a particularly natural way to avoid both outcomes. Make n−1n-1n−1 separate red groups, each containing m−1m-1m−1 vertices, and color every connection between groups blue. No red cycle can reach mmm vertices, while a blue clique can take at most one vertex from each group.

This construction uses (m−1)(n−1)(m-1)(n-1)(m−1)(n−1) vertices. The conjecture addressed by the manuscript says that, when m≥n≥3m\ge n\ge3m≥n≥3, just one additional vertex forces one of the desired patterns, with a single small exception. The claim is an exact threshold, not an asymptotic estimate.

2. Background and essential definitions

A simple graph consists of vertices and edges joining distinct pairs of vertices, without repeated edges. The complete graph KnK_nKn​ has every possible edge on its nnn vertices. A clique is a set of vertices whose pairs are all joined.

The cycle CmC_mCm​ has mmm distinct vertices arranged around a closed route, with consecutive vertices joined. Its order and length are both mmm. Finding CmC_mCm​ means finding exactly that cycle length; a longer cycle alone does not satisfy the requirement.

For two graphs HHH and JJJ, the Ramsey number R(H,J)R(H,J)R(H,J) is the smallest integer NNN such that every red–blue coloring of the edges of KNK_NKN​ contains a red copy of HHH or a blue copy of JJJ. Copies here need not be induced: extra edges between the chosen vertices are allowed.

There is an equivalent formulation using just one graph GGG. Declare its edges red and its missing edges blue. A blue clique becomes an independent set in GGG, meaning a set containing no edges. Thus the desired upper bound says that every graph on (m−1)(n−1)+1(m-1)(n-1)+1(m−1)(n−1)+1 vertices has a cycle of length mmm or an independent set of size nnn.

Write α(G)\alpha(G)α(G) for the largest size of an independent set and ω(G)\omega(G)ω(G) for the largest size of a clique. These two quantities measure opposite kinds of organization inside the same graph.

For a vertex set III, its closed neighborhood N[I]N[I]N[I] consists of III itself and every vertex adjacent to at least one member of III. A lower bound on ∣N[I]∣|N[I]|∣N[I]∣ expresses expansion: a small set must reach many vertices.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The cycle–clique problem developed through a long sequence of exact cases and general parameter ranges. The case of a blue triangle goes back to Chartrand and Schuster in 1971. Bondy and Erdős proved the formula in 1973 when the red cycle was sufficiently long, specifically for m≥n2−2m\ge n^2-2m≥n2−2. Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp’s 1978 paper is the conjectural reference used by M1.

A succession of papers resolved all conjectured cycle lengths for clique sizes n=4,5,6,7n=4,5,6,7n=4,5,6,7, together with several cases for n=8n=8n=8. Nikiforov obtained a much wider general range, m≥4n+2m\ge4n+2m≥4n+2 for n≥4n\ge4n≥4. These results progressively reduced the gap between a cycle much longer than the clique and the boundary case m=nm=nm=n.

A major later advance came from Keevash, Long, and Skokan. Their theorem establishes the formula whenever

m≥Clog⁡nlog⁡log⁡n,m\ge C\frac{\log n}{\log\log n},m≥Cloglognlogn​,

with an absolute constant CCC, using suitable logarithm conventions for small nnn. Their paper was published in 2021. In particular, its threshold is smaller than nnn once nnn is sufficiently large. It therefore already covers all sufficiently large pairs in the conjectured range m≥nm\ge nm≥n. Their article explains this near-logarithmic cycle-length regime.

For each of the finitely many remaining clique sizes, their theorem also covers all sufficiently large cycle lengths. Consequently, only finitely many pairs in the stated conjecture were left outside its reach.

M1 claims to complete that remaining range. Its structural argument produces an explicit finite calculation without requiring a numerical value for the constant in the Keevash–Long–Skokan theorem. The distinction is essential: the new claim completes an exact conjecture whose broad asymptotic range had already been settled.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. It states that for all integers m≥n≥3m\ge n\ge3m≥n≥3, except (m,n)=(3,3)(m,n)=(3,3)(m,n)=(3,3),

R(Cm,Kn)=(m−1)(n−1)+1.R(C_m,K_n)=(m-1)(n-1)+1.R(Cm​,Kn​)=(m−1)(n−1)+1.

The exceptional value is

R(C3,K3)=6.R(C_3,K_3)=6.R(C3​,K3​)=6.

Since C3C_3C3​ is itself a triangle, this is the familiar two-color triangle Ramsey number. The general formula would give five for this pair, so recording the exception changes the answer.

For example, the claimed formula gives R(C8,K6)=36R(C_8,K_6)=36R(C8​,K6​)=36. The lower construction uses five disjoint red complete graphs of order seven, for a total of 35 vertices. M1’s theorem says that every coloring on 36 vertices contains a red eight-cycle or a blue six-clique. This illustrates the formula; the novelty of the family lies in completing the whole stated parameter range, not in every individual numerical instance.

The cycle length remains exact, the copies remain ordinary rather than induced, and the hypothesis m≥nm\ge nm≥n is part of the theorem. The claim does not provide a formula for every pair of cycle and clique sizes outside that region.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5. An exact resolution of a long-standing Ramsey conjecture is a substantial contribution. The rating also reflects the strong earlier theorem: the unsettled portion was finite, rather than a previously unknown asymptotic range.

Exact Ramsey values expose extremal structure particularly clearly. Here the simplest obstruction, a union of small complete graphs, is claimed to remain optimal throughout the conjectured range. Adding a single vertex then forces a cycle of precisely the requested length or a larger independent set.

The argument is also an example of combining structural graph theory with a finite symbolic calculation. The computation described by M1 handles constrained path patterns after the general theory has compressed the problem. It is not an enumeration of all edge colorings up to an enormous vertex bound.

The scope is narrower than a general solution of Ramsey numbers. It nevertheless gives a complete answer for a natural two-parameter family and clarifies why the obvious lower construction has the correct size.

6. The main idea

A minimal obstruction must expand

Set k=m−1k=m-1k=m−1 and a=n−1a=n-1a=n−1. A counterexample to the upper bound would be a graph with

∣V(G)∣=ka+1,α(G)≤a,|V(G)|=ka+1,\qquad \alpha(G)\le a,∣V(G)∣=ka+1,α(G)≤a,

and no cycle of length k+1k+1k+1. Here V(G)V(G)V(G) is the vertex set. The argument holds kkk fixed and chooses a counterexample with the smallest possible aaa.

That minimality makes independent sets expand. M1 obtains, for every nonempty independent set III,

∣N[I]∣≥k∣I∣+1.|N[I]|\ge k|I|+1.∣N[I]∣≥k∣I∣+1.

The intuition is deletion. If III and its neighbors occupied too few vertices, the remaining graph would be large enough to contradict minimality: an independent set there could be combined with III, because no edges connect the two sets.

In particular, a one-vertex set shows that every vertex has at least kkk neighbors. The graph cannot avoid the desired patterns merely by being sparse or split into small isolated pieces.

Use a clique as a reservoir of closing edges

The next structural step finds a clique QQQ of order ttt with

max⁡{3,⌊k/2⌋}≤t≤k.\max\{3,\lfloor k/2\rfloor\}\le t\le k.max{3,⌊k/2⌋}≤t≤k.

The floor symbol means rounding down to an integer. M1 obtains this through distance layers from a root vertex and controlled changes to paths, building on established cycle–clique ideas.

A clique is useful because its vertices can be joined in many orders. The argument considers paths whose endpoints lie in QQQ and whose interior vertices lie outside it. Their interiors must be disjoint, and their endpoint connections form disjoint chains. Combining these excursions with edges inside the clique can create cycles of specified lengths.

Call the total number of outside interior vertices the system’s amount. The manuscript chooses a system with maximum amount below k+1−tk+1-tk+1−t, breaking ties by using fewer paths. This optimization puts it just below the point where suitable closing edges could produce the forbidden cycle.

Possible improvements now become restrictions. If a new path or edge would increase the amount appropriately, it would close a cycle of length k+1k+1k+1, so that possibility must be absent. The resulting separations between neighborhoods allow independent sets to be assembled. Expansion makes those sets too large for the assumed bound on α(G)\alpha(G)α(G).

Reduce the final cases to finite patterns

The structural analysis treats cliques of order t≥9t\ge9t≥9. The remaining range satisfies

3≤t≤8,5≤k≤17,3\le t\le8,\qquad 5\le k\le17,3≤t≤8,5≤k≤17,

after the smaller cycle cases are handled separately.

A pattern records the numbers of interior vertices along the chains, identifying descriptions that differ only by reversing chains or reordering components. M1 reports 3,099 such parameter-pattern instances across 42 admissible pairs (k,t)(k,t)(k,t).

Its finite argument applies rules for replacing paths, closing exact cycles, growing neighborhoods, and packing independent sets. The manuscript reports two exact implementations and accompanying deduction traces that exclude every remaining pattern. This describes the stated computational component of the argument; the mathematical object being processed is the compressed path system, not an arbitrary colored complete graph.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem claims full coverage of m≥n≥3m\ge n\ge3m≥n≥3, with the one explicit exception. It makes no claim that the same formula holds without the order condition on mmm and nnn. Much of cycle–clique Ramsey theory outside that range remains a different question.

A cycle copy can have chords, because the theorem is not induced Ramsey theory. Likewise, a cycle on more than mmm vertices is not a substitute for the specified CmC_mCm​. Both distinctions are important when translating the result into ordinary graph language.

The manuscript’s finite computation is part of its reported argument. The existence of programs or traces is not itself a claim about an efficient general-purpose algorithm for finding the red cycle or blue clique in a large input coloring.

Natural further directions include sharper descriptions of colorings just below the threshold and stronger results when the cycle is shorter than the clique. Those questions ask for information beyond the exact numerical formula completed here.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Keevash, Long, and Skokan, Cycle-complete Ramsey numbers, for the earlier near-logarithmic cycle-length threshold.
  • Bondy and Erdős, Ramsey numbers for cycles in graphs, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 14 (1973), 46–54, for an early general range.
  • Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp, On cycle–complete graph Ramsey numbers, Journal of Graph Theory 2 (1978), 53–64, for the conjecture and structural antecedents.

M1 lists the primary papers for the successive small clique sizes and describes its finite path-pattern calculation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why rare ordered binary patterns can be hard to remove
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 190 · Combinatorics
Importance 2/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Suppose a large table contains only zeros and ones. A small forbidden pattern appears when certain rows and columns, read in their original orders, reproduce a prescribed binary matrix. If the table contains very few such appearances, can we eliminate all of them by changing a small number of entries?

A qualitative removal theorem says yes: sufficiently few appearances imply that the table is close to one with none. The quantitative question is how few appearances are needed. Can the relation between the fraction of changed entries and the density of forbidden patterns always be expressed by a fixed power?

The manuscript in this family claims a negative answer for a single explicitly specified 66×6666\times6666×66 binary pattern. Its examples contain exceptionally few copies relative to the amount of editing needed to remove the pattern.

A subtlety drives the construction. Changing one cell can destroy an existing occurrence while creating another. A small set of cells touching all current violations therefore need not give a cheap repair. Ordered binary matrices provide a setting where that distinction becomes a strong quantitative obstruction.

2. Background and essential definitions

Copies preserve both orders and both symbols

Let AAA be an n×nn\times nn×n matrix with entries in {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1}, and let HHH be a fixed k×kk\times kk×k binary matrix. An ordered copy of HHH is a choice of rows and columns

r1<⋯<rk,c1<⋯<ckr_1<\cdots<r_k,\qquad c_1<\cdots<c_kr1​<⋯<rk​,c1​<⋯<ck​

such that A(ri,cj)=H(i,j)A(r_i,c_j)=H(i,j)A(ri​,cj​)=H(i,j) for every i,ji,ji,j. The row and column choices are separate; their indices need not be equal.

The chosen positions need not be consecutive. However, we may not rearrange them after selection. A copy must match zeros as well as ones, so it is not enough to find all the locations where HHH has a one.

Write NH(A)N_H(A)NH​(A) for the number of copies. The matrix is HHH-free if this count is zero. Its normalized editing distance from being HHH-free is

dist⁡H(A)=1n2min⁡B is H-free∣{(r,c):A(r,c)≠B(r,c)}∣.\operatorname{dist}_H(A)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{B\text{ is }H\text{-free}}\bigl|\{(r,c):A(r,c)\ne B(r,c)\}\bigr|.distH​(A)=n21​B is H-freemin​​{(r,c):A(r,c)=B(r,c)}​.

Both kinds of changes, zero to one and one to zero, are allowed. Saying that AAA is ε\varepsilonε-far means that every successful repair changes at least εn2\varepsilon n^2εn2 cells.

What a polynomial removal bound would say

There are at most n2kn^{2k}n2k choices of kkk rows and kkk columns, so NH(A)/n2kN_H(A)/n^{2k}NH​(A)/n2k is a convenient copy-density normalization. A polynomial removal statement would provide constants cH,CH>0c_H,C_H>0cH​,CH​>0, depending only on the fixed pattern, such that

NH(A)n2k≥cHεCHwheneverdist⁡H(A)≥ε.\frac{N_H(A)}{n^{2k}}\ge c_H\varepsilon^{C_H}\quad\text{whenever}\quad\operatorname{dist}_H(A)\ge\varepsilon.n2kNH​(A)​≥cH​εCH​wheneverdistH​(A)≥ε.

In words, a table requiring substantial editing would necessarily contain a polynomially large density of visible violations. The exponent may be large, but it must stay fixed as the table and accuracy parameter vary.

A qualitative removal bound asks only for some positive function of ε\varepsilonε, which can decrease far faster than every power. The distinction between these two demands is the problem’s central issue.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Alon, Fischer, and Newman developed efficient testing results for forbidden binary matrix patterns when row and column order is ignored. Their 2007 work also raised the ordered question. Retaining order changes which patterns count as copies, so the unordered conclusion cannot simply be transferred.

Alon, Ben-Eliezer, and Fischer established qualitative removal for ordered matrices in 2017. Thus a fixed positive editing distance already guaranteed a positive density of forbidden patterns. The open issue was the rate at which that guarantee deteriorates as the permitted editing fraction shrinks. Their paper treats ordered graphs and matrices in a broader testing framework.

Alon and Ben-Eliezer’s Efficient removal lemmas for matrices obtained polynomial bounds in important cases, including finite forbidden families closed under row permutations, or under column permutations by transposition. They also proved a useful result relating many copies that are disjoint in cells to polynomial copy density. Their work formulated the remaining general binary-matrix question. The article supplies these positive results and the quantitative problem.

A singleton version, concerning just one forbidden binary matrix, appears in the first version of Gishboliner and Shapira’s 2025 survey. M1 claims to disprove that version, and consequently the more general finite-family proposal as well.

Earlier negative examples used a third symbol in the large host matrix. Even if the forbidden pattern used only two symbols, that additional symbol changed the available repairs. M1’s construction keeps both the pattern and the host genuinely binary. It also concerns separate row and column orders, rather than the single order and symmetric adjacency of an ordered graph.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. It specifies a fixed binary matrix HHH of size 66×6666\times6666×66. For every integer h≥1h\ge1h≥1, it constructs a square binary matrix AhA_hAh​ of side length

nh=(386h+2)2hn_h=(386h+2)2^hnh​=(386h+2)2h

and sets

εh=(386h+2)−2.\varepsilon_h=(386h+2)^{-2}.εh​=(386h+2)−2.

The claimed estimates are

dist⁡H(Ah)≥εh,NH(Ah)nh132≤εh2−h.\operatorname{dist}_H(A_h)\ge\varepsilon_h,\qquad\frac{N_H(A_h)}{n_h^{132}}\le\varepsilon_h2^{-h}.distH​(Ah​)≥εh​,nh132​NH​(Ah​)​≤εh​2−h.

The exponent 132 is twice the pattern size, because a copy selects 66 row positions and 66 column positions. The same HHH is used for every hhh.

The distance parameter decreases roughly as h−2h^{-2}h−2, while the additional factor 2−h2^{-h}2−h decreases exponentially. For every fixed positive ccc and CCC, the ratio of the displayed copy-density upper bound to cεhCc\varepsilon_h^CcεhC​ eventually tends to zero. This is how the claimed sequence contradicts every polynomial removal bound for that one pattern.

M1 also states a consequence for a specific canonical tester: independently sample qqq row positions and qqq column positions, inspect their ordered submatrix, and reject only if it contains HHH. Along the construction sequence, a fixed positive rejection probability requires

q≥exp⁡(Ω(εh−1/2)).q\ge \exp\bigl(\Omega(\varepsilon_h^{-1/2})\bigr).q≥exp(Ω(εh−1/2​)).

Here Ω\OmegaΩ indicates a positive constant multiple in the exponent for sufficiently large hhh. The sample has qqq positions on each axis and q2q^2q2 inspected entries. This is a statement about that sampling procedure, not every conceivable testing algorithm.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 2/5. The claim settles a specific quantitative conjecture in ordered matrix removal and supplies a concrete obstruction to a natural sampling strategy. Its significance is concentrated in property testing and extremal matrix theory.

A removal lemma connects a global property, distance from any successful repair, with local evidence, the number of forbidden patterns. Polynomial bounds make that connection especially useful because the required local search remains controlled as the accuracy demand becomes stricter.

The claimed construction shows that ordering and binary editing can frustrate this expectation even for one fixed pattern. Its conceptual lesson is wider than the numerical size 66: repairing violations is a dynamic problem, because changing a cell can move the obstruction rather than eliminate it.

The result preserves the qualitative removal theorem. For each fixed positive distance there is still some positive copy-density guarantee. What fails is the expectation that a fixed power always suffices.

6. The main idea

A small pattern transmits constraints

The lower-right corner of HHH is the two-by-two pattern

P=(1011).P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.P=(11​01​).

The other 64 rows and columns form an anchor: a larger pattern that identifies which rows and columns may play the roles in this small corner. This prevents an intended local restriction from drifting to unrelated positions in the host matrix.

Avoiding PPP can impose inequalities between binary entries. For example,

(1a1b)≠P⟺b≤a,a,b∈{0,1}.\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\1&b\end{pmatrix}\ne P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\le a,\qquad a,b\in\{0,1\}.(11​ab​)=P⟺b≤a,a,b∈{0,1}.

The forbidden case is exactly a=0,b=1a=0,b=1a=0,b=1. Such a restriction can transmit a known zero or one from one location to another. M1 uses anchored versions of these implications in both row and column directions.

Arrange the implications on a tree

The host positions are organized around a binary tree of depth hhh. Each internal node has plus and minus blocks on both axes. At a leaf, the two named blocks coincide. The row and column orders are chosen differently so that an ordered copy imposes the intended relation between successive levels.

Two root entries begin with opposite values. If an edited matrix avoids the forbidden pattern while retaining suitable anchors, the restrictions propagate those values down a common tree path. At the bottom, the plus and minus roles occupy the same positions. They cannot still carry opposite values.

To turn this contradiction into a distance estimate, the paper samples a path and the necessary anchor and auxiliary positions. Its argument states that fewer than 4h4^h4h edits leave a suitable selection untouched. The propagation contradiction then forces every successful repair to make at least 4h4^h4h changes, which equals εhnh2\varepsilon_h n_h^2εh​nh2​.

Make all original violations rare

A separate part of the argument locates every copy in the unedited host. The anchor contains dense rows and columns together with a block encoding all five-bit words. According to M1, these features force any occurrence into the prescribed roles.

The resulting copies must use one of only 2h2^h2h distinguished leaf cells. That bottleneck gives the small copy count and the sampling lower bound: a randomly selected submatrix is unlikely even to encounter a cell through which every violation must pass.

Notice the two scales. All original copies meet a set of 2h2^h2h cells, yet the claimed minimum repair uses at least 4h4^h4h edits. Simply changing the cells in that small meeting set does not solve the problem, because the edits can create new copies. The tree mechanism is designed to make that gap persist.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The counterexample uses one particular 66×6666\times6666×66 pattern. It does not claim that all ordered binary patterns have nonpolynomial removal bounds, or that 66 is the smallest possible size for a negative example.

Matching both symbols and preserving both orders are essential parts of the model. Ignoring order, allowing a third host symbol, forbidding only selected one-entries, or permitting only one direction of editing would pose different questions.

The lower bounds occur along the explicit sequence εh\varepsilon_hεh​. That is enough to refute a bound intended to hold for every positive ε\varepsilonε. It is not an exact determination of the best removal function at every distance.

The testing consequence concerns independent uniform row and column sampling followed by rejection only on a witnessed copy. Claims about adaptive queries, different rejection rules, or unrestricted testing complexity would require additional arguments.

A natural remaining task is to classify which ordered binary patterns admit polynomial bounds and to locate the smallest obstructions. The manuscript supplies a negative example, while the earlier positive subclasses show that the landscape is not uniform.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Alon, Ben-Eliezer, and Fischer, Testing hereditary properties of ordered graphs and matrices, for qualitative ordered removal.
  • Alon and Ben-Eliezer, Efficient removal lemmas for matrices, for polynomial positive cases and the earlier question.
  • Gishboliner and Shapira, Polynomial property testing, version 1, for the singleton conjecture cited by M1.

M1 gives the complete binary anchor, the ordered tree matrices, and the stated repair and copy-count estimates.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Keeping every triangle larger than the predicted scale
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 191 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Place nnn points in a square of side one. You would like every triangle formed by three of them to have reasonably large area. How well can you do?

This is Heilbronn’s triangle problem. It asks about the smallest triangle in a configuration, so one unfortunate triple can spoil an otherwise well-spread arrangement. Keeping points far apart is not sufficient: three widely separated points can lie almost on a line and form a very thin triangle.

The original conjecture predicted that every configuration would contain a triangle of area at most a constant times n−2n^{-2}n−2. That prediction was disproved decades ago by constructions improving the scale by a logarithmic factor. A weaker expectation allowed every arbitrarily small loss in the exponent: perhaps a triangle of area at most n−2+εn^{-2+\varepsilon}n−2+ε, up to a constant depending on ε\varepsilonε, would always exist.

The manuscript in this family claims a fixed power improvement in the opposite direction. For one absolute η>0\eta>0η>0, it constructs arbitrarily large configurations in which every triangle has area at least a constant times n−2+ηn^{-2+\eta}n−2+η. The exponent gain is extremely small, but fixed. That is enough to contradict the weaker expectation as well.

2. Background and essential definitions

The quantity being optimized

For a set PPP of points in the unit square [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2, define

Δ(P)=min⁡{p,q,r}⊂PArea⁡(pqr),\Delta(P)=\min_{\{p,q,r\}\subset P}\operatorname{Area}(pqr),Δ(P)={p,q,r}⊂Pmin​Area(pqr),

where the minimum runs over triples of distinct points. Then define

Δ(n)=max⁡P⊂[0,1]2∣P∣=nΔ(P).\Delta(n)=\max_{\substack{P\subset[0,1]^2\\|P|=n}}\Delta(P).Δ(n)=P⊂[0,1]2∣P∣=n​max​Δ(P).

Thus Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n) is the largest minimum triangle area achievable with nnn points. A lower bound requires constructing a good configuration. An upper bound must apply to every configuration. The directions can be easy to confuse because the definition combines a maximum and a minimum.

A collinear triple has area zero. A positive lower bound therefore guarantees, among other things, that no three selected points lie on a line.

Area as a determinant

For plane points p,q,rp,q,rp,q,r, elementary linear algebra gives

Area⁡(pqr)=12∣det⁡(q−p,r−p)∣.\operatorname{Area}(pqr)=\frac12\left|\det(q-p,r-p)\right|.Area(pqr)=21​∣det(q−p,r−p)∣.

The determinant measures the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two displacement vectors. Taking its absolute value and dividing by two gives the triangle area.

The construction uses another form of the same identity. An integer column u=(u1,u2,u3)Tu=(u_1,u_2,u_3)^{\mathsf T}u=(u1​,u2​,u3​)T, with positive third coordinate, represents the point

π(u)=(u1u3,u2u3).\pi(u)=\left(\frac{u_1}{u_3},\frac{u_2}{u_3}\right).π(u)=(u3​u1​​,u3​u2​​).

If three columns form a matrix AAA, then their projected triangle has area

∣det⁡A∣2A31A32A33.\frac{|\det A|}{2A_{31}A_{32}A_{33}}.2A31​A32​A33​∣detA∣​.

The entries A3jA_{3j}A3j​ are the third coordinates. Keeping them in a controlled range turns a lower bound on integer determinants into a geometric area bound.

Logarithmic and power improvements

A factor of log⁡n\log nlogn grows without bound, but more slowly than nηn^\etanη for every fixed η>0\eta>0η>0. Consequently, replacing n−2n^{-2}n−2 by (log⁡n)n−2(\log n)n^{-2}(logn)n−2 contradicts a constant-factor bound but does not contradict all bounds of the form n−2+εn^{-2+\varepsilon}n−2+ε. A fixed positive exponent gain crosses that second barrier.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Roth’s 1951 paper records Heilbronn’s original question and an elementary construction associated with Erdős. The construction uses a parabola over a finite field, producing grid points with nonzero triangle determinants before scaling. It reaches a minimum area comparable to n−2n^{-2}n−2. Random sampling followed by deleting points in small triangles also reaches that basic scale.

Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi obtained the stronger lower bound

Δ(n)≥clog⁡nn2\Delta(n)\ge c\frac{\log n}{n^2}Δ(n)≥cn2logn​

for a positive constant ccc. Their 1982 paper therefore disproved the original constant-factor conjecture. Their method treats small-area triples as forbidden triples in a hypergraph, then selects a large subset containing none. A hypergraph generalizes a graph by allowing an edge to contain more than two vertices. The original paper develops this lower-bound approach.

Upper bounds followed a separate trajectory. Roth obtained the first improvement over the elementary inverse-linear scale. Later work by Schmidt, Roth, and Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi sharpened the estimates, the last reaching exponents arbitrarily close to −8/7-8/7−8/7.

Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov introduced further incidence-geometric methods. Their 2023 work passed the −8/7-8/7−8/7 exponent by a fixed amount, and their subsequent Lower bounds for incidences gives

Δ(n)≤Cεn−7/6+ε\Delta(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{-7/6+\varepsilon}Δ(n)≤Cε​n−7/6+ε

for every fixed positive ε\varepsilonε. An incidence records a point lying on, or suitably near, a geometric object such as a line; controlling many such relationships can force a small triangle. Their paper develops the incidence estimates and the triangle consequence.

These upper and lower bounds remain widely separated. M1 addresses the lower-bound side and claims to disprove the almost-n−2n^{-2}n−2 formulation. It does not close the overall exponent gap or determine the correct asymptotic order of Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n).

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. It states that there are absolute constants η,c1>0\eta,c_1>0η,c1​>0 and an integer n0n_0n0​ such that

Δ(n)≥c1n−2+ηfor every integer n≥n0.\Delta(n)\ge c_1n^{-2+\eta}\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0.Δ(n)≥c1​n−2+ηfor every integer n≥n0​.

The constants are independent of the number of points. In particular, the improvement is available for every sufficiently large cardinality, not merely for a special sequence.

The weaker conjectural upper bound would say that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 there is a constant CεC_\varepsilonCε​ with

Δ(n)≤Cεn−2+ε\Delta(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{-2+\varepsilon}Δ(n)≤Cε​n−2+ε

for all sufficiently large nnn. Taking ε=η/2\varepsilon=\eta/2ε=η/2 makes the ratio of M1’s lower bound to the proposed upper bound grow like a positive constant times nη/2n^{\eta/2}nη/2. Thus the two statements cannot both hold for large nnn.

The manuscript gives an explicit admissible expression for η\etaη in terms of its fixed construction parameters, while emphasizing that it is extremely small and unoptimized. The claim is a qualitative change in the exponent, not a practically large numerical improvement for ordinary-sized point sets.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed result would overturn a persistent exponent-level expectation in a classical problem of discrete geometry. It also introduces a combination of arithmetic restrictions and random selection that goes beyond the earlier logarithmic improvement.

A tiny fixed exponent matters asymptotically because it eventually exceeds every logarithmic factor. The result would therefore change the plausible long-term scale of the extremal quantity, even if its explicit constants make the construction unsuitable for small examples.

The method connects geometric area to integer determinants, finite-field algebra, and congruences. This suggests a useful way of looking at the problem: instead of distributing points uniformly and then searching for bad triples, build arithmetic restrictions that make most bad triples impossible before sampling.

The rating reflects the conjectural barrier being crossed. It does not treat the claim as a complete solution of Heilbronn’s problem, since the optimal exponent remains undetermined.

6. The main idea

Build rational points through integer columns

The paper starts with integer columns satisfying

0≤u1,u2<N,N≤u3<2N.0\le u_1,u_2<N,\qquad N\le u_3<2N.0≤u1​,u2​<N,N≤u3​<2N.

Their projected points lie in the unit square. If every retained triple has determinant larger than a threshold τ\tauτ in absolute value, the area identity gives

Area⁡(pqr)>τ16N3.\operatorname{Area}(pqr)>\frac{\tau}{16N^3}.Area(pqr)>16N3τ​.

The task is therefore to sample many columns while making small determinants rare. Zero determinants need particular care because they represent collinear projected triples.

Use finite-field labels to obstruct small nonzero determinants

A finite field is a finite number system in which addition, multiplication, and division by nonzero elements obey the usual field rules. For distinct field elements x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z, the three columns

(1,x,x2)T,(1,y,y2)T,(1,z,z2)T(1,x,x^2)^{\mathsf T},\quad(1,y,y^2)^{\mathsf T},\quad(1,z,z^2)^{\mathsf T}(1,x,x2)T,(1,y,y2)T,(1,z,z2)T

have nonzero determinant. This is the algebraic reason that a finite-field parabola avoids collinear triples.

M1 assigns random labels in a fixed-degree field extension. A field norm, a multiplicative map from the extension to its smaller base field, packages the nonvanishing determinant information into a polynomial over the base field.

The construction then encodes this polynomial in a selected digit of a much larger integer determinant. A sufficiently large base controls carries between digits. Distinct labels thereby obstruct a small determinant modulo a prescribed modulus. Repeated labels are exceptional events whose probabilities can be made small.

A shared random invertible change of coordinates mixes the residue columns while preserving their determinant. The manuscript combines this with lattice counts to estimate how many integer lifts can have a given small nonzero determinant. A lattice is a discrete set of integer linear combinations of basis vectors; here it organizes the possible lifts satisfying the congruences.

Treat collinearity separately

The nonzero-determinant estimates do not automatically control determinant zero. The latter allows many columns to lie in a common plane before projection, so it requires a separate restriction.

At another prime modulus, M1 uses residues from a small part of a quadratic surface with no three points on a line. Random transformations provide enough flexibility for counting, while the chosen portion excludes certain short integer relations. The Chinese remainder theorem combines the restrictions at the two coprime moduli into compatible integer coordinates.

This second layer supplies the missing control of collinear triples, including degenerate residue patterns. Avoiding those triples is essential because even one would make the minimum area zero.

Delete the few exceptional choices

The final step is an alteration argument: sample more columns than ultimately needed, count repeated projected points and small-determinant triples, and delete one point from each offending pair or triple.

The manuscript’s estimates make the expected number of deletions smaller than the available surplus. Hence a retained set has no bad triples and still contains many points. Relating that count to the determinant threshold gives the fixed exponent gain.

The construction first produces certain cardinalities associated with growing primes. Bounds on the spacing of those sizes then permit passage to every sufficiently large nnn: retain any nnn points from a suitably sized configuration. Deleting points cannot introduce a smaller triangle.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns ordinary Euclidean triangle area in the unit square. Changing the region by a fixed scaling changes areas by a constant factor, but higher-dimensional simplex questions are not covered by its statement.

All triples must satisfy the bound, including nearly collinear ones. The result is stronger than a statement about average area or about most triples. At the same time, it says nothing about maximizing pairwise distances or controlling the shape of each triangle.

The exponent is fixed but extremely small, and the constants and size threshold are not optimized. The paper’s random construction establishes existence; the stated theorem is not an efficient numerical recipe for optimal configurations at a requested modest size.

The principal remaining problem is the correct decay rate of Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n). The claimed lower bound still lies far below the cited upper bounds. Improving either side, or simplifying the arithmetic mechanism enough to obtain a meaningful exponent, would provide further progress.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Roth, On a problem of Heilbronn, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 26 (1951), 198–204, for the early formulation and finite-field construction.
  • Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi, A lower bound for Heilbronn’s problem, for the logarithmic improvement that disproved the original conjecture.
  • Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov, A new upper bound for the Heilbronn triangle problem and Lower bounds for incidences, for the recent upper-bound developments.

M1 gives the determinant construction, the separate treatment of zero determinants, and the stated fixed power improvement.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A Boolean function can beat the square-root degree bound by any factor
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 192 · Combinatorics
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A Boolean function takes a string of binary inputs and returns one binary answer. Use signs −1-1−1 and +1+1+1 for the two values. Some functions closely follow individual inputs; others depend on complicated interactions among many inputs.

There are two different ways to measure this behavior. The function’s linear Fourier coefficients record its correlations with individual inputs. Its polynomial degree measures the largest interaction needed to express it exactly as a polynomial.

A conjecture of Gopalan and Servedio proposed a square-root relationship: the sum of the linear correlations should be at most the square root of the degree. Such a statement would replace the total number of input bits by a much more intrinsic measure of the function’s complexity.

The manuscript in this family claims that the proposed bound fails by arbitrarily large factors. For every chosen constant C>0C>0C>0, it constructs a finite Boolean function whose summed linear correlations exceed Cdeg⁡(f)C\sqrt{\deg(f)}Cdeg(f)​. A linear bound in the degree survives, so the question becomes how large the gap between these two scales can be.

2. Background and essential definitions

Fourier analysis on binary inputs

Let X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)X=(X1​,…,Xn​) be independent uniform random signs. For a subset S⊆{1,…,n}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}S⊆{1,…,n}, define

f^(S)=E[f(X)∏i∈SXi].\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E\left[f(X)\prod_{i\in S}X_i\right].f​(S)=E[f(X)i∈S∏​Xi​].

The empty product is one, so f^(∅)=E[f(X)]\widehat f(\varnothing)=\mathbb E[f(X)]f​(∅)=E[f(X)]. These coefficients express every function on the sign cube uniquely as

f(x)=∑S⊆{1,…,n}f^(S)∏i∈Sxi.f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\widehat f(S)\prod_{i\in S}x_i.f(x)=S⊆{1,…,n}∑​f​(S)i∈S∏​xi​.

Each variable appears with exponent at most one; this is the multilinear representation. Its degree is

deg⁡(f)=max⁡{∣S∣:f^(S)≠0}.\deg(f)=\max\{|S|:\widehat f(S)\ne0\}.deg(f)=max{∣S∣:f​(S)=0}.

The degree is over the real numbers and represents the function exactly. It is not degree modulo two, approximate polynomial degree, or the number of input queries used by an algorithm.

For a singleton set {i}\{i\}{i}, the coefficient f^({i})=E[f(X)Xi]\widehat f(\{i\})=\mathbb E[f(X)X_i]f​({i})=E[f(X)Xi​] measures agreement with input iii: it is the probability of agreement minus the probability of disagreement.

Their signed sum satisfies

L(f):=∑i=1nf^({i})=E[f(X)∑i=1nXi].L(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f(\{i\})=\mathbb E\left[f(X)\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right].L(f):=i=1∑n​f​({i})=E[f(X)i=1∑n​Xi​].

Thus L(f)L(f)L(f) measures correlation with the total input sum. Since a Boolean function has f(X)2=1f(X)^2=1f(X)2=1, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives L(f)≤nL(f)\le\sqrt nL(f)≤n​. The conjecture asks whether deg⁡(f)\sqrt{\deg(f)}deg(f)​ can replace n\sqrt nn​.

A surviving general bound

The influence of coordinate iii is the probability that flipping only that input changes the output. Write it as Inf⁡i(f)\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)Infi​(f), and let I(f)I(f)I(f) be the sum over coordinates.

The standard Fourier identities imply

∑i∣f^({i})∣≤I(f)=∑S∣S∣f^(S)2≤deg⁡(f).\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|\le I(f)=\sum_S|S|\widehat f(S)^2\le\deg(f).i∑​∣f​({i})∣≤I(f)=S∑​∣S∣f​(S)2≤deg(f).

The last step uses ∑Sf^(S)2=1\sum_S\widehat f(S)^2=1∑S​f​(S)2=1, the analogue of Parseval’s identity for a Boolean function. So there is already a dimension-independent linear degree bound. The disputed claim is the much smaller square-root scale.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nisan and Szegedy’s 1994 work developed the study of Boolean functions through their exact real polynomial degree. This connects a discrete input-output rule with algebraic constraints on which interactions can occur. The influence identities above belong to that established framework.

O’Donnell’s problem list attributes the square-root conjecture to Gopalan and Servedio around 2009. It also records a stronger proposal based on majority. If ddd independent signs are available, define

Bd=E∣X1+⋯+Xd∣≤d.B_d=\mathbb E|X_1+\cdots+X_d|\le\sqrt d.Bd​=E∣X1​+⋯+Xd​∣≤d​.

Majority on those signs, with a fixed output chosen at ties, has summed linear correlation BdB_dBd​. The stronger proposal would bound a degree-ddd function’s sum by this majority benchmark. The problem list records the two related questions.

Jha and Wang gave reformulations of the majority proposal and settled some special degree ranges. Kudin and Pašalić established additional low-degree cases and disproved the majority bound at degree four. That was a counterexample to the stronger inequality; it did not by itself contradict the weaker square-root bound. M1 carefully separates these statements despite varying terminology in the literature.

Another source of positive evidence came from decision trees. These compute a function by revealing information about the inputs. O’Donnell and Servedio related correlation to the expected amount of information revealed in ordinary decision trees; Blais, Tan, and Wan obtained a square-root bound involving parity decision-tree depth, where a query reveals a product of input signs.

M1’s construction uses a different kind of observation. It controls the polynomial degree of each possible output event rather than requiring the observation to be a sequence of simple queries. Algebraic cancellation then permits behavior that the earlier decision-tree bounds do not rule out.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. Its main statement is that for every real C>0C>0C>0, there are a positive integer nnn and a nonconstant Boolean function f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1} such that

∑i=1nf^({i})>Cdeg⁡(f).\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f(\{i\})>C\sqrt{\deg(f)}.i=1∑n​f​({i})>Cdeg(f)​.

This excludes every constant-factor version of the square-root conjecture. It is stronger than finding a single function that barely exceeds the proposed constant one.

The conclusion also applies to the sum of absolute values:

sup⁡n≥1, f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}deg⁡(f)>0∑i∣f^({i})∣deg⁡(f)=∞.\sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\\\deg(f)>0}}\frac{\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|}{\sqrt{\deg(f)}}=\infty.n≥1, f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}deg(f)>0​sup​deg(f)​∑i​∣f​({i})∣​=∞.

Indeed, reversing any input sign changes the sign of its linear coefficient while preserving polynomial degree. A universal bound for signed sums would therefore also bound absolute sums after suitable input reversals. M1’s examples already produce a large positive signed sum directly.

Every example in the theorem has finitely many inputs. Limits enter the construction to establish that sufficiently large finite choices exist. The source explicitly does not give useful bounds on how the dimension or replication counts grow with the requested violation factor.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5. The claimed result resolves a concrete conjecture in the analysis of Boolean functions and rules out its entire constant-factor relaxation. It clarifies that exact polynomial degree can underestimate this kind of accumulated linear correlation by more than a fixed square-root factor.

Linear Fourier information is a natural way to detect which inputs align with an output. Polynomial degree is a different structural measure, central to connections between algebra and computation. Understanding their limitations helps separate forms of complexity that initially appear closely related.

The claim is also conceptually stronger than the earlier failure of the majority benchmark. A modest violation of an exact extremal candidate might still leave a universal square-root law intact. An unbounded ratio rules out that broader law too.

At the same time, the surviving linear degree bound remains valid, and the manuscript does not determine the optimal replacement. The advance changes the range of possible answers without completing the full extremal picture.

6. The main idea

First retain information, then output a sign

Instead of immediately designing the Boolean function, M1 constructs a finite-valued observation FFF of a block of input signs. It can have more than two possible outputs. Let

HN=X1+⋯+XN,TF=E[HN∣F].H_N=X_1+\cdots+X_N,\qquad T_F=\mathbb E[H_N\mid F].HN​=X1​+⋯+XN​,TF​=E[HN​∣F].

Conditional expectation means the best mean-square prediction of the input sum when the observation is known. The random variable TFT_FTF​ records that prediction. Since the input sum has mean zero, so does TFT_FTF​.

Define the retained variance by

v(F)=E[TF2].v(F)=\mathbb E[T_F^2].v(F)=E[TF2​].

A large retained variance means that observing FFF reveals substantial information about the sum. Meanwhile, impose a degree bound DDD on every event indicator 1{F=a}\mathbf1_{\{F=a\}}1{F=a}​, which is one when the output is aaa and zero otherwise.

Every function of FFF is a linear combination of those indicators, so it also has degree at most DDD. In particular, reading out the sign of TFT_FTF​ gives a Boolean function with controlled degree and correlation E∣TF∣\mathbb E|T_F|E∣TF​∣.

The construction seeks observations with v(F)/Dv(F)/Dv(F)/D arbitrarily large.

Independent averaging turns variance into correlation

Take MMM independent copies of the same observation on disjoint input blocks, with scores T1,…,TMT_1,\ldots,T_MT1​,…,TM​. Their sum has variance Mv(F)Mv(F)Mv(F). The central limit theorem says that, after normalization, this sum approaches a standard Gaussian variable as MMM grows.

Choose the final output to be the sign of that score sum, assigning either fixed sign at zero. Its degree is at most MDMDMD, while its linear correlation behaves asymptotically like

2πMv(F).\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\sqrt{Mv(F)}.π2​​Mv(F)​.

Thus the correlation divided by the square root of the degree bound is governed by v(F)/D\sqrt{v(F)/D}v(F)/D​. An arbitrarily large retained-variance ratio would give the desired Boolean counterexamples using a sufficiently large but finite number of copies.

Cancellation improves the information-to-degree ratio

The central construction starts with m+1m+1m+1 independent standardized scores, each having mean zero and variance one. Simply revealing mmm of them retains mmm units of variance.

M1 designs a more selective reporting rule. Usually it reports all but one score. On a specially chosen exceptional event it reports a single tag, and that tag predicts the total sum with mean-square error smaller than the one unit normally lost by hiding one score.

The source claims that this retains strictly more than mmm units of variance. Yet each output indicator can be expressed as a linear combination of functions depending on at most mmm of the input observations. When the observations themselves have degree bound DDD, this gives degree at most mDmDmD.

The crucial feature is cancellation in that indicator expansion. An output can depend on all m+1m+1m+1 scores without requiring their full combined degree. The saving does not come from permanently ignoring one fixed input.

A Gaussian model supplies intervals and reporting rules with a definite gain. Independent averaging transfers those rules to finite sign inputs. Repeating the gain a finite number of times makes the retained-variance ratio exceed any prescribed level, after which the sign readout completes the stated construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the sum of linear coefficients, not their squared sum. Parseval’s identity still bounds the total squared Fourier mass by one. A large sum of many small linear correlations is compatible with that restriction.

The degree is exact real multilinear degree. The statement does not transfer automatically to approximate degree, arithmetic over a finite field, decision-tree depth, or circuit size. Each of those measures carries different constraints.

The construction establishes arbitrarily large violations but does not supply useful dimension bounds in terms of the desired factor. It also does not claim a simple small formula giving an optimal example at every degree.

The surviving estimate ∑i∣f^({i})∣≤deg⁡(f)\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|\le\deg(f)∑i​∣f​({i})∣≤deg(f) leaves substantial room above the square-root scale. Determining the true extremal growth, finding simpler examples, and identifying important subclasses where square-root behavior survives are natural further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Nisan and Szegedy, On the degree of Boolean functions as real polynomials, for the exact-degree framework and influence identities.
  • O’Donnell, Open Problems in Analysis of Boolean Functions, for the square-root and majority proposals.
  • Kudin and Pašalić, Proving the conjecture of O’Donnell in certain cases and disproving its general validity, for the earlier majority-bound counterexample.
  • Blais, Tan, and Wan, An inequality for the Fourier spectrum of parity decision trees, for the distinct decision-tree setting.

M1 develops the finite-observation construction, Gaussian comparison, and repeated amplification used in its claimed counterexamples.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Unbounded Violations of the Square-Root Degree Bound (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The precise residue of random triangle removal
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 188 · Combinatorics
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Begin with a complete network on nnn vertices: every pair is joined by an edge. Choose one of its triangles uniformly at random and erase that triangle’s three edges. Repeat, always choosing uniformly among the triangles still present. Eventually there is no triangle left, so the procedure stops.

How many edges survive? The answer is not zero in general. The final graph can contain many edges without containing a triangle, and the choices made along the way affect which edges become stranded. This is a simple example of a random greedy algorithm: make an available local move, without planning for the final outcome.

Write FnF_nFn​ for the number of surviving edges. Earlier work identified its principal scale as n3/2n^{3/2}n3/2, up to a factor of the form no(1)n^{o(1)}no(1). The manuscript in this family claims the precise leading constant:

Fn≈n3/222.F_n\approx \frac{n^{3/2}}{2\sqrt{2}}.Fn​≈22​n3/2​.

It also claims a strong form of concentration around that value. The interesting issue is how the last stages of a dependent process can be described accurately enough to recover a constant, after most of the original edges have already disappeared.

2. Background and essential definitions

Triangles, packings, and the leftover graph

A graph here is finite, undirected, and simple: there are no loops or repeated edges. A triangle consists of three vertices and all three edges between them. The complete graph KnK_nKn​ has (n2)=n(n−1)/2\binom n2=n(n-1)/2(2n​)=n(n−1)/2 edges.

Every triangle deleted by the procedure is disjoint in edges from every triangle deleted earlier. Thus the removed triangles form a triangle packing. Thinking of each triangle as a three-element subset of the vertex set, no pair of vertices belongs to more than one chosen triple. This is also called a partial Steiner triple system.

The leave is the graph of unused edges. At termination it is triangle-free, since otherwise another deletion would be possible. Triangle-free does not mean empty: a graph whose vertices split into two groups and whose edges run only between groups has no triangle, even when many edges are present.

If TnT_nTn​ triangles were removed, then

3Tn+Fn=(n2).3T_n+F_n=\binom n2.3Tn​+Fn​=(2n​).

Consequently, understanding the leave also describes how close the greedy packing comes to covering all pairs. The claimed leave occupies a vanishing proportion of all edges, but still has order n3/2n^{3/2}n3/2.

What kind of convergence is claimed?

For random variables XnX_nXn​, convergence in probability to aaa means that the chance of ∣Xn−a∣>ε|X_n-a|>\varepsilon∣Xn​−a∣>ε tends to zero for every fixed positive ε\varepsilonε. Convergence in mean square, also called L2L^2L2 convergence, means

E[(Xn−a)2]⟶0.\mathbb E[(X_n-a)^2]\longrightarrow0.E[(Xn​−a)2]⟶0.

Here E\mathbb EE denotes expectation. Mean-square convergence controls both typical behavior and the contribution of unusually large deviations. It implies convergence in probability and convergence of the expectations.

The notation o(1)o(1)o(1) means a quantity tending to zero as nnn grows. A statement holding with high probability has probability tending to one. Neither phrase says that a particular small instance must behave close to the limiting formula.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The manuscript traces the prediction that the expected leave should have order n3/2n^{3/2}n3/2 to Bollobás and Erdős in 1990. The broader setting is the study of random greedy packings, where a very simple rule can create an almost complete combinatorial design.

Spencer’s 1995 branching-process treatment and work of Rödl and Thoma in 1996 established asymptotic packing results: the unused fraction tends to zero. For triangle removal, this corresponds to a leave of size o(n2)o(n^2)o(n2). Such a result shows that the procedure is efficient at first order, while leaving the much smaller residue largely undetermined.

Subsequent work progressively reduced bounds on that residue. Grable obtained bounds approaching an exponent of 11/611/611/6, and described a further improvement. Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky’s 2010 paper gave an upper bound of order n7/4(log⁡n)5/4n^{7/4}(\log n)^{5/4}n7/4(logn)5/4. Their later Random triangle removal, published in 2015, established

Fn=n3/2+o(1)F_n=n^{3/2+o(1)}Fn​=n3/2+o(1)

with high probability. This settled the main exponent, but an no(1)n^{o(1)}no(1) factor can still drift and therefore does not determine a leading constant.

Joos and Kühn’s 2025 work developed a much broader theory of hypergraph removal processes. Its triangle-removal conjecture specifies the constant 1/(22)1/(2\sqrt2)1/(22​). The present manuscript claims that constant and mean-square convergence, rather than another improvement to the exponent alone.

The source explicitly uses the earlier Joos–Kühn analysis for a sufficiently long initial portion of the process. Its new argument concerns the continuation into the final regime. This distinction matters: the claimed advance builds on existing control of the early evolution instead of replacing the whole history of random greedy analysis.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. Its main statement is

E[(Fnn3/2−122)2]⟶0.\mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{F_n}{n^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\right)^2\right]\longrightarrow0.E[(n3/2Fn​​−22​1​)2]⟶0.

The randomness is exactly that of successive uniform choices among the currently available triangles, starting from KnK_nKn​.

The stated consequences include

Fnn3/2→P122,E[Fn]=(122+o(1))n3/2.\frac{F_n}{n^{3/2}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}\frac{1}{2\sqrt2},\qquad\mathbb E[F_n]=\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}+o(1)\right)n^{3/2}.n3/2Fn​​P​22​1​,E[Fn​]=(22​1​+o(1))n3/2.

The arrow denotes convergence in probability. Mean-square convergence also entails that the variance of FnF_nFn​ is o(n3)o(n^3)o(n3); variance measures the mean squared distance from a random variable’s expectation.

This is an asymptotic theorem about the terminal number of edges. It does not identify a limiting distribution for the finer fluctuations, an exact finite-size expectation, or a formula for an arbitrary starting graph. Nor does it assert that every maximal triangle packing has this leave. Uniform randomness is part of the statement.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5. The claimed result completes a substantial prediction about a central example of a random greedy process. Its significance lies in determining the terminal constant and controlling fluctuations at the main scale, after the exponent was already known.

The distinction between an exponent and a constant is particularly meaningful here. During most of the process, averages and approximate uniformity offer useful descriptions. Near termination, an edge’s fate depends on a web of earlier choices. A sharp answer must retain enough of that dependence to distinguish one constant from another.

The method also explains why a branching-process prediction can survive this complicated finite environment. That is potentially useful intuition for other greedy algorithms, although M1’s theorem remains specific to triangle removal from a complete graph.

For designs, the conclusion quantifies the defect left by an uncomplicated construction procedure. It does not say that the leave is the smallest possible defect, or that a carefully planned packing could not do better.

6. The main idea

Stop early enough to retain a regular environment

The argument first pauses the process at a stage where the remaining graph has edge density ppp, with ppp slightly larger than n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2. At that point it has approximately

m=n2p2m=\frac{n^2p}{2}m=2n2p​

edges, and a typical surviving edge belongs to about

D=np2D=np^2D=np2

triangles. The letter mmm in this explanation counts remaining edges. The parameter DDD measures how many competing deletion opportunities surround one edge.

The cited earlier theory supplies a sufficiently regular graph at this stopping point. The remaining task is to follow the continuation all the way to the end, where straightforward uniform-density approximations become inadequate.

Give possible deletions random priorities

One can represent the continuation by assigning independent uniform priorities between zero and one to the triangles present at the pause. Scan them in priority order and accept a triangle precisely when all three of its edges are still available. The manuscript uses the equivalence of this representation with the required random greedy continuation.

To decide whether a particular edge survives up to priority ttt, inspect earlier triangles containing it. Whether one of those triangles deletes the edge depends on whether its other two edges have survived until that earlier priority. Their survival produces further questions, and so on.

This backward exploration resembles a tree of dependencies. An idealized version gives different appearances of a triangle independent randomness, even when the finite graph would identify them. In the approximately uniform setting, the corresponding survival probability has the scalar form

q(t)=11+2Dt.q(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2Dt}}.q(t)=1+2Dt​1​.

Here ttt is a priority cutoff, not the number of deleted triangles. The shape of this formula reflects the fact that deletion of one edge needs two other surviving edges.

Recover the constant, then justify the approximation

At the final cutoff t=1t=1t=1, the idealized number of survivors is

mq(1)=n2p21+2np2.mq(1)=\frac{n^2p}{2\sqrt{1+2np^2}}.mq(1)=21+2np2​n2p​.

Because the chosen stopping point has D=np2D=np^2D=np2 tending to infinity, the leading factors of ppp cancel:

mq(1)n3/2⟶122.\frac{mq(1)}{n^{3/2}}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}.n3/2mq(1)​⟶22​1​.

This calculation explains the constant; it is not by itself the finite-process argument. Actual dependency explorations can meet the same edge or triangle more than once. Such collisions create correlations absent from the idealized tree.

M1 describes two ingredients for controlling the discrepancy. First, information about local neighborhoods stabilizes the survival equations despite small irregularities. Second, it counts the patterns that can witness a collision in one or two simultaneous explorations, keeping track of the order of their priorities.

The two-exploration estimate is crucial. One randomly selected edge reveals the expected surviving fraction; two independently selected edges reveal its second moment. The claimed comparison error is smaller than their joint survival probability. This supplies enough precision for the first and second moments to yield mean-square convergence, rather than only a plausible estimate of the mean.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The initial graph and the selection rule are essential. Starting with a different dense graph, choosing triangles with a bias, or deleting another fixed shape gives a different problem. The broader removal-process literature motivates such extensions, but M1 does not state a universal version of its constant.

The terminal graph is triangle-free, yet it is not sampled uniformly from triangle-free graphs. It is also distinct from the usual triangle-free process, which starts with no edges and adds edges while avoiding triangles. Similar vocabulary should not obscure these different probability distributions.

The theorem concerns the total leave, rather than a complete description of its geometry. It does not specify the degree distribution, component structure, or the smaller scale and shape of the remaining fluctuations. Those are natural further questions once the leading constant is fixed.

Finally, the asymptotic result supplies no optimized numerical cutoff beyond which the approximation has a chosen accuracy. Its explanatory achievement is a limiting law for a concrete algorithm, supported in the manuscript by control of the dependent final phase.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky, A note on the random greedy triangle-packing algorithm, for the earlier quantitative upper bound.
  • Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky, Random triangle removal, for the n3/2+o(1)n^{3/2+o(1)}n3/2+o(1) scale and the process’s development.
  • Joos and Kühn, The hypergraph removal process, version 2, for the broader removal framework, the early-stage input, and the sharp-constant conjecture discussed by M1.

M1 supplies the detailed references to the early packing results and the stated terminal analysis.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The sharp terminal leave in random triangle removal (September 25, 2026).

entry.title: The full BSD formula from a small Selmer group
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 002 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An elliptic curve can have infinitely many rational points even though its equation is very simple. The curve y2=x3+ax+by^2=x^3+ax+by2=x3+ax+b, when nonsingular and completed by its point at infinity, carries a group law. A basic arithmetic question asks how many independent rational points are needed to generate all the others, apart from a finite torsion subgroup.

The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, usually abbreviated BSD, predicts that this arithmetic information is encoded in an analytic function built from counting points modulo primes.
