Inhomogeneous overlap is difficult even when numerators are unrestricted. Ramírez constructed nonmonotone counterexamples to unweighted divergence for prescribed countable collections of shifts. These have finite totient-weighted sum, so they do not contradict the statement considered here. His primary paper explains the distinction.

Yu obtained results with additional divergence or size assumptions and restrictions on the shift. Chow and Technau proved the weak conjecture for certain structured approximation functions arising in multiplicative approximation. Beresnevich, Hauke and Velani proved the weak statement for every rational shift and obtained further irrational-shift results under additional conditions. Their 2024 paper is the immediate predecessor for the arbitrary-shift question.

There is also a crucial warning about the stronger numerator condition. The manuscript cites September 2026 counterexamples by Hauke-Treuer–Maynard–Pollington and independently He–Liao to the ordinary coprime-numerator formulation for broad classes of shifts. Thus “weak” is not a cosmetic adjective.

For a rational shift γ=A/B\gamma=A/Bγ=A/B, the earlier positive theorem can impose the adapted condition gcd⁡(A+aB,q)=1\gcd(A+aB,q)=1gcd(A+aB,q)=1. This is different from gcd⁡(a,q)=1\gcd(a,q)=1gcd(a,q)=1. Family 022’s stated advance is to allow a completely arbitrary fixed irrational shift together with an arbitrary sparse, nonmonotone tolerance function, while leaving numerators unrestricted.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript. Theorem 1.1 states that, for every fixed γ∈R\gamma\in\mathbb Rγ∈R and finite-valued ψ\psiψ,

∑q=1∞φ(q)qψ(q)=∞\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(q)}q\psi(q)=\inftyq=1∑∞​qφ(q)​ψ(q)=∞

implies

∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q)for infinitely many q\|qx-\gamma\|<\psi(q)\quad\text{for infinitely many }q∥qx−γ∥<ψ(q)for infinitely many q

for Lebesgue-almost every x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R.

There is no Diophantine restriction on γ\gammaγ. It may be rational, badly approximable, or extremely well approximated by rationals. No monotonicity is required of ψ\psiψ, even on its support. The conclusion is a divergence implication, not an asymptotic count of solutions.

The quantifiers are worth keeping explicit: first fix γ\gammaγ and ψ\psiψ; then almost every xxx works. The theorem does not give one universal exceptional null set valid simultaneously for all real shifts and all tolerance functions.

A Hausdorff-measure consequence

Corollary 1.2 extends the divergence statement to a finer measure of size. A gauge f(r)f(r)f(r) assigns a cost to a covering interval of small diameter rrr; Hausdorff fff-measure is obtained by minimizing total cost over increasingly fine covers. The familiar Hausdorff dimension uses gauges f(r)=rsf(r)=r^sf(r)=rs.

Assume fff is continuous, positive and nondecreasing on positive arguments, tends to zero as r↓0r\downarrow0r↓0, and has monotone ratio f(r)/rf(r)/rf(r)/r. If

∑q=1∞φ(q)f ⁣(ψ(q)q)=∞,\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\varphi(q) f\!\left(\frac{\psi(q)}q\right)=\infty,q=1∑∞​φ(q)f(qψ(q)​)=∞,

then for every bounded interval III,

Hf(I∩Wγ(ψ))=Hf(I).\mathcal H^f(I\cap W_\gamma(\psi))=\mathcal H^f(I).Hf(I∩Wγ​(ψ))=Hf(I).

The corollary uses the mass transference principle of Beresnevich and Velani. It retains the fixed shift and unrestricted numerators, and asserts no convergence converse.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Taken as stated, this settles a major general form of metric approximation with an additive shift. Both sources of irregularity remain unrestricted: the shift can have any rational-approximation behavior, and the denominator support can be arbitrarily sparse.

The conclusion shows that the totient-weighted divergence condition is robust enough to overcome the resulting overlaps for unrestricted numerators. The Hausdorff consequence connects the theorem to fractal-size questions as well as ordinary length.

The mathematical significance lies in the uniformity of the hypotheses, not in a pointwise claim for every real number. This is a broad theorem about almost-everywhere approximation, with arithmetic correlations replacing the independence that elementary probability would prefer.

6. The main idea

Keep enough mass while controlling overlap

For independent events, divergent total probability often implies infinitely many occurrences. These approximation events are far from independent. A standard replacement is a second-moment estimate: if a nonnegative counting function has substantial average and its squared average is controlled, it cannot concentrate all its mass on an arbitrarily tiny set.

The paper works with arbitrarily late finite blocks of denominators whose totient-weighted mass lies in a fixed small range. Within each block it constructs a weighted sum of interval indicators, supported inside the original approximation events. It aims to retain enough first-moment mass while bounding the second moment.

A comparison sum follows the same prime-step updates but omits certain additional deletions. This sum is equidistributed on fixed spatial intervals. Small loss of mass and control of the retained second moment then rule out a positive-measure set avoiding every sufficiently late block. The argument approximates such an avoided set by one fixed finite union of intervals, rather than assuming an unproved zero-one principle for the shifted problem.

Close shifted fractions reveal denominator structure

Two centers can be close only when an integer combination of their numerators and shifted denominators is small. At very small scales there is too little room for direct averaging.

An inverse estimate shows that large weighted overlap forces the prime-exponent patterns of the denominators to cluster around a common integer. This builds on the common-pivot ideas from homogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer proofs, but the shifted phases require additional analysis.

Varying permitted factors then gives either a rotation estimate controlling the overlap or a precise rational model for the phase offsets. Exact coincidences in those models are handled by explicit numerator restrictions. Those restrictions are tools used on selected weighted subevents; the final theorem still permits all numerators.

Expose primes without pretending the tests are independent

Large common primes can create repeated correlations when previously separate collections of rows begin to interact. The manuscript assigns each denominator an integer multiple and exposes its prime factors in stages. Before all factors are exposed, a row is represented on a finer projected grid containing its eventual true centers.

At a prime step, nearby grid entries are grouped. Some weights survive only when a numerator passes a divisibility test; linked portions of other weights are suppressed to offset the strongest correlated contributions. The rules preserve the required first-moment normalization.

The construction also remembers earlier alignments when intermediate labels disappear. At the first meeting of two previously separate collections, a backward comparison accounts for covariance through entries that passed their tests. A squared-mass bound limits the total contributions assigned to them.

This history-sensitive accounting is the paper’s response to dependencies across many scales. It averages common residue translations, while keeping γ\gammaγ fixed throughout; it does not assume independent outcomes or randomize the shift. Once the finite-block estimates are established, the almost-everywhere conclusion follows, and mass transference yields the Hausdorff version.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem does not impose ordinary numerator coprimality. Adding gcd⁡(a,q)=1\gcd(a,q)=1gcd(a,q)=1 changes the statement and, according to the cited counterexamples, can make it false.

Convergence of the totient-weighted sum is not claimed to force a null approximation set. A simple sufficient null-set criterion comes instead from convergence of the unweighted sum ∑qψ(q)\sum_q\psi(q)∑q​ψ(q), by the first Borel–Cantelli lemma and interval-length bounds. The gap between these conditions should not be erased by calling the new result a complete convergence-divergence law.

The result gives no rate or asymptotic formula for the number of successful denominators. It also does not treat an arbitrary changing sequence of shifts γq\gamma_qγq​, nor recover the approximation behavior of a specified exceptional real number.

Further questions include quantitative counting, finer dependence on the tolerance support, and meaningful numerator restrictions adapted to particular shifts.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 gives the Lebesgue-measure statement; Corollary 1.2 and Section 11 give the Hausdorff consequence. The introduction carefully distinguishes unrestricted, reduced and shift-adapted numerators. Sections 5–10 develop the weighted finite-block construction and overlap estimates.

The Ramírez and Beresnevich–Hauke–Velani papers linked in section 3 explain the earlier obstruction and rational-shift theorem. The cited counterexample preprints explain why the stronger coprime formulation must remain separate. Optional background on the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture and Hausdorff measure provides additional context.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Weak Inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer Conjecture (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The small positive bias in cubic Gauss sums
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 023 · Number theory
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Add many points on the unit circle in the complex plane. If their directions are balanced, their sum should be much smaller than the number of points. But “balanced in the limit” does not rule out a smaller systematic bias.

Cubic Gauss sums provide an arithmetic example. Their normalized values become equidistributed around the unit circle as the prime varies, yet computations suggest a persistent positive first moment. Patterson predicted the scale and constant of that bias.

Family 023 claims an unconditional asymptotic for the sum over all primary Eisenstein primes with a sharp upper cutoff. It also claims cancellation for every fixed nonzero angular Fourier mode and for certain higher powers of the Gauss sums. The precise indexing and normalization determine the leading constant, so they deserve explicit treatment.

2. Background and essential definitions

Cubes and exponential sums

Write e(t)=exp⁡(2πit)e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)e(t)=exp(2πit). For a rational prime ppp, Kummer’s cubic sum is

Sp=∑x mod pe(x3/p).S_p=\sum_{x\bmod p}e(x^3/p).Sp​=xmodp∑​e(x3/p).

The summands have absolute value one, but their phases can cancel. If p≡2(mod3)p\equiv2\pmod3p≡2(mod3), cubing permutes the residues modulo ppp, so the sum is zero. The interesting rational primes satisfy p≡1(mod3)p\equiv1\pmod3p≡1(mod3), where nonzero cubes occupy only one third of the nonzero residue classes.

For the natural cubic characters, it is convenient to work with the Eisenstein integers

O=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.\mathcal O=\mathbb Z[\omega],\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}.O=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.

These form a triangular lattice in the complex plane. Complex conjugation sends ω\omegaω to ω2\omega^2ω2. The norm and trace are

N(z)=zzˉ=∣z∣2,Tr⁡(z)=z+zˉ.N(z)=z\bar z=|z|^2,\qquad\operatorname{Tr}(z)=z+\bar z.N(z)=zzˉ=∣z∣2,Tr(z)=z+zˉ.

In particular, N(a+bω)=a2−ab+b2N(a+b\omega)=a^2-ab+b^2N(a+bω)=a2−ab+b2.

An element prime to three is primary when it is congruent to one modulo three. This chooses one generator for each ideal prime to three. The sum in the manuscript counts prime ideals through these chosen generators. For a split rational prime p≡1(mod3)p\equiv1\pmod3p≡1(mod3), both conjugate prime ideals are included.

Normalized Gauss sums

For a primary prime ϖ\varpiϖ, the cubic residue character χϖ\chi_{\varpi}χϖ​ takes values in {1,ω,ω2}\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}{1,ω,ω2} on nonzero residues. It records the cubic residue class and is extended by zero at zero. Concretely, its value is the cube root of unity congruent to v(Nϖ−1)/3v^{(N\varpi-1)/3}v(Nϖ−1)/3 modulo ϖ\varpiϖ.

The manuscript normalizes the Gauss sum as

G(ϖ)=1Nϖ∑v mod ϖχϖ(v)e ⁣(Tr⁡(v/ϖ)).G(\varpi)=\frac1{\sqrt{N\varpi}}\sum_{v\bmod\varpi}\chi_{\varpi}(v) e\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}(v/\varpi)\right).G(ϖ)=Nϖ​1​vmodϖ∑​χϖ​(v)e(Tr(v/ϖ)).

For a prime argument its absolute value is one. A first moment is the sum of these complex values, rather than the sum of their absolute values. It detects a preferred direction that absolute values cannot see.

An angular Fourier mode weights a prime by

(ϖ∣ϖ∣)ℓ,ℓ∈Z.\left(\frac{\varpi}{|\varpi|}\right)^\ell,\qquad\ell\in\mathbb Z.(∣ϖ∣ϖ​)ℓ,ℓ∈Z.

This probes how the bias correlates with the direction of the prime in the complex plane. The mode ℓ=0\ell=0ℓ=0 is the ordinary first moment.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kummer’s nineteenth-century computations suggested a positive bias in cubic sums. Heath-Brown and Patterson proved equidistribution of normalized cubic Gauss sums on the unit circle. That says the distribution is balanced on the prime-counting scale X/log⁡XX/\log XX/logX, but leaves room for a smaller average of order X5/6/log⁡XX^{5/6}/\log XX5/6/logX.

Patterson proposed this finer first-moment scale in 1978. Heath-Brown’s cubic large sieve supplied an unconditional upper bound Oε(X5/6+ε)O_\varepsilon(X^{5/6+\varepsilon})Oε​(X5/6+ε). An upper bound close to the expected power is still different from an asymptotic: it does not identify the sign, leading constant or a remainder smaller than the main term.

The analytic background comes from cubic theta series and metaplectic forms, which encode Gauss sums in automorphic objects with functional equations. Patterson and Yoshimoto developed the relevant coefficient and twist calculations.

Dunn and Radziwiłł proved a smoothed first-moment asymptotic conditional on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Hecke LLL-functions. Their 2024 Annals paper introduced an explicit level-aspect Voronoi summation formula and a corrected dispersion argument. Some nonzero cube frequencies contribute to the main term, so treating all nonzero frequencies as errors would lose the bias itself.

The current manuscript imports their unconditional summation formula and residue calculations, together with established large-sieve and mean-square estimates. It states that its new cancellation arguments do not use their GRH-dependent estimates. It also removes smoothing to obtain the ordinary sharp-cutoff sum.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Define

c∗=(2π)2/33Γ(2/3),c_* =\frac{(2\pi)^{2/3}}{3\Gamma(2/3)},c∗​=3Γ(2/3)(2π)2/3​,

where Γ(s)=∫0∞ts−1e−t dt\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dtΓ(s)=∫0∞​ts−1e−tdt for s>0s>0s>0 is the gamma function. Theorem 1.1 claims

∑Nϖ≤Xϖ≡1(mod3) primeG(ϖ)=65c∗X5/6log⁡X+o ⁣(X5/6log⁡X).\sum_{\substack{N\varpi\le X\\\varpi\equiv1\pmod3\ \mathrm{prime}}}G(\varpi)=\frac65c_*\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}+o\!\left(\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}\right).Nϖ≤Xϖ≡1(mod3) prime​∑​G(ϖ)=56​c∗​logXX5/6​+o(logXX5/6​).

The sum is over all primary Eisenstein primes. The little-oh remainder is smaller than the first-moment scale. There is no smoothing function suppressing the endpoint near XXX.

Partial summation gives the corresponding logarithmically weighted statement:

∑Nϖ≤XG(ϖ)log⁡Nϖ=65c∗X5/6+o(X5/6),\sum_{N\varpi\le X}G(\varpi)\log N\varpi=\frac65c_*X^{5/6}+o(X^{5/6}),Nϖ≤X∑​G(ϖ)logNϖ=56​c∗​X5/6+o(X5/6),

with the same primary-prime convention.

Converting to rational primes

For a split rational prime p=ϖϖˉp=\varpi\bar\varpip=ϖϖˉ, the manuscript records

G(ϖ)+G(ϖˉ)=Spp.G(\varpi)+G(\bar\varpi)=\frac{S_p}{\sqrt p}.G(ϖ)+G(ϖˉ)=p​Sp​​.

Inert prime ideals have norm p2p^2p2, and their total contribution below norm XXX is O(X)O(\sqrt X)O(X​), negligible here. Therefore the rational-prime consequence is

∑p≤Xp≡1(mod3)Sp2p∼35c∗X5/6log⁡X=(2π)2/35Γ(2/3)X5/6log⁡X.\sum_{\substack{p\le X\\p\equiv1\pmod3}}\frac{S_p}{2\sqrt p}\sim\frac35c_*\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}=\frac{(2\pi)^{2/3}}{5\Gamma(2/3)}\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}.p≤Xp≡1(mod3)​∑​2p​Sp​​∼53​c∗​logXX5/6​=5Γ(2/3)(2π)2/3​logXX5/6​.

The factor of two comes from counting both conjugate Eisenstein primes versus the rational-prime summand normalized by 2p2\sqrt p2p​. The manuscript explicitly notes conflicting printed constants in two historical formulations and identifies its theorem with the all-primary-prime formulation. The formulas above preserve its stated conversion rather than silently identifying those conventions.

Fixed angular modes and higher powers

Appendix A claims that, for each fixed nonzero integer ℓ\ellℓ,

∑Nϖ≤XG(ϖ)(ϖ∣ϖ∣)ℓ=oℓ ⁣(X5/6log⁡X).\sum_{N\varpi\le X}G(\varpi)\left(\frac{\varpi}{|\varpi|}\right)^\ell=o_\ell\!\left(\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}\right).Nϖ≤X∑​G(ϖ)(∣ϖ∣ϖ​)ℓ=oℓ​(logXX5/6​).

Together with the cubic Gauss-sum identity, this gives cancellation at the same scale for every fixed power G(ϖ)kG(\varpi)^kG(ϖ)k with 3∤k3\nmid k3∤k and ∣k∣>1|k|>1∣k∣>1. The first powers k=±1k=\pm1k=±1 retain the bias. Nonzero multiples of three are not included in this higher-power conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. Taken as stated, this removes a major conditional hypothesis from a classical first-moment prediction and proves it at a sharp cutoff. It identifies a subtle arithmetic bias that ordinary equidistribution cannot detect.

There is no contradiction between the two scales. The main term divided by the number of prime ideals is of order X−1/6X^{-1/6}X−1/6, so the average still tends to zero. Yet the accumulated sum has a positive and precisely predicted asymptotic.

The methodological contribution is also focused: the paper obtains stronger cancellation for structured prime sequences without claiming a generally stronger cubic large sieve for arbitrary coefficients. Its rating reflects a substantial advance in exponential sums and analytic number theory, with several complementary moments still outside the theorem.

6. The main idea

Compare with a simple arithmetic model

The analytic target is to compare G(ϖ)G(\varpi)G(ϖ), after summation, with

c∗(Nϖ)−1/6.c_*(N\varpi)^{-1/6}.c∗​(Nϖ)−1/6.

This is not a pointwise approximation: ∣G(ϖ)∣=1|G(\varpi)|=1∣G(ϖ)∣=1, while the model tends to zero. It is an average model for the small directional bias.

The prime ideal theorem and partial summation give

∑Nϖ≤X(Nϖ)−1/6∼65X5/6log⁡X.\sum_{N\varpi\le X}(N\varpi)^{-1/6}\sim\frac65\frac{X^{5/6}}{\log X}.Nϖ≤X∑​(Nϖ)−1/6∼56​logXX5/6​.

The exponent 5/65/65/6 and the factor 6/56/56/5 thus arise naturally from integrating a weight of degree −1/6-1/6−1/6 against prime density. The difficult task is proving that the Gauss-sum average matches that model closely enough.

Preserve the cube-frequency main term

Prime sums are decomposed into sums with one main variable and bilinear sums involving products. Voronoi summation transforms the first kind. For bilinear sums, Poisson summation introduces dual frequencies.

The nonzero frequencies that are cubes yield the model term. The corrected dispersion method subtracts it explicitly before estimating the remaining frequencies. Existing large sieves handle most ranges, but two configurations of conductor and length require additional work.

The manuscript uses moments at several lengths to move a hypothetical large contribution into a range where a Gram-matrix estimate is stronger. A Gram matrix records pairwise inner products, so control of its off-diagonal entries limits how coherently a family can align. These estimates apply to smooth convolutions of prime sequences with independent coefficients, not arbitrary coefficient arrays.

Keep independence through the prime decomposition

A decomposition chosen by a least-prime condition can couple the two variables, invalidating an estimate that requires independent coefficients. The paper instead orders prime norm bins and stops according to counts in the final bin. A binomial weight separates the two sides exactly.

The remaining narrow transition involves three primes of nearly equal norm. Their sparsity supplies the extra saving needed there. This is one reason the structure of prime coefficients matters.

Remove the smoothing

A smoothed cutoff is analytically convenient because its Mellin transform decays quickly. Approximating a sharp cutoff more finely introduces larger imaginary parts of the Mellin variable, often called heights. The paper must control heights up to slightly beyond X1/6X^{1/6}X1/6.

At low heights it compares the Gauss sum with its model. At large heights it estimates the Gauss-sum term directly. Localizing both norm variables improves the diagonal contribution near a product boundary; away from that boundary, oscillation in the Mellin height produces the saving.

Combining these ranges permits removal of the smooth weight. Appendix A keeps the additional fixed angular factors through the same framework, with constants allowed to depend on the mode.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Every angular mode is fixed before XXX grows. The theorem does not give uniformity for a mode that increases with XXX, nor automatically imply equally strong results in angular sectors shrinking with XXX.

The complementary higher-moment prediction is only partly covered. Nonzero powers divisible by three require stronger information about angular Hecke prime sums. The little-oh error does not specify a power-saving rate.

The main term is a collective bias; it says nothing like G(ϖ)≈c∗(Nϖ)−1/6G(\varpi)\approx c_*(N\varpi)^{-1/6}G(ϖ)≈c∗​(Nϖ)−1/6 for each prime. It also does not prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis or a stronger general cubic large sieve. The unconditional claim comes from estimates tailored to the structured families in this first-moment problem.

The normalization caveat is mathematical rather than cosmetic. Counting one rational prime, both conjugate prime ideals, or a differently scaled real cubic sum changes the constant. Any comparison with another formulation must carry those factors explicitly.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 states the primary-prime first moment. Section 1.2 gives the rational-prime conversion and its normalization caveat. Theorem A.1 and equation (A.14) specify the fixed-angular and higher-power consequences.

Dunn–Radziwiłł’s paper linked in section 3 is the principal analytic predecessor. The manuscript’s references identify Kummer, Patterson, Heath-Brown and Yoshimoto for the historical and metaplectic inputs. Optional background on Gauss sums and Eisenstein integers helps visualize the characters and complex prime lattice.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An unconditional first moment for cubic Gauss sums (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Counting distinct values of Euler’s totient function
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 024 · Number theory
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Euler’s totient function φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) counts the integers from one to nnn that are coprime to nnn. Its values repeat: φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4\varphi(5)=\varphi(8)=\varphi(10)=\varphi(12)=4φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4. Other integers never occur. How many different outputs are at most xxx?

This is not the same as counting inputs n≤xn\le xn≤x, or even counting all inputs whose outputs are at most xxx. Every output must be counted exactly once, regardless of how many preimages it has.

Family 024 claims an explicit asymptotic equivalent for the number of distinct totients. It also answers a simpler-looking question of Erdős and Hall: if the output bound is multiplied by a fixed constant ccc, does the number of outputs asymptotically multiply by ccc too? The manuscript’s answer is yes.

2. Background and essential definitions

The product formula is

φ(n)=n∏p∣n(1−1p),\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right),φ(n)=np∣n∏​(1−p1​),

where the product is over distinct prime divisors. In particular, φ(p)=p−1\varphi(p)=p-1φ(p)=p−1 for a prime, and φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b)\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) when a,ba,ba,b are coprime.

Let

V={φ(n):n≥1},V(x)=#{v∈V:v≤x}.\mathcal V=\{\varphi(n):n\ge1\},\qquadV(x)=\#\{v\in\mathcal V:v\le x\}.V={φ(n):n≥1},V(x)=#{v∈V:v≤x}.

The symbol V\mathcal VV denotes the set of outputs, while V(x)V(x)V(x) counts them. The prime outputs alone show that V(x)V(x)V(x) is at least roughly x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx, but products of shifted primes contribute many additional values.

An asymptotic equivalent V(x)∼M(x)V(x)\sim M(x)V(x)∼M(x) means V(x)/M(x)→1V(x)/M(x)\to1V(x)/M(x)→1. This is stronger than V(x)≍M(x)V(x)\asymp M(x)V(x)≍M(x), which only places the ratio between two positive constants. A bounded but unknown multiplicative factor can still prevent a limiting ratio from being known.

All logarithms here are natural, and log⁡jx\log_j xlogj​x means the logarithm iterated jjj times. Thus log⁡2x=log⁡log⁡x\log_2 x=\log\log xlog2​x=loglogx, while log⁡3x=log⁡log⁡log⁡x\log_3 x=\log\log\log xlog3​x=logloglogx. Formulas involving several such logarithms are intended for sufficiently large xxx.

For a totient value vvv, define its least preimage by

ℓ(v)=min⁡{n≥1:φ(n)=v}.\ell(v)=\min\{n\ge1:\varphi(n)=v\}.ℓ(v)=min{n≥1:φ(n)=v}.

For example, ℓ(4)=5\ell(4)=5ℓ(4)=5. Counting distinct outputs, counting all preimages and locating the least preimage are three different problems; the manuscript addresses the first and gives an additional result on the third.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Pillai proved that totient values have density zero among the positive integers. Erdős sharpened upper bounds using the typical factorization of p−1p-1p−1, and his work on products of two shifted primes improved the elementary lower bound.

Erdős and Hall obtained a much larger lower-order factor and asked whether V(cx)/V(x)→cV(cx)/V(x)\to cV(cx)/V(x)→c for fixed c>1c>1c>1. Their 1976 paper is the source of this dilation question. Pomerance brought the upper bound to the same logarithmic scale; Maier and Pomerance then identified the leading constant in the exponent:

V(x)=xlog⁡xexp⁡ ⁣((C0+o(1))(log⁡3x)2),C0≈0.8178146.V(x)=\frac{x}{\log x}\exp\!\left((C_0+o(1))(\log_3x)^2\right),\qquad C_0\approx0.8178146.V(x)=logxx​exp((C0​+o(1))(log3​x)2),C0​≈0.8178146.

Ford’s 1998 work went much further, determining the count up to a bounded multiplicative factor and describing the prime-factor structure of typical preimages. The current manuscript uses the revised 2013 version of that paper as its structural input.

Ford also proved that a fixed multiplicative interval (x,cx](x,cx](x,cx] contains a number of totients comparable to V(x)V(x)V(x). This guarantees many outputs in that interval, but does not specify the limiting ratio or remove the bounded factor in the total count.

The remaining task is delicate because multiple prime factorizations can produce the same output. Approximating every factorization by a continuous volume can overcount. The new manuscript retains the short arithmetic tail exactly and controls collisions between the long prefixes before claiming an asymptotic for distinct values.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A scale with an arithmetic phase coefficient

The explicit main term uses constants defined by a positive recurrence. Put

aj=(j+1)log⁡(j+1)−jlog⁡j−1(j≥1),a_j=(j+1)\log(j+1)-j\log j-1\qquad(j\ge1),aj​=(j+1)log(j+1)−jlogj−1(j≥1),

and let ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1)ρ∈(0,1) be the unique solution of

∑j≥1ajρj=1.\sum_{j\ge1}a_j\rho^j=1.j≥1∑​aj​ρj=1.

Define

λ=log⁡(1/ρ),g0=1,gj=∑d=1jadgj−d.\lambda=\log(1/\rho),\qquadg_0=1,\qquad g_j=\sum_{d=1}^{j}a_dg_{j-d}.λ=log(1/ρ),g0​=1,gj​=d=1∑j​ad​gj−d​.

For large xxx, set

B=log⁡2x,m=⌊log⁡B−log⁡2Bλ⌋,θ=log⁡B−log⁡2Bλ−m,B=\log_2x,\qquadm=\left\lfloor\frac{\log B-\log_2B}{\lambda}\right\rfloor,\qquad\theta=\frac{\log B-\log_2B}{\lambda}-m,B=log2​x,m=⌊λlogB−log2​B​⌋,θ=λlogB−log2​B​−m,

so 0≤θ<10\le\theta<10≤θ<1, and put

Gm=Bmm!∏j=1mgj.G_m=\frac{B^m}{m!\prod_{j=1}^{m}g_j}.Gm​=m!∏j=1m​gj​Bm​.

Theorem 2.1 claims

V(x)∼xlog⁡xGmA(1;θ).\boxed{V(x)\sim\frac{x}{\log x}G_m A(1;\theta).}V(x)∼logxx​Gm​A(1;θ).​

The factor A(1;θ)A(1;\theta)A(1;θ) is positive and bounded above and away from zero. It is a function of a phase, not asserted to be a single constant. It is defined independently of V(x)V(x)V(x) as a uniform limit of explicit approximants AH(1;s)A_H(1;s)AH​(1;s) built from finite prime and integer data.

The notation “1” means that every tail value receives weight one. Section 6 below describes the construction. The coefficient is not defined tautologically by dividing the unknown count by its proposed scale.

Fixed dilation

The same theorem claims, for every fixed real c>0c>0c>0,

V(cx)V(x)⟶c.\frac{V(cx)}{V(x)}\longrightarrow c.V(x)V(cx)​⟶c.

This is called regular variation of index one. For example, (x,2x](x,2x](x,2x] contains asymptotically as many distinct totients as [1,x][1,x][1,x], even though the proportion of all integers that are totients tends to zero.

The manuscript proves this by comparing counts at common endpoint parameters. It does not infer the conclusion from an unproved continuity property of the phase coefficient. No continuity or other regularity of s↦A(1;s)s\mapsto A(1;s)s↦A(1;s) is asserted.

Where least preimages lie

For a fixed positive integer kkk, let

Nk(x)=#{v∈V:v≤x, kx<ℓ(v)≤(k+1)x}.N_k(x)=\#\{v\in\mathcal V:v\le x,\ kx<\ell(v)\le(k+1)x\}.Nk​(x)=#{v∈V:v≤x, kx<ℓ(v)≤(k+1)x}.

Define the bounded nonnegative weight

fk(r)=min⁡{1,(k+1)/r}−min⁡{1,k/r}.f_k(r)=\min\{1,(k+1)/r\}-\min\{1,k/r\}.fk​(r)=min{1,(k+1)/r}−min{1,k/r}.

Theorem 2.2 claims a corresponding weighted formula,

Nk(x)=xlog⁡xGm(A(fk;θ)+o(1)).N_k(x)=\frac{x}{\log x}G_m\bigl(A(f_k;\theta)+o(1)\bigr).Nk​(x)=logxx​Gm​(A(fk​;θ)+o(1)).

If there is even one totient ddd with ℓ(d)>kd\ell(d)>kdℓ(d)>kd, then A(fk;s)A(f_k;s)A(fk​;s) is uniformly positive and Nk(x)≍kV(x)N_k(x)\asymp_k V(x)Nk​(x)≍k​V(x). If there is no such seed, Nk(x)=0N_k(x)=0Nk​(x)=0 for every x>0x>0x>0. The positive alternative is established for k=1,2k=1,2k=1,2; the manuscript does not determine all larger kkk.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. Taken as stated, the theorem closes a longstanding gap between order-of-magnitude estimates and an asymptotic equivalent for the range of a fundamental arithmetic function. It also answers the Erdős–Hall fixed-dilation question.

The main term retains genuinely discrete arithmetic information. A continuous approximation captures most prime-factor geometry, but it cannot simply erase collisions among the smaller factors. The coefficient records these collisions through a finite union before taking a limit.

This is a substantial advance in the distribution of arithmetic-function values. Its scope is precise: it counts distinct totients and locates certain least preimages, without resolving all multiplicity or inverse-totient questions.

6. The main idea

Separate a long prime prefix from a short exact tail

Order the prime factors of a suitable preimage from largest to smallest. Ford’s structural estimates place their double logarithms in a region resembling a simplex, a higher-dimensional generalization of a triangle.

The manuscript splits this list twice. A long prefix is treated continuously by volume. A shorter collection of smaller primes, together with a smooth cofactor whose prime factors are bounded, is kept as exact arithmetic data. The two cuts are separated so the discarded part is small enough to absorb the tail’s complexity.

For a fixed tail cutoff HHH, the retained tail possibilities are finite and independent of xxx. The proof first lets xxx grow with HHH fixed, and only then lets HHH grow. Reversing that order would lose the finite-arithmetic interpretation.

Count outputs rather than descriptions

Different long prefixes might yield the same totient. The paper compares equations between products of shifted primes and shows that the total contribution of such prefix collisions is negligible. It uses a layered method descended from Maier–Pomerance and Ford; each sieve application involves only two or three linear forms even though the number of layers grows.

The structural coverage must also be strong enough for the least-preimage analysis: outside a negligible exceptional set, every relevant preimage has the required form. Finding one convenient preimage would not by itself control the least one.

After prefix collisions have been removed, different exact tails can still give the same value. They are deliberately not declared unique. Instead, all regions permitted by tails with the same totient are combined by taking their union. Inclusion–exclusion counts that union once.

What the coefficient records

A concrete probabilistic description makes the finite union easier to interpret. Fix a phase sss, set

αs=λeλs,γ=(∑j≥1jajρj)−1,\alpha_s=\lambda e^{\lambda s},\qquad\gamma=\left(\sum_{j\ge1}j a_j\rho^j\right)^{-1},αs​=λeλs,γ=(j≥1∑​jaj​ρj)−1,

and enumerate the permitted bounded tails η\etaη. Each tail is an integer w(η)w(\eta)w(η) expressed using a prescribed finite list of primes and a smooth cofactor. It has a totient d=φ(w(η))d=\varphi(w(\eta))d=φ(w(η)).

If the tail primes are indexed by l<Hl<Hl<H, their double logarithms vlv_lvl​ determine thresholds

D(h,η)=∑lah−lvl(h≥H).D(h,\eta)=\sum_l a_{h-l}v_l\qquad(h\ge H).D(h,η)=l∑​ah−l​vl​(h≥H).

The sums run over the retained tail indices. The manuscript’s explicit bounded inequalities specify which lists are permitted. The continuous prefix volume allowed by a tail is represented by an event

Eη=⋂h≥H{Eh≥γαsρhD(h,η)},E_\eta=\bigcap_{h\ge H}\left\{E_h\ge\frac{\gamma}{\alpha_s}\rho^hD(h,\eta)\right\},Eη​=h≥H⋂​{Eh​≥αs​γ​ρhD(h,η)},

where the EhE_hEh​ are independent exponential random variables of mean one. These auxiliary variables encode volumes; the theorem does not model prime factors as literally independent random variables.

The approximant AH(f;s)A_H(f;s)AH​(f;s) is a normalized sum over distinct tail totients ddd, with weight f(ℓ(d)/d)/df(\ell(d)/d)/df(ℓ(d)/d)/d, multiplied by the probability of the union of the events for all tails producing ddd. The normalization is

ρH(H−1)/2(γαs)H.\rho^{H(H-1)/2}\left(\frac{\gamma}{\alpha_s}\right)^H.ρH(H−1)/2(αs​γ​)H.

There are finitely many tails for each HHH. Intersections of their events use the maximum threshold at each coordinate, so exponential probabilities and finite inclusion–exclusion give an explicit formula with absolutely convergent series. The main coefficient uses f=1f=1f=1, requiring no least-preimage search. For weighted coefficients, a tail witness itself bounds the finite search for ℓ(d)\ell(d)ℓ(d).

Uniform convergence in the phase produces A(1;s)A(1;s)A(1;s) and the particular A(fk;s)A(f_k;s)A(fk​;s) needed above. Counting the largest prime supplies the factor x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx and the tail weight 1/d1/d1/d; normalized prefix volumes supply GmG_mGm​ and the remaining coefficient.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The coefficient is explicit through finite arithmetic approximants and a uniform limit. The theorem does not assert that it is constant, continuous or easy to evaluate efficiently. No numerical convergence rate for computing it is part of the headline statement.

The dilation factor ccc is fixed. The result does not automatically give uniform estimates for ccc depending on xxx, or asymptotics in short additive intervals.

Most importantly, uniqueness of the long prefix is not uniqueness of the whole preimage. Large fibers of φ\varphiφ, including those discussed in family 011, are compatible with this theorem and are not an input to it.

The question whether ℓ(d)/d\ell(d)/dℓ(d)/d is unbounded remains unresolved here. Equivalently, the least-preimage positive alternative is not established for every integer kkk. An asymptotic formula for the range does not settle all inverse problems for the function.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorems 2.1–2.2 give the main and weighted asymptotics. Section 2.2, especially equations (2.5)–(2.8), gives the complete finite-tail definition of the coefficient. Sections 4–5 control prefix collisions, Section 6 proves the limiting formula, and Section 7 treats least preimages.

The Erdős–Hall paper and Ford’s revised distribution paper linked in section 3 are the principal historical sources. The manuscript also cites Pillai, Erdős, Pomerance and Maier–Pomerance for the earlier bounds. Optional background on Euler’s totient function helps connect the product formula to its range.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An asymptotic formula for the number of totients (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Large prime gaps occur with positive frequency
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 026 · Number theory
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The primes become less frequent as numbers grow. Near a large number xxx, their average spacing is about log⁡x\log xlogx, where log⁡\loglog denotes the natural logarithm. Some consecutive primes are much closer together, while others are much farther apart. How frequently does a gap exceed, say, ten times the local average?

Write pnp_npn​ for the nnnth prime. The manuscript claims that, for every fixed positive number CCC, a positive proportion of the gaps satisfy

pn+1−pn>Clog⁡pn.p_{n+1}-p_n>C\log p_n.pn+1​−pn​>Clogpn​.

The proportion may depend on CCC and become very small as CCC grows. Nevertheless, it stays bounded away from zero as we inspect longer initial segments of the prime sequence.

There are two different questions here. One asks whether an exceptionally large gap exists somewhere. The other asks whether large gaps constitute a positive fraction of all gaps. A single enormous desert between primes answers the first question but contributes only one gap to the second. The new claim concerns the second question, with each prime gap counted once.

2. Background and essential definitions

The prime-counting function π(x)\pi(x)π(x) counts primes at most xxx. The prime number theorem says

π(x)∼xlog⁡x,\pi(x)\sim\frac{x}{\log x},π(x)∼logxx​,

meaning that the ratio of the two sides tends to one. Consequently, the average gap on a large scale is logarithmic. Define the normalized gap by

gn=pn+1−pnlog⁡pn.g_n=\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}.gn​=logpn​pn+1​−pn​​.

Dividing by the local average makes gaps at different heights comparable.

A set AAA of positive integers has positive lower asymptotic density if

lim inf⁡N→∞∣A∩{1,…,N}∣N>0.\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N}>0.N→∞liminf​N∣A∩{1,…,N}∣​>0.

The vertical bars count elements. This condition says that some fixed positive fraction works for every sufficiently large cutoff. It is stronger than obtaining a positive fraction along a selected sequence of cutoffs. It does not assert that the fraction has a limit.

Two ways to sample empty space

One can choose a prime and examine the gap following it. Alternatively, one can choose an integer mmm and ask whether (m,m+h](m,m+h](m,m+h] contains a prime. These experiments weight the same prime desert differently. A gap of length DDD may contain roughly D−hD-hD−h starting points of empty intervals of length hhh, but it is still only one consecutive prime gap.

This distinction is central. A statement that many integer-start intervals are empty does not automatically imply that many prime-start gaps are large. The latter needs control of how many interval starts can correspond to the same gap.

A probabilistic model in which primes appear independently with probability roughly 1/log⁡x1/\log x1/logx suggests an exponential tail for normalized gaps. Such a model is useful intuition, not a theorem about the primes. The manuscript establishes positivity of every fixed tail, without identifying that tail with the model’s value.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Westzynthius proved in 1931 that normalized prime gaps are unbounded. Erdős and Rankin subsequently improved quantitative lower bounds for exceptionally large gaps. More recently, Ford, Green, Konyagin and Tao, and independently Maynard, strengthened these constructions; their joint work gave further improvements. These are developments in the size of the largest gaps, rather than a complete description of how often large gaps occur.

The frequency problem needs different care. Bazzanella, Languasco and Zaccagnini’s Prime numbers in logarithmic intervals explicitly distinguishes integer-start intervals from prime-start gaps. As the new manuscript records, their Theorem 5 gives positive prime-start proportions for fixed thresholds below approximately 0.5790380.5790380.579038 times the average spacing. Other conclusions in their work concern integer-start intervals and therefore cannot simply be read as prime-gap proportions above the average.

There are also much more detailed conditional predictions. Gallagher obtained Poisson statistics for prime counts in logarithmic intervals from a sufficiently uniform Hardy–Littlewood prime-tuple hypothesis. Roughly, that hypothesis estimates how often several specified integer shifts are simultaneously prime. Uniformity matters because the shifts and the intervals being counted vary. More recent conditional work extends the parameter ranges, but still uses strong assumptions about prime tuples.

The manuscript’s analytic ancestry includes the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem, which controls prime distribution in arithmetic progressions after averaging over the moduli. It also builds on Goldston–Yıldırım’s correlations of divisor sums and Maynard’s smooth multidimensional sieve weights. A sieve weight is a numerical function designed to emphasize integers with chosen divisibility properties. Its usefulness comes from having averages that can be evaluated even when the corresponding prime pattern cannot be counted directly.

The proposed advance combines these ideas to handle arbitrary fixed CCC, unconditionally as stated, in the prime-start counting measure. It also addresses a 1962 question of Erdős and Prachar concerning the sequence pn/np_n/npn​/n.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

There is one manuscript in this family. Its main theorem states that for every fixed real C>0C>0C>0, there are constants c(C)>0c(C)>0c(C)>0 and N0(C)N_0(C)N0​(C) such that

#{1≤n≤N:pn+1−pn>Clog⁡pn}≥c(C)N(N≥N0(C)).\#\{1\le n\le N:p_{n+1}-p_n>C\log p_n\}\ge c(C)N\qquad(N\ge N_0(C)).#{1≤n≤N:pn+1​−pn​>Clogpn​}≥c(C)N(N≥N0​(C)).

Here #\## means the number of indices satisfying the condition. Both constants may depend on CCC. In particular, the threshold is fixed before NNN tends to infinity.

The theorem gives ordinary lower density among prime indices. It requires neither an average over cutoffs nor a logarithmic weighting of indices. It is also not merely an assertion of infinitely many examples.

An application to the ratio of a prime to its index

The manuscript deduces that

{n:pn+1n+1>pnn}\left\{n:\frac{p_{n+1}}{n+1}>\frac{p_n}{n}\right\}{n:n+1pn+1​​>npn​​}

has positive lower density. To understand the connection, multiply by n(n+1)n(n+1)n(n+1). The displayed inequality is equivalent to

pn+1−pn>pnn.p_{n+1}-p_n>\frac{p_n}{n}.pn+1​−pn​>npn​​.

The prime number theorem gives pn/n∼log⁡pnp_n/n\sim\log p_npn​/n∼logpn​. Thus a gap exceeding twice log⁡pn\log p_nlogpn​ eventually suffices. The main theorem with C=2C=2C=2 supplies a positive proportion of such indices. This is the stated affirmative answer to the Erdős–Prachar question.

Although pn/np_n/npn​/n has an overall tendency to grow, that broad asymptotic behavior alone would not imply a positive proportion of individual increases. The corollary concerns the local steps of this sequence.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisionally. The claim is a substantial advance in the distribution of prime gaps: it reaches every fixed multiple of the average spacing with a frequency conclusion, and resolves a specific longstanding question. The rating also reflects its limits. It does not determine the full gap distribution or settle the most precise conjectures about extreme gaps.

The result would sharpen the qualitative picture of prime irregularity. Arbitrarily large normalized gaps would be accompanied by a stronger statement: for any fixed level, exceeding that level is a recurring phenomenon with positive lower frequency.

The method also addresses a general counting problem. A weighted or geometric argument can count many witnesses while repeatedly witnessing the same object. Here the manuscript introduces a nearby prime as an anchor, giving a uniform bound on that repetition. That counting step makes the sieve construction relevant to the desired statistic.

6. The main idea

Put a prime immediately before an empty block

Choose a fixed λ>C\lambda>Cλ>C, and let h=⌊λlog⁡X⌋h=\lfloor\lambda\log X\rfloorh=⌊λlogX⌋. For integers mmm between XXX and 2X2X2X, consider two adjacent intervals:

Jm=(m,m+h],Im=(m+h,m+2h].J_m=(m,m+h],\qquad I_m=(m+h,m+2h].Jm​=(m,m+h],Im​=(m+h,m+2h].

The target is a prime in JmJ_mJm​ and no primes in ImI_mIm​. If ppp is the last prime in the first interval, its successor lies beyond the second interval, so the gap after ppp exceeds hhh.

Crucially, a fixed prime ppp can be selected by at most hhh different starting integers mmm, since m<p≤m+hm<p\le m+hm<p≤m+h. This bound does not grow with the length of the actual prime gap. Therefore δX\delta XδX successful interval starts yield at least δX/h\delta X/hδX/h distinct prime gaps, where δ>0\delta>0δ>0. Since hhh is logarithmic, this is the same order of magnitude as the number of primes in the region.

Build a weight with unequal behavior in adjacent intervals

The manuscript constructs nonnegative weights WX(m)W_X(m)WX​(m). Under these weights, the first interval retains substantial prime mass, while the expected prime count in the second can be made arbitrarily small. The weights are normalized to have average tending to one.

Two second-moment controls serve different purposes. One prevents the first interval’s detected prime mass from concentrating on too little weighted mass. The other bounds the average of WX(m)2W_X(m)^2WX​(m)2, preventing the useful weighted mass from concentrating on too few ordinary integers. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality then converts the weighted statements into a positive ordinary proportion of successful starts.

The order of choices matters: the constant controlling prime detection in the first interval is independent of how strongly primes are suppressed in the second. The bound for the weights’ own second moment can depend on that suppression. Everything is fixed before XXX grows.

Obtain suppression by cancellation inside a square

A nonnegative weight cannot cancel directly. Instead, the paper forms a signed sum of smooth divisor sums and then squares it. Each divisor sum corresponds to a set of shifts in the second interval. Different set sizes act like different dimensions of the construction.

The chosen test functions make distinct shift sets orthogonal in an unmarked average: their cross terms disappear in the limiting formula. If one marks a particular shift as prime, a support restriction forces its divisor coordinate to be one. Removing that coordinate couples terms whose dimensions differ by one. Alternating coefficients make those neighboring contributions nearly cancel.

Thus the square retains positive total mass while its interaction with primes in the second interval is small. Smooth divisor correlations, averaged prime distribution and averages of the prime-tuple singular series evaluate the required moments. The singular series records compatibility with divisibility conditions at each prime. The manuscript keeps all dimensions and test functions fixed, proving the uniform estimates needed to sum over the shifts.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem gives a positive lower bound depending on each fixed CCC. It does not supply a sharp expression for that bound, establish a limiting gap distribution, or give the exponential tail suggested by an independent random model.

It does not permit replacing CCC by an arbitrary function growing with NNN. Results on the largest prime gap investigate a different regime and remain relevant independently.

The distinction between lower density and density also remains: the proportions are bounded away from zero eventually, but need not be shown to converge. Likewise, the corollary does not identify the exact proportion of indices where pn/np_n/npn​/n increases.

All conclusions here report the manuscript’s claims. The central conceptual gain is the conversion from empty intervals to distinct consecutive gaps with controlled multiplicity; the resulting assertion is stronger than an empty-interval frequency statement alone.

8. Sources and further reading

The source manuscript below contains the precise weight proposition, its moment identities and the passage to lower density in prime indices.

For the history of extreme gaps, see Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao, Long gaps between primes. For the divisor-sum method, see Goldston and Yıldırım, Small gaps between primes I, and Maynard, Small gaps between primes. These primary sources explain why related sieve technology can address quite different statistics.

The bibliography of M1 identifies the original Westzynthius, Erdős–Rankin, Erdős–Prachar, Gallagher and Bazzanella–Languasco–Zaccagnini papers. Its introduction also separates their counting measures and hypotheses, which is essential when comparing the results.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Positive lower density of large prime gaps (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Short Egyptian fractions and doubly exponential families
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 025 · Number theory
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An Egyptian fraction writes a positive rational number as a sum of distinct reciprocals of positive integers. For example,

23=12+16,1=12+13+16.\frac23=\frac12+\frac16,\qquad1=\frac12+\frac13+\frac16.32​=21​+61​,1=21​+31​+61​.

Every positive rational number has such an expansion, but how many terms are needed in the worst case? If the denominator of the original fraction is bbb, can every numerator 1≤a<b1\le a<b1≤a<b be handled using only a constant multiple of log⁡log⁡b\log\log bloglogb terms?

Family 025 claims this conjecture of Erdős. It also derives two striking consequences: the number of distinct-term expansions of one grows doubly exponentially with the allowed exact length, and every integer below a doubly exponential threshold can occur as an exact denominator in some expansion of that length.

The length is optimized without any prescribed upper bound on the new denominators. That tradeoff is essential to understanding the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

A unit fraction has numerator one. For integers 1≤a<b1\le a<b1≤a<b, define N(a,b)N(a,b)N(a,b) to be the least kkk for which

ab=1n1+⋯+1nk,2≤n1<⋯<nk.\frac ab=\frac1{n_1}+\cdots+\frac1{n_k},\qquad 2\le n_1<\cdots<n_k.ba​=n1​1​+⋯+nk​1​,2≤n1​<⋯<nk​.

The denominators are positive integers and must be distinct. They are written in increasing order so that permuting terms does not produce a new representation. The original fraction need not be reduced.

The worst numerator at denominator bbb is measured by

N(b)=max⁡1≤a<bN(a,b).N(b)=\max_{1\le a<b}N(a,b).N(b)=1≤a<bmax​N(a,b).

This is a maximum of minimum lengths. It does not say every fraction needs that many terms: N(1,b)=1N(1,b)=1N(1,b)=1 for all b≥2b\ge2b≥2.

The greedy algorithm repeatedly subtracts the largest unit fraction no greater than the current remainder. If the remainder is a/ba/ba/b, it chooses denominator ⌈b/a⌉\lceil b/a\rceil⌈b/a⌉. This proves existence because the numerator of the new remainder decreases after reduction, but existence alone does not supply the desired uniform length bound.

For expansions of one, let

F(k)=#{(n1,…,nk):1≤n1<⋯<nk, ∑i=1k1ni=1}.F(k)=\#\left\{(n_1,\ldots,n_k):1\le n_1<\cdots<n_k,\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac1{n_i}=1\right\}.F(k)=#{(n1​,…,nk​):1≤n1​<⋯<nk​, i=1∑k​ni​1​=1}.

The length is exactly kkk. For k>1k>1k>1, no denominator can be one, since its reciprocal already accounts for the whole sum.

Let DkD_kDk​ be the set of integers m≥2m\ge2m≥2 occurring as a denominator in at least one such expansion, and define

v(k)=min⁡({2,3,…}∖Dk).v(k)=\min\bigl(\{2,3,\ldots\}\setminus D_k\bigr).v(k)=min({2,3,…}∖Dk​).

Each m∈Dkm\in D_km∈Dk​ may use a different expansion. The statement that every m<v(k)m<v(k)m<v(k) occurs does not mean one expansion contains all those denominators.

“Doubly exponential in kkk” means growth comparable on the double-logarithmic scale: log⁡log⁡F(k)\log\log F(k)loglogF(k) or log⁡log⁡v(k)\log\log v(k)loglogv(k) is bounded above and below by positive multiples of kkk. It is stronger than ordinary exponential growth and does not specify one exact exponential base.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The representation itself is ancient, but the modern problem concerns uniform bounds. Nakayama studied arithmetic criteria for short expansions. In 1950, Erdős improved a bound reported from de Bruijn to order log⁡b/log⁡log⁡b\log b/\log\log blogb/loglogb, proposed the O(log⁡log⁡b)O(\log\log b)O(loglogb) upper bound, and proved a matching lower order already using the numerator b−1b-1b−1.

Vose’s 1985 paper improved the uniform upper bound to order log⁡b\sqrt{\log b}logb​. The double-logarithmic scale remained the conjectural target. The new manuscript’s lower bound is classical; its claimed advance is the matching upper bound for every numerator and every sufficiently large denominator.

A related problem restricts denominator sizes as well as length. Tenenbaum and Yokota obtained a length at most (1+ε)log⁡b/log⁡log⁡b(1+\varepsilon)\log b/\log\log b(1+ε)logb/loglogb, for fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and large bbb, while keeping every denominator at most 4b(log⁡b)2log⁡log⁡b4b(\log b)^2\log\log b4b(logb)2loglogb. The present theorem optimizes only length and should not be read as improving both constraints simultaneously.

Erdős and Graham also asked how many expansions of one have a given length, and which denominators can appear. Konyagin obtained a lower bound for the count whose double logarithm has order k/log⁡kk/\log kk/logk. Elsholtz obtained this order even with specified congruence restrictions on denominators. Elsholtz–Planitzer established an upper bound with double logarithm O(k)O(k)O(k), including a setting that allows repetitions.

For prescribed denominators, van Doorn and Tang proved v(k)≥exp⁡(ck2)v(k)\ge\exp(ck^2)v(k)≥exp(ck2) and developed operations that increase the length while preserving an exact chosen denominator. Their paper also anticipates the connection between uniform short expansions and a double-exponential threshold. Family 025 supplies the stronger length theorem and the required denominator-avoidance arguments.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 states that absolute constants c1,c2>0c_1,c_2>0c1​,c2​>0 exist such that, for all sufficiently large integers bbb,

c1log⁡log⁡b≤N(b)≤c2log⁡log⁡b.\boxed{c_1\log\log b\le N(b)\le c_2\log\log b.}c1​loglogb≤N(b)≤c2​loglogb.​

The upper bound applies to every integer numerator 1≤a<b1\le a<b1≤a<b. The constants do not depend on that numerator or denominator. No upper bound on the resulting nin_ini​ is prescribed.

Corollary 1.2 claims absolute constants c,C>0c,C>0c,C>0 with

ck≤log⁡log⁡F(k)≤Ckck\le\log\log F(k)\le Ckck≤loglogF(k)≤Ck

for every sufficiently large integer kkk. In particular, the conclusion concerns all sufficiently large exact lengths, not merely an infinite subsequence of lengths.

Corollary 1.3 claims

exp⁡(exp⁡(k/600))≤v(k)≤1+k2k−1\exp(\exp(k/600))\le v(k)\le1+k^{2^{k-1}}exp(exp(k/600))≤v(k)≤1+k2k−1

for sufficiently large kkk, and gives the sharper slope bounds

log⁡2257≤lim inf⁡k→∞log⁡log⁡v(k)k≤lim sup⁡k→∞log⁡log⁡v(k)k≤log⁡2.\frac{\log2}{257}\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\log\log v(k)}k\le\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{\log\log v(k)}k\le\log2.257log2​≤k→∞liminf​kloglogv(k)​≤k→∞limsup​kloglogv(k)​≤log2.

Equivalently, every fixed c<log⁡2/257c<\log2/257c<log2/257 eventually gives v(k)≥exp⁡(exp⁡(ck))v(k)\ge\exp(\exp(ck))v(k)≥exp(exp(ck)). These inequalities determine the double-logarithmic order, not an exact asymptotic coefficient. The convenient elementary upper bound is not presented as the sharpest available public upper estimate.

The prescribed-denominator conclusion retains the exact term 1/m1/m1/m. Merely keeping a denominator divisible by mmm would not satisfy it. The counting consequence needs a weaker divisibility feature, so the two corollaries require different constructions.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 3/5. Taken as stated, the result reaches the optimal order in a longstanding uniform Egyptian-fraction problem. Its elementary formulation conceals a difficult demand: no numerator may be left in an exceptional set.

The consequences quantify how much flexibility remains among exact-length expansions of one. Short representations enable both an enormous number of choices and inclusion of every moderately sized prescribed denominator, on a doubly exponential scale.

The advance is substantial within additive and combinatorial number theory. It does not settle all famous fixed-length problems, such as asking for a particular three-term pattern for every denominator, and it makes no simultaneous claim that the new denominators are small.

6. The main idea

First solve almost every numerator over a useful denominator

Set S=log⁡bS=\log bS=logb. A short greedy prefix either finishes the expansion or leaves a remainder A/CA/CA/C, with A≤bA\le bA≤b and CCC in a controlled exponential range in SSS.

The manuscript then constructs an auxiliary integer MMM, also exponential in SSS, for which a dense set of numerators uuu gives short expansions of u/(MC)u/(MC)u/(MC). “Dense” here is strong enough that a suitable multiple gAMgAMgAM can be written as the sum of two good numerators. Adding their expansions and dividing every term by ggg produces an expansion of the original remainder A/CA/CA/C.

This is the passage from almost every numerator in a carefully designed interval to every original numerator. A probabilistic or density result alone would not establish the theorem without this final step.

Use divisors to reduce the numerator

For a divisor t∣Mt\mid Mt∣M, choose

z=⌈Qtu⌉,h=uz−Qt,z=\left\lceil\frac{Qt}{u}\right\rceil,\qquad h=uz-Qt,z=⌈uQt​⌉,h=uz−Qt,

where QQQ is the current denominator factor. Then

uMQ=1(M/t)z+1zhMQ.\frac{u}{MQ}=\frac1{(M/t)z}+\frac1z\frac{h}{MQ}.MQu​=(M/t)z1​+z1​MQh​.

One unit fraction has been removed, and the residual numerator is hhh, a small nonnegative residue when ttt is chosen well. The construction selects MMM so that many of its divisors produce useful residues for most numerators at each scale.

Deterministic products of distinct primes handle larger numerator ranges, while independent random products supply estimates at smaller ranges. The paper descends through O(log⁡S)O(\log S)O(logS) ranges, changing the denominator factor from CCC to one when appropriate. At the bottom, an all-numerator reduction and a binary expansion finish the process.

Keep exceptional sets from accumulating

Each stage may have bad numerators. It is not enough that each bad set is small separately: many earlier numerators could map into the same bad set later.

For fixed t,ht,ht,h, a predecessor uuu must divide Qt+hQt+hQt+h. The manuscript proves a uniform moment bound for the number of small divisors in shifted intervals. Hölder’s inequality then controls how many predecessors a small exceptional set can have. This keeps the exceptional proportion small across the whole descent.

Intermediate lists can repeat denominators. A separate replacement argument removes repetitions while preserving the number of terms when the sum is below one. The proof uses identities replacing two equal reciprocals by two different ones and a finiteness argument to ensure termination. The expansion-of-one case receives its own treatment.

Produce many expansions, or preserve one exact denominator

For the counting corollary, short expansions are arranged to contain a denominator with many prime factors. Splitting its reciprocal using its divisors creates many distinct choices. An injective length-increasing operation extends the count to every sufficiently large prescribed length.

For the marker problem, reserve 1/m1/m1/m first and construct the rest while avoiding that denominator. A greedy prefix is chosen so the remaining positive sum is smaller than every reserved reciprocal. Any positive unit-fraction expansion of that remainder must then use larger denominators, so it cannot collide with the reserved terms.

A separate padding lemma increases the length without losing 1/m1/m1/m. A direct quantitative construction gives the coefficient 257/log⁡2257/\log2257/log2 in the sufficient length bound, hence the explicit lower slope for log⁡log⁡v(k)\log\log v(k)loglogv(k). It does not require making the unspecified constant in the general length theorem explicit.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The optimal-order statement concerns N(b)N(b)N(b), the worst numerator. Many individual fractions have much shorter expansions. It does not claim that each numerator needs Θ(log⁡log⁡b)\Theta(\log\log b)Θ(loglogb) terms.

The denominators in the expansion can be large, and the theorem gives no efficient algorithm or practical runtime bound for finding a shortest expansion. Controlling length and denominator size simultaneously remains a separate optimization problem.

The count F(k)F(k)F(k) uses distinct positive denominators and exact length. The bounds do not identify a limiting value of log⁡log⁡F(k)/k\log\log F(k)/kloglogF(k)/k. Likewise, the lower and upper slopes for v(k)v(k)v(k) are not equal, so its precise doubly exponential growth is still undetermined.

Finally, denominator coverage is a collection of existence statements, one for each mmm. It does not demand that a single kkk-term representation contain all integers below the threshold.

8. Sources and further reading

Theorem 1.1 gives the uniform length bound, and Corollaries 1.2–1.3 give the counting and prescribed-denominator consequences. Sections 2–5 explain the dense-family reduction, divisor moments and multiscale descent. Sections 6–8 distinguish counting, exact-marker preservation and the quantitative marker construction.

Vose and van Doorn–Tang are linked in section 3. The manuscript’s bibliography identifies Erdős’s original theorem and conjecture, Tenenbaum–Yokota’s simultaneous denominator bounds, and the earlier counting results. Optional background on Egyptian fractions gives further examples and classical algorithms.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Short Egyptian fractions (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Integral points throughout character varieties of curves
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 027 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Imagine carrying a vector around loops on a surface. After returning to its starting point, the vector may have changed by a matrix. A compatible collection of these matrices is called a representation of the surface’s fundamental group. Such representations vary in families, described by algebraic spaces called character varieties.

These spaces are usually studied over the complex numbers. The arithmetic question is whether they contain many points whose coordinates are algebraic integers. More precisely, can one choose a single number field so that integral points over its ring of integers are dense in the algebraic sense?

The manuscript claims an affirmative answer for the determinant-one character varieties of all smooth complex algebraic curves, in every rank. It also allows prescribed behavior around missing points of the curve, including exact nondiagonalizable matrix types. The word “single” matters: the number field is fixed for the whole space, rather than enlarged separately for every point.

2. Background and essential definitions

From loops to matrices

The fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X)π1​(X) records loops in a connected space XXX, with multiplication given by following one loop after another. A rank-rrr representation is a homomorphism

ρ:π1(X)⟶SL⁡r(C),\rho:\pi_1(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{SL}_r(\mathbb C),ρ:π1​(X)⟶SLr​(C),

where SL⁡r\operatorname{SL}_rSLr​ is the group of rrr-by-rrr matrices with determinant one. Changing the basis of the vector space conjugates all matrices simultaneously, so it should not change the represented object.

For a curve of genus ggg with sss punctures, generators can be chosen with relation

∏j=1g[Aj,Bj]∏i=1sMi=I,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1.\prod_{j=1}^{g}[A_j,B_j]\prod_{i=1}^{s}M_i=I,\qquad [A,B]=ABA^{-1}B^{-1}.j=1∏g​[Aj​,Bj​]i=1∏s​Mi​=I,[A,B]=ABA−1B−1.

The matrices MiM_iMi​ describe travel around the punctures and are called boundary monodromies. The relation says that these journeys fit together globally.

A representation is semisimple if it is a direct sum of irreducible representations. This condition concerns all the matrices together. It does not mean that each individual matrix is diagonalizable: an irreducible group action can contain nontrivial unipotent matrices.

The character variety Mr(X)M_r(X)Mr​(X) parametrizes semisimple representations up to isomorphism. Algebraically, one first writes the matrix relations as polynomial equations, then takes the ring of polynomial functions invariant under simultaneous conjugation. This produces a natural affine model over Z\mathbb ZZ, even when the original complex curve itself is not defined over a number field.

Integral and dense have specific meanings

A number field LLL is a finite extension of Q\mathbb QQ. Its ring of integers OL\mathcal O_LOL​ consists of elements satisfying monic polynomial equations with integer coefficients. For example, 2\sqrt22​ is integral, whereas 1/21/21/2 is not.

An integral point of the character variety means a point defined over this full ring OL\mathcal O_LOL​. One is not allowed to invert an arbitrary finite list of primes. A set is Zariski dense if no additional polynomial equations cut out a proper closed subset containing it. This is algebraic density, not closeness in ordinary Euclidean distance.

Finally, a matrix is quasi-unipotent if all its eigenvalues are roots of unity. Prescribing its conjugacy class specifies both those eigenvalues and its Jordan block sizes. The matrices III and (1101)\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}(10​11​) have the same characteristic polynomial in rank two but belong to different conjugacy classes. Exact boundary conditions distinguish them.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The arithmetic of local systems developed partly through questions about rigidity. A local system is another way of describing a representation: it assigns vector spaces locally, with compatible transport along paths. A rigid local system has no appropriate nontrivial deformations. Simpson conjectured integrality for rigid irreducible local systems in the projective setting.

Esnault and Groechenig proved integrality for cohomologically rigid irreducible local systems with finite determinant and quasi-unipotent boundary monodromy. Cohomological rigidity is a precise condition on infinitesimal deformations. This is a theorem about individual rigid objects, not density in large deformable families.

De Jong and Esnault established a different existence result without rigidity. Under the relevant determinant and boundary assumptions, the existence of a complex irreducible local system implies existence of integral irreducible systems for each prime ℓ\ellℓ, in the ℓ\ellℓ-adic setting. Such prime-by-prime existence is distinct from obtaining a Zariski-dense collection over the full ring of integers of one number field.

Litt formulated questions about potential integral density, explicitly asking whether a single field suffices. Coccia and Litt subsequently proved full-ring potential integral density in rank two for SL⁡2\operatorname{SL}_2SL2​ and PGL⁡2\operatorname{PGL}_2PGL2​ on a broad class of smooth varieties. Their surface results permit arbitrary algebraic-integer boundary traces and an extension of degree at most four over the trace field. The manuscript explains that their results also imply the ambient-integral exact-class conclusion in rank two.

The new claim extends the curve theorem to every rank, including nongeneric and nonsemisimple quasi-unipotent boundary data. It does not subsume every feature of the earlier rank-two theorem: arbitrary algebraic-integer traces are more general than the quasi-unipotent boundary condition used here.

Geometric predecessors also matter. Mellit and Su obtained decompositions of character varieties with suitable generic semisimple boundary conditions into tractable pieces. Such complex geometry does not by itself guarantee full-ring integral points: parametrizations may require denominators or may fail at special Jordan types. The new argument works with integral gluing data throughout its rank reduction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let XXX be any smooth connected complex algebraic curve, and let r≥1r\ge1r≥1. Prescribe quasi-unipotent conjugacy classes C1,…,CsC_1,\ldots,C_sC1​,…,Cs​ at its punctures. Let YYY be the locus in the complex character variety whose semisimple representations have precisely those boundary classes.

Choose a number field K⊂CK\subset\mathbb CK⊂C containing the boundary eigenvalues. The main theorem claims that some finite extension L/KL/KL/K satisfies

Mr(X)(OL)∩Y(C)is Zariski dense in Y.M_r(X)(\mathcal O_L)\cap Y(\mathbb C)\quad\text{is Zariski dense in }Y.Mr​(X)(OL​)∩Y(C)is Zariski dense in Y.

The conclusion holds on every irreducible component, with the same field LLL for all components. There is no restriction on genus or Jordan block shape. Empty loci contribute no existence assertion.

The theorem also allows prescribing only boundary characteristic polynomials, provided their roots are roots of unity. Without any boundary restrictions, it asserts potential integral density for the entire character variety. For nonprojective curves with no boundary conditions, density already holds over Z\mathbb ZZ, because their fundamental groups are free and integral determinant-one matrices are Zariski dense.

For the prescribed-boundary and projective cases, the manuscript gives a possible field explicitly in terms of an intermediate extension:

F=K(2,ζpq),L=F(ζr,{u1/r:u∈OF×}),F=K(\sqrt2,\zeta_{pq}),\qquadL=F\bigl(\zeta_r,\{u^{1/r}:u\in\mathcal O_F^\times\}\bigr),F=K(2​,ζpq​),L=F(ζr​,{u1/r:u∈OF×​}),

where p,q>rp,q>rp,q>r are distinct primes, ζm\zeta_mζm​ denotes a primitive mmmth root of unity, and OF×\mathcal O_F^\timesOF×​ is the group of units. Although the notation involves all units, this extension is finite because the unit group is finitely generated. In the projective case one starts with K=QK=\mathbb QK=Q.

Where exactness is imposed

Integrality is measured in the ambient character variety. Exact Jordan conditions are imposed on the corresponding complex semisimple representation. The theorem does not require the same Jordan type to survive reduction modulo every prime ideal of OL\mathcal O_LOL​. Such a requirement would define a different arithmetic problem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisionally. The claimed theorem settles an all-rank curve case of a broad arithmetic question about moduli spaces. Its strength lies in combining a fixed number field, the full ring of integers, every component and exact boundary data.

The statement connects two seemingly different kinds of structure. Character varieties encode the topology of surfaces through matrix equations. Integral points impose arithmetic restrictions at all finite primes simultaneously. Density says these restrictions still leave enough points to escape every proper algebraic subvariety of each component.

The scope also explains the rating’s limits. This is not a solution for character varieties of arbitrary higher-dimensional varieties in every rank, nor for every reductive group or arbitrary boundary eigenvalues. The reusable contribution is a mechanism for carrying integral density through rank reduction and gluing.

6. The main idea

Replace a difficult representation by smaller pieces

The construction initially uses general invertible matrices, GL⁡r\operatorname{GL}_rGLr​, because subspaces, quotients and direct sums are easier to handle without fixing determinants. A matrix with a specified Jordan type preserves a flag: a chain of nested subspaces. On suitable successive quotients it acts by scalar roots of unity.

The paper turns a surface with such boundary data into a diagram of surfaces connected by flags and identifications of their quotient spaces. Attaching disks carrying scalar local systems turns boundary behavior into gluing instructions. The argument then inducts on the largest rank present in the diagram.

A maximal-rank surface with boundary is cut into disks. On a disk, a selected proper subspace and its quotient have smaller ranks. The missing extension data are recovered by choices of linear maps. Comparing and rearranging flags lets the pieces fit together, including cases with repeated eigenvalues or nonregular Jordan forms.

The arithmetic difficulty is that a convenient complex splitting need not exist integrally. The manuscript carries free graded modules and integral splittings as part of the data. This allows reconstruction over the full number ring, with no unannounced inversion of primes.

Deal with closed surfaces

Closed surfaces have no boundary from which to start the same reduction. The paper cuts along a nonseparating circle and first fixes a convenient spectrum for its monodromy. A Dehn twist is the operation of cutting along a circle, rotating one side and regluing; it acts on surface representations by explicit transformations of their matrices.

Powers of these twists preserve the integral construction while enlarging its algebraic closure. At a suitable smooth representation, the resulting torus motions vary the spectrum in all needed directions. An irreducibility statement for the relevant twisted surface equation then extends density across the closed-surface case. The paper obtains that statement through finite-group character counts and the Lang–Weil link between finite-field point counts and algebraic geometry.

Restore determinants and select the exact classes

The constructed handle determinants are units in OF\mathcal O_FOF​. Adjoining their rrrth roots in the single field LLL permits scalar corrections that make every determinant one. Finite generation of the unit group makes this correction uniform across the construction.

Finally the argument passes from representations to their characters. This order matters because semisimplifying a representation can shrink Jordan blocks of its boundary matrices. Exact classes are therefore selected on the quotient by excluding the closed loci where a required matrix rank drops. Density in the appropriate closed locus then gives density in the desired open part, component by component.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Potential integral density allows a finite extension of the ground field. It is not an assertion of density over Z\mathbb ZZ in every case, and it does not provide a count of points of bounded height.

The fixed boundary eigenvalues must be roots of unity. The all-rank theorem does not cover arbitrary integral eigenvalues merely because earlier rank-two results permit more general traces. Likewise, exact complex Jordan forms should not be confused with preservation of those forms in all finite-characteristic reductions.

Zariski density need not imply Euclidean density or an effective procedure for finding a nearby integral point. The field construction supplies a common arithmetic setting, rather than a sharp bound for the smallest field or the heights of its points.

The higher-dimensional, higher-rank density question remains outside this manuscript. Extending the integral rank-reduction method beyond surface fundamental groups would require additional structure.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the integral model, the exact-class convention and the common field extension. For the preceding rank-two theorem, see Coccia and Litt, Density of integral points in the Betti moduli of quasi-projective varieties. Litt’s Motives, mapping class groups, and monodromy places the density question in a broader setting.

The primary references for the earlier rigidity and existence results are Esnault–Groechenig, Cohomologically rigid local systems and integrality (2018), and de Jong–Esnault, Integrality of the Betti moduli space (2024), both listed in M1. Their conclusions use different hypotheses and notions of arithmetic existence from the density theorem explained here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Integral points on character varieties of curves (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The Gaussian moat: why bounded steps cannot go forever
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 028 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

On the ordinary number line, arbitrarily long gaps between primes prevent an infinite journey through distinct primes with a fixed maximum step length. In the plane, a traveler can go around an obstacle. Does that extra freedom allow an endless walk through the Gaussian primes?

Gaussian integers are complex numbers a+bia+bia+bi with integer coordinates. Their prime elements form a scattered set of points in the plane. The Gaussian moat problem asks whether one can visit infinitely many distinct such primes while keeping every step below some fixed distance.

The manuscript claims that the answer is no, in a stronger uniform form: for each fixed step bound, every connected group of reachable Gaussian primes contains at most a certain finite number of vertices. The bound works everywhere in the plane, including on the coordinate axes. It is not given explicitly.

The challenge is genuinely two-dimensional. Finding enormous empty disks does not suffice: a path might travel around every one of them. The proposed argument instead constructs a finite collection of divisibility restrictions that collectively prevent any infinite bounded-step route.

2. Background and essential definitions

The Gaussian integers form the ring

Z[i]={a+bi:a,b∈Z},i2=−1.\mathbb Z[i]=\{a+bi:a,b\in\mathbb Z\},\qquad i^2=-1.Z[i]={a+bi:a,b∈Z},i2=−1.

Their norm is N(a+bi)=a2+b2N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2N(a+bi)=a2+b2, and their Euclidean length is ∣a+bi∣=N(a+bi)|a+bi|=\sqrt{N(a+bi)}∣a+bi∣=N(a+bi)​. Norms multiply, which makes factorization compatible with planar geometry.
