Suppose two nonnegative integers are supplied as binary strings of length nnn. Their product has at most 2n2n2n bits. School multiplication forms and adds many shifted partial products, taking quadratic time in a straightforward implementation.

The output is only twice as long as either input. How close can multiplication come to the linear time required simply to read and write these strings?

For decades, a central benchmark was nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. Sophisticated algorithms eventually attained this upper bound, while a matching general lower bound remained conjectural. The manuscript claims an exact deterministic algorithm with running time

O ⁣(n(log⁡n)1−κ),κ=2−182>0.O\!\left(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa}\right),\qquad \kappa=2^{-182}>0.O(n(logn)1−κ),κ=2−182>0.

Since the logarithmic exponent is smaller than one, the ratio of this bound to nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn tends to zero. That remains true however tiny the fixed positive constant κ\kappaκ is.

2. Background and essential definitions

What counts as computation

A multitape Turing machine has a fixed finite number of tapes, each divided into cells from a fixed finite alphabet. Its heads move locally, at most one cell per step. Reading, writing, and moving data all contribute to running time.

This model does not give free random access to an enormous array or charge one operation for multiplying arbitrarily large integers. A claim about bit complexity must account for moving the actual encoded data.

“Uniform” means one fixed machine works for every input length. There is no separate uncharged circuit or advice table for each nnn. “Worst case” means the time bound applies to every pair of inputs of that length.

Multiplication as convolution

Split each input into blocks of bits, interpreted as digits in a base BBB. Write

a=∑iaiBi,b=∑jbjBj.a=\sum_i a_iB^i,\qquad b=\sum_j b_jB^j.a=i∑​ai​Bi,b=j∑​bj​Bj.

Before carrying, the product has coefficients

ck=∑i+j=kaibj.c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_i b_j.ck​=i+j=k∑​ai​bj​.

This sequence is the convolution of the digit sequences. For example, multiplying digit polynomials (a0+a1z)(b0+b1z)(a_0+a_1z)(b_0+b_1z)(a0​+a1​z)(b0​+b1​z) produces the middle coefficient a0b1+a1b0a_0b_1+a_1b_0a0​b1​+a1​b0​. After convolution, ordinary carry propagation converts the coefficients into valid base-BBB digits.

A discrete Fourier transform changes coordinates so that convolution becomes pointwise multiplication. Transform both sequences, multiply corresponding transformed entries, and apply an inverse transform. This is the source of fast multiplication’s connection with harmonic analysis.

Exact answers from approximate intermediates

An algorithm may use approximate complex numbers internally and still return an exact integer product. It needs a rigorous error bound: if every recovered integer coefficient is within strictly less than one half of its true value, rounding to the nearest integer recovers it exactly.

Working precision, intermediate scaling, and rounding therefore belong to the complexity analysis. An arithmetic-operation count alone cannot establish the manuscript’s bit-time theorem.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Karatsuba and Ofman’s 1962 work showed that splitting an integer into two parts need not require all four large products suggested by direct expansion. Their three-product identity gives subquadratic multiplication. Toom subsequently developed further splitting methods. These early advances made recursion an essential tool.

Schönhage and Strassen’s 1971 paper, Schnelle Multiplikation großer Zahlen, used transform methods to achieve O(nlog⁡nlog⁡log⁡n)O(n\log n\log\log n)O(nlognloglogn) multitape time. They proposed nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn as the optimal order. The distinction between this conjecture and their proven upper bound is central to the present family.

Fürer’s 2007 algorithm reduced the remaining overhead to a very slowly growing factor involving the iterated logarithm. Later work by Harvey, van der Hoeven, and Lecerf further developed fast transform and precision techniques.

Harvey and van der Hoeven’s integer multiplication algorithm, published in 2021, attained the unconditional O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) bound. Gaussian resampling allowed the required transforms to be organized into convenient multidimensional shapes. Reaching the conjectured scale settled an upper-bound question, but did not prove that faster algorithms were impossible.

The cost of rearranging data remained relevant. Harvey and van der Hoeven’s 2025 work related integer multiplication to matrix transposition in the tape model, emphasizing that arithmetic and data movement cannot be separated casually.

The new manuscript builds on the established transform reduction while claiming savings in both transform layers and address rearrangements. Its target is precisely the overhead that a sequence of full-array scans would otherwise preserve.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that one deterministic Turing machine, with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes, multiplies every pair of nnn-bit integers exactly in

T(n)=O ⁣(n(lg⁡n)1−2−182),lg⁡n=max⁡{⌈log⁡2n⌉,1}.T(n)=O\!\left(n(\lg n)^{1-2^{-182}}\right),\qquad \lg n=\max\{\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,1\}.T(n)=O(n(lgn)1−2−182),lgn=max{⌈log2​n⌉,1}.

The clipped logarithm simply makes the expression meaningful at small lengths. The input allows leading zeroes, and the output is the product padded to exactly 2n2n2n bits.

The bound holds at every input length and in the worst case. It is not an average over random integers, a randomized success guarantee, or a result restricted to a sparse sequence of convenient lengths.

The manuscript also states corresponding worst-case bounds for exact quotient-and-remainder division by a nonzero integer and for integer square root. The latter returns ⌊a⌋\lfloor\sqrt a\rfloor⌊a​⌋, an exact integer, not a floating-point estimate.

The constants and thresholds are explicitly described as extremely large. The theorem is intended as a bit-complexity result, without a claim of competitive performance on practical input sizes.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the claim refutes the proposed nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn optimality threshold in a standard and restrictive model of computation. Integer multiplication is a basic operation underlying exact arithmetic and many number-theoretic algorithms, so its asymptotic complexity has unusually broad significance.

The size of the saving and its conceptual force should be distinguished. The factor gained over nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn is a power (log⁡n)κ(\log n)^{\kappa}(logn)κ. Because κ\kappaκ is so small, this grows imperceptibly over ordinary scales. Yet a fixed positive exponent saving disproves an eventual lower bound of the conjectured form.

The model also makes the result more demanding than a formal manipulation of arithmetic circuits. Moving bits to where they are needed is charged. A method that saves multiplications but spends the same nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn time reorganizing data would not establish the theorem.

The rating reflects the central problem and the claimed change in its asymptotic answer. It does not imply a useful replacement for current multiplication libraries.

6. The main idea

Two costs must fall together

A transform on a large array typically has many levels. If each level scans a linear volume of stored bits, logarithmically many levels produce the familiar nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn cost. The manuscript develops two procedures to reduce this burden.

The first exchanges two fields within array addresses. For example, an address may encode a row and a column; exchanging them reorganizes the data as a transpose. The final action is an exact permutation, but intermediate steps are allowed to mix data by exclusive-or operations.

The second processes many transform “butterflies” together. A basic normalized butterfly maps a pair to

(u,v)⟼(u+v2,u−v2).(u,v)\longmapsto\left(\frac{u+v}{2},\frac{u-v}{2}\right).(u,v)⟼(2u+v​,2u−v​).

Instead of charging a full separate pass for every coordinate direction, the construction combines operations across several directions. Numerical values use carefully chosen fixed-point representations, and truncation follows completed layers under controlled bounds.

Change the representation during the computation

The paper’s linear networks use different invertible coordinate systems for arrays at different stages. A stored array may represent a transformed version of the logical array. When a gate acts linearly on several arrays in the same coordinate system, applying the gate commutes with that common change of coordinates.

This makes it possible for intermediate coordinate changes to cancel, leaving the desired transformation only at the endpoints. Auxiliary values are restored, so they need not begin as a specially prepared store of zeroes.

One can think of this as computing with encoded data while keeping track of the encoding. It is an explanatory analogy: the paper supplies exact linear identities and charges the work needed to implement them on tapes.

A strict recursive saving

The finite network arranges that a larger task splits into fewer smaller calls than a direct volume-times-dimension accounting would predict. If WWW is the number of data streams and the parameter grows by a factor mmm, the key inequality has the form s<Wms<Wms<Wm, where sss counts recursive calls.

After normalizing by stored volume, the recursive growth is strictly smaller than linear in the parameter. This produces a small positive power saving. The rest of the argument must preserve it through padding, shifts, precision management, and layout changes.

Return to exact integer arithmetic

The algorithm places these procedures inside convolution reductions involving multidimensional transforms and polynomial rings. Forward transforms retain compatible frequency orders, so some expensive permutations cancel across pointwise multiplication and the reverse transform.

Finally, the paper bounds the coefficient error below one half, rounds, and propagates carries. This is how approximate internal transform computations deliver the exact binary output required by the theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The statement is model-specific: fixed finite tapes, local head motion, and explicitly charged bit operations. It should not be restated merely as “a faster Fourier transform” or as an arithmetic bound over exact complex numbers. Family 130 studies a different transform model.

The result leaves open the optimal complexity of multiplication. It does not attain linear time, nor does it supply a matching lower bound for its new exponent. Improving the extremely small saving, reducing constants, and determining whether any ideas are practical are separate questions.

The algorithm also uses established multiplication machinery inside its construction. A faster final bound can arise even when some subroutines use an older bound, provided those subproblems are sufficiently small and the full cost accounting fits together.

8. Sources and further reading

The Harvey–van der Hoeven paper linked above explains the nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn baseline and the resampling framework. M1’s introduction separates its two tape procedures from the later convolution, precision, and carry steps; that separation is a useful guide through an otherwise technical algorithm.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Integer multiplication below n log n (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Optimal-order randomized k-server on arbitrary metrics
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 110 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

A cache, a fleet of service vehicles, and a collection of movable resources share a basic difficulty: each request must be handled before the next request is known. Family 110 claims an optimal-order guarantee for a general mathematical model of this situation. A companion turns the existence result into a computable policy on finite rational inputs, with an important qualification about its initial cost.

1. The question

There are kkk servers in a metric space. A request specifies a point, and a server must move there unless one is already present. The algorithm pays the distance traveled. It knows past requests but not future ones.

A greedy rule might always move the nearest server. But preserving a slightly farther server for an imminent request can be better, and the online algorithm cannot know that request is coming. The natural benchmark is an offline optimum that sees the whole sequence in advance.

How much more movement must an online policy pay? Randomization can help by preventing a fixed request sequence from exploiting one predictable pattern of decisions. The manuscripts claim a guarantee of order log⁡2(k+1)\log^2(k+1)log2(k+1) on every metric, independent of the number of locations or their geometric arrangement.

2. Background and essential definitions

Metrics and configurations

A metric d(x,y)d(x,y)d(x,y) is a distance function: distances are nonnegative, symmetric, zero exactly when the points agree, and satisfy the triangle inequality. The latter says a detour cannot be shorter than the direct distance.

A configuration lists the positions of all kkk labeled servers. Different servers may start at the same point. At each request, the stated model chooses one server to move directly to the requested location, leaving the others fixed. A zero-length move is allowed.

For a finite request sequence σ\sigmaσ, let OPT⁡(σ)\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)OPT(σ) be the least movement cost attainable with advance knowledge of the sequence, starting from the same initial configuration.

Competitive analysis

A randomized policy AAA has competitive ratio RRR if

E[cost⁡A(σ)]≤ROPT⁡(σ)+B\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)]\le R\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+BE[costA​(σ)]≤ROPT(σ)+B

for every allowed request sequence. The expectation is over the policy’s random choices. The additive constant BBB may depend on the fixed instance and initial configuration, but must not depend on the sequence or its length.

The term BBB can absorb an initial disadvantage. It cannot absorb losses that continue growing faster than the optimum over arbitrarily long sequences. Nevertheless, a very large BBB can make an asymptotic guarantee uninformative for ordinary finite workloads.

What the adversary knows

The request sequence is oblivious: it is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. It may be chosen with full knowledge of the policy, but cannot adapt to the realized random choices.

An adversary that watches the actual server positions and chooses the next request accordingly is stronger. The family does not assert the same guarantee in that model.

Paging as an example

When every pair of distinct points has distance one, servers represent pages currently held in a cache. A request to a missing page costs one move; choosing a server corresponds to choosing which cached page to evict. General metrics allow different replacement costs and much richer geometry.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Manasse, McGeoch, and Sleator introduced the kkk-server framework and its competitive viewpoint. For deterministic policies, the classical lower bound is kkk on metrics with more than kkk points. Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou proved a 2k−12k-12k−1 guarantee for the work function algorithm.

Randomized paging suggested a much smaller scale. Fiat and collaborators obtained logarithmic guarantees, and McGeoch and Sleator attained the harmonic ratio

Hk=1+12+⋯+1k.H_k=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1k.Hk​=1+21​+⋯+k1​.

Since HkH_kHk​ grows like log⁡k\log klogk, it was tempting to expect a logarithmic ratio on every metric.

The history took a different turn: Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani established metrics requiring order log⁡2k\log^2 klog2k. As explained and cited in M1, this disproved the original randomized logarithmic conjecture. A matching universal upper bound would therefore settle the revised worst-case scale, not confirm the old conjecture.

A major upper-bound approach approximates a metric by hierarchical trees. Such trees group nearby points at successively larger distance scales. Fakcharoenphol, Rao, and Talwar proved an expected distortion of order log⁡n\log nlogn for an nnn-point metric.

Randomized server algorithms on these trees improved substantially, including squared-logarithmic dependence on kkk. But transferring a tree guarantee through a static embedding typically introduced another factor depending on nnn. That fails to give a bound depending on the server count alone.

M1 discusses dynamic embeddings and partition methods as predecessors, while explicitly distinguishing its argument from a withdrawn general guarantee in earlier work. M2 compares its implementation with stronger per-request time and random-bit guarantees available for tree-based algorithms whose general-metric ratio still depends on nnn.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that an absolute constant CCC works for every metric with at least k+1k+1k+1 points and every k≥2k\ge2k≥2: one randomized online policy satisfies

E[cost⁡A(σ)]≤Clog⁡2(k+1)OPT⁡(σ)+B\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)]\le C\log^2(k+1)\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+BE[costA​(σ)]≤Clog2(k+1)OPT(σ)+B

for every finite oblivious sequence. The same policy serves all horizons. The metric may be infinite, unbounded, or nondiscrete. If the initial positions are distinct, the paper states that B=0B=0B=0 is possible.

This first result makes no computational-efficiency claim. M2 supplies a uniform randomized implementation when the metric is finite and all distances are rational.

Let LLL be the complete binary input length, including the metric, server count, and initial positions. M2 claims polynomial preprocessing and, at request number ttt, at most

p ⁣(L+⌈log⁡2(t+1)⌉)p\!\left(L+\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\right)p(L+⌈log2​(t+1)⌉)

bit operations for one fixed polynomial ppp. The bound holds for every reachable internal state. Only unbiased random bits are required.

The implementation retains the squared-logarithmic competitive ratio but permits an unrestricted finite additive movement constant. Its useful policy may activate only after an enormous initial number of requests. Polynomial preprocessing and per-request work therefore do not imply a practical startup period.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The kkk-server problem is a central model of online decision-making. A ratio matching the known worst-case order across arbitrary metrics would identify the scale of the unavoidable cost of lacking future information.

The independence from the size and geometry of the metric is decisive. A bound containing log⁡n\log nlogn can deteriorate as more possible locations are added even when the number of servers stays fixed. The claimed result makes the server count the controlling parameter.

The family also illustrates an important distinction in theoretical algorithms: existence, computability, and practical efficiency are different achievements. M1 addresses the universal policy; M2 gives a finite computation with formal time bounds, while its additive constant limits what that says about actual service quality over moderate horizons.

6. The main idea

Compare distributions without revealing the future

M1 first studies a finite probability distribution on request sequences. For each complete sequence, choose an offline optimum. At an intermediate time, consider the conditional distribution of that optimum’s server positions given only the revealed requests.

This distribution is a mathematical comparator, not information about the realized future handed to the online algorithm. The argument later converts guarantees for finite distributions into one policy working against all fixed sequences.

Allocate fractional servers across scales

A hierarchy partitions the metric at different distance scales. Instead of immediately choosing integer server positions, the construction maintains fractional amounts of server mass in subtrees. Rank-related constraints express which allocations can satisfy the service requirements.

Some mass may remain temporarily at internal tree vertices. This allows the allocation to change gradually when the conditional comparator changes, instead of repeatedly committing all resources to fine-scale locations.

The paper claims a logarithmic loss in allocating this mass. Its partition construction contributes another logarithm, while subsequent steps preserve their product.

Pay for moving the hierarchy too

Changing partitions can help adapt to requests, but it is not free. A representation of parked mass by a point in the original metric may move even when no mass crosses a tree edge.

The manuscript introduces potentials—quantities stored in the analysis whose decreases can pay for movement—to account for partition edits and this additional travel. A rounding procedure then turns fractional mass into exactly kkk actual servers with only a constant-factor loss.

Finally, finite minimax and compactness arguments produce a single policy for all finite histories, including on arbitrary infinite metrics. These are existence tools rather than an efficient recipe for computing probabilities.

The companion’s delayed construction

M2 replaces finite-horizon policy probabilities by rational transition tables satisfying linear constraints. It filters requests and organizes resets so a bounded table can support arbitrarily long service.

Constructing the table may take an uncontrolled but finite amount of time. At request ttt, the implementation simulates only a budget proportional to the binary length of ttt. Until construction finishes, it uses a simple fallback service. The total cost before activation is finite and is absorbed into BBB.

This explains both the formal per-request polynomial bound and its limitation: a finite constant can hide an exceptionally long initial phase.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The squared-logarithmic order is a worst-case statement over metrics. It does not mean every metric requires that ratio; paging already shows better behavior in a special geometry.

The guarantee is in expectation against oblivious requests. It is not a pathwise movement guarantee or a guarantee against an adversary reacting to the realized random choices.

On arbitrary spaces, M1 asserts existence without effective access assumptions. M2 requires an explicit finite rational metric. Its additive constant, activation time, and dependence on the request-counter length leave room for stronger computational results with usable initialization and uniform practical bounds.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the metric-independent existence theorem and the historical lower-bound comparison. M2 should be read alongside it: its introduction explains why the computational statement allows a large additive loss and a delayed transition to the constructed policy.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Squared-logarithmic randomized k-server on arbitrary metrics (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Uniform computation of the squared-logarithmic k-server bound (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One-sample matroid prophet inequalities against an almighty adversary
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 111 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Imagine selecting valuable opportunities as they arrive, with no chance to undo a decision. You know which collections can be accepted together, but you do not know the value distributions. You have only one historical sample for each opportunity. Family 111 claims that this limited information still suffices for a constant fraction of the expected best possible reward, even under a particularly powerful choice of arrival order.

1. The question

An offline chooser sees every value before selecting a feasible set. An online chooser sees one value at a time and must immediately accept or reject it. A prophet inequality compares their expected rewards: how much of the offline advantage can the online chooser recover?

The family asks this question under matroid feasibility constraints, which include choosing at most a fixed number of items and selecting linearly independent vectors. It assumes independent nonnegative values but does not give the online rule their distributions.

Before arrivals, the rule receives one independent sample from each item’s distribution. The arrival-order adversary then sees the samples, every actual value, and the rule’s entire random seed. It chooses an order exploiting all that information.

The manuscript claims a universal positive reward fraction. The fraction is tiny, and no polynomial-time implementation is asserted. The advance concerns how little statistical information is sufficient in this strong adversarial model.

2. Background and essential definitions

Matroids encode flexible independence

A finite matroid consists of a set EEE of labeled elements and a collection I\mathcal II of feasible, or independent, subsets. Every subset of an independent set is independent. In addition, if I,J∈II,J\in\mathcal II,J∈I and ∣I∣<∣J∣|I|<|J|∣I∣<∣J∣, some element of J∖IJ\setminus IJ∖I can be added to III while preserving independence.

The second condition is the augmentation axiom. It captures the familiar fact that a smaller linearly independent set can be extended using a larger one.

For example, a uniform matroid permits every set of at most rrr elements. A linear matroid associates elements with vectors and permits linearly independent selections. A graphic matroid associates elements with graph edges and permits selections containing no cycle.

The rank r(S)r(S)r(S) of a subset S⊆ES\subseteq ES⊆E is the largest size of an independent subset of SSS. Rank measures the available number of independent choices, rather than their monetary value.

Samples, values, and the benchmark

For each element eee, let SeS_eSe​ be its preliminary sample and VeV_eVe​ its actual online value. Both have the same unknown distribution, and all these random variables are mutually independent. Distributions may differ across elements.

For a realized value vector vvv, the offline optimum is

OPT⁡M(v)=max⁡I∈I∑e∈Ive.\operatorname{OPT}_M(v)=\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}v_e.OPTM​(v)=I∈Imax​e∈I∑​ve​.

The expected optimum is assumed finite. This excludes cases where the comparison would involve an infinite reward benchmark.

The rule sees the complete sample vector before arrivals, then sees actual labels and values one at a time. It must keep its accepted set independent throughout.

Why the order of expectation matters

A guarantee for every fixed arrival order is weaker than a guarantee against an order chosen after seeing the random seed. In the first case one controls a minimum of expected rewards. In the second one needs to control the expected minimum over orders:

E ⁣[min⁡πreward⁡(π)]≤min⁡πE[reward⁡(π)].\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{\pi}\operatorname{reward}(\pi)\right]\le\min_{\pi}\mathbb E[\operatorname{reward}(\pi)].E[πmin​reward(π)]≤πmin​E[reward(π)].

Here π\piπ ranges over permutations of the elements. The adversary may pick a different damaging order for each realization. This is why simply reusing a fixed-order theorem would not answer the question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical prophet inequalities began with selecting one value from a sequence of independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions. The sharp reward fraction is one half. Krengel and Sucheston’s early work records the foundational factor-two comparison.

Kleinberg and Weinberg extended the one-half guarantee to matroid constraints when distributions are known, in their specified arrival model. This showed that matroid feasibility itself need not destroy constant competitiveness.

Unknown distributions motivate sample-based information. Azar, Kleinberg, and Weinberg developed limited-information prophet inequalities and connected one-sample rules with order-oblivious secretary algorithms. Rubinstein, Wang, and Weinberg obtained the optimal one-sample one-half guarantee in the single-choice setting.

For general matroids, Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen gave an order-oblivious secretary algorithm with a doubly logarithmic loss in rank, yielding a related one-sample prophet inequality. Thus the earlier obstruction was not obtaining any useful one-sample guarantee, but removing its dependence on matroid rank under strong order selection.

Another route used more samples. Fu and collaborators obtained constant guarantees with a sample count growing polylogarithmically in the ground-set size. Later sample-complexity work improved this dependence in a framework allowing an almighty adversary.

M1 also discusses one-sample results with better constants for orders independent of samples, values, and random choices. Those results address a different information pattern. Its claimed contribution combines one sample, arbitrary finite matroids, a rank-independent constant, and full exposure of the seed to the ordering adversary.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every known finite labeled matroid and every collection of independent nonnegative value distributions with finite expected optimum, M1 states that a distribution-independent measurable online rule achieves

E ⁣[∑e∈AVe]≥2−310 E[OPT⁡M(V)].\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{e\in A}V_e\right]\ge 2^{-310}\,\mathbb E[\operatorname{OPT}_M(V)].E[e∈A∑​Ve​]≥2−310E[OPTM​(V)].

The accepted set AAA is independent. The rule receives exactly one preliminary sample per element and uses its own seed independent of the samples and values.

The guarantee permits any measurable order-selection rule depending on the matroid, distributions, all samples, all actual values, and the complete seed. The online rule itself receives neither future values nor the future permutation.

The constant is independent of ground-set size, rank, and distributions. The proof states a stronger internal constant, with slack left in the main theorem, but the displayed main guarantee is the relevant headline.

The paper also derives a secretary consequence. For fixed weights, observe and reject a random initial segment of a uniformly random permutation. An informed adversary may then reorder the remaining labels after seeing all weights, the observation prefix, and the seed. A constant reward guarantee still holds in that model.

Neither statement includes a polynomial running-time or polynomial independence-oracle bound.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The claim would establish that one labeled observation per distribution contains enough information for constant competitiveness across all matroids, even when randomness cannot be hidden from the ordering adversary.

This is a substantial structural result about online selection. It separates the information requirement from the difficulty of computing a useful rule. The data budget is minimal in a natural sense, while the computational budget remains unrestricted.

The tiny constant limits immediate applications. A fraction of 2−3102^{-310}2−310 is not a persuasive operational reward guarantee for a hiring system or marketplace. Its role is to remain positive independently of the problem size, thereby changing the qualitative dependence on rank and sample count.

The rating also reflects the importance of the adversary model. A larger numerical guarantee in an easier order model does not automatically subsume this statement, and this statement does not replace all more efficient algorithms in those models.

6. The main idea

First hide fixed weights, then reveal a random subset

The paper initially removes distributional complications. Fix a vector of nonnegative weights, randomly reveal some coordinates, and sacrifice those elements: they can inform the rule but cannot be accepted.

The goal is a reward bound that holds after taking the worst arrival order for each seed. A coupling then connects this fixed-weight experiment with the sample model. On sacrificed labels use the preliminary sample; on other labels use the actual online value. Independence and matching distributions make this combined vector have the correct product distribution.

This transfers a suitably robust fixed-vector guarantee to the desired one-sample setting.

Organize value and dependence together

Weights are rounded into geometric levels, grouping values of comparable magnitude. Within each group, the construction builds nested matroid flats.

A flat is a subset closed under span: adding an element already in its closure does not increase rank. This generalizes the span of vectors in linear algebra. Differences between nested flats create layers in which the algorithm can make local greedy selections while keeping their union globally feasible.

A density calculation compares how many revealed elements a region contains with how much independent rank it provides. This helps distinguish a large pile of redundant opportunities from a set supporting many genuinely independent selections.

Protect useful rank from several losses

Lower-value arrivals can occupy capacity before valuable elements appear. The construction uses an additional independent selection of revealed elements as guards, expanding flats early enough to control this obstruction.

A second difficulty is that revealed elements have been sacrificed. Their apparent richness must imply that enough useful rank remains among unrevealed elements. The paper bounds exceptional patterns in which the informative sample captures too much of the relevant structure.

Finally, later expansions of flats can reduce available rank in earlier layers. A telescoping rank identity charges these losses across the whole construction rather than repeatedly charging the same dependence.

The resulting accepted-count estimates hold simultaneously for all permutations before the expectation is taken. That order of analysis is what allows the adversary to see every random choice. Reverse exposure of random masks is a proof device, not secretly preserved randomness unavailable to the adversary.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Independence is essential to the stated setup. Correlated values, correlated preliminary samples, negative rewards, or an unknown matroid are outside the theorem as presented.

The adversary controls arrival order, not the realized values themselves. Values are still generated from the independent distributions specified by the model. Giving the adversary arbitrary power over both values and order would be a different problem.

The rule’s existence and measurability do not establish efficient implementation. Better constants, efficient oracle algorithms under this same full-information ordering model, and guarantees under weaker statistical assumptions remain natural further targets.

The secretary consequence should also retain its precise observation-prefix and adversarial-suffix conventions. It is stronger in one order-related direction than ordinary random-order secretary selection, but it is not a statement about every possible secretary information model.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the exact adversary interface in Theorem 1.1 and the fixed-weight formulation in Proposition 2.1. The earlier papers linked above help separate three resources that are easily confused: knowledge of distributions, the number of samples, and the amount of control over arrival order.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, One Sample Suffices for Matroid Prophet Inequalities against an Almighty Adversary (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Beyond the square-root exponent for depth-three circuits
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 112 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

A calculation can be easy when performed through many successive steps and expensive when forced into only three layers of logic. Family 112 claims an explicit example of this phenomenon beyond a longstanding quantitative threshold. The result concerns a restricted circuit architecture, while allowing that architecture unrestricted fan-in, shared gates, and a separate design for every input length.

1. The question

A Boolean circuit computes a function of bits by connecting logical gates. An AND gate outputs one when all its inputs are one; an OR gate outputs one when at least one input is one.

The circuits here have three layers: OR gates at the bottom, AND gates in the middle, and an OR gate at the top. Every bottom gate may read arbitrarily many input literals, where a literal is a bit or its negation.

Can a function that is efficiently computable by an ordinary algorithm nevertheless require an enormous number of gates in this shallow architecture? Classical examples already require roughly a square-root exponential, of the form 2cn2^{c\sqrt n}2cn​ for a fixed positive constant ccc.

The manuscript asks for one polynomial-time language whose required circuit size eventually exceeds 2An2^{A\sqrt n}2An​ for every fixed constant AAA. The function must be explicit and efficiently evaluable; merely counting how many difficult Boolean functions exist would not suffice.

2. Background and essential definitions

Languages and their membership functions

A language L⊆{0,1}∗L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*L⊆{0,1}∗ is a set of finite binary strings. For each length nnn, its membership function fnf_nfn​ takes an nnn-bit string and outputs one exactly when the string belongs to LLL.

Saying LLL is in deterministic polynomial time means one fixed algorithm decides membership in at most C(n+1)aC(n+1)^aC(n+1)a steps, for fixed constants C,aC,aC,a. The algorithm works across all lengths.

By contrast, the circuits may be nonuniform: a different circuit can be chosen independently for each nnn, with no requirement that an efficient algorithm construct it. This makes a lower bound stronger than one restricted to efficiently generated circuit families.

Clauses and three-layer circuits

A clause is an OR of literals, such as x1∨¬x3∨x7x_1\lor\neg x_3\lor x_7x1​∨¬x3​∨x7​. A conjunction of clauses is a formula in conjunctive normal form, abbreviated CNF.

An OR–AND–OR circuit is therefore an OR of CNFs. The width of a clause is the number of variables it contains. Width is unrestricted in the target circuit model.

Let S3(f)S_3(f)S3​(f) be the smallest total number of AND and OR gates needed to compute fff in this model. All three layers count, including bottom clauses and the top output gate. Input negations are free, and gates may feed several later gates.

Counting only the number of middle CNFs would be misleading: every Boolean function has some CNF representation, although that CNF may contain exponentially many clauses. The total gate budget prevents those clauses from being treated as free.

Reading the growth rate

The notation

S3(fn)=2ω(n)S_3(f_n)=2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}S3​(fn​)=2ω(n​)

uses the asymptotic symbol ω\omegaω, meaning growth faster than every constant multiple in the exponent. It is unrelated to the matrix multiplication exponent in family 107.

Precisely, the assertion is

lim⁡n→∞log⁡2S3(fn)n=∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 S_3(f_n)}{\sqrt n}=\infty.n→∞lim​n​log2​S3​(fn​)​=∞.

This is stronger than one bound 2cn2^{c\sqrt n}2cn​, but weaker than a bound 2n1/2+ε2^{n^{1/2+\varepsilon}}2n1/2+ε for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. An unbounded multiplier of n\sqrt nn​ could grow much more slowly than any positive power of nnn.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Håstad’s random-restriction and switching methods established major lower bounds for constant-depth circuits. A random restriction fixes many input bits and leaves the others free. A shallow circuit often simplifies dramatically under such a restriction, while the target function retains enough difficulty to force a large original circuit.

For parity—the function recording whether the number of one bits is odd—the depth-three lower-bound exponent has square-root order. Håstad, Jukna, and Pudlák developed a top-down approach and improved quantitative bounds for parity and majority.

Paturi, Pudlák, and Zane’s Satisfiability coding lemma, cited in M1, determined the depth-three parity scale sharply up to a constant factor in circuit size. Thus simply improving the analysis of parity cannot produce the desired unbounded multiplier in the exponent: parity itself has matching upper bounds at the older scale.

Connections with satisfiability algorithms also yielded lower bounds for code-membership functions. These remained within a constant times n\sqrt nn​ in the leading exponent. Paturi, Pudlák, Saks, and Zane developed an important algorithmic route through isolated satisfying assignments.

Much stronger bounds are possible when bottom gates have bounded fan-in. Paturi, Saks, and Zane obtained nearly full exponential bounds in a bottom-fan-in-two setting. More recent local enumeration work treats related majority questions with small bottom width.

Those restrictions change the problem. Family 112 claims to cross the square-root-exponent threshold while leaving bottom fan-in unrestricted, and with one fixed polynomial-time language witnessing every required constant.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that there is a language LLL, decided by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, whose length-nnn membership functions satisfy

for every A>0,S3(fn)>2Anfor every sufficiently large n.\text{for every }A>0,\quadS_3(f_n)>2^{A\sqrt n}\quad\text{for every sufficiently large }n.for every A>0,S3​(fn​)>2An​for every sufficiently large n.

The threshold length may depend on AAA. The language and its polynomial-time membership algorithm do not.

The bound holds at every sufficiently large length, not merely infinitely many selected lengths. It counts all AND and OR gates, permits arbitrary sharing, and imposes neither a uniformity requirement nor a bottom-fan-in bound on the circuits being ruled out.

The theorem is about exact computation: the circuit must agree with the membership function on every input. Correlation estimates under random inputs are tools inside the argument, rather than a replacement of the theorem by an average-case statement.

The manuscript explicitly presents its conclusion as weaker than a fixed-power improvement 2n1/2+ε2^{n^{1/2+\varepsilon}}2n1/2+ε. That stronger formulation should not be inferred from the notation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Explicit circuit lower bounds reveal limitations of computational architectures that are difficult to capture by ordinary algorithm analysis. Crossing a longstanding quantitative threshold for unrestricted depth-three circuits would be a substantial advance in these methods.

The result combines two kinds of strength. The target language remains efficiently computable by a general algorithm, while even nonuniform circuits in the specified shallow architecture require the claimed size. This isolates the cost of restricting depth rather than asserting that the underlying decision problem is generally intractable.

The conclusion does not separate P\mathsf PP from NP\mathsf{NP}NP, since the constructed language is itself in P\mathsf PP. It instead shows that a fixed shallow form cannot efficiently express all computations that become possible with a longer sequence of steps.

6. The main idea

Make every middle gate cover very little

Represent a Boolean target function by a sign ggg, equal to plus one on accepted inputs and minus one on rejected inputs. For a CNF indicator HHH, consider its correlation

∣E[g(x)H(x)]∣,\left|\mathbb E[g(x)H(x)]\right|,∣E[g(x)H(x)]∣,

where xxx is uniformly random.

If HHH is one middle component of an exact OR representation, it cannot accept a negative input: that would make the whole circuit accept incorrectly. Consequently gH=HgH=HgH=H, so the correlation equals the fraction of inputs that component accepts.

If every admissible component has tiny correlation but the target accepts a substantial fraction of inputs, many components are needed to cover the target’s positive inputs. This is the basic counting mechanism behind the lower bound.

Simplify tests without losing control of their number

The circuit’s clauses may be wide. The manuscript develops a random-restriction statement expressing a restricted moderately wide CNF as a signed combination of constant-width CNFs.

“Signed” means some coefficients may be negative. The useful quantity is the sum of their absolute values, whose expectation is bounded under the chosen restriction parameters. Crucially, this bound does not grow with the original number of clauses.

Thus a function poorly correlated with every narrow CNF also remains poorly correlated with the wider tests relevant to the circuit. Exceptional restrictions and coefficient sizes are accounted for together, without assuming an independence that need not hold.

Put the hard choice into the input

The constructed language has a data block and parameter blocks. Its evaluator hashes the data and evaluates a polynomial in an algebraic quotient described by the parameters. These are operations a fixed polynomial-time machine can carry out.

For a desired lower-bound constant, probabilistic arguments establish a choice of parameter bits giving a hard function of the data block. The evaluator never has to search for this choice: it simply uses the parameter bits supplied in its input.

Fixing those bits selects a slice of the full membership function. If the full function had a small circuit, substituting those fixed values would also give a small circuit for that hard slice.

From narrow tests back to the full circuit

The paper uses sparsification to organize constant-width CNFs into controlled collections with few clauses. Limited-independence constructions and moment bounds then establish small correlations simultaneously across the relevant tests.

Very wide clauses in a small candidate circuit can be removed with a small total error under uniform inputs, because a clause of width www is false on only a 2−w2^{-w}2−w fraction of assignments. Combining this truncation with the restriction argument shows that too few middle gates cannot cover the positive inputs.

The parameters used in this analysis vary with the desired constant AAA, while the language’s evaluator remains fixed.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower bound applies to the stated OR–AND–OR architecture with free input negations. It should not be generalized to arbitrary depth, threshold gates, or unrestricted Boolean circuits.

It is also not a fixed positive-power improvement over the square-root exponent. Establishing such a rate remains beyond the claimed conclusion.

The hard slice is proved to exist within an explicit polynomial-time language. This does not mean the digest supplies an efficient algorithm that, given a lower-bound target, outputs the particular parameter choice witnessing it. The separation between easy evaluation and finding useful parameters is part of the construction.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s first theorem states the quantifiers and gate-count convention precisely. Its introduction compares parity, code-membership, and bounded-bottom-width results. The linked historical papers explain why changing the target function and controlling clause count are both necessary to go beyond the older threshold.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Beyond the Square-Root Exponent for Depth-Three Boolean Circuits (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Approximate counting of common integer polymatroid bases
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 114 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Many allocation problems impose two overlapping systems of capacity constraints. Finding one feasible allocation can be tractable while counting all feasible allocations is much harder. Family 114 claims randomized relative counting for common bases of two arbitrary matroids, then extends this to integer polymatroids with potentially enormous binary-encoded capacities.

1. The question

Suppose resources must be allocated among several coordinates. One system limits combinations of coordinates in one way, while a second system imposes different limits. The task is to count allocations satisfying both systems and using the required total amount.

Even when each system separately has a well-behaved exchange structure, their intersection need not retain it. Moving one unit or swapping one selected element can violate one of the two sets of constraints.

A second challenge is numerical size. A capacity of a billion needs only about thirty binary digits. An algorithm that creates one object per capacity unit is not polynomial in the encoded input length.

The manuscripts address both issues. M2 treats ordinary matroid bases; M1 treats integer allocations and explicitly counts each vector once, without weighting it by the number of ways to assign labels to its units.

2. Background and essential definitions

Matroids and common bases

A matroid is a finite set EEE together with independent subsets. Independence is preserved by taking subsets, and any smaller independent set can be enlarged using an element of a larger one. Linear independence of vectors and cycle-free sets of graph edges are standard examples.

The rank r(A)r(A)r(A) is the maximum size of an independent subset of AAA. A basis is a maximal independent subset of the full ground set; all bases have the same size.

For two matroids on the same ground set and of equal rank, a common basis is a set that is a basis in both. If the ground set is the edges of a bipartite graph, one matroid can allow at most one selected edge at each left vertex and the other at most one at each right vertex. Their common full-size bases are perfect matchings.

Polymatroids permit integer amounts

A polymatroid replaces zero–one selection by nonnegative quantities. Its capacity function rrr assigns a nonnegative integer to every subset of EEE. It is normalized, meaning r(∅)=0r(\varnothing)=0r(∅)=0, nondecreasing, and submodular:

r(A)+r(B)≥r(A∪B)+r(A∩B).r(A)+r(B)\ge r(A\cup B)+r(A\cap B).r(A)+r(B)≥r(A∪B)+r(A∩B).

Submodularity expresses a diminishing-returns structure. The extra capacity associated with adding coordinates becomes smaller when more coordinates are already present.

For x=(xj)j∈Ex=(x_j)_{j\in E}x=(xj​)j∈E​, write x(A)=∑j∈Axjx(A)=\sum_{j\in A}x_jx(A)=∑j∈A​xj​. Given two such functions r1,r2r_1,r_2r1​,r2​ with equal total rank RRR, the family of common integer bases is

Ω={x∈Z≥0E:x(E)=R, x(A)≤ri(A) for all A⊆E, i=1,2}.\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}:x(E)=R,\ x(A)\le r_i(A)\text{ for all }A\subseteq E,\ i=1,2\}.Ω={x∈Z≥0E​:x(E)=R, x(A)≤ri​(A) for all A⊆E, i=1,2}.

Every distinct integer vector counts once. If the only constraint is allocating two units between two coordinates, the vectors (2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(2,0),(1,1),(0,2) are three objects. Giving the units distinct labels would represent the middle vector twice, changing the counting measure.

Oracle access and approximation

An exact rank-value oracle returns ri(A)r_i(A)ri​(A) when queried with a subset AAA. It avoids explicitly listing exponentially many inequalities. Oracle calls are counted separately from the algorithm’s other bit operations; the internal work of the oracle is not included.

An FPRAS, or fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, estimates Z=∣Ω∣Z=|\Omega|Z=∣Ω∣ within relative error ε\varepsilonε with failure probability at most δ\deltaδ, using polynomial resources in input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Edmonds’s matroid intersection theory established a fundamental distinction: finding and optimizing common independent sets can be efficient through independence queries. Counting all solutions requires additional ideas.

For one matroid, Feder and Mihail obtained sampling and counting results for balanced matroids, using negative dependence. Later work treated strongly Rayleigh distributions, another structured class with strong algebraic properties.

Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant removed these special assumptions for counting bases of a single arbitrary matroid. Their high-dimensional walks use log-concave polynomials to control random movement among bases.

Intersections remained harder. Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant obtained an exponential-in-rank factor approximation in polynomial time and relative approximation with exponential-in-rank running time. The latter becomes fully polynomial for small logarithmic rank, but not for arbitrary rank.

The permanent FPRAS of Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda already solves a special common-basis case arising from two partition matroids. Its strategy of balancing nearly feasible states is an important methodological predecessor.

For integer allocations, Brändén and Huh’s Lorentzian polynomial theory provides powerful concavity properties. However, a factorial-normalized generating polynomial weights integer vectors differently from a uniform count. Nor does good behavior for one polymatroid automatically transfer to the intersection of two.

M1 builds on M2 and on the cell-bounded contingency-table construction in family 115. Its added task is to handle arbitrary submodular rank constraints and large binary capacities while preserving the intended one-vector-one-vote count.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2 claims an FPRAS for common bases of two equal-rank matroids given only exact independence oracles. No matrix representation, graph representation, or generating-polynomial evaluation oracle is required.

It also derives counting schemes for common independent sets of prescribed, unrestricted, or maximum cardinality, including when the two matroid ranks differ. Its almost-uniform samplers always return feasible objects on nonempty instances and detect emptiness exactly.

M1 claims an FPRAS for the common integer bases defined above, with RRR supplied in binary and exact rank-value oracles. It returns a nonnegative rational estimate satisfying

Pr⁡[(1−ε)Z≤Z^≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ.\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z]\ge1-\delta.Pr[(1−ε)Z≤Z≤(1+ε)Z]≥1−δ.

On every execution, the number of oracle calls and the bit work outside the oracles are bounded by a fixed polynomial in ground-set size, binary input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

An empty feasible set always produces zero. If R=0R=0R=0, the unique common base is the zero vector. Lower-dimensional feasible regions are included; the theorem does not require an interior in the ambient coordinate space.

The polynomials have large fixed exponents. The claimed contribution is polynomial dependence on the correct input encoding, rather than an optimized implementation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5, provisional. The family would provide a general counting framework for intersecting combinatorial capacity systems, substantially extending the cases addressed by single-matroid methods.

Its oracle formulation is broad: a rank function can describe a feasible system without revealing an explicit matrix or an exponentially long list of inequalities. The result makes clear which information the counting algorithm actually needs.

Binary capacities are equally substantive. A theorem polynomial in the numerical capacity can be exponential in the length of the input. M1 claims to avoid that blowup while also avoiding the counting bias introduced by labeled expansions.

These are structural and asymptotic guarantees. The score reflects a substantial advance within counting and discrete optimization, while recognizing its specialized input model and the lack of a practical runtime claim.

6. The main idea

Turn two matroids into a paired selection problem

M2 makes two copies of the ground set, pairing corresponding elements. It combines the first matroid with the dual of the second. A dual matroid has as bases the complements of the original bases.

Selecting exactly one element from every pair is called a transversal. With the combined matroid chosen as in the paper, a transversal is a basis exactly when it represents a common basis of the original two systems.

The algorithm gives a positive but small weight to rank-deficient transversals. It also permits temporary defects: one empty pair and one doubly selected pair. These extra states provide routes between feasible selections that might otherwise be far apart.

Learn how to balance defects

Different defect types can have very different total weights. Multipliers are learned during an annealing schedule to keep them from overwhelming the target transversals or becoming too rare to be useful.

Algebraic inequalities control transport between conditional distributions and variation in the observables the algorithm estimates. The manuscript deliberately distinguishes this from proving fast mixing for every fluctuation inside every defect class.

A trace chain records successive returns to transversals. Controlling that chain and the relevant frequency estimates is sufficient for the counting procedure. The analytical partition sums and flows are not extra oracles supplied to the implementation.

Keep large ranges implicit

M1 cannot expand a huge capacity into that many pairs. Instead it finds a rational center of the common-base region and identifies near-tight constraints. These define partitions whose part totals have only polynomially many relevant discrete values.

Large remaining ranges are treated through weighted integration over free coordinates. Soft penalties suppress violations of the original constraints. Convex-volume approximation supplies numerical estimates of the resulting weights.

Integration preserves an ordinary form of log concavity, but the discrete counting framework needs stronger quadratic inequalities. The manuscript smooths and adjusts the weights, controls the difference between discrete changes and continuous derivatives, and establishes the needed inequalities for its particular construction.

Only bounded-range variables are expanded into paired labels. Factorial corrections cancel the multiplicities on target transversals, restoring unit mass per original integer vector.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The rank functions are promised to satisfy the polymatroid axioms and to be available through exact value queries. The theorem does not provide an efficient test that an arbitrary black box satisfies those promises, nor does it include the black box’s internal computational cost.

The main integer-base theorem assumes equal total ranks. M2’s unequal-rank consequences concern common independent sets and should not be substituted indiscriminately for that hypothesis.

Counting each integer vector once is part of the problem definition. Applications requiring distinguishable units, factorial weights, or a different probability law need their own translation.

The result leaves practical efficiency, sharper polynomial exponents, and extensions to broader non-submodular constraints as separate questions. Its methods exploit the particular exchange and concavity structure of matroids and polymatroids.

8. Sources and further reading

M2 gives the paired-matroid reduction and its independence-oracle guarantees. M1 states the binary-capacity theorem and identifies the exact companion inputs it uses. The primary historical papers linked above explain why optimization, single-system counting, and intersection counting require different levels of machinery.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An FPRAS for Common Integer Polymatroid Bases with Binary Capacities (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Approximate counting of common bases of two matroids (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Approximate counting and entropy of perfect matchings
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 113 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Finding one way to pair every vertex of a graph is very different from counting all such pairings. Family 113 brings together two claims about this gap: a randomized approximation scheme for the number of perfect matchings in any simple graph, and an entropy inequality describing how much randomness a matching distribution can retain when its edge probabilities are fixed.

1. The question

A graph has vertices and edges joining pairs of vertices. A perfect matching chooses edges so that every vertex belongs to exactly one chosen edge. One may think of pairing participants when edges specify compatible pairs.

An existence algorithm can answer whether a complete pairing is possible and return one. Counting asks how many different complete pairings exist. The answer can be exponentially large, even when finding one is easy.

The algorithmic question is whether that count can be estimated efficiently to any prescribed relative accuracy, without restricting the graph to a special class.

The entropy question starts from local data: the probability that each edge is chosen. How much uncertainty can remain about the whole matching? Local probabilities do not specify a joint distribution, because selected edges must cooperate to cover every vertex exactly once.

2. Background and essential definitions

Perfect matchings and relative approximation

Write M(G)\mathcal M(G)M(G) for the perfect matchings of a graph GGG, and

Z(G)=∣M(G)∣.Z(G)=|\mathcal M(G)|.Z(G)=∣M(G)∣.

An estimate has relative error at most ε\varepsilonε when it lies between (1−ε)Z(G)(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)(1−ε)Z(G) and (1+ε)Z(G)(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)(1+ε)Z(G). A ten-percent estimate of a million matchings may differ by a hundred thousand; the same requirement near a small count is much stricter.

A fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, or FPRAS, produces such an estimate with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta1−δ, in time polynomial in input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ). Here δ\deltaδ is the allowed failure probability.

When the count is zero, a multiplicative guarantee needs special attention. The manuscript explicitly tests existence and returns zero with certainty in that case.

Marginals and entropy

For a probability distribution ppp on matchings, the marginal xex_exe​ is the probability that edge eee belongs to the chosen matching. The entropy is

Ent⁡(p)=−∑M∈M(G)pMlog⁡pM,\operatorname{Ent}(p)=-\sum_{M\in\mathcal M(G)}p_M\log p_M,Ent(p)=−M∈M(G)∑​pM​logpM​,

using natural logarithms and the convention 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0. Entropy measures uncertainty: it is zero for a fixed matching and equals log⁡Z(G)\log Z(G)logZ(G) for the uniform distribution.

Not every vector of numbers in [0,1][0,1][0,1] is a feasible vector of marginals. At each vertex, incident-edge probabilities must sum to one. In general graphs, odd subsets impose further constraints: a perfect matching must cross the boundary of any odd vertex set at least once.

The perfect-matching polytope is the set of feasible marginal vectors, equivalently the convex hull of matching indicator vectors. A convex hull consists of all weighted averages with nonnegative weights summing to one.

For a feasible vector xxx, let H(x)H(x)H(x) be the maximum entropy among distributions having those marginals. This is a constrained optimization over whole matching distributions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Edmonds’s 1965 matching algorithm established polynomial-time optimization in general graphs. His polytope theorem also identified the odd-cut constraints that distinguish general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Valiant showed that exact counting is computationally difficult even for bipartite perfect matchings, through the permanent of a zero–one matrix. Bipartite means that vertices split into two parts and every edge crosses between them. Planar graphs admit special exact counting techniques based on Pfaffians, but arbitrary graphs need a different approach.

Jerrum and Sinclair developed efficient randomized approximation for counting all matchings, summed over every possible cardinality. Their perfect-matching result required control of the ratio between near-perfect and perfect matchings. Counting all matchings does not automatically isolate the potentially rare perfect ones accurately.

Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda removed this obstruction for bipartite graphs, giving an FPRAS for nonnegative permanents. Their method balances near-perfect configurations according to the vertices left unmatched.

Extending that particular chain to general graphs faces a documented obstacle. Štefankovič, Vigoda, and Wilmes constructed instances where the specified family of perfect-and-near-perfect chains either mixes slowly or assigns too little mass to perfect matchings. This leaves room for a different state space, rather than proving approximate counting impossible.

On the entropy side, bipartite inequalities of Schrijver and Gurvits give strong comparisons with edgewise expressions. Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant proposed an entropy-optimization approach for general matching and a linear-error conjecture, cited precisely in M2. The odd-cut geometry makes the general case different.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 claims an FPRAS for perfect matchings in every finite simple undirected graph:

Pr⁡ ⁣[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Z^≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥1−δ.\Pr\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\right]\ge1-\delta.Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Z≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥1−δ.

It returns a nonnegative rational estimate, detects a zero count exactly, and has a polynomial bit-time bound on every execution. Its consequences include counting matchings of a prescribed size and edge subsets with prescribed vertex degrees, together with almost-uniform feasible sampling.

M2 treats loopless labeled multigraphs on 2m2m2m vertices, where parallel edges count as distinct choices. Define

F(x)=−∑exelog⁡xe,B(x)=−∑e(1−xe)log⁡(1−xe).F(x)=-\sum_e x_e\log x_e,\qquadB(x)=-\sum_e(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e).F(x)=−e∑​xe​logxe​,B(x)=−e∑​(1−xe​)log(1−xe​).

For every feasible marginal vector, including boundary points, it claims

F(x)−(2−2m)B(x)≤H(x)≤F(x).F(x)-\left(2-\frac2m\right)B(x)\le H(x)\le F(x).F(x)−(2−m2​)B(x)≤H(x)≤F(x).

Boundary points allow some edge probabilities to equal zero or one. They cannot be discarded as pathological: forced and forbidden edges occur naturally.

Optimizing the edgewise binary entropy yields the consequence

log⁡Z(G)≤max⁡x{F(x)+B(x)}≤log⁡Z(G)+3m−2.\log Z(G)\le\max_x\{F(x)+B(x)\}\le\log Z(G)+3m-2.logZ(G)≤xmax​{F(x)+B(x)}≤logZ(G)+3m−2.

M2 also supplies a deterministic polynomial-bit-time approximation within factor 512n512^n512n for graphs with binary-encoded edge multiplicities, where nnn is the vertex count. This much coarser guarantee is distinct from M1’s arbitrarily accurate randomized scheme.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. General-graph perfect-matching approximation is a central counting problem. The claimed algorithm would close a major gap between bipartite and unrestricted graphs without requiring density or other structural promises.

The entropy statement offers a complementary kind of understanding. It relates the global diversity of feasible matchings to quantities computed from individual edge probabilities. Such inequalities connect combinatorial counting, convex optimization, and probability.

The family should not be read as making exact counting easy. Relative approximation permits controlled numerical error and, for M1, a small failure probability. Exact counting asks for every digit of the integer answer and remains a different computational task.

The two manuscripts also illustrate that a structural inequality can be useful even when it alone produces only an exponential-factor approximation. Its value includes count lower bounds and geometric information, not just the strongest algorithmic guarantee elsewhere in the family.

6. The main idea

Count by multiplying manageable ratios

M1 starts with a complete graph, whose perfect-matchings count is known, and gradually suppresses edges absent from the target graph. Each stage has a weighted sum of matchings, called its partition function.

If consecutive partition functions have ratios that can be estimated accurately, multiplying those estimates recovers the final count. This process is often called annealing. Its success depends on drawing useful samples from every intermediate distribution.

Change the sampling space

Rather than directly reuse the obstructed perfect-and-near-perfect chain, the manuscript enlarges the graph. Logical edges become weighted paths, and auxiliary edges connect vertices inside organized bags.

The construction controls the extra probability mass introduced by those auxiliary edges. Under the required balance, a sampled matching uses only the real path edges with probability at least one half. Such an event recovers a matching of the logical graph.

Marked auxiliary edges also expose ratios involving two unmatched vertices. Those observations update the balance conditions used in later counting stages.

The sampler works with several matching coordinates at nearby weight levels. It exchanges alternating cycles between coordinates: when two matchings are overlaid, their differing edges form alternating cycles along which assignments can be swapped. Replication across levels helps control variation that a two-coordinate estimate alone would miss.

The manuscript separately bounds random-bit use and arithmetic sizes, so inaccurate statistical estimates do not create an unbounded running-time path.

Entropy through the geometry of feasible means

M2 studies the smallest face of the matching polytope containing xxx. A face records constraints that are tight throughout the relevant portion of the polytope; its dimension counts the remaining independent directions of variation.

The paper claims the sharp geometric estimate

∣supp⁡x∣−dim⁡Fx≤3m−2,|\operatorname{supp}x|-\dim F_x\le3m-2,∣suppx∣−dimFx​≤3m−2,

where supp⁡x\operatorname{supp}xsuppx is the set of positive coordinates and FxF_xFx​ is the minimal face. Here FxF_xFx​ denotes a geometric face, distinct from the scalar function F(x)F(x)F(x).

Maximum-entropy distributions have an exponential-weight form on the matchings permitted by that face. Their covariance matrices describe how marginals respond to small changes in weights. The argument compares second derivatives of a proposed entropy deficit with the face-dimension estimate. A positive deficit beyond the claimed bound would violate that geometric constraint.

Working inside the minimal face lets the argument include boundary marginals without pretending the ambient covariance matrix is invertible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1’s headline input is an unweighted simple graph. M2’s entropy theorem permits distinguished parallel edges, and its deterministic algorithm handles binary multiplicities. These input conventions should stay attached to their respective guarantees.

The entropy coefficient cannot simply be replaced by the stronger bipartite coefficient one: M2 gives a nonbipartite counterexample. Its geometric sharpness examples do not establish that every constant in the entropy comparison is optimal.

The polynomial exponents and constants in the counting constructions are large. The claims settle asymptotic feasibility rather than provide benchmarked sampling software. Faster implementations and sharper structural inequalities remain separate directions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction distinguishes all-matchings counting, bipartite perfect-matchings counting, and general perfect-matchings counting. M2’s first two theorems separate the entropy inequality from its deterministic counting consequence. Reading these distinctions first avoids conflating their different approximation guarantees.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Perfect Matchings in General Graphs (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Entropy and Face Dimension of the Perfect-Matching Polytope (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Sampling and counting contingency tables with arbitrary margins
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 115 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

A table of counts can have many possible interiors while its row and column totals stay fixed. Drawing uniformly from these possibilities is a basic problem in statistics and combinatorics. Family 115 claims algorithms for arbitrary margins and variable dimensions, including exact sampling in expected polynomial time and approximate counting when individual cells have upper bounds.

1. The question

Suppose rows classify objects by one attribute and columns classify them by another. The entry in a cell counts objects with that combination. If only the totals for each attribute are prescribed, how many tables are possible? Can we draw one without favoring some possibilities over others?

Even a two-by-two example illustrates the distributional issue. If all row and column sums equal two, the feasible tables are

(0220),(1111),(2002).\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.(02​20​),(11​11​),(20​02​).

Uniform sampling gives each table probability one third. Randomly assigning distinguishable objects can instead favor the middle table, because more assignments produce it. Sampling assignments and sampling tables are different tasks.

The manuscripts seek algorithms whose cost is polynomial in the encoded input, even when both dimensions grow and some margins are enormous.

2. Background and essential definitions

Margins and cell bounds

Let r1,…,rmr_1,\ldots,r_mr1​,…,rm​ be nonnegative integer row sums and c1,…,cnc_1,\ldots,c_nc1​,…,cn​ nonnegative integer column sums, with common total NNN. A contingency table is a nonnegative integer matrix XXX satisfying

∑j=1nXij=ri,∑i=1mXij=cj.\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}=r_i,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{ij}=c_j.j=1∑n​Xij​=ri​,i=1∑m​Xij​=cj​.

Ordinary tables impose no additional forbidden positions or cell capacities. A cell-bounded table also satisfies Xij≤bijX_{ij}\le b_{ij}Xij​≤bij​, for supplied nonnegative integers bijb_{ij}bij​. A zero bound forbids that cell; such a restriction is often called a structural zero.

The margins and bounds are encoded in binary. Polynomial dependence on NNN would not suffice, since NNN may be exponential in its bit length. The relevant numerical size is roughly log⁡(N+1)\log(N+1)log(N+1), together with the dimensions and other input data.

Exact and approximate uniformity

If a finite feasible set is Ω\OmegaΩ, exact uniformity assigns probability 1/∣Ω∣1/|\Omega|1/∣Ω∣ to every table.

For distributions μ,ν\mu,\nuμ,ν, total variation distance is

dTV(μ,ν)=12∑X∈Ω∣μ(X)−ν(X)∣.d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)=\frac12\sum_{X\in\Omega}|\mu(X)-\nu(X)|.dTV​(μ,ν)=21​X∈Ω∑​∣μ(X)−ν(X)∣.

A distance at most η\etaη means that probabilities of all events differ by at most η\etaη. It measures the entire output law, rather than an error in one table entry. An approximately uniform sampler can still return a perfectly feasible table every time.

Expected time and bounded time

Expected polynomial time permits rare very long runs as long as their probability-weighted contribution is controlled. A polynomial bound on every execution is stronger and forbids such runs.

This distinction is central here: the exact sampler has an expected-time guarantee, while the approximate sampler has a deterministic cap on work for each accuracy request.

An FPRAS for counting estimates the number of feasible tables within relative error ε\varepsilonε, with failure probability at most δ\deltaδ, using time polynomial in input length, ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}ε−1, and log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Diaconis and Gangolli’s survey places fixed-margin arrays in a long statistical and combinatorial tradition. Producing one table is easy in the ordinary setting: repeatedly place the smaller of a remaining row and column total into their intersection. This does not make the result uniformly random.

Dyer and Greenhill obtained efficient approximate counting and sampling for arbitrary two-row margins. Kijima and Matsui developed exact uniform sampling for two rows through coupling from the past. Their computation model and dimension restriction are part of those earlier guarantees.

Cryan and Dyer extended approximate counting to any fixed number of rows. Cryan and collaborators proved rapid mixing of suitable local chains in that setting. A polynomial whose exponent depends on a fixed row count does not establish polynomial complexity when both dimensions are inputs.

Another line of work handles dense margins using volumes of transportation polytopes—the real-valued regions defined by the same row and column equations. Morris improved earlier dense-table bounds through expanded regions and rounding. Sparse-margin exact generation also has strong results under quantitative restrictions, including Arman, Gao, and Wormald.

For zero–one cell bounds, the problem becomes counting bipartite subgraphs with prescribed degrees. Permanent approximation methods already cover this important special case. Larger capacities require treating integer multiplicities without expanding a large number into an equally large explicit combinatorial structure.

M2 discusses earlier fixed-row and large-capacity results for capped tables, then claims to remove these restrictions simultaneously. M1 separately strengthens ordinary-table sampling to exact uniformity, using a correction method from Göbel, Liu, Manurangsi, and Pappik.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 considers ordinary tables with arbitrary nonnegative margins of equal total. Both dimensions may vary. For an accuracy parameter k≥1k\ge1k≥1, it claims a sampler whose law is within 2−k2^{-k}2−k of uniform and whose running time is polynomial in

m, n, log⁡(N+1), k.m,\ n,\ \log(N+1),\ k.m, n, log(N+1), k.

Thus the dependence on a requested total-variation tolerance η\etaη is polynomial in log⁡(1/η)\log(1/\eta)log(1/η). Every output is feasible.

It also claims an exactly uniform sampler that terminates almost surely and has expected bit time polynomial in m,n,log⁡(N+1)m,n,\log(N+1)m,n,log(N+1). No fixed-dimension, balance, density, or positivity hypothesis is imposed. This exact statement has no input cell bounds or forbidden positions.
